stories.title: During waves of separation ideation, national poll probes Canadians' attachment to Canada, their province, and each other
stories.summary: Not surprisingly, Quebecers had the least sentiment of strong attachment to Canada, while respondents in Atlantic Canada were the opposite.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
Facing renewed separatist ideation and agitation in Quebec and Alberta, a new national public opinion poll says Canadians feel a strong attachment to their country — stronger than to their province — and share an abiding affinity for fellow Canadians, no matter where they live.

With Albertans voting Monday in a referendum asking whether the province should begin the process of holding a vote on separating from Canada and a separatist government elected in Quebec earlier this month, Canadian unity is again eating up airtime, timelines and headlines.

A national poll dissecting the feelings Canadians have for Canada, their province and each other casts a light on our national hearts.

“Despite the outcome of the Quebec election and some of the increasingly negative rhetoric about Canada in Alberta, what stands out in our findings is the relative stability and resilience of Canadian identity. Political discourse May suggest a country pulling apart, but Canadians’ attachment to their country and, importantly, to one another remains remarkably strong,” said Jack Jedwab, president of the Montreal-based Association for Canadian Studies (ACS).

The nationwide poll of Canadian adults was conducted last week by Ekos Research for the ACS and provided to Postmedia.

Perhaps not surprisingly, considering decades of separatist ideation, Quebecers expressed the lowest sentiment of strong attachment to Canada, while respondents in Atlantic Canada were on the opposite end of the scale, being the most boisterous in Canadian attachment, by a wide margin.

In Alberta, which is currently probing its own separation sentiment, a strong majority of respondents said they are very attached to Canada — although the percentage of Albertans saying they felt no attachment at all to Canada was higher even than in Quebec.

Nationally, the combined results from all respondents in the 10 provinces polled, found 60 per cent described themselves as very attached to Canada. Another 27 per cent said they were somewhat attached. Eight per cent nationally described feeling not very attached and four per cent said not at all attached.

At 45 per cent, Quebec was the only region that did not have a majority expressing strong attachment to Canada; 33 per cent said they felt somewhat attached, 14 per cent said not very attached and seven per cent said not at all attached.

Alberta had 61 per cent of respondents say they felt very attached to Canada; 23 per cent said somewhat attached, eight per cent not very attached, and another eight per cent say not attached at all, higher than those in Quebec in expressing that level of alienation.

In Atlantic Canada (the pollsters combined New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland and Labrador) 79 per cent said they were strongly attached to Canada, and another 27 per cent said they felt somewhat attached. Only four per cent said not very attached and none said they felt no attachment at all.

The remaining provinces were roughly in the same territory on their expressions of attachment to Canada.

The proportion of respondents saying they felt very attached in the remaining provinces were: 62 per cent in B.C.; 63 per cent in Manitoba and Saskatchewan pooled together; and 65 per cent in Ontario. Those saying they felt somewhat attached were: 24 per cent in Manitoba and Saskatchewan; 28 per cent in Ontario; and 29 per cent in B.C.

Those expressing some alienation accounted for: 10 per cent in Manitoba and Saskatchewan; six per cent in B.C.; and five per cent in Ontario. Those expressing complete alienation were four per cent in Manitoba and Saskatchewan; three per cent in B.C.; and two per cent in Ontario.

The findings suggest that Quebecers continue to negotiate (provincial and Canadian) identities rather than simply choosing one over the other

Those in the Atlantic provinces not only have the strongest expression of attachment to Canada, but they also had the strongest attachment to their home province — 62 per cent said they felt very attached to their province.

Those who had the lowest proportion expressing strong attachment to their province were in Ontario, where only 27 per cent said they felt very attached, significantly lower than anywhere else.

The next lowest was Alberta, where 38 per cent said they felt very attached to their province, followed by Manitoba and Saskatchewan with 41 per cent, B.C. with 45 per cent, and Quebec with 47 per cent.

The national average was 39 per cent.

Despite disagreements and rivalries, the poll shows that Canadians feel a strong attachment to other Canadians.

Nationally, 63 per cent said they felt very strong attachment towards other Canadians and another 31 per cent said they felt somewhat attached. Only two per cent said they didn’t feel much attachment, and none said they felt no attachment at all.

The weakest in expressing affinity with other Canadians were Albertans.

Only 59 per cent of respondents in Alberta said they felt very much attachment to other Canadians, compared to 73 per cent in Atlantic Canada, 63 in Ontario, 62 in Quebec and B.C., and 60 in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

Albertans were also most likely to say they felt not very much attachment to other Canadians, but it was still only five per cent, where it was either one or two per cent everywhere else.

“Quebec remains the exception in the extent to which provincial and Canadian identities compete, but that’s hardly new,” Jedwab said. “The findings suggest that Quebecers continue to negotiate these identities rather than simply choosing one over the other. Indeed, while only 45 per cent of Quebecers say they’re very attached to Canada, 62 per cent feel very strongly attached to other Canadians. That’s an important distinction that often gets lost in debates over sovereignty.”

Curiously, in the context of Alberta’s separation referendum, more respondents in Alberta said they felt no attachment at all to their province than said they felt no attachment to their country.

Alberta had the highest proportion of respondents feeling alienated from their province, at 11 per cent, followed by Manitoba and Saskatchewan at 10 per cent, six per cent in both Quebec and Ontario, three per cent in Atlantic provinces, and two per cent in B.C.

“There’s an important distinction between political alienation and national identification,” said Jedwab. “Whatever frustrations some Albertans May have with Ottawa, an important majority remain attached to Canada and to other Canadians. The concerns are more with governance and much less so with identity.”

Poll respondents were also asked which description best fits with how they see themselves: Canadian only, Canadian first but also provincial, equally Canadian and provincial, provincial first but also Canadian, or provincial only.

Nationally, the average of those saying Canadian only was 29 per cent. The regional breakdown showed those in Ontario to be the outliers, at 46 per cent, followed by 29 per cent in Alberta, 24 per cent in Manitoba and Saskatchewan, 22 per cent in B.C., 13 per cent in the Atlantic provinces, and 10 per cent in Quebec.

Those who said Canadian first but also provincial reached a national average of 34 per cent. That sentiment was shared equally strongest in the Atlantic provinces and B.C., with 44 per cent. Next came Manitoba and Saskatchewan at 35, followed by Ontario and Alberta both at 33, and Quebec landing at 28.

A national average of 17 per cent declared equal national and provincial affinity. Atlantic Canada and Manitoba and Saskatchewan were highest in the regional breakdown on that choice at 20 per cent, closely followed by Quebec at 19, B.C. at 17, Ontario at 15, and Alberta at 13.

Next, those choosing province first but also Canadian accounted for 14 per cent of respondents nationally. Quebecers were the big outliers at 31 per cent, followed by those in Atlantic Canada at 22, Albertans at 16, those in B.C. and Manitoba and Saskatchewan all at 11, and Ontarians by far the lowest at just two per cent.

Finally, those declaring only a provincial affiliation were a slim four per cent nationally. In Quebec it was nine per cent, Manitoba and Saskatchewan at eight, Alberta at six, B.C. at two, and Ontario and Atlantic Canada both at zero.

“One of the lessons of the survey is that many Canadians don’t want to be forced into choosing between their regional and Canadian identities. That’s particularly relevant in Quebec, where the relationship is more divided, but it also applies to Alberta, where most identify primarily as Canadian or as Canadian and Albertan.

“Despite the political divisions, the bonds between Canadians appear stronger than some of the rhetoric would have us believe.”

The survey questioned 1,232 Canadian adults from Oct. 9 to 15. Participants were randomly recruited by telephone and confirmed by live interviewers. This sample size has a margin of error plus or minus 2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

Finally, those declaring only a provincial affiliation were a slim four per cent nationally. In Quebec it was nine per cent, Manitoba and Saskatchewan at eight, Alberta at six, B.C. at two, and Ontario and Atlantic Canada both at zero.

“One of the lessons of the survey is that many Canadians don’t want to be forced into choosing between their regional and Canadian identities. That’s particularly relevant in Quebec, where the relationship is more divided, but it also applies to Alberta, where most identify primarily as Canadian or as Canadian and Albertan.
“Despite the political divisions, the bonds between Canadians appear stronger than some of the rhetoric would have us believe.”

The survey questioned 1,232 Canadian adults from Oct. 9 to 15. Participants were randomly recruited by telephone and confirmed by live interviewers. This sample size has a margin of error plus or minus 2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: More than 1,800 arrested in France during violent protests leaving devastation in their wakes
stories.summary: Emmanuel Macron's centrist government and far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen both blamed "ultra-left" groups for the violence.
stories.author: AFP
stories.content:
France was reeling on Sunday from widespread damage caused in violent protests the day before that saw 1,800 people arrested, a historic town hall torched and widespread looting.

The convulsion, which officials described as of extraordinary intensity, raised the stakes for President Emmanuel Macron, who is in his final months in power before elections to replace him in six months’ time. It followed weeks of student protests that had also turned violent at times.

Around “1,800 people have been arrested and now investigations are under way to identify the perpetrators of these acts so they can be brought to justice,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on X on Sunday.

In Paris, where police said a “record” 855 people had been arrested, streets were littered with the burnt-out remains of barricades built by protesters using bikes and bins and other materials. Several streets had smashed shop windows and the remains of torched cars.

The capital experienced “a level of violence that we have never, I believe, seen before,” said Paris deputy mayor Lamia El Aaraje.

Paris and many other cities, including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Strasbourg, had scores of shops pillaged by masked youths during the protests, which had been called against high inflation and the cost of living.

The city of Limoges lost its 19th-century town hall to a fire the local prefect, Maurice Barate, told LCI television had been deliberately set by “a wild horde.” The fire was only brought under control early Sunday.

Political recriminations flew over the scenes of destruction.

Macron’s centrist government and far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen both blamed “ultra-left” groups for the violence.

Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who had prominently backed the demonstrations, late Saturday urged demonstrators to stay away from any looting, describing it as “contrary to our methods.”

Paris’s Socialist deputy mayor, Lamia El Aaraje, accused Le Pen’s party of fuelling tensions around the protests to further her ambition of becoming president next year.

The far-right National Rally party was “acting like a pyromaniac firefighter,” El Aaraje said.

U.S. Vice President JD Vance also waded in, implying that the unrest stemmed from immigration.

“Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility,” Vance said on X.

500 arrested in Paris

In Paris, where startled tourists had been seen Saturday running with suitcases along streets filled with tear gas and protesters, the prosecutor’s office said more than 500 people were in custody.

It said arrests had been carried out through the night until early Sunday, with most taken into custody on suspicion of receiving stolen goods, association with intent to commit violence, and vandalism.

Officials in Lyon said 160 people were in custody there.

Around 500 police, firemen and paramedics were hurt in the protests, Interior Minister Nunez said, adding that the figure was provisional.

The violence took place on the sidelines of nationwide cost-of-living protests that the interior ministry said were attended by 550,000 people. The CGT union said 800,000 people participated.

Police used tear gas and water cannon against protesters who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks.

A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Étienne.

Analyst Mujtaba Rahman of the Eurasia Group think tank said on X that Saturday’s “terrible scenes” were “not political protest in any true sense. Most of the real demonstrations against high oil prices and failing schools were peaceful”.

He added: “The violence came from a fringe of the ultra-left. The looting by opportunistic gangs from the poor suburbs. All good news for Marine Le Pen.”

During and after those demonstrations, gangs of youths roamed city streets, sporadically confronting police, while setting fires and attacking shuttered stores to break in and empty their shelves.

France’s Yellow Vest movement, which staged street protests eight years ago against Macron’s government over planned fuel-tax hikes, had called Saturday’s “yellow and youth” demonstrations.

The principal grievance was the cost of living, pushed up in part by the war in the Middle East that has helped send inflation soaring in Europe as elsewhere.

stories.title: Behind the push to make smoking and vaping illegal for a generation of Canadians
stories.summary: Ottawa - It's illegal for kids under 18 to buy tobacco products in Canada and there's a movement afoot to make sure today's youth are never allowed to light up a cigarette — even after they come of age.
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - It’s illegal for kids under 18 to buy tobacco products in Canada and there’s a movement afoot to make sure today’s youth are never allowed to light up a cigarette — even after they come of age.

Oct. 18, 2026

Updated 29 mins ago

GAC[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/behind-the-push-to-make-smoking-and-vaping-illegal-for-a-generation-of-canadians/article_e1f6712b-2e5b-53b2-9fab-7123211fdb60.html)

By Sarah Ritchie The Canadian Press

A law that will take effect in the United Kingdom in January will prohibit anyone born after 2008 from ever legally buying cigarettes.

In Canada, lobbyists are pushing the federal government to go even further by banning smoking and vaping products for the next generation entirely.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Sarah Sleet, CEO of Asthma + Lung U.K., said there has been broad public support for the move in Britain but it took decades of lobbying and advocacy.

“If you survey smokers, they do not want their children to be smoking. They know what a terrible thing it is, they know how bad it is for their health, they know how expensive it is,” she said.

The law also had cross-partisan support. It was proposed by a Conservative government in 2023 and eventually passed under the current Labour government.

The proposed bill initially included vaping products, but the final version is limited to smoking. The Lung Health Foundation in Canada wants to bring vaping into the conversation.

“Kids who vape are 3 1/2 times more likely to smoke tobacco in the future,” said Jessica Buckley, president and CEO of the foundation.

Sleet said some in the United Kingdom were concerned about the law limiting access to vaping products that are used to help people stop smoking. The law did bring in stronger rules on the sale of vapes, including plain packaging and a requirement that stores keep the products behind screens.

The British law didn’t come without pushback from the tobacco industry.

Eric Gagnon, vice-president of regulatory affairs for Imperial Tobacco Canada, said while he shares the goal of keeping cigarettes and vapes out of the hands of youth, the tobacco industry does not support a prohibition on smoking, however gradual.

He pointed out that Canada has gone in the opposite direction with cannabis by legalizing and regulating the product, despite research showing smoking and vaping cannabis is harmful. He also warned that a ban would feed the black market.

“Canada already has a huge illicit market, not only on cigarettes but on nicotine pouches, on vaping products,” Gagnon said.

Convenience store retailers are also opposed to such a ban and argue the illicit market has well-documented links to organized crime.

“Canada is unique in the illegal tobacco market, with one of the most sophisticated contraband trades in the world. Illegal tobacco products account for 50 per cent of the national market, and even more in some regions,” said Jeff Brownlee, vice-president of communications for the Convenience Industry Council of Canada.

Brownlee called for a national strategy to crack down on contraband.

In the United Kingdom, advocates’ research showed the size of the illicit market “is massively overestimated,” Sleet said. The British government said raising the smoking age to 18 from 16 in 2007 and 2008 led to a 25 per cent reduction in the number of illicit cigarettes consumed.

“What it takes is, obviously, strong enforcement,” she said.

U.K. research estimates smoking costs the equivalent of $5.6 billion a year in health and social services, and costs the wider economy some $32 billion. Sleet said those sums outweigh the estimated losses in government revenue from excise taxes and sales of cigarettes.

In Canada, the estimated public cost of tobacco use is $11.2 billion a year and as many as 46,000 people die from tobacco-related illnesses each year.

The federal government collected $2.6 billion in tobacco excise tax revenue in 2024, according to a report from the parliamentary budget officer.

Buckley and dozens of advocates plan to be on Parliament Hill next week for a lobbying push to convince the federal government that a generational tobacco ban could save health care funding desperately needed for Canada’s aging population.

“It’s very difficult to have levers to pull on the health-care side in order to reduce those costs long-term,” she said.

Buckley said they’ll also be armed with polling that suggests broad public support in Canada for a generational ban.

She said they have meetings scheduled with advisers to Health Minister Marjorie Michel and her parliamentary secretary Maggie Chi.

Canada has a national strategy to reduce tobacco use to five per cent of the population by 2035 — currently, about 11 per cent of Canadians smoke — and directs $66 million a year toward stop-smoking programs.

Michel’s office said in a statement that Canada isn’t currently considering introducing a prohibition.

“We continue to monitor measures taken by like-minded countries to reduce youth smoking, including the United Kingdom’s recent initiative,” said Alexandre Bergeron, Michel’s spokesperson.

From the other side of the pond, Sleet has a message for Canadian lawmakers.

“Be brave, go for it,” she said. “You’re not going to regret it.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 18, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Why this pay raise for politicians might make sense
stories.summary: Newfoundland and Labrador politicians haven’t seen a pay raise since 2009 — will that help the public swallow a proposed $22,000 bump?
stories.author: Garrett Barry
stories.content:
ST. John’s - The transition from summer to fall is much calmer these days for long-time Newfoundland and Labrador cabinet minister Siobhan Coady.

She is no longer busy preparing the province’s audited financial statements — as her successor did this week — or drafting a fall fiscal update. Instead, she has more time for her passions: a litter of small puppies and her three Labrador retrievers she is raising in her home in St. John’s.

“We’ve had puppies now for about 14 years,” Coady said, adding her husband Pat, is “very keen to have good Labradors coming from Newfoundland and Labrador.”

Since stepping away from politics in 2025 and declining to run in that year’s provincial election, Coady is on the outside looking in — neither campaigning nor holding public office for the first time since 2004.

She served as a provincial cabinet minister from 2015 to 2025, first as a minister of natural resources, then as finance minister.

“I miss the people,” Coady said “I miss the opportunity to contribute to Newfoundland and Labrador. But I always said 10 years was enough for me in public life… I always had said that I would give it my best 10 years.”

She believes her efforts pushed the province in a better direction — despite overseeing a particularly difficult portfolio. For five years, Coady was deputy premier and finance minister in the most indebted province in the country.

That meant delivering plenty of bad fiscal news — aside from a surprise, one-time budget surplus in 2022-23. For her trouble, she was paid just over $144,000 annually: the $95,357 base salary paid to every member of the House of Assembly, plus an additional $48,664 for her cabinet duties.

“Compensation becomes a very difficult conversation for people to have,” she said.

But as Newfoundland and Labrador’s politicians once again consider whether to grant themselves a raise, recommended this month by an arms-length report, Coady said it is an important conversation to have — and agreed to speak to CTV News about the demands of a life in politics.

“We want to attract attract the best and the brightest. We want to attract good people into the House of Assembly. So we have to compensate them as well,” Coady said. “[They work] a tremendous amount on behalf of the people of the province, and they give up an awful lot. Their families give up an awful lot.”

The independent report, prepared for the province’s Member Compensation Review Committee, recommends a roughly $23,000 yearly raise for all provincial politicians, alongside a mechanism to index the salaries to inflation.

The pay raise would bring Newfoundland and Labrador’s politicians to the middle of the pack, nationally after 17 years without a pay raise.

Prince Edward Island pays its politicians the lowest, at $86,924 annually, while Ontario pays the most, with salaries recently upgraded at Queen’s Park to $163,275.

“What other profession, job in this province — or I would dare say in Canada — hasn’t had an increase in salary since 2009?” Coady asked.

A similar increase proposed in 2024 received pushback from then-premier Andrew Furey, and was ultimately shelved.

“I think the general public doesn’t necessarily always appreciate the work of a politician,” Coady said, noting the job followed her everywhere — even to the grocery store.

In the report, lawyer Heather Jacobs wrote that MHAs in Newfoundland and Labrador who reached out to her said the demands of public life have increased.

“The influence of social media has increased expectations from the public for immediate attention from MHAs,” Jacobs wrote. “MHAs also said the job carries heavy personal costs, citing safety concerns, sometimes a hostile work environment including being harassed, minimal work-life balance, and career interruption.”

Jacobs noted that 35 of the province’s 40 members communicated with her, neither major political party has publicly endorsed the increase.

Premier Tony Wakeham told reporters Wednesday he had not yet read the report.

“There’s a process to be followed. It will go before the Management Commission. And I want to take a look, a deep look at exactly what’s being proposed,” Wakeham said.

The Management Commission is scheduled to meet on Oct. 21 to hear from Jacobs regarding her recommendations.

Every other province and territory has increased pay for its politicians since 2024. Newfoundland and Labrador stands alone as the single jurisdiction that has not, Jacobs wrote.

Coady believes political pay is becoming a disincentive for public life.

“That’s why I say this is an issue of democracy,” she said. “You May be able to get people like myself who have been successful in business and be able to enter into the House of Assembly and not be as concerned about the compensation or you May be able to get…not everyone can do that.”

“It limits the amount of people that can offer themselves. I would rather have a bigger pool of people who are able to come forward.”

stories.title: ‘It’s important’: New RCMP position to investigate livestock crimes in Manitoba
stories.summary: For Darren MacMillan, raising cattle is what he loves most. But working with livestock also comes with risk.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Warren, Man., – For Darren MacMillan, raising cattle is what he loves most. But due to recent livestock thefts in the area, working with them also comes with risk.

At his farm near Warren, Man., about 39 kilometres northwest of Winnipeg, MacMillan has a herd of cattle worth thousands of dollars each. He says protecting them is an ongoing concern, though he is constantly monitoring the herd.

“As a child, I remember seeing carcasses and animals that had been butchered,” he said.

“I know of neighbours who have lost trailer loads of cattle and I’m not sure where they ended up, and more or less police themselves are trying to track them down.”

While he personally hasn’t seen any theft on his property, he says it’s always on his mind.

According to a recent news release from the Manitoba government, 57 reported cases of cattle theft or fraud were reported to Manitoba RCMP between 2021 and 2025.

Incidents like this have now prompted the province to crack down on livestock crimes.

Manitoba’s Justice Minister Matt Wiebe and Agriculture Minister Ron Kostyshyn announced last week that the province is providing funding to Manitoba RCMP to hire a designated officer to investigate livestock-related crimes.

“Our government is strengthening enforcement, improving co-ordination with producers and law enforcement partners, and helping ensure those who commit crimes against Manitoba’s agriculture sector are held accountable,” Wiebe said last Thursday.

RCMP investigators will collaborate with producers and other law enforcement agencies to enforce provincial livestock legislation and the Criminal Code, with the goal of deterring cattle theft and fraud.

Producers have been calling on the province for years to implement a dedicated officer to support livestock inspections.

Similar models are already in place in both Saskatchewan and Alberta.

Back in August, a 52-year-old Saskatchewan man was charged with altering the brands of almost 200 cattle, which was investigated by that province’s livestock investigator.

‘Need that enforcement in place’

Carson Callum, the CEO of Manitoba Beef Producers, says Manitoba’s model will be based on initiatives in Saskatchewan and Alberta, which he says has proved successful.

“It’s been a long-debated topic to bring an inspection service here,” he said. “Over the years, there’s been a concern in the industry of theft and fraud.”

He says there are many factors that go into livestock-related crime, including rising input costs that go into operating and putting up feed for the animals.

He says another factor is the high cost of food, including beef. Food expert Sylvain Charlebois agrees.

“The incentive is clearly there for the black market, for people who want to not only get cheap beef, but there’s a black market for beef because of these price tags,” said Charlebois, who is the director of the Agri-Food Analytics Lab at Dalhousie University.

“What I’m hearing right now, is that more and more ranchers are basically getting the proper equipment to offer their herds some level of security to prevent theft.”

MacMillan said adding this position in Manitoba is a good step but believes more positions are needed to address this issue across the province.

“The province is a big area and there’s so many auction marts, so many places where someone steals some cattle, loads them up and hauls them somewhere to sell,” he said.

He hopes stronger enforcement moving forward will keep his cattle safe.

“We need people on the ground looking after this,” he said.

stories.title: Do other drivers have to let me out of the HOV lane?
stories.summary: There’s no Ontario rule that says drivers have to let you out of any lane – as long as they’re not deliberately blocking you
stories.author: Jason Tchir
stories.content:
When I’m signalling to leave the HOV (high-occupancy vehicle) lane, shouldn’t drivers in the adjacent lane let me merge? If they don’t, traffic in the HOV lane can slow to a crawl or even stop. People are trying to have a positive impact on the environment, but some drivers seem determined to block them. – Roger, Ontario

Here’s the lane truth: there’s no Ontario rule that says drivers have to let you out of any lane – as long as they’re not deliberately blocking you.

“There’s no obligation for someone to slow down and give you space,” said Sean Shapiro, a road safety consultant and former Toronto traffic cop. “That’s just courtesy, and everyone should do it, but [they’re] not legally obligated.”

In Ontario, the law states that anytime you’re changing lanes – whether from a regular lane or the HOV lane – you can’t make the move unless you’re sure “that it can be done safely.”

That generally means the driver who’s already there “owns that lane,” Shapiro said.

So they don’t have to slam on the brakes or move over to the next lane to let you in, for instance – but they can’t speed up or do anything else to intentionally block your move.

“The real issue is when I go to make a lane change, and buddy doesn’t like the fact that I’m going to be in front of him and accelerates to reduce the space,” Shapiro said. “That makes it unsafe for me to change lanes.”

If you’re caught blocking another driver’s lane change in Ontario, you could be charged with stunt driving , Shapiro said.

The rules vary by province. But in most, you could be charged with careless driving if you block someone from changing lanes or merging.

In British Columbia, for instance, drivers have to “reasonably yield” to merging traffic – but police would decide whether to lay charges on a case-by-case basis, RCMP Sergeant Michael McLaughlin, a spokesman for B.C. Highway Patrol, said in an email.

”Drivers in regular lanes of travel are required to allow a driver to merge from an HOV lane [or face careless driving charges ], provided that the driver changing lanes signals appropriately and has a reasonable amount of time, distance and space to merge," McLaughlin said. “However, if the driver who is merging is driving aggressively, they may themselves be charged.”

Give me a break?

If you’re in the HOV lane – which in Ontario is reserved mostly for carpoolers , motorcycles and electric vehicles with green licence plates – you’re legally allowed to enter or exit it only when there are breaks in the solid white lines .

And those breaks typically come every two to four kilometres, according to an Ontario Ministry of Transportation (MTO) webpage . We asked the MTO how long those breaks are and didn’t receive an immediate response.

If you can’t get out when you need to – for instance, because you need to make the next exit in 600 metres – then you’ll be stuck there until the next break.

Normally, getting out shouldn’t be a problem, unless the next lane is stalled in bumper-to-bumper traffic, Shapiro said.

“Rarely have I ever been in a situation where everyone’s doing the speed limit, or even above the speed limit, and there’s no room to get in,” he said. “When you’re transitioning out, you should be able to match [their speed] and merge just as though you were going to be getting on a highway from the on-ramp.”

If you can’t move into that lane because someone is directly beside you, slow down a little if you can and get in behind them – as long as you can do it safely, Shapiro said.

But, unless there’s already stop-and-go traffic in both lanes, it could be “really dangerous” to come to a stop in any lane while you’re waiting for someone to let you in, he said.

“The person behind you is absolutely responsible for not hitting you , [but] might just hit you anyway because they’re not paying attention,” Shapiro said.

Mind the gap?

If you can’t safely move over in time, you might have to keep going – even if you miss your exit.

“That might mean you [have to] double back and lose all sorts of time, but that was your choice,” Shapiro said. “[But] making dangerous manoeuvres [at the] last minute is the way to cause collisions.”

Instead, you should plan ahead and get out of the HOV lane a few kilometres before you need to – and not wait until the GPS tells you to move over immediately, he said.

“[That means] you’re looking at traffic, you’re gauging it, and you’re adjusting your speed,” Shapiro said.

In March, Ontario’s transportation minister said the province will be opening up HOV lanes to solo drivers during off-peak hours in a move to reduce gridlock. We asked when that’s happening and did not receive an immediate response.

But many drivers already treat the HOV lane as a “zoom zoom lane” to get past slow traffic in the main lanes and then have to slow down abruptly when it’s time to leave, Shapiro said.

“One of the biggest misconceptions [about] the HOV lane is that it’s a high-speed lane,” he said. “You should be travelling at a safe speed based on the speed [of traffic] beside you.”

That means not going over the speed limit, Shapiro said. And if cars in the next lane are slowed to a crawl, he recommends that you don’t go more than 30 kilometres an hour faster than they are going.

“Even if they’re doing 10 kilometres an hour, [then] you should not be exceeding 40 kilometres an hour,” Shapiro said. “Because [someone] to your right is going to [jump in] in front of you when you’re doing 100 and you’re going to break them in two.”

stories.title: Missing Person - Elijah Caissie-Thomas
stories.summary: General Releases
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (October 17, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 12-year-old Elijah Caissie-Thomas, of London.

The missing person is described as male, White, 5’9, slim build, short dark brown hair, last seen wearing a navy blue Nike t-shirt, grey jogging pants, and white Nike running shoes.

The missing person was last seen on October 17th 2026 at approximately 1pm in the area of Waterloo St and Grey St, in London.

Family and police are concerned for the missing person’s welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Why Canada's immigration cuts aren't fixing the system's problems
stories.summary: Some see a system still plagued by backlogs, changing rules and a lack of data on temporary residents already here.
stories.author: Nicholas Keung

ByNicholas Keung Senior Immigration Reporter

Om Kachhadiya picked Canada for his postgraduate studies because its immigration rules and pathways were clear and predictable.

The 26-year-old, who already had a civil engineering degree in India, knew the criteria to meet for his study permit and what he needed to do to qualify for the postgraduation work permit, so he could get a job and earn Canadian work experience — and ultimately his permanent residence.

But what has happened to Canada’s immigration system between his arrival in 2022 and graduation in 2024 — and thereafter — has been anything but clear and predictable.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

“The rules are changing every second month,” said Kachhadiya, who works as a construction estimator in Winnipeg and is struggling to obtain permanent residence. “It’s like I am just chasing my own tail.”

The Next Levels

Targets will be influenced by the stubborn math of a temporary resident population that’s proven challenging to shrink.

Facing public backlash over high immigration amid an affordable housing crisis and a high cost of living, Ottawa has slashed the admissions of new temporary and permanent residents since 2024 to curb the rapid immigration growth after the pandemic.

Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab, who took over the portfolio 17 months ago, has repeatedly said the Carney government is delivering a “controlled, sustainable, fair and secure” immigration system that Canadians can trust.

At an event on Friday, she said the government’s plan is working and the significant declines in new asylum seekers, international students and temporary foreign workers speak for themselves. Employers are hiring more Canadians and cutting their reliance on low-wage foreign workers — and asking rents have been falling for two years straight, she said.

“We are in control of immigration,” Diab told reporters.

So far, her policies have largely mirrored those of her predecessor Marc Miller. The levels plan due by Nov. 1 — her second — will offer a clearer signal yet of whether Carney is ready to put his own stamp on the immigration file.

While Diab has reined in immigration numbers, whether the immigration system is under control is another question altogether.

“A smaller immigration target is not the same thing as a smaller immigration problem,”said Mario Bellissimo, a Toronto-based immigration lawyer and policy analyst.

Depending on who you ask, Canada’s immigration system is either more controlled, stable and sustainable than it has been in years — or still very much a work in progress, plagued by persistent backlogs, constantly changing rules and a critical lack of data on the hundreds of thousands of temporary residents already here.

The question now is whether Ottawa can fix the deeper structural problems before Carney opens the tap again.

“Reducing numbers is comparatively straightforward,” said Bellissimo. “Building a predictable system that matches intake to capacity, deals fairly with people already here, targets genuine economic needs, reunites families, meets humanitarian obligations, uses technology responsibly, enforces the law and provides timely decisions is much harder.”

The government’s changes since 2024 have not always had the intended effects.

Ottawa has struggled to reduce immigration backlogs and address growing processing times despite huge investments in AI and advanced analytics to modernize the system. The Immigration Department’s website shows that there were more than one million pending permanent residence applications in the queue as of the end of July 2026.

It included 255,325 in the economic class, 165,445 awaiting family reunification, and 295,830 resettled refugees and people granted asylum in Canada, as well as 328,200 citizenship applications. In addition, 394,325 temporary resident applications were pending — 37,730 for study permits, 28,615 for work permits and 327,980 for visitor visas.

Although the department has introduced application caps for some programs,Bellissimo said the approach must be adopted across the board to control and manage application intakes based on processing capacity, which would improve efficiency and allow applicants to plan and decide whether to submit an application based on reliable timelines.

Right now, Bellissimo said, the biggest challenge for Ottawa to get a firm grip on the immigration system is the presence of hundreds of thousands of temporary residents already in the country, many with the intent to stay permanently.

“Control is not just control of new arrivals,” said Bellissimo. “It is control of the entire life cycle of an immigration file. You cannot call a system controlled if you just focus on the front door when you don’t know what’s going on in the hallways.”

The Temporary Canadians

To launch a new series, the Star spoke to temporary residents caught up in a numbers game and

In its effort to reduce the temporary resident population already in Canada,Calgary immigration lawyer Mark Holthe said, the Immigration Department has been changing rules with little consultation and tightening requirements without notice, leaving applicants unsure of what is expected of them.

“We’re in a world that’s very difficult to predict,” he said. “We always knew what we needed to do to get an approval, generally speaking. The policies were clear as long as we hit what they were expecting. We had a really good predictor of success. But now, everything that worked before, in many instances, all of a sudden isn’t good enough.”

Clear communication and transparency are crucial in Canada’s rapidly changing immigration landscape, Holthe noted, so cases don’t end in appeals, clogging up an already backlogged federal court.

Although Ottawa started incorporating targets of new students and foreign workers in its immigration levels plan after 2024, there’s little information on tracking the status of those already in Canada, which critics say should be part of the plan in order to determine yearly new admissions.

For all planning purposes, government officials need to know how many temporary residents are transitioning to permanent status, how many have had temporary permits extended and how many have left the country, said Naomi Alboim,a senior immigration policy fellow at Toronto Metropolitan University.

“You’re building a house of cards with no foundation and you’re developing policy without the information that you really need,”said Alboim, who worked at senior levels on immigration policy in the federal and Ontario governments.

“If you don’t know if they leave, or how many and what kind of status transitions they make, you are potentially going to have more and more of an insecure and possibly undocumented population, which is not good for the health of our society.”

Facing public backlash over high immigration amid an affordable housing crisis and a high cost of living, Ottawa has slashed the admissions of new temporary and permanent residents since 2024 to curb the rapid immigration growth after the pandemic.

Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab, who took over the portfolio 17 months ago, has repeatedly said the Carney government is delivering a “controlled, sustainable, fair and secure” immigration system that Canadians can trust.

stories.title: Deaths and injuries after explosion at Alberta military base: McGuinty
stories.summary: Wainwright - Canada’s defence minister is confirming deaths and injuries after an explosion and a fire at CFB Wainwright southeast of Edmonton.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Wainwright - Defence Minister David McGuinty says there have been deaths and injuries after a fire broke out Saturday at a military base in Alberta.

Fire crews scrambled late into the night as fierce winds whipped flames beyond CFB Wainwright, a massive military training base located 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

McGuinty, speaking to reporters in Ottawa, confirmed the casualties but had no other details to share, including numbers or what happened.

“I cannot recall such an incident in my short time for sure as a minister, but I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory,” McGuinty said.

“We will have more to say in the coming hours and days,” he added.

“At this time, our thoughts are with the families and with everyone impacted by this tragic event.”

He said Armed Forces members were at the scene and that RCMP were also involved. “This is an active and delicate situation and soon to be an active and delicate investigation.”

The Canadian Armed Forces said in a late evening statement that it wouldn’t confirm the number of casualties or injuries until next of kin had been notified.

“The full extent of the impact remains under assessment,” it said.

It also confirmed the fire had started about 4 p.m. and that military and local emergency crews responded. RCMP had said earlier Saturday that officers had also been called at the time.

“Early reports were that there was a fire at a training area,” police said.

In Wainwright late Saturday, at least 10 ambulances were seen parked in and around the local health centre, red lights flashing in the darkness. Paramedics and soldiers rushed about. One patient was seen being loaded into an ambulance.

Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan also didn’t provide details but said Saturday’s fire was a “profoundly difficult” event for the Armed Forces.

“While casualty identification and notification processes are ongoing, I extend my deepest condolences to the loved ones of those who have lost their lives,” Carignan said.

Alberta Conservative MP Dane Lloyd posted on social media that there had been an explosion and a fire that “resulted in significant casualties.”

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest bases and is used mainly to train soldiers and prepare units for combat operations.

Acute Care Alberta said late Saturday that significant medical resources were needed to respond to the incident and that a “Code Orange” had been activated at several hospitals across the province.

It said the code is declared when health resources need to be co-ordinated to respond “to an incident that results in multiple severe patients needing care at the same time.”

The agency advised people in the Edmonton area to avoid the University of Alberta Hospital emergency department and urged those with non-emergency issues to consider other care options.

“At this time, extremely few (Emergency Health Services-Alberta) response (units) are available in the Edmonton-area, and acute capacity is finite in several communities across Alberta.”

As McGuinty delivered the news, fire crews were battling flames raging between the base and the nearby town of Wainwright, which has about 7,000 people.

Firefighters faced a volatile situation. A windstorm hit large areas of the province during the day, with gusts up to 100 kilometres an hour. The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.

By 11 p.m., the Municipal District of Wainwright, ON social media, announced the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. No evacuation order was issued for residents.

“A fire watch will remain in place to monitor the affected area and address any changing conditions,” the statement said.

The fire also disrupted advance voting for Monday’s provincial referendum on whether Alberta should hold a binding separation vote. Elections Alberta said two advance polling locations — in Lloydminster and Vermilion — were closed early and the ballots transported securely.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a social media post that he was in close contact with Premier Danielle Smith

“Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected,” he said.

In Saskatchewan, Premier Scott Moe said his province is sending help.

Stars air ambulance reported sending two helicopters from Edmonton and Saskatoon.

B.C. Premier David Eby said his government has also reached out to offer help.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 17, 2026.

— with files from Jack Farrell in Edmonton

stories.title: Emergency crews respond to major fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta
stories.summary: An incident sparked a large fire at CFB Wainwright southeast of Edmonton Saturday evening.
stories.author: Edmonton Journal
stories.content:
Canada’s defence minister has confirmed that there were people killed and injured in an incident Saturday afternoon at CFB Wainwright.

“I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base,” David McGuinty said in a statement.

“The Canadian Armed Forces, Department of National Defence, partners across the federal government, including Public Safety are working with the government of Alberta and municipal governments to mobilize all necessary, support, and working through the details of what actually occurred,” McGuinty added.

McGuinty said he “cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory.”

Alberta MP Dane Lloyd, himself a Canadian Army reservist, posted to Facebook about the incident, which happened Saturday afternoon.

“Hearing terrible news out of CFB Wainwright,” Lloyd posted, adding that it resulted “in significant casualties.”

“Please keep our soldiers, their families and the community of Wainwright in your prayers.”

The Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton is currently under code orange — which is activated in a mass casualty event.

A doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital confirmed to Postmedia the code orange is due to the explosion at Wainwright.

The University of Alberta hospital was also under code orange Saturday night.

Wainwright RCMP, in a release just before 9 p.m. said they were called to the base about 4 p.m.

“Early reports were that there was a fire at a training area,” the release said.

“The RCMP sent numerous resources to assist. Our initial involvement is winding down, though we still have resources available if needed.”

A Saturday evening statement from Acute Care Alberta indicated that Emergency Health Services Alberta “is on scene, and supporting care and transport related to an incident at CFB Wainwright.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney indicated that the incident had created a “major fire.”

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, whose riding is home to CFB Wainwright expressed support for the base and the community.

“Thank you to the brave firefighters and emergency responders working to save lives,” Poilievre said in a statement.

“I have spoken to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence to offer our support to everyone on the base and in the community.”

Premier Danielle Smith referred to the incident as a “significant and tragic fire.”

In a Facebook post, Wainwright Fire & Rescue indicated that multiple agencies were responding to the resulting fire.

The fire also forced the closure of an advance voting station for the Alberta referendum.

stories.title: As the Lotto Max jackpot hits a record-breaking $90 million, what are the odds you’ll win?
stories.summary: Saturday’s record $90-million Lotto Max jackpot, the largest single lottery prize ever offered in Canada, is up for grabs. Canadians gave a variety of answers as how they would spend the money.
stories.author: John Vennavally-Rao
stories.content:
Pickering, Ont. – Mansions. Boats. Cottages. And, for at least one hopeful Ontarian, a lot more cats.

Those are just some of the dreams fuelling a rush on tickets for Saturday’s record $90-million Lotto Max jackpot, the largest single lottery prize ever offered in Canada. It got there after no winning ticket was sold for Tuesday’s $85-million draw.

At Smokers Corner, a convenience store in Pickering, Ont., the line to buy tickets has been long at times.

“It’s been crazy, actually,” said owner Issa Kakisa. “People coming in, spending a little more money than normal, and just everybody’s got a dream and wants that $90 million.”

Some are spending hundreds of dollars at a time, Kakisa said, and one customer dropped $2,000 on this draw alone. His store has some history with big wins, as they sold a winning ticket worth $1 million two years ago.

As for what people in line said they’d do with the money?

“I’d get a mansion, fill it with all of my cats ... I’d get more cats,” said Taylor Locke. She said she’d also buy a house for her mom, a boat and a cottage, and give a lot of the money to animal shelters and people experiencing homelessness.

Cindy O’Neill kept it practical. She said she’d pay off her mortgage, buy her brother a house, make sure her kids are looked after and save the rest for charity and travel.

Her husband, standing nearby, reminded her that he had his eye on a Land Rover. She laughed.

“Oh yeah, I’d buy him a Land Rover.”

Margaret Ward said she’d be happy with one of the smaller prizes of $100,000 or $1 million. But if she landed the full $90 million, she’d pay off a few debts and then go car shopping.

“I’d buy a new car, and I’d buy my husband a new car, and I’d buy my kids a car,” she said. “They’d all get a car.”

Javad Gezelbash, who is retired, bought two tickets for himself. He’d already bought three more the day before as part of a group purchase. If one of them hits, he has his plan ready.

“I’m going to be donating to a hospital, some of it,” he said. “And travelling around the world.”

Ralph Gomes isn’t retired yet, but he’d like to be. His wife had already bought a ticket, and he stopped in to buy a second one.

“I’m super excited,” he said.

The odds of winning the jackpot are roughly one in 33 million, which is about the same as flipping a coin and getting heads 25 times in a row.

What would it actually be like to win $90 million? According to one financial expert, it May not all be upside.

Wolfgang Klein, a Toronto-based portfolio manager with Canaccord Genuity Wealth Management who has worked with lottery winners, said a windfall that size can be a lot to handle.

“The psychological impact is something that they are really, really, probably not prepared for,” he said.

Klein said winners can feel euphoria, confusion and even guilt, and many feel obligated to help others out. People also tend to come out of the woodwork.

“It’d be fun to win $90 million … but be careful what you wish for,” he said. “All of a sudden, people you haven’t heard from in decades begin to communicate with you and become your friends once again.”

One of his clients won $5 million on Lotto 6/49 and found the experience bittersweet.

“Their children stopped working. They began to rely on the lottery winner for a monthly income,” Klein said. “Children, grandchildren, cousins, friends, charity. Where do you say no? When do you say no? And you have to learn to say no.”

His advice for the winner is to cash in on the ticket as soon as possible. He says even a very conservative portfolio of government bonds and GICs would produce a good income.

“Two per cent on $90 million? It’s $1.8 million a year,” he said. “You can do very well.”

Check your pockets

Some fortunes never get collected. In 2022, a $70-million Lotto Max ticket was sold in Toronto’s Scarborough area, but a winner never came forward, and after a year the prize went back into the pool.

Another big prize could soon meet the same fate. The Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation says a $40-million winning ticket sold last year in Grey County, Ont., is set to expire on Oct. 28.

As for who should win on Friday night?

“I hope someone who is a good person gets it,” said Locke, who has plans for her cats. “Hopefully it’s me.”

Another big prize could soon meet the same fate. The Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation says a $40-million winning ticket sold last year in Grey County, Ont., is set to expire on Oct. 28.
As for who should win on Friday night?
“I hope someone who is a good person gets it,” said Locke, who has plans for her cats. “Hopefully it’s me.”

stories.title: Deaths and injuries reported after fire breaks out at CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: Acute Care Alberta said EMS crews were on the scene providing care and transports related to the emergency at CFB Wainwright, located southeast of Edmonton.
stories.author: Amy Judd, Karen Bartko
stories.content:
A fire at the Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in central Alberta has claimed an unknown number of lives and injured others.

“I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory,” Federal Defence Minister David McGuinty said on Saturday night.

“This is a very, very active and delicate situation.”

Acute Care Alberta says EMS are on the scene providing care and transport related to the emergency at the military base about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

McGuinty said he was saddened to share that people have died and been injured as a result of “an incident on the base.”

“At this time, our thoughts are with the families and with everyone impacted by this tragic event,” McGuinty said.

“And I want to thank, in particular, the first responders and everyone providing assistance at a very difficult time.”

Alberta Member of Parliament Dane Lloyd said he heard there were “significant casualties” after an explosion and fire at the base.

Lloyd, who represents a riding west of Edmonton, asked in a social media post for people to pray for the soldiers and their families.

A fire on the base was spreading due to high winds, according to the Municipal District of Wainwright. Much of Alberta was under wind warnings on Saturday, and guts of up to 100 km/h were reported in parts of the province.

The municipality established an emergency coordination centre Saturday night. An update around 7 p.m. said the fire south of Wainwright crossed the base fence earlier in the day and was being actively managed. The active fire area is south of Township Road 44-0.

Firefighting resources from multiple jurisdictions are actively responding, the district said.

Premier Danielle Smith has also confirmed the incident, saying there has been a “significant and tragic fire” at CFB Wainwright.

In a post on social media, the premier added the incident has affected many military personnel.

She added that the province is in contact with the federal government and the prime minister.

McGuinty said the Canadian Armed Forces, the Department of National Defence and the federal government will have more to share in the coming days.

Prime Minister Mark Carney also posted on social media that his thoughts are with all the brave men and women affected.

Pierre Poilievre, Leader of the Official Opposition and Member of Parliament for Battle River—Crowfoot, put out a message saying: “Pray for Wainwright, everyone. There has been a serious incident that caused a fire at CFB Wainwright. Thank you to the brave firefighters and emergency responders working to save lives.

Poilievre said he spoke with the prime minister and the Minister of Defence to offer his support to everyone on the base and in the community.

Firms (Nasa’s Fire Information for Resource Management System) tracks active fires by satellite and shows a cluster of them on Saturday just to the southeast of the town of Wainwright.

Elections Alberta said it has been informed of the fire, which impacts the Wainwright Communiplex Advance Vote location, which has been closed.

There are two advance vote locations in Electoral Division 86:

Border Inn, Lloydminster

Vermilion Elks Hall, Vermilion

Ballot boxes and materials from Wainwright are being moved securely.

This is a breaking news story. More to come…

— with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Major fire reported at CFB Wainwright; leaders monitoring situation
stories.summary: A major fire at CFB Wainwright has prompted responses from both the Alberta and federal governments, with leaders describing the incident as serious and affecting military personnel at the base. Premier Danielle Smith said Alberta’s government is learning more about what she called a “significant and tragic fire” at the Canadian forces base, located about […
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By News Staff

Posted October 17, 2026 8:53 pm.

A major fire at CFB Wainwright has prompted responses from both the Alberta and federal governments, with leaders describing the incident as serious and affecting military personnel at the base.

Premier Danielle Smith said Alberta’s government is learning more about what she called a “significant and tragic fire” at the Canadian forces base, located about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

“We are learning of a significant and tragic fire at CFB Wainwright today that is affecting many of our brave military personnel,” Smith said in a post on social media.

Smith said Alberta officials are in close contact with the federal government and Prime Minister Mark Carney as the situation continues to develop.

The prime minister also issued a statement, describing the event as “a serious incident creating a major fire” at the base.

“Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected,” Carney said.

Neither government provided details on the cause of the fire, the extent of the damage, or whether anyone was injured.

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s largest military training facilities and is located in east-central Alberta. Authorities have not yet released additional information about the fire.

stories.title: Expert says bus model involved in deadly Calgary crash considered ‘extremely safe’
stories.summary: A chain-reaction crash happened when a transit bus hit several vehicles before rear-ending a parked bus, igniting an explosion that left three dead and more than a dozen injured.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
An expert on low-carbon transportation says the roughly 1,000 compressed natural gas buses running in Canada are still considered “extremely safe” after one such bus was involved in a deadly crash in Calgary that claimed the lives of three people.

On Thursday, a chain-reaction crash happened when a transit bus hit several vehicles before rear-ending a parked bus, igniting an explosion that also left more than a dozen others injured.

Calgary police said one officer was taken to the hospital with injuries after running towards a bus as fire erupted.

One of the 12-metre-long buses involved in the crash was powered by compressed natural gas, a kind of fuel considered cheaper and more environmentally friendly than diesel gas.

Buses that run on compressed natural gas are common in public transit and have been in operation for the past two decades, said Josipa Petrunic, president and CEO of Canadian Urban Transit Research and Innovation Consortium (Cutric), a national non-profit focused on low-carbon transit research and planning.

“It’s considered extremely safe technology, so we all need to find out what happened to create an unsafe environment in a crash situation,” Petrunic said.

There are 958 compressed natural gas-powered buses operating in Ontario, Alberta and B.C., according to a Cutric database report.

Petrunic said there are several heavy-duty safety mechanisms involved in building these buses, including a series of tools and technologies designed to manage leakage and reduce the risk of fire. Their tanks are also designed to withstand heavy impacts.

Usually, the most unsafe part of these buses, and any form of public transportation, is the lack of seatbelts, Petrunic said.

A spokesperson from Nova Bus confirmed that it was the manufacturer of the bus that was rear-ended in Thursday’s crash and the company is in contact with Calgary Transit .

The spokesperson also said that it was “ premature to speculate on the cause before a thorough investigation has been completed.”

“Safety remains Nova Bus’s highest priority, and we are offering our full cooperation to Calgary Transit and the relevant authorities as they work to establish the facts.“

Calgary Transit procures its buses from manufacturers that go through Altoona testing, a rigorous certification process for any new bus model to assess its durability and reliability before being rolled out into their fleet, said Petrunic.

The agency has nearly 250 CNG buses, which represents about 20 per cent of its fleet, according to the agency’s website. The website says the city plans to buy about 150 more this year to replace diesel buses.

As investigators continue to look into the cause of the crash, Petrunic said industry leaders will be looking into what factors went into the collision.

“A series of events had to have occurred in tandem for this cataclysmic event to occur leading to death,” said Petrunic. “A transit crash shouldn’t result in passenger deaths.”

stories.title: 2 RCMP officers charged after N.W.T. man died in police custody in 2025
stories.summary: The RCMP says it has laid charges against two of its own officers after a man from Yellowknife, Northwest Territories, died in their custody last year.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Yellowknife — The RCMP says it has laid charges against two of its own officers after a man from Yellowknife, Northwest Territories, died in their custody last year.

The Alberta RCMP, which led the investigation into the man’s death, says the two Yellowknife officers face charges of criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessities of life.

The charges stem from an incident in March 2025, police say, when the two officers responded to a report of a disturbance at a Yellowknife business.

When the officers arrived, the RCMP says they detained a man who was showing signs of intoxication and left him inside a police vehicle while they gathered more information at the scene.

Police say the officers returned to the car and found the man, 56-year-old Lawrence Blackduck, unresponsive.

He was ultimately pronounced dead at the scene, the RCMP says, after life-saving measures were attempted and paramedics were called.

The RCMP did not give further details about the officers’ alleged conduct which gave rise to the charges.

The national police service says it conducted an internal review in the aftermath of the incident and it has since made changes to police policy and training related to in-vehicle detentions.

Chief Superintendent Dyson Smith of the Northwest Territories RCMP extended his condolences to Blackduck’s family and community and called the incident “deeply troubling.”

““This is a difficult day for our organization and the communities we serve. We recognize the seriousness of this incident and remain committed to transparency, accountability and maintaining public trust and confidence,” Smith wrote in a statement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 17, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Voters head to polls in B.C. municipal elections
stories.summary: Residents will cast ballots for local representatives on councils, school boards and other regional posts until polls close at 8 p.m., local time
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The polls have closed in B.C.’s municipal elections.

Residents voted for local representatives on councils, school boards and other regional posts, choosing from 3,500 candidates across the province.

It was quiet at Vancouver’s city hall voting place Saturday, with about half a dozen voters casting their ballots and no lineups.

At the nearby SkyTrain station, volunteers with Cope stood with signs asking voters to “evict Ken Sim,” the city’s incumbent mayor, who is running for re-election.

The group was also present near Commercial-Broadway station, where Greens candidate Pete Fry campaigned with volunteers earlier in the day.

Advance voting in the provincial general election is also taking place Saturday and will continue until Oct. 21, ahead of final voting day on Oct. 24.

NDP Leader David Eby ’s decision to call a snap election two years early and in the middle of the planned municipal election period has been denounced by local and opposition politicians.

The Union of B.C. Municipalities passed a resolution at its annual convention last month imploring Eby not to call an election during the local campaign period, but days later he set off the provincial vote.

Cori Ramsay, who was the president of the union at the time of the resolution, said since then that the two elections have caused voter confusion and local campaigns lost staff to provincial candidates.

Many cities and municipalities have nevertheless reported increased or even record turnout at advance polls, including Vancouver, Richmond, Burnaby, Kamloops, Surrey, Kelowna, Prince George, Cranbrook and View Royal, among others.

Polling ahead of the Vancouver vote showed the mayor’s race to be a mostly two-person battle between Mr. Sim and two-term Green councillor Pete Fry, who cemented his place as the consensus progressive candidate after two challengers from the left-leaning parties withdrew.

Also in the ring was Kareem Allam, Mr. Sim’s former chief of staff turned adversary. Mr. Allam ran under a party called the Vancouver Liberals, which is not affiliated with the federal Liberal party.

Rebecca Bligh also ran for mayor under the new Vote Vancouver banner. Ms. Bligh is a two-term councillor who helped Mr. Sim win the previous election when she ran with his ABC party but she eventually broke with the mayor.

Former councillor Colleen Hardwick rounds out the mayor’s race under the Team banner.

Mr. Sim kept a low profile during the campaign, and his ABC party promised a steady-as-she-goes platform, touting what they say were successes in reducing crime and street disorder, and pushing through record numbers of new housing approvals. Critics noted that very few of those approved units actually have people living in them.

ABC also promised a zero per cent property tax increase for 2027 after having raised them almost 24 per cent since taking power in 2022.

All the candidates’ platforms emphasized quality-of-life issues, including affordability and public safety.

Many of Sim’s challengers also promised to undo many of the cuts made under Sim’s ABC-majority council, including re-establishing a renters office and a stand-alone climate and sustainability division.

Voters were faced with a ballot of 131 different candidates for mayor, city council, the parks board and school board trustees.

The election ballot also included two plebiscite questions on public safety.

The non-binding questions ask voters if they’re in favour of the city “strengthening its laws to forbid open-air hard drug use in public spaces,” which is already illegal in B.C.

The other asks if the city should ask the province to convert portions of the old St. Paul’s Hospital into a “secure medical facility” with 100-plus involuntary care beds.

Ms. Hardwick called the questions a “populist election tactic,” while other critics said they aren’t realistic.

Andy Yan, director of the City Program at Simon Fraser University, said ABC tried to frame the election around crime, public safety and street disorder, and the other parties tried to focus on housing and social supports.

He said this election was about a mix of cost-of-living and housing concerns, alongside a broader debate about whether Vancouver can maintain its services and quality of life–not just continue to approve more development.

“It’s a shift from, really, the role of growth to now the question of maintenance in Vancouver, how do you maintain the city,” Mr. Yan said.

Mr. Yan pointed to Abc’s success in approving high numbers of new housing, and also noted that market rents have come down in the city, helping to make housing more affordable – at least for some people.

But there’s a nuance: The top half of the rental market now has a vacancy rate of around three per cent, he said, which is considered relatively healthy. The bottom half of the market, though, is still very tight.

Mr. Yan said people struggling at the middle or bottom end of the rental ladder have seen almost no meaningful reduction in their housing costs.

“That’s really something that has kind of changed as [more] market rental come online. But yet, it hasn’t necessarily resulted in affordability for your typical renter,” Mr. Yan said.

He also pointed to a recent Auditor-General’s report that found that 73 per cent of Vancouver recreation centres are in poor or very poor shape. There are growing questions about aging street infrastructure as well, repeated costly repairs to the Vancouver seawall, the high costs of repairing the Kitsilano outdoor pool, and others.

“There isn’t an economic resiliency that we have in the city of Vancouver, which I think, really framed up a certain level of fragility – a brittleness in terms of economic activity,” Mr. Yan said.

Even the street disorder issue tends to mask underlying challenges around maintenance of public infrastructure, trash collection and graffiti – the sorts of issues that make people feel less safe even if they actually aren’t less safe, Mr. Yan said.

He said Vancouver is facing a “polycrisis” of aging infrastructure, climate change, and housing unaffordability, leaving Vancouver politics more fractured than usual and those issues are unlikely to fade regardless of who occupies the city’s council chambers, Mr. Yan said.

stories.title: RCMP officers charged in death of Yellowknife man left in police vehicle
stories.summary: Two officers face charges of criminal negligence causing death, failing to provide the necessities of life after an incident in March, 2025
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The RCMP says it has laid charges against two of its own officers after a man from Yellowknife, Northwest Territories, died in their custody last year.

The Alberta RCMP, which led the investigation into the man’s death, says the two Yellowknife officers face charges of criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessities of life.

The charges stem from an incident in March, 2025, police say, when the two officers responded to a report of a disturbance at a Yellowknife business.

When the officers arrived, the RCMP says they detained a man who was showing signs of intoxication and left him inside a police vehicle while they gathered more information at the scene.

Police say the officers returned to the car and found the man, 56-year-old Lawrence Blackduck, unresponsive.

He was ultimately pronounced dead at the scene, the RCMP says, after life-saving measures were attempted and paramedics were called.

The RCMP did not give further details about the officers’ alleged conduct which gave rise to the charges.

The national police service says it conducted an internal review in the aftermath of the incident and it has since made changes to police policy and training related to in-vehicle detentions.

Chief Superintendent Dyson Smith of the Northwest Territories RCMP extended his condolences to Blackduck’s family and community and called the incident “deeply troubling.”

“This is a difficult day for our organization and the communities we serve. We recognize the seriousness of this incident and remain committed to transparency, accountability and maintaining public trust and confidence,” Smith wrote in a statement.

stories.title: Retirement home inviting public to ‘Walk the Kindness Way’ fundraiser
stories.summary: Craigwiel Gardens in Ailsa Craig is inviting the public to its first ‘Walk the Kindness Way’ walk fundraiser.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Craigwiel Gardens in Ailsa Craig is inviting the public to its first ‘Walk the Kindness Way’ walk fundraiser.

There are two distance options, 10 kilometres or 19.4 kilometres, with proceeds funding Craigwiel’s Spread Kindness initiatives. Those initiatives include creating outdoor paths and gardens.

“The annual Walk the Kindness Way fundraiser has raised in excess of $250,000, helping to complete healing gardens at Fairview Community in Cambridge and Parkwood Community in Waterloo,” said Elaine Shantz, president and CEO, Fairview Parkwood Craigwiel Communities.

“This year, we are pleased to launch the walk at Craigwiel Gardens, adding a third day to the event. Each campus has set its sights on raising $20,000 to support their Spread Kindness initiatives, including the creation of outdoor paths and gardens for nearly 150 older adults living at Craigwiel Gardens. Whether you walk 10 kilometres or the full 60 kilometres option, every step makes a difference.”
