stories.title: London Acorn brings back ‘Slummies’ awards to call out worst landlords
stories.summary: London Acorn members gathered at Victoria Park on Saturday to name the city’s worst landlords as part of the group’s second annual ‘Slummies’ awards.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
London Acorn members gathered at Victoria Park on Saturday to name the city’s worst landlords as part of the group’s second annual ‘Slummies’ awards.

The event, held at 1 p.m. at the park’s bandshell, highlighted tenant complaints about delayed repairs, pest infestations, and landlords who fail to respond to concerns.

The awards are based on tenant nominations and votes, with three categories recognizing landlords for poor maintenance, excessive rent increases and a lack of communication.

Claire Wittnebel, chair of London Acorn, said the group collected tenant testimonies and survey responses to highlight the conditions renters are facing across the city.

“We’re presenting three main awards today,” Wittnebel said.

The categories include the Golden Cockroach Award for landlords accused of neglecting maintenance, the Rent Gouger Award for landlords criticized for significant rent increases, and the Ghost Landlord Award for those who allegedly fail to respond to tenants.

Christina Bobb, an Acorn tenant who has lived at 235 Gray Street for 16 years, said it’s difficult to get a response from her landlord.

“We’re waiting months to get simple repairs done, or even a response to requests for repairs,” Bobb said.

Wittnebel said the problems extend beyond individual buildings and reflect a broader issue for renters in London.

“This is not an isolated incident. This is a systemic issue happening across the city,” she said.

Acorn is calling on the City of London to introduce landlord licensing, which the group says would help hold landlords accountable through proactive inspections of common areas and stronger enforcement of existing bylaws designed to protect tenants.

Members also displayed petitions collected across the city in support of landlord licensing and called on mayoral and ward candidates to commit to the proposal ahead of the Oct. 26 municipal election.

The organization says the awards are intended to draw attention to tenants’ experiences and build support for stronger protections for renters.

stories.title: More than one in four Montreal-area adults experienced poverty over eight years
stories.summary: Montreal - More than one in four adults in Greater Montreal experienced poverty at some point between 2016 and 2023, according to a new study suggesting poverty is more widespread than annual statistics indicate.
stories.author: Stéphane Rolland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - More than one in four adults in Greater Montreal experienced poverty at some point between 2016 and 2023, according to a new study suggesting poverty is more widespread than annual statistics indicate.

The study, conducted by Quebec’s Institut national de la recherche scientifique in collaboration with Centraide of Greater Montreal, found that 26 per cent of adults in the metropolitan area — which includes Montreal, Laval and surrounding suburbs — lived below the poverty line for at least one year between 2016 and 2023.

“Poverty really affects a lot of people,” said Tasha Lackman, president and CEO of Centraide of Greater Montreal, a charity that funds community organizations fighting poverty and social exclusion.

While annual poverty rates have hovered between 10 and 12 per cent since 2020, the study released Thursday found that financial hardship affected a much larger share of the population when measured over several years.

Using Statistics Canada data that tracked people’s circumstances over several years, researchers found that 14 per cent of adults experienced poverty for at least three years, while another 12 per cent lived below the poverty line for one or two years.

Lackman said escaping poverty can be difficult because even seemingly minor expenses can become major obstacles.

She pointed to families struggling to afford public transit fares so their children could participate in educational activities, or adults unable to cover transportation costs to attend job interviews or get to work before receiving their first paycheque.

The study found that persistent poverty was particularly common among immigrants, affecting 22 per cent of recent immigrants and 20 per cent of those who had lived in Canada for more than a decade.

Poverty has also become a longer-term problem for seniors. Among adults aged 65 and older, the proportion who spent seven or eight years below the poverty line rose from one per cent between 1992 and 1999 to 11 per cent between 2016 and 2023.

Xavier St-Denis, a professor at the Institut national de la recherche scientifique and the study’s author, said Canada has been relatively successful at reducing poverty among seniors through programs such as Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement.

However, significant wealth inequalities remain, he said, particularly among seniors who reach retirement with little savings and do not own a home.

The report recommends increasing government benefits, particularly social assistance payments, to help reduce poverty.

Single adults under 65 are especially disadvantaged compared with seniors and families, who receive greater government support.

In Quebec, a single adult without health-related employment limitations can receive $845 a month in social assistance, compared with $1,014 for someone with qualifying health-related limitations, according to the provincial government’s website.

The report argues that neither amount is sufficient to escape poverty.

St-Denis said concerns that increasing benefits would discourage employment have not materialized in the case of government support for families.

“Benefits increased without having a negative effect on mothers’ participation in the labour market,” he said, adding that the payments had a particularly positive effect on reducing poverty among single mothers.

Lackman also emphasized the importance of social housing, saying the study found that people living in neighbourhoods with more social housing were less likely to fall into poverty.

She welcomed the focus on homelessness by the Parti Québécois, which won Quebec’s Oct. 5 election and is preparing to form a minority government. Its leader, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, has pledged to make reducing homelessness a priority.

“We need to make sure our politicians and society in general understand the urgency of the situation when one in four people has experienced poverty,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 17, 2026.

stories.title: Failed Toronto 18 terror plot ringleader granted full parole
stories.summary: Conditions linked to his parole include stipulation that Amara can’t communicate with anyone involved in crime or with extremists.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
As previously reported by National Post , he was one of 18 people arrested in sweeping national security raids in June 2006. Amara and an accomplice recruited people for a jihadist group that planned to carry out terrorist acts demanding Canadian troops be withdrawn from Afghanistan.

The group splintered in two, with Amara taking the lead role in a plot that included plans to detonate powerful truck bombs at key financial, military and intelligence targets. They also planned to storm Parliament, the CBC, as well as take hostages and behead the prime minister.

Amara has been on day parole with multiple conditions since 2022. The parole board moved his release forward after they reviewed his case last week. The two-member panel said Amara, 41, demonstrated “positive change, both in attitude and behaviour” after undergoing a deradicalization process while in jail.

The board’s decision notes Amara wants to live in his own home, get a full-time job, attend a mosque, see family and participate in leisure activities. It says he was closely supervised while on day parole. His internet use, friendships and relationships were monitored, with no reported concerns or breaches.

The conditions linked to his full parole include a stipulation that Amara can’t communicate with anyone involved in crime, including others arrested in the anti-terrorism raids of June 2006. He also can’t be in contact with extremists, except in his work as a consultant with a specialized program.

He also has to continue to attend counselling, undergo financial monitoring and have restrictions on his phone and Internet use.

In response to the Parole Board decision, Senator Leo Housakos wrote on X, “Don’t worry, Canadians! The terrorist who plotted to storm Parliament Hill and bomb Toronto has been miraculously cured of extremism. The Parole Board says Canadians can sleep soundly.”

Amara pleaded guilty in October 2009 to participating in a terror group with the intention of setting off explosions likely to cause serious bodily harm or death. He was sentenced to life in prison with no chance of parole for 10 years.

stories.title: Record $90M Lotto Max jackpot unclaimed in Friday’s draw
stories.summary: There was no winner of the record $90 million Lotto Max jackpot on Friday night, meaning Canadians will have yet another opportunity to claim the largest lottery prize ever offered. While no single ticket matched the winning numbers of 1, 11, 13, 36, 41, 43, 51 and the bonus number 52, five tickets holders have […]
stories.author: John Marchesan
stories.content:
By John Marchesan

Posted October 17, 2026 12:37 pm.

There was no winner of the record $90 million Lotto Max jackpot on Friday night, meaning Canadians will have yet another opportunity to claim the largest lottery prize ever offered.

While no single ticket matched the winning numbers of 1, 11, 13, 36, 41, 43, 51 and the bonus number 52, five tickets holders have won just over $154,000 after matching six of the seven numbers drawn plus the bonus number. Three of those tickets were sold in Ontario, while one each was sold in Alberta and Winnipeg.

There were five Maxmillion winning tickets worth $1 million each sold in London, Oxford County, Essex County, Quebec and online at OLG.ca.

There were also 14 Maxplus tickets worth $100,000 each sold across Ontario including in Ottawa, London, Etobicoke, Vaughan, Milton, Whitby, and two in Toronto.

The $90 million prize will once again be up for grabs on Tuesday, October 20, with an estimated 20 $1 million Maxmillion prizes and 90 $100,000 Maxplus prizes, making for a total of $119 million in prizes available.

stories.title: 2 seriously hurt, 11 others injured in B.C. crash that shut down Highway 99
stories.summary: Surrey police initially reported no serious injuries in the crash, but said late Friday night that two among the injured were seriously hurt and one was airlifted to a hospital.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Police in British Columbia say 13 people were sent to the hospital after a semi-truck and trailer, a bus and several other vehicles were involved in a crash on Highway 99 on Friday.

The Surrey Police Service initially reported no serious injuries in the crash, but said late Friday night that two among the injured were seriously hurt, one of whom was airlifted to a hospital.

The force says the other 11 injured were hospitalized in stable condition.

Police say the probe into the cause of the crash is still in the early stages but investigators believe the semi-truck and trailer crossed into incoming traffic.

The multi-vehicle collision shut down traffic for several hours on Highway 99.

BC Emergency Health Services say several ambulances, paramedics and an air ambulance responded to the crash.

stories.title: Quebec author abandons effort to document novel’s origins amid AI allegations
stories.summary: Quebec author Thélyson Orélien has abandoned efforts to compile evidence supporting his denial that artificial intelligence was used to write his novel, his publisher confirmed.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
Quebec author Thélyson Orélien has abandoned efforts to compile evidence supporting his denial that artificial intelligence was used to write his novel, his publisher has confirmed.

Éditions du Boréal says it supported Orélien in the process to compile evidence, which it had publicly disclosed in September, but that the author ultimately decided to end it.

The publisher says it respects his decision, although it would have preferred to provide definitive answers to the allegations surrounding his novel, “C’était ça ou mourir.”

Boréal also confirms that sales of the novel have slowed since the controversy began, but declined to provide specific figures.

The novel remains available in bookstores, but Boréal says it is currently out of stock at the publishing house, with a new printing expected next week.

The novel was removed from the running for France’s prestigious Prix Goncourt earlier this month amid allegations of AI use and separate plagiarism allegations involving Orélien’s earlier writings, which he has since acknowledged.

stories.title: Stellantis workers begin two-day vote on strike mandate
stories.summary: Union remains at odds with automaker over plans to sell its idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to defence contractor Roshel
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Stellantis Stla-N workers in Canada begin voting today on whether to give their union a strike mandate as collective bargaining negotiations remain stalled.

The two-day votes will wrap up tomorrow, with Unifor set to announce results on Monday.

Unifor says potential strike action remains its last resort as it still hopes to reach a negotiated deal with the company.

However, the union remains at loggerheads with the automaker after Stellantis announced plans to sell its idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to defence contractor Roshel.

Stellantis says market and trade conditions have hurt the business case for keeping the plant, but that the move to sell could support future jobs there.

More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when it halted operations in 2023, as Stellantis later moved production of its Jeep Compass from the site to Illinois.

stories.title: B.C. Municipal Election Day Live: The latest news, results and reaction
stories.summary: Check back throughout the day for coverage of the election, results as they come in, and dispatches from reporters across Metro Vancouver.
stories.author: Stephanie Ip, J.J. Adams
stories.content:
It’s general election day across B.C.

British Columbians head to the polls today beginning at 8 a.m. to vote for the mayors, councillors, and school trustees who will lead their cities for the next four years. (And in the case of Vancouver, voters will also select park board commissioners.)

Once polls close at 8 p.m., results will start to trickle in about who’s been elected and who’s out across the Lower Mainland.

Bookmark this live-blog and check back throughout the day for coverage of the day’s events, results as they come in, and dispatches from reporters stationed in municipalities across Metro Vancouver.

5:32 p.m.: Kindness, art and pools top Vancouver’s 2026 Kids Vote ballot

While the adults figure out who’s going to run city hall next, Vancouver’s younger generation have cast their ballots for kindness.

Kids who visited one of 20 Vancouver Public Library branches between Oct. 3 to 17 were invited to participate in an early democracy activity by voting on four major issues, including what they like to do for fun, what qualities they want a leader to have, and what activity they wish they could do more of.

Some 36 per cent of early voters said they liked to visit swimming pools for fun in Vancouver, instead of beaches or playgrounds, libraries or community centres. When asked about the qualities a leader should have, 38 per cent noted kindness as the top quality, followed by 31 per cent who said fun was the most important. (Swag was not listed as a voting option.)

Vancouver Election 2026: 8 hot topics and where the 7 major parties stand

Surrey Election: 6 hot topics and where candidates stand

Finally, 40 per cent said firefighters, ambulance and police officers were the most important aspect of Vancouver. Gardens, parks and nature came in a close second with 28 per cent, while libraries, theatres and fun events took 16 per cent of the votes.

Preliminary results show 1,047 kids cast a ballot this year, up 121 per cent from 2022. A total of 223 ballots were spoiled, “a sign that some young voters had more to say than the ballot allowed.”

4 p.m.: Endorsement controversy in Coquitlam

Richard Stewart is retiring from the mayorship after nearly two decades at the helm of Coquitlam, and the race to replace him is a heated one.

He’d originally endorsed Craig Hodge, a city councillor since 2011, but since switched his support to two-time councillor Trish Mandewo. Stewart had asked Hodge to remove a video of him endorsing him, but as of Saturday, it was still up, leading Stewart to post on Facebook, calling it “misleading.”

1 p.m.: Political Polymarket bets

Apropos of nothing, and not to encourage gambling, but political observers can bet on the outcome of B.C. Elections on the platform Polymarket. The U.S.-funded, Panama-based crypto-based prediction market exists in a murky ethical and legal area, as it includes wars, deaths and sports among its bets.

Playnow.com, B.C.’s legal betting website, doesn’t offer the option.

Polymarket predicts Pete Fry will likely be the new mayor in Vancouver, and Brenda Locke is a shoo-in for Surrey. Will the numbers be borne out in reality? It remains to be seen.

11:30 a.m.: Thind says vote — just not for me

An incumbent Surrey school board trustee encourages everyone to vote in this election, including for school board trustees — but not to cast his vote for him.

Gary Thind is running as a Conservative MLA for Surrey-Guildford in the upcoming provincial election, and isn’t seeking to be re-elected to the school board. But the snap provincial election came too late for him to withdraw from the local trustee election.

Thind, who’s served on the board since 2014 and is currently the vice-chair, would have to vacate his trustee seat if elected in both positions.

11 a.m.: Ballots begin to be cast

We know at least one vote for mayor in Vancouver. Well, probably.

Incumbent Ken Sim cast his vote in Vancouver as polls opened across the province in the municipal elections.

“Our door knockers, including the team and me, are out across the city right now, talking with neighbours and reminding people to vote, as we have been doing for many months,” he wrote. “Thank you to every one of you for the time, energy and heart you’ve given this campaign. If you haven’t voted yet, there’s still time.”

Sim won in 2022, becoming the first candidate in more than a decade to unseat an incumbent mayor when he dethroned Kennedy Stewart.

Stewart, Larry Campbell (2005) and Sam Sullivan (2008) were the only one-term mayors in the city’s history since 1950. Sim is looking to avoid those ranks.

8 a.m.: Polls open while Vancouver reports record-high advance voter turnout

The polls are open! We won’t know until after polls close at 8 p.m. what the turnout looks like for the 2026 municipal elections. However, after the first day of advance voting on Oct. 3, the city of Vancouver announced it had seen a record-high turnout .

In the first 12 hours of opening day, a total of 21,824 voters cast their ballots for Vancouver’s next mayor, council, park board and school board. All told, more than 103,000 ballots were cast before today — a 60 per cent increase from 2022.

And Vancouver wasn’t alone . Richmond was up 141 per cent compared to the last election, with New Westminster close behind at 121 per cent and Victoria at 101 per cent. Abbotsford’s numbers jumped by 93 per cent while Surrey, Langley, Burnaby, Nanaimo and Port Coquitlam were all on track to blow the old numbers out of the water.

stories.title: Pete Fry unseats Ken Sim to become Vancouver's first Green mayor as city hall swings left
stories.summary: ABC Vancouver, which swept to power in 2022 as a new centre-right party, was almost wiped out. Find out more.
stories.author: Dan Fumano
stories.content:
Pete Fry is Vancouver’s guy.

At the Green party of Vancouver’s election-night party on Saturday night, the jubilant crowd chanted to celebrate their candidate’s win in the mayor’s race: “Our guy, Pete Fry! Our guy, Pete Fry!”

Fry, a two-term Vancouver councillor, unseated the incumbent mayor, Ken Sim of ABC Vancouver, in an election that saw the city government swing to the left.

Fry will become Vancouver’s first Green mayor, and he will be joined in a new-look civic administration with other Greens, as well as representatives of the city’s other major left-leaning parties, Cope and OneCity.

ABC Vancouver, which swept to power in 2022 as a new centre-right party, was almost wiped out. After ABC won the mayor’s office by a wide margin four years ago with its 18 affiliated candidates topping the polls for council, school board, and park board, the once-dominant party was reduced this year to a single seat.

With 148 of 149 voting places reporting, at past midnight Saturday, Fry had 89,706 votes, well ahead of Sim’s 63,072.

Shortly after 10:30 p.m., Fry took the stage at the Greens’ event, and told the crowd Sim had just phoned him to concede. Fry said the outgoing mayor was “very gracious in offering his assistance in making sure that I steward the city well.”

Colleen Hardwick of Team for a Livable Vancouver was in a distant third in the mayoral race, followed by the Vancouver Liberals’ Kareem Allam, and Vote Vancouver’s Rebecca Bligh. None of those three parties’ candidates were elected to council, park board, or school board.

Fry will oversee a diverse, more left-leaning council, with four different parties and no majority. He said he looks forward to working with councillors from across the spectrum, including ABC.

B.C. Municipal Election Results Map: Who's your new mayor?

Surrey Election Results: Brenda Locke unseated by former mayor Doug McCallum

While ABC won seven of 10 council seats in 2022, incumbent Coun. Mike Klassen was the only one of the party’s nine council candidates elected this year.

Incumbent Cope Coun. Sean Orr won more votes than any other council candidate and will be joined by fellow Cope councillors Chloe Leslie, Devyani Singh, and Solomon Yi-Kieran. Four Green council candidates were elected: Annette Reilly, Stephanie Smith, Camil Dumont, and Bridget Burns. Incumbent OneCity Coun. Lucy Maloney was the only member of her party’s five candidates elected to council.

Fry said Vancouverites should not worry about the new council’s ability to get things done, despite having no majority.

“I’ve spent eight years on the Union of B.C. Municipalities, where the majority of mayors and councils don’t have political parties, and they function just fine. We have this anomaly in Vancouver with political parties … and I recognize that that’s a function of our electoral politics. But we can leave that at the door and focus on how we work together,” Fry said.

“My interest is in cultivating a culture where we’re all working for Vancouver, not for our political parties.”

Fry said ABC “really tried to run on very negative and fear-based messaging, and a lot of attack ads that we didn’t really respond to. Instead, we took a very positive, upbeat approach, and a love for our city that, I think, shone through.”

ABC failed to elect a single candidate to the park board or school board, which will be filled with a mix of Cope, OneCity, and Green politicians.

One of the biggest stories of Sim’s term in office was his attempt to abolish Vancouver’s elected park board, a unique body among B.C. cities. The move surprised the public and some members of Sim’s own party, but he eventually changed course and ABC ran a slate of park board candidates this year.

Incumbent Green park commissioner Tom Digby topped the park board race, and will be joined by fellow Greens Spencer van Vloten and Breanne Smart, as well as Cope candidates T’uy’t’tanat Cease Wyss, Tamiko Suzuki, Jamie Han and Sacia Burton.

Watching the results roll in Saturday night, Digby commented: “Ken Sim tried to abolish the park board, but it turns out tonight might be the revenge of the park board, because I think we’re going to succeed in abolishing Ken Sim.”

Recent polling suggested a desire for change at Vancouver city hall. But with seven established parties running slates of council candidates and five mayoral hopefuls between them, there were several possibilities for what change could look like.

Sim and ABC dominated the 2022 election, with the new party’s entire slate of candidates topping the polls. But over the course of the four-year term, the size of that ABC caucus shrank with a series of politicians leaving the party, many of whom ran against their former party this year.

A record number of Vancouverites cast their votes before election day. More than 103,000 voters cast a ballot over four advance voting days this year, the city reported , a 59 per cent increase over 2022, and more than 21,000 voters requested vote-by-mail packages this year, more than double the last election. In Vancouver’s 2022 election , a total of 171,494 ballots were cast, equating to 36.3 per cent of registered voters.

The Vancouver ballot also featured two non-binding plebiscite questions this year, which were added by the ABC-majority council. The first question was about cracking down on public drug use, and another about converting part of the old St. Paul’s Hospital, or a similar site, into an “involuntary-care” facility for 100 or more people with severe mental-health and substance-use problems.

The plebiscite results were not released Saturday night, but are expected to be released by Wednesday.

The Greens, Cope and OneCity, as the city’s main left-leaning parties, entered into an agreement earlier this year to limit the number of candidates among them so as to not split the progressive vote. In early September, Cope and OneCity’s mayoral candidates withdrew from the race, paving the way for Fry as a unity candidate.

At the ABC Vancouver party in the Sheraton Vancouver Wall Centre, Sim addressed the crowd after he conceded defeat.

“Obviously tonight, voters wanted to go in a different direction — not just in the mayor’s office but with council, park and school board as well,” a subdued Sim told supporters. “I think it’s important we acknowledge that.”

Sim said he entered political life so he could create a better city for his children. But he acknowledged that the job meant he wasn’t always there for his kids.

“For that, boys, I totally apologize. I love you. You’re going to see a lot more of dad over the next little while.”

Sim described being elected to the mayor’s office as “the highlight of my life.”

“When I’m on my death bed, I’ll look back at this time as probably the most meaningful thing I’ve been involved with. And with that, thank you again, and we’ll see you out on the streets somewhere, I’m sure.”

stories.title: Backstreet Boys’ 12-show Toronto run offers millennials a ticket to simpler times
stories.summary: Nearly three decades after their commercial peak, the Backstreet Boys have booked a staggering 12 shows at Toronto’s Rogers Centre in 2027, citing “overwhelming demand.”
stories.author: Alex Nino Gheciu
stories.content:
When Chelsea Smith heard the Backstreet Boys were coming to Toronto, she had a simple message for the five men who soundtracked her childhood.

“Here’s my credit card, take all my money.”

The 35-year-old Vancouver fan wasn’t bluffing. Having already travelled to Las Vegas to see her teenybopper crushes, she’s now preparing to fly across the country for two Toronto concerts, spending roughly $600 on tickets alone. And she’s hardly the only millennial willing to pay a tidy sum to party like it’s 1999.

Nearly three decades after their commercial peak, the Backstreet Boys have booked a staggering 12 shows at Toronto’s Rogers Centre in 2027, citing “overwhelming demand.” The run doubles the venue’s previous record of six shows, set by Taylor Swift during her Eras Tour in 2024.

While some current major artists are cancelling tours amid sluggish ticket sales, the once-baggy-jeaned quintet is proving nostalgia is a hell of a drug.

“I haven’t seen a Top 40 artist in so many years,” says Smith, a self-described “Y2K-era girlie” who made two trips to the Backstreet Boys’ Las Vegas Sphere residency last year.

She suspects millennials are seeking comfort in the past.

“I feel like during COVID we all retreated back to our nostalgia,” says the customer support professional.

“Times are tough. You’re going back to when it was simpler and just living in that moment.”

Bill Welychka remembers when the Backstreet Boys could bring downtown Toronto to a standstill.

At the height of the boy-band craze in the late ’90s, the former MuchMusic VJ watched thousands of screaming teenagers descend on the channel’s Queen Street West headquarters, hoping to glimpse the five American heartthrobs.

“There were certain bands where we knew we’d have to hire security, where we would have to close the street down. The Backstreet Boys were certainly one of those bands,” he recalls.

“I think they fed off of that energy and the applause and the screams and the tears.”

The Toronto residency is dubbed “Into the Millennium — Homecoming: Live in Canada,” fittingly so: Canada was the first North American market to embrace the group.

Welychka remembers the frenzy spreading from Europe to Quebec, then across Canada, with MuchMusic putting their videos into heavy rotation.

“We latched on to them very, very early on,” he says.

But the boy-band bubble eventually burst. As tastes shifted in the 2000s, the Backstreet Boys faded from the charts, trading stadium-scale hysteria for more theatres and casinos.

Now, with their original fans approaching middle age, Welychka reckons they’re yearning for a time when their biggest responsibility was keeping a Tamagotchi alive.

“It’s a different day and age now. It’s a lot more frustrating,” says Welychka, citing unemployment and the cost-of-living crisis.

“A lot of people want to get those feelings back you once had. If you’re a 45-year-old woman and screaming and crying, nothing wrong with that.”

Eleni Papamichelakis knows the feeling. The 39-year-old Durham Region mother drifted away from the Backstreet Boys as adulthood took over, only to rediscover her teenage obsession when she caught their Sphere residency last year. Now she’s taking her 11-year-old daughter to see the group, just as she did at that age in 1998.

Part of the appeal is revisiting a pre-smartphone era, when having fun just required a CD and some friends to dance with.

“The world and, like, life has changed and it’s become so digital and sometimes a little bit impersonal,” says the mortgage agent.

“We lived in such a fun era where we had to kind of entertain ourselves.”

A grown-up bank account helps, though: “We have the money to go and see these concerts in a better seat than when we were younger.”

Not every artist is benefiting from that spending power.

The concert industry has been grappling with so-called “blue dot fever,” named for the unsold seats dotting Ticketmaster seating charts.

This year, Meghan Trainor scrapped her tour, Zayn Malik cancelled his U.S. dates and Post Malone scaled back his stadium run. Though the artists cited varying reasons, the cancellations have fuelled speculation about sluggish ticket sales.

The Backstreet Boys, meanwhile, are once again larger than life at the box office. Their Toronto residency could draw nearly half a million concertgoers, with tickets ranging from around $100 to well over $1,000 for VIP packages.

Nostalgia has always sold concert tickets. But Scott Henderson, a professor of popular culture at Trent University, says it’s becoming an increasingly vital draw for major venues amid an uncertain touring market.

“It’s kind of fuelling the industry in ways it never used to,” Henderson says. “That used to be a separate market, that nostalgia market. Now it’s what big venues like the Rogers Centre are going to have to look for.”

Sentimental millennials, he says, now have deeper pockets and a willingness to splurge on premium tickets.

“That’s your guaranteed audience.”

For Vanessa Capozi, a 39-year-old Montreal-area mother of two, the Backstreet Boys offer something priceless: a break from adulthood.

“Life has taken over right now,” says the special education technician. “Rarely do people my age take time for themselves.”

But when her favourite boy band hits the stage, she gets to be 15 again.

“For those two hours, nothing else exists. I’m just there as me, that teenager, watching the Backstreet Boys.”

stories.title: Stellantis workers begin voting on strike mandate as talks remain stalled
stories.summary: Stellantis workers in Canada begin voting today on whether to give their union a strike mandate as collective bargaining negotiations remain stalled.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Stellantis workers in Canada begin voting today on whether to give their union a strike mandate as collective bargaining negotiations remain stalled.

The two-day votes will wrap up tomorrow, with Unifor set to announce results on Monday.

Unifor says potential strike action remains its last resort as it still hopes to reach a negotiated deal with the company.

However, the union remains at loggerheads with the automaker after Stellantis announced plans to sell its idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to defence contractor Roshel.

Stellantis says market and trade conditions have hurt the business case for keeping the plant, but that the move to sell could support future jobs there.

More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when it halted operations in 2023, as Stellantis later moved production of its Jeep Compass from the site to Illinois.

stories.title: How Canada’s fractured immigration consensus is starting to show up at ballot boxes
stories.summary: It's no secret the long-held Canadian consensus on immigration has fractured — pulled apart by a rapid increase in new arrivals post-pandemic and growing affordability challenges.
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
It’s no secret the long-held Canadian consensus on immigration has fractured — pulled apart by a rapid increase in new arrivals post-pandemic and growing affordability challenges. Now, that fracture is starting to show up at the ballot box.

The Parti Québécois won a minority mandate in Quebec on a platform that included promises of tighter immigration controls, which the party linked to protecting French culture and easing pressure on public services and housing.

And when Albertans head to the polls Monday to vote on whether to hold a future referendum on separation from Canada, they’ll also be answering five separate questions on immigration being pushed by the government of Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

Those questions include:

— Should the province should have more say over economic immigration?

— Should provincially funded services should be restricted to citizens, permanent residents and those with “Alberta-approved” immigration status?

— Should non-permanent immigrants should be charged a fee for accessing health care and education services?

— Should non-permanent residents should have to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for provincially funded social supports?

— Should voters should have to present proof of citizenship when voting provincially?

Jason Kenney, a former Alberta premier and federal immigration minister, said Canada needs a broader debate on immigration policy based on facts.

“We do need a serious debate on immigration because demography is destiny. There are very few things that are more important,” Kenney told The Canadian Press in an interview.

“But we have to do it in a disciplined and respectful, thoughtful way, as much as possible, based on evidence and data and experience around the world.”

Kenney warned that debates on immigration policy can easily become sidetracked by more extreme political views — by accusations of racism from the far left and by actual racism on the far right.

While Kenney said he doesn’t see the immigration questions on the Alberta ballot as race-based or xenophobic, the Alberta separatist movement itself is something else entirely.

“If you listen to the key separatist leaders like Mitch Sylvestre, who’s the leader of the primary separatist organization, he says that in his republic of Alberta, no one will have citizenship unless you’re born there,” Kenney said.

“So I do think there are some currents on the extreme right of Alberta politics that we should all be concerned about. I do not think that necessarily means we cannot have an adult, grown-up conversation about immigration policy.”

But the immigration questions on the ballot are not sitting well with some diaspora communities in the province.

Lawyer Avnish Nanda, co-founder of the advocacy group Our Alberta Advantage, is campaigning for people to vote “no” on the immigration-related questions.

He said reactions to the questions from Alberta’s cultural communities and from individuals who have considered running for the United Conservative Party have been overwhelmingly negative.

“They view these questions as targeting them, their journey here and the roots they’ve established over the past 60 years,” he said.

“There’s fear, there’s confusion and anger at this government. They think this is not necessary. They think it’s wrapped up in the separatism effort. They think that Danielle Smith is scapegoating them to continue to maintain the support of the more extreme separatist elements that brought her to power.”

Nanda said the referendum is bringing out some ugly undercurrents in Alberta. He said his parents were recently “jeered by a couple of white guys in a car” while out for a walk — something that had never happened to them since coming to Canada in the 1970s.

Nanda said if the immigration ballot measures pass on Monday, they could undermine Canada’s multicultural identity, while restricting access to provincial services would make it harder for newcomers to integrate.

Across the country in Quebec, the new minority Parti Québécois government campaigned on a promise to tighten immigration controls. Quebec has maintained far more control over the immigration system than other provinces since 1991.

The PQ immigration platform included, among other things, promises to reduce annual permanent resident admissions from 45,000 to 35,000, to impose a moratorium on permanent immigration from outside Quebec, to prioritize permanent status for temporary residents already in the province, and to tighten the selection criteria for temporary workers.

Catherine Xhardez, a political-science professor at the University of Montreal, said the outgoing Coalition Avenir du Quebec government politicized Quebec’s immigration debate by introducing restrictions the new government now wants to strengthen.

“Before that, they have kind of a consensus between political parties, how migration is good for the economy … good for demography, but even for French language,” she said.

Xhardez said before 2018, Quebec’s main parties generally agreed on the positive role immigration played in strengthening francophone culture by prioritizing certain immigrants.

“But then (the CAQ) broke this consensus between the parties by saying it was too much, too quickly, they needed less,” she said.

Xhardez said there’s a key difference between the Quebec and Alberta immigration debates — the debate in Alberta is built around populist pushback blaming social service shortages on immigrants, while the debate in Quebec puts identity and culture at the forefront.

She added immigration has also become a bargaining chip for the Quebec government in its engagements with Ottawa.

Premier Smith wants a bargaining chip of her own. In a video released Wednesday, Smith encouraged Albertans to vote in favour of the nine immigration and constitutional questions in the referendum to “send Ottawa a message.” She said the goal of one question on the ballot is to “give us the same power as Quebec to recruit economic migrants.”

During a pro-unity campaign stop in Calgary on Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney urged his audience to vote “no to the nine” — repeating a phrase that has become a rallying cry among those opposed to separatism.

Kenney said he’s a “skeptic when it comes to greater provincial control” over a “sensitive” matter like immigration policy. He said provincial governments lack the federal government’s ability to detect fraud and are inclined to focus solely on local issues — not on how immigration affects the national economy.

“In the Western provinces, very typically, the permanent residents that they recommend have been low-skilled temporary foreign workers who they’re flipping into permanent residency because the local MLAs get tired of being browbeaten by the Tim Hortons franchise owners,” Kenney said.

Reflecting on his time as Alberta’s premier, he said “certain premiers” told Ottawa after the COVID-19 pandemic that their biggest priority was to increase immigration — despite early evidence of the housing and youth unemployment challenges currently driving the immigration debate.

“When you don’t have social permission to discuss these issues, again, that creates the kind of conditions where popular opinion gets totally detached from elite opinion. And if you want to know what that looks like, look at the politics of Europe today,” Kenney said.

“So if you want to avoid (Alternative für Deutschland), Front National, U.K. Reform-style politics, then yes, we need a proper, open debate about these issues.”

Xhardez, who is originally from Belgium, said the Canadian political scene is very different from Europe and the U.S. — Canada has no mainstream anti-immigrant political party at the federal level. But public feelings about immigration have shifted — and no one knows for certain how that will affect Canada’s politics going forward.

“Canada is maybe not so exceptional, we don’t know. Or maybe it will become exceptional as being just less politicized, but it’s not true that there is still this consensus and strong public support,” Xhardez said.

Nanda said some of the loudest voices opposing the immigration questions in Alberta have been chambers of commerce, which represent businesses that have been struggling to recruit staff.

He said someone in politics needs to champion the idea that immigrants lift up economies, expand the tax base and help to fund social programs and services.

“If you go to rural Alberta hospitals or long-term care facilities, most nurses and support staff are immigrants because we can’t find local workers to work there. The same is true in many educational facilities.”

Reflecting on his time as Alberta’s premier, he said “certain premiers” told Ottawa after the COVID-19 pandemic that their biggest priority was to increase immigration — despite early evidence of the housing and youth unemployment challenges currently driving the immigration debate.

“When you don’t have social permission to discuss these issues, again, that creates the kind of conditions where popular opinion gets totally detached from elite opinion. And if you want to know what that looks like, look at the politics of Europe today,” Kenney said.
“So if you want to avoid (Alternative für Deutschland), Front National, U.K. Reform-style politics, then yes, we need a proper, open debate about these issues.”

Xhardez, who is originally from Belgium, said the Canadian political scene is very different from Europe and the U.S. — Canada has no mainstream anti-immigrant political party at the federal level. But public feelings about immigration have shifted — and no one knows for certain how that will affect Canada’s politics going forward.

“Canada is maybe not so exceptional, we don’t know. Or maybe it will become exceptional as being just less politicized, but it’s not true that there is still this consensus and strong public support,” Xhardez said.
Nanda said some of the loudest voices opposing the immigration questions in Alberta have been chambers of commerce, which represent businesses that have been struggling to recruit staff.
He said someone in politics needs to champion the idea that immigrants lift up economies, expand the tax base and help to fund social programs and services.

“If you go to rural Alberta hospitals or long-term care facilities, most nurses and support staff are immigrants because we can’t find local workers to work there. The same is true in many educational facilities.”

content_blocks.text: It’s no secret the long-held Canadian consensus on immigration has fractured — pulled apart by a rapid increase in new arrivals post-pandemic and growing affordability challenges. Now, that fracture is starting to show up at the ballot box.

The Parti Québécois won a minority mandate in Quebec on a platform that included promises of tighter immigration controls, which the party linked to protecting French culture and easing pressure on public services and housing.

And when Albertans head to the polls Monday to vote on whether to hold a future referendum on separation from Canada, they’ll also be answering five separate questions on immigration being pushed by the government of Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.
Those questions include:
— Should the province should have more say over economic immigration?
— Should provincially funded services should be restricted to citizens, permanent residents and those with “Alberta-approved” immigration status?
— Should non-permanent immigrants should be charged a fee for accessing health care and education services?
— Should non-permanent residents should have to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for provincially funded social supports?
— Should voters should have to present proof of citizenship when voting provincially?

content_blocks.alt: Smith
content_blocks.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith listens to a question during a press conference at the Canadian Forces Base in Edmonton on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. James MacIennan/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Jason Kenney, a former Alberta premier and federal immigration minister, said Canada needs a broader debate on immigration policy based on facts.
“We do need a serious debate on immigration because demography is destiny. There are very few things that are more important,” Kenney told The Canadian Press in an interview.
“But we have to do it in a disciplined and respectful, thoughtful way, as much as possible, based on evidence and data and experience around the world.”

content_blocks.alt: Notley
content_blocks.caption: Former Alberta premiers Rachel Notley, left, and Jason Kenney discuss their assessment of the possible economic cost of Alberta’s referendum at an Edmonton Chamber luncheon, in Edmonton, on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. John Ulan/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Kenney warned that debates on immigration policy can easily become sidetracked by more extreme political views — by accusations of racism from the far left and by actual racism on the far right.
While Kenney said he doesn’t see the immigration questions on the Alberta ballot as race-based or xenophobic, the Alberta separatist movement itself is something else entirely.

“If you listen to the key separatist leaders like Mitch Sylvestre, who’s the leader of the primary separatist organization, he says that in his republic of Alberta, no one will have citizenship unless you’re born there,” Kenney said.

“So I do think there are some currents on the extreme right of Alberta politics that we should all be concerned about. I do not think that necessarily means we cannot have an adult, grown-up conversation about immigration policy.”
But the immigration questions on the ballot are not sitting well with some diaspora communities in the province.
Lawyer Avnish Nanda, co-founder of the advocacy group Our Alberta Advantage, is campaigning for people to vote “no” on the immigration-related questions.

content_blocks.alt: stampede
content_blocks.caption: Stampede Princess Breanna Correia carries the Canadian flag as the national anthem is sung prior to rodeo action at the Calgary Stampede in Calgary, Alta., Friday, July 4, 2025. Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: He said reactions to the questions from Alberta’s cultural communities and from individuals who have considered running for the United Conservative Party have been overwhelmingly negative.
“They view these questions as targeting them, their journey here and the roots they’ve established over the past 60 years,” he said.

“There’s fear, there’s confusion and anger at this government. They think this is not necessary. They think it’s wrapped up in the separatism effort. They think that Danielle Smith is scapegoating them to continue to maintain the support of the more extreme separatist elements that brought her to power.”

Nanda said the referendum is bringing out some ugly undercurrents in Alberta. He said his parents were recently “jeered by a couple of white guys in a car” while out for a walk — something that had never happened to them since coming to Canada in the 1970s.

Nanda said if the immigration ballot measures pass on Monday, they could undermine Canada’s multicultural identity, while restricting access to provincial services would make it harder for newcomers to integrate.

content_blocks.alt: Plamondon
content_blocks.caption: Parti Quebecois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon speaks to supporters after winning the provincial election in Montreal, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Across the country in Quebec, the new minority Parti Québécois government campaigned on a promise to tighten immigration controls. Quebec has maintained far more control over the immigration system than other provinces since 1991.

The PQ immigration platform included, among other things, promises to reduce annual permanent resident admissions from 45,000 to 35,000, to impose a moratorium on permanent immigration from outside Quebec, to prioritize permanent status for temporary residents already in the province, and to tighten the selection criteria for temporary workers.

Catherine Xhardez, a political-science professor at the University of Montreal, said the outgoing Coalition Avenir du Quebec government politicized Quebec’s immigration debate by introducing restrictions the new government now wants to strengthen.
“Before that, they have kind of a consensus between political parties, how migration is good for the economy … good for demography, but even for French language,” she said.
Xhardez said before 2018, Quebec’s main parties generally agreed on the positive role immigration played in strengthening francophone culture by prioritizing certain immigrants.
“But then (the CAQ) broke this consensus between the parties by saying it was too much, too quickly, they needed less,” she said.

content_blocks.alt: asylum seeker
content_blocks.caption: Asylum seeker Mahamed Yusef Niazi, from Afghanistan, carries his seven-month-old daughter Sahaba, across the border at Roxham Road from New York into Canada Friday March 24, 2023 in Champlain, NY.. The irregular border crossing will be closed permanently tonight at midnight. Ryan Remiorz/The Canadian Press

stories.title: Three-quarter of Canadians want Carney to press ahead with his economic changes: poll
stories.summary: Three-quarters of Canadians believe Mark Carney should press forward with his economic changes without seeking another election mandate
stories.author: John Marchesan
stories.content:
By John Marchesan

Posted October 17, 2026 9:03 am.

Three-quarters of Canadians surveyed believe Prime Minister Mark Carney should press forward with his economic changes without seeking another election mandate, feeling there is no time to waste as the trade war with the United States drags on.

A new Canada Pulse Insights poll of just over 1,500 Canadians shows 73 per cent want Carney to move ahead with fast-tracking infrastructure projects, relaxing certain environmental reviews, altering labour strike rules and pursuing closer economic ties with Europe. That support is strong all across the country with 83 per cent in British Columbia, 77 per cent in Quebec, 73 per cent in Atlantic Canada, 71 per cent in Ontario, 67 per cent in Saskatchewan/Manitoba and 65 per cent in Alberta.

Just over a quarter believe that the changes proposed are so big that the Prime Minister should call a federal election to seek a fresh mandate. Among Conservative voters, 53 per cent want him to call an election while 47 per cent say Carney should press ahead with his plans.

If that election were held, the poll finds the Liberals with 46 per cent support nationally compared to 34 per cent for the Conservatives. The NDP have nine per cent support with the Bloc Quebecois at six per cent and the Green Party with three per cent. One in 10 eligible voters say they are undecided.

Of note, 15 per cent of those who voted Conservative in the 2025 election now say they would vote for the Liberals while only two per cent of Liberal voters say they would switch allegiance.

The Liberals maintain double-digit support over the Conservatives in Atlantic Canada (65 per cent to 24 per cent), British Columbia (52 per cent to 27 per cent), Ontario (48 per cent to 38 per cent) and Quebec (39 per cent to 27 per cent). The gap is much closer in Alberta, where the Conservatives lead 46 per cent to 41 per cent, and in Saskatchewan/Manitoba, with 42 per cent support for the Conservatives and 38 per cent for the Liberals.

The survey was conducted among 1,531 Canadian adults using an online panel from October 1-8, and has a margin of error of +/- 2.5 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: Support for Alberta remaining in Canada steadily rises ahead of Oct. 19 referendum: Leger poll
stories.summary: Albertans supporting the province remaining in Canada steadily rises ahead of Oct. 19 referendum, according to a new Leger poll.
stories.author: Cindy Tran
stories.content:
As the Oct. 19 referendum approaches, there is a rise in the number of Albertans supporting Option 1 — for the province to remain in Canada, according to a Leger poll.

The new October poll by Leger shows support for remaining in Canada has increased from 65 per cent in August to 74 per cent this month. Support for voting in favour of Option 2 has decreased from 23 per cent in August to 21 per cent in the latest poll.

Andrew Enns, executive vice-president at Leger, said those campaigning in favour of Option 1 have consistently driven the message about the benefits of Alberta remaining in Canada and have done an effective job at communicating to people the importance of voting despite earlier concerns about voter apathy.

“They’ve done a very good job of ensuring and communicating to people the importance of Alberta remaining in Canada and voting Option 1, but also, they’ve been fairly aggressive in terms of making sure people get out to vote,” Enns said.

On the other side, those campaigning in favour of independence were falling short in comparison, said Enns.

According to the poll, those who were previously undecided or had no opinion have now begun to choose sides. The latest numbers show only four per cent of respondents expressed no opinion, down significantly from the 12 per cent reported in August.

“I think it’s safe to say that the remain campaign got more of those individuals to say they’re gonna vote remain versus the option two campaign — they just didn’t do enough to convince those fence sitters who I would argue probably were somewhat convincible to either argument,” Enns said.

Among decided voters, 78 per cent intend to vote in favour of Option 1 — remaining in Canada — and 22 per cent are in favour of Option 2 — beginning the legal process of holding a binding referendum on separation.

According to the poll, since June when the two-part separation question was put on the Oct. 19 ballot, there’s been a steady rise in Albertans who are choosing to vote against separation. Leger says in June, 64 per cent of respondents indicated they’d vote for Option 1, October’s number show a 10 per cent increase since then.

In comparison, the number of people choosing to vote for Option 2 has gone from 24 per cent in June to now 21 per cent in October.

The poll was conducted from Oct. 14 to 16 among 1,000 adult Albertans.

stories.title: Rallies planned in final weekend before Alberta separation referendum
stories.summary: Edmonton - It's all over but the rallies in the final weekend before Albertans vote on their place in Confederation.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Some separatists who rallied in Alberta’s capital on the final weekend before a historic vote on the province’s place in Confederation insisted their gathering was no last hurrah.

Alberta’s separation movement will continue, they said, despite early polls indicating massive support for the province staying in Canada.

“I don’t listen to what polls say … This battle doesn’t stop,” said Madison Holmes, a 23-year-old from Calgary, during the rally on Saturday outside the provincial legislature in Edmonton.

“The cat’s out of the bag when it comes to independence,” said her 22-year-old sister, Maycee.

The sisters, each wearing the $200 pro-independence shirts they’ve been selling online since Premier Danielle Smith announced in May the vote on separation, said they’ve already cast their votes to leave and so have the dozens who braved the chilly weather to wave the Alberta flag at Saturday’s gathering.

“Most of these people don’t believe this stops because this is not a political whim,” said Madison. “This is a fight for our future.”

A few counter protesters wearing red hats and shirts and holding Canadian flags attended the rally.

On Monday, voters go to the polls to decide if Alberta should stay in Canada or if it’s time for a second, binding referendum on whether to leave the country. The results on the separation question are set to trickle in the next day.

On Friday, Prime Minister Mark Carney wrapped up a two-day barnstorming tour of the province.

During speeches in Edmonton and Calgary, he called the separatist sentiment a dangerous bluff and pointed to his government’s plan to fast-track an oil pipeline from Alberta to the B.C. coast as proof that a united Canada can still get things done.

Opposition Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has also spoken multiple times in recent days for a united Canada in front of his party supporters.

A unity rally is scheduled for Sunday also at the Edmonton legislature.

Smith, who announced this week she has cast her vote to stay, has defended the referendum.

She has said it is necessary because frustration with Ottawa has reached a boiling point among some Albertans, and a vote would finally put the question of independence to rest.

Critics, however, have said Smith isn’t resolving a broad-based existential debate and has validated latent fringe separatist sentiment, rolling the dice on the future of the country to appease hardliners in her United Conservative Party.

Jeffrey Rath, one of the leading figures of the separatist movement in Alberta, said Saturday he won’t be disappointed if his side doesn’t see a majority after Monday’s vote.

“It doesn’t matter what we get at this point if we have people voting for independence,” he said during the rally.

“This is just the first battle.”

He said that Smith has betrayed her party members who have supported her and efforts to replace her will get underway after Tuesday’s vote.

“We’re Albertans. We roll up our sleeves and we work harder,” he said.

“It’s time that we have a leader that respects the wishes of their members … A lot of us feel Danielle Smith needs to go. Once we get her replaced, we’ll keep moving forward toward an independent Alberta.”

Aside from the 10th question on separation, Smith has put nine other questions on the referendum ballot.

Those nine ask whether her government should take more control and impose new rules on immigration, and pursue constitutional changes that take power away from Ottawa. Smith has said she needs that mandate to negotiate a better deal with Ottawa.

Saturday was the final day for advance voting in the referendum.

Elections Alberta said over one million had voted already.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 17, 2026.

stories.title: Separation, immigration, the Constitution: A look at Alberta's referendum questions
stories.summary: Edmonton - Here are the 10 questions Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is sending to a provincewide referendum on Monday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Here are the 10 questions Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is sending to a provincewide referendum on Monday.

Question 1: Do you support the government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?

What you need to know: Smith has said she wants to see Alberta have a similar accord as Quebec, which has an agreement with Ottawa that lets the province set its own eligibility requirements for economic migrants.

She said in February that a “normal” and “sustainable” level of immigration would represent less than one per cent of the population, or about 50,000 newcomers per year. But critics say Smith has failed to plan for the population growth it invited with a countrywide ad campaign in recent years.

Question 2: Do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status will be eligible for provincially funded programs, such as health care, education and other social services?

What you need to know: The premier has blamed overburdened public services on rapid population growth in the past five years.

The government’s website claims temporary residents cost the province more than $1 billion in health care, education and social services. Critics say those numbers don’t add up and that the government is ignoring the economic contributions and benefits they bring to Alberta.

The specific effect of a yes vote is unclear, since the government says it won’t define “Alberta-approved immigration status” until after the referendum.

Question 3: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially funded social support programs?

What you need to know: The government says it won’t determine which programs would be affected until after the referendum, should Albertans vote yes.

Temporary workers are already ineligible for some provincial programs, such as Assured Income for the Severely Handicapped, and the Canadian Bar Association’s provincial chapter says this could run afoul of the Canada Health Act or the Charter’s equality provisions.

Question 4: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for public health care and education as they do now, do you support the government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family’s use of the health care and education systems?

What you need to know: A potential new charge wouldn’t be determined by the government until after the vote, though the premier told Calgary business leaders on Sept. 22 that a health premium could be as much as $1,900.

Education leaders in the province have come out against restricting access to schooling, saying it goes against internationally agreed children’s rights.

Question 5: Do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate, or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election?

What you need to know: Voting is already restricted to Canadian citizens, and both Elections Canada and Elections Alberta have reported very few cases of ineligible voting.

Smith has said it’s about strengthening the integrity of provincial elections. Critics say this policy would only make lineups at the polls more time-consuming and open the door to racial or ethnic bias at the voting booth.

Question 6: Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King’s Bench and Appeal courts?

What you need to know: If approved by voters, this proposal would only commit Alberta’s government to working with other provinces and federal lawmakers to make changes to the Constitution.

Changes generally need approval from seven provincial legislatures covering 50 per cent of Canada’s population, as well as from the House of Commons and Senate in Ottawa.

Question 7: Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?

What you need to know: Abolishing the Senate would be even more difficult than other general constitutional amendments. It would need to be unanimously approved by all provinces and ratified by the Senate and the House of Commons.

Question 8: Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs?

What you need to know: The federal “spending power” authority allows Ottawa to attach conditions to its funding for provinces, with health-care funding under the Canada Health Act as a key example.

A permanent provincial “opt-out” clause would require the Constitution to be amended.

Question 9: Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province’s laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province’s laws and federal laws conflict?

What you need to know: Under the Constitution, federal laws are given standing over provincial laws when jurisdictional issues arise.

This change to the Constitution would require approval from the Senate, the House of Commons and seven provinces representing at least half the country’s population.

Question 10: Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?

What you need to know: Advocates for separation say the province needs to get out from under federal taxation and regulation, freeing up wealth and sparking economic development. Federalists say the split would only hurt businesses and saddle landlocked Alberta with debt and the massive cost of delivering formerly federal services.

Smith has framed her other nine other questions on immigration and constitutional reform as a political compromise that could address Alberta’s grievances, gain leverage with Ottawa and avoid dismantling the country.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 17, 2026.

stories.title: What Albertans need to know about voting in the referendum
stories.summary: Edmonton - Referendum day in Alberta is on Monday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Referendum day in Alberta is on Monday.

The provincial referendum has 10 questions about immigration policy, constitutional reform, and whether Alberta should remain in Canada or hold a binding, second referendum on quitting the country.

Advance voting locations opened Tuesday and close Saturday night.

Over 1,400 polling stations will be open Monday from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Here’s what to expect when you go to vote:

How long will it take?

Get familiar with the ballot questions ahead of time, which are on the Elections Alberta website. Officials say it will help avoid confusion and delays.

They say they’re expecting a record turnout of between 80 and 85 per cent of Alberta’s nearly three million electors.

You have as much time as you want to fill in the 10 ballots, but officials estimate it will take most people about two minutes.

What identification is needed?

You should get a “where to vote” card in the mail ahead of time if you’re registered. Otherwise, visit Elections Alberta’s website to find out where to vote.

You must vote in your electoral division during advance voting or at your assigned location on Monday.

You’ll need one government-issued ID with your correct name, current address and photo, such as a driver’s licence. You can use two pieces of ID that both have your full name, with one showing your current address.

There are 50 forms of acceptable ID listed on Elections Alberta’s website that can be one of those two pieces, from a library card or a hunting licence to a bank statement or vehicle registration.

Elections Alberta says it will accept expired forms of ID, including a certificate of Indian Status Card, provided it still has the correct name.

Another option, in special circumstances, is to bring an attestation form signed by an authorized person such as a First Nation band manager or a student housing staffer.

What if I’m not registered to vote?

A voting officer will ask you to sign a declaration that confirms your eligibility — including that you are a Canadian citizen, at least 18 years old and that you normally reside in Alberta.

How many ballots are there?

There are 10 ballots, in different colours for easy identification. You can mark some of them, all of them or none. Your choice.

The ballots go into separate boxes to make it easier to count them and to lessen the chances of a mistake spoiling one long ballot.

What if I’m still in line when the polls close at 8 p.m.?

Stay in line. Don’t leave. You will be allowed to vote.

How long before I know the results?

By law, the votes need to be counted by hand within 48 hours.

Question 10 — about separation — is to be counted first. Officials say early results are to be released after 8 p.m. Monday, with the final count announced in the early hours Tuesday.

The results of the other nine questions should be completed and announced by Wednesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 17, 2026.

stories.title: How Canadian artists are reimagining the age-old quilt
stories.summary: As all things analog exert a pull, quilts are emerging as statement pieces in the design world
stories.author: Alexandra Petros
stories.content:
Homespun interiors are having a moment.

As digital innovations such as artificial intelligence evolve, the desire for design that tells a story – one that’s personal, memorable and most importantly, uniquely human – is growing.

Interior designers and local makers are seeing an increased demand for warmer, more tactile spaces . Once mainly considered family heirlooms, quilts are emerging as statement pieces, with today’s artisans bringing a contemporary approach to the age-old craft.

As all things analog continue to exert a pull, Canadian creatives are reinventing the quilt with fresh techniques, styles and customizations.

The charm of a quilt often lies in its originality and the sentimental connection to the person who made it.

“We want to see the artist’s hand when we look at a piece,” said Clare Forndran, principal and co-founder of Toronto design firm Forward Interiors. “We want to know who they are, what inspires them, where they learnt their craft.” It’s all part of the story we want our homes to tell, she added.

Beyond adding visual interest to a space, quilts can foster a sense of community with local artists.

Forndran said handmade qualities can fit within any design aesthetic – it’s just about selecting the right pieces. For example, a wholecloth quilt, where the top layer is made from a solid piece of fabric rather than a patchwork design, would suit a modern, minimalist space.

For a recent project at a Muskoka cottage, the Forward Interiors team incorporated quilt bedspreads throughout the home. Toronto-based textile artist Shayla Bond, founder of Esbe Studio, handcrafted the pieces. She also created custom product tags for the quilts, featuring the name of the cottage and an illustration of a type of bear local to the area.

Bond, who creates luxury quilts and textile art, aims to bridge traditional and contemporary approaches to making.

“I want my work to balance feeling familiar and refreshing,” she said. “I think designers and clients are looking for that, too. Not overly nostalgic, but also not disconnected from tradition.”

Bond preserves the familiar language of quilting through traditional blocks and construction methods, while shifting scale, spacing, colour and placement to reduce visual density. The resulting pieces have more breathing room, with negative space and unexpected compositions.

Clients often seek modern interpretations of heirlooms, Bond explained. Bond is currently seeing a growing interest in linen, burgundy tones and mid-century modern aesthetics, alongside checkered patterns, stripes and customizations.

“This has been a standout year in terms of bespoke work,” she said. “Homeowners and interior designers are looking for quilts that are specifically made for a room, a person or a particular story.

Marilyn Armand, founder of quilting studio Le Point Visible in Stanbridge East, Que., is noticing a similar trend. She said she’s having a record year, with commissions already scheduled through next spring.

“People are wanting something meaningful, beautiful, warm and welcoming,” said Armand, who works primarily with reclaimed textiles. “Quilts carry this power.” Graphic compositions, clean lines and a restrained aesthetic characterize her pieces.

Armand learned traditional quilting in 2017 through a women’s knowledge-sharing circle based in Longueuil, Que., called Les Cercles de Fermières du Québec. At the time, she was working in administration while completing her master’s degree in international relations. The next year, Armand changed course, quitting her job and launching her studio, eventually opening a storefront in 2024.

One of her recent pieces, Dear John , a quilt mural created in collaboration with a client to honour her late father, exemplifies Armand’s approach. Inspired by the connection that the client’s father had to aviation, she incorporated the curves of aircraft turbines. A classical music concert he attended at a landmark venue inspired another set of architectural lines. Using the father’s old shirts and a colour palette chosen by the client, Armand created a piece that transformed memories and materials into a new visual language.

On the east coast, Halifax-based quilt artist and founder of 3rd Story Workshop, Andrea Tsang Jackson, takes a more structural approach.

With a background in architecture, Tsang Jackson shapes her practice around geometry, repetition and the relationship between textiles and the built environment. In a recent quilt, Ginkgo , Tsang Jackson used one of her signature techniques called “ordered improvisational piecing,” where each curve is uniquely cut and organized in a rectangular grid.

“After years of very minimal interiors, those spaces are starting to feel stale because we’re craving connection and less neutrality,” she said. “People want more character, dimension and tactility, especially now that we’re so inundated with screens that flatten everything.”

As a new generation of quilters brings their perspectives and experiences to the medium, their one-of-a-kind pieces offer something increasingly sought-after in interiors: a human touch, a symbol of when life moved more slowly.

As Bond put it, “Quilts are comforting and, in a way, an icon of a simpler time.”

“After years of very minimal interiors, those spaces are starting to feel stale because we’re craving connection and less neutrality,” she said. “People want more character, dimension and tactility, especially now that we’re so inundated with screens that flatten everything.”
