stories.title: 'Now is not a time to tremble': Casey Babb's Moral Case for Zionism
stories.summary: His new book argues Zionism is not the colonialist caricature commonly presented by its critics, but a Jewish national-liberation movement.
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
At a time when “Zionist” has become, for many, an accusation, Casey Babb’s new book, The Moral Case for Zionism, attempts to reclaim Zionism as a powerful and rational idea — one rooted, he argues, in Jewish peoplehood, historical continuity, national self-determination, cultural revival and democratic aspiration.

Babb, director of the Promised Land Project at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute in Ottawa, contends Zionism is not the caricature commonly presented by its critics: neither colonialism nor racism, but a Jewish national-liberation movement rooted in a long historical relationship with the land of Israel.

Further, Babb suggests, the spirit of Zionism – the ethos of early Zionist thinkers – remains very much alive, and applicable today, for both Jews and non-Jews alike.

The book, coming from Wicked Son publishers on Oct. 22, is needed because the argument over Zionism has become emotionally charged, morally reductive, and often detached from history, he says. Babb seeks to arm readers — Jewish or not — with language, context and confidence: to distinguish criticism of Israeli governments from the repudiation of Jewish collective rights, to confront antisemitism expressed through anti-Zionist terms, and to recover an idea he believes has been deliberately distorted with the express purpose of destroying the Jewish story.

Babb is also an international fellow at Tel Aviv’s Institute for National Security Studies, and an associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London. His research has appeared in peer-reviewed publications in Canada, the United States, Europe and the Middle East. He holds a BA in political science and international development from Saint Mary’s University, an MA in international relations from York University, and a PhD in international relations from Carleton University.

This interview was edited for brevity.

What was the impetus to write the book?

I had, like many people, over time, and especially following October 7, become increasingly alarmed by the rise of anti-Zionism and the normalization of anti-Zionist rhetoric. I felt like if I wrote a book just on anti-Zionism, I might be putting the cart before the horse, because if you’re going to talk about anti-Zionism, in my view, you first have to talk about Zionism, what it really means, what it represents, and what it has achieved and continues to achieve for the Jewish people. I feel like yes, we have to defeat anti-Zionism, but Zionism itself is also worth saving.

Your book draws on decades of scholarship about antisemitism, Zionism, and related ideas, yet you’ve chosen a personal voice. What was behind that decision?

When I set out on this path a few years ago, it became clear to me rather quickly that there was decades worth of literature, thought, and material that needed to be taken into account. At the same time, I wanted this book to be accessible to everybody. I didn’t want it to be some highbrow book that people in the back of coffee shops are reading, only to be understood by a select few.

For me, it was about taking an expansive body of literature and contemplation, and distilling it down into something I hope is quite easily understood for the masses. It’s a bit challenging. But I tried to limit, to a certain extent, some of the intellectual details and historical debates on the topic that, in my opinion, would probably do the community a disservice right now. I wanted something that people could read and support, and which would leave them feeling good, and perhaps, a bit more confident about Zionism, and their place in the Zionist story.

Amongst your research, throughout the writing, what one particular thing was revelatory to you?

Israel is the most powerful unifying force in the history of the Jewish world. It is the force, vis-à-vis Zionism, that has taken the Jewish world from the private into the public. In other words, it is Israel which led Jews out the synagogue, the living, and the shtetl, into the light of public living. Prior to the reestablishment of the state of Israel in 1948, Jewish life was largely a private matter, and it no longer is. And that’s why an Orthodox rabbi in Crown Heights can relate with a secular Jewish kid in Fredericton, because it is highly likely that a part of their Judaism is woven into the Zionist spirit. Indeed, it’s probably the only thing uniting them on such a deep level.

That hadn’t really been so clear to me prior to writing this book. Similarly, I realized the true existential dangers of anti-Zionism and the underlying objective of anti-Zionists. I argue in the book, their aim is to ultimately destroy the Jewish story, the Jewish spirit and, in the end, the Jewish people.

Towards the end of the book, you have recommendations, actionables.

No part of this book is me pontificating about Zionism or how to live a Jewish life or a Zionist life. In fact, as I mention in the book, the recommendations I make in the book are for me, too.

That said, one of the ideas I raise is to remember that the Jewish people and our allies have never been stronger, never in history, and that now is not a time to tremble. There’s a distinction between fear that sharpens your attention, which I think is what we need now, and fear that paralyzes action, and the second kind is the enemy of Jewish life in virtually every era.

There’s no need for us to retreat inwards. We need to really remember who we are, embrace our story, and all that comes with it, and muster up a new level of chutzpah and courage, because that’s what it’s going to take to get through this. We cannot allow ourselves to fall victim to the gaslighting and the moral inversion that has characterized not just Jewish life, but most of our society the last number of years.

People need to know who they are, know the story that they’re part of, and know that they aren’t alone. Another thing, is to do Zionist things. Help people in your community. Start living a more Zionist life. There’s a temptation to orient ideas and day-to-day living around opposition and defensiveness. I understand that, but we can’t allow that to shape who we become. That’s no way to live. We have to say yes to things like Shabbat. We have to say yes to the Hebrew language. We have to say yes to Israeli culture, have the full fullest expression of what living a Zionist life actually means – a genuine abundance of meaning, of connection, of beauty, of purpose, of pride, and of exhilaration.

How is your book different from Alan Dershowitz’s “The Case for Israel”?

OK, so that was published 25 years ago and much has changed since then. Too much. Dershowitz’s is principally a prosecutorial defence of Israel against historical, legal, and political accusations. It is legalistic and forensic.

I make a more affirmative moral, historical, and civilizational argument for Zionism itself. I speak of dignity, belonging, return, liberation, tikkun olam, democratic pluralism, Jewish historical continuity. He speaks of legal context, double standards, anti-Israel demonization. I’m not refuting charges against Israel; I’m building a case for Zionism as a morally serious, positive ideal – one of the most morally inspiring stories and ideas in all of history.

I think there’s a lot to be said about keeping Zionism alive and modernizing it and renewing it. If Dershowitz’s book asks, “Why is Israel not what its detractors say it is?” mine asks, “What valuable moral ideas are its detractors failing to see?”

In other words, it is Israel which led Jews out the synagogue, the living, and the shtetl, into the light of public living. Prior to the reestablishment of the state of Israel in 1948, Jewish life was largely a private matter, and it no longer is. And that’s why an Orthodox rabbi in Crown Heights can relate with a secular Jewish kid in Fredericton, because it is highly likely that a part of their Judaism is woven into the Zionist spirit. Indeed, it’s probably the only thing uniting them on such a deep level.

That hadn’t really been so clear to me prior to writing this book. Similarly, I realized the true existential dangers of anti-Zionism and the underlying objective of anti-Zionists. I argue in the book, their aim is to ultimately destroy the Jewish story, the Jewish spirit and, in the end, the Jewish people.
Towards the end of the book, you have recommendations, actionables.
content_blocks.html: Towards the end of the book, you have recommendations, actionables.

content_blocks.text: No part of this book is me pontificating about Zionism or how to live a Jewish life or a Zionist life. In fact, as I mention in the book, the recommendations I make in the book are for me, too.

That said, one of the ideas I raise is to remember that the Jewish people and our allies have never been stronger, never in history, and that now is not a time to tremble. There’s a distinction between fear that sharpens your attention, which I think is what we need now, and fear that paralyzes action, and the second kind is the enemy of Jewish life in virtually every era.

There’s no need for us to retreat inwards. We need to really remember who we are, embrace our story, and all that comes with it, and muster up a new level of chutzpah and courage, because that’s what it’s going to take to get through this. We cannot allow ourselves to fall victim to the gaslighting and the moral inversion that has characterized not just Jewish life, but most of our society the last number of years.

People need to know who they are, know the story that they’re part of, and know that they aren’t alone. Another thing, is to do Zionist things. Help people in your community. Start living a more Zionist life. There’s a temptation to orient ideas and day-to-day living around opposition and defensiveness. I understand that, but we can’t allow that to shape who we become. That’s no way to live. We have to say yes to things like Shabbat. We have to say yes to the Hebrew language. We have to say yes to Israeli culture, have the full fullest expression of what living a Zionist life actually means – a genuine abundance of meaning, of connection, of beauty, of purpose, of pride, and of exhilaration.

content_blocks.text: How is your book different from Alan Dershowitz’s “The Case for Israel”?
content_blocks.html: How is your book different from Alan Dershowitz’s “The Case for Israel”?

content_blocks.text: OK, so that was published 25 years ago and much has changed since then. Too much. Dershowitz’s is principally a prosecutorial defence of Israel against historical, legal, and political accusations. It is legalistic and forensic.

I make a more affirmative moral, historical, and civilizational argument for Zionism itself. I speak of dignity, belonging, return, liberation, tikkun olam, democratic pluralism, Jewish historical continuity. He speaks of legal context, double standards, anti-Israel demonization. I’m not refuting charges against Israel; I’m building a case for Zionism as a morally serious, positive ideal – one of the most morally inspiring stories and ideas in all of history.

I think there’s a lot to be said about keeping Zionism alive and modernizing it and renewing it. If Dershowitz’s book asks, “Why is Israel not what its detractors say it is?” mine asks, “What valuable moral ideas are its detractors failing to see?”

stories.title: Toronto’s Studio La Beauté custom textile work stands out in a sea of mass-produced decor
stories.summary: Most of Studio La Beauté’s commissions require hours of labour
stories.author: Gayle MacDonald
stories.content:
Most of us give little thought to where our window coverings come from. We choose curtains from an online catalogue or machine-made panels from a retailer, looking for something attractive, affordable and readily available.

At Studio La Beauté in Toronto, curtains are made very differently.

In the middle of the workshop are two large sewing tables, surrounded by bolts of fabric, spools of thread and drawers overflowing with samples. Tassels, appliqués, ribbons, beads and bits of embroidery are everywhere.

Here, curtains are couture: Sketches are drawn, pleats are measured, rosettes are shaped by hand and linings are handstitched into place.

Presiding over it all is Camal Pirbhai, the studio’s owner and creative director, who trained in bespoke curtain making in Europe more than three decades ago. Alongside him are four women, ranging in age from 23 to 63, whose skills include beadwork, patchwork, painting on silk and padded stitching, called trapunto, a traditional Italian quilting technique dating back to the 13 th century.

Together, they make curtains, cushions, blankets, bespoke chandeliers (one is made of thousands of pieces of chartreuse string), headboards, chair backs and wall coverings.

“I like to think that our work bridges artistry and craftsmanship,” says Pirbhai, a multidisciplinary artist whose work with artist Camille Turner has been exhibited internationally and at the Art Gallery of Ontario.

The kind of work he and his small team do is also increasingly rare.

Pirbhai says the knowledge required to make such beautiful things is disappearing, overtaken by machine-made mass production and a culture used to getting things quickly and cheaply.

Interior designers, too, bear some responsibility, he says. They May spend hours selecting an expensive fabric, then give little thought to how it is cut, stitched, pleated and hung.

“The last decade I’ve been pounding the table, saying to designers, ‘Please don’t just mail it in. Let’s have a little discussion.’

“What disappears when a craft dies is not simply a way of making an object, but the knowledge accumulated and passed from one pair of hands to another.”

For centuries, textiles for the home were both necessities and creative expressions. Before mechanized production, curtains, cushions, quilts and tapestries were cut, sewn and embellished by hand, using skills passed between generations and across cultures. Beautifully made curtains, for example, would often remain in a family home for decades.

Today, computer-aided machines can reproduce elaborate patterns and embroidery quickly and inexpensively, while many consumers furnish homes with affordable pieces they don’t expect to keep for a lifetime.

Most of Studio La Beauté’s commissions require hours of labour. Pirbhai designs the hardware, too, commissioning carpenters, metalworkers and glass blowers to fabricate rods, brackets and finials.

His career began at 19. After leaving a fine-arts program in Toronto, Pirbhai moved to London, England, where he apprenticed with a custom curtain maker. Soon after, he returned home, where there was a scarcity of bespoke curtain makers.

He built Studio La Beauté slowly, through word of mouth. Today his soft furnishings can be found in the homes of Toronto’s toniest neighbourhoods, as well as in New York, London and Europe.

Toronto interior designer Colette van den Thillart, who discovered Pirbhai during COVID-19, understands his frustration.

She spent 13 years working in Britain with celebrity designer Nicky Haslam and holds a master’s degree in decorative arts. History informs her interiors, and she sees curtains as part of the architecture and narrative of a room, not simply a covering for a window.

“There really aren’t a lot of people who do what he does in North America,” she says. “There also just isn’t the demand for this any more, except from a few of us.”

Van den Thillart believes a culture focused on convenience and resale has contributed to the lack of interest. Realtors advise homeowners not to personalize too much, she says. “Everywhere people are living their lives in these boxes, painted white with furniture from Restoration Hardware, designed for resale,” she says. “I find it utterly depressing.”

For the past six years she has been bringing much of her custom drapery work to Studio La Beauté, spending hours at the work tables with Pirbhai and his team, exchanging ideas.

“Curtain making is like dressmaking,” she says. “You can think it’s just a curtain, or it’s just a blazer. If that’s the case, why do they have Savile Row? It’s the way you cut, how you hem, how you do the beautiful edge details.”

A current commission makes her point.

For a client’s country house in Ireland, van den Thillart and Pirbhai are creating a café curtain for a bathroom overlooking the garden. It could easily have been ordered online. Instead, it will be hand-stitched with wildflowers, a reflection of the ones the homeowner can see outside her window.

“When she sits in her tub, I want her to have a Proustian moment,” van den Thillart says. “The café curtain is going to look like a specimen vase of what she loves most growing on her property.”

The survival of such carefully considered work depends on finding new artisans to carry it forward, van den Thillart says.

Memengwaans Isaac-Sands, 31, has worked at Studio La Beauté for a decade. She studied visual and creative arts at Sheridan College and fashion at George Brown College before hearing about a curtain maker named Camal who valued a skill she had grown up with. Isaac-Sands is Ojibwa, and beadwork has been passed down through generations of her family.

“It was just something I knew how to do,” she says. “It wasn’t until I started studying and working in the city that I realized how rare it is. It means so much that the work I do here is valued.”

Ultimately, that is what Pirbhai is asking for, too. Not a return to a world in which every curtain is sewn by hand, but an appreciation of what is lost when speed, price and convenience become the primary measures of value.

There is an appetite among discerning customers for things made by human beings, with the tiny irregularities that go along with them.

Pirbhai says a machine can reproduce a pattern faster and more precisely. “What it can’t do is possess the accumulated knowledge and judgment of a craftsperson who knows, through doing, how a fabric should fall, where a stitch should sit, when an embellishment is enough and when it is too much.

“That knowledge survives only when it is used,” he says. “Someone has to teach it. Someone has to learn it. And someone has to believe the difference is worth paying for.”

stories.title: iGaming didn’t ‘keep Ontarians safe’ – not by a long shot
stories.summary: Skyrocketing use by students and record visits to emergency departments have brought light to the failure to regulate a destructive industry
stories.author: Darragh McGee
stories.content:
Darragh McGee is the author of Imitation Games: How Gambling Hijacked Sports.

It is grimly ironic to think that it all began with “tech issues,” via a choppy live stream, ON that “monumental” Monday of April 4, 2022, when Canada’s gambling establishment triumphantly gathered at the Toronto Stock Exchange to launch Ontario as the first province to permit a regulated online gambling market – or “iGaming” as they rebranded it.

True to form, the industry pitch was absurdly upbeat: iGaming Ontario would “encourage competition while incentivizing capital investment, job creation, and economic growth.” Paradoxically, for an extractive business model that only profits when people lose, all of this would be achieved while “protecting consumers and keeping Ontarians safe.” To that end, there was an earnest pledge to uphold “rigorous standards of game integrity, fairness, player protections and social responsibility,” with “controls preventing underage access and measures to enable more responsible gambling.”

Then the market launch buzzer sounded, confetti streamed down, and the cutthroat realities of recruiting and retaining bettors in an increasingly crowded, tech-fuelled marketplace instantly kicked in.

What happened next depends on who you ask. Industry-friendly business pages proudly hail Ontario as the single most competitive gambling market in North America – by which they mean that it has the highest concentration of private companies, with 49 licensed brands operating 84 online platforms today. Record-breaking revenues also dominate headlines, including news of $4-billion yearly revenue in 2025, a 34-per-cent increase on 2024 alone. Overall, the $10-billion barrier has already been broken since April, 2022. The tax yield during that same period exceeds $2-billion. On that front, the origin pledge of free-flowing capital and jobs has been delivered on, and then some.

Yet as Ontarians are learning amid a wave of new research published on the once-hidden human costs behind this relentless growth trajectory, it is unwise to trust the platitudes and pledges of a provincial government or a sporting fraternity in partnership with a known addictive industry that causes life-altering harm on a societal scale. That essential conflict of interest makes a mockery of empty pledges to “keep Ontarians safe.” In reality, the promised guardrails don’t even protect the province’s children and teenagers.

The findings from the latest Ontario Student Drug Use and Health Survey, published by Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, lay this bare. In a sample of 11,000 students enrolled in Grades 7 to 12 across the province, more than 80 per cent reported having seen or heard an online gambling advert in the past month. Roughly a quarter reported exposure daily. None of those surveyed were legally entitled to bet.

Not coincidentally, a quarter also admitted spending five or more hours a day on social-media platforms, which not only account for an ever-increasing share of overall gambling marketing spend, but house some of the industry’s invasive forms of digital surveillance and behavioural targeting too. Data are the primary asset of virtually every online business model today, and gambling brands are leading the way. Algorithms track our every move online and aggregate vast troves of granular data that can be used to profile our behavioural attributes and even target our vulnerabilities . Propensity to gamble and susceptibility to marketing are but two of the attributes that feed into customer profiles that can be used to profitable effect.

Concerningly, the behavioural effects of exposure to marketing are already evidenced among students, 12 per cent of whom reported gambling online – a 50-per-cent jump in two years – with boys significantly more likely to participate, and sports betting increasing twofold between Grade 7 and 12.

A related survey from the Chartered Professional Accountants of Canada, published in June, also found that 50 per cent of 18- to 34-year-olds participated in some form of online gambling over the past year, with more than one-third (37 per cent) indicating that marketing influenced them to place a wager.

And wager they have, to the tune of $82.7-billion in 2024-25, a 31-per-cent annual increase that is on course to be shattered again this year. The Fifa World Cup alone sparked a $1-billion bumper yield from sports betting in June, 2026, including legions of first-time casual bettors who downloaded apps, linked their bank account, and consented to the dark nudges of a digital architecture that is not only designed to convert sports fans into gamblers, but to cross-sell them even more ruinously addictive casino products. This is one of the uncomfortable truths that lurk beneath the clean-cut veneer of sports gambling today: It is but the recruitment ground and the gateway to the viciously predictable outcomes of the online casino.

Let that sink in: An entire new generation of smartphone-savvy Ontarians are never more than a few clicks away from activating a casino slot machine in their pockets. For the record, such cross-selling feeds into an online casino market that topped $8-billion in June – eight times that of the World Cup betting fever .

If none of this previously induced concern, it’s not altogether surprising. Whether we know it or not, many of us have been subconsciously conditioned to accept “iGaming” as a mainstream entertainment sector, a legitimate part of sport media and fandom, and therefore a normalized feature of modern society. We’ve also been schooled to accept industry manufactured labels like “responsible gambling” and “problem gambling,” both of which act as a smokescreen, individualizing harm and addiction at every turn, diverting the gaze of governments and policy makers away from the promotional culture, product design and business practices of the gambling industry. In Ontario, as elsewhere, that has too often led to public-health harms being narrowly attributed to flawed psychology, individual deviance, or irresponsibility.

An urgent reckoning with such harms must be a priority for Ontarians going forward. After all, evidence of “clinically significant harms” is corroborated by a series of studies by researchers at the University of Toronto, including findings published by the Canadian Medical Association Journal of a “substantial increase” in gambling-related calls to ConnexOntario, the province’s mental health and addictions helpline, since April, 2022. Most concerningly, they reported that helpline contacts skyrocketed by 317 per cent among boys and men aged 15 to 24.

Allied to this was a study published last month that reported a 154-per-cent increase in gambling-related visits to emergency rooms by boys and men aged 10 to 29 across Ontario during the same period. The authors not only flagged the comorbidity of mental health conditions, including depression, alcohol use or self-harm among those affected, but found they were more likely to live in the lowest-income neighbourhoods.

A landmark report by the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction also found that 69.4 per cent of young adults aged 18 to 29 who gambled online met the criteria for harmful gambling, with a quarter reporting serious harm such as income loss, debt and relationship conflict. Compared to lottery products, online gambling was 45 times more likely to lead to harm.

No doubt many reading this will have their own anecdotal tales of affected family members, friends or colleagues who opted to conceal their harm, suffering in silence and internalizing the stigma that still shrouds gambling, which was only formally ratified as the first behavioural addiction in 2014. Still, today, reliable statistics on the true prevalence of gambling harm remain elusive to all but the private limited companies who sit atop a mountain of granular propriety data that could be used by clinicians and researchers to pinpoint where harm is most concentrated and guide intervention when certain patterns are identified.

This is the elephant in the room when it comes to preventing the dangers posed by the digital rebirth of gambling, the complicity of professional sports and the conveyor belt of high-octane products that are subject to no independent safety assessment as a condition of licensing. It is contingent on ending a partnership model which renders the provincial government dependent on industry revenue streams and thereby disincentivized to put public health before profit margins.

Achieving that is no small feat, but Ontarians are not alone. Across the Atlantic in Europe – and south of the Canadian border – the movement for gambling reform is increasingly nested in a wider political and legal concern with online safety, surveillance capitalism and digital consent processes. As with the backlash against Big Tech and social-media platforms – many of which have been ruled as “harmful and defective” – a robust legal reckoning May be the principal mechanism of holding sport, government and their gambling partners to account.

Until then, there is no silver bullet for the risk-filled predicament which Ontarians find themselves in, but at least the unsustainably short-sighted, greed-ridden nature of the economic model underpinning it is being exposed for what it is. Just short of five years in, however, it’s difficult not to wager on the quantum of harm escalating still further before public consciousness reaches a critical tipping point. Lives as much as livelihoods, we now know, are on the line.

stories.title: The separatists who helped bring Danielle Smith to power are trying to unseat her
stories.summary: Alberta’s Premier paved the way for Albertans to make themselves heard on secession, but her federalist position has alienated key political allies
stories.author: Carrie Tait
stories.content:
Mitch Sylvestre didn’t see it coming.

Premier Danielle Smith , in a television address in May, promised to put the question of Alberta separation to a provincial vote. But first, she declared herself a federalist.

Up until then, Mr. Sylvestre believed the leader of Canada’s most prosperous province would stay neutral on whether Alberta should divorce itself from the rest of the country. Before secession was even on the ballot, Mr. Sylvestre had asked Ms. Smith about her plans for the aftermath.

“I have said to her multiple, multiple times: ‘Premier, will you lead the new country if we win this referendum?’” Mr. Sylvestre recounted over breakfast at a Smitty’s restaurant this summer.

“She said: ‘I don’t want to David Cameron myself by committing.’”

Alberta’s referendum on Monday includes 10 questions, but the one drawing comparisons to Brexit asks voters if they want to remain in Canada or start the process to hold a binding referendum on separation. In Britain, Mr. Cameron resigned a prime minister in July, 2016, after voters opted to leave the European Union, rejecting his remain campaign.

“She told me that three times,” Mr. Sylvestre said. “She doesn’t want to have to take a side and then resign.”

Prior to the announcement, Ms. Smith had taken significant steps to ease the separatists’ path, including changing provincial legislation. So Mr. Sylvestre, a United Conservative Party constituency president who was once Ms. Smith’s most reliable hype man, is stumped.

Alberta’s most prominent separatist just can’t figure out why the Premier would risk her job by siding with the federalists.

“It’s like running back into a burning house to get pictures,” Mr. Sylvestre said.

Like Mr. Cameron’s Brexit, Ms. Smith’s referendum is a gamble. But for her, it could be a Catch-22.

If voters opt to stay in Canada, as Ms. Smith has advocated and as polls predict, the result would likely inflame the now-powerful separatist bloc within her party already calling for her removal. If the secessionists win, there would likely be immediate calls for her resignation, given her opposition to them.

The same conservative activists who were angry at government restrictions during the COVID-19 pandemic and worked to depose her predecessor Jason Kenney elevated her as the Ucp’s leader.

Now, the faithful who helped her become Premier are trying to unseat her.

Two years ago, Ms. Smith was at the height of her power.

Roughly 6,000 party members gathered in Red Deer at the Ucp’s annual general meeting to vote on dozens of policy proposals, none of which referenced Alberta independence.

And in her first leadership review, Ms. Smith won support from 91 per cent of the 4,633 members who voted.

“Our party is more united than it has ever been,” she told the crowd in November, 2024.

Talk of Alberta secession ignited four months later, kicking off a delicate dance to maintain party unity.

The first notable public murmurs came from Jeff Rath, a lawyer allied with Mr. Sylvestre and other conservative activists. He said he and other activists were planning a trip to Washington to seek U.S. statehood.

His comments gained little traction in the mainstream in Alberta, let alone the rest of the country.

However, Ms. Smith amplified separatist sentiments a couple of weeks later, in the days between Mark Carney being sworn in as Prime Minister and calling a snap election.

“I provided a specific list of demands the next Prime Minister, regardless of who that is, must address within the first six months of their term to avoid an unprecedented national unity crisis,” she warned, referring to Ottawa’s energy regulations, in a government press release after she met Mr. Carney on March 20, 2025.

The day after Mr. Carney won the federal election last April, Ms. Smith announced a change that would give the secessionist movement a boost. She would lower the number of petition signatures required to force the legislature to consider putting proposed constitutional questions to a province-wide vote.

The changes kicked in July 4, 2025. That morning, Mr. Sylvestre, Mr. Rath and Dennis Modry applied to Elections Alberta to launch a citizen-led petition demanding the government call a referendum asking whether Alberta should become a “Sovereign Country and cease to be a province in Canada.”

Alberta’s chief electoral officer asked the court to determine whether the Alberta Prosperity Project’s proposed question contravened the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms or treaty rights, putting a pause on signature collection.

With the separatist effort on hold, Ms. Smith signed a deal for a proposed pipeline with Mr. Carney last November. She held that agreement up as proof Canada could work.

A few days later, Ms. Smith was met with resistance at her party’s annual general meeting in Edmonton.

UCP members booed when she mentioned the deal with Ottawa and again when she said she supported a sovereign Alberta within a united Canada. Mr. Rath, ON the other hand, received a standing ovation from the packed crowd when he asked who supported independence.

Days later, Ms. Smith’s government again made legislative changes to clear the way for the separatists.

On Dec. 4, 2025, her government tabled amendments that would end the petition court case and, separately, permit citizen-led referendum questions regardless of their constitutionality.

“The legal consequence of discontinuing this proceeding prior to a decision would be to silence the Court,” Justice Colin Feasby wrote the next day, in a document explaining his decision to rule the Alberta Prosperity Project’s proposed question offside. “Legislating an end to litigation is extraordinary.”

Shortly after that, Mr. Sylvestre and Mr. Rath filed fresh paperwork with Elections Alberta in pursuit of a secession vote.

On May 4, Mr. Sylvestre delivered 300,000 signatures to the legislature. The following week, a judge struck down the petition, concluding First Nations must be consulted first.

But on May 21, flanked by the flags of Canada and Alberta, Ms. Smith said her government would put a question about separation on the Oct. 19 referendum ballot.

The Premier has stayed on the side of federalism in the lead-up to the vote.

“Our government, party, and caucus support Alberta remaining in Canada,” Ryan Fournier, a spokesman for the Premier, said in a statement. He said the province has “welcomed the change in direction” from the federal government on energy resource development.

Mr. Fournier reiterated Ms. Smith’s position that she advanced the secession question to reflect the will of Albertans who signed Mr. Sylvestre’s separatist petition and those who put their name on a pro-Canada petition.

He did not address questions about challenges to Ms. Smith’s leadership or Mr. Sylvestre’s account of their conversations.

The Premier’s predecessor, Mr. Kenney, who engineered the creation of the UCP through a merger of the Wildrose Party and the Progressive Conservatives in 2017, has spent much of the past year advocating for Alberta to remain in Canada.

He now says the UCP must sweep out the separatists.

“If there are folks who want to advocate for separatism, they have every right as citizens to do so in separatist parties,” he told reporters Friday. “The UCP needs to lay down the law.”

Such housecleaning would be difficult.

Party president Rob Smith said in the spring that he believed most UCP members would vote to leave Canada, and that the party would not take a position on the referendum.

This week, he said there would be no purity test for party members.

“No one will be ‘banned’ or disqualified from membership,” Mr. Smith wrote on social media this week. “Under no circumstances will that happen. No way. Never.”

With Ms. Smith in the federalist camp, the conservative activists who supported her rise are now openly campaigning against her.

“I AM Thankful That @ABDanielleSmith won’t be premier very much longer,” Mr. Rath said on X in response to the Premier’s Thanksgiving message.

At town halls and online seminars, Mr. Sylvestre and his supporters are urging like-minded citizens to buy UCP memberships so they can force a leadership review and install a leader friendlier to their cause.

Thousands of UCP members are expected to attend the party’s annual meeting in Calgary at the end of next month. Ms. Smith’s leadership is not on the agenda, but talk of her future will dominate the weekend.

“I’m not that smart, but it seems to me if she would have stayed neutral, she would have stayed Premier, no matter what, forever,” Mr. Sylvestre said.

With reports from Matthew Scace

stories.title: No early parole for first-degree murder, a crime like no other
stories.summary: A B.C. court ruling that overturns the minimum 25-year wait for parole for first-degree murder cannot be allowed to stand
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
For breathtaking judicial arrogance – not to mention upside-down logic – it would be hard to top the first-degree murder case of Luciano Mariani in British Columbia.

Two judges on the province’s Supreme Court combined to strike down the mandatory penalty of life with no parole for 25 years, and replace it with a chance at early parole after 15 years. Not just for Mr. Mariani – who committed an especially brutal, gut-wrenching murder of his former intimate partner – but retroactively, for the scores of killers who committed a single first-degree murder since Dec. 2, 2011, and for everyone who might henceforth commit a single planned and deliberate killing. The ruling took immediate effect, but its scope is unclear.

All of this is built on the supposed logic that it is unfair to punish those who kill just one person the same way as those who kill more than one. Yet the reason Canada has the same parole rules for multiple killers is that, four years ago, the Supreme Court of Canada disallowed a law that permitted judges to stack up the 25-year ineligibility periods. Some punishments, it said, no matter how deserved, do not comport with Canadian values. Now along comes a judge who says people who kill just one person must therefore be in line for a lighter sentence, yet another example of judicial activism from B.C. courts.

Mr. Mariani used a baseball bat to murder Caroline Bernard, a mother of a four-year-old, for having an abortion without his say-so. His crime needs to be denounced and punished in the strongest terms. But here we come to layers of nonsense.

Long-standing precedent allowed Mr. Mariani’s lawyers to invent a stand-in for their client, to demonstrate the unfairness of a 25-year ineligibility period. They offered an imaginary lawyer who becomes homeless and paranoid and kills. As unfathomable as it seems, Parliament’s chosen punishment for murder could be struck down if shown to be unfair to an imaginary character.

In this case, Justice David Crossin rejected the fictional creation and substituted an actual killer from a separate case – a gang member who May have abetted a killing rather than firing the fatal bullet. (Juries don’t explain their reasons for finding an accused guilty, so Justice Crossin accepted, for the purposes of his hypothetical, that this killer did not fire the bullet.) This man received early release at 17.5 years, under a previous system, ended in 2011 (except for murders committed before that time), that allowed first-degree murderers to apply at the 15-year mark. The judge said the difference between release at 15 years and 25 was grossly disproportionate, and therefore cruel and unusual punishment.

More nonsense. Nowhere does the judge explain what grossly disproportionate means in Canadian law: a punishment that “shocks the conscience” – of regular Canadians, not those on the bench. Does the difference between a 15-year wait to apply for a parole hearing rather than 25 for first-degree murder make Canadians heartsick? It’s true that juries often granted people early release under the old rules. But does it follow logically that the political decision to end early release shocks the Canadian conscience? Not even close.

Nowhere does the judge seriously grapple with Parliament’s role, as the elected representatives of the Canadian people, to set punishment policy, including the determination that abetting be punished as first-degree murder.

And nowhere does the judge appear to understand that murder is unlike any other crime. To say, as Justice Crossin does, that first-degree murder covers a wide range of moral culpability, which has led courts to reject many minimum sentences over the past decade, is to ignore that the deliberate taking of a life is in a moral universe of its own. Parliament has made clear that, in the absence of the death penalty, first-degree murder needs to be denounced and punished in the clearest of terms, albeit within the parameters sensibly set by the country’s highest court.

Compounding the British Columbia court’s manifold failures, when Justice Crossin retired, Justice Robin Baird took over and instead of asking Parliament to repair the law, restored the former system of early release for Mr. Mariani and, retroactively, for all first-degree murderers of one person since late 2011.

British Columbia’s appeal court heard the Mariani case in June. The senior court needs to overturn the ruling, and restore sanity to the punishment of first-degree murder in B.C.

stories.title: Toe to toe with Dolph Lundgren, an unbreakable and far-from-expendable icon
stories.summary: The Rocky IV action veteran gets vulnerable in Dolph: Unbreakable, a new documentary about his life, struggles and career
stories.author: Will Sloan
stories.content:
Anticipation fills the air as we await the arrival of one of those rare stars identifiable just by their first name. He has landed in Toronto for a gruelling schedule of at least 30 interviews, and a publicist remarks that she had seldom received such an overwhelming response to a press release. Who is this icon? Is it Tom? Or Leo? Did Timothée pick our city to kick off his press rounds for Dune: Part Three ?

No, it’s Dolph. Dolph Lundgren, of course – the 68-year-old action veteran best known for playing the fearsome Ivan Drago from 1985’s Rocky IV . In the 1980s, he emerged into a cinematic landscape dominated by heavily accented musclemen: Arnold Schwarzenegger, Sylvester Stallone and Jean-Claude Van Damme among them. Lundgren’s peaks were not as high as theirs, but he has arguably weathered the years more gracefully. If you’re of a certain age, he has likely been with you all your life. Maybe you saw Rocky IV with your dad when you were a kid. Maybe you also just saw him pop up in the Masters of the Universe reboot this summer. How many stars can claim such longevity?

If you tell people you’re going to interview Dolph Lundgren, without exception their eyes light up. How does Lundgren explain the fondness he engenders?

“I guess these action movies we made back in the day, people love them, and there’s a nostalgic element to it,” he says. “And also, they inspire people because everybody has their own kind of hero’s journey. Everybody’s going through those struggles.”

Lundgren is in town to promote Dolph: Unbreakable , a new documentary on his life and career that gives ample attention to his struggles. Begun in 2020, its production was upended by the star’s difficult but ultimately triumphant battle with cancer, which the film documents with candor. Its greatest focus is on the animating trauma of Lundgren’s life: the physical and emotional abuse he endured in Sweden at the hands of his father. For a man who burst into public consciousness as the embodiment of physical perfection, Lundgren has never been afraid to be vulnerable.

“Until I got to terms with my childhood trauma, work was a way to hijack it, to feel better,” he says. “It was, you know, training too much, working too much, drinking a little too much, steroids, the rest of it. [I was] a crazy, kind of shot-out-of-a-cannon guy from Sweden. It was just like I could never relax.

“But now, there’s more of a balance in my life. I can relax, and I can work, and I don’t need to kill myself doing it.”

The Swedish-born Hans Lundgren (he renamed himself “Dolph” for Rocky IV ) was a chemical engineering student, Fulbright Scholar and karate black-belt whose life took an unlikely turn when he became bodyguard for the singer and model Grace Jones. She made him her boyfriend, took him to Studio 54 and brought him to movie sets – including the James Bond film A View to a Kill , in which he played a bit role. To prepare for that film, Lundgren worked with an acting coach, the late Warren Robertson, who unlocked an interest in performance.

“He was very smart, so he saw I had something, some kind of trauma,” Lundgren remembers of Robertson. “He kind of brought it out of me and I got very emotional, and then I did a scene kind of using that emotion. And it always made me feel great afterwards. That’s when I decided to become an actor.”

Dolph: Unbreakable gives admirable attention to how Lundgren and Robertson built the character of Drago into something more than just a body. Sylvester Stallone is on hand for a talking-head interview attesting to the power of Lundgren’s stillness – how, in contrast to the scenery-chewing actors up for the role, Lundgren communicated so much with just his eyes.

With overnight fame came a string of fondly remembered video-store staples: Masters of the Universe (1987), Showdown in Little Tokyo (1991), and Universal Soldier (1992), to name three. It also brought drink, drugs and a lifestyle of hard partying. Marriage and family in the 1990s brought a period of emotional stability, but with his family home in Spain and his career in the U.S., things slowly unravelled through the 2000s. The movies got worse; the drinking returned; the marriage collapsed.

Today, Lundgren attributes many of his wrong turns to the unresolved traumas of his childhood. He first publicly discussed his father at a 2015 TED Talk, portions of which appear in the documentary.

“It was quite hard for me to open up in front of an audience, but it was therapeutic for me as well, and I knew people responded well to it,” he says. “So, I wanted to do it on a bigger stage in the documentary ... but also I think to show other people that it’s okay. You don’t have to keep it in and hold it.”

Lundgren channelled some of these feelings into Creed II (2018), where he reprised Drago as a bitter cast off seeking personal redemption through his son. He gave a nuanced, lived-in performance that surprised many – the kind of acting he says it took him years to grow into.

“I like to study things from the ground up, whether it’s chemical engineering or martial arts. But in acting, I started and within a year I was auditioning for this big movie, Rocky IV . I was sort of focused on one character. That movie was a huge hit, and now I had offers to star in my own movies, but I didn’t really have the technical skill. It took me many, many films to find that.”

He points to his return as Drago as an example of that growth. “Now he’s an older, bitter guy who reminded me of my own dad. A guy who wants to use his son to sort of get back at the world. My brother actually said when he saw the movie that it reminded him of our dad immediately.”

For those who kept up with Lundgren’s direct-to-video work of the past 15-or-so years, he had already been revealing new depths. Both he and Van Damme brought genuine gravitas to John Hyams’ thoughtful, stylish Universal Soldier: Day of Reckoning (2012). More recently, Lundgren has ably directed himself in likeable potboilers such as Castle Falls (2021) and Wanted Man (2024), in which his screen presence has grown affable and textured. In these films and others, he’s has grown older gracefully – partly because, unlike some of his contemporaries, he actually looks his age.

In The Expendables (2010), Lundgren’s portrayal of the gang’s troubled, substance-abusing black sheep is the film’s emotional core. By the fourth instalment (released in 2023), his anguished performance was not entirely acting. The documentary reveals that production of Expend4bles and Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom occurred during the height of Lundgren’s cancer battle, and shows how taxing they were. Was the struggle worth it?

“On the whole, it was good for me to work,” he says. “I think it kept me feeling stronger, more youthful, got my mind off the actual treatments and the cancer. And I enjoyed the Expendables , of course. You know, Sly and Statham and Randy Couture, the rest of them – I could hang out with them a little bit.

“It was a tough experience, but no, I didn’t feel like, ‘Oh, I’m going to sit home and be depressed and work on my will,’ or something.”

Dolph: Unbreakable ends on an upbeat note, with Lundgren now cancer-free, in a new marriage and with an apparent handle on his traumas. Lundgren’s 2015 TED Talk was called “On Healing and Forgiveness,” and I ask him if forgiveness of his father meant reconciliation.

“I forgave him actually pretty early on,” says Lundgren. “I realized he was a troubled guy who had problems in his life, who ended up getting divorced and ended up dying kind of an old, bitter man. I felt really sorry for him. But I never could really talk to him about what happened because he just refused to own up to what he’d done.”

He adds, “But like my therapist said, we’re victims of victims. He was probably beaten a lot. He grew up in the thirties in Sweden when people starved to death. It was a hard time.”

Lundgren’s father died in 2000, living long enough to see his son become internationally famous.

“He was very impressed by the martial arts and also by the movies. I think he had aspirations when he was young to travel, go to America and not to be an engineer… but he didn’t have the will to change his life in that way. So, I kind of did it for him, I think.”

paragraphs: Anticipation fills the air as we await the arrival of one of those rare stars identifiable just by their first name. He has landed in Toronto for a gruelling schedule of at least 30 interviews, and a publicist remarks that she had seldom received such an overwhelming response to a press release. Who is this icon? Is it Tom? Or Leo? Did Timothée pick our city to kick off his press rounds for Dune: Part Three ?

No, it’s Dolph. Dolph Lundgren, of course – the 68-year-old action veteran best known for playing the fearsome Ivan Drago from 1985’s Rocky IV . In the 1980s, he emerged into a cinematic landscape dominated by heavily accented musclemen: Arnold Schwarzenegger, Sylvester Stallone and Jean-Claude Van Damme among them. Lundgren’s peaks were not as high as theirs, but he has arguably weathered the years more gracefully. If you’re of a certain age, he has likely been with you all your life. Maybe you saw Rocky IV with your dad when you were a kid. Maybe you also just saw him pop up in the Masters of the Universe reboot this summer. How many stars can claim such longevity?
If you tell people you’re going to interview Dolph Lundgren, without exception their eyes light up. How does Lundgren explain the fondness he engenders?

“I guess these action movies we made back in the day, people love them, and there’s a nostalgic element to it,” he says. “And also, they inspire people because everybody has their own kind of hero’s journey. Everybody’s going through those struggles.”

Lundgren is in town to promote Dolph: Unbreakable , a new documentary on his life and career that gives ample attention to his struggles. Begun in 2020, its production was upended by the star’s difficult but ultimately triumphant battle with cancer, which the film documents with candor. Its greatest focus is on the animating trauma of Lundgren’s life: the physical and emotional abuse he endured in Sweden at the hands of his father. For a man who burst into public consciousness as the embodiment of physical perfection, Lundgren has never been afraid to be vulnerable.

“Until I got to terms with my childhood trauma, work was a way to hijack it, to feel better,” he says. “It was, you know, training too much, working too much, drinking a little too much, steroids, the rest of it. [I was] a crazy, kind of shot-out-of-a-cannon guy from Sweden. It was just like I could never relax.
“But now, there’s more of a balance in my life. I can relax, and I can work, and I don’t need to kill myself doing it.”

The Swedish-born Hans Lundgren (he renamed himself “Dolph” for Rocky IV ) was a chemical engineering student, Fulbright Scholar and karate black-belt whose life took an unlikely turn when he became bodyguard for the singer and model Grace Jones. She made him her boyfriend, took him to Studio 54 and brought him to movie sets – including the James Bond film A View to a Kill , in which he played a bit role. To prepare for that film, Lundgren worked with an acting coach, the late Warren Robertson, who unlocked an interest in performance.

“He was very smart, so he saw I had something, some kind of trauma,” Lundgren remembers of Robertson. “He kind of brought it out of me and I got very emotional, and then I did a scene kind of using that emotion. And it always made me feel great afterwards. That’s when I decided to become an actor.”

Dolph: Unbreakable gives admirable attention to how Lundgren and Robertson built the character of Drago into something more than just a body. Sylvester Stallone is on hand for a talking-head interview attesting to the power of Lundgren’s stillness – how, in contrast to the scenery-chewing actors up for the role, Lundgren communicated so much with just his eyes.

With overnight fame came a string of fondly remembered video-store staples: Masters of the Universe (1987), Showdown in Little Tokyo (1991), and Universal Soldier (1992), to name three. It also brought drink, drugs and a lifestyle of hard partying. Marriage and family in the 1990s brought a period of emotional stability, but with his family home in Spain and his career in the U.S., things slowly unravelled through the 2000s. The movies got worse; the drinking returned; the marriage collapsed.
Today, Lundgren attributes many of his wrong turns to the unresolved traumas of his childhood. He first publicly discussed his father at a 2015 TED Talk, portions of which appear in the documentary.

“It was quite hard for me to open up in front of an audience, but it was therapeutic for me as well, and I knew people responded well to it,” he says. “So, I wanted to do it on a bigger stage in the documentary ... but also I think to show other people that it’s okay. You don’t have to keep it in and hold it.”

Lundgren channelled some of these feelings into Creed II (2018), where he reprised Drago as a bitter cast off seeking personal redemption through his son. He gave a nuanced, lived-in performance that surprised many – the kind of acting he says it took him years to grow into.

“I like to study things from the ground up, whether it’s chemical engineering or martial arts. But in acting, I started and within a year I was auditioning for this big movie, Rocky IV . I was sort of focused on one character. That movie was a huge hit, and now I had offers to star in my own movies, but I didn’t really have the technical skill. It took me many, many films to find that.”

He points to his return as Drago as an example of that growth. “Now he’s an older, bitter guy who reminded me of my own dad. A guy who wants to use his son to sort of get back at the world. My brother actually said when he saw the movie that it reminded him of our dad immediately.”

For those who kept up with Lundgren’s direct-to-video work of the past 15-or-so years, he had already been revealing new depths. Both he and Van Damme brought genuine gravitas to John Hyams’ thoughtful, stylish Universal Soldier: Day of Reckoning (2012). More recently, Lundgren has ably directed himself in likeable potboilers such as Castle Falls (2021) and Wanted Man (2024), in which his screen presence has grown affable and textured. In these films and others, he’s has grown older gracefully – partly because, unlike some of his contemporaries, he actually looks his age.

In The Expendables (2010), Lundgren’s portrayal of the gang’s troubled, substance-abusing black sheep is the film’s emotional core. By the fourth instalment (released in 2023), his anguished performance was not entirely acting. The documentary reveals that production of Expend4bles and Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom occurred during the height of Lundgren’s cancer battle, and shows how taxing they were. Was the struggle worth it?

“On the whole, it was good for me to work,” he says. “I think it kept me feeling stronger, more youthful, got my mind off the actual treatments and the cancer. And I enjoyed the Expendables , of course. You know, Sly and Statham and Randy Couture, the rest of them – I could hang out with them a little bit.
“It was a tough experience, but no, I didn’t feel like, ‘Oh, I’m going to sit home and be depressed and work on my will,’ or something.”

stories.title: How lost police evidence derailed a historic P.E.I. cold case murder prosecution
stories.summary: One of P.E.I.’s most high-profile murder cases has been upended after prosecutors withdrew all charges this week, saying police lost the overwhelming majority of critical physical evidence.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Charlottetown - One of P.E.I.’s most high-profile murder cases has been upended after prosecutors withdrew all charges this week, saying police lost the overwhelming majority of critical physical evidence.

The decision halted the planned trial of Todd Joseph Gallant, who was also known as Todd Joseph Irving, in the 1988 killing of teacher Byron Carr. Gallant had pleaded not guilty.

The Crown also pointed to gaps in how evidence was identified and tracked, raising concerns about the reliability of what remains.

“The loss of crucial evidence, together with the issues identified concerning the remaining evidence, means that there is no longer a reasonable likelihood of conviction and that the prosecution can no longer proceed,” the Crown Attorneys’ Office wrote in a statement shared with CTV News.

The office called it a “deeply disappointing outcome.”

Carr was found dead in the bedroom of his Charlottetown home, stabbed and strangled with a towel, after what police have described as a consensual sexual encounter with another man. On the wall, there was a scribbled threat: “I will kill again.”

The case went cold before advances in genetic genealogy brought a big break in 2024. Police arrested Gallant, saying his DNA was found on a pair of underwear left at the crime scene.

The towel believed to have been used to strangle Carr, and a knife are among the items police can’t account for.

“What we endeavoured to do was talk to the people who were responsible in 1988, and they didn’t have answers for us,” said Darren MacDougall, Charlottetown’s interim chief of police, ON Wednesday.

He added that some of those involved are no longer employed by the service, while others had died.

Several physical items collected at the time were sent to a forensic lab for analysis, MacDougall said. New investigators took over the file in 2007 and couldn’t find some of them, despite lab reports indicating they had been processed and returned to Charlottetown police in 1989.

However, biological material extracted from the items had been preserved at the lab, allowing investigators to produce a DNA profile. They forged ahead, MacDougall said, relying on that evidence while hoping the original items would turn up.

“We take this very seriously. We really do,” MacDougall said. “We are looking inward to see what has gone wrong.”

The service had no electronic database tracking evidence in the 80s and investigators couldn’t find a paper trail or notes explaining what happened to the items after their return. It has since introduced new policies and updated its evidence-management systems over the years, MacDougall said, describing today’s standards as consistent with those of police departments across the country.

Charlottetown police are considering a third-party review to get recommendations that could benefit the institution moving forward.

“We take this very seriously. We really do,” MacDougall said. “We are looking inward to see what has gone wrong.”

The service had no electronic database tracking evidence in the 80s and investigators couldn’t find a paper trail or notes explaining what happened to the items after their return. It has since introduced new policies and updated its evidence-management systems over the years, MacDougall said, describing today’s standards as consistent with those of police departments across the country.
Charlottetown police are considering a third-party review to get recommendations that could benefit the institution moving forward.

The decision halted the planned trial of Todd Joseph Gallant, who was also known as Todd Joseph Irving, in the 1988 killing of teacher Byron Carr. Gallant had pleaded not guilty.
The Crown also pointed to gaps in how evidence was identified and tracked, raising concerns about the reliability of what remains.

stories.title: Meet Canada’s first ever Parliamentary Visual Artist Laureate
stories.summary: For the first time in Canadian history, there’s an artist appointed by Parliament to promote the arts in this country, and the man chosen says he feels as if he’s been handed a blank roll of film.
stories.author: Rachel Aiello
stories.content:
Ottawa – For the first time in Canadian history, there’s an artist appointed by Parliament to promote the arts in this country, and the man chosen says he feels as if he’s been handed a blank roll of film.

“The fact that this is the first time for this role, it’s a great opportunity to explore what this can or cannot be,” said Paul Wong, the first ever Parliamentary Visual Artist Laureate, in an interview with CTV News.

“As artists, we use our imaginations to think outside the box, out of practical kinds of things, to tell stories and to engage audiences in all kinds of ways. So, it really is about letting our imaginations go and inviting other people’s imaginations to embrace the visions of art and artists.”

After years of advocacy from the Canadian arts community, and a lengthy legislative push to create the position, Wong – considered a pioneer of Canadian visual, multimedia, and large-scale public art installations – says he’s very grateful and feeling lucky to get to chart new territory.

“To have this kind of parliamentary position being made available to celebrate and empower arts and culture in this country, I think is really progressive,” he said.

“This gives me an opportunity to be amongst parliamentarians, the lawmakers, the people who create opportunities, and perhaps be able to inspire and influence and create dialogue that’s going to generate more interest and more support for Canadian art and artists.”

Wong lives in Vancouver, B.C., and his art spans many disciplines: film, video, sound, photography, installation, sculpture, printmaking, neon art, performance and writing. As an active curator, critic and community activist, he told CTV News he’s feeling very excited to get to work.

“We have tremendous filmmakers… we have we have incredible sculptors, craftspeople, storytellers. What we’ve been doing in this country is really different than what other people are doing in other places, and it needs it needs to be recognized and celebrated.”

What is an artist laureate?

Wong’s mandate is to “promote the arts in Canada, through Parliament, including by fostering knowledge, enjoyment, awareness and development of the arts.” The “arts” in this context include drawings, paintings, sculptures, printmaking, design, crafts, photography, videography, ﬁlmmaking and other digital creations.

To carry this responsibility out over his two-year term, Wong May be asked to produce artistic creations at the request of either the House of Commons or Senate speakers, including for use in Parliament during major occasions, but the position extends far beyond that.

As essentially an artist-in-residence – albeit one who is able to work remotely – Wong can also develop programming to promote visual arts in Canada, sponsor artistic events such as exhibitions and provide advice to the parliamentary librarian about the Library of Parliament’s collection and acquisitions to enhance the institution’s cultural holdings.

Because Wong primarily works in English, the next appointee will be someone who primarily works in French. This linguistic compromise was made when the position was created, “to ensure that Canada’s official languages are equitably represented.”

Wong said at this point he’s still “just nosing around what’s available on the Hill and what kind of resources there are,” that he can leverage in the execution of his mandate and potential new art projects.

“Art continues to be – and the creative process continues to be – somewhat undervalued compared to other trades and other kinds of career paths, and I think that hopefully this position will also shift and put some attention, value, and more respect for what art and artists in this country do,” he said.

‘A dynamic and multidisciplinary creative voice’

The speakers of the House of Commons and Senate announced Wong’s appointment last week, selecting him from a shortlist of three candidates, following an open nomination process.

The shortlist was prepared by a selection committee that included the director of the National Gallery of Canada, the commissioner of official languages of Canada, the chair of the Canada Council for the Arts, the president of the Royal Canadian Academy of Arts, and the parliamentary librarian as chair.

“Paul Wong has built an extraordinary career across many facets of the visual arts, from creating and exhibiting his own work to curating, writing and producing,” said House Speaker Francis Scarpaleggia.

“His longstanding commitment to building community, supporting artists and creating opportunities for connection will bring a dynamic and multidisciplinary creative voice to the role.”

Over his decades-long career, Wong – considered one of Canada’s leading video and multimedia artists – has received an honorary doctorate of letters from the Emily Carr University of Art + Design, the Audain Prize for Lifetime Achievement in the Visual Arts, and the Governor General’s Award in Visual and Media Arts.

“I’ve always been an artist,” Wong said. “I’ve worked with hundreds, if not thousands of artists across this country.”

Self-taught, he’s still creating. In addition to taking on this new role, Wong has several other projects on the go, including an upcoming public art installation at the new St. Paul’s Hospital campus in Vancouver.

“It’s called ‘ Mother’s Cupboard Mural ,’ and it it’s a collection of 43 of my mother’s recycled jars of Chinese herbs, medicines, and elixirs,” he said.

“Having Paul Wong be the inaugural Parliamentary Visual Artist Laureate is wonderful. He’s such a well-known artist. His work deals with so many of the issues that the Senate and various committees are working on, ON an ongoing basis,” said former senator Patricia Bovey, who tabled the bill that led to the creation of the artist laureate position, after a winding parliamentary saga.

Wong’s work is known for pushing boundaries, tackling issues including immigrant identity, media manipulation, death, memory, and homophobia. His pieces also celebrate Chinese culture, queer and activist communities, and Vancouver’s diversity.

“The arts can convey and do convey ideas and concerns and solutions to concerns, in many instances, long before the rest of society is aware that there May be a problem,” Bovey said.

Role the result of years of artist advocacy

The role was established in 2024, through an amendment to the Parliament of Canada Act.

That amendment was made in Bill S-202, a piece of Senate legislation that came as the result of years of advocacy from the arts community as well as several attempts to pass the proposal through Parliament.

The artist who first proposed the idea of a Canadian parliamentary visual artist laureate – inspired by the parliamentary poet laureate position that’s existed since 2001 – was Peter Gough.

A decade ago, then-senator Wilfred Moore brought forward the first version of a Senate public bill proposing a parliamentary artist laureate. That bill passed the upper chamber with wide support in 2018 but died after failing to secure a House sponsor.

What came next was a series of procedural struggles, but that didn’t deter Gough. He kept pushing, even while undergoing rounds of chemotherapy for an aggressive form of cancer.

“I’m just going to keep fighting for it,” he told CTV News in early 2019. “I can’t drop it, it’s too important to the arts in this country.”

Gough passed away in late 2020. A year later, a fourth version of the bill – the version that ultimately became law – was introduced in the upper chamber, by then-senator Bovey.

“Peter worked very, very hard on this,” she said. “I think it’s very sad that its passage was after he passed away. But every time I think about it, I think about Peter… A great tribute goes his way.”

Closely connected to the Canadian art scene throughout her life as a gallery director, curator, and art historian, Bovey saw it pass the Senate before her retirement in 2023, but it took another year before MPs followed suit.

“Artists are very excited by it. I had a number of calls from people who wanted to apply for it this time around, and there were some very, very good applicants. I also had calls from people who would like to apply, but this wasn’t the best time for them,” she said.

“So, I’m confident that when Paul’s two years are up, that there will be a number of very, very good applicants.”
