stories.title: What the Alberta referendum on separation could mean for the province and Canada, according to our reporters
stories.summary: Readers asked about the impact of the other nine questions, what would happen if Alberta ever separated and the fight against foreign interference
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
Alberta’s Oct. 19 referendum could be the province’s most consequential vote yet, as Albertans decide whether to remain in Canada or move toward a binding referendum on independence, among a number of questions on the ballot .

On Oct. 15, Alberta-based reporters Carrie Tait and Matthew Scace and opinion editor Tyler Dawson answered reader questions on the referendum, how both sides have been campaigning and what the result could mean for the province – and Canada as a whole.

In the lead-up to the pivotal vote, The Globe has covered how some Alberta separatists have received tactical assistance from U.S. political operatives and offered the province’s natural resources in exchange , the federalist side’s cash-strapped efforts to keep the province within Canada , and much more .

Readers asked about the impact of the other nine questions, what would happen if Alberta ever separated and the fight against foreign interference. Here are some highlights from the Q&A.

The question on separation aside, what impact will the other questions have if Albertans vote yes?

Matthew Scace: Premier Smith has put the full weight of her government behind those nine questions, including a massive $4-million ad spend aimed at passing them. The campaigns to reject those questions are trying to frame a “No” vote as a referendum on the premier herself. And that May well be the case. She has tied herself to those questions, and a majority rejection of them could be perceived as a rejection of her. Don’t forget: Albertans are voting in a provincial election next October (at the latest).

And if Albertans endorse the nine? Smith says she wouldn’t have legislation ready for at least a year. It would stand to reason, then, that the details of that legislation will be a key plank of her 2027 re-election campaign.

What is your opinion on the referendum affecting foreign investments in Canada and investments in Alberta?

Tyler Dawson: There has been a lot of talk about the referendum leading to instability that leads to a decline in foreign investment. The business community has raised alarms about this. However, is it a certainty that this ‘has’ happened – as opposed to ‘could’ happen if Alberta separates? I think that’s fundamentally less clear.

How did the story on the separatists’ repeated meetings and promises to the GOP come about?

Carrie Tait: We first heard about separatists meeting with officials in Washington because, well, the separatists boasted about it publicly. Other news organizations confirmed the U.S. State Dept. met with secessionists, but details were scarce.

So, we wanted to learn more. Who did the separatists meet? What did they discuss? When? Where? And so we just...asked around.

Independence advocate Dennis Modry provided details on the record. Jeff Rath, another separatist who was in the meetings, dismissed Modry’s account, which we noted in the story.

We still don’t know who represented the U.S. in the meetings. If you do, please reach out!

What is the strategy to track foreign interference during the referendum to make the public aware of such and to tackle such misinformation?

Scace: Within Alberta, Elections Alberta has been trying its darndest to track this and address misinformation on social media. But as we reported in January , experts are generally concerned about EA’s ability to manage this issue. Beyond foreign interference, EA has been sounding the alarm for more than a year about underfunding and chronic burnout/staff turnover.

Why is voter turnout expected to be so high? Are you anticipating long lines at polling stations on Monday?

Dawson: Elections Alberta has forecast a turnout of 80-85%, so it’s projected to be huge, compared to past general elections or past referendum campaigns. I think part of this is probably just a projection based on how many advance ballots were requested: We got X, therefore we can forecast actual turnout to be Y. But I also suspect that these are the sorts of questions – not just the secession ones but the ones about immigration – that really motivate people on both sides, so they’re more likely to come out.

Scace: My grandparents in Red Deer waited in line for 90 minutes yesterday. One of my colleagues told me it took him 10 minutes to vote. It’s anyone’s guess. The general expectation has been that it’ll be busy – partly due to the fact that voters have to fill out 10 separate ballots on questions they May be processing in real time.

The wording of the Alberta referendum questions is highly complex, super long and, honestly, confusing. Why do you think they were created/worded this way?

Scace: I’ve heard this criticism from readers and friends for months now. Opponents of the premier’s questions have argued that these questions are designed to achieve her desired outcome.

Say nothing of their readability, these questions are challenging for voters partly because they lack context and crucial details about how the government will implement them. Polling also shows swaths of Albertans still aren’t familiar with these questions, so many voters could be relying on their intuition when they arrive at the polls.

Tait: The separation question is a doozy. It is not a yes/no question. Instead, voters will choose their own adventure, marking an X by either Option 1 or Option 2.

Here’s the wording:

Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?

Option 1: Alberta should remain a province of Canada.

Option 2: The Government of Alberta should commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.

What will Smith do with referendum results?

Dawson: Likely, she will use a win on the immigration questions to try and change provincial policy. Whether that succeeds – it requires some negotiation with the federal government – is less clear. Ditto for the constitutional questions – Alberta cannot do those unilaterally, but she May push for negotiations with the rest of Canada. Likely she will fail, as Jason Kenney did with his referendum on equalization . On the secession question, if the separatists lose, she will likely try and put the issue to bed but will receive pushback from within her own party. If the separatists win, she’ll then have an awful lot of consultative work to do before holding a referendum at some point in the future.

What has Carney’s role been in all of this? What has been his involvement in Alberta since taking office last year?

Dawson: His role has primarily been on the policy front, I think it’s safe to say. There was the repeal or modification of several pieces of legislation that the Alberta government viewed as problematic. Much of this was part of an accord signed between the PM and Premier Danielle Smith, which also included the eventual construction of a new West Coast pipeline. But he has not involved himself in the day-to-day rollicking fight over Alberta’s future in the way that, for example, Naheed Nenshi or former premier Jason Kenney have. Probably at least part of the reason is because having a Liberal in that fight could backfire on federalist forces.

What are the legitimate complaints of those who want to separate?

Dawson: I think there are a couple legitimate grievances. The first would be with Trudeau-era legislation that seemed to hem in the oil industry, though many have since been withdrawn. The outcomes have not been as dire as people often suggest, but the better way to think of it is: Imagine how much more prosperous Alberta would have been without 10 years of federal interference.

The second would be with the equalization program. Even though it’s not a transfer payment – it’s paid for with federal taxes, not the Alberta government cutting a cheque – the structure of the system probably does suppress economies in other parts of the country.

First Nations have indicated they want to remain part of Canada having Treaties 6, 7 and 8 with the Crown prior to Alberta becoming part of Confederation. How could a separatist government become a party to the Treaty?

Tait: Those are big, big, double-big questions. It would require years of complex negotiations with multiple parties to sort out.

So, like so many questions around separation, throw these in the unknowable pile.

Is the threat of Alberta separating different than Quebec’s last referendum?

Dawson: I think it is different in many ways. Quebec, for example, has a distinct culture, a distinct language, a distinct history, at one point a largely distinct shared religion. Quebec, in other words, has more in common with other sovereigntist movements around the world, as opposed to Alberta, which does not have a distinct language or religious history. There is arguably a distinct culture here, but Alberta does not stand out as unique in a way that Quebec does.

It’s also very different in that Quebec has sovereigntist parties that run in – and win – elections . Alberta’s vote happened because of a citizen-initiated process as opposed to a separatist party winning elections.

However, both, in my view, are part of a similar problem, which is that regions in the country do at times feel left out of the national project, feel they don’t share enough in national prosperity, feel they don’t have enough say in the future and direction of the country.

In 1980, six days before the first Quebec referendum, Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau told an audience in Quebec that a “no” vote – that’s the stay in Canada side – wouldn’t be an affirmation that all was well in Canada. A renewed partnership would be needed. A similar situation, I think, exists now: Even a vote to remain in Canada is not an endorsement, necessarily, of the status quo.

If Alberta separates, will their residents retain Canadian citizenship, and will they be able to use the Canadian dollar as their official currency?

Dawson: The short answer is, I think, it depends. On the currency one: that would depend if an independent Alberta decided to adopt the Canadian dollar or create its own currency. Quebec has had the same debate because adopting a foreign currency means you don’t have control over monetary policy – that would still be set by the Bank of Canada.

On the citizenship question, the answer is really, at least as far as I understand it: it depends. It depends on what negotiations ensue and what the government of Canada decides.

paragraphs: Alberta’s Oct. 19 referendum could be the province’s most consequential vote yet, as Albertans decide whether to remain in Canada or move toward a binding referendum on independence, among a number of questions on the ballot .

On Oct. 15, Alberta-based reporters Carrie Tait and Matthew Scace and opinion editor Tyler Dawson answered reader questions on the referendum, how both sides have been campaigning and what the result could mean for the province – and Canada as a whole.

In the lead-up to the pivotal vote, The Globe has covered how some Alberta separatists have received tactical assistance from U.S. political operatives and offered the province’s natural resources in exchange , the federalist side’s cash-strapped efforts to keep the province within Canada , and much more .
Readers asked about the impact of the other nine questions, what would happen if Alberta ever separated and the fight against foreign interference. Here are some highlights from the Q&A.
The question on separation aside, what impact will the other questions have if Albertans vote yes?

Matthew Scace: Premier Smith has put the full weight of her government behind those nine questions, including a massive $4-million ad spend aimed at passing them. The campaigns to reject those questions are trying to frame a “No” vote as a referendum on the premier herself. And that May well be the case. She has tied herself to those questions, and a majority rejection of them could be perceived as a rejection of her. Don’t forget: Albertans are voting in a provincial election next October (at the latest).

And if Albertans endorse the nine? Smith says she wouldn’t have legislation ready for at least a year. It would stand to reason, then, that the details of that legislation will be a key plank of her 2027 re-election campaign.
What is your opinion on the referendum affecting foreign investments in Canada and investments in Alberta?

Tyler Dawson: There has been a lot of talk about the referendum leading to instability that leads to a decline in foreign investment. The business community has raised alarms about this. However, is it a certainty that this ‘has’ happened – as opposed to ‘could’ happen if Alberta separates? I think that’s fundamentally less clear.
How did the story on the separatists’ repeated meetings and promises to the GOP come about?

Independence advocate Dennis Modry provided details on the record. Jeff Rath, another separatist who was in the meetings, dismissed Modry’s account, which we noted in the story.
We still don’t know who represented the U.S. in the meetings. If you do, please reach out!
What is the strategy to track foreign interference during the referendum to make the public aware of such and to tackle such misinformation?

Why is voter turnout expected to be so high? Are you anticipating long lines at polling stations on Monday?

stories.title: The Alberta voters who want leverage – but not independence
stories.summary: Separatist organizers are trying to persuade fence-sitters that they can use their vote to send a message to the rest of the federation
stories.author: Joe Friesen
stories.content:
Ask the Albertans

Here’s how our Alberta-based reporters and editors answered your questions about the referendum as voting day draws near.

On a cool night in September, a flotilla of pickup trucks flying Alberta flags sits in the parking lot outside a community hall in Sylvan Lake. The community of 17,000 people is about halfway between Edmonton and Calgary, surrounded by rolling farmland and central Alberta’s oil and gas industry.

A crowd of about 120 people has gathered for a town hall organized by the Alberta Prosperity Project, a pro-sovereignty group.

Greg and Debbie Anderson, who run a cattle and grain farm in the area, step into the modest, brightly lit hall shortly before the speeches start. They haven’t yet chosen a side but are attending a pro-independence event for the first time. They’re contemplating a vote for Option 2, which would trigger an independence referendum. They’ve come tonight hoping to learn more. “I don’t know if we’re up for separation,” Ms. Anderson says. “Alberta needs a voice. That’s what we’re thinking.”

The Andersons and thousands of Albertans like them hold the future of the province in their hands.

On Oct. 19, citizens will be asked whether they want to maintain the status quo, or whether the province should hold another vote on separation.

At a time when a secessionist party has won power in Quebec and when the U.S. president has made clear his desire to subjugate Canada economically, the Alberta referendum is another destabilizing force pulling at the fabric of the country.

A landslide for the remain side could put the question to bed. But if Option 2 prevails, or if the vote is close, Canada could be in for years of constitutional negotiations, angst and economic uncertainty.

The idea of Alberta sovereignty has spread like a fever in some parts of the province in recent years.

In country halls, at hockey rinks and coffee shops, independence supporters have been galvanized by the progress of their grassroots uprising. An old idea has been given new energy by a group that coalesced around their opposition to COVID-19 pandemic restrictions. When contempt for Justin Trudeau burned white hot, and when the trucker convoy captured their anti-establishment anger, they made common cause with other groups looking to make change.

They see themselves as guardians of freedom and democracy, which lends their campaign an evangelical zeal. And their goal is the carving up of the country.

The many factions of the pro-independence side have dozens of talking points that often boil down to this: Alberta may be rich, but it ought to be richer. They argue the province will never reach its potential if it’s forced to share its wealth with the rest of Canada. And they rail at federal elections decided in Ontario and Quebec.

The remain side has powerful arguments of its own, such as a University of Calgary study that foresees a transition to independence costing up to $170-billion over five years, not to mention the long-term economic uncertainty and the fundamental divides it would create in families and communities.

Support for Option 2 has hovered around the 25 per cent mark in recent months, so the pro-independence side isn’t expected to approach the 50 per cent threshold for victory.

But referendum campaigns are unpredictable. Much depends on each side’s motivation to get to the polls.

The sovereignty movement, in these last days of the campaign, has been trying to win over sympathetic fence-sitters – the one-tenth or so of Albertans who aren’t necessarily in favour of secession, but aren’t satisfied by the status quo.

One argument they’ve pushed with some success is that a vote for Option 2 gives the province leverage for a future renegotiation of terms with Canada. It appeals to those who want to lodge a protest vote, but are uneasy about breaking up the country. The result could turn on how persuasive this idea proves.

In the Sylvan Lake hall, as the Andersons and the rest of the crowd take their seats, the organizers begin with a prayer. They acknowledge it’s unusual for a civic event, and offer an apology should anyone be offended.

The event’s main speaker is Mitch Sylvestre, one of the leading figures in the independence movement. The tall, square-jawed Mr. Sylvestre owns a sporting goods store in Bonnyville, Alta., and over the last several years his dogged campaigning, including delivering more than 300,000 signatures on a petition demanding Premier Danielle Smith hold a vote on independence, has pushed him to the political fore.

His political awakening, like that of many of his followers, occurred in the COVID-19 emergency. What pushed him to action was being forced to keep his store closed while larger, corporate competitors were allowed to open.

Mr. Sylvestre is not polished, but he holds the audience rapt. A gleam in his eye as he paces back and forth, Mr. Sylvestre calls this a “belly to belly” campaign. He urges those in the crowd to fight back against government overreach, the surveillance state and shadowy elites by taking advantage of their democratic opportunity.

They need 1.5 million votes to win, he says. Committed supporters number about 250,000, so he needs each of them to deliver five additional votes. That means persuading friends, family, neighbours and co-workers. “We have to do it ourselves. No one is coming to save you,” he says.

He recounts how he gained control of his local United Conservative Party constituency association a few years ago. He called his friends and relatives and made sure they showed up to vote. Then he did something similar to extend his influence in the broader party. When Jason Kenney resigned after a leadership review in 2022, he toasted victory. Persuade them one by one: That’s how power works, he tells them.

Support for independence has been remarkably stable over the past year, sitting between 20 and 30 per cent, according to Alberta pollster Janet Brown. In her view, there’s very limited room for growth.

But her polling also indicates about 11 per cent of the population could be categorized as “soft separatists.”

These are people who don’t necessarily want Alberta to leave Canada, but who think the current set-up isn’t working.

They’re open to voting for Option 2 but aren’t necessarily in favour of breaking up the country. Sovereignty to them could mean a strong and sovereign Alberta within a united Canada, as Premier Smith has put it.

If support for Option 2 is to grow, it’s likely with this category of voter. And if Option 2 ends up above 40 per cent, the vote share achieved by Quebec’s separatists in the 1980 referendum, the issue could simmer for years to come.

“What really differentiates the committed separatist from the soft separatist is the committed separatist doesn’t just want to separate; they want to create a right-wing utopia. The soft separatists are frustrated with Ottawa. They see some merit in the separatist argument. But they’re not quite as right-wing,” Ms. Brown says.

Mr. Sylvestre spends about 10 minutes of his Sylvan Lake speech on the nuts and bolts of winning.

The rest of his time is devoted to topics he appears to have covered many times before: Alberta loses billions of the tax revenue it generates to other provinces through equalization, it has fewer House of Commons seats per capita than the Atlantic provinces, it’s underrepresented in the Senate and at the Supreme Court. Immigration is too high, he says, and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s proposed new pipeline is a bad deal.

But as the speech goes on, he veers into strange territory.

He plays a clip from a documentary that suggests there is a “centralization of control in the hands of unelected officials at supranational organizations.” It hints darkly at a new world order, digital ID, digital currency.

And “like it or not, chemtrails are real,” Mr. Sylvestre adds. The theory that the white vapour airplanes leave across the sky is full of toxic chemicals has been debunked. But what he’s describing is that Alberta has been cloud seeding – releasing silver iodide into storm clouds in an attempt to shrink the size of hailstones – for about 30 years.

Most of the audience nods along with him. A few chime in with a loud “yeah” or “yup.” While the presentation contains recognizable elements of Western alienation, it also reflects efforts to build a coalition with people outside the political mainstream.

Mr. Sylvestre found some receptive responses in Sylvan Lake, but not everyone was sold. Leah Hennel/The Globe and Mail

It’s Jessica Westlund’s first time at a political event.

The 41-year-old stay-at-home mother and former health-care worker brought her young children to the meeting in Sylvan Lake. She says she arrived unsure what to think, but after hearing Mr. Sylvestre speak she feels persuaded to vote for Option 2.

“It’s really scary to have little ones, you know? What does their future look like with this government? The whole world is going crazy. It’s scary,” she says. “The surveillance state stuff is terrifying. Just freedoms in general [are threatened]. The way the government spends money is insane and has no accountability.”

But as for full separation from the country she has known, she’s not sure. “I don’t know where I go with that,” Ms. Westlund says. “You’re just trading control from one shady government to the next, right?”

The Andersons also emerged from the meeting largely persuaded to support Option 2, seeing an opportunity to seize on the province’s economic success and give it more leverage. Political revolts are often nourished by economic hardship, but the Andersons say they’ve rarely seen a better time for cattle farming. Beef prices are about 60 per cent higher than just five years ago.

They’re not sold on full independence, though. “I can’t see where that would go,” Ms. Anderson says. “But Alberta wants their say. They want more rights. They want to be heard.”

The economy’s impact on the referendum is difficult to gauge. Over the past six months, oil prices have surged in response to the U.S. war with Iran. By one calculation, oil industry profits have doubled this year. Alberta’s deficit will likely vanish.

Already, the median annual after-tax household income for families in 2024 was about $10,000 higher than it is nationally, and the average annual salary about 20 per cent higher.

Increased investment in new projects, such as the $2.9-billion Yellowhead Mainline natural gas pipeline that broke ground this week, or the Pacific Link oil pipeline designated a project of national interest a few weeks ago, will boost employment. Incomes could rise further still.

But many Albertans don’t feel optimistic. Some are struggling to afford the life they’re accustomed to. Polling shows that support for separatism is particularly high among those earning between $150,000 and $200,000 who feel it’s become hard to make ends meet.

“I used to crack the joke that separatists are rich people who think they should be richer, but that’s a little ungenerous,” the pollster, Ms. Brown, says.

A $150,000 salary “is a fabulous income if you’re 65, or if you’re 30,” she adds. “But it might not make ends meet if you’ve got a couple of kids going to college and you’ve got parents going into a senior home and you’re trying to maintain your multi-generational farm.”

Her surveys, done mainly for CBC Calgary, have found that support for Alberta independence tends to be lowest in the big cities and among those with the highest levels of education.

Rural central Alberta is where support is strongest. Men are likelier to support it than women, as are those who say religion is important in their daily lives.

Ms. Brown says it could come down to voter turnout. “It’s going to be about mobilization, about who gets their vote out.”

After healthy participation in advance polls this week, Elections Alberta is preparing for the possibility that turnout will be high.

The question related to secession is just one of 10 being posed to Albertans, with the other nine concerning immigration policies and possible constitutional amendments.

The time needed to read and consider each question could lead to slower voting and lines at the ballot box, which ultimately could have an impact on total ballots cast, Ms. Brown says.

Young people have historically asserted themselves at moments of political upheaval. But at most pro-separation events, the crowd is overwhelmingly made up of older adults.

Ms. Brown’s polling bears this out: Voters aged 18-24, 10 per cent of the electorate, represent only two per cent of committed separatists.

Some young people say they view the referendum as the preoccupation of an older generation, but others see its merits.

The vote takes place just a few days after Drayson Uwazny’s 18th birthday and will be his first opportunity to cast a ballot. He’s grateful for the federal student aid that supports his studies at Red Deer Polytechnic, but he doesn’t like the idea of one day paying higher Canadian taxes.

“I do think I’d be able to make more money if Alberta separates,” he says. “A big issue for me is housing. I probably won’t be able to afford a house by myself.”

Although he dreams of being a visual artist, he expects to find a job in construction, which he has worked part-time, when his studies are over. He comes from a conservative family and says the blue-collar guys he’s been around talk about how Quebec threatened to leave in the past and got a better deal from the federal government. That resonates for him.

“I’d say I’m more proud to be Albertan than I am Canadian,” he says. “I should be worth just as much as Quebec.”

After weighing the referendum question for a moment, he says he’ll probably vote with his family for Option 2. And if it comes to a separation vote next year, he might even vote to leave, he adds.

Avery Kapser, a 19-year-old student from Rocky Mountain House, plans to vote in favour of Option 2, but wouldn’t vote to leave Canada.

She describes herself as Catholic and conservative, is opposed to MAID and abortion, and has what she calls “traditional” values on same-sex marriage and gender identification. Her father works in the oil business and she agrees with those who argue that despite its economic strength, Alberta’s views aren’t well reflected in the federal government.

“I do think that we need to send Ottawa a message,” Ms. Kapser says.

The idea of sending a message is one that organizers on the separatist side have been pushing in recent weeks as they try to sway undecided voters.

Keith Wilson, a lawyer and leading figure in the independence movement, reminded voters in a recent video on social media that independence isn’t on this ballot.

A vote to remain says Alberta is fine with the status quo, he argued. A vote for Option 2, however, gives the province leverage.

“We want a better deal.”

For Valerie Richards, a safety officer in the oil and gas industry and a young parent, the argument is working. After meeting separatist canvassers at a sports complex in Blackfalds, just north of Red Deer, Ms. Richards says she doesn’t think Alberta should leave the country, but she hopes a vote for Option 2 will spark change.

When she was growing up, her father’s earnings from the oil rigs could pay for his children to play hockey.

“I’m not going to be able to do that for my kids, and that’s just extremely frustrating. I can’t give them the simple, middle-class life,” Ms. Richards said. “Canada now is not the Canada I grew up with.”

Four years after anti-government protesters blockaded the nearby border crossing, referendum fever has taken hold in Coutts, Alta. One house has ‘Republic of Alberta’ and Montana flags. Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press

On a recent Wednesday night, more than a hundred people fill the German Canadian Harmony Club in Redcliff – a town of 5,000 just outside Medicine Hat, about 300 kilometres southeast of Calgary.

The Canadian symbols affixed to the club’s walls clash with the merchandise tables, where stickers, banners and flags cry out for an independent republic.

The event was organized by Let’s Talk Alberta, which describes itself as dedicated to open debate about Alberta’s future. Although the content is heavily informed by pro-sovereignty views, the group says it doesn’t advocate for any single outcome.

At the start of the meeting, speaker Christopher Scott asks how many people have never attended a meeting before (it’s his fourth time in this community, he says). About 10 per cent raise their hands, an indication that interest is growing but not booming.

Mr. Scott, who has been speaking at town halls like this for weeks, is the owner of the Whistle Stop Cafe in Mirror, Alta., a business that became a focal point for those opposed to public-health restrictions during the pandemic. He was charged in 2021 under the Public Health Act for ignoring rules against large gatherings but was later acquitted. His legal fight has helped him rise to political prominence in Alberta.

His view is that a win for Option 2 “is not the end of Canada.”

“If Ottawa negotiates, Canada gets fixed,” he says in one of his pamphlets. “If Ottawa refuses even then, Albertans will have learned something worth knowing.”

The people in this room see their situation as a power struggle with a federal government determined to keep Alberta down. When Alberta joined Confederation in 1905, created along with Saskatchewan out of what had been the North-West Territories, it didn’t get to negotiate its own deal, as B.C., Manitoba and Prince Edward Island had.

“We weren’t invited, we were told,” says Regina Neufeld, who is attending her first meeting. She heard about the event from someone she spotted in Costco wearing an Alberta Freedom sweatshirt.

Ms. Neufeld describes herself as a homemaker who also works seasonally in a greenhouse. She says she was dismayed by Ottawa’s response to the truckers’ protests in early 2022. It motivated her to stand up for her beliefs, she says.

Though she’s on the fence about Alberta independence, she’s impressed by Mr. Wilson’s plain-spoken arguments about getting better deal with Canada.

During the discussion period after Mr. Scott’s speech, the most pointed question comes from Joe Repetski, who is seated near the front.

He asks: What about the possibility of Alberta becoming the 51st U.S. state?

Mr. Scott replies that he wouldn’t want to win sovereignty only to immediately concede it again, and argues it would be constitutionally complicated for the U.S., and therefore unlikely.

Mr. Repetski, who is retired and lives with his wife in Medicine Hat, says he has no interest in seeing Alberta join the U.S., but it’s a scenario that has to be considered.

Mr. Repetski says without hesitation that Canada has been good to his family, having grown up the son of immigrants displaced by the Second World War. Recently, though, his perception is that government rule-making is increasing and freedoms are eroding.

“I think the biggest one for me was what happened in Ottawa over the truckers’ conflict, particularly where the government took exceptional, extreme emergency powers when they didn’t have to,” Mr. Repetski says.

A former high school social studies teacher and principal in Saskatchewan, he remembers handing out copies of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to students, speaking of it with reverence, only for it to be unjustly trampled to curtail a political protest, in his view. The Federal Court of Appeal this year upheld a ruling that said Ottawa’s use of the Emergencies Act was unreasonable.

“If Pierre Trudeau alienated the West, Justin did more damage,” he says.

He believes the referendum process is about constitutional reform more than independence. The nine other questions on the ballot, about the Senate, control of immigration and judicial selection, look to him like an agenda for constitutional talks.

When he pauses to think through the likely outcome of the Oct. 19 vote, Mr. Repetski says he doubts Option 2 will prevail.

It’s a complex idea, he says, and it lands just as relations with Canada’s largest trading partner are at a low point, heaping economic uncertainty on potential political instability.

“People are afraid of the unknown. That’s the truth,” he says.

Still, he hopes the referendum is a wake-up call to those who have taken Alberta for granted.

“This is to have a serious conversation. Not to be dismissed as a bunch of moronic idiots,” he says.

Where that conversation goes next will shape Alberta for years to come.

Increased investment in new projects, such as the $2.9-billion Yellowhead Mainline natural gas pipeline that broke ground this week, or the Pacific Link oil pipeline designated a project of national interest a few weeks ago, will boost employment. Incomes could rise further still.

But many Albertans don’t feel optimistic. Some are struggling to afford the life they’re accustomed to. Polling shows that support for separatism is particularly high among those earning between $150,000 and $200,000 who feel it’s become hard to make ends meet.
“I used to crack the joke that separatists are rich people who think they should be richer, but that’s a little ungenerous,” the pollster, Ms. Brown, says.

A $150,000 salary “is a fabulous income if you’re 65, or if you’re 30,” she adds. “But it might not make ends meet if you’ve got a couple of kids going to college and you’ve got parents going into a senior home and you’re trying to maintain your multi-generational farm.”
Her surveys, done mainly for CBC Calgary, have found that support for Alberta independence tends to be lowest in the big cities and among those with the highest levels of education.
Rural central Alberta is where support is strongest. Men are likelier to support it than women, as are those who say religion is important in their daily lives.
Ms. Brown says it could come down to voter turnout. “It’s going to be about mobilization, about who gets their vote out.”
After healthy participation in advance polls this week, Elections Alberta is preparing for the possibility that turnout will be high.
The question related to secession is just one of 10 being posed to Albertans, with the other nine concerning immigration policies and possible constitutional amendments.
The time needed to read and consider each question could lead to slower voting and lines at the ballot box, which ultimately could have an impact on total ballots cast, Ms. Brown says.
Young people have historically asserted themselves at moments of political upheaval. But at most pro-separation events, the crowd is overwhelmingly made up of older adults.
Ms. Brown’s polling bears this out: Voters aged 18-24, 10 per cent of the electorate, represent only two per cent of committed separatists.
Some young people say they view the referendum as the preoccupation of an older generation, but others see its merits.

The vote takes place just a few days after Drayson Uwazny’s 18th birthday and will be his first opportunity to cast a ballot. He’s grateful for the federal student aid that supports his studies at Red Deer Polytechnic, but he doesn’t like the idea of one day paying higher Canadian taxes.
“I do think I’d be able to make more money if Alberta separates,” he says. “A big issue for me is housing. I probably won’t be able to afford a house by myself.”

Although he dreams of being a visual artist, he expects to find a job in construction, which he has worked part-time, when his studies are over. He comes from a conservative family and says the blue-collar guys he’s been around talk about how Quebec threatened to leave in the past and got a better deal from the federal government. That resonates for him.
“I’d say I’m more proud to be Albertan than I am Canadian,” he says. “I should be worth just as much as Quebec.”
After weighing the referendum question for a moment, he says he’ll probably vote with his family for Option 2. And if it comes to a separation vote next year, he might even vote to leave, he adds.
Avery Kapser, a 19-year-old student from Rocky Mountain House, plans to vote in favour of Option 2, but wouldn’t vote to leave Canada.

She describes herself as Catholic and conservative, is opposed to MAID and abortion, and has what she calls “traditional” values on same-sex marriage and gender identification. Her father works in the oil business and she agrees with those who argue that despite its economic strength, Alberta’s views aren’t well reflected in the federal government.
“I do think that we need to send Ottawa a message,” Ms. Kapser says.
The idea of sending a message is one that organizers on the separatist side have been pushing in recent weeks as they try to sway undecided voters.
Keith Wilson, a lawyer and leading figure in the independence movement, reminded voters in a recent video on social media that independence isn’t on this ballot.
A vote to remain says Alberta is fine with the status quo, he argued. A vote for Option 2, however, gives the province leverage.
“We want a better deal.”

For Valerie Richards, a safety officer in the oil and gas industry and a young parent, the argument is working. After meeting separatist canvassers at a sports complex in Blackfalds, just north of Red Deer, Ms. Richards says she doesn’t think Alberta should leave the country, but she hopes a vote for Option 2 will spark change.
When she was growing up, her father’s earnings from the oil rigs could pay for his children to play hockey.

“I’m not going to be able to do that for my kids, and that’s just extremely frustrating. I can’t give them the simple, middle-class life,” Ms. Richards said. “Canada now is not the Canada I grew up with.”

Four years after anti-government protesters blockaded the nearby border crossing, referendum fever has taken hold in Coutts, Alta. One house has ‘Republic of Alberta’ and Montana flags. Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press
On a recent Wednesday night, more than a hundred people fill the German Canadian Harmony Club in Redcliff – a town of 5,000 just outside Medicine Hat, about 300 kilometres southeast of Calgary.
The Canadian symbols affixed to the club’s walls clash with the merchandise tables, where stickers, banners and flags cry out for an independent republic.

The event was organized by Let’s Talk Alberta, which describes itself as dedicated to open debate about Alberta’s future. Although the content is heavily informed by pro-sovereignty views, the group says it doesn’t advocate for any single outcome.

At the start of the meeting, speaker Christopher Scott asks how many people have never attended a meeting before (it’s his fourth time in this community, he says). About 10 per cent raise their hands, an indication that interest is growing but not booming.

Mr. Scott, who has been speaking at town halls like this for weeks, is the owner of the Whistle Stop Cafe in Mirror, Alta., a business that became a focal point for those opposed to public-health restrictions during the pandemic. He was charged in 2021 under the Public Health Act for ignoring rules against large gatherings but was later acquitted. His legal fight has helped him rise to political prominence in Alberta.
His view is that a win for Option 2 “is not the end of Canada.”
“If Ottawa negotiates, Canada gets fixed,” he says in one of his pamphlets. “If Ottawa refuses even then, Albertans will have learned something worth knowing.”

The people in this room see their situation as a power struggle with a federal government determined to keep Alberta down. When Alberta joined Confederation in 1905, created along with Saskatchewan out of what had been the North-West Territories, it didn’t get to negotiate its own deal, as B.C., Manitoba and Prince Edward Island had.
“We weren’t invited, we were told,” says Regina Neufeld, who is attending her first meeting. She heard about the event from someone she spotted in Costco wearing an Alberta Freedom sweatshirt.

Ms. Neufeld describes herself as a homemaker who also works seasonally in a greenhouse. She says she was dismayed by Ottawa’s response to the truckers’ protests in early 2022. It motivated her to stand up for her beliefs, she says.
Though she’s on the fence about Alberta independence, she’s impressed by Mr. Wilson’s plain-spoken arguments about getting better deal with Canada.
During the discussion period after Mr. Scott’s speech, the most pointed question comes from Joe Repetski, who is seated near the front.
He asks: What about the possibility of Alberta becoming the 51st U.S. state?
Mr. Scott replies that he wouldn’t want to win sovereignty only to immediately concede it again, and argues it would be constitutionally complicated for the U.S., and therefore unlikely.
Mr. Repetski, who is retired and lives with his wife in Medicine Hat, says he has no interest in seeing Alberta join the U.S., but it’s a scenario that has to be considered.

Mr. Repetski says without hesitation that Canada has been good to his family, having grown up the son of immigrants displaced by the Second World War. Recently, though, his perception is that government rule-making is increasing and freedoms are eroding.

“I think the biggest one for me was what happened in Ottawa over the truckers’ conflict, particularly where the government took exceptional, extreme emergency powers when they didn’t have to,” Mr. Repetski says.

A former high school social studies teacher and principal in Saskatchewan, he remembers handing out copies of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to students, speaking of it with reverence, only for it to be unjustly trampled to curtail a political protest, in his view. The Federal Court of Appeal this year upheld a ruling that said Ottawa’s use of the Emergencies Act was unreasonable.
“If Pierre Trudeau alienated the West, Justin did more damage,” he says.

He believes the referendum process is about constitutional reform more than independence. The nine other questions on the ballot, about the Senate, control of immigration and judicial selection, look to him like an agenda for constitutional talks.
When he pauses to think through the likely outcome of the Oct. 19 vote, Mr. Repetski says he doubts Option 2 will prevail.
It’s a complex idea, he says, and it lands just as relations with Canada’s largest trading partner are at a low point, heaping economic uncertainty on potential political instability.
“People are afraid of the unknown. That’s the truth,” he says.
Still, he hopes the referendum is a wake-up call to those who have taken Alberta for granted.
“This is to have a serious conversation. Not to be dismissed as a bunch of moronic idiots,” he says.
Where that conversation goes next will shape Alberta for years to come.

stories.title: Canada war-gamed a U.S. invasion. A former Norad commander explains why
stories.summary: Retired Gen. Glen VanHerck says military trust endures, but political friction could hurt North American defence.
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — In recent weeks, we’ve learned that Canadian military leaders war-gamed U.S. military action against Canada earlier this year, with Prime Minister Mark Carney having described it as an “extreme tail risk,” in an interview last month with the New York Times.

That revelation was a stark reflection of an increasingly strained relationship amid the tariff war, even as Arctic, missile, drone, and homeland-defence threats continue to rise. To understand how the Canada-U.S. defence alliance is holding up amid these tensions, National Post spoke with retired General Glen VanHerck, commander of U.S. Northern Command and North American Aerospace Defense Command (Norad) from 2020 to 2024.

This Q&A has been edited for clarity and length.

Gen. Glen VanHerck: It did not affect the military relationship or defence cooperation on a day-to-day basis. What it did was, at times, create doubt about the political commitment to the military mission — to Canada’s responsibility to its Norad commitment and continental defence in general. That’s what I would say it created questions or doubt about at times.

From a military perspective, I never doubted the commitment of the Chief of Defence staff (of Canada), the military personnel assigned to Norad, the military personnel I interacted with at Canadian Joint Operations Command (Cjoc) or anyplace else.

But when you see politically questionable support for that military institution at times — when you see statements that express, ‘Yes, we’re going to do Norad modernization,’ but no money comes with it; when you see that there’s discussion of a new strategy, but that strategy is delayed a year or two — then that creates questions in one’s mind about commitment and long-term support.

I don’t have concerns that the trade challenges we’re experiencing will impact the relationship or military commitment … The commitment is there. The trade challenges and relationships could ultimately impact their ability to support (that commitment) because of a lack of money, resources, platforms that are capable, interoperable, and integrated.

Well, I think the greatest thing Canada commits to and has is its posture, its location in the Arctic, the geography that it offers. Certainly, the United States can replace material things, whether it’s radars or airplanes. It cannot replace a government that is committed to a binational relationship. That’s the most powerful thing you can have. And that relationship — and even expanding that to Nato — is an asymmetric advantage that the United States, Canada, and our partners and allies have had. I would say that relationship has actually prevented the great powers from going to war.

The friction we have politically, in my mind, makes that relationship and that support questionable and erodes strategic stability, because potential adversaries see that and they question our alignment, our support for each other. Are we going to have each other’s back, and are we committed to defence and going to war over each other’s sovereignty and the things that we support as an alliance? That’s the worst thing that could happen.

I think both countries are at fault. I think countries have reacted based on emotion rather than fact. At times, there’s been immaturity in the relationship both ways, and it would be better if we sat down and looked at the positives of the relationship rather than making emotional decisions out of political positions by leaders on both sides.

I do think Canada needs to do more for its defence posture and support. I think that has eroded over the years. With various elected officials who have been in power, Canada’s support for the defence apparatus did wane a little bit. But at the same time, I think the U.S. could have had these discussions behind closed doors, in non-emotional terms, and gotten to a better place.

I think the strongest evidence is that North America has been kept safe. We have fielded operable capabilities. Canada and the United States have gone to war, into conflicts around the globe, attached at the hip, side-by-side. Certainly the commitments from each country look different, but that doesn’t mean that the commitment from the political (realm) and the people has been any different. That’s just a fact of gross domestic product and the size of industry that has limited Canada’s commitment.

I think the biggest weakness is that the partnership and relationship, as we’re seeing it play out, can be significantly influenced by single leaders and emotional leaders in ways that impact an entire country. The rest of the people, and the military apparatus, our national security, our prices of goods — all become affected by two individuals who don’t necessarily agree over policy.

Canada’s very exposed to that. From a defensive perspective and being able to track, it’s going to require a satellite constellation to track hypersonics that are going to attack North America. The United States is committed to building a Low Earth Orbit constellation to do that. To my knowledge, Canada has not yet built radars that’ll be able to bridge that gap. So both the United States and Canada are vulnerable to that threat.

Since I’m not the commander, I don’t see under the tent and see what’s going on necessarily — but my understanding is that Prime Minister Carney has absolutely furthered the commitment to Norad. He made sure the money that was committed but never really provided under the last administration in Canada has gone forward, and he’s added to that.

On the 2 per cent (of GDP for Nato defence), I think that number is just pulled out of thin air and doesn’t mean anything for the United States, Canada, or Nato. We need to figure out what the threat requires, what stability requires, and then get a commitment of all nations, whether that’s 2 per cent, 5 per cent, 2.5 per cent, 1.5 per cent. I don’t know where the number is, but just arbitrarily putting percentages out as a goal, in a military planner’s mind, is not really the way to do business.

If you’re looking at it from a Norad perspective, there are terms of agreement — there are rules that you must follow that require political leaders on both sides to commit to. So Canada has all the influence and power it needs in that agreement. That would be for Norad support. If the United States feels differently or Canada feels differently, then you can take actions outside of the Norad construct through your forces or additional U.S. forces.

We saw that play out in some way with Northcom taking action to shoot down the (Chinese high-altitude surveillance) balloon, which flew over both countries’ airspace. The legal justification to shoot it down was under U.S.-only law and policy, and therefore the authority used was a Northcom authority.

Not to my knowledge. During my timeframe, I never saw anything remotely close to that.

And I think it’s really important that we get this right, that we partner with Canadians to look at what the next century is going to be for the two countries and how to make that happen.

That’s what I would say it created questions or doubt about at times.

From a military perspective, I never doubted the commitment of the Chief of Defence staff (of Canada), the military personnel assigned to Norad, the military personnel I interacted with at Canadian Joint Operations Command (Cjoc) or anyplace else.

But when you see politically questionable support for that military institution at times — when you see statements that express, ‘Yes, we’re going to do Norad modernization,’ but no money comes with it; when you see that there’s discussion of a new strategy, but that strategy is delayed a year or two — then that creates questions in one’s mind about commitment and long-term support.

I don’t have concerns that the trade challenges we’re experiencing will impact the relationship or military commitment … The commitment is there. The trade challenges and relationships could ultimately impact their ability to support (that commitment) because of a lack of money, resources, platforms that are capable, interoperable, and integrated.

I would say that relationship has actually prevented the great powers from going to war.

The friction we have politically, in my mind, makes that relationship and that support questionable and erodes strategic stability, because potential adversaries see that and they question our alignment, our support for each other. Are we going to have each other’s back, and are we committed to defence and going to war over each other’s sovereignty and the things that we support as an alliance? That’s the worst thing that could happen.

I think both countries are at fault. I think countries have reacted based on emotion rather than fact. At times, there’s been immaturity in the relationship both ways, and it would be better if we sat down and looked at the positives of the relationship rather than making emotional decisions out of political positions by leaders on both sides.

With various elected officials who have been in power, Canada’s support for the defence apparatus did wane a little bit. But at the same time, I think the U.S. could have had these discussions behind closed doors, in non-emotional terms, and gotten to a better place.

And I think it’s really important that we get this right, that we partner with Canadians to look at what the next century is going to be for the two countries and how to make that happen.

We are going to meet this month in Baltimore, Maryland, and we’ll meet in the spring in Montreal. We’ll draft reports, and that will likely, through editing and recommendations, and coordination, take us about 18 months to complete.

stories.title: B.C. votes for mayors and councillors before general election next week
stories.summary: Vancouver - It’s voting day in British Columbia but if you are confused, you're probably not alone.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Pete Fry is Vancouver’s next mayor.

Fry won the municipal election Saturday, defeating incumbent Ken Sim and six other challengers vying to lead British Columbia’s largest city.

He celebrated with supporters at a campaign party in Vancouver and held a lead throughout the night.

Fry embraced his mother, longtime Liberal MP Hedy Fry, and thanked his supporters and fellow candidates in a speech.

“We love this city a lot, and we’re here to work for the city, to fight for the city,” he said.

Fry leads the municipal Green Party and was first elected as a city councillor in 2018.

Preliminary results show he received about 90,000 votes while SIM received about 63,000.

He won a mayoral race that highlighted quality-of-life issues and campaigned on promises about housing, transportation, and the economy.

Fry bested incumbent mayor Sim, whose re-election platform emphasized affordability and public safety and included a promise of a zero per cent property tax increase.

He frequently clashed with Sim and his more right-leaning ABC councillors during council meetings and has acknowledged benefiting from the narrowing of the progressive field after several other candidates withdrew from the race.

Fry said Vancouverites elected him as the city’s first Green mayor because the party prioritizes values-based policy over partisan issues, and said he would take an idealistic approach to governance.

“The values that we bring are about respect for the earth, participatory democracy, working together, non-violence, being supportive, being nice. And I think that’s really where we can shine,” he told reporters on Saturday.

He said investments in housing are a key ask for the federal government, and that he will ask the province to support community safety, including help dealing with street disorder.

Vancouver’s preliminary election results suggest Fry will be working with a big progressive majority on council, with Green and Cope candidates poised to take four seats each out of 10.

Sim’s ABC Vancouver appears reduced to one councillor, alongside a single OneCity candidate.

Vancouver’s preliminary election results show that voters elected a mix of candidates for city council, including from Fry’s Green party, OneCity, Cope, and ABC Vancouver.

Fry said he was going to dive in and put partisan politics aside.

“At the end of the day, we’re going to have a council that’s working for Vancouver,” he said.

When asked whether the mix of slates could prevent council from getting anything done, Fry said a similar makeup in 2020 only didn’t work because of difficulties during the COVID-19 pandemic.

“I think we’re going to be able to make it work,” he said. “My priority is to get folks who are working for the betterment of Vancouver. Not their political interests, not their partisan interests, but they want to get stuff done for Vancouverites. That’s where we’re going to make a difference.”

Also on the ballot were two plebiscite questions brought forward by Sim.

One asks voters if they’re in favour of the city “strengthening its laws to forbid open-air hard drug use in public spaces,” which is already illegal in B.C., while the other asks if the city should ask the province to convert portions of the old St. Paul’s hospital into a “secure medical facility” with 100-plus involuntary care beds.

The results of the plebiscite questions won’t be known until Oct. 21.

Fry’s victory in Vancouver was among hundreds of local elections that took place across the province on Saturday.

In Surrey, Doug McCallum beat incumbent Brenda Locke in the mayoral race.

McCallum served three terms as mayor but lost to Locke in 2022.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 17, 2026.

stories.summary: General Releases
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (October 16, 2026 ) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 34-year-old Michael Thibert, of London.

The missing person is described as male, White, approximately 5’10”, weighing 150lbs.

The missing person was last seen on October 5, 2026. He was reported missing on October 6, 2026.

Family and police are concerned for his/her welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Althia Raj: A closer look at six controversial powers inside Mark Carney’s Building Canada Strong Act
stories.summary: The Star's Althia Raj breaks down aspects of Bill C-39, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Building Canada Strong Act.
stories.author: Althia Raj
stories.content:
The Halifax MP accused opposition members of lying about Bill C-39 , Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Building Canada Strong Act, telling them the bill does not do things it does.

“I have spent my entire career fighting for the environment, and I would never support something that would weaken environmental protections,” she said.

I don’t know if Miedema read the bill. Having read and listened to MPs’ speeches, it seems many Liberals have not.

The stated goal behind C-39 is to speed up project approvals and permitting so that things get built faster. The government speaks of concurrent reviews instead of consecutive ones, limiting duplication across governments and agencies, strengthening trade corridors and supporting paperless commerce. But there is much more packed into this omnibus bill. As MPs begin six days of hearings (prime minister Justin Trudeau’s Impact Assessment Act, C-69, in comparison, faced 51 days of study in the House and Senate), here are a few controversial aspects explained.

I have never seen a bill drafted to be as deceitful as this one.

— Green Party Leader Elizabeth May

C-39 makes C-5 permanent

Bill C-39’s summary mysteriously does not identify a key controversial change, the removal of the five-year sunset clause imposed on C-5, the Building Canada Act , by the opposition last year. Cabinet now gets permanent powers to select what projects are in the national interest (through criteria it determines and can change), those that will be green lit regardless of the outcome of environmental reviews, and to decide whether to exempt projects from certain laws and regulations, for example, the Species at Risk Act (Sara) which prevents wildlife extinction and protects biodiversity, the Fisheries Act, which protects fish habitat and controls the amount of wastewater and industrial discharge released into Canada’s lakes and rivers, and the Migratory Birds Convention Act, which protects nearly all native birds in Canada.

A crisis that is already frightening enough for Canadians and Quebecers is being used to justify major legislative changes that will shake the very foundations of the temple of values that we thought were otherwise secure, and that took years to build.

— Bloc Québécois MP Christine Normandin

C-39 creates “regions of national interest” where environmental reviews can’t stop projects

Bill C-39 builds on C-5 by allowing cabinet to designate new “regions of national interest.” These regions will be defined by cabinet, which also decides what kind of activity can happen in them and under what criteria (which cabinet can change or remove).

A regional assessment is required before a region is designated, but the report is not binding on cabinet. There is also no requirement that the assessment consider the types of projects that could be authorized in a region, or that it covers the full geographical area of the designated region.

When the designated minister — currently Intergovernmental Affairs Minister Dominic LeBlanc — is satisfied a project in a region of national interest meets the criteria, he must provide the project’s proponent with a document “deemed” to be every required permit and authorization (all the federal green lights). Indigenous Peoples whose rights May be adversely affected must be consulted prior to the document being issued; and reviews still happen, but they only influence a project’s conditions. They can’t find that the project is too polluting, too dangerous for endangered species, or that it will destroy crucial fish habitat and should not go ahead.

And while an impact assessment is required, C-39 eliminates the planning phase that mandates meaningful public participation.

When the economic zones were first floated last spring, the government’s consultation report said Indigenous participants cautioned that “pre-approval” of projects could limit the ability of rights-holders to assert their rights within their territories and would “likely lead to litigation.”

When we’re at the table from the start, projects get built. When we are shut out, they end up in court and nobody gets certainty.

— Teme Augama Anishinabek Chief Shelly Moore-Frappier

C-39 reduces protections for species at risk and opens the door for industry lawsuits

In May, after the Star reported the federal government was proposing to skirt the Species at Risk Act (Sara)’s jeopardy test so projects, such as the new west coast pipeline, could go ahead despite threatening the existence of the endangered Southern Resident Killer Whales, a public outcry temporarily shelved the government’s plans.

“We heard directly from Canadians that they did not like this,” Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said . “They pushed back very strongly, and the proposal is not in this bill.”

That’s true. But C-39 still weakens protections under Sara — the law designed to prevent wildlife species from becoming extinct.

Currently, activities that affect endangered species or their critical habitat need approval from either the environment, fisheries, or Parks Canada minister. Only if the minister believes all reasonable alternatives to the activity have been considered, that all feasible measures will be taken to minimize the impact on the species or their habitat, and that the activity will not jeopardize the survival or recovery of the species, is the minister allowed to permit the activity and lay out conditions the proponent must abide by, for example, mitigation and monitoring measures.

Bill C-39 changes that in two ways. First, as noted above, if a project in a “region of national interest” meets cabinet’s criteria, Sara’s preconditions — that a project can’t jeopardize the survival of species — don’t appear to matter. This would be an end-run around the jeopardy test.

Second, C-39 obliges the responsible minister to take into account the technical, economic and practical feasibility of the conditions it considers imposing. This happens already in practice, but adding it to the law raises two issues: it risks watering down conditions and protection for threatened species, and it opens the door for industry lawsuits, if conditions are deemed too financially onerous.

The economic feasibility should help determine how an environmental obligation is achieved. It should not become a substitute for achieving the environmental outcome.

— B.C. Liberal MP Patrick Weiler

C-39 allows construction to begin on projects before an impact assessment is completed

Bill C-39 amends the Impact Assessment Act to allow a minister to permit a project proponent to do “that act or thing,” subject to potential conditions, including remediation, prior to the project receiving a decision statement from the minister. (The Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission gets similar powers, though entire projects can’t be permitted this way.)

Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson’s office offered as an example, a mining project proponent granted permission to build a road before the project is approved so a construction season isn’t missed. In his speech to the House, B.C. Liberal MP Patrick Weiler called on Parliament to define the kind of work that can and can’t be done.

“It should not be irreversible, it should not prejudge the final decision or replace the assessment itself, and it should continue to respect Indigenous consultation and environmental requirements,” he said.

(C-39) will assure a weary industry that the time to build is now, and there is a path to a decision that will lead to greater investment, jobs creation and, ultimately, strengthening our economic sovereignty.

— Canadian Chamber of Commerce Senior Director Bryan Detchou

C-39 allows a designated minister to override project conditions

The new legislation also allows LeBlanc — the designated minister — to remove conditions on a project that was conditionally approved but is now listed as a project of national interest by cabinet. For example, the Roberts Bank Terminal 2 (RBT2) Project was approved in 2023 subject to 370 legally binding conditions .

In August, the government announced plans to list RBT2 as a project of national interest . This would allow the project to move forward, possibly without enacting some of the conditions intended to protect southern resident killer whales, the Chinook salmon, or the Western sandpipers. By listing RBT2 as a project of national interest, not only could its conditions be removed, but it could also jump over the constraints of the Species at Risk Act’s jeopardy test.

When ministers, like LeBlanc speaking to the Senate on Oct. 6 , say: “We removed the government’s ability to completely exempt projects from the application of that (Species at Risk) Act” — that is not quite accurate.

The modus operandi of the Carney government in amending federal environmental legislation, rather than doing full repeals and just owning the political fallout of that, it’s been to narrow, exempt, and build in so much discretion that they can, when they need to, for their political purposes, make the laws either not apply at all, or apply in a toothless way. And that way, they can say: ‘Well, we still have these laws.’ But what are they worth now?

— Ecojustice Program Director Charlie Hatt

C-39 cements the federal government’s ability to shut down legal strikes

Bill C-39 introduces pro-labour policies to protect truck drivers from misclassification and airport workers from having their collective agreements scrapped when a new employer takes over. To limit port disruptions, it lets employers, the Canada Industrial Relations Board (Cirb), or the minister seek a single bargaining agent for smaller bargaining units. The most controversial measure — denounced by unions across the country — is the power the labour minister retains to end a strike — without a parliamentary vote.

The government sets out a path to avoid that. Parties who had a binding arbitration imposed, or who had a strike or lockout, or whose agreement ran five years or more, must begin the process earlier. The conciliation period is extended by 30 days, and the minister can appoint a special mediator who, after 21 days, reports on the issues, the parties’ positions, their participation, and the likelihood of a deal. The report will be made public, unless the parties reach an agreement.

The Star, simplified

Breaking news, interactive polls, video, and voice notes. Star stories you’ll want to share, delivered where you’re already chatting. Follow the Star on WhatsApp .

“This is designed as a package to drive people to getting their own deals earlier and at the table,” Jobs and Families Minister Patty Hajdu told the Star. She believes public reporting will shame parties into behaving better.

If they don’t, Hajdu can use section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to take measures she considers necessary, including imposing a binding resolution, but only if she believes the strike or lockout adversely affects or might adversely affect the national interest. She can consider, but is not obliged to, whether the lockout or strike has or May have a significant impact on the Canadian economy, if it’s causing or May cause any serious social disruption, or whether the direction to the Board impacts freedom of association.

The Carney government has yet to release the Charter statement on C-39 potential effects.

Unions argue their bargaining power comes from employers knowing a strike will cause real pain; if Ottawa swoops in to ensure that doesn’t happen, their rights are diminished. In C-39’s background document , the federal government calls workers in federally-regulated sectors (ports, rail, air transportation, telecommunications, etc.) “ essential” to Canada’s economic growth — raising questions whether a constitutionally protected right to strike that can’t be exercised is a right at all.

Unions hoped Ottawa would limit government intervention, instead the government’s consultation document suggests it sided with employers who wanted s. 107 maintained or strengthened.

Canada’s unions fought hard for the right to strike, and we’re gonna fight equally hard to make sure that we can defend it.

— Canadian Labour Congress President Bea Bruske

While some cabinet ministers and Liberal MPs argue there’s nothing to see in this legislation, a closer look suggests otherwise.

Bill C-39 amends 19 acts and four regulations, it repeals one law, and creates a new one. It deserves careful study from Parliamentarians, whether that’s raising some of the issues outlined here, or pressing for details to ensure some of the government’s changes aren’t an attempt to limit judicial oversight or that job cuts at Environment Canada and Fisheries and Oceans won’t mean reviews are shortchanged. This legislation isn’t a temporary Band-Aid to address the current U.S. administration’s threats. It sets up a system that May be with us for decades to come.

She can consider, but is not obliged to, whether the lockout or strike has or May have a significant impact on the Canadian economy, if it’s causing or May cause any serious social disruption, or whether the direction to the Board impacts freedom of association.
The Carney government has yet to release the Charter statement on C-39 potential effects.

Unions argue their bargaining power comes from employers knowing a strike will cause real pain; if Ottawa swoops in to ensure that doesn’t happen, their rights are diminished. In C-39’s background document , the federal government calls workers in federally-regulated sectors (ports, rail, air transportation, telecommunications, etc.) “ essential” to Canada’s economic growth — raising questions whether a constitutionally protected right to strike that can’t be exercised is a right at all.
Unions hoped Ottawa would limit government intervention, instead the government’s consultation document suggests it sided with employers who wanted s. 107 maintained or strengthened.
Canada’s unions fought hard for the right to strike, and we’re gonna fight equally hard to make sure that we can defend it.
— Canadian Labour Congress President Bea Bruske
While some cabinet ministers and Liberal MPs argue there’s nothing to see in this legislation, a closer look suggests otherwise.

Bill C-39 amends 19 acts and four regulations, it repeals one law, and creates a new one. It deserves careful study from Parliamentarians, whether that’s raising some of the issues outlined here, or pressing for details to ensure some of the government’s changes aren’t an attempt to limit judicial oversight or that job cuts at Environment Canada and Fisheries and Oceans won’t mean reviews are shortchanged. This legislation isn’t a temporary Band-Aid to address the current U.S. administration’s threats. It sets up a system that May be with us for decades to come.
