stories.title: Canada's immigration upheaval in 6 charts: from Trudeau to Carney
stories.summary: The government’s changes since 2024 have not always had the intended effects.
stories.author: Nicholas Keung
stories.content:
Newcomers have been tied, fairly or not, to many of Canadians’ socioeconomic woes in recent years, prompting Ottawa to slam the brakes on the country’s rapid immigration growth .

International students were blamed by many Canadians for the affordable housing crisis; foreign workers for depressing wages and stealing jobs; and asylum seekers for draining government resources.

Since 2024, when Justin Trudeau was still prime minister, the federal government has drastically reduced the entry of new students and workers to Canada while restricting eligibility and access to asylum .

Since many study and work permits are for multiple years — and in part due to gaps in data collection, the share of temporary residents in the overall population has only crept down slowly from the peak of 7.6 per cent in 2024 to 6.7 per cent as of July 2026.

The post-secondary education sector has been the hardest hit by the international student caps , struggling with revenue loss, program cancellations and layoffs, said Larissa Bezo, president and CEO of the Canadian Bureau for International Education.

What keeps her up at night, she added, is how to sustain a healthy international talent pipeline to support the Carney government’s ambitious nation-building projects.

Bezo pointed to an example of what that talent shortfall would look like with the recent release of Canada’s nuclear energy strategy, and its projected demand for thousands of mechanical engineers, skilled trades and nuclear workers required in the coming years.

“International education operates on a multi-year cycle,” she said. “A scalpel could have been used rather than a hammer. I think we could have blunted and mitigated the risks to our future talent pipeline had there been a more careful approach applied.”

The government’s blunt measures to reduce the temporary population have also affected different sectors and local communities differently across Canada , said David Pierce, vice-president of government relations at the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.

Certain sectors such as manufacturing, food processing, hotels and restaurants are in particular trouble in some areas when it comes to finding workers, he added.

A survey by Hotels Canada, for instance, found 72 per cent of hotels reported difficulty attracting local workers and 58 per cent anticipated workforce shortages while 46 per cent lost temporary foreign workers due to expiring permits.

“Canada is so big that the reality in Montreal is not going to be the reality in Thunder Bay,” said Pierce, whose organization consists of more than 400 local chambers of commerce and boards of trades across the country.

“While some markets and some sectors appear to be saturated and there are too many people and job applicants, others need more people.”

Parisa Mahboubi of the C.D. Howe Institute said a smaller number of people coming here is bound to affect the growth of the labour force, Gross Domestic Product, job numbers and demand for goods and services.

At the aggregate level, she said she hasn’t seen significant negative impacts on the labour market in terms of employment, though she recognized there are regions facing labour shortages. However, she said that has been a chronic challenge for smaller communities, and immigration can’t address all labour needs.

Some labour market imbalances are not necessarily a bad thing, said Mahboubi, who chairs the Toronto think tank’s immigration targets council. A labour shortage can mean the economy is creating more jobs than workers available, and result in improvements in wages and working conditions, prompting capital investments in technology and automation when possible, she added.

“That’s something that Canada desperately needs right now,” she said. “We saw a reduction in productivity when we had high immigration and cheap labour available.”

Mahboubi said one positive outcome of the immigration shift is that GDP per capita has shown some improvement. GDP per capita is the total value of all goods and services produced and divided by the population of the country, widely considered as a measure of the standard of living.

The recent population slowdown has also offered relief for those in the housing market in terms of vacancy rates and rents, as well as lowering unemployment rates, she noted.

However, reduced population can also affect the housing market in other ways.

In its 2026 outlook report, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. said new home construction is set to decline through 2028 as developers face high costs, weaker demand and more unsold homes amid geopolitical and trade uncertainty, significantly lower population growth, soft labour markets and modest income growth.

“Certainly rents have stabilized,” said Stein Monteiro, lead immigration researcher at Signal49 Research, formerly known as The Conference Board of Canada.

“Are we still building the same amount of homes as we were when we had high immigration numbers? I would say no, because a lot of the pre-developments are pretty much stopped. Developers are choosing to keep land vacant rather than continue building.”

Not only are some of the bureaucratic regulations and zoning issues affecting housing supply not resolved yet, Ottawa’s immigration levels also signal to developers future demand for housing, which in turn provides the incentive to build, he said.

“It gives confidence,” said Monteiro. “From my perspective, immigration was boosting some of that housing supply.”

Mahboubi of the C.D. Howe Institute said it’s not possible to isolate immigration impacts given all the other factors involved in these issues, but immigration policy changes certainly play a role.

“There are always losers and winners when it comes to immigration,” she said. “The biggest question is how to mitigate negative impacts and maximize the benefits of those reforms.”
paragraphs: Newcomers have been tied, fairly or not, to many of Canadians’ socioeconomic woes in recent years, prompting Ottawa to slam the brakes on the country’s rapid immigration growth .
International students were blamed by many Canadians for the affordable housing crisis; foreign workers for depressing wages and stealing jobs; and asylum seekers for draining government resources.

Since 2024, when Justin Trudeau was still prime minister, the federal government has drastically reduced the entry of new students and workers to Canada while restricting eligibility and access to asylum .

Since many study and work permits are for multiple years — and in part due to gaps in data collection, the share of temporary residents in the overall population has only crept down slowly from the peak of 7.6 per cent in 2024 to 6.7 per cent as of July 2026.

The post-secondary education sector has been the hardest hit by the international student caps , struggling with revenue loss, program cancellations and layoffs, said Larissa Bezo, president and CEO of the Canadian Bureau for International Education.
What keeps her up at night, she added, is how to sustain a healthy international talent pipeline to support the Carney government’s ambitious nation-building projects.

Bezo pointed to an example of what that talent shortfall would look like with the recent release of Canada’s nuclear energy strategy, and its projected demand for thousands of mechanical engineers, skilled trades and nuclear workers required in the coming years.

“International education operates on a multi-year cycle,” she said. “A scalpel could have been used rather than a hammer. I think we could have blunted and mitigated the risks to our future talent pipeline had there been a more careful approach applied.”

The government’s blunt measures to reduce the temporary population have also affected different sectors and local communities differently across Canada , said David Pierce, vice-president of government relations at the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.
Certain sectors such as manufacturing, food processing, hotels and restaurants are in particular trouble in some areas when it comes to finding workers, he added.

A survey by Hotels Canada, for instance, found 72 per cent of hotels reported difficulty attracting local workers and 58 per cent anticipated workforce shortages while 46 per cent lost temporary foreign workers due to expiring permits.

“Canada is so big that the reality in Montreal is not going to be the reality in Thunder Bay,” said Pierce, whose organization consists of more than 400 local chambers of commerce and boards of trades across the country.
“While some markets and some sectors appear to be saturated and there are too many people and job applicants, others need more people.”

Parisa Mahboubi of the C.D. Howe Institute said a smaller number of people coming here is bound to affect the growth of the labour force, Gross Domestic Product, job numbers and demand for goods and services.

At the aggregate level, she said she hasn’t seen significant negative impacts on the labour market in terms of employment, though she recognized there are regions facing labour shortages. However, she said that has been a chronic challenge for smaller communities, and immigration can’t address all labour needs.

Some labour market imbalances are not necessarily a bad thing, said Mahboubi, who chairs the Toronto think tank’s immigration targets council. A labour shortage can mean the economy is creating more jobs than workers available, and result in improvements in wages and working conditions, prompting capital investments in technology and automation when possible, she added.
“That’s something that Canada desperately needs right now,” she said. “We saw a reduction in productivity when we had high immigration and cheap labour available.”

Mahboubi said one positive outcome of the immigration shift is that GDP per capita has shown some improvement. GDP per capita is the total value of all goods and services produced and divided by the population of the country, widely considered as a measure of the standard of living.
The recent population slowdown has also offered relief for those in the housing market in terms of vacancy rates and rents, as well as lowering unemployment rates, she noted.

stories.title: What’s it really like for patients ‘trapped’ in seclusion? ‘I feel sometimes I’m losing my soul’
stories.summary: Their accounts offer a rare look at life in long-term isolation inside Ontario's Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care.
stories.author: Jacques Gallant
stories.content:
Barron Jenner moves close to the camera and describes the feeling of being held in seclusion in hospital.

“Anxious. Trapped. Stranded.”

It’s early August, and the 40-year-old is in his eleventh year of being detained at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care in Penetanguishene, the province’s only maximum-security psychiatric hospital with more than 300 patient beds.

He’s been an involuntary patient in various Ontario hospitals his entire adult life, after being found not criminally responsible (NCR) for mischief in 2004 at the age of 18.

His crime: standing in a Chatham-Kent restaurant and refusing to leave.

20 years in isolation: Part 1

Hamblett May be the person who has spent the most time in psychiatric seclusion in any Ontario hospital. In a four-part series, the Star

While the Star’s coverage this year has included interviews with lawyers, doctors, advocates and relatives of patients, this is the first time that the voices of those experiencing seclusion have been featured, offering a rare look at life inside Waypoint.

The four men have all been found NCR, some for non-violent incidents. Two of them, including Jenner, are presently out of seclusion, but all have experienced being in isolation for prolonged periods.

For Jenner, who has been diagnosed with schizophrenia and obsessive-compulsive disorder, it was months at a time. He said seclusion only makes him feel worse.

“It just bogs me down and makes me feel uncomfortable and unhappy and stuck in a trap,” he said. “I tell them I don’t like being in seclusion. They don’t usually ask what it feels like.”

Waypoint’s own policy states that seclusion is to be used as a last resort — and for as brief a time as possible — to deal with patients who pose an imminent risk of bodily harm to themselves or others. The Star’s investigation has revealed that Waypoint is keeping patients in seclusion for years, including Camelott Hamblett, who has been held for 20 years and counting .

The four patients spoke in August and September in the company of their lawyers, Golnaz Nayerahmadi and Pritpal Mann of Toronto firm Rochon Genova, which had tried to certify a class-action lawsuit against Waypoint; the courts dismissed the case, finding that seclusion is an individualized process and patients would have to bring individual claims. The firm is exploring other ways of pursuing the lawsuit.

“What’s it like being in seclusion? It’s not fun,” said patient Richard DeJong. “It feels like there’s no oxygen. It feels like you can’t breathe.”

The men described strikingly similar experiences: feeling that they’ve been placed in seclusion as punishment rather than because they were a threat; staff not checking on them regularly or telling them why their seclusion was being maintained each day; and being left in their room for days at a time without being escorted out for seclusion relief — even though hospital policies say staff must offer two hours a day.

They also spoke about staff failing to de-escalate when they’re in a state of crisis, and instead resorting to the nuclear option: seclusion.

“They’ll just push your buttons and make no effort to calm you down,” said Christopher Ducharme. “You’re gonna get even more angry. You’re gonna slam your fist or slam a door. You’re just gonna lose more and more self-control.”

Monteiro concluded that Waypoint appears to be using seclusion to pre-emptively manage seriously mentally ill patients who might become violent later, a practice she said is now prohibited in many prisons. She found that patients in prolonged seclusion are being held in conditions the United Nations has “deemed to constitute torture” in similar settings.

Craig Thompson has been “closely following” the Star’s investigation into the use of long-term seclusion at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care.

Waypoint is appealing that decision, with president and CEO Dr. Nadiya Sunderji saying the Orb’s orders “raise concerns about the board’s jurisdiction and intrusion upon both clinical decision-making and the management of hospital operations.”

Asked for a response regarding the experiences of the patients interviewed, Sunderji said she couldn’t comment due to patient confidentiality requirements.

“Person-centred care, reflecting the unique circumstances of each patient, is at the core of the work we do at Waypoint,” she said in a statement.

In the 13 years that Sukhbir Mann has spent mostly locked in seclusion at Waypoint, he’s written close to 500 poems.

One excerpt reads: “Sometimes, I come out of my room and don’t shower for weeks/I feel sometimes I’m losing my soul and at 41, my body is turning weak.”

Mann, who spoke to the Star on a tablet while in seclusion in his room, has been detained at Waypoint since being found NCR for a random knife attack in a Toronto gas station in 2013.

“I just keep thinking over and over about the things I’m going to do with my life,” he said.

Barron Jenner — ‘It’s very bland and dull and empty’

As he spoke, Jenner was polite and focused on giving a full picture of his life at Waypoint — “I think I covered most of the stuff, so you got an understanding, right?” He also spent several minutes making sure the camera angle was right as he was sketched over Zoom by artist Alexandra Newbould.

He described himself as someone who likes to have fun and is interested in “high energy stuff” — “I like to interact with people that I like and am close to.”

Jenner had had numerous run-ins with police over trespassing before his May 2004 arrest, which came after he locked himself in a restaurant bathroom, left after police arrived, then returned a short time later.

“Police were again called and upon arriving at the restaurant met Mr. Jenner, who was standing just inside it,” says a summary from the ORB. “Mr. Jenner was then arrested for mischief.”

Noting that Jenner has been “in the forensic system for over three decades,” the ORB ordered last year that he remain detained at Waypoint. Pointing to hospital records that Jenner had assaulted people at Waypoint in the past after going off his medication, the ORB found it was “highly likely” that if he no longer fell under the board’s jurisdiction, Jenner would again stop taking his medication and become violent.

Since being transferred to Waypoint in January 2016, he’s been “subjected to multiple periods of seclusion,” including several instances lasting more than 100 consecutive days, according to a 2022 affidavit from Jenner filed as part of the proposed class-action lawsuit. Sometimes, he was also put in restraints while in the room, even though he was locked in.

He described seclusion to the Star as a “waste of time,” where he does little more than lie in bed: “It’s very bland and dull and empty.”

Jenner feels he’s secluded as punishment for his behaviour, mainly swearing at staff. And while Waypoint policy mandates that staff check on secluded patients every 15 minutes, it’s more like once an hour, Jenner said.

He spent about 12 days in seclusion in March, after the hospital said he made repeated phone calls to the security office and became angry when prevented from making more calls. He yelled at staff and attempted to punch a staff member in the face, according to a hospital report.

The document does not indicate why Jenner’s seclusion was maintained each day. While he’ll generally be told the reason he’s initially put in seclusion, Jenner said he’s kept in the dark when his seclusion is maintained on a daily basis.

“I don’t feel like they have a reason, like day to day,” he said.

The hospital report says he accepted seclusion relief every day it was offered earlier this year, but on four days he got no time out of his room due to “operational requirements”; in her assessment, Monteiro found that Waypoint lacks the staff to provide meaningful seclusion relief to all secluded patients on a daily basis.

“The panel is directing Waypoint’s treatment of (Andrew Azevedo) to be in compliance with its

Jenner’s first interview with the Star in August happened after having just spent a night in seclusion; he said he swore at staff and asked, “want to fight?” after they cut off his access to the phone, when he maintained he still had time left.

That behaviour would not meet the standard of imminent risk of harm warranting seclusion, said U.S.-based psychologist Janice LeBel — “Hard stop.”

“It’s a strain on my body to be in there, for even short periods of time,” Jenner said of seclusion. “It’s especially strenuous on my mind. It feels torturous.”

Now that he’s no longer in seclusion, Jenner likes to go outside and watch music videos on the computer. Sitting in front of a wall covered in bumblebee stickers and the words “Bee-lieve in yourself,” Jenner talks about what he would do if he were no longer in hospital.

“I’d try to get a girlfriend and just try to make the most of my life.”

Richard DeJong — ‘I’m dying slowly in here’

As Richard DeJong puts it: “I’ve been locked up for over 23 years for stealing a car.”

The 53-year-old grandfather has been detained in hospitals since being found NCR in December 2002 for auto theft in Windsor and for leaping from the prisoner’s box in court following his arrest and setting off the fire alarm.

Diagnosed with treatment-resistant schizophrenia and alcohol-use disorder, he’s been held continuously at Waypoint since June 2020. He said in a 2022 affidavit he’d spent several prolonged periods in seclusion, including one instance of more than 60 consecutive days.

“In solitary confinement, I cannot help but think about all that I have missed out on in life, specifically time with my children and grandchildren,” he said in the affidavit.

DeJong, described by his doctor in medical records as “sexually preoccupied,” said in his interview he was held in seclusion last year for asking a staff member for a “blow job.”

“I’m stuck in here alone; I haven’t had a girlfriend in years,” he said. “I don’t know where my life is going. I wish I could have somebody to talk to.”

His hospital report notes he was secluded for a month last year due to his “escalating sexually inappropriate requests to female staff,” after he stopped taking clozapine, a medication used to treat schizophrenia when other drugs have failed. He was told that his comments made staff “very uncomfortable.”

Huckshorn and LeBel have said that things such as swearing, hurling insults at staff, and making sexualized comments — all said as a result of an underlying mental illness — would not meet the high threshold for seclusion.

Once placed in isolation, DeJong lamented that there’s a lack of clear explanation on what to do to get out.

“Like what’s your plan?” he said. “What steps do I have to do?”

DeJong has not been in seclusion so far this year; he’s no longer fighting with staff after restarting clozapine. In keeping DeJong at Waypoint, the ORB ruled this year that while he’s to be “congratulated” for returning to the medication, he will need to demonstrate a longer commitment to being treated before he can be potentially transferred to a less secure hospital.

He repeatedly returned to a much larger issue in his interview: the fact that people found NCR can find themselves serving indefinite sentences — “being warehoused” — if their condition isn’t deemed to have improved, potentially spending far longer in custody than a person convicted of the same offence.

“It does not make a difference if you are in seclusion or not. There is no release date,” he said. “I’m dying slowly in here. People’s lives are being stolen.”

DeJong said Waypoint should be shut down with severance paid to the staff. As for the patients, he said group homes should be established. He wants to work on setting them up and would like to live in one himself.

“I’m an honest guy,” he said. “I care about other people.”

If he wasn’t detained, he’d like to work in a motorcycle shop.

“I just like driving them,” he said. “Feel the freedom, you know?”

Christopher Ducharme — ‘They’ll push your buttons’

Ducharme spoke on a tablet from his room, which includes a window overlooking Georgian Bay and a mattress on the floor — at his request, as a proper bed would take up too much space and he likes to breakdance. Describing himself as a “very passionate entertainer,” he also spends his time drawing, writing music and doing magic tricks.

The 34-year-old, who has been diagnosed with schizophrenia and cannabis-use disorder, has been found NCR twice, both in Quebec.

In 2014, he left a Montreal restaurant without paying, stole a steak knife, then put it to a taxi driver’s throat, ordering him out of the vehicle and driving off. He was again found NCR for punching a hospital attendant in the face in 2016.

He’s been held continuously at Waypoint since 2018, where he insists on staying in seclusion as he weans himself off his antipsychotic medication, maintaining the drugs only made him more violent and aggressive. He doesn’t want to come out until he feels that he can safely be around other people.

“I feel amazing,” he said. “The thoughts of violence, the voices, are going away. Feelings of aggression haven’t completely gone away, but are dissipating significantly.”

The ORB decision from his latest hearing in May indicates he committed no violent incidents or displayed aggression over the previous year, yet he was kept in seclusion because he repeatedly told staff he felt the medication would make him dangerous and harm them.

Ducharme went off his medication after regaining the ability to make his own treatment decisions in June, when the Consent and Capacity Board overturned a finding made by Ducharme’s Waypoint psychiatrist, Dr. Craig Hudson, that he’s incapable of consenting to treatment. Hudson is appealing that decision.

Ducharme said it’s “sick” that a number of patients are being held involuntarily in prolonged seclusion; while Waypoint refuses to divulge a number, it’s understood to be at least a dozen.

He said many of the patients in seclusion are “harmless” while “some of them are actually dangerous,” but he believes that’s because “They’re being treated like monsters, because they’re continuously secluded.”

For the patients in the latter category, Ducharme proposed they have their own enclosed space, including a bit of the courtyard, along with a shower and a TV behind a screen that can’t be damaged.

“It would be like their own little house that’s just very secure,” he said.

Ducharme has also been placed in seclusion against his will, including when he first arrived at Waypoint and was in a state of crisis. In his affidavit, he said he was secluded for 317 consecutive days and would turn down the “rare” offers of seclusion relief because it meant being placed in restraints, which were a trigger for his anxiety.

In his interview, he spoke about staff not listening to him or trying to understand his behaviour. “They’ll push your buttons, bring up situations they know are going to piss you off,” he said.

One of the Six Core Strategies to reduce seclusion focuses on proper de-escalation. The staff behaviour described by Ducharme “sounds coercive and punitive — not therapeutic,” said LeBel, one of the strategies’ co-creators.

Ducharme said he wishes staff would have tried to understand what he needs when in crisis.

“More of a negotiation,” he said, as he thought back to his arrival at Waypoint: “Not once did anybody come to me and say, ‘Chris, what’s wrong? What can I do to help?’”

But Ducharme also acknowledged there are some really nice staff “who have done a lot for me.”

If not detained, he said, he’d be an international superstar.

“I’d be bigger than Drake,” he said, laughing. “My goal is to revolutionize entertainment.”

He has a big smile on his face as he talks about the prospect of performing for an audience.

“I want people to know that I’m a really freaking nice guy who tries to help the world and tries to be the best person you can be,” Ducharme said.

The smile then disappears, and Ducharme goes quiet after he says:

“Although I’ve done some stupid s-​-​-, I don’t deserve this.”

Sukhbir Mann — ‘At the end of the day, this is a hard life’

Mann studied criminology at the University of Windsor, but was unable to finish his degree. He spoke of turning to alcohol and cannabis after a friend died, which had a detrimental effect on his mental health.

On New Year’s Day in 2013, he slashed a stranger’s face with a knife, in an unprovoked attack from behind in a gas station that included a Tim Hortons. He then threw his hot coffee on a woman. He was found NCR, and his diagnoses include schizophrenia, anti-social personality disorder and substance use disorders.

“Looking back, it’s wrong what I did,” he said.

Mann has spent most of his time in seclusion due to aggressive behaviour since being transferred to Waypoint in December 2013; his hospital records note that when he’s allowed out of his room, he eventually assaults someone. The records describe his attacks on staff as “opportunistic.”

He disputes that, chalking up his behaviour to the fact that he’s been locked in his room for so long.

“It’s f-​-​-ing mad pressure,” he said of being out of his room. “I get a hostile feeling because I’ve been locked for so long in one room and when I get out, I can’t frigging adjust to it.”

paragraphs: Barron Jenner moves close to the camera and describes the feeling of being held in seclusion in hospital.
“Anxious. Trapped. Stranded.”

It’s early August, and the 40-year-old is in his eleventh year of being detained at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care in Penetanguishene, the province’s only maximum-security psychiatric hospital with more than 300 patient beds.
He’s been an involuntary patient in various Ontario hospitals his entire adult life, after being found not criminally responsible (NCR) for mischief in 2004 at the age of 18.
His crime: standing in a Chatham-Kent restaurant and refusing to leave.
20 years in isolation: Part 1
Hamblett May be the person who has spent the most time in psychiatric seclusion in any Ontario hospital. In a four-part series, the Star

While the Star’s coverage this year has included interviews with lawyers, doctors, advocates and relatives of patients, this is the first time that the voices of those experiencing seclusion have been featured, offering a rare look at life inside Waypoint.
The four men have all been found NCR, some for non-violent incidents. Two of them, including Jenner, are presently out of seclusion, but all have experienced being in isolation for prolonged periods.
For Jenner, who has been diagnosed with schizophrenia and obsessive-compulsive disorder, it was months at a time. He said seclusion only makes him feel worse.
“It just bogs me down and makes me feel uncomfortable and unhappy and stuck in a trap,” he said. “I tell them I don’t like being in seclusion. They don’t usually ask what it feels like.”

Waypoint’s own policy states that seclusion is to be used as a last resort — and for as brief a time as possible — to deal with patients who pose an imminent risk of bodily harm to themselves or others. The Star’s investigation has revealed that Waypoint is keeping patients in seclusion for years, including Camelott Hamblett, who has been held for 20 years and counting .

The four patients spoke in August and September in the company of their lawyers, Golnaz Nayerahmadi and Pritpal Mann of Toronto firm Rochon Genova, which had tried to certify a class-action lawsuit against Waypoint; the courts dismissed the case, finding that seclusion is an individualized process and patients would have to bring individual claims. The firm is exploring other ways of pursuing the lawsuit.
“What’s it like being in seclusion? It’s not fun,” said patient Richard DeJong. “It feels like there’s no oxygen. It feels like you can’t breathe.”

The men described strikingly similar experiences: feeling that they’ve been placed in seclusion as punishment rather than because they were a threat; staff not checking on them regularly or telling them why their seclusion was being maintained each day; and being left in their room for days at a time without being escorted out for seclusion relief — even though hospital policies say staff must offer two hours a day.
They also spoke about staff failing to de-escalate when they’re in a state of crisis, and instead resorting to the nuclear option: seclusion.

“They’ll just push your buttons and make no effort to calm you down,” said Christopher Ducharme. “You’re gonna get even more angry. You’re gonna slam your fist or slam a door. You’re just gonna lose more and more self-control.”

Monteiro concluded that Waypoint appears to be using seclusion to pre-emptively manage seriously mentally ill patients who might become violent later, a practice she said is now prohibited in many prisons. She found that patients in prolonged seclusion are being held in conditions the United Nations has “deemed to constitute torture” in similar settings.
Craig Thompson has been “closely following” the Star’s investigation into the use of long-term seclusion at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care.

Waypoint is appealing that decision, with president and CEO Dr. Nadiya Sunderji saying the Orb’s orders “raise concerns about the board’s jurisdiction and intrusion upon both clinical decision-making and the management of hospital operations.”
Asked for a response regarding the experiences of the patients interviewed, Sunderji said she couldn’t comment due to patient confidentiality requirements.
“Person-centred care, reflecting the unique circumstances of each patient, is at the core of the work we do at Waypoint,” she said in a statement.
In the 13 years that Sukhbir Mann has spent mostly locked in seclusion at Waypoint, he’s written close to 500 poems.
One excerpt reads: “Sometimes, I come out of my room and don’t shower for weeks/I feel sometimes I’m losing my soul and at 41, my body is turning weak.”
Mann, who spoke to the Star on a tablet while in seclusion in his room, has been detained at Waypoint since being found NCR for a random knife attack in a Toronto gas station in 2013.
“I just keep thinking over and over about the things I’m going to do with my life,” he said.
Barron Jenner — ‘It’s very bland and dull and empty’

As he spoke, Jenner was polite and focused on giving a full picture of his life at Waypoint — “I think I covered most of the stuff, so you got an understanding, right?” He also spent several minutes making sure the camera angle was right as he was sketched over Zoom by artist Alexandra Newbould.
He described himself as someone who likes to have fun and is interested in “high energy stuff” — “I like to interact with people that I like and am close to.”

Jenner had had numerous run-ins with police over trespassing before his May 2004 arrest, which came after he locked himself in a restaurant bathroom, left after police arrived, then returned a short time later.
“Police were again called and upon arriving at the restaurant met Mr. Jenner, who was standing just inside it,” says a summary from the ORB. “Mr. Jenner was then arrested for mischief.”

Noting that Jenner has been “in the forensic system for over three decades,” the ORB ordered last year that he remain detained at Waypoint. Pointing to hospital records that Jenner had assaulted people at Waypoint in the past after going off his medication, the ORB found it was “highly likely” that if he no longer fell under the board’s jurisdiction, Jenner would again stop taking his medication and become violent.

Since being transferred to Waypoint in January 2016, he’s been “subjected to multiple periods of seclusion,” including several instances lasting more than 100 consecutive days, according to a 2022 affidavit from Jenner filed as part of the proposed class-action lawsuit. Sometimes, he was also put in restraints while in the room, even though he was locked in.
He described seclusion to the Star as a “waste of time,” where he does little more than lie in bed: “It’s very bland and dull and empty.”

Jenner feels he’s secluded as punishment for his behaviour, mainly swearing at staff. And while Waypoint policy mandates that staff check on secluded patients every 15 minutes, it’s more like once an hour, Jenner said.

He spent about 12 days in seclusion in March, after the hospital said he made repeated phone calls to the security office and became angry when prevented from making more calls. He yelled at staff and attempted to punch a staff member in the face, according to a hospital report.

The document does not indicate why Jenner’s seclusion was maintained each day. While he’ll generally be told the reason he’s initially put in seclusion, Jenner said he’s kept in the dark when his seclusion is maintained on a daily basis.
“I don’t feel like they have a reason, like day to day,” he said.

The hospital report says he accepted seclusion relief every day it was offered earlier this year, but on four days he got no time out of his room due to “operational requirements”; in her assessment, Monteiro found that Waypoint lacks the staff to provide meaningful seclusion relief to all secluded patients on a daily basis.
“The panel is directing Waypoint’s treatment of (Andrew Azevedo) to be in compliance with its

Jenner’s first interview with the Star in August happened after having just spent a night in seclusion; he said he swore at staff and asked, “want to fight?” after they cut off his access to the phone, when he maintained he still had time left.
That behaviour would not meet the standard of imminent risk of harm warranting seclusion, said U.S.-based psychologist Janice LeBel — “Hard stop.”
“It’s a strain on my body to be in there, for even short periods of time,” Jenner said of seclusion. “It’s especially strenuous on my mind. It feels torturous.”

Now that he’s no longer in seclusion, Jenner likes to go outside and watch music videos on the computer. Sitting in front of a wall covered in bumblebee stickers and the words “Bee-lieve in yourself,” Jenner talks about what he would do if he were no longer in hospital.
“I’d try to get a girlfriend and just try to make the most of my life.”
Richard DeJong — ‘I’m dying slowly in here’
As Richard DeJong puts it: “I’ve been locked up for over 23 years for stealing a car.”

The 53-year-old grandfather has been detained in hospitals since being found NCR in December 2002 for auto theft in Windsor and for leaping from the prisoner’s box in court following his arrest and setting off the fire alarm.

Diagnosed with treatment-resistant schizophrenia and alcohol-use disorder, he’s been held continuously at Waypoint since June 2020. He said in a 2022 affidavit he’d spent several prolonged periods in seclusion, including one instance of more than 60 consecutive days.
“In solitary confinement, I cannot help but think about all that I have missed out on in life, specifically time with my children and grandchildren,” he said in the affidavit.
DeJong, described by his doctor in medical records as “sexually preoccupied,” said in his interview he was held in seclusion last year for asking a staff member for a “blow job.”
“I’m stuck in here alone; I haven’t had a girlfriend in years,” he said. “I don’t know where my life is going. I wish I could have somebody to talk to.”

His hospital report notes he was secluded for a month last year due to his “escalating sexually inappropriate requests to female staff,” after he stopped taking clozapine, a medication used to treat schizophrenia when other drugs have failed. He was told that his comments made staff “very uncomfortable.”

Huckshorn and LeBel have said that things such as swearing, hurling insults at staff, and making sexualized comments — all said as a result of an underlying mental illness — would not meet the high threshold for seclusion.
Once placed in isolation, DeJong lamented that there’s a lack of clear explanation on what to do to get out.
“Like what’s your plan?” he said. “What steps do I have to do?”

DeJong has not been in seclusion so far this year; he’s no longer fighting with staff after restarting clozapine. In keeping DeJong at Waypoint, the ORB ruled this year that while he’s to be “congratulated” for returning to the medication, he will need to demonstrate a longer commitment to being treated before he can be potentially transferred to a less secure hospital.

He repeatedly returned to a much larger issue in his interview: the fact that people found NCR can find themselves serving indefinite sentences — “being warehoused” — if their condition isn’t deemed to have improved, potentially spending far longer in custody than a person convicted of the same offence.
“It does not make a difference if you are in seclusion or not. There is no release date,” he said. “I’m dying slowly in here. People’s lives are being stolen.”

DeJong said Waypoint should be shut down with severance paid to the staff. As for the patients, he said group homes should be established. He wants to work on setting them up and would like to live in one himself.
“I’m an honest guy,” he said. “I care about other people.”
If he wasn’t detained, he’d like to work in a motorcycle shop.
“I just like driving them,” he said. “Feel the freedom, you know?”
Christopher Ducharme — ‘They’ll push your buttons’

Ducharme spoke on a tablet from his room, which includes a window overlooking Georgian Bay and a mattress on the floor — at his request, as a proper bed would take up too much space and he likes to breakdance. Describing himself as a “very passionate entertainer,” he also spends his time drawing, writing music and doing magic tricks.
The 34-year-old, who has been diagnosed with schizophrenia and cannabis-use disorder, has been found NCR twice, both in Quebec.

In 2014, he left a Montreal restaurant without paying, stole a steak knife, then put it to a taxi driver’s throat, ordering him out of the vehicle and driving off. He was again found NCR for punching a hospital attendant in the face in 2016.

He’s been held continuously at Waypoint since 2018, where he insists on staying in seclusion as he weans himself off his antipsychotic medication, maintaining the drugs only made him more violent and aggressive. He doesn’t want to come out until he feels that he can safely be around other people.
“I feel amazing,” he said. “The thoughts of violence, the voices, are going away. Feelings of aggression haven’t completely gone away, but are dissipating significantly.”

The ORB decision from his latest hearing in May indicates he committed no violent incidents or displayed aggression over the previous year, yet he was kept in seclusion because he repeatedly told staff he felt the medication would make him dangerous and harm them.

Ducharme went off his medication after regaining the ability to make his own treatment decisions in June, when the Consent and Capacity Board overturned a finding made by Ducharme’s Waypoint psychiatrist, Dr. Craig Hudson, that he’s incapable of consenting to treatment. Hudson is appealing that decision.
Ducharme said it’s “sick” that a number of patients are being held involuntarily in prolonged seclusion; while Waypoint refuses to divulge a number, it’s understood to be at least a dozen.

He said many of the patients in seclusion are “harmless” while “some of them are actually dangerous,” but he believes that’s because “They’re being treated like monsters, because they’re continuously secluded.”
For the patients in the latter category, Ducharme proposed they have their own enclosed space, including a bit of the courtyard, along with a shower and a TV behind a screen that can’t be damaged.
“It would be like their own little house that’s just very secure,” he said.

Ducharme has also been placed in seclusion against his will, including when he first arrived at Waypoint and was in a state of crisis. In his affidavit, he said he was secluded for 317 consecutive days and would turn down the “rare” offers of seclusion relief because it meant being placed in restraints, which were a trigger for his anxiety.
In his interview, he spoke about staff not listening to him or trying to understand his behaviour. “They’ll push your buttons, bring up situations they know are going to piss you off,” he said.

One of the Six Core Strategies to reduce seclusion focuses on proper de-escalation. The staff behaviour described by Ducharme “sounds coercive and punitive — not therapeutic,” said LeBel, one of the strategies’ co-creators.
Ducharme said he wishes staff would have tried to understand what he needs when in crisis.
“More of a negotiation,” he said, as he thought back to his arrival at Waypoint: “Not once did anybody come to me and say, ‘Chris, what’s wrong? What can I do to help?’”
But Ducharme also acknowledged there are some really nice staff “who have done a lot for me.”

stories.summary: General Releases
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
Update – London, ON (October 17, 2026) – There will be an increased police presence in the Chelsea Green area while members of the London Police Service continue to search for George. Investigators are asking members of the public in the Chelsea Green area to search their properties, outbuildings and vehicles for George.

The missing vulnerable person is described as male, white, approximately 5’2” and 120lbs, blue eyes, and white balding hair. The missing person was last seen wearing a light blue shirt, dark blue striped jacket, casual pants, and a beige baseball cap.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Record $90-million Lotto Max jackpot up for grabs again Tuesday

Ontarians hoping to take home a record $90-million Lotto Max jackpot will have another chance next week.

A total of $119 million in prizes will be available to win in Tuesday’s draw, according to OLG.

stories.title: ‘Significant and tragic’ fire in Wainwright, Alta. spreading after starting near military base
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney posted on X Saturday night that “a serious incident creating a major fire” had occurred.
stories.author: Joshua Smith
stories.content:
A major blaze following a reported explosion at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta has led to “fatalities and injuries,” Canada’s defence minister told reporters Saturday night .

“I am saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident at the base,” Defence Minister David McGuinty said.

“I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory,” McGuinty said. He would not confirm there had been an explosion — nor the number of deaths and injuries — at the base when asked by reporters.

MP Dane Lloyd, who represents the Parkland riding west of Edmonton, said in Facebook post that an “explosion and fire during these high winds has resulted in significant casualties” at the base, southeast of Edmonton.

CFB Wainwright, located 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, is one of Canada’s busiest and is used mainly to train soldiers and prepare units for combat operations.

McGuinty added that he would have more to say “in the coming hours and days.” He said the RCMP are also involved.

“This is an active and delicate situation and soon to be an active and delicate investigation.”

As McGuinty delivered the news, fire crews in Alberta were battling a blaze raging between the base and the nearby town of Wainwright.

Asked if the town was threatened by the fire, McGuinty said he understands people there are helping the base with the injured and the fire.

Firefighters in the area faced a volatile situation after large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 km/ that toppled trees and sent signs flying.

CFB Wainwright is a massive military training base located 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton. It’s one Canada’s busiest and is used mainly to train soldiers and prepare units for combat operations.

It’s also the site of the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which prepares military units to operate together in realistic battlefield conditions, as well as the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides basic infantry training.

Alberta RCMP spokesperson Cpl. Gina Slaney said in a statement that Wainwright RCMP responded to a request for assistance at CFB Wainwright at about 4 p.m., and that early reports were that there was a fire at a training area.

“The RCMP sent numerous resources to assist,” the statement said. “Our initial involvement is winding down, though we still have resources available if needed. Any further details regarding the incident will come from the Canadian Armed Forces.”

“A large fire originating near the Canadian Forces Base has spread rapidly due to high winds and has crossed into the Municipal District of Wainwright No. 61,” the Municipal District of Wainwright wrote in a post on social media .

“Emergency responders are actively assessing the situation and working to protect people, property, and critical infrastructure,” the post read. The municipality wrote in a subsequent post that there is “no evacuation order at this time.”

“The fire south of Wainwright crossed the base fence earlier today and is being actively managed,” the town added.

Multiple agencies are responding to the fire, Wainwright Fire & Rescue said in a social media post of its own.

Prime Minister Mark Carney posted on X Saturday night that “a serious incident creating a major fire” occurred at CFB Wainwright, while extending his thoughts to those affected.

“We are working closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities,” Carney wrote, adding that he and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith “are in close contact as are our relevant ministers and officials.”

A serious incident creating a major fire has occurred at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta. Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected. We are working closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities. Premier Smith and I are in close contact as are our relevant ministers and officials. — Mark Carney (@MarkJCarney) October 18, 2026

Smith also posted Saturday night about what she called “a significant and tragic fire” at the base “that is affecting many of our brave military personnel.”

Smith echoed Carney’s statement that the provincial and federal governments are in “close contact” over the incident. She also thanked first responders and those providing care and support to those affected.

We are learning of a significant and tragic fire at CFB Wainwright today that is affecting many of our brave military personnel. Alberta’s government is in close contact with the Government of Canada and Prime Minister Mark Carney as this situation evolves. Thank you to the first responders and all those providing care and support to those affected. — Danielle Smith (@ABDanielleSmith) October 18, 2026

The town of Wainwright is in Conservative Party leader Pierre Poilievre’s riding of Battle River—Crowfoot.

“Pray for Wainwright, everyone,” Poilievre wrote on social media . He also thanked first responders and said he’s spoken to Carney and McGuinty to those in the base and in the community.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe wrote in a post that his province has sent resources to Alberta and is ready to provide more if required to assist in responding to the incident.

Federal Minister of Emergency Management Eleanor Olszewski wrote in a post that she was “deeply distressed and thinking of everyone at CFB Wainwright and the families anxiously awaiting news about their loved ones.”

Olszewski wrote that she’s been in contact with her Alberta counterpart, Mike Ellis, the province’s deputy premier and minister of public safety and emergency services. Ellis reposted Smith’s X post Saturday night and added that he’s keeping everyone in his thoughts .

Elections Alberta has closed the Wainwright Communiplex advance voting location for Monday’s referendum after being informed of the fire, the agency said in a news release.

Ballot boxes and materials from Wainright are being moved securely, Elections Alberta said.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Dissident Turkish author says she was unable to enter Canada for book tour
stories.summary: Ece Temelkuran’s travel difficulties arose just as Prime Minister Mark Carney is due to visit Turkey
stories.author: Steven Chase
stories.content:
A dissident Turkish author says she was unable to obtain authorization to enter Canada for a book tour due to begin Saturday.

Ece Temelkuran’s 2019 book, How to Lose a Country: The 7 Steps from Democracy to Facism , is among the writings that have earned her international acclaim.

Her travel difficulty arises just as Prime Minister Mark Carney is due to travel to Turkey next week to deepen ties with the government of Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Freedom House, a U.S.-based democracy watchdog, said in its 2026 report that Mr. Erdogan, who has led Turkey as prime minister or president for more than 20 years, has grown increasingly authoritarian over the past decade, including imprisoning political opponents and independent journalists.

Ms. Temelkuran was supposed to visit Calgary and Vancouver where she was going to talk about her latest book on homelessness: Nation of Strangers: Rebuilding Home in the 21st Century .

“Today I was supposed to travel to Canada but unfortunately I wasn’t issued” an authorization, she said in a message to The Globe and Mail.

She said she holds a European Union country’s citizenship and EU citizens normally only require a Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) from the Canadian government if arriving by air. Ms. Temelkuran said she had expected the ETA within 72 hours but it never arrived.

She said she received a follow-up message last week regarding her application which asked if she had “replied to the below question truthfully: Have you been denied entry by any country?”

Ms. Temelkuran said she’d never been denied entry by any country.

The author left Turkey in 2016, in the aftermath of a failed military coup attempt that the government blamed on a U.S.-based cleric. A crackdown by Ankara followed, closing media outlets and jailing journalists. She now lives mainly in Berlin.

The author has provided writers festival organizers with a statement to read in her absence.

“Dear strangers in Canada,” part of her statement said. “I’ve written a book declaring that we are all becoming homeless. That the world is unhoming all of us, one way or another, physically, politically, morally and spiritually.”

She said: “We, the immigrants, exiles, refugees, and the homeless, are only the scouts of the human condition- moving only a bit ahead of the rest.”

Calgary’s Wordfest said on its website that “Ece Temelkuran is unable to join us this year due to unexpected delays in receiving her Canadian travel authorization.”

And the Vancouver Writers Fest similarly on its website said Ms. Temelkuran “is unfortunately no longer able to join us in-person due to an unforeseen visa delay.” It said she would be making a virtual appearance instead for one of the talks she was originally scheduled to join.

Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab’s office did not immediately respond to queries on Friday about the travel authorization difficulties faced by the Turkish author.

-With files from Doug Saunders in Toronto

stories.title: Mark Carney makes final pitch for Canadian unity ahead of Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney pushed a message of Canadian unity for an Edmonton crowd of over five thousand people Friday night.
stories.author: Liam Newbigging
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney pushed a message of Canadian unity for a hometown crowd of over five thousand people Friday night, while encouraging people to vote for Alberta to remain in Canada in Monday’s referendum.

At the Edmonton Expo Centre, Carney boasted of the benefits Canada provides for the province and warned of the risks Alberta’s separation could pose during a time when the world is becoming more dangerous and divided.

“There are some outside our borders working to break us, so they can own us,” Carney said.

He also warned people not to think any outcome was assured, and urged people to vote and bring others out to do the same.

The rally comes days before a historic vote for the province, as Albertans will have their say on five questions related to immigration, four questions related to constitutional changes and one on separation.

Carney has been touring the province ahead of the vote, making stops across Calgary, Red Deer and Edmonton.

He was met with a wall of applause and stomping feet when he walked on-stage to the Sam Roberts Band’s “We’re all in This Together.”

He told the crowd what he thought of the welcome, saying, “I was at an event in Calgary, and it was fantastic. But this is Edmonton. This is the city of champions.”

Repeating the sentiment he delivered to Calgary Thursday night, he said he believed this to be the worst time for a referendum, and that it would be foolish to gamble with the province’s future, “just to send a message.”

Still, his speech was loaded with regional references, like his childhood skating rink in Laurier Heights, Boyle Street Community Services, and the Edmonton Oilers .

In his bid for Albertans to vote to remain in Canada, Carney didn’t shy away from the energy topic and Alberta’s past grievances with the federal government.

“The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” Carney said. “Growing up, I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own, and more recently, we were made to feel that our energy contributions were running against the tides of history.”

“Canada isn’t perfect. But we are the best.”

“And we are getting better,” he added, saying that Alberta is at the centre of his government’s nation-building plans.

He touted plans to spend more on local infrastructure, and how the Pacific Link pipeline became the first item for his major projects office. He said Alberta will help unlock Canada’s full “energy potential” and reduce the country’s dependence on the U.S.

Those sentiments around energy issues were shared by some in the audience.

John Buie said he spent much of his career in the oil industry, working in Fort McMurray. While he’s fully in support of staying in Canada, he said he understands some of the anger Albertans feel.

“You had Trudeau senior, and there was a lot of anger, and rightfully so,” John said, alluding to Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau’s national energy program and the rage it fueled in the oil industry.

“I understand some of the sentiment about how Alberta is being treated. But separation’s not the answer,” John said.

While Carney headlined the rally, Forever Canadian leader Thomas Lukaszuk, retired CBC radio host Mark Connolly, and hockey legend Kevin Lowe all added words of support for Canadian unity. Former Premier Rachel Notley also sent a recorded video message.

Lukaszuk told the crowd that they were making history.

“Fifty to 150 years from now, our children and our grandchildren will be studying about this in their social studies classes,” he said.

Mayor Andrew Knack asked the crowd to also consider the nine other questions, including those on immigration. He argued those questions were meant to divide Albertans, and referenced the city’s famous Heritage Festival as an example of strong diversity in Edmonton.

He also said that the referendum removes focus from “real priorities” that the province should be addressing.

“I believe Edmontonians would rather see Premier Smith spend their money on new schools,” Knack said. “Or maybe a new hospital.”

The audience responded to Knack, chanting “no to nine.”

Saturday marks the last day people can vote in the advance polls ahead of referendum day. Elections Alberta is expecting a strong turnout, estimating between 80 and 85 percent of registered voters will cast a vote.

As of Friday night, more than one million Albertans had cast votes. Voting stations open at 9 a.m. Monday and close at 8 p.m.

stories.title: Health Ministers secure funding extensions from Ottawa, but long-term commitments remain in limbo
stories.summary: Federal health minister declines to make any commitments beyond what she described as ‘bridge dollars’ until further negotiations, including for the Canada Health Transfer
stories.author: Temur Durrani, Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
By the end of a two-day interjurisdictional meeting, Canada’s provincial and territorial health ministers were able to receive assurances on funding extensions from Ottawa, but will need to convene again before 2027 to confirm the future of expiring transfer programs.

Federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel declined to make any commitments on Friday beyond what she described as “bridge dollars” until further negotiations, including for the Canada Health Transfer, the country’s primary vehicle for provincial and territorial funding.

“The work is starting today. It’s not like a big announcement – it’s a bridging,” Ms. Michel said in Winnipeg, where ministers from across Canada gathered to meet their counterparts this week, as they attempted to reach a consensus on issues related to health care.

Despite jurisdictional differences on many policies, such as the privatization of health care and access to medical assistance in dying, the ministers presented a united front against challenges that have been bogging down Canada’s strained hospitals and medical facilities. Their most wholehearted agreement, the ministers told reporters, was on the need for longer-term and stable commitments from the federal government.

Ms. Michel, however, answered the ministers calls by saying that the federal budget cycle has changed. Traditionally, the government’s fiscal blueprint has been tabled in the spring, but it will arrive in the House of Commons this fall, a date for which has not yet been announced.

Securing an agreement from Ottawa to extend funding for mental health, substance-use treatment and home care had been a key priority for the provincial and territorial ministers.

They issued warnings for weeks leading up to their meeting, repeatedly calling out Ottawa’s silence on programs set to expire next year, portraying the expiration as a potential spending cut that would affect multitudinous parts of the health sector.

But on the night before their meeting, Ms. Michel announced via social media late Wednesday that her government will extend those expiring programs for at least one year, which she said would represent $1.2-billion in funding.

Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones said the temporary change came at the last minute and lacked clarity. “Respectfully, I would say that a one-year extension of an existing 10-year [agreement] about to expire does not fill us with a lot of joy,” she said Thursday.

On Friday, Uzoma Asagwara, Manitoba’s health minister, said officials were pleased to see Ms. Michel “asking really important questions, getting clarification, and really hearing our concerns and pledging their support to work with us.”

Mx. Asagwara added that, as a direct result of Friday’s discussions, another interjurisdictional meeting will take place by December this year.

Provincial and territorial health ministers want the Canada Health Transfer to grow at a minimum of 5 per cent annually, rather than the 3-per-cent growth rate it is expected to reach in 2028, Mx. Asagwara said.

Ms. Michel assured the health ministers that the next stage of discussions will be on funding through the Canada Health Transfer and other bilateral agreements.

The Canadian Medical Association and the Canadian Nurses Association, both of which were in Winnipeg as well, said they wish there was more clarity from Ottawa this week.

“We really need to see a more sustainable path towards funding and staffing for our nurses and physicians,” said Valerie Grdisa, chief executive of the CNA, in an interview. “We can’t really actually plan anything without those proper commitments.”

Speaking on behalf of all 13 territories and provinces as the meeting’s host, Mx. Asagwara said several other topics had come up during the ministerial discussions, such as targeted care for Indigenous communities and equitable access in the pharmaceutical sector.

But recent federal changes toward medical assistance in dying, commonly referred to as Maid, which were expected to be discussed, were not a major factor this week.

Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser said last week that Ottawa intends to introduce legislation to bar Maid for patients whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness.

He said the federal government intends to amend the Criminal Code to legally decriminalize the provision of Maid where there is an advance request. It allows patients to formalize their wishes ahead of when they no longer have the capacity to offer consent to end their lives by Maid.

Ottawa’s approach, however, will not mean that Canadians across the country would automatically be able to make advance requests once the bill becomes law. It will be up to each province and territory to decide whether it will offer that choice and to determine the framework for that.

Mr. Fraser has not provided further details on the bill, while Ms. Michel declined to address the matter Friday.

National consultations, conducted from November 2024 to February 2025 by the federal government on advance requests found that a majority of Canadians are supportive of advance requests.

Mr. Fraser said he expects conversations on Maid to unfold at the provincial level.

But Ms. Jones from Ontario said federal, provincial and territorial ministers did not have those discussions this week. Ms. Michel offered a small update related to Maid on Friday that was “helpful,” Ms. Jones said, without providing further details.

In October, 2024, Quebec became the only Canadian jurisdiction to allow patients diagnosed with a serious and incurable illness that leads to incapacity – such as Alzheimer’s – to apply in advance for Maid. Ottawa did not challenge Quebec’s law, but it did not change the Criminal Code either.

Sonia Bélanger, Quebec’s health minister, who was also in Winnipeg this week, declined to comment on the matter.

Ms. Jones said Ontario is “very appreciative” that the federal government does not plan to expand access to Maid. “Moving forward, we will obviously individually assess for how it impacts our residents provincially and territorially.”

stories.title: London Knights beat Sudbury Wolves 4-1 on home ice
stories.summary: The London Knights earned a 4-1 win over the Sudbury Wolves on home ice, scoring twice in the third period to secure the victory.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
The London Knights earned a 4-1 win over the Sudbury Wolves on home ice, scoring twice in the third period to secure the victory.

Marcus Nordmark opened the scoring for London at 18:00 of the first period.

Cohen Bidgood added to the lead at 17:29 of the second period, giving the Knights a 2-0 advantage heading into the final frame.

Jaxon Cover scored at 3:23 of the third period before Adam Nemec found the back of the net at 8:38 to make it 4-0.

Cooper McAslan scored for Sudbury to put the Wolves on the board.

London outshot Sudbury 32-26 and won 38 faceoffs compared with 18 for the Wolves.

stories.title: Delayed municipal funding for homeless services having predictable impact in the Old East Village
stories.summary: Months after city council allowed municipal bridge funding to expire for some frontline homelessness services, this week a procurement process re-allocated $350,000 between four agencies.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Months after city council allowed municipal bridge funding to expire for some frontline homelessness services, this week a procurement process re-allocated $350,000 between four agencies.

On Wednesday, the Executive Director of Ark Aid Street Mission Sarah Campbell told CTV News about conditions in the Old East Village (OEV) since municipal funding stopped on July 31 and the agency had to slash daytime drop-in spaces and hours.

“Pressure has actually intensified as the number of people on the street is growing and the services are reducing,” Campbell explained.

She says without municipal funding for an encampment support strategy, people living in encampments relocated to the OEV to meet their basic needs like food and bathrooms.

At the same time, the growing number of unsheltered Londoners arriving in the business district discovered that the capacity of daytime drop-in shelters had been greatly reduced when municipal funding wasn’t renewed.

The result has been a greater number of homeless Londoners on Dundas Street and in the nearby alleys and parking lots.

The current situation can be traced back to funding uncertainty six months ago.

On March 31, the federal government’s Unsheltered Homelessness and Encampments Initiative (Uhei) expired.

The next day, it was announced that the fund would be renewed-- but the federal government’s timeline to disburse the money was uncertain.

In response, council provided $350,000 of bridge funding (until July 31) to extend daytime drop-in space at The Ark and encampment outreach services by 519Pursuit.

It was early August when the federal government notified City Hall that it would receive $2.5 million from the renewed Uhei fund, but council directed most of that money ($2.1 million) towards the upcoming Winter Response to Homelessness, and a municipal reserve account that had been the source of stopgap funding for The Ark and 519Pursuit was reimbursed with the remaining $350,000.

At the time, Council also directed staff to conduct a fair and transparent procurement process to determine how the $350,000 could best be utilized by frontline agencies.

Recently a report to the Community and Protective Services Committee recommended dividing those dollars four-ways:

519Pursuit street outreach and system navigation services ($100,000)

The Salvation Army London Centre of Hope for enhanced shower and basic-needs access

Ark Aid Street Mission for the stabilization of drop-in services ($130,000)

However, ON Wednesday Coun. Susan Stevenson objected to the use of municipal dollars to fund the services that would be provided on the main street of the OEV Business Improvement Area (BIA), in accordance with a previous direction by Council.

“Ark Aid used to be a volunteer charity organization, and now these organizations are becoming taxpayer-funded contracts at a time when people need shelter beds,” Stevenson told council colleagues. “They need a space to sleep at night. The other stuff the public can, and is willing to, do through charity.”

Despite Stevenson’s objections, a majority of council supported dividing the funds four-ways.

After the meeting, Campbell responded to Stevenson’s comment.

“The assertion was these services have been provided by volunteers in the past,” Campbell explained. “The truth is they’re provided by organizations with the help of volunteers. But we can’t rely on volunteers alone to do this work.”

The Ark had submitted three proposals totaling $548,716 to the procurement process to demonstrate what the agency believes is the coordinated system response needed at this time.

“This is a fractional improvement,” Campbell said about the $130,000 approved by council. “This is adding one or two staff so we could have 20 or 30 more people come inside for a period of time. It does not cover the costs.”

Since the bridge funding expired, The Ark’s limited drop-in hours have been funded through public donations and with the support of volunteers.

Campbell emphasizes it will be is being left to the generosity of donors to cover the remaining costs related to the drop-in service.

The Salvation Army London Centre of Hope for enhanced shower and basic-needs access
Ark Aid Street Mission for the stabilization of drop-in services ($130,000)

However, ON Wednesday Coun. Susan Stevenson objected to the use of municipal dollars to fund the services that would be provided on the main street of the OEV Business Improvement Area (BIA), in accordance with a previous direction by Council.

“Ark Aid used to be a volunteer charity organization, and now these organizations are becoming taxpayer-funded contracts at a time when people need shelter beds,” Stevenson told council colleagues. “They need a space to sleep at night. The other stuff the public can, and is willing to, do through charity.”
Despite Stevenson’s objections, a majority of council supported dividing the funds four-ways.
After the meeting, Campbell responded to Stevenson’s comment.

“The assertion was these services have been provided by volunteers in the past,” Campbell explained. “The truth is they’re provided by organizations with the help of volunteers. But we can’t rely on volunteers alone to do this work.”
The Ark had submitted three proposals totaling $548,716 to the procurement process to demonstrate what the agency believes is the coordinated system response needed at this time.

“This is a fractional improvement,” Campbell said about the $130,000 approved by council. “This is adding one or two staff so we could have 20 or 30 more people come inside for a period of time. It does not cover the costs.”
Since the bridge funding expired, The Ark’s limited drop-in hours have been funded through public donations and with the support of volunteers.
Campbell emphasizes it will be is being left to the generosity of donors to cover the remaining costs related to the drop-in service.
