stories.title: Smith, Carney rally support for Alberta to remain in Canada ahead of referendum
stories.summary: Political leaders from across the country, including Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, rally in province to boost pro-Canada vote
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
The campaign to keep Alberta in Confederation hit a fever pitch on Friday as politicians from across the country crisscrossed the province, aiming to drive up turnout and boost the pro-Canada vote ahead of Monday’s referendum on secession.

Premier Danielle Smith stood beside Prime Minister Mark Carney at a federalist rally in Red Deer. The two have shared a stage on numerous occasions over the past year in their bid to build a bitumen pipeline to the West Coast, a plan both leaders have endorsed as a sign that Canada can work for Alberta.

“As you know, we don’t always agree on everything. We often disagree quite publicly on several things,” Ms. Smith told a crowd of pro-Canada supporters decked in red and white.

“But today we can all agree that on Question 10, that we are voting for Option 1 to remain in Canada.”

A day earlier, a crack appeared in the thawing relationship between Mr. Carney and Ms. Smith, when he urged Albertans to vote “no to the nine,” referring to the Premier’s nine proposals on immigration and constitutional changes also on Monday’s referendum ballot.

But the Premier, who had responded on social media, stood her ground on her plan to wrest more control over immigration from Ottawa.

“I have bad news for you, Prime Minister: All of the premiers are interested in talking about immigration and how we might be able to reform it,” she told Mr. Carney in Red Deer, handing him Alberta government literature advertising her proposals.

Former Alberta premier Ed Stelmach, who co-authored an op-ed this week also calling for voters to reject Ms. Smith’s immigration questions , stood next to her.

Ms. Smith says she is seeking to fortify her mandate by getting the electorate’s approval on those questions, which she argues would provide leverage to gain more autonomy within Confederation.

Those questions propose restricting some newcomers’ access to social services and charging some non-permanent residents for their access to health and education.

The gathering in Red Deer was one of several events on Friday where politicians made the case for a united Canada.

At a rally in Edmonton in the evening, Mr. Carney delivered a speech very similar to the one he gave the night before in Calgary, reminding Albertans to “vote like Canada depends on it.” He walked up to the lectern to We’re all in this together by the Sam Roberts Band.

Prime Minister Mark Carney told thousands rallying in Calgary on Thursday that Albertans should vote to keep the province in Canada.

The Canadian Press

The Prime Minister spoke of how the province and the city is his home, where he grew up and that the future of the country is “too precious to play games with.”

“This referendum is about something larger than any of us,” he said at an event organized by Forever Canadian, one of the province’s most prominent federalist groups. “It is about the province and country we love, and it’s about what we can build together.”

Mr. Carney reiterated a point he made the night before, saying that recently Albertans were made to feel their “energy contributions were running against the tides of history.”

“What should have brought us together began to divide us. Contributing to a half-century of politics that have too often pulled us apart.”

Mr. Carney went on to tout the plan to build the Pacific Link pipeline, which he described as “true nation building.”

“Now is the time to build, not break. Now it’s our turn to stand up for Canada.”

Ms. Smith followed up her lunchtime appearance alongside Mr. Carney with a keynote address and on-stage conversation at the Canada Strong and Free Network conference, a conservative gathering, in downtown Calgary.

Ms. Smith struck a positive tone on her relationship with Mr. Carney’s government, saying that Alberta and Ottawa are “moving together,” and spent much of the on-stage conversation discussing conservative party politics.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, at the same conference earlier in the day, made his case to Albertans to reject choosing a second, binding separation referendum.

Mr. Poilievre argued that many of the frustrations Albertans feel are no different from those shared by Canadians across the country.

He pointed to concerns about immigration, affordability and energy policy as the issues driving separatism.

“Much of this referendum debate has rightly focused on the flaws of the country. But while we focus on those things, we must not forget – and we must not ignore – what Canada has done for Alberta,” he told the crowd of roughly 200 people.

“But here’s the thing: there are Canadians right across the country that wonder the very same things,” Mr. Poilievre said.

Some leaders in Alberta’s separatist movement argue that Monday’s referendum is a chance to voice dissatisfaction with Ottawa or use the threat of separation to extract concessions from the federal government.

On Friday, Mr. Poilievre offered a patriotic appeal to voters, saying it was not the best vehicle for protesting policies from Ottawa.

“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation, I say this: Canada is more than a government. It is a people, a flag, a land, a history, a promise.”

While Mr. Poilievre didn’t mention Ms. Smith’s nine other referendum questions, he encouraged voters to “lock arms with Quebeckers who want to have full autonomy over their provincial jurisdiction, just like we Albertans do.”

Conservative MP Dane Lloyd, the man spearheading the party’s pro-Canada campaign, told The Globe and Mail that the Conservatives’ door-knocking campaign has met few big-city Albertans who are voting for a second referendum. Support for a separation vote is higher in rural areas, he said, but they’re still “overwhelmingly pro-Canada.”

Mr. Lloyd said he’s expecting high turnout. He thinks that bodes well for the federalist camp.

“I would like to see a very decisive, high number. I think we need a very high number,” he said on the sidelines of the conference.

Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney, speaking to reporters at the conference, credited Mr. Carney with his campaign strategy leading into the referendum.

He pointed to the Prime Minister’s push for an oil pipeline to the West Coast, which was preceded by rolling back numerous energy and environmental policies implemented under former prime minister Justin Trudeau. Mr. Kenney added that it was “powerful” to hear Mr. Carney refer to himself as an Albertan. (Mr. Carney was raised in Edmonton.)

“I think he’s played it just about right. He’s not been here constantly, and he’s not telling us, telling Albertans how to think or what to do,” he said.

“He’s one of us; he’s saying, ‘Let’s get this done together.’”

The crowd at Friday night’s Forever Canadian rally in Edmonton brought roughly 5,500 federalist supporters, where people wrapped themselves in Canadian flags and danced to hits by one of Canada’s biggest country stars, Shania Twain.

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack, speaking to the crowd before Mr. Carney took the stage, encouraged people to vote against the other nine referendum question. The crowd responded by chanting, ‘No to the nine.’

Barb Anderson, a 56-year-old military veteran, wore a white sweater with ‘Canada’ emblazoned on it. She singled out the immigration questions, which, among other things, would restrict social services to certain classes of newcomers.

Josue Hernandez, 20, a student in human geography and political science, said talk about separation is “overall a horrible idea.”

“I think it’s extremely stupid.”

Daisy Nellis, 19, a University of Alberta political science student, said she is from Grande Prairie, a conservative-leaning city northwest of Edmonton, and so she was “happy to see that people are coming out.” She hoped that Mr. Carney would speak out strongly not just about separatism, but also about the other nine questions.

“It’s time for him to step up and be a leader about the nine,” Ms. Nellis said, prompting cheers from her friends.

Albertans continued to vote at advance polls on Friday. Saturday is the final day of early voting before referendum day on Monday.

Roughly a million Albertans had voted in the referendum as of 10:30 p.m. on Thursday night – about a third of all electors in the province – Elections Alberta wrote in an e-mail.

With reports from Tyler Dawson

stories.title: Tackling Toronto congestion May be a key issue for mayoral candidates, but it’s not all bad
stories.summary: Indicators show that gridlock has lessened in the past few years
stories.author: Patrick White
stories.content:
With 10 days remaining in a campaign where Toronto’s notoriously clogged roads have been a central issue, the City has released figures that could shift the tone of the mayoral debate.

A key indicator the municipality uses to measure traffic congestion has actually declined in recent years, according to numbers provided to The Globe and Mail, countering some campaign rhetoric and a deepening sense in Toronto and beyond that gridlock has become one of the city’s defining features.

“The trend over the last few years is showing that congestion is decreasing,” Andrew Posluns, Toronto’s chief congestion officer, said in an e-mail.

Such a mundane statement qualifies as provocation in a metropolis that, just three years ago, had the worst traffic in North America, according to the Amsterdam-based geolocation company TomTom.

But Mr. Posluns has the data to back it up.

Like many cities worldwide, Toronto uses a measurement called Travel Time Index (TTI) to record congestion levels within city limits. The index is a ratio comparing rush-hour travel times with free-flow speeds.

A TTI of 2.00, for example, would mean that a trip takes twice as long at peak traffic as the same trip when there’s no traffic.

This July, the most recent period for which figures were provided, Toronto’s city-wide TTI was 1.587. During same month last year, the TTI was 1.698. And in July, 2024, it was 1.738.

That recent improvement is incremental, but it’s a substantial reduction from 2.324 in June, 2018, when Toronto recorded it’s highest monthly TTI out of the 11 full years of figures provided to The Globe.

Toronto uses navigation data from a third-party vendor to calculate the indicator. The city also provided TTI figures for the downtown core dating back to 2019. They show a similar decrease of late.

It’s not an anomalous finding. Since its first-place showing as having the worst congestion among TomTom’s continentwide city rankings in 2023, Toronto clocked in at ninth place in 2025. Inrix, a traffic analytics firm, places Toronto as the 13th-worst among North American cities in the same year, with average peak speeds actually improving by 1.6 km/h since 2023.

So, things are better, but still not great.

The spreadsheets provided by the city give no explanation for why the TTI has dropped, and Mr. Posluns was unavailable for an interview. He did say by e-mail that the city has increased traffic agents on roads, reduced construction closures and adjusted transit signal priorities.

Construction is typically the biggest contributor to gridlock in the city, according to a city congestion management document, which states that, as of July, 2024, 18 per cent of Toronto road capacity was closed for construction.

That could help explain the recent decline, with major projects on the Gardiner Expressway and Eglinton Avenue wrapping up in recent years.

Gridlock has emerged as a top voter concern in multiple polls and the leading mayoral candidates have sparred over plans to address the problem with a combination of road and transit improvements.

Mayor Olivia Chow’s campaign has touted a number of recent traffic measures. She landed a $73-million deal with the province to expedite Gardiner rehabilitation, established a Scarborough Busway, restored prepandemic service levels across much of TTC, hired 127 traffic agents and hired the first congestion czar, Mr. Posluns, the campaign said.

In another term, she’s proposing to drive up TTC usage by offering free rides after 10 weekly trips and improving transit signal priority.

A spokesman for Brad Bradford, Ms. Chow’s main challenger in the Oct. 26 election, said the candidate welcomes any progress on roads, but that small improvements are nothing to celebrate.

Mr. Bradford will be announcing further congestion plans in coming days, according to the campaign, including a seven-point strategy focusing on adaptive traffic controls, overnight construction, faster streetcar service, bike lane construction on quiet roads and AI pothole detection.

There is a glass-half-full way to look at overall traffic in the city, which remains enervating despite recent progress.

Congestion is a sign of a successful city, said Eric Miller, a University of Toronto professor specializing in transportation engineering. “Throughout history, cities have been congested places,” he said. “The whole point of cities is to bring people together so they can get congested, so they can interact.”

Part of Toronto’s seemingly intractable problem is that the regional population has grown by 100,000-plus people a year for the past two decades without commensurate investment in roads and transit.

“If you go back to the 50s and 60s, we were building transit for the 80s,” he said. “And in the 1980s, things were looking good, so we stopped building transit even though we didn’t stop growing.”

In the 90s, then-premier Mike Harris cut off operating subsidies to local transit. “We haven’t had the money to properly maintain the TTC since then let alone grow it over time,” Dr. Miller said. “You get what you pay for, and we haven’t paid for transit.”

stories.title: Millions in funding put toward Manitoba First Nations Police, safety officers
stories.summary: Manitoba First Nations police and safety officers will receive $163.5 million from the provincial and federal government, but some First Nation leaders say it's not enough.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
The Manitoba First Nations Police Service (Mfnps) and safety officers will receive a total of $163.5 million from the provincial and federal governments, but some First Nation leaders say it’s not enough and are hoping for more support.

Mfnps is getting $121 million over four years, while the Manitoba First Nations Safety Officer Program will get $42.5 million to expand its program, making it accessible for any community that wants it.

“Where someone lives should not determine the level of policing or investigational services they receive,” said Mfnps Police Chief Jason Colon. “The expectations placed on our police service are the same as the expectations placed on any other police service in Manitoba, but we need the capacity to meet those expectations.”

Manto Sipi Cree Nation relies on safety officers to respond to crime and potentially detain any suspect, while they wait for the nearest RCMP detachment to fly into their community, said Chief Michael Yellowback. The nearest RCMP station is more than 50 kilometres away. RCMP response time can lag up to three hours during the winter as officers trek through winter roads, said Yellowback.

Indigenous leaders have long been advocating for funding, as safety officers are the first line of defence scanning who and what is coming in and out of a community.

“There’s 63 first nations in Manitoba and $42 million won’t go a long way,” he said. “I’m hoping it’s a win-win situation for everybody, especially for our community, because our First Nation officers need that much needed training and equipment.”

Long Plain First Nation Chief David Meeches said his community received around $1 million for the safety of its community and is appreciative of the funding from the government, so they can put resources in other needs, but there needs to be ongoing support.

“We need to go beyond today’s announcement. We need to go beyond and seek continued support,” said Meeches.

stories.title: Kenney says UCP must ‘lay down the law’ with separatist members, Smith skirts question on enforcement
stories.summary: Danielle Smith said she won't decide how to handle separatist sentiment in the UCP party until after the referendum votes are counted.
stories.author: Noah Brennan
stories.content:
With Albertans preparing to head to the polls Monday, questions are mounting over how Premier Danielle Smith will navigate divisions within the United Conservative Party over Alberta separation in the aftermath of the referendum.

A Leger poll released last week suggested UCP supporters are almost evenly divided on the separation question, raising questions about whether the party’s membership can get back on the same page following the Oct. 19 vote.

Former premier Jason Kenney, who founded the UCP in 2017, says the party must enforce its founding commitment to a “strong Alberta within a united Canada,” suggesting the party’s leadership could screen out separatist candidates and potentially expel members who violate its core principles.

“When I created the UCP in 2017, it was with a clear commitment to a federalist party supporting (a) strong Alberta in a united Canada,” Kenney told reporters at a Canada Strong and Free Network event in Calgary on Friday.

“If there are folks who want to advocate for separatism, they have every right as citizens to do so in separatist parties.”

Kenney said the UCP leadership has a responsibility to “lay down the law” with members who are “not committed to the core principles of the party,” including its commitment to Canadian unity.

He pointed to his own tenure as party leader, saying prospective UCP candidates with a history of advocating for Alberta separation were barred from running under the party’s banner.

“We invalidated all of them. Just said ‘no, sorry,’” he said. “You can’t bring separatism into it to represent us on the ballot.”

His comments come as the party faces an increasingly apparent divide over Alberta’s future, with polling suggesting a substantial portion of its supporters favour beginning the process toward a second, binding referendum on separation.

Smith, who addressed attendees at the same event shortly after Kenney’s remarks, acknowledged that “loyalty to a united Canada” is among the Ucp’s founding principles.

But when asked whether she would take steps similar to those described by her predecessor — including screening out separatist candidates or expelling members who violate the party’s principles — Smith stopped short of making any commitment.

She suggested the outcome of Monday’s referendum would help determine how the party approaches members who might waver in their commitment to national unity following Monday’s vote.

If the government receives “affirmation” that remaining committed to a united Canada is a principle Albertans want the party to maintain, Smith said it would do so.

Pressed on whether that could mean taking enforcement action against members who continue to advocate for separation, the premier deferred an answer until after the vote.

“I don’t want to prejudge how people are going to interpret the result on Monday,” Smith said.

“Maybe ask me that on October 20th once I have a chance to see what people’s reaction is.”

Smith suggested some separatist sentiment within the party May prove temporary, arguing that members who have recently embraced separation could still be persuaded that “Canada can work.”

Others, she said, have turned to separatism as a way to “express their anger,” suggesting support within her party for breaking away from Canada could diminish following Monday’s referendum.

On Oct. 19, Albertans will head to the polls to vote on 10 referendum questions, including one that asks whether they want Alberta to remain a province of Canada, or begin the legal process toward holding a second, binding referendum on separation.

paragraphs: With Albertans preparing to head to the polls Monday, questions are mounting over how Premier Danielle Smith will navigate divisions within the United Conservative Party over Alberta separation in the aftermath of the referendum.

A Leger poll released last week suggested UCP supporters are almost evenly divided on the separation question, raising questions about whether the party’s membership can get back on the same page following the Oct. 19 vote.

Former premier Jason Kenney, who founded the UCP in 2017, says the party must enforce its founding commitment to a “strong Alberta within a united Canada,” suggesting the party’s leadership could screen out separatist candidates and potentially expel members who violate its core principles.

“When I created the UCP in 2017, it was with a clear commitment to a federalist party supporting (a) strong Alberta in a united Canada,” Kenney told reporters at a Canada Strong and Free Network event in Calgary on Friday.
“If there are folks who want to advocate for separatism, they have every right as citizens to do so in separatist parties.”
Kenney said the UCP leadership has a responsibility to “lay down the law” with members who are “not committed to the core principles of the party,” including its commitment to Canadian unity.
He pointed to his own tenure as party leader, saying prospective UCP candidates with a history of advocating for Alberta separation were barred from running under the party’s banner.
“We invalidated all of them. Just said ‘no, sorry,’” he said. “You can’t bring separatism into it to represent us on the ballot.”

His comments come as the party faces an increasingly apparent divide over Alberta’s future, with polling suggesting a substantial portion of its supporters favour beginning the process toward a second, binding referendum on separation.
Smith, who addressed attendees at the same event shortly after Kenney’s remarks, acknowledged that “loyalty to a united Canada” is among the Ucp’s founding principles.

But when asked whether she would take steps similar to those described by her predecessor — including screening out separatist candidates or expelling members who violate the party’s principles — Smith stopped short of making any commitment.
She suggested the outcome of Monday’s referendum would help determine how the party approaches members who might waver in their commitment to national unity following Monday’s vote.
If the government receives “affirmation” that remaining committed to a united Canada is a principle Albertans want the party to maintain, Smith said it would do so.
Pressed on whether that could mean taking enforcement action against members who continue to advocate for separation, the premier deferred an answer until after the vote.
“I don’t want to prejudge how people are going to interpret the result on Monday,” Smith said.
“Maybe ask me that on October 20th once I have a chance to see what people’s reaction is.”
Smith suggested some separatist sentiment within the party May prove temporary, arguing that members who have recently embraced separation could still be persuaded that “Canada can work.”
Others, she said, have turned to separatism as a way to “express their anger,” suggesting support within her party for breaking away from Canada could diminish following Monday’s referendum.

On Oct. 19, Albertans will head to the polls to vote on 10 referendum questions, including one that asks whether they want Alberta to remain a province of Canada, or begin the legal process toward holding a second, binding referendum on separation.

stories.title: Canada’s largest-ever jackpot is up for grabs. What would you do with $90 million?
stories.summary: Tonight’s record $90-million Lotto Max jackpot, the largest single lottery prize ever offered in Canada, is up for grabs. Canadians gave a variety of answers as how they would spend the money.
stories.author: John Vennavally-Rao
stories.content:
Pickering, Ont. – Mansions. Boats. Cottages. And, for at least one hopeful Ontarian, a lot more cats.

Those are just some of the dreams fuelling a rush on tickets for tonight’s record $90-million Lotto Max jackpot, the largest single lottery prize ever offered in Canada. It got there after no winning ticket was sold for Tuesday’s $85-million draw.

At Smokers Corner, a convenience store in Pickering, Ont., the line to buy tickets has been long at times.

“It’s been crazy, actually,” said owner Issa Kakisa. “People coming in, spending a little more money than normal, and just everybody’s got a dream and wants that $90 million.”

Some are spending hundreds of dollars at a time, Kakisa said, and one customer dropped $2,000 on this draw alone. His story has some history with big wins, as they sold a winning ticket worth $1 million two years ago.

As for what people in line said they’d do with the money?

“I’d get a mansion, fill it with all of my cats ... I’d get more cats,” said Taylor Locke. She said she’d also buy a house for her mom, a boat and a cottage, and give a lot of the money to animal shelters and people experiencing homelessness.

Cindy O’Neill kept it practical. She said she’d pay off her mortgage, buy her brother a house, make sure her kids are looked after and save the rest for charity and travel.

Her husband, standing nearby, reminded her that he had his eye on a Land Rover. She laughed.

“Oh yeah, I’d buy him a Land Rover.”

Margaret Ward said she’d be happy with one of the smaller prizes of $100,000 or $1 million. But if she landed the full $90 million, she’d pay off a few debts and then go car shopping.

“I’d buy a new car, and I’d buy my husband a new car, and I’d buy my kids a car,” she said. “They’d all get a car.”

Javad Gezelbash, who is retired, bought two tickets for himself. He’d already bought three more the day before as part of a group purchase. If one of them hits, he has his plan ready.

“I’m going to be donating to a hospital, some of it,” he said. “And travelling around the world.”

Ralph Gomes isn’t retired yet, but he’d like to be. His wife had already bought a ticket, and he stopped in to buy a second one.

“I’m super excited,” he said.

The odds of winning the jackpot are roughly one in 33 million, which is about the same as flipping a coin and getting heads 25 times in a row.

What would it actually be like to win $90 million? According to one financial expert, it May not all be upside.

Wolfgang Klein, a Toronto-based portfolio manager with Canaccord Genuity Wealth Management who has worked with lottery winners, said a windfall that size can be a lot to handle.

“The psychological impact is something that they are really, really, probably not prepared for,” he said.

Klein said winners can feel euphoria, confusion and even guilt, and many feel obligated to help others out. People also tend to come out of the woodwork.

“It’d be fun to win $90 million … but be careful what you wish for,” he said. “All of a sudden, people you haven’t heard from in decades begin to communicate with you and become your friends once again.”

One of his clients won $5 million on Lotto 6/49 and found the experience bittersweet.

“Their children stopped working. They began to rely on the lottery winner for a monthly income,” Klein said. “Children, grandchildren, cousins, friends, charity. Where do you say no? When do you say no? And you have to learn to say no.”

His advice for the winner is to cash in on the ticket as soon as possible. He says even a very conservative portfolio of government bonds and GICs would produce a good income.

“Two per cent on $90 million? It’s $1.8 million a year,” he said. “You can do very well.”

Check your pockets

Some fortunes never get collected. In 2022, a $70-million Lotto Max ticket was sold in Toronto’s Scarborough area, but a winner never came forward, and after a year the prize went back into the pool.

Another big prize could soon meet the same fate. The Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation says a $40-million winning ticket sold last year in Grey County, Ont., is set to expire on Oct. 28.

As for who should win on Friday night?

“I hope someone who is a good person gets it,” said Locke, who has plans for her cats. “Hopefully it’s me.”

stories.title: How safe are natural gas buses after Calgary’s deadly crash?
stories.summary: Calgary Transit is reviewing its fleet of nearly 350 natural gas-powered buses after the tragic chain-reaction crash that claimed three lives and injured more than a dozen others.
stories.author: Andrew Johnson
stories.content:
Vancouver – Calgary Transit is reviewing its fleet of nearly 350 natural gas-powered buses after the tragic chain-reaction crash that claimed three lives and injured more than a dozen others.

The second bus involved, powered by compressed natural gas (CNG) was on fire before an explosion occurred, according to Calgary police. Three passengers on the bus were killed.

Investigators have not yet determined what caused the crash, which has sparked concern about the safety of CNG buses in service across Canada, including in Hamilton, Ont., Metro Vancouver, and Victoria.

Gordon McTaggart-Cowan, a professor in the School of Sustainable Energy Engineering at Simon Fraser University, does not believe the Calgary tragedy, ON its own, provides a reason to reconsider CNG bus fleets across Canada.

“There’s a lot of time and effort that’s gone into trying to make them as safe as a conventional bus,” said McTaggart-Cowan. Unlike conventional gasoline and diesel buses, CNG buses store their fuel in high-pressure cylinders.

The gas must be compressed to reduce the amount of space it needs, allowing the bus to carry enough fuel to travel a useful distance, McTaggart-Cowan explained.

He noted that the storage cylinders undergo extensive testing. “They go through drop tests, they go through puncture tests, they sort of shoot things at them. They do all sorts of tests to make sure that they’re going to withstand extreme events,” McTaggart-Cowan told CTV News.

The tanks are also equipped with pressure-release safety valves designed to release gas if a cylinder becomes dangerously hot. When ignited, the venting gas can appear as a torch-like flame shooting from the vehicle.

That appears to be what is taking place in videos from the Calgary crash that show flames shooting from the roof of the bus, although McTaggart-Cowan cautioned that he had not examined the crash scene and could not confirm what was happening.

The pressure release system is intended to reduce the risk of a cylinder rupturing, which can have serious consequences, including explosions.

Jim McMenemy, a former Transportation Safety Board of Canada investigator, said the Calgary crash will need to be examined from multiple angles.

That includes the design of the vehicles, their operation, driver training, and maintenance.

“You can’t leave any stone unturned,” McMenemy said.

McMenemy said a preliminary report could typically be released within about 6-8 weeks, although a complex investigation could take close to a year.

stories.title: Murder charges laid in 2022 double homicide of Coquitlam couple
stories.summary: The families of Kiesha Garie and Umair Kasim finally see the results of four years of investigation into their murders in Burnaby.
stories.author: J.J. Adams
stories.content:
Almost four years after two bodies were discovered in a car on a quiet street in Burnaby, charges have been laid.

Mohammed Arif Ansari, 27, is charged with two counts of second-degree murder and one count of indignity to human remains in the 2022 homicide of Coquitlam couple Kiesha Garie, 31, and her fiancée, Umair Kasim, 30.

The Integrated Homicide Investigation Team spent four years piecing together the circumstances and timeline surrounding the homicides. With few publicly released leads, Garie’s family started a Facebook group to raise awareness of the lack of progress in the case, which became the subject of a true crime podcast.

Garie and Kasim had been reported missing to the Coquitlam RCMP a few days before a passerby spotted their bodies inside a parked car near Alpha Secondary School around 1:45 p.m.

Christine Angelis, Garie’s mother, held a protest in front of RCMP headquarters in Surrey in February, saying she’d been “kept in the dark.”

“This was a complex investigation that demanded years of dedicated work by investigators who were committed to finding answers,” said Ihit Sgt. Freda Fong. “Through the persistent pursuit of multiple investigative avenues and the meticulous examination of evidence, this case has reached a significant milestone with the approval of charges.”

Wong said the case dragged on for more than three years delay is primarily due to the “high threshold” set by the B.C. Prosecution Service which Crown demands substantial likelihood of conviction before proceeding with a case.

stories.title: ‘Committed to the long term‘: Hitachi Energy to build $479M transformer insulation factory in London, Ont.
stories.summary: Hitachi Energy has announced a $479-million investment in a new transformer insulation factory, with support from the federal and provincial governments.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Amid a trade war with the United States, a global energy company is making a major investment in London, Ont.

Hitachi Energy has announced a $479-million investment in a new transformer insulation factory, with support from the federal and provincial governments.

The 226,000-square-foot (21,000-square-metre) facility will be built at Huron Street and Veterans Memorial Parkway.

“This new facility will create over 100 permanent skilled manufacturing and engineering jobs,” said Carla Vicente of Hitachi Energy Canada.

Latest updates on company news here

The federal and provincial governments are contributing a combined $50 million.

“More than 20,000 tonnes of wood fibre will be turned into electric grid pressboard and will strengthen the domestic supply chain and our forest sector,” said federal Industry Minister Melanie Joly at a news conference at the site.

Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli said the facility will be the first transformer pressboard factory in Canada and the largest of its kind in the world.

Ontario Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce said global thinking is at the forefront of the investment.

“We’re building an end-to-end supply chain made in Canada, made by Canadians and for Canadians, and I think that is the ultimate illustration of success that we can punch back and stand up for the good of Canada.”

Although construction is underway, the factory is not expected to be ready until late 2028.

The project marks Hitachi Energy’s second venture into London. Last year, the company purchased Canduct Industries, a manufacturer of transformer cooling equipment.

Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.CA

Hitachi Energy executives told CTV News London that site easements and access to electrical power were critical to the final decision to build in the city.

Mayor Josh Morgan echoed the importance of reliable energy infrastructure in attracting major investments.

“Safe, secure, reliable power, and power infrastructure are critical — critical — to these investments.”

Hitachi Energy says the factory remains on track for completion despite potential changes in economic conditions.

“We have a very solid foundation to make sure the factory is ready on time. Hitachi Energy and Hitachi are committed to the long term,” said Bruno Melles, CEO of Hitachi Energy’s Transformers business unit.

stories.title: Toronto 18 jihadi terror boss granted full parole
stories.summary: A ringleader of the failed Toronto 18 terror plot has been granted full parole by the Parole Board of Canada. Read more.
stories.author: Brian Towie
stories.content:
Canada

Parole Board of Canada says would-be terrorist who planned to bomb Csis no longer shows signs of extremism

Last updated 14 hours ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/national/toronto-18-jihadi-terror-boss-granted-full-parole/wcm/db72ba2d-c377-4dae-9e48-512bde379391#comments-area)

Zakaria Amara getting arrested in 2006.Photo by Screengrab

A ringleader of the failed Toronto 18 terror plot has beengranted full parole after the Parole Board of Canada concluded he no longer shows “any signs of holding onto extremist beliefs or radical ideologies.”

Zakaria Amara helped recruit members of a group that planned to storm Parliament Hill and bomb several places across Toronto. He’s been on day parole with multiple conditions for the past four years, and the board moved his release forward after they reviewed his case last week.

The two-member panel says Amara, 41, demonstrated “positive change, both in attitude and behaviour” after taking a deradicalization process while he was in jail. The panel’s decision, which included redactions, says Amara wants to live in his own home, work a full-time job, attend a mosque, see family and participate in “appropriate leisure activities.”

Amara can’t communicate with anyone involved in crime, including others arrested in the anti-terrorism raids of June 2006. He can’t come into contact with extremists, except in his work as a consultant with a specialized program.

He also has to continue to attend counselling, undergo financial monitoring and have restrictions on his phone and Internet.

Amara and an accomplice recruited people with jihadist ideologies to carry out terror attacks to prompt the withdrawal of Canadian troops from Afghanistan. Amara specifically masterminded a plot focused on building truck bombs targeting the headquarters of the Canadian Security Intelligence Services, the Toronto Stock Exchange, and a military base.

Amara pleaded guilty in October 2009 to participating in a terror group with the intention of causing explosions that were likely to cause serious bodily harm or death.

He was sentenced to life in prison with no chance of parole for 10 years. Amara challenged the sentence but it was upheld.

stories.title: Margaret Atwood tells journalists to 'search deep within your hearts' over Steven Galloway coverage
stories.summary: The case of the UBC professor fired over student's unsubstantiated claim of sexual assault is now the subject of a defamation trial.
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
Canada’s most respected writer gave a backhanded scolding to the country’s media establishment at a charity gala for failing to cover the firing and blacklisting of author and former professor Steven Galloway, and for only coming late to this scandalous story of sex, creative writing and alleged defamation.

“Finally the Canadian press is covering it, after eight years of mostly not,” Margaret Atwood said while accepting an award from Journalists for Human Rights in Toronto. “As one of those attacked online, trashed and derided as a ‘due processer’ for asking for an open investigation with information and evidence from the University of British Columbia, I’m happy to see that.

“Luckily, I couldn’t be fired from a university, blacklisted from festivals, or, if I was, I’d have noticed,” Atwood said. This joke got a laugh, but it was also a poignant criticism of the assembled journalistic decision makers, still waiting on their main course of chicken and kale.

“But did the press stand up for Article 10 (of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights) back then, the right of every human being to a fair, open and impartial trial? Search deep within your hearts,” she told them.

Galloway was suspended and later fired by UBC over a former student’s allegation of sexual assault, and subsequent complaints of other misconduct. A judge’s review found on a balance of probabilities he had not committed sexual assault, and he was later awarded $167,000 from UBC through arbitration. He filed a lawsuit in 2018.

The civil trial, over his libel claim against four women, is hearing evidence now in Vancouver over the events from 2015, in the intense early days of Canada’s cultural reckoning with sexual violence, just before the criminal trial of Jian Ghomeshi.

Atwood’s audience Thursday night included many of Canada’s top media executives, editors and writers. The fundraiser gala for Journalists for Human Rights, a charity that sponsors media training in developing countries, also included remarks by prominent journalists including Lyse Doucet, chief international correspondent for the British Broadcasting Corporation, and Lisa LaFlamme, former anchor of CTV National News.

Atwood is one of several dozen major Canadian arts and literary figures who signed a 2016 letter called UBC Accountable advocating for Galloway’s right to due process.

She also recently wrote a commentary alleging UBC, where she once taught and wrote, mishandled public money by giving it to Galloway’s accuser, a former student with whom he claims to have had a consensual affair, and who is now one of the civil defendants. The school is not a party to the trial, though Atwood wrote it was “instrumental in trashing Galloway’s life by jumping the gun before a smidgen of due diligence.”

At the gala, Atwood spoke of “mobs” that “can be right in principle but wrong in application,” from the Paris mob of the French Revolution with its legitimate complaints of socioeconomic inequality to the moral crusades of modern social media. “But just principles can inspire and enrage hate-filled, vicious piling on. Verdict first, no trial, guilty by identity.”

Atwood was accepting an award, and focused most of her speech on the wider issues of human rights abuses by governments and other powerful interests, and the role of the journalist in confronting them, specifically legacy media companies, which have less money both for investigating and for defending against litigation.

“This has made them more cautious. I won’t say timid. And it has emboldened their enemies, would-be power grabbers who don’t like criticism in the press and wish to squash and exclude,” she said.

Atwood, who spoke from a lectern for about 10 minutes, was keenly familiar with the gala’s setting, the Arcadian Court ballroom, high in the Simpson’s tower on Bay Street near Toronto’s Old City Hall.

In The Blind Assassin, the 2000 historical novel that won her the first of two Booker Prizes, it is the fictional setting for a fateful lunch meeting between the narrator protagonist Iris Chase and her manipulative sister-in-law Winifred Griffen Prior, which begins with the memorable and menacing introduction: “Call me Freddie. All my chums do, and I want us to be great chums.”

“This was where the ladies lunched,” Atwood wrote, “up at the top of Simpsons department store, ON Queen Street – a high, wide space, said to be “Byzantine” in design (which meant it had archways and potted palms), done in lilac and silver, with streamlined contours for the lighting fixtures and the chairs. A balcony ran around it halfway up, with wrought-iron railings; that was for men only, for businessmen. They could sit up there and look down on the ladies, feathered and twittering, as if in an aviary.”

In The Blind Assassin, the 2000 historical novel that won her the first of two Booker Prizes, it is the fictional setting for a fateful lunch meeting between the narrator protagonist Iris Chase and her manipulative sister-in-law Winifred Griffen Prior, which begins with the memorable and menacing introduction: “Call me Freddie. All my chums do, and I want us to be great chums.”

A balcony ran around it halfway up, with wrought-iron railings; that was for men only, for businessmen. They could sit up there and look down on the ladies, feathered and twittering, as if in an aviary.”

content_blocks.text: Canada’s most respected writer gave a backhanded scolding to the country’s media establishment at a charity gala for failing to cover the firing and blacklisting of author and former professor Steven Galloway, and for only coming late to this scandalous story of sex, creative writing and alleged defamation.

“Finally the Canadian press is covering it, after eight years of mostly not,” Margaret Atwood said while accepting an award from Journalists for Human Rights in Toronto. “As one of those attacked online, trashed and derided as a ‘due processer’ for asking for an open investigation with information and evidence from the University of British Columbia, I’m happy to see that.

“Luckily, I couldn’t be fired from a university, blacklisted from festivals, or, if I was, I’d have noticed,” Atwood said. This joke got a laugh, but it was also a poignant criticism of the assembled journalistic decision makers, still waiting on their main course of chicken and kale.

“But did the press stand up for Article 10 (of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights) back then, the right of every human being to a fair, open and impartial trial? Search deep within your hearts,” she told them.

Galloway was suspended and later fired by UBC over a former student’s allegation of sexual assault, and subsequent complaints of other misconduct. A judge’s review found on a balance of probabilities he had not committed sexual assault, and he was later awarded $167,000 from UBC through arbitration. He filed a lawsuit in 2018.

The civil trial, over his libel claim against four women, is hearing evidence now in Vancouver over the events from 2015, in the intense early days of Canada’s cultural reckoning with sexual violence, just before the criminal trial of Jian Ghomeshi.

Atwood’s audience Thursday night included many of Canada’s top media executives, editors and writers. The fundraiser gala for Journalists for Human Rights, a charity that sponsors media training in developing countries, also included remarks by prominent journalists including Lyse Doucet, chief international correspondent for the British Broadcasting Corporation, and Lisa LaFlamme, former anchor of CTV National News.
Atwood is one of several dozen major Canadian arts and literary figures who signed a 2016 letter called UBC Accountable advocating for Galloway’s right to due process.

She also recently wrote a commentary alleging UBC, where she once taught and wrote, mishandled public money by giving it to Galloway’s accuser, a former student with whom he claims to have had a consensual affair, and who is now one of the civil defendants. The school is not a party to the trial, though Atwood wrote it was “instrumental in trashing Galloway’s life by jumping the gun before a smidgen of due diligence.”

At the gala, Atwood spoke of “mobs” that “can be right in principle but wrong in application,” from the Paris mob of the French Revolution with its legitimate complaints of socioeconomic inequality to the moral crusades of modern social media. “But just principles can inspire and enrage hate-filled, vicious piling on. Verdict first, no trial, guilty by identity.”

stories.title: 10/3 Podcast: What's driving Alberta separatists?
stories.summary: Will Albertans vote to remain a part of Canada, or will they vote to start the process to hold a vote on separation?
stories.author: Dave Breakenridge
stories.content:
Will Albertans vote to remain a part of Canada, or will they vote to start the process to hold a vote on separation?

That question is the main focus in Monday’s referendum in Alberta, which features a host of questions on immigration and constitutional issues.

For many Canadians, the question of “Who are these separatists?” has proven elusive.

National Post Western Canada correspondent Jesse Snyder joins host Dave Breakenridge to discuss why separatists feel so emboldened despite lacking popular support, what is driving their movement, and what things could look like in Alberta politics after Monday’s vote.

Further reading: God, guns and grievances: Alberta’s separatists make their case for independence

stories.title: Feds confirm funding for rare disease research as other questions unanswered
stories.summary: Winnipeg - The federal government confirmed at a meeting of Canadian health ministers that it is extending a funding deal on rare disease research, while wider questions on health-care funding remain unanswered.
stories.author: Ian Bickis The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Winnipeg - The federal government confirmed at a meeting of Canadian health ministers that it is extending a funding deal on rare disease research, while wider questions on health-care funding remain unanswered.

Federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel told her provincial and territorial counterparts at the meeting in Winnipeg that the $500 million in annual funding for the National Strategy for Drugs for Rare Diseases that was set to expire next year will now be funded on an ongoing basis.

stories.title: Multi-million-dollar expansion unveiled at Canada Life Place
stories.summary: The ribbon cutting has been held and the $33-million expansion at Canada Life Place in downtown London was unveiled on Friday.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
The ribbon cutting has been held and the $33-million expansion at Canada Life Place in downtown London was unveiled on Friday.

The project which started in June of 2024 took more than two year to complete.

The 10,000 sq. ft. expansion includes the new Casey’s Club Lounge on the main level as well as the new MNP District Lounge on the upper level.

“It can be used to host VIP events or different community gatherings,” said Kelly Austin, the General Manager with Oak View Group at Canada Life Place.

There is also a new larger back of stage area, along with expanded locker and training facilities for the London Knights Hockey Club.

Austin says the expansion is bound to help attract more events at Canada Life Place.

“When we have those national or international events like the Junos or the Memorial Cup prior to the expansion a lot of time we would have to build tents out in the parking lot or out on Dundas Street for example to host media,” she added. “Now we are able to bring them in-house which makes us a lot more competitive when going after those bids.”

Austin says a lot of planning and work went into the project but in the end, “We’re extremely happy about how it all turned out.”

stories.title: A federal IVF program will harmonize ‘patchwork’ approach, experts say
stories.summary: Data collected by Ipsos for Fertility Matters Canada (FMC) found that 46 per cent of Canadians with an opinion on it support the proposed federal IVF funding program.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Nearly half of Canadians support federal funding for in vitro fertilization (IVF) treatment, according to a new study, which experts say would help harmonize the patchwork of public provincial funding available across nine of the 10 provinces.

Data collected by Ipsos for Fertility Matters Canada (FMC) found that 46 per cent of Canadians with an opinion on it support the proposed federal IVF funding program.

During his 2025 campaign, Prime Minister Mark Carney promised Canadians up to $20,000 for a single round of IVF treatment.

While that campaign promise has yet to materialize, Carolynn Dubé, executive director of FMC, told Global News she has had conversations with the federal government and they seem to be listening.

“There is certainly a keen interest in really understanding what this looks like for Canadians and how to get the right program in place so that it’s done well,” she said.

Nine out of ten provinces provide some sort of IVF programs, grants or tax credits, which the industry says are working.

According to the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society (Cfas), 5,466 patients in Ontario and 3,606 patients in Quebec received provincial funding for IVF treatment in 2025.

“This is actually life-changing. Not everybody can afford fertility treatments and so these funded programs are what provides that hope and that pathway to build a family,” Emily McIntosh, executive director of Cfas, told Global News.

The Ontario Ministry of Health told Global News in an email that 132,900 women have received publicly funded fertility support since 2015.

One round of IVF treatment costs around $20,000, but McIntosh said the average heterosexual couple will require three rounds before they have a successful outcome.

“What that tells us is that provincial funding programs are not enough. They are an important, critical start, but we need federal support. We need insurance programs to be stepping up because the financial barrier is massive and this should be an opportunity for every single Canadian that wants to build a family,” she said.

Support for a federal IVF financial program is highest among Canadians aged 18 to 34, according to the survey, with 26 per cent saying it would affect their families’ building plans or those of someone close to them.

This is also one of the age groups hardest hit by the cost-of-living crisis.

“Fertility care is health care. It should be accessible to everybody,” McIntosh said

Dubé said education and awareness are also an important piece of the puzzle. As she speaks to patients across the country, she said they express how they didn’t know about the costs and barriers to IVF until they found themselves needing fertility treatments.

She said this not only creates a financial burden, but a mental toll as well.

“Research shows that being diagnosed with infertility has the same negative impact on one’s mental health as a diagnosis of a more significant health concern like cancer or heart disease. And we don’t treat it the same,” Dubé said.

“Anytime we can have an opportunity to drive public awareness about the issue is certainly helpful for tens of thousands of Canadians who are still waiting to take their baby home.”

A spokesperson for federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel told Global News in a statement that the ministry recognizes that fertility treatments come with many challenges, including financial burdens.

“We recognize the importance of this issue for many Canadians, and we’ll have more to say on this in due course,” they said.

stories.title: Mark Carney makes case against Alberta separatism to his boomer base
stories.summary: On a tour of Alberta days before the province’s referendum on independence, the prime minister said Canadians are more united than divided
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
RED Deer, Alta. — Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday made his final plea to Albertans to vote against separating from Canada, part of his ongoing tour of the province aimed at swaying public opinion just days before Monday’s independence referendum.

At a brief stop in Red Deer, Alta., Carney told a gathering of supporters that the country must remain united at a time when it faces “threats to our sovereignty,” claiming also that the days of a fractured relationship between Alberta and Ottawa are no longer.

“We as a country, we are co-operating again, Canada is working again,” Carney said. “We are coming together, we are taking advantage of all of what we have.”

The prime minister’s address comes as Albertans were voting this week in advance polls for the referendum, with the official voting day on Monday. Voters are asked to respond to 10 questions on the referendum ballots, including one that asks whether they wish to remain in Canada or commence the process of officially separating from the federation.

Carney supporters in attendance crammed inside the Red Hart brewery in Red Deer to hear the address, while others waited outside the venue. More than 100 people, many of them seemingly aged 60 or older, waved miniature Canadian flags and wore red. When Carney arrived at the venue, they belted out the national anthem in unison.

In a brief speech to the crowd, Carney sought to play up his Alberta bona fides, saying that many people in the province have distinct memories of the catastrophic federal energy policies from decades past that had severely handicapped its oil and gas sector. Without naming former prime minister Justin Trudeau, Carney also appeared to suggest that similar policies had been introduced by his Liberal predecessor.

“I want to acknowledge that there have been times within the federation where that trust was put to the test,” he said. “In my lifetime, when I was growing up… we as Albertans were made to feel that sometimes our resources weren’t our own. We were later made to feel that we were developing those resources against the tides of history.”

Carney appeared alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who also gave a brief speech. A collection of other political hangers-on, including Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas and Liberal MP Matt Jeneroux, also attended the event.

The prime minister talked about what he called a “tough collaboration” with Smith, with whom Ottawa has announced a flurry of major projects and investments in the months leading up to the vote. Those include Alberta’s proposed Pacific Link pipeline to the West Coast, a proposed high-speed rail line between Edmonton and Calgary, and $8 billion in military spending at Alberta bases, among other things.

Carney and Smith were chummy at the event, exchanging light-hearted jokes and talking about all the policy ambitions they have in common. Smith claimed that the federal government’s support on major projects is just one example of how the province is working with Ottawa to support Alberta’s economic priorities. Like many Albertans, Smith said she was at first hesitant to believe that the prime minister was truly prepared to spend political capital to advance the province’s interests.

“When people do ask me if it’s real, and if it’s changed, I say ‘well he did grow up in his formative years in Alberta, and he remains an Edmonton Oilers fan,’” Smith said to laughter from the crowd.

The premier also addressed the other nine questions on the ballot, many of which ask voters whether Alberta should work with other provinces to restrict immigration rates or cut public services to some non-permanent residents.

“I have bad news for you, prime minister, all of the premiers are interested in talking about immigration and how we might be able to reform it.”

Standing outside the event and wearing a Maple Leaf-shaped hat, Tom Gwin, 74, said he disagreed fundamentally with the Smith government’s decision to hold a referendum on independence, and wanted to show his support for the prime minister.

“I think Alberta should stay in Canada, and I think Canada is too fabulous a place to be riven by this kind of referendum, which in lots of ways is completely unnecessary,” he said.

At a brief stop in Red Deer, Alta., Carney told a gathering of supporters that the country must remain united at a time when it faces “threats to our sovereignty,” claiming also that the days of a fractured relationship between Alberta and Ottawa are no longer.
“We as a country, we are co-operating again, Canada is working again,” Carney said. “We are coming together, we are taking advantage of all of what we have.”

The prime minister’s address comes as Albertans were voting this week in advance polls for the referendum, with the official voting day on Monday. Voters are asked to respond to 10 questions on the referendum ballots, including one that asks whether they wish to remain in Canada or commence the process of officially separating from the federation.

Carney supporters in attendance crammed inside the Red Hart brewery in Red Deer to hear the address, while others waited outside the venue. More than 100 people, many of them seemingly aged 60 or older, waved miniature Canadian flags and wore red. When Carney arrived at the venue, they belted out the national anthem in unison.

In a brief speech to the crowd, Carney sought to play up his Alberta bona fides, saying that many people in the province have distinct memories of the catastrophic federal energy policies from decades past that had severely handicapped its oil and gas sector. Without naming former prime minister Justin Trudeau, Carney also appeared to suggest that similar policies had been introduced by his Liberal predecessor.

“I want to acknowledge that there have been times within the federation where that trust was put to the test,” he said. “In my lifetime, when I was growing up… we as Albertans were made to feel that sometimes our resources weren’t our own. We were later made to feel that we were developing those resources against the tides of history.”

Carney appeared alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who also gave a brief speech. A collection of other political hangers-on, including Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas and Liberal MP Matt Jeneroux, also attended the event.

The prime minister talked about what he called a “tough collaboration” with Smith, with whom Ottawa has announced a flurry of major projects and investments in the months leading up to the vote. Those include Alberta’s proposed Pacific Link pipeline to the West Coast, a proposed high-speed rail line between Edmonton and Calgary, and $8 billion in military spending at Alberta bases, among other things.

Smith claimed that the federal government’s support on major projects is just one example of how the province is working with Ottawa to support Alberta’s economic priorities. “When people do ask me if it’s real, and if it’s changed, I say ‘well he did grow up in his formative years in Alberta, and he remains an Edmonton Oilers fan,’” Smith said to laughter from the crowd.

stories.title: Cause of fiery Calgary bus crash that killed 3 passengers, injured 16 under investigation
stories.summary: Calgary police are working to determine the cause of a fiery city bus crash that killed three passengers and injured 16 others, including a police officer who helped save a child.
stories.author: Bill Graveland
stories.content:
Police were working Friday to determine the cause of a fiery bus crash in Calgary that killed three passengers and injured 16 others , including a police officer who helped save a child.

Two transit buses and several other vehicles were involved in the chain-reaction crash just after 1 p.m. Thursday, along the 800 block of Saddletowne Circle N.E., a busy road in the city’s northeast.

Police said one Calgary Transit bus first struck a truck, which then side-swiped an SUV and hit the back of a box truck.

The bus then hit the back of a sedan, pushing the vehicle through the intersection. That car then hit a truck.

The bus eventually hit the rear of another City of Calgary bus running on compressed natural gas.

A large, fierce fire broke out on top of the bus as it also hit a sedan and then came to a stop, with flames and thick, black smoke shooting from the roof.

“During the collision, the natural gas tanks on the second bus ignited. The second bus continued forward before striking a sedan,” said a news release.

“Within seconds, the fire intensified resulting in an explosion and significant fire inside the bus.

“Three passengers on the second bus were found deceased.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Three passengers on the second bus were found deceased."

The driver of that bus was able to escape, police said, while the driver of the first bus was trapped, had to be extricated, and was taken to hospital with what police said were life-altering injuries.

“In the middle of the chaos, one brave Calgary police officer ran into a burning bus to save the life of a child,” Mayor Jeromy Farkas said Thursday.

Police said the officer was recovering at home and that she and the others who were hurt had minor injuries.

The three who died have been identified and their families notified.

The mayor said there would be a full investigation into what happened.

“At this time, it is too early to determine whether impairment, speed or distraction contributed to the collision,” added police.

“All possible factors remain under investigation.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "All possible factors remain under investigation."

Mike Mahar, the head of Calgary’s transit union, said Thursday that it’s not clear why the fire was so extreme and that natural gas buses are generally safe.

Calgary Transit says on its website that it has nearly 250 compressed natural gas-powered buses, representing about 20 per cent of its fleet.

It says it acquired this type of bus in 2014 and since then the fleet’s emissions have reduced significantly.

The website says the city plans to buy 153 more natural gas buses this year to replace diesel buses.

With files from Karen Bartko, Global News

stories.title: London’s Traffic Crunch: Can the City Keep Moving?
stories.summary: From roadway rehabilitation to rapid transit projects, London's construction plan for 2026 comprises more than...
stories.author: Callum Contursi
stories.content:
From roadway rehabilitation to rapid transit projects, London’s construction plan for 2026 comprises more than 100 lane-kilometers of roadwork as well as many intersection projects, bridge projects, and underground infrastructure projects. According to the city, the project is designed to repair aging infrastructure in the city and cope with the expansion of the city, but residents are having to deal with reduced lanes, detours, and delays.

One of the biggest areas of focus is Highbury Avenue South.

The rehabilitation project stretches from Hamilton Road toward Bradley Avenue and involves reconstructing the roadway and improving stormwater foundations. The project is expected to continue until November 2027.

The discussion comes at a time when London is preparing for its municipal elections on October 26, 2026, and residents can look at the construction planning, roadway capacity, transit, and mobility concerns of the candidates.

“The most important thing is growth; that’s where big challenges are in the city.” Ward 10 City Councillor Candidate Lois Ward says.

As London continues to grow, the challenge will be finding a balance between building for the future and keeping the city moving today.

stories.title: ‘We are very sorry’: Company apologizes for Owen Sound printing plant closure and loss of 360 jobs
stories.summary: Flags at TC Transcontinental’s Owen Sound printing plant are at half mast today, marking the news nearly 400 employees received on Tuesday. The facility is closing by the end of January, leaving 360 employees without jobs.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Flags at TC Transcontinental’s Owen Sound printing plant are at half mast today, marking the news nearly 400 employees received on Tuesday. The facility is closing by the end of January, leaving 360 employees without jobs.

“A very, very challenging week for our plant up in Owen Sound, and for the entire organization. We are very sorry for the impact that this decision is going to have on all those impacted employees, as well as on the Owen Sound community,” said TC Transcontinental Chief Operating Officer, Patrick Brayley.

The Montreal based company, that is one of Canada’s largest printers of magazines, direct mail, and flyers, says with a steady decline in demand for printed marketing materials, they needed one less plant to meet demand.

“Work that is currently produced in Owen Sound will be redistributed to five other plants across Canada within our national network. And so, that process will take about three and a half months,” said Brayley.

Brayley says U.S. tariffs had nothing to do with their decision. This is entirely based on Canadian market conditions.

The TC Transcontinental closure, and it’s 360 job losses came one day after the city learned Owen Sound’s grain elevators will be closing come December, putting 6 more people out of work.

“We’ve reached out to Bruce Power, which is one of our biggest employers in the area, and are always looking for people. So, it’s scrambling trying to make sure that we’re ready to go when the deadline comes at the end of January, that we’ve got as many jobs available and/or retraining to help the members of our community,” said Owen Sound’s Mayor, Ian Boddy.

Brayley says personalized job counselling, mental health counselling, retraining, and severance packages are being offered by the company, and community. Some jobs will be made available at TC’s other Canadian printing plants.

“We have retained the services of a career placement firm that’s going to be providing individualized support to each affected employee, helping them establish what their best next step could be, whether that’s helping them find employment elsewhere, considering returning to school, or other forms of reskilling.

So we’re going to work with each and every person that’s been impacted by this decision to help them out in that respect. There will be opportunities for at least some employees to explore opportunities elsewhere within Transcontinental’s operating network in Ontario, and elsewhere.

As difficult as this week is, we’re going to proceed with the utmost care in the circumstances. And we are very sorry for the impact that it is going to have,” said Brayley.

He’d much rather see the printing plant stay open, but Boddy believes TC Transcontinental’s empty Owen Sound factory which will be sold by the company, could eventually be repurposed.

“It can be an asset, but you’ve got to find that next company to come in. So, I’m partly optimistic, but, you know, at the same time worried about those people let go, and the families that are involved,” said Boddy.
paragraphs: Flags at TC Transcontinental’s Owen Sound printing plant are at half mast today, marking the news nearly 400 employees received on Tuesday. The facility is closing by the end of January, leaving 360 employees without jobs.

“A very, very challenging week for our plant up in Owen Sound, and for the entire organization. We are very sorry for the impact that this decision is going to have on all those impacted employees, as well as on the Owen Sound community,” said TC Transcontinental Chief Operating Officer, Patrick Brayley.

The Montreal based company, that is one of Canada’s largest printers of magazines, direct mail, and flyers, says with a steady decline in demand for printed marketing materials, they needed one less plant to meet demand.

“Work that is currently produced in Owen Sound will be redistributed to five other plants across Canada within our national network. And so, that process will take about three and a half months,” said Brayley.

The TC Transcontinental closure, and it’s 360 job losses came one day after the city learned Owen Sound’s grain elevators will be closing come December, putting 6 more people out of work.

stories.title: Flu virus hits harder and earlier as some provinces adjust vaccination plans
stories.summary: Nova Scotia and PEI started earlier, while Alberta is adjusting availability of shots
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
The flu virus has hit earlier and harder this fall, forcing some provinces to adjust vaccination plans and adding urgency to the immunization campaign in Ontario, where seniors have reported difficulties obtaining shots.

The latest figures from the national FluWatch+ surveillance program, released Friday, show that the percentage of positive tests had crossed the 5-per-cent mark.

If the rate remains above that threshold next week, the start of the influenza season will be declared, according to the surveillance program.

For the week ending Oct. 10, the percentage of positive tests rose to 5.3 per cent, from 4.7 per cent the previous week. In British Columbia, the province with the highest flu activity, the positivity rate was 14.9 per cent.

“This is a clear, strong indication that flu is circulating and we need to continue to watch whether that increase continues and whether it translates clinically into more medical visits and hospitalizations,” said Don Vinh, an infectious disease specialist at McGill University.

Rates this fall are several times higher than the numbers recorded in previous years, Dr. Vinh noted. “We are definitely having an earlier start to the flu season.” The influenza activity started before vaccination campaigns began to deploy fully “and that’s a situation that we want to avoid.”

However, he added, starting vaccines too early can be problematic as well, because then their protection wane prematurely. Also, vaccination campaigns have to be set months in advance to address manufacturing, procurement and distribution issues. “The flu doesn’t really care about our agenda,” Dr. Vinh said.

Most provinces set their vaccination launches for Oct. 13. But the escalating rates prompted Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island to start at an earlier date and Alberta to adjust the availability of flu shots.

PEI held pop-up clinics on Oct. 7. “Flu season has arrived earlier than usual in Prince Edward Island,” its Department of Health and Wellness said in a Sept. 28 communiqué that urged islanders to book appointments.

Nova Scotia started appointments on Oct. 9.

Alberta was to launch its vaccination drive on Oct. 19, but it has now told pharmacies to give shots as soon as they receive the doses.

“Albertans are encouraged to contact their local pharmacy or clinic to see if they are able to administer fall immunizations prior to October 19th,” the province’s Ministry of Primary and Preventative Health Services said in a statement.

Ontario originally said high-risk and priority groups could get vaccinated starting the week of Sept. 28. However, some people found that shots wouldn’t be available until Oct. 13, after Thanksgiving.

Frustrated seniors said they contacted multiple pharmacies without success; in other cases appointments were cancelled because the vaccine hadn’t arrived. Ontarians who spoke to The Globe and Mail reported they had trouble making bookings for relatives in their 80s and 90s in Niagara, North Bay and London, with appointments not opening before Oct. 28 or Nov. 1.

“Only the most determined might go through all that hassle,” 68-year-old Toronto retiree Sue Gowans said, recounting her difficulties finding online options for herself and an older relative.

Michelle Cohen, a family doctor in Brighton, Ont., said her practice usually receives flu vaccines in early October. This year, the delivery arrived Thursday and contained fewer shots and less of the high-dose formulation recommended for seniors.

“It is frustrating because people are checking out the pharmacy, not sure what to do, looking online,” she said. “I have many patients who are in their 80s and 90s, and it’s hard for them simply to get out of the house a lot of the time and come into the office. … They’re asking for a flu shot and I’m saying, sorry, try again later.”

Ontario’s Ministry of Health said 679,000 doses were distributed as of Oct. 8 and priority was given to hospitals, long-term care homes and other high-risk settings.

The main viral subtype detected so far is influenza A (H1N1), which can cause severe disease in younger adults, pregnant women and those with underlying medical conditions, Dr. Vinh said, explaining that vaccination shouldn’t be limited to older people.

Preliminary data suggest that this year’s vaccine has been a “moderately good match” for the viral strain circulating, he added.

In Quebec, vaccination begins Oct. 20. Starting this fall, shots are free only for those in vulnerable groups, including people 65 and over, nursing home residents and pregnant women. The association of Quebec pharmacy owners says people who don’t qualify for free shots can expect to be charged $30 to $40 for a flu jab.
