stories.title: Expert explainer: Western’s chief information security officer on staying safe online
stories.summary: Western's chief information security office Brent Fowles offers cybersecurity strategies to stay safe online.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
Western Technology Services builds security into the technology and services used every day at the university, protecting the campus community and blocking millions of automated attempts to identify vulnerabilities.

At home, you don’t have a cybersecurity team working behind the scenes – it’s just you.

Brent Fowles is Western University’s chief information security officer and a recognized leader in cybersecurity. He received the 2026 Toronto Orbie Enterprise Ciso Award and regularly speaks to businesses across Southwestern Ontario about cybersecurity through Western Continuing Studies.

Fowles shared his top tips to stay safer online.

Brent Fowles (BF):Our CyberSmart team uses this phrase: Stop, think, verify.You don’t need to be a cybersecurity expert to protect yourself. A little suspicion can go a long way.

Cybercriminals are getting better at making scams look and sound legitimate. A fake text can look like it came from your bank. An email can appear to be from your boss. A phone call can even sound like someone you know. Even a QR code on a poster could take you somewhere you weren’t expecting.

A lot of scams work by getting you to react emotionally. They create fear, excitement, curiosity or urgency That’s where ‘stop, think, verify’ comes in. Here’s how you can use this approach to your benefit:

Stop. Give yourself a few seconds. Pay attention to how the message is making you feel. If it makes you afraid, angry, excited or like you need to act right now, slow down.

Think. Does this make sense? Was I expecting this? What are they asking me to provide? Be especially cautious if someone unexpectedly asks for a password, verification code, personal information, gift cards, cryptocurrency or money.

Verify. Check out the ask in another way. If you receive a suspicious message from your bank, for example, call the number on the back of your card instead of using the contact information in the message.

BF: Don’t assume something is true just because it looks convincing or has been widely shared. With artificial intelligence (AI), it’s easier than ever to create misinformation and scams.Start by looking for the original source. Check who published the information, when it was shared, and whether other trusted sources are reporting the same thing.

If you’re unsure about a photo, try a reverse image search using a tool such as Google Lens. This can help you find where else the image appears online and whether it is older than the post, from a different event or being shared without the right context. Remember, a real photo can still be used to spread false or misleading information.

You can also use fact-checking websites. Snopes.com has been investigating rumours, viral posts, news claims, scams, urban legends and misinformation since 1994. Snopes can be a useful first stop, but don’t rely on one source alone. Whenever possible, check a primary source and compare information across several reputable sources.

BF: One of the best places to start is using a different, strong password for every important account. If you reuse the same password and one account is compromised, criminals can try it on your other accounts.

You can visit haveibeenpwned.com to check whether your email and password has appeared in a known data breach.

A password manager can also do a lot of the work for you. It can create and securely store strong, unique passwords so you don’t have to remember them all.

Turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA) wherever you can. It adds another layer of protection, so having your password alone isn’t enough to access your account. And remember: never approve an MFA request you didn’t initiate or give someone your verification code.

If a service offers a passkey, that’s another good option. Passkeys let you sign in using something tied to your device, such as your fingerprint, face or device PIN, and are much harder to steal through phishing.

BF: Think about what you’re agreeing to when you download an app, create an account or use a new service.

Take a look at your privacy and security settings. What information is being collected? Who can see what you share? What have you given the app permission to access?

For example, does an app really need your contacts, location, microphone and photos to do what you downloaded it for? If a permission doesn’t make sense, consider turning it off.

It’s also worth checking these settings from time to time, especially as apps and services change.

BF:Act quickly. The sooner you respond, the more you May be able to do to protect your accounts, money and information.

Start by saving screenshots, emails, text messages, receipts and other evidence. If money or financial information is involved, contact your bank immediately. They can help you determine what steps to take, which could include locking cards or accounts, lowering transaction limits or adding other protections.

Change the password on any affected account — and anywhere else you used that same password. Review your security settings and turn on MFA if you haven’t already.

You should also report the incident when appropriate. Contact your local police using their non-emergency line andreport fraud and cybercrime to theCanadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

BF: Start with what matters most.Think about it this way: you wouldn’t put an old pair of tennis shoes in a high-security vault, but you might put a valuable family heirloom there. Your digital life is no different.

Start with the accounts that would cause the most harm if someone got into them. Your primary email is especially important because it can often be used to reset passwords for other accounts. Your banking and accounts containing sensitive personal information should also be priorities.

Protect those first using strong, unique passwords, MFA or passkeys, and then work your way through the rest. Keep your devices updated – these updates patch security vulnerabilities.

Technology is changing quickly, and scams are changing with it. You don’t have to know everything about cybersecurity to protect yourself. Being a little suspicious – and taking the time to stop, think and verify – can make a big difference.

Faculty or staff at Western? Register for the upcoming CyberSmart: Staying Safer Online session on Zoom on October 21, from 1-2 PM.

Think. Does this make sense? Was I expecting this? What are they asking me to provide? Be especially cautious if someone unexpectedly asks for a password, verification code, personal information, gift cards, cryptocurrency or money.

Verify. Check out the ask in another way. If you receive a suspicious message from your bank, for example, call the number on the back of your card instead of using the contact information in the message.

With artificial intelligence (AI), it’s easier than ever to create misinformation and scams.Start by looking for the original source. Check who published the information, when it was shared, and whether other trusted sources are reporting the same thing.

If you’re unsure about a photo, try a reverse image search using a tool such as Google Lens. This can help you find where else the image appears online and whether it is older than the post, from a different event or being shared without the right context. Remember, a real photo can still be used to spread false or misleading information.

You can also use fact-checking websites. Snopes.com has been investigating rumours, viral posts, news claims, scams, urban legends and misinformation since 1994. Snopes can be a useful first stop, but don’t rely on one source alone. Whenever possible, check a primary source and compare information across several reputable sources.

If a service offers a passkey, that’s another good option. Passkeys let you sign in using something tied to your device, such as your fingerprint, face or device PIN, and are much harder to steal through phishing.

Take a look at your privacy and security settings. What information is being collected? Who can see what you share? What have you given the app permission to access?
For example, does an app really need your contacts, location, microphone and photos to do what you downloaded it for? If a permission doesn’t make sense, consider turning it off.
It’s also worth checking these settings from time to time, especially as apps and services change.

Start by saving screenshots, emails, text messages, receipts and other evidence. If money or financial information is involved, contact your bank immediately. Change the password on any affected account — and anywhere else you used that same password. Review your security settings and turn on MFA if you haven’t already.
You should also report the incident when appropriate. Contact your local police using their non-emergency line andreport fraud and cybercrime to theCanadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

stories.title: Nackawic mill workers and union push for government action as shutdown looms
stories.summary: The Nackawic mill is set to temporarily idle on Nov. 4. The company attributed the decision to "prevailing market conditions" and other challenges.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Reeti Rohilla
stories.content:
Hundreds of workers at the AV Nackawic Mill in New Brunswick are now less than three weeks away from losing their jobs, and their fight to save the mill has become part of a nationwide push for government action.

AV Group NB Inc. announced in September it would be temporarily idling its facility, located west of Fredericton. That shutdown is slated for Nov. 4.

The company attributed the decision to “prevailing market conditions” and other challenges.

“We’re devastated at the announcement of the idling of the Nackawic Mill. Hundreds of good paying jobs, hundreds of families living in great uncertainty,” said Jennifer Murray, Unifor’s Atlantic regional director.

“We will not stop fighting regardless of deadlines or whatever happens after Nov. 4.”

On Friday, forestry workers were joined by Unifor’s national leadership at a rally in Nackawic to call for government intervention to protect the industry.

The union says the shutdown will have an impact beyond the mill’s workers.

“It affects about 240 unionized workers and about 300 to 350 overall direct jobs plus thousands of spin-off jobs with truckers and woods workers and other contractors,” said Grant Charlton, president of Unifor Local 219, which represents some of the mill workers.

Amid trade pressures with the U.S. and soaring energy costs, Unifor is asking for a national forestry strategy.

Locally, it’s pushing for a joint government task force. Murray says a provincial review could help identify what it would cost to modernize the mill, create a long-term plan, and make a pitch to potential investors.

Lana Payne, Unifor’s national president, says she herself has been approaching potential buyers for the mill.

“I, myself, have contacted other players in the forestry industry to say, ‘Look, there’s a great mill there, there’s great workforce, would you go have a look at it and see if this is something that you would be interested in taking on?'” she said.

The local union is also asking for the mill to be heated through the winter in order to preserve the possibility of reopening.

The province says it is working with AV Nackawic NB Inc. and the municipality on options, while Working NB helps employees access federal and provincial benefits.

“We’re turning over every rock to see what the possibilities are for employment and a different use of either the facility, the land, all of the pieces. (We’re) engaging with the sector,” said Premier Susan Holt.

The province is also organizing job fairs for the workers.

The mill faced a similar situation in 2004, closing its doors for over a year before a different operator took over.

stories.title: Police identify suspect van after caregiver, 60, left to die on side of road in Vaughan
stories.summary: The woman from Richmond Hill was travelling to her job as a live-in caregiver when she was hit. Her body laid on the side of the road for two days before a passerby spotted it.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Police in York Region say they have identified the vehicle involved in a fatal hit-and-run earlier in October that left a 60-year-old woman dead.

The woman’s body laid on the side of the road for two days before she was found.

Investigators say the woman stepped off a bus on Major Mackenzie Drive in Vaughan and was walking north on Pine Valley Drive around 8:30 p.m. on Oct. 4, when she was hit.

The woman from Richmond Hill was travelling to her job as a live-in caregiver when she was hit, said York Region Police Const. Kevin Nebrija.

On Oct. 6 the woman was spotted by an area resident, who called police.

“The caller got close enough to see someone was there and not responding,” he said.

Officers arrived to find she was dead. Her suitcase was found nearby, he said.

“It is absolutely tragic that she was struck and essentially left on the side of the road for two days,” he said.

“We don’t know if she was killed instantly or if she was suffering.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We don't know if she was killed instantly or if she was suffering."

Police announced Friday the suspect vehicle is a white 2020 to 2022 Mercedes-Benz sprinter van.

The local community provided video and police found vehicle debris at the scene, which led them to determine the make of the van, said Nebrija.

“We hope that the driver sees the video, talks to legal and turns himself in,” said Nebrija, adding that police are confident the driver is well-aware they hit someone.

Investigators are appealing to any body shops or auto repair shops to be on the lookout for a sprinter van with damage to the front area.

“To the driver: consult legal counsel and turn yourself in. We already have the vehicle on video. It’s going to be a matter of time before our investigators are able to determine who the driver is,” he said.

“We want the driver to do the right thing here, bring some closure to the victim’s family.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We want the driver to do the right thing here, bring some closure to the victim's family."

stories.title: As Alberta referendum nears, seeds to dispute results planted online: report
stories.summary: McGill’s Media Ecosystem Observatory has been keeping tabs on the occasionally fraught online discourse surrounding the Alberta referendum.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Just days after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said strikes on Russian bot farms halted some of that traffic online, social media researchers at McGill University say they’ve found no significant change in “inauthentic” online discourse connected to the Alberta referendum.

However, they’re warning that significant narrative groundwork has been laid to contest the validity of the next week’s vote.

Researchers are McGill’s Media Ecosystem Observatory (MEO) have been keeping tabs on the online discourse around the province’s referendum which will ask, among other questions, if Albertans want a binding provincial vote on independence from Canada.

With widespread concerns about foreign interference in the vote, a narrative began circulating last week that Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centres had led to a drop in online separatist accounts — suggesting those accounts were inauthentic “bots.”

The McGill researchers found no evidence the purported changes in Russian traffic had any effect on either pro- or anti-separatism voices online. But Aengus Bridgman, one of the researchers, said the viral claims provide a window into the fraught nature of the debate.

“The (separatist) movement, as a whole, is very active online, it has this disproportionate footprint, that people look at it and think ‘this feels inauthentic … how is support in this province low for this movement, but their online presence is so big?’” Bridgman said in an interview.

“And the answer that has really been reached for in the national discourse is that there is large, inauthentic activity driving this.”

That hasn’t been the Meo’s observation, Bridgman said. Instead, he said a very passionate, very online community of Albertans is pushing the separatist cause. And because they’re so online, they appear to be a larger movement than they are in terms of voting power.

But the distortion also has an effect on the online separatists, who have started to believe “somehow that their information environment online and the events that they go to online are somehow representative of a broad swath of Middle Alberta,” Bridgman said.

Bridgman gave the example of online separatist seeing a poll of thousands of people online on X.com that indicated 80 per cent support for independence, and have a hard time squaring that with professional polling that almost universally shows the opposite when specifically asking people who are eligible to actually vote in the referendum.

“You have all political communities feeling like the other one is inauthentic, or is dishonest, or is cheating,” Bridgman said.

Federal politicians, including Prime Minister Mark Carney and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, traveled to Alberta this week to bolster the pro-Canada campaigns that have been working against the separatists for months.

National pollsters have consistently suggested that the separatists are significantly outnumbered. An Ipsos poll for Global News in mid-September suggested seven out of 10 Albertans intended to vote against holding a separation referendum.

But Bridgman warned that significant groundwork has been laid online for separatists to call into question the results of the vote, should that side lose.

“This is now normal, we see this in every electoral event … but this is the largest number we’ve seen, and it’s happening earlier,” Bridgman said.

He noted that while trust in electoral administration agencies has been dropping on the political right, in Alberta that declining trust cuts across the political spectrum.

“It doesn’t feel like a great moment, and I think those in Alberta are really feeling it,” Bridgman said.

“And I think part of the frustration with this whole process … is reflective of (it) not feeling as legitimate or as clear as we would like. That’s something that, ON Oct. 20, there’s going to have to be a rebuilding of that trust, and some real work to do that.”

stories.title: Ontario hospital in deficit cutting over 100 nursing roles, adding other positions
stories.summary: A hospital in London, Ont., is cutting more than 100 registered nurse positions in its mental health programs, the latest in a growing list of hospitals across the province making similar moves in the face of deficits.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A hospital in London, Ont., is cutting more than 100 registered nurse positions in its mental health programs, the latest in a growing list of hospitals across the province making similar moves in the face of deficits.

St. Joseph’s Health Care London said Friday in a statement that it is removing 83 full-time and 31 part-time RN roles, and adding close to the same number of registered practical nurse, personal support worker, occupational therapist, physiotherapy assistant, social worker and therapeutic recreation assistant roles.

stories.title: What France’s spiking bond yields, rising debt mean for Canadian borrowers
stories.summary: Canadian borrowers May wind up paying more for some mortgages and other loans as government bond yields continue to rise worldwide, including in France.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
As France grapples with continued protests, high government debt, and growing speculation from economists about whether the country is on the verge of another euro zone crisis, Canadian investors and borrowers watching government bond yields rise worldwide are raising concerns.

“France’s government bond yields have risen more sharply than those of the United States and many other developed economies during the recent sell-off. The underperformance reflects growing concern about political uncertainty and a weak fiscal outlook,” said senior economist Vikram Rai at TD Bank in a statement on Wednesday.

“France stands out among its developed-market peers in the recent global bond sell-off. Long-term yields have risen across major markets, but French government bonds have seen an outsized move.”

Bonds are loan investment products issued by governments and companies over fixed terms, and over the course of that term, the bond pays a regular yield or interest payment to the owner. Bond yields fluctuate regularly based on a combination of various economic factors, as well as supply and demand.

Since the start of the year, especially since the Iran war began, bonds have been selling-off, which has driven up their yields in order to win back investors.

The U.S. Treasury yield has shot up over five per cent in recent months, and some French government bonds are following in lockstep.

France’s government, like many others around the world, has a debt problem.

The nation’s sovereign debt is now close to 120 per cent of its GDP, which means a substantial amount of revenue the government brings in, including from taxes, goes just to paying the interest on the money it’s had to borrow. Those rising interest costs are putting pressure on the government’s public finances.

If investors are losing confidence in a government’s ability to pay off its debt, they May sell their bonds because of perceived risk.

Another potential concern for investors, in this context, is the fact that France is about to go into an election period, which dials up the uncertainty about the country’s future financial strategies.

“The French government debt is like 120 per cent of GDP, and that is twice as high as what it’s supposed to be by the EU standard, and I think investors are more concerned about the future prospect,” says finance professor Yoshio Nozawa at the University of Toronto.

“If the populist leaders are elected, the deficit problem is expected to be even worse. So, this combined effect is contributing to the concern about the French government’s ability and willingness to narrow the gap between what they are spending and how much they are raising in tax revenue.”

Rai notes how the 10-year French government bond, known as the Obligation assimilable du Trésor (or OAT), is hovering at close to five per cent, which is the highest level since 2002, and up from about 3.5 per cent in June.

The 10-year U.S. treasury yield was about five per cent as of publication, and although that’s down from a recent peak of 5.3 per cent, it’s still up from roughly four per cent in March.

Meanwhile, the 10-year Canadian bond yield was about 3.8 per cent, and up from just over three per cent in March.

“The bond sell-off took a darker turn this week, with yields in much of Europe suddenly ratcheting higher, especially in France,” said Doug Porter, chief economist at the Bank of Montreal in a note to investors from Oct. 2.

Both Porter and Rai note how the spread, or difference between France’s and Germany’s 10-year yields, has increased to over 1.5 per cent in recent weeks, the highest since the euro crisis peaked around 2011/2012.

At the time, Greece was facing massive sovereign debt problems, which raised fears of wider financial instability and threatened the future of the euro as a currency.

Nozawa says that although this May be reminiscent of that euro zone crisis, France’s economic positioning means there May be less cause for concern right now.

“But here, in terms of France, it’s a big economy and they are not Greece, and in that sense, it is worrying, in some respect, because it’s a big member of the EU, but in terms of the observed cost of borrowing and also the amount of deficit they have, we are not really talking about 2010.”

The Bank of Canada sets the floor for borrowing rates that commercial banks can offer loans to Canadian households and businesses, which usually affects variable rate loans. But longer-term fixed rate products are more often determined by global bond yields.

Even though France’s debt issue May not directly impact Canada’s economy, if France’s bond yields rise, so too May Canada’s in order to stay competitive.

But so far, Canadian borrowers May be in a relatively better position compared to the U.S. and France.

“Canadian yields have clearly felt the gravitational pull of rising global yields, but have mostly managed to remain calmer,” said Porter.

“Canada’s cooler growth backdrop, in part because of the trade tussle, slightly milder inflation, and less-fraught government finances have all played a role in dampening the yield back-up. Note that Canada’s fiscal sustainability is much less of an issue than for others.”

Nozawa says that regardless of Canada’s bond market performance compared to other nations, the relative cost of borrowing some loan products is still likely going to increase.

“The interest rates on long-term government bonds tend to move in lockstep across countries. So that is a tendency that we have and that is often explained by the fact that there are these big global investors who have a diversified portfolio consisting of Canadian government bonds, U.S. government bonds and French government bonds,” says Nozawa.

“When the interest rate of one thing goes up, the other thing has to go up so that they kind of strike a balance between these three.”

Meanwhile, the 10-year Canadian bond yield was about 3.8 per cent, and up from just over three per cent in March.

“The bond sell-off took a darker turn this week, with yields in much of Europe suddenly ratcheting higher, especially in France,” said Doug Porter, chief economist at the Bank of Montreal in a note to investors from Oct. 2.

Both Porter and Rai note how the spread, or difference between France’s and Germany’s 10-year yields, has increased to over 1.5 per cent in recent weeks, the highest since the euro crisis peaked around 2011/2012.
At the time, Greece was facing massive sovereign debt problems, which raised fears of wider financial instability and threatened the future of the euro as a currency.
Nozawa says that although this May be reminiscent of that euro zone crisis, France’s economic positioning means there May be less cause for concern right now.

“But here, in terms of France, it’s a big economy and they are not Greece, and in that sense, it is worrying, in some respect, because it’s a big member of the EU, but in terms of the observed cost of borrowing and also the amount of deficit they have, we are not really talking about 2010.”

content_blocks.text: What does this mean for Canadians?

The Bank of Canada sets the floor for borrowing rates that commercial banks can offer loans to Canadian households and businesses, which usually affects variable rate loans. But longer-term fixed rate products are more often determined by global bond yields.
Even though France’s debt issue May not directly impact Canada’s economy, if France’s bond yields rise, so too May Canada’s in order to stay competitive.
But so far, Canadian borrowers May be in a relatively better position compared to the U.S. and France.
“Canadian yields have clearly felt the gravitational pull of rising global yields, but have mostly managed to remain calmer,” said Porter.

“Canada’s cooler growth backdrop, in part because of the trade tussle, slightly milder inflation, and less-fraught government finances have all played a role in dampening the yield back-up. Note that Canada’s fiscal sustainability is much less of an issue than for others.”
Nozawa says that regardless of Canada’s bond market performance compared to other nations, the relative cost of borrowing some loan products is still likely going to increase.

“The interest rates on long-term government bonds tend to move in lockstep across countries. So that is a tendency that we have and that is often explained by the fact that there are these big global investors who have a diversified portfolio consisting of Canadian government bonds, U.S. government bonds and French government bonds,” says Nozawa.
“When the interest rate of one thing goes up, the other thing has to go up so that they kind of strike a balance between these three.”

stories.title: Canadians living in the United States charged with voting in U.S. federal elections
stories.summary: Neither of the accused are US citizens. Non-citizens voting in a US federal election carries a maximum $100,000 fine and a year in prison.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
Two Canadian citizens living in New York have been charged with voter fraud after voting in United States federal elections, authorities and court documents allege.

Paula Stitt, 57, has been living in Albany, N.Y., for 31 years as a lawful permanent resident but never became a U.S. citizen, according to a criminal complaint filed in court.

She is accused of voting in at least two federal elections in 2024: a primary election in June for the U.S. Senate and U.S. House of Representatives, and the U.S. general election in November that elected Donald Trump as U.S. president.

A special agent with U.S. Homeland Security Investigations swore in a criminal complaint that officials compared past New York voting records to immigration records. The agent said records showed she voted in federal elections despite not being a U.S. citizen.

Stitt was stopped in August at the Peace Bridge border crossing between Fort Erie, Ont., and Buffalo, N.Y., when returning from a family reunion in Canada. She was interviewed at the border “regarding her voting history” in the United States, according to the agent’s statement.

The agent’s statement, filed in court, said Stitt told him she remembers registering to vote and showed him her voter registration card. Stitt said she had asked an unnamed immigration official if she was able to vote and was told “not until you get your permanent residency card.” She allegedly said that since being granted permanent residency she had voted in local and state elections and every presidential election for 30 years, including the most recent.

She was charged Oct. 9 with two counts of voting by an alien.

Jacques Patry, 64, another Canadian, has lived in Tupper Lake, N.Y., for the past five years, according to a criminal complaint filed in court. The scenic town in the Adirondacks is about 200 kilometres south of Montreal.

Records from the Franklin County Board of Elections show he voted in the 2022 U.S. federal midterm elections that elected members to the Senate and the House, among other elections, while immigration records show he has never been a U.S. citizen, according to a complaint by a different Homeland Security Investigations special agent.

Patry was interviewed on Oct. 1, according to court documents. The circumstances of his interview were not included in court records. It is not known if it also took place at a border crossing.

He allegedly told the agent he knows he is not a U.S. citizen, that he registered to vote when he was in high school, and has voted in U.S. elections.

He is charged with one count of voting by an alien.

The criminal complaints against both Canadians — along with similar charges against two British citizens and a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina who also were permanent residents — were filed last week under seal, meaning they were not public until unsealed by a judge on Wednesday when they appeared in court.

Patry had a lawyer. Stitt requested the appointment of a public defender after swearing she was financially unable to retain a lawyer. They were both released on conditions they promise to appear for future court dates, not to breach any law, and to tell the court before changing their address.

Neither lawyer responded to the National Post prior to deadline.

It is a federal crime in the United States for non-U.S. citizens to vote in a federal election. The crime carries a maximum punishment of $100,000 fine and one year’s imprisonment.

John A. Sarcone III, the first assistant United States attorney for the Northern District of New York, said in a written statement that the five people are accused of voter fraud.

“The law is clear that only U.S. citizens can vote in elections that have candidates running for federal office. When non-citizens vote, the public loses confidence in the integrity of the election process and its outcome,” he said. “Our office, working with our federal law enforcement partners, will work tirelessly to prosecute those who should not have voted, but did.”

stories.title: Advocacy group issues urgent call to combat radicalization after youth found guilty of plan to kill Ottawa Jews
stories.summary: "This case reinforces (that) antisemitism is a matter of national security,” says the Cija’s Josh Landau.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
A Canadian Jewish advocacy group has issued an urgent call to confront the radicalism that generates terrorism after an Ontario criminal court judge found a male youth guilty of two terrorism-related charges arising from a 2023 plan to kill Jewish people in Ottawa.

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs released a statement via X late Friday saying that “Jewish Canadians should not have to wait for a mass-casualty attack before every tool available is used to confront this threat.”

“This case reinforces what the Government of Canada has recently affirmed: antisemitism is a matter of national security – a threat to both the personal safety of Canadians and our democratic way of life,” says Josh Landau, the Cija’s senior director for government affairs in Ontario.

“Governments must act with urgency to confront the radicalization that fuels terrorism, ensure our security agencies have the resources they need to identify and disrupt threats, and enforce our laws to hold those responsible accountable.”

Ontario Superior Court Justice Kerry McVey found the young person guilty of conspiracy to commit murder through involvement with a terrorist group, reports the Canadian Press . She also found him guilty of facilitating terrorist activity due to an effort to acquire a prohibited firearm.

The male youth, who cannot legally be identified due to his age, pleaded not guilty to all three charges. McVey did not find the accused guilty of facilitating terrorist activity in making instructional material and propaganda available.

The judgement was issued a day after his co-accused, also a young person who cannot be identified, was found guilty on four charges. McVey concluded that the youth found guilty conspired with his co-accused as well as another individual who was not charged.

stories.title: What time is it? Confusion as Canada’s approach to daylight time shifts
stories.summary: There is more confusion and a reignited debate over the seasonal time change as millions of Canadians get set to turn the clocks back while some provinces scrap the move altogether.
stories.author: Katie Griffin
stories.content:
Ottawa - There is more confusion and a reignited debate over the seasonal time change as millions of Canadians get set to turn the clocks back while some provinces scrap the move altogether.

On Nov. 1, British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba and the Northwest Territories will no longer turn the clocks back one hour in favour of remaining on daylight time.

Most of Ontario, Quebec and Atlantic Canada will, although parts of northwestern Ontario including Kenora, won’t so the region can align with neighbouring Manitoba.

“The Canadian time landscape is a real mess right now, I can’t even keep up with it,” said Patricia Lakin-Thomas, a biology professor at York University. “We desperately need some kind of organization to try to come up with something more systematic than this patchwork approach.”

As of Nov. 1, when it is noon in Toronto, it will be 10 a.m. in Vancouver. Alberta will now be only one hour behind most of Ontario.

Some experts argue the semi-annual change can be harmful to your health and that switching to permanent standard time is the way to go.

Lakin-Thomas said that is particularly true when considering the sunrise in Calgary on some mornings this winter won’t be until 9:30 a.m.

“You’re going to find it very hard and you’re going to feel and be essentially jet-lagged,” she said.

At Kaya’s Watch and Clock Shop in Ottawa, Mustafa Kaya uses the semi-annual time change as a reminder to replace the batteries in the dozens of clocks in his store.

“The time change is a good time for me to go over all the clocks and make sure they’re in sync again,” Kaya said. “Keeping it consistent would be huge, especially for a business like us.”

Ontario has said it would end the semi-annual switch, but only if Quebec and New York do so as well.

Ontario has said it would end the semi-annual switch, but only if Quebec and New York do so as well.

stories.title: Environment Canada issues overnight frost advisory for Toronto
stories.summary: The agency issued a yellow warning Friday morning and said “freezing temperatures are expected tonight into Saturday morning.”
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Some cold weather is arriving for Toronto as Environment Canada has issued a frost advisory.

The weather agency issued a yellow alert Friday morning and said “freezing temperatures are expected tonight into Saturday morning.” A “yellow” advisory indicates “moderate, short-term” impacts, according to the Environment Canada website.

Temperatures are expected to fall near or slightly below the freezing mark overnight into Saturday morning. It will particularly affect areas north of Highway 401, the national agency said. Areas closer to Lake Ontario should be a few degrees warmer.

Environment Canada also said damage to trees, plants and crops is possible. It advises taking preventative measures to protect plants, trees and crops that are sensitive to cold weather.

stories.title: Carney and Smith link up to pitch pro-Canada vote ahead of Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney, standing with Alberta's premier and other politicians, channelled author Charles Dickens in saying the referendum comes at the best and worst of times.
stories.author: Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and Premier Danielle Smith joined forces at an Alberta brewery to make a last-ditch plea for Albertans to vote to stay in Canada.

Carney, standing with Smith and other politicians, channelled author Charles Dickens in saying Monday’s referendum comes at the best and worst of times.

He says the worst is globalist forces and policies threatening the country, while the best is a nation and a province on the cusp of unprecedented growth and success.

His remarks come as his opponent is also in Alberta, making the same plea.

Speaking in Calgary, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said he understands separatist disillusionment with the state of affairs in Canada but that quitting isn’t the answer.

Carney is scheduled to attend a Forever Canadian rally in Edmonton on Friday, as well as meet with business leaders alongside Premier Danielle Smith in Red Deer.

It comes after he gave a speech Thursday night at another Forever Canadian rally in Calgary, saying the frustrations in Alberta are real but that Canada is working in a spirit of co-operative federalism.

A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that could lead to years of lost opportunities, he said.

Voters are being asked whether the province should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on separation.

It’s one of 10 questions on the ballot, as Smith also wants Albertans to endorse her proposals for more control and rules around immigration and a mandate to pursue constitutional changes to wrest power from Ottawa.

While Carney and Smith agree on a united Canada, the prime minister has urged Albertans to reject the other nine ballot questions, and the premier says she will work to change his mind.

More to come…

stories.title: Canadian firms signed deals worth almost $300M during India trade mission: Ottawa
stories.summary: Ottawa - International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu says trade talks between Canada and India advanced over the last week, as he led a major trade mission to New Delhi and Mumbai.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said trade talks between Canada and India advanced over the past week as he led a major trade mission to New Delhi, Bengaluru and Mumbai.

A statement from his office said the mission included representatives from nearly 300 Canadian businesses and exporters, and resulted in 34 commercial agreements worth almost $300 million.

It said the agreements spanned multiple sectors, including aerospace, clean technology and energy transitions, information and communications technologies, infrastructure, life sciences and tourism.

Sidhu’s office also said the minister met with Indian Industry Minister Piyush Goyal in both New Delhi and Mumbai to push forward trade talks. Canada and India are looking to conclude negotiations on a new Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement by the end of the year.

The ministers have now met 10 times since May 2025.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi formally launched trade negotiations almost a year ago on the sidelines of the G20 leaders’ summit in South Africa.

Carney confirmed on Thursday Modi will visit Toronto and Ottawa on Dec. 11 and 12, just ahead of this year’s G20 summit in Miami.

The Liberals have set out to double non-U.S. exports over the next decade and have also set a goal of doubling two-way trade with India to $70 billion annually by 2030.

In 2025, two-way goods and services trade between Canada and India amounted to $30.4 billion.

In May, Goyal said Carney’s visit to his country paved the way for a complete overhaul of the Canada-India relationship.

Canada and India have been in trade talks since 2010. But those talks were shut down in 2023 after the federal government accused New Delhi of playing a role in the assassination of a Canadian Sikh activist in Surrey, B.C.

Carney, who made resetting relations with India a priority after he became prime minister in 2025, visited Mumbai and New Delhi in March. It was the first visit there by a Canadian prime minister in eight years.

That trip concluded with a meeting with Modi and the signing of a series of agreements — including a $2.6-billion deal to supply India with about 22 million pounds of uranium for energy generation and 10 commercial agreements worth more than $5.5 billion.

“From energy and critical minerals to aerospace, Canadian companies have built valuable connections that will strengthen our long-term partnership with one of the world’s fastest-growing major economies,” Sidhu said in a statement.

“Canada is ready to be the reliable partner India needs, and the opportunities secured on this mission will deliver lasting benefits for our workers and businesses.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

stories.title: Grand Chief Stewart Phillip endorses B.C. Greens' Lowan, while backing Eby as premier
stories.summary: Victoria - Grand Chief Stewart Phillip, a longtime British Columbia NDP ally whose late wife was a legislator for the party, has thrown his support behind Green Party Leader Emily Lowan in her bid to win in her Vancouver Island riding.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - Jim Leard had just cast his ballot for Emily Lowan on Friday when he ran into the British Columbia Green Party leader outside a high school in Greater Victoria.

“We have a saying in the family, because we all vote Green, ‘someone has to talk for the trees,’” he said with a chuckle.

Lowan had also just voted in the advance ballot at the school when Leard approached her. She told him the party’s prospects were looking good as the election approaches on Oct. 24, including in West Vancouver-Sea to Sky, where Green candidate Jeremy Valeriote is running as the incumbent.

“But it would be incredible to have a few more breakthroughs,” she said. “So, tell your friends, get everybody out to vote.”

Lowan lives in the nearby riding of Victoria-Beacon Hill, not in Saanich North and the Islands where she is running. Residents can vote at any advance voting place in B.C., although they must cast the ballot for a candidate in their own riding.

Lowan voted alongside her father and grandparents on Friday.

“We are all just so thrilled to be casting our ballots,” she said.

Lowan had her own personal breakthrough earlier in the week, when she appeared in the only televised debate of B.C.‘s snap election.

“It helped introduce me to the province,” she said.

Lowan became the party’s leader little more than a year ago, running on a platform that opposed large resource projects and a pledge to tax the wealthiest residents to fund social programs.

The promises, coupled with a strong commitment to the Declaration of the Rights of the Indigenous Peoples Act, earned her the endorsement of Grand Chief Stewart Phillip in her leadership campaign, and again on Friday in her bid to win in the Vancouver Island riding.

Lowan posted the endorsement from the president of the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs on social media.

Phillip said he was “totally honoured” to support the candidate for Saanich North and the Islands.

With days left in the election campaign, Lowan said she would be spending a lot of time in the riding and others on Vancouver Island, which the party has targeted.

The Greens have held the Saanich North riding since 2017, but the party has never won more than three seats in an election.

The NDP on Friday also issued a statement saying Phillip had endorsed Eby as premier, saying he was “the best choice as leader of this province.”

“David Eby has a good heart, and true genuine friends and allies are forever,” Stewart said in the statement.

Phillip has been a strong supporter of the NDP, with his wife Joan elected as a New Democrat legislator in 2024 before she died this past summer.

He backed the NDP in 2024, standing alongside Eby and telling an audience in Victoria that a vote for the Greens was a vote for the B.C. Conservatives.

In his statement posted by Lowan, Phillip said the Green leader’s understanding of the climate crisis as well as her “proactive, principled, evidence-based approach” to finding solutions were key reasons for his endorsement.

“She is a strong and courageous ally for Indigenous Peoples in B.C. and approaches environmental stewardship with full respect for Indigenous rights,” the statement said.

Phillip said he was supporting Lowan “in a riding that the Greens have held for the past three elections, because she has earned my full respect and admiration and is part of our future.”

Phillip previously had a falling out with Eby over the NDP government’s handling of B.C.‘s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act.

Eby backed down earlier this year on changing or suspending parts of the legislation in the face of opposition from Stewart and his late wife, among others.

Phillips’ statement about Eby on Friday said he strongly supports “the principles and ideology” of the NDP under Eby and called on voters to place their trust in him.

“I have been a longtime supporter of the BC NDP since Dave Barrett, and my late wife Joan Phillip was a proud BC NDP (legislator) in David Eby’s government,” he said.

“We have known David Eby and his family for over 20 years. He attended Joan’s funeral and went to her graveside in our community cemetery.”

Eby said during an unrelated campaign announcement on Friday that his government had points of disagreement and differences with Indigenous leadership.

“But at the end of the day, the only way this province will be successful is working in partnership with First Nations,” he said. “It not just lifts up the whole province, it lifts up First Nations communities that have been living in grinding poverty.”

Eby said he and Lowan share a commitment to working with First Nations and noted the Conservatives have proposed to toss out the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act and other economic partnerships.

“Doing so will create unbelievable chaos at a time we need to be building up this province,” he said.

Eby was in Coquitlam on Friday, while interim Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson was in Port Moody, both in Metro Vancouver.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

stories.title: B.C. begins voting without Conservatives' costed platform, Doerkson calls it imminent
stories.summary: Port Moody - British Columbians have started voting without the release of a costed platform from the B.C. Conservatives, whose leader says it will be announced "imminently."
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
British Columbians have started voting in the provincial election without the release of a costed platform from the B.C. Conservatives, whose leader says it will be announced “imminently.”

Interim leader Lorne Doerkson said at a Metro Vancouver campaign stop on Friday that he has seen the platform but wants to make sure they’re aren’t going to promise anything the party “can’t make happen.”

“We’re working on it, but I want it to be right,” Doerkson said while in Port Moody, B.C.

“I want the numbers to be right and I want to know with an absolute clear conscience that the things that we are promising British Columbians in that platform, we will be able to achieve.”

Doerkson said earlier this week that British Columbians would see a “fulsome plan” from the party before voters go to the polls, although advance polls opened Friday through to Wednesday before election day on Oct. 24.

The provincial New Democrats led by David Eby and Emily Lowan’s BC Greens both released their costed platforms earlier this week.

Doerkson said he wants to avoid what Eby’s New Democrats did by breaking promises after the last election, such as a doctor for every resident who wants one and giving people a $1,000 rebate.

“None of those things happened, and our deficit is now $14 billion,” he said, explaining the delay on his party’s costed platform.

The B.C. campaign is entering its last full weekend before the election, and all three major party leaders made pitches to voters on Friday to secure votes in key swing ridings.

Doerkson’s stop in Port Moody included doubling down on his party’s plans to build a women’s and children’s hospital in Surrey, along with scrapping the Massey Tunnel replacement between Delta and Richmond in favour of a bridge.

The Conservatives have also pledged to cut income taxes by up to $1,000 a year “for nearly every working British Columbian,” Doerkson said, as he criticized the former NDP government on a range of topics, from emergency department wait times and affordability to small businesses being “strangled by taxes and red tape.”

“It doesn’t have to be this way, you guys,” Doerkson told the gathering at the campaign stop. “David Eby has a record of devastating this province. We have a plan to build British Columbia, and we have a plan to build it back so that people can afford to make life in this place where we are so lucky to call home.”

Eby, making an NDP campaign stop nearby in the Metro Vancouver city of Coquitlam, said Friday that the Conservatives are unwilling to share their plans to make cuts by not releasing a costed platform.

The New Democrat Leader said the Conservatives’ promises would cost $5 billion and they have not explained how they would pay for it.

“Now, you might think to yourself, ‘Well, that’s weird, why wouldn’t he explain it?’” Eby said, referring to Doerkson.

“It’s not that he doesn’t know the answer. He knows the answer of how he’s going to pay for that $5 billion. He is going to pay for it the same way that conservative parties in B.C. have always paid for these promises, by cutting the services that you and your family depend on.”

The NDP made a series of promises Friday on what a re-elected Eby government would do, including bringing in urgent primary care centres in Greater Victoria and Port Hardy, expanding involuntary care to the Okanagan Correctional Centre in Oliver, and building a new middle school in Coquitlam’s Burke Mountain neighbourhood.

Eby also criticized a Conservative candidate in the swing riding of Juan de Fuca-Malahat for comments about B.C.‘s treaties with First Nations.

Video appeared to show Mike Hicks saying “in law, we have to conquer or sign a treaty with the First Nations.”

“We just arrived, we settled in, and we didn’t do any of it,” he appeared to say, explaining the need for treaties.

Hicks said his comments were being taken “out of context.”

The Conservatives had one day earlier removed another candidate, Jordan McIntosh in Vancouver-Strathcona, for alleged online comments about Hitler and the Holocaust.

Eby said Hicks’ comments show Conservatives’ extremism, with Hicks responding that he “inartfully” explained B.C.‘s need “for developing modern treaties” as time was running out on his answer.

Green Party Leader Emily Lowan scored a major endorsement on Friday as Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs president Grand Chief Stewart Phillip stated his support for her in the Saanich North and the Islands riding.

Phillip’s wife Joan was elected and served as an NDP member of the legislature before she died this summer, and he has been a strong supporter of the New Democrats in the 2024 provincial campaign.

The NDP later issued a statement saying Stewart Phillip had endorsed Eby as premier, calling him “the best choice as leader of this province.”

“David Eby has a good heart, and true genuine friends and allies are forever,” Stewart says in the statement.

“I supported Emily Lowan in her candidacy in Saanich North and the Islands, a riding that the Greens have held for the past three elections, because she has earned my full respect and admiration and is part of our future,” Phillip’s statement adds.

Lowan also became the first major party leader to vote in the race, casting her ballot in the Vancouver Island community of Saanichton, B.C., ON Friday.

— With files by Wolfgang Depner in Victoria

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

stories.title: Former politician Perrin Beatty tragically loses second son, who died four days after his wedding
stories.summary: Tragedy follows death of Beatty's other son, who died in a motorcycle accident in Thailand in 2008.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Tragedy has struck the Beatty family for a second time. After losing his oldest son, Christopher, in a motorcycle accident in 2008, former federal cabinet minister Perrin Beatty has had to say goodbye to his only other child after an automobile accident last month took the life of Patrick Caverhill Beatty.

Patrick died just four days after his wedding to Nabiha Paracha, in a crash that injured his wife. The two had been married at an outdoor ceremony overlooking Lake Muskoka, in cottage country North of Ontario and made an offer on a home there, before setting off for Ottawa to attend Patrick’s 20-year high school reunion.

But they never made it.

A celebration of life will take place Saturday in Ottawa for Patrick, who was 38 years old. His brother, Christopher, was just 24 when he died in a motorcycle accident in Thailand. Patrick will be laid to rest in Beechwood Cemetery beside his brother.

Patrick’s father, 76-year-old Perrin Beatty, served as a Progressive Conservative Member of Parliament for more than 20 years, having first won election at the age of 22 in the 1972 election. He married his wife, Julie, in February of 1974.

In 1979 Beatty became, at the time, the youngest person ever appointed to a Cabinet position when then prime minister Joe Clark named him to the Treasury Board.

According to an obituary from Beechwood , Patrick and Nabiha were married on Sept. 19.

“The happiest days of Patrick’s life came just before his death,” the obituary says. “Nabiha was the star Patrick’s solar system orbited around; he was filled with joy whenever he was with her, and she inspired him always to be his best. The wedding allowed them to share their utmost happiness with friends and family, many of whom had travelled long distances to celebrate with them.”

The following Monday, the newlyweds made an offer on a home in Muskoka, a move the obituary calls “the realization of a longstanding dream.”

Two days after that, they set off for Ottawa, where Patrick planned to attend a reunion with high school classmates at Ashbury College. The accident happened on the way there. His wife was sent to hospital but her injuries are not life-threatening, Ashbury said in a Facebook post .

“Ashbury introduced Patrick to the close-knit group of friends who would remain an important part of his life, many of whom became familiar faces in the Beatty household,” the obituary says. “It also fostered a lifelong passion for learning. It was at Ashbury that Patrick discovered his love of the dramatic arts and creative writing, interests that, for a time, inspired dreams of becoming a film director.”

Patrick earned his undergraduate degree at Western University in London, and a Master of Public Policy at the University of Calgary. At the time of his death, he was more than halfway through an MBA from Dalhousie University.

Patrick was just 19 when Christopher died.

“Losing Christopher taught Patrick about the fragility of life, the importance of relationships, and the need to use our time to make a difference,” Beechwood said. “He promoted organ donation and became active in politics to contribute to his country and community. He respected anyone who made a similar commitment regardless of political belief.”

Patrick worked in the Canadian energy sector, first with Suncor Energy in Calgary and most recently with Pattern Energy in Toronto, where his responsibilities included fostering relationships between the energy sector and Canada’s Indigenous peoples. He had a book on the topic with him at the time of his accident, his obituary notes.

The celebration of Patrick’s life will take place at 10 a.m. on Saturday, Oct. 17 in the Great Hall at Ashbury College in Ottawa, followed by his interment. Ashbury College has also created the Patrick Caverhill Beatty ’06 Memorial Fund in his memory.

After the 1984 election of Brian Mulroney, Perrin was made Minister of National Revenue and Minister responsible for Canada Post. He subsequently served as Solicitor General, Minister of National Defence, Minister of National Health and Welfare, and Minister of Communications. He was Secretary of State for External Affairs in the short-lived Kim Campbell government but lost his seat in the 1993 election, which returned only two Tory MPs.

“A sincere thanks to everyone who has reached out following the loss of our beloved Patrick Beatty,” he wrote in a post on LinkedIn. “Julia, Nabiha and I greatly appreciate your thoughtfulness at this sad time.”

stories.title: Pierre Poilievre urges Albertans not to ‘quit’ on Canada ahead of separation vote
stories.summary: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says he understands the disillusionment with the state of affairs in Canada, but quitting is the easy way out and Albertans are not quitters.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson
stories.content:
Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says he understands separatist disillusionment with the state of affairs in Canada but that quitting isn’t the answer.

Poilievre says quitting is the easy way out and Albertans are not quitters.

He says the solution is to restore the greatness of a country that has been defended and built up through generations.

Poilievre made the comments Friday in a speech in Calgary, three days head of the Alberta referendum in which Albertans will weigh in on independence.

He and Prime Minister Mark Carney are in the province making last-ditch appeals to Albertans to vote to stay in Canada.

Albertans go to the polls Monday to decide whether the province should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on leaving Confederation.

That is one of 10 questions; the other nine have to do with immigration and the Canadian Constitution.

— More to come…

stories.title: Joly warns Stelco owner to uphold jobs or risk forced sale of Canadian assets
stories.summary: Industry Minister says Ottawa open to taking equity stakes in key industries
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Friday the U.S.-based owner of Stelco Inc. must uphold job commitments it made when it purchased the Ontario-based steel maker or risk being forced to sell its Canadian assets.

In a speech at the Canadian Club in Toronto, she also raised the possibility of the federal government taking equity positions in strategic industries.

But Joly stopped short of explicitly saying Ottawa was prepared to take an ownership stake in Stelco.

The minister singled out Stelco owner Cleveland-Cliffs CLF-N , accusing the American company of supporting U.S. tariffs that are damaging its own Canadian operations.

“Cleveland-Cliffs must uphold its commitments, full stop,” she said. “We will apply the full force of the law and every tool in the tool box to ensure that this strategic capacity remains operational.”

Joly added: “They must keep the jobs in Canada or face the prospect of having to sell their Canadian assets.”

Cleveland-Cliffs made legally binding commitments under the Investment Canada Act when it acquired Stelco in 2024, including to maintain at least the same number of unionized workers and the vast majority of non-unionized employees for five years.

Stelco announced plans last month to lay off up to 500 workers across its Hamilton and Lake Erie facilities, citing the ongoing trade crisis, weak demand and continued import pressure.

The steelmaker’s Hamilton operations produce cold-rolled and galvanized steel. The company said it would indefinitely idle both operations.

“Stelco’s Hamilton plant produces steel essential to our advanced manufacturing industrial base,” Joly said.

She said the federal government is prepared to provide financing or even take ownership stakes in companies to keep important industries and jobs in Canada.

“We must ensure that strategic production capabilities remain right here at home,” Joly said in her speech. “We will provide the financing . . . and even take equity positions.”

When asked how soon Ottawa expected to resolve the dispute over Stelco’s planned layoffs or pursue legal action, Joly said it was “a question of days.”

She later told reporters that Ottawa has hired lawyers as it reviews the possibility of taking action against Cleveland-Cliffs.

“It is the government’s position that Stelco has breached its commitments,” Joly said. “Since we believe there’s been multiple breaches of the commitments, the Investment Canada Act under Section 40 offers options through a court process.”

Under the act, Ottawa can ask a superior court to enforce commitments made by foreign investors, impose financial penalties or order the sale of their Canadian businesses.

“We’re looking at all of these options,” Joly said. “And I’m always ready to sit down again with Stelco to find a solution, but it’s not true that they will cut the jobs in Hamilton and continue to ship their steel from the U.S. to Canada meanwhile. No way.”

Stelco was founded in 1910 as the Steel Company of Canada and remained an independent Canadian steel maker until 2007 when it was acquired by Pittsburgh-based U.S. Steel Corp.

The steel maker entered creditor protection in 2014 amid financial difficulties and was later acquired by Bedrock Industries before its eventual sale to Ohio-based steel maker Cleveland-Cliffs in 2024.

“Cleveland-Cliffs came to Canada . . . to be part of the solution,” Joly said. “Now they have spoken in favour of U.S. tariffs, ones that are directly harming Stelco’s own business right here at home and putting hundreds of Canadian jobs at stake.”

stories.title: Interest-rate myth distracts from Canada’s continuing housing crisis
stories.summary: Home prices, carrying costs and the time needed to save for a down payment are much greater for young Canadians than they were for most boomers
stories.author: Paul Kershaw
stories.content:
Do young people really have it so hard in Canada’s housing market today? I get this question regularly from baby boomers. Don’t today’s lower interest rates offset housing’s much higher sticker price?

It’s time to drive a stake through this myth because it is harmful to our national housing debate. It implies lower interest rates are a solution to affordability when they have often been part of the problem. They allow buyers to bid more for housing and inflate prices higher.

Fifty years of data from Statistics Canada and the Canadian Real Estate Association tell a clear story.

Let’s start with the interest rates that boomers understandably found so hard to manage. They were brutal in the early 1980s, peaking at about 18 per cent in 1982 for a conventional five-year mortgage. The increase from around 10 per cent just five years earlier made life difficult for many, especially homeowners with variable-rate loans. The work required to cover annual mortgage costs rose from the equivalent of four months of full-time earnings to six months.

While painful, those peak rates did not last. Within five years, rates had fallen back to levels seen in the mid-1970s. They continued declining through the 1990s and, by 2002, fell below 7 per cent, where they have since remained.

That sounds like good news. But mortgage payments are only one of three factors in the affordability equation. Two other measures matter just as much: the work required to save a down payment and the scale of mortgage risk that accompanies buying a home.

Lower borrowing costs often make both of those measures worse by allowing buyers to qualify for larger loans that further fuel bidding wars. Over the past quarter-century, cheaper credit contributed to skyrocketing home values , especially during the pandemic when rates fell toward 3 per cent.

So while interest rates are much lower today, the three cost pressures associated with home ownership have grown dramatically.

Back in 1982, a typical young person buying an average-priced home needed about five years to save a 20-per-cent down payment, assuming they could set aside 15 per cent of gross earnings. After doing so, they needed a mortgage of roughly $173,000 in today’s dollars to purchase an average home.

A typical young Canadian now needs 13 years to save a comparable down payment. Thereafter, they must take on more than $540,000 in mortgage debt and devote the equivalent of seven months of full-time earnings to pay the annual carrying costs – a full month more than during peak interest rates in the 1980s.

In Ontario and British Columbia, the picture is bleaker. Saving enough for a down payment takes 16 to 18 years. Mortgage debt rises to roughly $609,000 in Ontario and $763,000 in B.C. Annual mortgage costs absorb eight to nine months of work.

These numbers reveal two hard truths. First, the dream that hard work should bring home ownership within reach is far more difficult to achieve today than in 1982 on all three measures of affordability.

Second, the rise in home prices that now hinders younger Canadians generated substantial wealth for homeowners who weathered the interest-rate shock of the early 1980s. After adjusting for inflation, the average Canadian homeowner accumulated roughly $463,000 in additional home equity between 1982 and 2025. In Ontario and British Columbia, the increase exceeded $625,000.

The population is shrinking in pockets of Vancouver and Toronto. What if we put more housing there?

While unaffordability is greatest in Ontario and B.C., the pattern extends across the country. Even in the Prairies and Newfoundland and Labrador, where home prices rose by a more modest $180,000 to $240,000, younger residents must work four to five additional years to save a down payment than did young people in 1982.

There is one counterpoint in these less expensive regions. At the 1982 interest-rate peak, homeowners in the Prairie provinces and Newfoundland worked between 10 additional days and seven additional weeks to cover principal and interest payments than young buyers entering those markets today. On this measure alone, some boomers briefly had it tougher.

There is no denying that the early 1980s were frightening for many Canadians. Some could not cope as credit became much more expensive.

Today, younger Canadians don’t just face a temporary spike in borrowing costs. They confront a housing system in which the work required to save for, buy and carry a mortgage is generally far greater than the peak hardship faced by boomers in 1982.

Imagine enduring that level of fear and uncertainty not for a few difficult years, but as a defining feature of your housing future. It’s no wonder so many young people feel shut out of the housing market today.

Dr. Paul Kershaw is a policy professor at UBC and founder of Generation Squeeze , Canada’s leading voice for generational fairness. You can follow Gen Squeeze on X , Facebook , Bluesky , and Instagram , as well as subscribe to Paul’s Hard Truths podcast.

stories.content:
Calgary - Police were working Friday to determine the cause of a fiery bus crash in Calgary that killed three passengers and injured 16 others, including a police officer who helped save a child.

Two transit buses and several other vehicles were involved in the chain-reaction crash Thursday on a busy road in the city’s northeast.

stories.title: Vancouver officer tells Myles Gray hearing of ‘unnerving’ call for help
stories.summary: No charges have been laid over Gray’s death, which a 2023 coroner’s inquest ruled a homicide
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A Vancouver police officer involved in the fatal arrest of Myles Gray has addressed the man’s family, telling them the “tragic” outcome was never the intention of police.

But Const. Beau Spencer had told the public hearing in Vancouver earlier Friday there was nothing he would change about his use of force in the violent arrest on Aug. 13, 2015.

He spoke to Gray’s family as he ended his testimony. “I know there’s no words that I can say to you to take the pain away,” he said in a shaky voice.

“I can’t imagine losing a member of my family like you did. The intention of us was not to end it this way, and it was very tragic.”

Spencer is among seven Vancouver officers under investigation by British Columbia’s Office of the Police Complaint Commissioner, which called the hearing over whether they committed misconduct during the confrontation that ended with Gray’s death or neglected their duties by failing to take notes in the immediate aftermath.

They have all denied wrongdoing.

Spencer, testifying for a second day, said Gray was the strongest man he had ever encountered in 15 years of policing, and the incident was “biggest moment” of his life.

“It was very traumatizing to me,” he said, adding that when he now saw someone who looked like Gray it would “bring me back to that moment … it constantly stays with me.”

Spencer said his involvement began while he and his partner were having ice cream at a Dairy Queen, when they heard an “unnerving” call for assistance from a colleague who encountered Gray on a residential street in Burnaby, near the Vancouver boundary.

The hearing was told earlier that Const. Hardeep Sahota had retreated to her vehicle, away from Gray, when she radioed for help.

Spencer said he knew Sahota and her tone of voice on the call raised immediate concern, while an “animalistic roar” he later heard as he and his partner headed to the scene was like nothing he had ever heard on a police radio.

Spencer, whose lawyer said he was over six feet tall and weighed more than 90 kilograms, or about 200 pounds, said that when he arrived he found other officers who appeared to be “exhausted” as they struggled to subdue Gray.

Spencer testified that for the first time in his career he felt physically unable to restrain someone as he and another officer, Const. Joshua Wong, tried unsuccessfully to get Gray’s arm behind his back to apply handcuffs and make sure he did not have a weapon.

“I needed to up my level of force,” Spencer said. He recalled delivering three or four “closed-fist strikes” as hard as he could to Gray’s right shoulder while pulling on the man’s wrist with his other hand.

“Each time there was nothing … (his arm) was not moving at all which was incredibly concerning for me,” Spencer said, given his and Wong’s size and strength.

“This was the strongest man I’d dealt with at that point and the strongest man I’ve dealt with” in 15 years of policing, he said.

Spencer said he held onto Gray’s arm “with all my might.”

No charges have been laid over Gray’s death, which a 2023 coroner’s inquest ruled was a homicide, a term that does not assign legal blame.

The commissioner’s notice of public hearing said an earlier disciplinary process had dismissed misconduct allegations, but the discipline authority found the process “strangely lopsided” and had to decide the case despite “discrepancies and inconsistencies in statements made by (Vancouver Police Department) members.”

The earlier inquest heard Gray was left with injuries that included a fractured eye socket, crushed voice box and ruptured testicles, while a paramedic said Gray’s bruising was so severe, he initially thought Gray was not a white man.

Spencer told the hearing on Friday that Gray passed out, but when he came to he exhibited a “crazy change of behaviour.”

“He looked at me and said ‘what’s going on,’” Spencer said, adding the moment of apparent lucidity from Gray gave the officer an immediate sense of relief.

Spencer recalled telling Gray he had been involved in a fight with officers and an ambulance was on the way. Gray was like someone in “the dead of sleep” who had woken up and said “where am I,” he said.

But the moment only lasted seconds, before Gray went into a “rage” again, throwing the officer onto his back and “manhandling” him despite the officer’s larger stature, Spencer said.

When Gray fell unconscious a second time “he went from pure strength, pure power, to no flex in his muscles,” and going limp, Spencer said.

That was when Spencer said he stepped back from the scene.

“I was not a person I believed could help in a medical sense,” thinking he would be in the way, he said.

Gray died at the scene, which was by then attended by paramedics and firefighters.

Spencer said he was in a state of “shock or disbelief” at what had occurred, as officers involved in the arrest were called to meet at Vancouver police headquarters on Cambie Street that day.

There, he said he found out he was under investigation by B.C.’s police watchdog, the Independent Investigations Office, and the officers met union representatives.

A moment “soaked in” when one or more union representatives told him “don’t write anything down, don’t write notes, we will tell you when to write something,” he said.

“I thought it was odd,” Spencer said, although he believed it made sense in the context of not having legal representation.

He later wrote a statement on his personal laptop before it was entered into the police data system Prime around March 2016. He said he did not consult other officers.

The ongoing public hearing started in January but has experienced repeated delays.

Const. Eric Birzneck was the first of the seven officers to testify earlier this week.

He likened Gray’s strength to “the Hulk” and said the man appeared “impervious to pain” as police tried to subdue him.

Adjudicator Elizabeth Arnold-Bailey has adjourned the hearing until Nov. 16.
