stories.title: Hitachi announces $479M plan to build transformer insulation factory in London, Ont.
stories.summary: The 21,000-square-metre facility would be the first in Canada to produce pressboard — a material made from paper pulp that's key to keeping transformers cool.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
Hitachi Energy and the federal and Ontario governments have announced a $479-million plan to build a new transformer insulation factory to help meet skyrocketing demand from data centres, green energy and industrial development.

“All those investments are creating more demand for components, and transformers are a major element in the customer energy chain,” Bruno Melles, chief executive of Hitachi’s transformers business unit, said in an interview ahead of Friday’s announcement in London, Ont.

“Because in every place where there is power generation and in every place where there is a connection, there is a transformer.”

The 21,000-square-metre facility would be the first in Canada to produce pressboard — a material made from paper pulp that’s key to keeping transformers cool — and the first Hitachi would establish in the Americas. Currently in Canada that material sourced from Europe, Melles said.

Construction is set to be complete by the end of 2028 and the project is expected to create 100 permanent skilled jobs.

Hitachi is shouldering the bulk of the investment, with the federal and Ontario governments collectively contributing $50 million.

Of that, $20 million is through the federal strategic response fund, $10 million is from Natural Resources Canada and up to $20 million is through the Invest Ontario Fund.

The power industry has been dealing with supply chain challenges as electricity demand booms. The factory aims to ease at least one of the big pinch points.

“Today we are in a situation where the industry for transformer manufacturing is going at a very high speed, but not all the industrial parts are going at the same speed,” Melles, who is based in Zurich, said.

“This is why we want to give a strong message to the market and say, ‘We want to be an integral part of the supply chain resilience and we are going to invest in order to ensure that the market is not going to have any shortage.'”

In May, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Canada’s new electricity strategy, which aims to double the country’s electricity grid by 2050.

“Electricity demand in Canada is growing at an unprecedented pace, something we’ve never seen before,” said Carla Vicente, managing director of Hitachi Energy’s Canadian division, in an interview.

“By ensuring that we have this factory operational by the end of 2028, we will be able to respond to the higher needs and demand for the transformers that are an essential part of anything that we want to do to be able to electrify.”

Building new infrastructure has been a key focus for Carney’s government, and several power and transmission projects have been referred to the major projects office for a streamlined review.

“By investing in the critical infrastructure needed to power our future, we are supporting economic growth, creating good-paying jobs and strengthening Canada’s economic security,” Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said in a news release.

Vic Fedeli, Ontario’s minister for economic development, job creation and trade, said in a news release that the Hitachi investment will help position the province as a central hub for advanced manufacturing projects.

“In the face of global economic uncertainty, our government continues to foster the competitive conditions needed for global companies to confidently expand their presence in Ontario and invest in long-term projects.”

Melles said the site for the new factory in London was not chosen “as a coincidence.”

He said it will be a good fit with another operation Hitachi has in the southwestern Ontario city. In June, it announced the acquisition of Canduct, a manufacturer of insulation kits and components.

“To have a location that is very, very close to Canduct will allow a simplification of the supply in the value chain, a dramatic reduction of the risks connected to logistics, and then of course we can count on having access to fresh and clean water that is an integral element for the production of insulation material.”

“To have a location that is very, very close to Canduct will allow a simplification of the supply in the value chain, a dramatic reduction of the risks connected to logistics, and then of course we can count on having access to fresh and clean water that is an integral element for the production of insulation material.”

stories.title: Claims made by Jewish Canadian Armed Forces members in $150M racism class action rejected: report
stories.summary: One member is taking legal action on behalf of other Jewish members, according to recent reporting by the Canadian Jewish News.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
More than two dozen Jewish members of the Canadian Armed Forces who made claims in a $150-million racial discrimination settlement against the military were told they did not meet the racial identity criteria, according to the Canadian Jewish News.

One member, Capt. Rabbi Jonathan Jaffit, is taking legal action .

He alleges that Deloitte, the accounting firm in charge of processing the claims, is not applying the terms of the final settlement agreement and is denying access to funds for claimants “who squarely meet the class definition,” according to court documents obtained by CJN.

Jewish CAF members told CJN they were harassed and discriminated against during their time serving in the military due to their identity. One member, who said they served for eight years, gave 14 examples of antisemitism in a claim application.

“You people really are tight with money,” they were once told. The same member was accused of cheating because they could not take an exam on Shabbat, they said.

“The fact that we are just rejected once again from this lawsuit about discrimination is at the height of irony, and really the height of pain for the Jewish soldiers in the army,” the member said.

Another Jewish member who made a claim that was rejected said they “were forced to attend church on Sundays” and “comments about them having a big nose (were) published in the Royal Military College yearbook,” the CJN reported.

That same member said a swastika was drawn on their helmet by a colleague.

They filed a complaint with the military after they were called a “f—ing” Jewish “c—t” and told they couldn’t take a training course. Despite the complaint, “nothing was done,” they said.

Another Jewish CAF member said “it’s gotten harder to be Jewish in the military, just like every other public institution.”

“But I kind of knew, or I shouldn’t say I knew, I had a feeling going into it that we would be left in the cold, we being Jews,” they said. After October 7 — when Hamas terrorists murdered 1,200 people in Israel, sparking a war in the Middle East country — “things took a turn.”

A Zoom meeting that was dedicated to “Talking About Race” was set up for CAF members to join, but they said it “very quickly devolved into Israel-bashing and peddling false narratives about Israel and about Zionism.”

They said their claim was considered “ineligible” by Deloitte.

In a response from the firm, the member was told: “While an individual May have experienced discrimination and/or harassment based on other personal characteristics such as gender, sexuality, disability, religion, culture, or language, claims that are not based on racial discrimination and/or racial harassment are outside the scope and intent of this class action.”

The racial discrimination settlement stems from a 2016 lawsuit. Three army veterans — who identified as Indigenous and Black, including one person of Haitian descent — alleged they were discriminated against based on race.

The class action was certified in 2024. Current and former CAF members who experienced racial discrimination and/or racial harassment in connection with their military service at any time since April 17, 1985 were eligible to make a claim.

The claims period closed on Oct. 15.

Claimants can receive a settlement ranging from $5,000 to $30,000, depending on the duration and severity of impacts, according to a settlement notice .

In 2025, the Canadian military issued an apology for racial discrimination and harassment.

Deloitte Canada told National Post in a statement that the matter “is governed by the terms of the agreement approved by the Federal Court.”

“Deloitte Canada performs its work in strict accordance with the highest professional standards and takes very seriously the confidentiality requirements of the work we do for our clients,” the statement said, adding that the firm could not comment further on any matters relating to its clients.

When asked what they wanted to happen, a Jewish CAF member told CJN: “I would like the CAF to take ownership of this file away from Deloitte. Clearly, they’re not qualified to be able to do this job without bias. The CAF needs an adjudicator that is not indoctrinated in this anti-Jewish ideology. And I don’t know if that’s an internal system.”

Department of National Defence spokesperson Cheryl Forrest told National Post in a statement that Deloitte was appointed by the Federal Court.

Within the final settlement agreement, there is a section that says “decisions by the administrator are final and binding and are not subject to judicial review” and there is no “mechanism for appeal,” she said.

National Defence and CAF are not involved in eligibility assessments, added Forrest.

“DND and the CAF are taking deliberate, coordinated action to eliminate racism, discrimination, biases, harmful stereotypes, and systemic barriers. We are committed to fostering an environment in which everyone is treated with dignity and respect,” she said.

stories.title: Court documents show Fsin knew ISC audit decision months before informing members
stories.summary: Documents show the Fsin applied for a judicial review in August, alleging procedural unfairness following Isc’s decision that the organization owes $12.4 million.
stories.author: Grace Miller
stories.content:
Federal Court documents show the Federation of Sovereign Indigenous Nations (Fsin) knew the details of money owed to the federal government months prior to the organization’s recent public disclosure.

Documents show in August that the Fsin applied for a judicial review, alleging procedural unfairness following Indigenous Services Canada (ISC)’s decision in July that the organization owed $12.4 million to the federal government due to ineligible and unsupported expenses between April 2019 and March 2024.

The Fsin publicly announced the revised figure Wednesday in a media release, stating it does not accept Isc’s final decision and sharing that it has commenced legal action.

“ISC May have concluded its process, but this matter is not concluded for the Fsin,” said Fsin Chief Bobby Camerson in the release.

“We remain confident that when this matter is subjected to a fair and independent review, that all expenditures will be proven eligible and the allegations proven false.”

Political analyst Jennifer Laewetz is questioning how much information is being shared with First Nations leaders.

“We’re seeing a lot of communication now from the Fsin in the last year regarding the audit almost strictly on social media and then sent to certain media outlets,” says Laewetz.

“So rather than seeing this proper communication coming frequently from the federation to the chiefs and assembly, you know through email or whatever, it might be they’re finding out about a lot of these things, they’re finding out a lot about the Fsin and its stance on things, through the media.”

Court documents show the Fsin claims loss of “finite reserves” and experienced staff. The organization has listed postings for multiple jobs since July.

Fsin Vice Chief Fabian Head said in a statement he supports the Fsin’s efforts to criticize Isc’s decision.

“Based on the evidence before me, the expenditures that ISC has classified as ineligible are legitimate, reasonable, and consistent with both the funding agreements and the realities of serving First Nations communities,” said Head.

ISC originally found $34.2 million in estimated questionable expenditures and lowered the amount following a line-by-line review. The Fsin said the two sides had substantially narrowed the amount in dispute by June 12.

Laewetz suggests the dispute is part of a broader problem of the federation focusing on defending itself and not representing member nations.

“Money is obviously a big piece. There should be some accountability. But I think on the other side of that, we also need to be asking, is this money getting to where it needs to go when in terms of resources,” Laewetz said.

“This organization has been largely silent and kind of missing on part of the bigger conversations impacting treaty, Bill C-5, 39, Bill S-2, child welfare reform. Where have you been?”

Indigenous Services Canada said the money owed is now considered a debt owed to the Crown.

ISC is seeking repayment in full by Nov. 13 and warns the money could instead be deducted from future federal funding if it isn’t paid.

Laewetz said that shouldn’t become a financial burden for member nations.

“I would hope that First Nations people understand this is not up to our nations to pay. Under no circumstances should our First Nations be transferring money to the federation to make these payments or to pay back this money,” said Laewetz.

Global News has repeatedly sought interviews with Chief Cameron and other vice chiefs. Cameron agreed to a Friday morning virtual interview with Global News, but later cancelled, citing a death on Red Earth Cree Nation.

The court challenge remains ongoing.

stories.title: Pitching in: Family helping raise $8-million for BC Children’s Hospital
stories.summary: Six-year-old Eliana Gappan, who was treated for a rare autoimmune condition, and her family have become hospital spokespeople
stories.author: Paul Waldie
stories.content:
The organizers: Eliana Gappan, Abd Alaziz Gappan, Maysaa Alabtah and Selena Gappan

The pitch: Helping raise more than $8-million

The cause: BC Children’s Hospital

Back in April, five-year-old Eliana Gappan came down with a cough and fever that soon turned far worse. Within a couple of weeks her legs felt numb and she couldn’t walk.

Her parents – Abd Alaziz Gappan and Maysaa Alabtah – took her to the hospital near their home in Nanaimo, B.C., but doctors couldn’t diagnose the problem. When she started developing weakness in her face, Eliana was rushed by helicopter to BC Children’s Hospital in Vancouver.

Her parents were distraught. “This is your kid just dying between your hands, and you can’t do anything,” recalled Mr. Gappan.

The family had immigrated to Canada from Syria, by way of Saudi Arabia, in 2022 and Mr. Gappan was preparing for his final exams to become a veterinarian.

He accompanied his daughter to Vancouver, and from the moment they arrived at BC Children’s, he couldn’t believe the care she received. “It was a Sunday and they called in the whole staff, the MRI responsible staff and other technicians and doctors,” he said.

Doctors diagnosed Eliana with Guillain-Barré Syndrome, a rare condition that occurs when the body’s immune system attacks nerves. A team of doctors, including a neurologist who specialized in GBS, treated Eliana for three weeks. She also received extensive physiotherapy at the Sunny Hill Health Centre involving music, painting and pet owners who visited the centre.

Eliana slowly regained her strength and soon she was able to walk. She was discharged on June 5, her sixth birthday. “She went back to her school, playing and jumping with her friends, talking again,” said Mr. Gappan.

Eliana and her family – she also has a younger sister Selena – have become spokespeople for the hospital, which recently held its Dream Lottery. The annual draw raises around $8-million for research each year.

Mr. Gappan plans to become an active donor once he starts his veterinarian practice and he’s already been making presentations about the hospital at Eliana’s school. “I will do whatever it takes,” he said.

“Any kid can have this disease but you will not get this care in any other part of the world,” he added. “We need to support these researchers and these doctors and these workers.”

The pitch: Helping raise more than $8-million
The cause: BC Children’s Hospital
Back in April, five-year-old Eliana Gappan came down with a cough and fever that soon turned far worse. Within a couple of weeks her legs felt numb and she couldn’t walk.

Her parents – Abd Alaziz Gappan and Maysaa Alabtah – took her to the hospital near their home in Nanaimo, B.C., but doctors couldn’t diagnose the problem. When she started developing weakness in her face, Eliana was rushed by helicopter to BC Children’s Hospital in Vancouver.
Her parents were distraught. “This is your kid just dying between your hands, and you can’t do anything,” recalled Mr. Gappan.
The family had immigrated to Canada from Syria, by way of Saudi Arabia, in 2022 and Mr. Gappan was preparing for his final exams to become a veterinarian.

He accompanied his daughter to Vancouver, and from the moment they arrived at BC Children’s, he couldn’t believe the care she received. “It was a Sunday and they called in the whole staff, the MRI responsible staff and other technicians and doctors,” he said.

Doctors diagnosed Eliana with Guillain-Barré Syndrome, a rare condition that occurs when the body’s immune system attacks nerves. A team of doctors, including a neurologist who specialized in GBS, treated Eliana for three weeks. She also received extensive physiotherapy at the Sunny Hill Health Centre involving music, painting and pet owners who visited the centre.

Eliana slowly regained her strength and soon she was able to walk. She was discharged on June 5, her sixth birthday. “She went back to her school, playing and jumping with her friends, talking again,” said Mr. Gappan.

Eliana and her family – she also has a younger sister Selena – have become spokespeople for the hospital, which recently held its Dream Lottery. The annual draw raises around $8-million for research each year.

Mr. Gappan plans to become an active donor once he starts his veterinarian practice and he’s already been making presentations about the hospital at Eliana’s school. “I will do whatever it takes,” he said.
“Any kid can have this disease but you will not get this care in any other part of the world,” he added. “We need to support these researchers and these doctors and these workers.”

stories.title: France to decide next month on extradition of ex-Manitoba law dean in fraud case
stories.summary: A former law dean at the University of Manitoba wanted on a fraud charge is expected to learn next month if he will be extradited from France.
stories.author: Brittany Hobson
stories.content:
A former law dean at the University of Manitoba wanted on a fraud charge is expected to learn next month if he will be extradited from France.

A court document says Jonathan Black-Branch was in the Investigating Chamber of the Versailles Court of Appeal today opposing his extradition.

The court reserved its decision to Nov. 6.

Black-Branch was arrested in a municipality west of Paris in April, after a Canada-wide arrest warrant was issued for fraud over $5,000.

The disbarred lawyer is accused of misusing more than $600,000 from the university to pay his bills, buy pricey meals at a members-only club and spend on his education at Ivy League schools.

Black-Branch was hired as the Winnipeg university’s law dean in 2016 but suddenly left the post in 2020 and moved to Europe.

stories.title: Canadians most likely to be born on Sept. 20, Statistics Canada reports
stories.summary: Statistics agency found that Sept. 20 was the most likely date on which to be born over the past 30 years. Least likely? Christmas.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
If you had a birthday last month, happy belated. Also, you’re not that special.

Statistics Canada has just released information on the number of live births in Canada, broken down by month and, even further, by date. Upon crunching the numbers, they determined that Sept. 20 was the most likely date on which to be born between 1995 and 2025.

That might seem random, but it’s part of a larger trend. The second most common birthday is just two days earlier, ON Sept. 18. Third is Sept. 25.

You have to dig down to the ninth most common birthday to find one that falls in another month — July 5 to be exact. In all, 16 of the 20 most common days on which to be born are in September. July and August were also home to larger-than-average numbers of birthdays.

One of the first comments in response to the agency’s tweet about the topic was: “Technically all those September babies are Christmas babies.” That’s true. The average human gestation from conception to birth is about 267 days. Subtract that from Sept. 20 and you get Dec. 28, right in the middle of the Christmas holidays.

Some of the (many) people born on Sept. 20 include hockey star Guy Lafleur, author George R.R. Martin and Italian actress Sophia Loren.

The least common birthday, not surprisingly, was Feb. 29, since that date only occurs once every four years. Next least common was a cluster of three days — Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and Boxing Day. Far more babies were born in summer months that winter ones.

One of the more surprising revelations was that Dec. 31 and Jan. 1 were unlikely days on which to be born, falling 359th and 362nd, respectively. Some famous New Year’s babies include Australian actress Angourie Rice, authors E.M. Forster and J.D. Salinger, and FBI director J. Edgar Hoover.

It can even be lucrative. Reader’s Digest reports that, in 2022, Dignity Health St. Rose Dominican Hospital in Las Vegas gave its first baby of the year a large gift basket filled with diapers and baby supplies. The following year, Kaleida Health’s Oishei Children’s Hospital in Buffalo, N.Y., presented New Year’s twins with a basket of baby essentials and a $1,000 savings bond.

And last year Prudential Financial rolled out a $150 “Generation Beta Baby Bonus” for any baby born in the U.S. on Jan. 1, the official start of the next generation. It was a nice bit of PR and a nudge for new parents to start saving early for things like education and their own retirement.

Perhaps people aren’t doing the math required to have a baby born at the stroke of midnight on New Year’s Eve. Or maybe they’re too busy worrying about taxes in early April to get busy with other things.

stories.title: Youth found guilty in Ottawa 2023 terror plot to kill Jewish people
stories.summary: A judge has found a youth guilty of two terrorism-related charges stemming from an alleged 2023 plan to kill Jewish people in Ottawa.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
A judge has found a youth guilty of two terrorism -related charges stemming from an alleged 2023 plan to kill Jewish people in Ottawa.

In 2023, the RCMP said the youth was charged with “facilitating” a terrorist activity by spreading “instructional material” about building bombs, and “knowingly instructing” someone to carry out a terrorist attack.

Crown attorneys at the time charged the youth facilitating terrorist activity, possession of explosives and making or possessing an explosive substance.

More coming.

stories.title: Youth found guilty of terrorism charges tied to alleged plan to kill Jewish people
stories.summary: Person guilty of conspiracy to commit murder through involvement with terrorist group, facilitating terrorist activity by seeking to acquire a prohibited firearm
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
A judge has found a youth guilty of two terrorism-related charges stemming from an alleged 2023 plan to kill Jewish people in Ottawa.

In a verdict delivered Friday, Ontario Superior Court Justice Kerry McVey found the young person guilty of conspiracy to commit murder through involvement with a terrorist group, and of facilitating terrorist activity by seeking to acquire a prohibited firearm.

McVey found him not guilty of facilitating terrorist activity by making instructional material and propaganda available.

The youth, who cannot legally be identified due to his age, had pleaded not guilty to all three charges.

His trial began in April, a day after his co-accused was found guilty on four charges.

The co-accused, who also cannot be named due to provisions of the Youth Criminal Justice Act, pleaded not guilty to the charges but admitted to a statement of facts and invited a judge to find him guilty. The unusual move preserved his right to appeal pretrial rulings in his case, as well as the findings of guilt.

McVey concluded the youth found guilty Friday conspired with his co-accused and another individual who was not charged in a plan to kill a large number of people.

“The planned attack was intended to intimidate a segment of the public, namely members of the Jewish community, with respect to their security,” McVey said.

The attack was intended to cause serious harm through violence, she said.

“The communications between the participants reveal detailed discussions concerning the scale of the intended killing, the weapons required to accomplish it, the quantity of ammunition necessary and the possible use of explosives,” McVey said.

“Their shared objective was the mass killing of innocent people.”

The youth found guilty Friday was arrested in February, 2024.

In her reasons, McVey noted the Crown alleged that in the summer of 2023, the young person and his co-accused communicated regularly online and shared violent extremist material.

The judge said that by August of that year, the two young people clearly shared an interest in violent extremist content and expressed hostility toward particular communities, including Jewish people.

She said much of the material sent by the young person to his co-accused could be characterized as propaganda or instructional material – including videos created by the extremist Islamic State group and documents about firearms, explosives and methods of killing.

The judge noted that, according to the Crown, those communications evolved over time and by late October, 2023, a concrete plan had emerged to carry out a mass casualty attack in which the co-accused youth intended to take his own life.

McVey said she found the young person not guilty Friday of facilitating terrorist activity by making instructional material and propaganda available because she was not sure that he knew he was furthering terrorist activity when he sent the material to his co-accused.

McVey said she was not satisfied that his co-accused’s plans had even advanced that far at the time.

McVey said that when the youth was aware of his co-accused’s plan for a large-scale attack, he did more than simply express support or interest. She said he contacted potential sources of firearms, made inquiries about availability and pricing, and relayed information back to his co-accused for decision-making.

McVey said that, put simply, attempting to obtain an assault rifle for use in a preplanned, religiously and ideologically motivated mass shooting plainly facilitates that terrorist activity.

After delivering her verdict, McVey addressed the youth directly.

“Based on all of the evidence, I am satisfied that you genuinely intended to help advance this act of deadly violence,” she said.

McVey said the young person was a participant in the conspiracy, even though he did not intend to fight or die as part of it, and even though he May not have known of, or intended to be involved in, every aspect of it.

“In Canada, people are not prosecuted for holding unpopular, offensive or extremist views,” McVey told him.

“You are not being found guilty because of what you believed. You are being found guilty because of what you did. The evidence establishes that your beliefs led you to take concrete steps with others toward the commission of terrorist activity.”

stories.title: Temperatures set to plunge across southwestern Ontario this weekend
stories.summary: Cooler conditions are expected to be short-lived. High pressure moving into the region will bring mainly sunny skies through the weekend.
stories.content:
Prepare for a sharp drop in temperatures as a colder air mass settles into the region following the passage of a cold front.

Temperatures Friday afternoon ranged from about 9 C to 14 C across the region, but conditions are expected to cool rapidly overnight, with temperatures nearing the freezing mark by Saturday morning, according to CTV News London’s Reta Ismail.

“We’re going to get close to that freezing mark overnight,” Ismail said.

The colder air follows a large low-pressure system that brought overnight rainfall to parts of southwestern Ontario. While the rain is expected to taper off later Friday evening, Ismail said some lake-effect showers developing off Lake Huron could affect areas between about 6 p.m. and 9 p.m.

The more significant change, she said, will be the arrival of strong northwesterly winds and a noticeably colder air mass.

“The real big story with this one is the colder air and the strong gusty northwesterly winds that are going to start to build this evening and into tomorrow,” said Ismail.

North winds of 20 to 40 km/h are expected Friday evening, contributing to a chilly start to the weekend. Overnight temperatures are forecast to fall to around 1 C before rebounding under sunny skies Saturday.

Despite abundant sunshine, temperatures are expected to remain below seasonal norms.

“We’re forecasting a high of 10 degrees and with that chilly northwesterly wind, it will actually feel close to about 7 or 8 degrees tomorrow,” Ismail said.

The cooler conditions are expected to be short-lived. High pressure moving into the region will bring mainly sunny skies through the weekend, while temperatures should gradually return to seasonal levels from Sunday through Wednesday.

stories.title: Charges laid against two Nova Scotia businesses accused of illegal lobster buying
stories.summary: Yarmouth - The Nova Scotia government has laid charges against two businesses accused of buying illegally caught lobsters in the province.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Yarmouth - The Nova Scotia government has laid charges against two businesses accused of buying illegally caught lobsters in the province.

Two firms in southwestern Nova Scotia, Independent Fisheries in Lockeport, N.S., and a numbered company in Shelburne County are facing charges under the Fisheries and Coastal Resources Act.

The Department of Natural Resources says these charges follow a two-year investigation into the lobster trade.

Both companies face charges for buying, selling or processing fish that were caught without a valid licence.

The numbered company, 3329874 Nova Scotia Ltd., faces the same charges and an additional charge for buying, selling or marketing fish in Nova Scotia without the required licence.

Neither firm could be reached for comment on Friday afternoon.

Nova Scotia raised the maximum fine under the act in 2024, to $1 million for a first offence, up from $100,000.

The cases are scheduled for a court date in Yarmouth Provincial Court next month.

Colin Sproul, president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance, said the organization is “extremely pleased” to see charges have been laid.

“The lobster fishery is the most important segment of Nova Scotia’s economy. It’s our largest export and our biggest employer. And it’s all being placed in extreme jeopardy by an industrial-scale, out-of-season fishery that’s taking place across the province, and across the Maritimes for that matter,” Sproul said in an interview Friday.

Canada’s lobster fishery had a landed value of $1.97 billion in 2024. Almost half of that, about $962 million, was caught in Nova Scotia.

Sproul said Nova Scotia’s government has ramped up illegal fishing enforcement over the past couple of years, and he thanked Premier Tim Houston and provincial Fisheries and Aquaculture Minister Kent Smith for their efforts.

“We give our heartfelt thanks to Minister Smith and to Premier Houston for today. It’s a really important day for fishermen in Nova Scotia,” he said.

The group that represents thousands of independent, multi-species commercial fishers and associations across the Maritimes filed a lawsuit against Independent Fisheries Ltd. in November 2024.

A court hearing about the lawsuit was held last month, but there hasn’t been a ruling yet.

Sproul said he’s hopeful the province and public prosecution moves ahead with these charges in a timely manner, adding that the group’s lawsuit has faced multiple delays.

“Seeing this prosecution move forward would definitely be beneficial to a lawsuit that seeks to recompense fishermen across Nova Scotia for what’s been done to their industry,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

— By Lyndsay Armstrong in Halifax.

stories.title: 4 in 10 women don’t know where to seek support for menopause: report
stories.summary: Around four in 10 (40 per cent) Canadian women reported that they do not know where to seek menopause care, a report by health care and insurance organization GreenShield said.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
While roughly half of the population will experience menopause , many women in Canada struggle to find resources that can help them through this phase, a new report has found.

Around four in 10 (40 per cent) Canadian women reported that they do not know where to seek menopause care, a new report by health care and insurance organization GreenShield says.

The barriers are particularly striking for racialized women in Canada, 45 per cent of whom say they are unaware of where to seek help for perimenopause or menopause symptoms.

Only one-third of racialized women said they had discussed their symptoms with a health professional, compared to roughly half of women respondents overall. While some workplaces have supports available for menopause, nearly one in four said those supports at their workplace were not “culturally appropriate.”

“Menopause symptoms can be complex and interconnected, and too often, women are left playing detective with their own bodies, trying to understand symptoms that May initially seem unrelated and searching for credible answers on their own,” said Harriet Ekperigin, vice president of clinical services growth at GreenShield Health.

Another GreenShield survey, conducted by Ipsos in March, found that 33 per cent of Canadian women “wait more than two years for effective menopause care.”

The March survey said that this was due to “a complex series of barriers ranging from confusion over symptoms and dismissed concerns to not knowing where to turn for help.”

Menopause occurs when the ovaries cannot consistently make the hormones of reproduction called estrogen and progesterone. Perimenopause, which typically occurs between the ages of 40 and 50, is a transitional phase that occurs when a person’s periods start to change and ends when they have not had a period of 12 months.

According to Health Canada, the average age of menopause in Canada is 51. The most common symptoms could include fatigue, hot flashes, night sweats, sleep disturbance, heart palpitations, anxiety, mood swings, weight gain, and brain fog.

According to the Menopause Foundation of Canada’s 2022 research report , 46 per cent of Canadian women “feel unprepared for this stage of life and, in a world where no topic is off limits, more than half (54%) believe menopause is still a taboo subject.”

The March survey said that this was due to “a complex series of barriers ranging from confusion over symptoms and dismissed concerns to not knowing where to turn for help.”

Menopause occurs when the ovaries cannot consistently make the hormones of reproduction called estrogen and progesterone. Perimenopause, which typically occurs between the ages of 40 and 50, is a transitional phase that occurs when a person’s periods start to change and ends when they have not had a period of 12 months.

According to Health Canada, the average age of menopause in Canada is 51. The most common symptoms could include fatigue, hot flashes, night sweats, sleep disturbance, heart palpitations, anxiety, mood swings, weight gain, and brain fog.

According to the Menopause Foundation of Canada’s 2022 research report , 46 per cent of Canadian women “feel unprepared for this stage of life and, in a world where no topic is off limits, more than half (54%) believe menopause is still a taboo subject.”

stories.title: Highway 401 eastbound reopens after three-vehicle crash
stories.summary: Police said one of the transport trucks was fully loaded, and crews are currently unloading its contents so the vehicle can be turned over and removed from the highway.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
The eastbound lanes of Highway 401 at Highway 2 in Woodstock have reopened following a three-vehicle collision involving two commercial motor vehicles and a passenger vehicle early Friday morning.

Ontario Provincial Police first reported the closure shortly after 4 a.m. as emergency crews responded to the crash.

Police said the driver of the passenger vehicle was taken to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries. The drivers of the two transport trucks were not injured.

Police said one of the transport trucks was fully loaded, and crews had to unload its contents so the vehicle can be turned over and removed from the highway.

Motorists were being asked to avoid the area and use alternate routes while the cleanup and investigation continue.

stories.title: NewsAlert: Youth guilty of two charges tied to alleged plan to kill Jewish people
stories.summary: Ottawa - A judge has found a youth guilty of two terrorism-related charges stemming from an alleged 2023 plan to kill Jewish people in Ottawa.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - A judge has found a youth guilty of two terrorism-related charges stemming from an alleged 2023 plan to kill Jewish people in Ottawa.

In a verdict delivered Friday, Ontario Superior Court Justice Kerry McVey found the young person guilty of conspiracy to commit murder through involvement with a terrorist group, and of facilitating terrorist activity by seeking to acquire a prohibited firearm.

McVey found him not guilty of facilitating terrorist activity by making instructional material and propaganda available.

The youth, who cannot legally be identified due to his age, had pleaded not guilty to all three charges.

His trial began in April, a day after his co-accused was found guilty on four charges.

The co-accused, who also cannot be named due to provisions of the Youth Criminal Justice Act, pleaded not guilty to the charges but admitted to a statement of facts and invited a judge to find him guilty. The unusual move preserved his right to appeal pretrial rulings in his case, as well as the findings of guilt.

McVey concluded the youth found guilty Friday conspired with his co-accused and another individual who was not charged in a plan to kill a large number of people.

“The planned attack was intended to intimidate a segment of the public, namely members of the Jewish community, with respect to their security,” McVey said.

The attack was intended to cause serious harm through violence, she said.

“The communications between the participants reveal detailed discussions concerning the scale of the intended killing, the weapons required to accomplish it, the quantity of ammunition necessary and the possible use of explosives,” McVey said.

“Their shared objective was the mass killing of innocent people.”

The youth found guilty Friday was arrested in February 2024.

In her reasons, McVey noted the Crown alleged that in the summer of 2023, the young person and his co-accused communicated regularly online and shared violent extremist material.

The judge said that by August of that year, the two young people clearly shared an interest in violent extremist content and expressed hostility toward particular communities, including Jewish people.

She said much of the material sent by the young person to his co-accused could be characterized as propaganda or instructional material — including videos created by the extremist Islamic State group and documents about firearms, explosives and methods of killing.

The judge noted that, according to the Crown, those communications evolved over time and by late October 2023 a concrete plan had emerged to carry out a mass casualty attack in which the co-accused youth intended to take his own life.

McVey said she found the young person not guilty Friday of facilitating terrorist activity by making instructional material and propaganda available because she was not sure that he knew he was furthering terrorist activity when he sent the material to his co-accused.

McVey said she was not satisfied that his co-accused’s plans had even advanced that far at the time.

McVey said that when the youth was aware of his co-accused’s plan for a large-scale attack, he did more than simply express support or interest. She said he contacted potential sources of firearms, made inquiries about availability and pricing, and relayed information back to his co-accused for decision-making.

McVey said that, put simply, attempting to obtain an assault rifle for use in a preplanned, religiously and ideologically motivated mass shooting plainly facilitates that terrorist activity.

After delivering her verdict, McVey addressed the youth directly.

“Based on all of the evidence, I am satisfied that you genuinely intended to help advance this act of deadly violence,” she said.

McVey said the young person was a participant in the conspiracy, even though he did not intend to fight or die as part of it, and even though he May not have known of, or intended to be involved in, every aspect of it.

“In Canada, people are not prosecuted for holding unpopular, offensive or extremist views,” McVey told him.

“You are not being found guilty because of what you believed. You are being found guilty because of what you did. The evidence establishes that your beliefs led you to take concrete steps with others toward the commission of terrorist activity.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

The judge noted that, according to the Crown, those communications evolved over time and by late October 2023 a concrete plan had emerged to carry out a mass casualty attack in which the co-accused youth intended to take his own life.

McVey said she found the young person not guilty Friday of facilitating terrorist activity by making instructional material and propaganda available because she was not sure that he knew he was furthering terrorist activity when he sent the material to his co-accused.
McVey said she was not satisfied that his co-accused’s plans had even advanced that far at the time.

McVey said that when the youth was aware of his co-accused’s plan for a large-scale attack, he did more than simply express support or interest. She said he contacted potential sources of firearms, made inquiries about availability and pricing, and relayed information back to his co-accused for decision-making.
McVey said that, put simply, attempting to obtain an assault rifle for use in a preplanned, religiously and ideologically motivated mass shooting plainly facilitates that terrorist activity.
After delivering her verdict, McVey addressed the youth directly.
“Based on all of the evidence, I am satisfied that you genuinely intended to help advance this act of deadly violence,” she said.

McVey said the young person was a participant in the conspiracy, even though he did not intend to fight or die as part of it, and even though he May not have known of, or intended to be involved in, every aspect of it.
“In Canada, people are not prosecuted for holding unpopular, offensive or extremist views,” McVey told him.

“You are not being found guilty because of what you believed. You are being found guilty because of what you did. The evidence establishes that your beliefs led you to take concrete steps with others toward the commission of terrorist activity.”

stories.title: University of Guelph’s rowdy homecoming party cost police $91,000
stories.summary: Report says the police response involved approximately 88 officers and civilian members – and hundreds of hours of overtime
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
As many as 15,000 people gathered during an unsanctioned homecoming party in Guelph, Ont., last month, a new report said, and policing the chaos that ensued cost more than $90,000.

A report presented to the Guelph Police Service Board Thursday said police responded to approximately 250 incidents related to the Sept. 26 gathering on Chancellor’s Way near the University of Guelph.

The police response involved approximately 88 officers and civilian members and hundreds of hours of overtime with the cost totalling about $91,000, it said.

Police made six arrests during the event and about 70 provincial offence notices were also issued that day, mostly liquor- related.

Videos from the off-campus homecoming party showed massive crowds of young people in the streets, with some throwing bottles and other objects as police officers tried to control the situation.

Police said officers were also dealing with people climbing buildings, as well as shoplifting and vandalism at nearby businesses.

University of Guelph president Rene Van Acker said the party risked the safety of students and neighbours and the university was reviewing the incident.

Guelph police said earlier this month that they’re establishing a “homecoming working group” to manage large unsanctioned gatherings in the future. The group includes the city, the University of Guelph and Guelph General Hospital.

stories.title: ‘It’s dangerous’: MPP Flack adds voice to those concerned about rural south London intersection
stories.summary: Calls continue to grow for the City of London to make improvements at the intersection of Wonderland Road and Glanworth Drive.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Calls continue to grow for the City of London to make improvements at the intersection of Wonderland Road and Glanworth Drive.

The MPP for Elgin-Middlesex-London is the latest to raise safety concerns about the rural south London crossing.

“It’s dangerous,” said Rob Flack.

With the area surrounded by farmland, the intersection has long served the agricultural community. In recent years, however, Wonderland Road has become a heavily used commuter route between London and St. Thomas.

“I’ve talked to a lot of my farmer friends. They’re up and down combining right now. Safety is paramount. We need to do something now,” Flack said.

His comments come after what area farmers describe as a significant increase in serious collisions at the intersection in recent years, including multiple crashes over the Thanksgiving weekend, according to area farmer Richard Smibert.

“We need to be able to use the road and not have to fear for our lives,” Smibert said.

He is among several area farmers calling for both immediate and long-term safety improvements.

“We need traffic lights to slow down the traffic, stop the traffic, allow for breaks in the traffic and the congestion. Or a roundabout. I know that will take time, but we need something now,” he added.

The city points to a Ministry of Transportation construction project as a contributing factor. Colonel Talbot Road is closed at Glanworth Drive as part of reconstruction work on the Highway 401 interchange south of the intersection.

Traffic is being detoured onto Glanworth Drive to reach Wonderland Road as an alternate north-south route.

Doug MacRae, London’s director of transportation and mobility, said the city continues to monitor the intersection but no improvements are planned in the immediate future.

“We’ve really looked at every alternative, including short-term changes, but we’re really limited by the limitations of the road itself. Also considering operational risks of short-term changes, driver reaction to unexpected changes and then short-term changes again. Our recommended path forward is an intersection fully improved that meets standards,” MacRae said.

He said that could include traffic signals or a roundabout in the future.

However, advocates say maintaining the status quo should not be an option.

“We just need somebody to step up, take a leadership role and let’s get this done,” Smibert said.

“We would seriously ask the city to fulfill its obligation with respect to that crossing,” Flack added.

In the meantime, the Colonel Talbot Road interchange is expected to reopen in late November.

stories.title: Carney continues pro-Canada campaign in Red Deer and Edmonton with referendum days away
stories.summary: Smith has put 10 questions on Monday’s referendum, including one on whether Alberta should stay in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on leaving
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canada’s prime minister and Alberta’s premier tapped a keg, had a beer, sang O Canada and made a last-ditch pitch Friday for the province to stay in Confederation.

It was a Maple Leaf love affair for Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

About 50 people squeezed in and jockeyed for position inside Red Hart Brewing in Red Deer, Alta. They wore Canada shirts, hats, sweaters, jerseys and pins. There were mayors, members of parliament and former Alberta premier Ed Stelmach.

Smith walked in first, followed by the prime minister to the chants of “Carney! Carney!”

Outside, there were another 100 supporters. Across the street, a lone protester with an Alberta flag strode back and forth.

In a short speech, Carney channelled author Charles Dickens. The prime minister said Monday’s separation referendum comes as globalist forces and policies threaten Canada and the province as it stands on the cusp of unprecedented growth and success.

“We’re here in both the best and worst of times,” said Carney.

Albertans are being asked whether the province should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on separation.

Smith has said it’s time for Albertans to decide on the issue and that she prefers a sovereign Alberta in a united Canada. She said earlier this week that she voted at an advance poll for Alberta to stay.

At the brewery, she and Carney praised each other as sharp-eyed, flinty negotiators who fight for their positions but want the best for Canada. They said they’re making progress, including with a proposed fast-tracked oil pipeline from Alberta to the B.C. coast.

“For the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada are walking together,” Smith said.

They are, however, agreeing to disagree when it comes to the rest of Smith’s referendum.

The leaving-Canada question is one of 10 on the ballot. Smith wants Albertans to endorse nine other proposals.

Those proposals urge her government to take more control and impose new rules surrounding immigration and to pursue constitutional changes that wrest power from Ottawa. Smith has said she needs that mandate to negotiate a better deal with Ottawa.

On Thursday, Carney urged Albertans to reject the nine proposals. Smith said she’ll work to change his mind.

As the brewery crowd looked on, Smith handed Carney an explanatory booklet, adding, “I have bad news for you, prime minister, all of the premiers are interested in talking about immigration and how we might be able to reform it.”

When it was all over, Carney and one of the brewery owners tapped a keg, and Carney and Smith were handed a beer.

Earlier Friday, Poilievre, in a speech in Calgary, said he understands separatist disillusionment with the state of affairs in Canada but said quitting isn’t the answer.

“Quitting is the easy way out – and Albertans are not quitters,” Poilievre said.

“We don’t just take our ball and go home. We don’t walk away. We stand and fight for what we believe in, and we reflect upon all that we have.”

Poilievre said countries like Canada are built, defended, reimagined and reinforced by generations honouring those who came before.

“Some even died (in wars) so that we can have the country that we have today,” Poilievre said. “They had to be strong so that we could be free.”

He said he gets how people are unhappy with rising costs and what he characterized as a lax justice system, an out-of-control immigration program and federal policies that curtail resource development. But he urged Albertans to see the bigger picture.

“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government.

“It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”

Later Friday, Carney was to attend a rally in Edmonton with the federalist group Forever Canadian. He attended a similar one in Calgary on Thursday night.

At that event, he told a crowd of roughly 5,000 that a vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that could lead to years of lost opportunities.

Polls have suggested a strong majority of Albertans will vote to stay in Canada, but leaders stress that voter apathy could open the door to a winning vote for separation.

Albertans have been voting by mail and, for the past few days, at advance polls in numbers that suggest the final count could set a record.

Smith called the referendum earlier this year. She said bubbling discontent with past federal policies recently reached a boiling point with hundreds of thousands signing petitions for and against staying in Confederation. She said a referendum is needed to resolve the issue once and for all.

Critics, however, say Smith isn’t resolving a broad-based existential debate. Instead, they say, she has inflamed and validated latent fringe separatist sentiment, rolling the dice on the future of the country to appease hardliners in her United Conservative Party.
paragraphs: Canada’s prime minister and Alberta’s premier tapped a keg, had a beer, sang O Canada and made a last-ditch pitch Friday for the province to stay in Confederation.
It was a Maple Leaf love affair for Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

About 50 people squeezed in and jockeyed for position inside Red Hart Brewing in Red Deer, Alta. They wore Canada shirts, hats, sweaters, jerseys and pins. There were mayors, members of parliament and former Alberta premier Ed Stelmach.
Smith walked in first, followed by the prime minister to the chants of “Carney! Carney!”
Outside, there were another 100 supporters. Across the street, a lone protester with an Alberta flag strode back and forth.

In a short speech, Carney channelled author Charles Dickens. The prime minister said Monday’s separation referendum comes as globalist forces and policies threaten Canada and the province as it stands on the cusp of unprecedented growth and success.
“We’re here in both the best and worst of times,” said Carney.
Albertans are being asked whether the province should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on separation.

Smith has said it’s time for Albertans to decide on the issue and that she prefers a sovereign Alberta in a united Canada. She said earlier this week that she voted at an advance poll for Alberta to stay.

At the brewery, she and Carney praised each other as sharp-eyed, flinty negotiators who fight for their positions but want the best for Canada. They said they’re making progress, including with a proposed fast-tracked oil pipeline from Alberta to the B.C. coast.
“For the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada are walking together,” Smith said.
They are, however, agreeing to disagree when it comes to the rest of Smith’s referendum.
The leaving-Canada question is one of 10 on the ballot. Smith wants Albertans to endorse nine other proposals.

Those proposals urge her government to take more control and impose new rules surrounding immigration and to pursue constitutional changes that wrest power from Ottawa. Smith has said she needs that mandate to negotiate a better deal with Ottawa.
On Thursday, Carney urged Albertans to reject the nine proposals. Smith said she’ll work to change his mind.

As the brewery crowd looked on, Smith handed Carney an explanatory booklet, adding, “I have bad news for you, prime minister, all of the premiers are interested in talking about immigration and how we might be able to reform it.”
When it was all over, Carney and one of the brewery owners tapped a keg, and Carney and Smith were handed a beer.
Earlier Friday, Poilievre, in a speech in Calgary, said he understands separatist disillusionment with the state of affairs in Canada but said quitting isn’t the answer.
“Quitting is the easy way out – and Albertans are not quitters,” Poilievre said.
“We don’t just take our ball and go home. We don’t walk away. We stand and fight for what we believe in, and we reflect upon all that we have.”
Poilievre said countries like Canada are built, defended, reimagined and reinforced by generations honouring those who came before.
“Some even died (in wars) so that we can have the country that we have today,” Poilievre said. “They had to be strong so that we could be free.”

He said he gets how people are unhappy with rising costs and what he characterized as a lax justice system, an out-of-control immigration program and federal policies that curtail resource development. But he urged Albertans to see the bigger picture.
“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government.
“It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”
Later Friday, Carney was to attend a rally in Edmonton with the federalist group Forever Canadian. He attended a similar one in Calgary on Thursday night.
At that event, he told a crowd of roughly 5,000 that a vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that could lead to years of lost opportunities.
Polls have suggested a strong majority of Albertans will vote to stay in Canada, but leaders stress that voter apathy could open the door to a winning vote for separation.
Albertans have been voting by mail and, for the past few days, at advance polls in numbers that suggest the final count could set a record.

Critics, however, say Smith isn’t resolving a broad-based existential debate. Instead, they say, she has inflamed and validated latent fringe separatist sentiment, rolling the dice on the future of the country to appease hardliners in her United Conservative Party.

stories.title: Toyota commits to making cars in Canada as rivals downsize
stories.summary: The Japanese automaker’s commitment to making cars in Canada comes at a time when U.S. rivals are shrinking production in the country.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Toyota Motor Corp.’s latest compact crossover will roll out of a plant in Ontario starting in December, a sign of the Japanese automaker’s commitment to making cars in Canada at a time when U.S. rivals are shrinking production in the country and newly arrived Chinese competitors are ramping up sales.

The updated, hybrid-only Lexus NX is one of three models made at Toyota’s 38-year—old factory complex in Cambridge, Ontario, along with the Toyota RAV4 crossover and Lexus RX SUV. While some of those are sold locally, about 85 per cent are earmarked for export — mostly to the much larger and more lucrative US market.

It also builds the RAV4 at another Ontario facility located about 48 km away. The plants produced a combined 537,518 vehicles last year, making Toyota the largest vehicle manufacturer in Canada.

The U.S. is a crucial market for vehicles made in Canada and the sector has been hit hard by President Donald Trump’s tariffs on imports, which have eroded profitability and spurred some carmakers to downsize their operations in the country. The White House has threatened to increase tariffs on autos to 50 per cent if a broader trade deal isn’t reached by Jan. 1.

Toyota invested $1.1 billion in its Canadian operations for the latest RAV4 model, which began production in January, and hundreds of millions of dollars more for the newest NX. With all of the carmaker’s factories are running at or close to full capacity, Toyota sees Canada as a vital cog in its global manufacturing network and key to its four-decade-long localization efforts.

“We’re fully committed to making cars in Canada for the long-term,” Scott MacKenzie, director of corporate affairs at Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada, said in an interview, noting its local factories run two full shifts plus regular overtime. “We continue to invest here and think Canada is a great place to make cars.”

Right now, those operations are at “well over 100%” of capacity, but that fast production pace May not be sustainable with even higher tariffs. “Would we, for instance, manufacture at the same rate today that we would if we were facing an exorbitant tariff? We’d have to see,” MacKenzie said.

The commitment to Canada by Toyota and fellow Japanese automaker Honda Motor Co. comes at a time when competition is being stoked by the entry of Chinese-made cars. While the number of permitted imports from China remains relatively small — about 50,000 vehicles a year — that allotment will steadily grow under a deal Ottawa reached earlier this year with Beijing.

China’s Geely Automobile Holdings Ltd. has plans to launch sales in Canada next year, positioning it to be the first Chinese mass-market electric vehicle maker to establish a presence in the country.

General Motors Co. has long been the market leader in Canada with 2025 sales of about 300,000 cars and trucks. But Toyota is rapidly closing the gap, with record deliveries of 249,445 vehicles last year — a gain of 4.4 per cent. But that came against a backdrop of a market that has been growing more slowly, rising 2.1% to some 1.9 million new car sales.

Heightened trade tensions between the U.S. and Canada have exacerbated a longer-term decline in Canadian vehicle production due in part to labor and other fixed costs. The number of cars assembled in the country has fallen from around 3 million in 2000 to 1.3 million in 2024.

The three major Detroit-based automakers have scaled back their production footprint in Canada in recent years.

GM eliminated a shift at its truck plant outside Toronto earlier this year, and ended output at another factory in Ingersoll, Ontario, last year. Stellantis NV, which owns the Jeep and Ram brands, halted production in 2023 at a Toronto-area factory it now plans to sell, and cut a hybrid version of its Pacifica minivan from the production lines at a sibling plant in Windsor, Ontario, near Detroit.

Ford Motor Co. has reconfigured its vehicle manufacturing operations at its Canadian vehicle assembly plant to concentrate solely on heavy-duty truck production, shifting in 2024 from a plan to make all-electric vehicles there and its prior focus on crossover SUVs.

Even Honda, which makes the compact Civic sedan and CR-V crossover in Canada, has paused plans to expand capacity. It scrapped plans earlier this year to build a $15 billion EV battery supply chain near its existing Ontario plant as part of a broader strategic pivot.

stories.title: Carney's comment irks Smith, and a jab at sensitive Americans: 6 key moments from PM's Calgary visit
stories.summary: From hitting back at the U.S., talking about his overweight cat and a request to sign someone's chest, Carney had a busy day in Calgary.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Calgary on Thursday, where he visited Cinnamon Indian Cuisine and Bar to enjoy some pakoras, met with volunteers from Public Interest Alberta and gave a speech at a Forever Canadian rally.

On Friday, Carney will attend another rally in Edmonton and visit Red Deer with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, all as part of his efforts to drum up support for keeping Alberta in Confederation.

“A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff,” the PM warned in his speech, adding, “There are some outside our borders who are working to break us so they can own us.”

From displays of patriotism to moments of friction, here are six key moments from the PM’s visit to Calgary.

Speaking to a crowd in Calgary, Carney encouraged Albertans to vote “no to the nine,” referencing a federalist advertising campaign urging voters to reject the nine ballot questions on Oct. 19, as well as voting to remain in Canada.

Four of those questions ask whether the province should work to amend Canada’s Constitution, while the other five relate to immigration — including whether Alberta should have increased control over immigration.

The comment has caused friction with Premier Smith, who responded with the counter message of “yes to the rest” in a post on X.

“The Prime Minister and I have found common ground on many things over the last 18 months. However, it appears that he has yet to fully understand just how damaging the open-border policies of his predecessor were,” she wrote.

“That’s why I’m encouraging Albertans to vote ‘yes to the rest’ to give our government a strong mandate to take more control over our immigration system.”

Later in the day, Carney visited the student hall food court at the University of Calgary, where he greeted students by shaking their hands and answering questions.

While he was there, one man asked the prime minister to sign his chest. “I’m not gonna sign your chest,” Carney replied.

During his speech at the Forever Canadian rally, Carney made reference to recent comments from U.S. Ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, about potential election interference.

“We are closely watching Canadian activities because it appears that some of this, from our perspective, and the way that we view our elections, could be inferred to be election interference,” Hoekstra said in a podcast appearance on Tuesday. “Keep your nose out of American politics,” he added .

Carney said in his speech on Thursday that the Pacific Link pipeline will reduce Canada’s dependence on the U.S., a statement that prompted the crowd to erupt in applause.

“Careful. They might think that’s election interference. They’re a little touchy down there. We’re not. We’re getting on with it,” he added.

“This referendum comes at the worst possible time,” Carney said. “The world has become more dangerous and divided. There are some outside our borders who are working to break us so they can own us.”

Though the PM didn’t directly mention the U.S. or President Donald Trump, he’s made similar comments in past speeches. “The new U.S. tariffs are designed to hurt and divide us,” he previously said in a statement following the breakdown of trade negotiations between the two countries in August. “They are a miscalculation, because Canadians will always take care of each other. We know we’re stronger together.”

Meanwhile, Carney’s speech in Calgary came the day after Trump reignited his “51st state” rhetoric at a campaign rally in Arizona on Wednesday.

“Don’t be fooled by the idea you can ‘send a message’ with your vote,” the PM also said. “This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty.”

Partway through his speech, Carney paused to address a medical emergency in the crowd.

“Can we get help…there at my 11 o’clock,” he directed first responders from on stage, pointing to a crowd member who needed assistance.

After a pause while the emergency was being dealt with, the crowd started chanting “Carney, Carney,” to which the PM responded by prompting them to shout “Canada” instead.

During the ensuing lull while the medical emergency was being dealt with, a member of the crowd asked the PM about his cat, Nico.

“Nico’s home alone, actually,” he responded. “He’s put on a bit of weight…he’s good,” he added, before clarifying to the crowd that Nico is his cat. “A Canadian cat,” he said, prompting cheers from his audience.

stories.title: EverWind announces $10B investment in N.S. data centre campus, wind projects
stories.summary: EverWind has announced plans for $10 billion in private investment in a data centre campus at its existing Point Tupper site near Port Hawkesbury, N.S.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Energy and infrastructure company, EverWind , has announced plans for $10 billion in private investment in a data centre campus at its existing Point Tupper site near Port Hawkesbury, N.S.

The funding includes $8 billion to develop, construct, own, and finance the data centre, as well as $2 billion to advance the company’s onshore wind projects.

“This is the largest injection of private capital, we believe, in Nova Scotia history, and we could not be prouder to be here today,” said EverWind CEO Trent Vichie

Vichie said the company has reached a long-term lease agreement with a “leading AI company — a very, very large one,” which will identify itself later Friday.

The campus will begin with an initial 95-megawatt (MW) phase in late 2027. This will be followed by a 325-megawatt expansion targeted for 2028 subject to regulatory conditions.

At full development, EverWind expects the campus to reach a capacity of 420 megawatts to “meet growing demand for artificial intelligence and digital services.”

EverWind’s plan is to fund the electricity infrastructure costs attributed to the project so costs aren’t passed to ratepayers. The company noted the the data centre will have “several hundred megawatt hours” of battery storage to support the facility.

“Canada doesn’t have enough compute power. We need more compute power in this country. The data we use every day in our health-care system for all of our banking needs, everything on our phones. Business is run on on this data. Government runs on it,” said Premier Tim Houston.

“We need more secure infrastructure, more secure data infrastructure. This is part of that puzzle. This is really important for Nova Scotia, but also for our country.”

Vichie said the investment will mean 2,000 jobs during construction, followed by 215 “high paying permanent operating positions,” as well as indirect jobs.

“The investment here is anchored by a long-term commitment, so this will be here for a long, long time,” he said.

“This is investment that is in the ground here, supporting (not only Nova Scotia’s) energy economy, but its knowledge economy as well.”

Data centres are used in artificial intelligence (AI) and other high-tech industries, and require massive amounts of electricity not just to run, but also to cool the computer servers.

There have been concerns across the country about the environmental and health impacts of such centres.

When asked if the province would be legislating rules or requirements for data centres, the premier said there are a “number of checks and balances along the way” currently.

“There’s an industrial approval process … that process will be ongoing. The environmental approvals, industrial approvals. There’s a very stringent process for industrial entities that set up in the province that doesn’t change,” he said.

NDP Leader Claudia Chender reacted to Friday’s announcement by saying she didn’t believe the premier was protecting Nova Scotians from data centre risks.

“Nova Scotians have deep concerns about the impact of data centres, including on power rates and fresh water,” she said in a statement.

“Meanwhile the Houston government is supporting this project without any discussion, consultation, legislation or regulations. The Premier is saying people should just trust his word that Nova Scotians will be protected.”

In June, Canada announced a new AI strategy that includes proposals for the building of “large-scale” data centres .

Residents in the community of Lorneville, in Saint John, N.B., have been vocally against a proposed AI data centre .

Several municipalities in Ontario have voted on whether to place moratoriums on the centres while they study possible guardrails.

There’s also been opposition in Alberta, where several provincial townhalls were dominated by heated questions and angry remarks over possible environmental risks, water usage and the cost of energy associated with the data centres.

EverWind’s plan for Point Tupper indicates it will use a closed-loop cooling system where a water–glycol mixture circulates through a sealed loop rather than being routinely discharged.

“Heat will be removed primarily using air, with water-assisted cooling used during the hottest weather,” EverWind said in a release.

“Nova Scotia’s cooler climate reduces cooling-water requirements for much of the year.”

The company said under current design assumptions, the initial phase would use about 100,000 litres of water per day, which it compared to the daily water use of a large shopping mall.

At the planned 420-megawatt full build-out, average water use is expected to be about 500,000 litres per day.

The company said it will fund water infrastructure costs and “comply with applicable requirements for water use, noise and emissions.”

Representatives from all three levels of government were on hand, lauding the project.

“Richmond County has been clear that the project of this scale must address questions about electricity, water, environment, existing infrastructure with clear answers supported by sound technical evidence,” said Lois Landry, warden of the Municipality of the County of Richmond.

“Today we’ve received very encouraging information about proposed technology to minimize water consumption, arrangements intended to protect electricity ratepayers, and commitments concerning infrastructure costs and renewable energy generation.”

She said the community is open to opportunities, “provided they are developed responsibly, protect the interests of our residents and deliver meaningful, lasting benefits.”

“There is still much to learn and important work ahead, but we welcome the opportunity for our community to be part of that conversation,” she said.

EverWind said it is committed to funding community programs, which could include local infrastructure and recreation facilities, and housing initiatives.

The company also expects the data centre and wind development project to generate over $400 million in municipal tax revenues over the projects’ lives.

Negotiations are also underway, it added, with a First Nations consortium led by Membertou Development Corporation for a potential ownership stake in the data centre.

“Membertou is proud to have a long established partnership with EverWind, sharing in ambitious development projects like those announced today,” said Membertou First Nation Chief Terry Paul in a statement.

“The world of tech is changing and advancing, there’s no question about that. What we as a community can control is how we develop it safely, with responsibility to our resources.”
