“The investment here is anchored by a long-term commitment, so this will be here for a long, long time,” he said.
“This is investment that is in the ground here, supporting (not only Nova Scotia’s) energy economy, but its knowledge economy as well.”
Concerns about data centres
Data centres are used in artificial intelligence (AI) and other high-tech industries, and require massive amounts of electricity not just to run, but also to cool the computer servers.
There have been concerns across the country about the environmental and health impacts of such centres.
content_blocks.html: There have been concerns across the country about the environmental and health impacts of such centres.

content_blocks.text: When asked if the province would be legislating rules or requirements for data centres, the premier said there are a “number of checks and balances along the way” currently.

“There’s an industrial approval process … that process will be ongoing. The environmental approvals, industrial approvals. There’s a very stringent process for industrial entities that set up in the province that doesn’t change,” he said.
NDP Leader Claudia Chender reacted to Friday’s announcement by saying she didn’t believe the premier was protecting Nova Scotians from data centre risks.
“Nova Scotians have deep concerns about the impact of data centres, including on power rates and fresh water,” she said in a statement.

“Meanwhile the Houston government is supporting this project without any discussion, consultation, legislation or regulations. The Premier is saying people should just trust his word that Nova Scotians will be protected.”
In June, Canada announced a new AI strategy that includes proposals for the building of “large-scale” data centres .
content_blocks.html: In June, Canada announced a new AI strategy that includes proposals for the building of “large-scale” data centres.

content_blocks.text: Residents in the community of Lorneville, in Saint John, N.B., have been vocally against a proposed AI data centre .
content_blocks.html: Residents in the community of Lorneville, in Saint John, N.B., have been vocally against a proposed AI data centre.

content_blocks.text: Several municipalities in Ontario have voted on whether to place moratoriums on the centres while they study possible guardrails.
content_blocks.html: Several municipalities in Ontario have voted on whether to place moratoriums on the centres while they study possible guardrails.

content_blocks.text: There’s also been opposition in Alberta, where several provincial townhalls were dominated by heated questions and angry remarks over possible environmental risks, water usage and the cost of energy associated with the data centres.
content_blocks.html: There’s also been opposition in Alberta, where several provincial townhalls were dominated by heated questions and angry remarks over possible environmental risks, water usage and the cost of energy associated with the data centres.

content_blocks.text: EverWind’s plan for Point Tupper indicates it will use a closed-loop cooling system where a water–glycol mixture circulates through a sealed loop rather than being routinely discharged.
“Heat will be removed primarily using air, with water-assisted cooling used during the hottest weather,” EverWind said in a release.
“Nova Scotia’s cooler climate reduces cooling-water requirements for much of the year.”
The company said under current design assumptions, the initial phase would use about 100,000 litres of water per day, which it compared to the daily water use of a large shopping mall.
At the planned 420-megawatt full build-out, average water use is expected to be about 500,000 litres per day.
The company said it will fund water infrastructure costs and “comply with applicable requirements for water use, noise and emissions.”
Representatives from all three levels of government were on hand, lauding the project.

“Richmond County has been clear that the project of this scale must address questions about electricity, water, environment, existing infrastructure with clear answers supported by sound technical evidence,” said Lois Landry, warden of the Municipality of the County of Richmond.

“Today we’ve received very encouraging information about proposed technology to minimize water consumption, arrangements intended to protect electricity ratepayers, and commitments concerning infrastructure costs and renewable energy generation.”
She said the community is open to opportunities, “provided they are developed responsibly, protect the interests of our residents and deliver meaningful, lasting benefits.”
“There is still much to learn and important work ahead, but we welcome the opportunity for our community to be part of that conversation,” she said.
EverWind said it is committed to funding community programs, which could include local infrastructure and recreation facilities, and housing initiatives.
The company also expects the data centre and wind development project to generate over $400 million in municipal tax revenues over the projects’ lives.
Negotiations are also underway, it added, with a First Nations consortium led by Membertou Development Corporation for a potential ownership stake in the data centre.

“Membertou is proud to have a long established partnership with EverWind, sharing in ambitious development projects like those announced today,” said Membertou First Nation Chief Terry Paul in a statement.
“The world of tech is changing and advancing, there’s no question about that. What we as a community can control is how we develop it safely, with responsibility to our resources.”

stories.title: 'Dateline Canada' dives deep into past cases as appetite for true crime grows
stories.summary: Toronto - When Diana Swain stepped away from her journalism career after more than 35 years, she thought she was ready to slow down.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - When Diana Swain stepped away from her journalism career after more than 35 years, she thought she was ready to slow down.

That was until the veteran reporter learned about the opportunity with “Dateline Canada,” a spinoff of the long-running American investigative newsmagazine TV show.

“I’m not sure there is anything else that would have pulled me out of what I was doing,” said Swain, who notably worked on the investigative team during her tenure at CBC before leaving to start her own communications consulting firm in 2024.

"Dateline" correspondent Keith Morrison and "Dateline Canada" host Diana Swain discuss bringing the long-running investigative news series to Canada. (Oct. 16, 2026)

“I was happily winding down my professional life, but it’s ‘Dateline’ and it’s the legacy of that program. It’s the power of that program and it is the chance to tell a story in a fulsome way.”

Swain was named the new host of “Dateline Canada,” which will premiere on Citytv next month with a two-hour special that delves into the high-profile cold case of Elizabeth Bain, a University of Toronto student who disappeared from Scarborough, Ont., in 1990. It marks the first international expansion of the long-form NBC news program.

“It is hard to keep a program going as long as ‘Dateline’ has on either side of the border. And it has a very specific understanding with its audience about the kinds of stories it’s going to tell, how it’s gonna tell them, and it’s why people keep coming back,” Swain said. “They feel like they can depend on that kind of relationship they have with ‘Dateline.’ So, I think being able to bring that to Canadian audiences through the lens of Canadian stories is a really special opportunity.”

“Dateline” first aired in 1992 on NBC as a general interest program, but eventually evolved to focus primarily on true crime investigations.

“Dateline” NBC correspondent and Canadian Keith Morrison was on hand alongside Swain at a downtown Toronto studio and said it was “a delight” to help usher in the show’s north-of-the-border era, given his Canuck roots.

“I’ve always been a Canadian and I will remain a Canadian until I die,” said Morrison, who won’t be reporting for the homegrown spinoff. “That’s what my blood is and that’s how I feel about things, so to be associated with this makes me very happy.”

The 79-year-old was born in the Alberta-Saskatchewan provincial border city of Lloydminster and got his start working in local news before landing national roles with CTV and CBC. He joined “Dateline” in 1995 and has been a fixture on the series since.

Asked about the show’s enduring legacy, Morrison said through trial and error, “Dateline” learned how to tell stories in a way that drew viewers in and helped them make sense of what had happened.

True crime as a genre has grown in popularity in recent years, especially through steaming documentaries and podcasts.

“I suspect it has something to do with the unsettled nature of the world we live in right now,” Morrison said. “Somehow people need to be aware of the possibilities and maybe try to look a little deeper into the human psyche than normally we do.”

Morrison’s signature delivery — a drawn-out, rhythmic cadence with dramatic pauses — has also become synonymous with “Dateline” and he was even parodied on “Saturday Night Live” by former cast member Bill Hader. Morrison said he didn’t develop his style intentionally, but rather has just been himself all these years.

Nonetheless, Swain interjected to commend the veteran host on his iconic sound.

“You could probably list on one hand ... the number of journalists on either side of the border who are as well known for their voice and their style of speaking as Keith is,” Swain said. “That’s an extraordinary thing.”

Swain said “Dateline Canada,” which has so far only released information on its first episode, will resemble its American counterpart, but with “a singular focus on Canadian stories.”

The first episode will examine the 36-year-old Bain case and home in on key aspects of the investigation, including the wrongful conviction of Robert Baltovich, who was Bain’s boyfriend at the time of her disappearance and spent eight years incarcerated before he was acquitted in 2008. The show also re-examines evidence and unearths previously unreported information.

Swain said what she found compelling about the case is that more than three decades after Bain first went missing, “the question of what happened to her, who was involved, has never been answered.”

“Those questions need to be answered and if we can pull together the threads of this story (and) what’s known, because often details come out over time. And that’s the luxury of ‘Dateline’ is that we have two hours to pull these threads together, show people what’s known about what happened and see if we start to make more sense of things that didn’t make sense at the time.”

“Dateline Canada” will debut on Nov. 26 at 8 p.m. ET/PT on Citytv and Citytv+.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

stories.title: How common is your birthday? Stats Canada releases chart of ranked birth dates
stories.summary: Have you ever wondered where your birthday ranks in commonality? Statistics Canada has released a chart detailing how common each birthday is throughout the year, ranked from first, most common, to 366th, the least common. The least common birthday was no surprise as it only happens once every four years, leap day or Feb. 29. […]
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
By Meredith Bond

Posted October 16, 2026 11:40 am.

Have you ever wondered where your birthday ranks in commonality? Statistics Canada has released a chart detailing how common each birthday is throughout the year, ranked from first, most common, to 366th, the least common.

The least common birthday was no surprise as it only happens once every four years, leap day or Feb. 29.

September 20 took the prize for the most common birthday with most September birthdays not falling far behind.

July is also a fairly common month to celebrate your birthday, apart from Canada Day which ranked 332.

Other notable days, Christmas, Christmas Eve and Boxing Day ranked the three least common after Feb. 29.

The chart was built based on the most live births on a given day between 1995 and 2025.

stories.title: Astronaut Jeremy Hansen brings moon mission lessons to Western
stories.summary: Artemis II astronaut Jeremy Hansen shared lessons on teamwork and integrity at Western University during Staff and Leader Learning Day.
stories.author: Colleen MacDonald
stories.content:
Col. Jeremy Hansen, the first Canadian to travel to the moon, brought lessons from his mission to space back to Western University, where some of his training took place. The celebrated astronaut and Canadian fighter pilot addressed about 1,000 Western employees Oct. 14 at the annual Staff and Leader Learning Day.

Hansen made history in April as a mission specialist on Nasa’s Artemis II mission, becoming the first non-American to travel beyond low Earth orbit and around the moon. He and crewmates Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Reid Wiseman travelled farther from Earth than anyone before them, taking a 10-day journey aboard the Orion spacecraft Integrity. They tested its life-support systems and observed the moon’s far side, paving the way for future lunar landings.

The mission’s success, Hansen said, came from a team approach to turning problems into solvable challenges. When the four crew members began training together in 2023, they soon learned they were a good team that needed to understand what it takes to become a great team.

Staff get a chuckle out of astronaut Jeremy Hansen’s light-hearted take on an intense moment: “You get this tower of terror effect for five seconds,” he said of the trans-lunar injection burn, sized and timed to precisely propel the Orion spacecraft toward the moon. (Nicole Osborne/NEO Image Creations)

“There was a lot of times we were making it harder for each other,” Hansen said. “We knew we needed to start to figure out how to be a better and higher functioning team.”

The team, including the substitute members for the Artemis II mission – Nasa astronaut Andre Douglas and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jenni Gibbons – actively worked to improve their group dynamics. They added protected time to their training schedule, including in Iceland where a team-building expert taught that integrity isn’t a trait but rather a state people move in and out of through their actions. The lessons learned from achieving shared goals as a team apply to higher education as much as a mission to space, Hansen told the audience.

“You are contributing directly to something that matters to our collective futures, making an institution run and equipping our next generation,” he said.

stories.title: Ottawa adding new express entry points for immigrants in ‘high-wage’ jobs
stories.summary: Ottawa is adding new express entry points for permanent residency applicants in "high-wage" jobs.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Ottawa is adding new express entry points for some permanent residency applicants in “high-wage” jobs, Immigration Minister Lena Diab said Friday.

The government also plans to remove the requirement for an employer to prove they can’t find a qualified Canadian for those jobs.

The policies, which will take effect on Nov. 3, will apply to applicants who already have Canadian work experience, or who have a job offer in a high-wage field such as engineering.

The government considers a high-wage job one that pays at least 1.3 times the national median wage. The new policy offers more points for an occupation’s wage level, with higher paying jobs being worth more express entry points.

Statistics Canada says the median annual income in Canada in 2024 was $46,300.

The government is also introducing a temporary policy to remove the requirement for an employer to include a Labour Market Impact Assessment for a qualifying job that’s eligible for the new express entry points.

The government says this change is meant to simplify the application process and is part of its efforts over the past year to attract more immigrants in high-paying fields to Canada.

The government has introduced measures to give more express entry points to those working in medicine, the skilled trades, transportation and research.

Permanent residency candidates who are already in the express entry pool will have their scores modified to reflect the new points for Canadian work experience and job offers.

The Immigration Department says it May take up to two weeks for the new totals to be calculated and invitations to apply for permanent residency will be paused during that time.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Tesla says its newly unveiled Roadster 2 vehicle ‘can fly’
stories.summary: Tesla just unveiled its latest vehicle, the Roadster 2, which it says will be available with performance options that will allow it to 'fly.'
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Tesla just unveiled its latest vehicle, the Roadster 2, which it says will be available with performance options that will allow it to “fly.”

Details of the new sports car were displayed by Tesla at an event late Thursday, which included demonstrations showing the car appearing to jump over obstacles, and even drive vertically and upside down off a ramp using a suction system to help it stay glued to the road.

The car, which was developed in collaboration with CEO Elon Musk ‘s rocket company SpaceX, has a top tier “Rocket” package that Tesla says uses a series of built-in fans and thrusters that allow it to “take flight” for a brief period — “defying gravity.”

It wasn’t made clear if these capabilities are intended for any legal use on public roads in the future.

Under the “Rocket” category, Tesla notes the package is “Not approved for public road use,” and adds that it’s “air ready,” with a “full flight system.”

“Air ready with seating for one. Features a multi-mode suction system paired with cold-gas thrusters positioned around the perimeter of the vehicle that support forward and upward acceleration as well as lateral rotational movement. So yes, it can fly,” Tesla says on its website.

Other lower tier packages include the “Thrust” package, which it says will have limited availability, and “is subject to each region’s legal requirements and applicable laws.”

The base model is known as the “Performance” package, and is described as “road ready.”

Tesla said at the unveiling that the Roadster 2 will start production in 2028, but customers can reserve theirs now online with a deposit, including in Canada.

The estimated sale price was not disclosed, but Musk quoted a price of US$200,000 about a decade ago, when the idea for the Roadster 2 was first being floated.

According to Tesla’s website for Canada, reservations can be placed for the Performance and Thrust packages, although the terms state that a reservation “does not constitute the purchase or order of a vehicle.”

Reservations for the Performance package require a deposit of CA$7,000, followed by an additional $63,000 within 10 days. For the higher tier Thrust package, an initial $7,000 deposit is also required, plus another $343,000 within 10 days.

Tesla says the Rocket package is available by “invite only,” with no options to reserve online.

The Roadster 2 has been delayed for several years, with the original prototype being revealed in 2017. At the time, Tesla said deliveries would begin in 2020.

Tesla has been facing fierce competition from other car companies as electric vehicles and hybrids become more popular, including in Canada.

Statistics Canada revealed this week that August saw sales of fully electric and hybrid electric vehicles rise 55 per cent from a year earlier.

Musk has played down the new Roadster’s importance to Tesla’s finances, describing it in 2023 as a “small potato situation” that would not “move the needle in a major way financially.”

Tesla has been under pressure from investors to maintain profit margins amid the heightened competition, including by driving up demand for more affordable models, as well as brand awareness through what one analyst describes as a “halo car.”

The Roadster 2 May be the one to carry that symbolic weight.

“Tesla does not currently have a halo car, or high-performance luxury vehicle designed to showcase an automaker’s best engineering and technology. The Roadster will be Tesla’s new halo car,” Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein said in a note last month.

Goldstein expects Tesla to sell around 2,000 Roadsters a year — a fraction of the 1.6 million vehicles Tesla sold last year.

In the wake of the unveiling event, Tesla’s stock price was up over five per cent before trading opened on Wall Street Friday morning.

The original Roadster, released in 2008 and on sale until 2012, was Tesla’s first-ever EV and used a Lotus Elise chassis. It helped change the world’s view of what an electric vehicle could be. The company has since been known for its Model Y and Model X SUVs and Model S and Model 3 sedans.

The reveal of the second-generation Roadster also comes amid a sharp shift in Tesla’s focus to artificial intelligence-led self-driving tech and robotics, from manufacturing cars for human drivers.

This year, Tesla stopped selling Model S and X vehicles to make space for production of its Optimus humanoid robots. It also launched Cybercab – a two-seater robotaxi that comes without manual controls such as a steering wheel, pedals and mirrors.

content_blocks.text: Tesla just unveiled its latest vehicle, the Roadster 2, which it says will be available with performance options that will allow it to “fly.”
content_blocks.html: Tesla just unveiled its latest vehicle, the Roadster 2, which it says will be available with performance options that will allow it to “fly.”

content_blocks.text: Details of the new sports car were displayed by Tesla at an event late Thursday, which included demonstrations showing the car appearing to jump over obstacles, and even drive vertically and upside down off a ramp using a suction system to help it stay glued to the road.

The car, which was developed in collaboration with CEO Elon Musk ‘s rocket company SpaceX, has a top tier “Rocket” package that Tesla says uses a series of built-in fans and thrusters that allow it to “take flight” for a brief period — “defying gravity.”
content_blocks.html: The car, which was developed in collaboration with CEO Elon Musk‘s rocket company SpaceX, has a top tier “Rocket” package that Tesla says uses a series of built-in fans and thrusters that allow it to “take flight” for a brief period — “defying gravity.”

content_blocks.text: It wasn’t made clear if these capabilities are intended for any legal use on public roads in the future.
Under the “Rocket” category, Tesla notes the package is “Not approved for public road use,” and adds that it’s “air ready,” with a “full flight system.”

“Air ready with seating for one. Features a multi-mode suction system paired with cold-gas thrusters positioned around the perimeter of the vehicle that support forward and upward acceleration as well as lateral rotational movement. So yes, it can fly,” Tesla says on its website.
Other lower tier packages include the “Thrust” package, which it says will have limited availability, and “is subject to each region’s legal requirements and applicable laws.”
The base model is known as the “Performance” package, and is described as “road ready.”
What could it cost?
Tesla said at the unveiling that the Roadster 2 will start production in 2028, but customers can reserve theirs now online with a deposit, including in Canada.
The estimated sale price was not disclosed, but Musk quoted a price of US$200,000 about a decade ago, when the idea for the Roadster 2 was first being floated.

According to Tesla’s website for Canada, reservations can be placed for the Performance and Thrust packages, although the terms state that a reservation “does not constitute the purchase or order of a vehicle.”

Reservations for the Performance package require a deposit of CA$7,000, followed by an additional $63,000 within 10 days. For the higher tier Thrust package, an initial $7,000 deposit is also required, plus another $343,000 within 10 days.
Tesla says the Rocket package is available by “invite only,” with no options to reserve online.
Is the Roadster 2 Tesla's 'halo' car?
content_blocks.html: Is the Roadster 2 Tesla's 'halo' car?

content_blocks.text: The Roadster 2 has been delayed for several years, with the original prototype being revealed in 2017. At the time, Tesla said deliveries would begin in 2020.
Tesla has been facing fierce competition from other car companies as electric vehicles and hybrids become more popular, including in Canada.
Statistics Canada revealed this week that August saw sales of fully electric and hybrid electric vehicles rise 55 per cent from a year earlier.
content_blocks.html: Statistics Canada revealed this week that August saw sales of fully electric and hybrid electric vehicles rise 55 per cent from a year earlier.

content_blocks.text: Musk has played down the new Roadster’s importance to Tesla’s finances, describing it in 2023 as a “small potato situation” that would not “move the needle in a major way financially.”

Tesla has been under pressure from investors to maintain profit margins amid the heightened competition, including by driving up demand for more affordable models, as well as brand awareness through what one analyst describes as a “halo car.”
The Roadster 2 May be the one to carry that symbolic weight.

“Tesla does not currently have a halo car, or high-performance luxury vehicle designed to showcase an automaker’s best engineering and technology. The Roadster will be Tesla’s new halo car,” Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein said in a note last month.
Goldstein expects Tesla to sell around 2,000 Roadsters a year — a fraction of the 1.6 million vehicles Tesla sold last year.
In the wake of the unveiling event, Tesla’s stock price was up over five per cent before trading opened on Wall Street Friday morning.

The original Roadster, released in 2008 and on sale until 2012, was Tesla’s first-ever EV and used a Lotus Elise chassis. It helped change the world’s view of what an electric vehicle could be. The company has since been known for its Model Y and Model X SUVs and Model S and Model 3 sedans.
The reveal of the second-generation Roadster also comes amid a sharp shift in Tesla’s focus to artificial intelligence-led self-driving tech and robotics, from manufacturing cars for human drivers.

This year, Tesla stopped selling Model S and X vehicles to make space for production of its Optimus humanoid robots. It also launched Cybercab – a two-seater robotaxi that comes without manual controls such as a steering wheel, pedals and mirrors.

stories.title: Supreme Court decision says sexual history relevant in some cases
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada has upheld a decision ordering new trials for two people facing human trafficking and sexual services offences, after concluding they should have been able to cross-examine a complainant about the commercial aspect of her prior sex work.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Supreme Court of Canada has upheld a decision ordering new trials for two people facing human trafficking and sexual services offences, after concluding they should have been able to cross-examine a complainant about the commercial aspect of her prior sex work.

The case looked at the application of section 276 of the Criminal Code, known as the rape shield law, which limits use of evidence about a complainant’s sexual history in court proceedings.

Two individuals faced human trafficking and sexual services offences arising out of their relationship with the complainant.

Sexual services and human trafficking offences are not listed in section 276.

Supreme Court Justice Mary Moreau wrote in the unanimous decision that section 276 doesn’t categorically apply to those two offences and there are cases where evidence of sexual history is relevant.

Moreau said in this case the evidence focused on the commercial aspect of the complainant’s prior sex work and was meant to show she had previously worked voluntarily in the sex industry and was not recruited by the accused.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: RCMP end dangerous person alert for Red Earth Cree Nation area
stories.summary: Saskatchewan RCMP ended a dangerous person alert Thursday night, saying it no longer believes there’s an imminent public safety risk.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Saskatchewan RCMP ended a dangerous person alert Thursday night, saying it no longer believes there’s an imminent public safety risk.

Police issued the alert earlier Thursday for Red Earth Cree Nation in northeastern Saskatchewan and the surrounding area.

Officers were responding to reports of a person armed with a gun.

Authorities were asking people to stay inside, seek immediate shelter and to lock their doors and windows.

RCMP said late Thursday no arrests have been made.

The investigation remains ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Police identify suspect vehicle in fatal hit-and-run crash in Vaughan, Ont.
stories.summary: Vaughan - Police in Vaughan, Ont., say they have identified a vehicle believed to have fatally struck a woman whose body was found by a passerby two days later.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vaughan - Police in Vaughan, Ont., say they have identified a vehicle believed to have fatally struck a woman whose body was found by a passerby two days later.

York regional police say the woman, a live-in caregiver, was walking on Pine Valley Drive on her way to work around 8:30 p.m. on Oct. 4 when she was hit by a vehicle that then left the scene.

stories.title: Guelph homecoming drew up to 15,000 people, generated $91K in policing costs
stories.summary: A University of Guelph homecoming party that became unruly last month drew up to 15,000 people and resulted in roughly $91,000 in policing costs, a new report indicates.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A University of Guelph homecoming party that became unruly last month drew up to 15,000 people and resulted in roughly $91,000 in policing costs, a new report indicates.

The report presented to the Guelph Police Service Board Thursday showed a sharp increase in demand for police services on Sept. 26, the day of the off-campus gathering .

“A post-event assessment estimated that approximately 13,000 to 15,000 people were present within a selected area of Chancellor’s Way, east of Edinburgh Road,” the report states.

“The Guelph Police Service recorded approximately 550 incidents across the city. Of these, approximately 250 were identified as directly associated with Homecoming.”

The report said the average Saturday in September generated approximately 250 incidents. The 550 recorded incidents represented an increase of more than 100 per cent over the average Saturday call volume cited in the report.

The highest hourly call volume occurred at 2 p.m. Police received 31 service calls during that hour, roughly one call every two minutes.

Video from the event showed partygoers throwing objects into large crowds, while students described glass bottles, metal water bottles, sticks and other debris being hurled through the air.

Some students told Global News they chose to leave when the situation escalated.

Police were out in full force during the gathering and eventually deployed tactical officers to help restore order.

Emergency responders treated multiple people for injuries, including cuts and lacerations, and also responded to several intoxication-related medical calls.

The report identified 11 criminal incidents associated with the gathering, including seven assaults, one offensive weapons occurrence, one disturb-the-peace occurrence, one mischief involving public property and one mischief involving a vehicle.

Six arrests were made during the event. Four involved public intoxication, one involved an alleged assault and one involved causing a disturbance.

Roughly 70 provincial offence notices were issued as well, with most involving open liquor.

Four property damage reports were made, including damage to a Guelph Transit bus shelter, two vehicles on Chancellor’s Way and other personal property. Several businesses also filed complaints that remain under investigation, the report said.

“Homecoming operations involved approximately 88 police and civilian members and generated 874.5 overtime hours as of the date of this report,” the report reads.

“Total costs were approximately $91,000. The University of Guelph supported the deployment of 22 officers to support this event.”

The report added the investigation remains ongoing and additional charges are expected.

Police announced earlier this month that they are forming a working group with the city, the University of Guelph and Guelph General Hospital to help manage large, unsanctioned gatherings.

stories.title: How to apply to The Globe and Mail’s Academic Internship Program
stories.summary: The five-week program is open to student journalists who require a work placement to graduate
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
The Globe and Mail’s foundational dedication to journalistic excellence has always gone beyond our daily headlines. We have a longstanding commitment to nurturing and developing the next generation of reporters, editors and visual storytellers, to lend our institutional knowledge to help prepare young journalists to carry on the vital work of informing, engaging and inspiring Canadians. These objectives are embodied in The Globe’s Academic Internship Program.

Each spring, the program invites Canadian postsecondary students to spend five weeks working and learning at The Globe, either in our Toronto newsroom or our bureaus across the country, in a variety of roles that make up a modern news operation. The students work with our editors and receive coaching and mentorship to help them improve and grow as young journalists, in a challenging environment that teaches them the importance of high journalistic standards and practices.

We are looking for the brightest and most talented student journalists, regardless of their field of study. This includes students in journalism and media programs who require work experience in order to receive their degree, as well as students in other disciplines who require work terms in their programs, including co-op students. In all cases, we require that applicants have relevant experience working in journalism, either inside or outside your degree program.

Interested? If you are in a journalism/media studies program, talk with your program’s internship coordinator. If you are a student journalist in another academic program that offers work placements, contact our internship committee co-chairs, David Parkinson ( DParkinson@globeandmail.com ) and Madeleine White ( MWhite@globeandmail.com ), to learn next steps. Application deadline is Friday, Nov. 6, 2026.

stories.title: EverWind says $10B AI data centre proposal largest private investment in N.S. history
stories.summary: Point Tupper - A company pursuing an ambitious wind and hydrogen development in Nova Scotia says it now has plans for a $10-billion AI data centre in Cape Breton.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Point Tupper - A company pursuing a wind and hydrogen development in Nova Scotia says it has plans for a $10-billion AI data centre in Cape Breton that it describes as the largest private investment in provincial history.

EverWind Fuels announced Friday that U.S. AI company Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for a 18,600-square metre data centre in Point Tupper, N.S., that would draw 95 megawatts of electricity during its first phase.

EverWind officials declined to disclose the value of the lease with the company, which says the site will power its Claude AI assistant and growing Canadian demand. Anthropic, led by CEO Dario Amodei, said in a press release that Canada is the sixth-largest user of Claude worldwide.

The data centre is scheduled to come online late next year. A 325-megawatt expansion is expected in mid-2028, which would bring the development’s total energy demand to 420 megawatts, the company said.

“Speed matters, and capable partners matter and this is something that we can do,” Vichie told a news conference in Point Tupper. “We can set an example for the rest of the country on how we can bring this industry to Canada and to protect Canadian sovereignty.”

The plan includes $8 billion to build a data centre campus and $2 billion to advance onshore wind energy projects. The company said the project will create 2,000 construction jobs and 215 permanent positions.

Permanent data centre jobs will pay between $135,000 and $185,000 per year, and the project will create millions of dollars in spinoff benefits, the company said.

Vichie, who is based in New York, launched EverWind about four years ago to build wind and green hydrogen projects in Atlantic Canada. He was previously a senior managing director and co-founder at New York alternative investment firm Stonepeak Infrastructure Partners. Prior to that, he was a senior managing director at alternative investor The Blackstone Group and a managing director at Australia’s Macquarie Bank.

Vichie said EverWind is still pursuing its hydrogen development at Point Tupper. He said the hydrogen and data centre projects will compliment each other as both are expected to be powered by Nova Scotia’s abundant renewable wind resources.

“You often hear that Canada is a resource economy, (but) it’s also an intellectual economy,” Vichie said.

“And we need this type of investment to support that part of the equation. They both play off each other very well, resources and knowledge. And Canadians have that in spades.”

EverWind plans to spend its own capital on the data centre, and with a long-term lease in place, will now pursue financing from banks and pension plans.

Premier Tim Houston said the data centre project was a major vote of confidence in the rural area about 200 kilometres east of Halifax. He said Canada does not have enough secure data infrastructure to meet the requirements of its businesses, governments and health-care institutions.

“This represents the connection between the high-technology possibilities and potential of our province, and the energy generation potential that we have,” said Houston, who is also promoting an ambitious $60-billion offshore wind project called Wind West.

Data centres are typically massive operations that require immense amounts of electricity to run and cool off computer servers.

Water from nearby Landrie Lake will be used to cool the Point Tupper data centre’s servers, and the company stressed it will safeguard the water supply.

EverWind said the cooling system will be closed-loop, similar to a car’s radiator, with cooling fluid recycled or disposed of off site, not in local waterways. The system will use an average of 100,000 litres of water per day in the first phase, which EverWind said is about the same as a large shopping mall.

That will expand to an average draw of 500,000 litre per day when the expansion is complete, about one per cent of the lake’s safe daily yield of 34 million litres.

The firm already has environmental approvals for four wind farms in mainland Nova Scotia with capacity to produce 650 megawatts of power. A consortium of First Nations, led by the Membertou First Nation in Cape Breton, own 51 per cent of those projects.

The company has begun preliminary construction work at some sites. And three more wind farms are in the planning stages.

The company said negotiations are underway with the Membertou Development Corporation to take a nine per cent equity stake in the data centre project. As well, the company says it’s planning extensive public consultations.

EverWind said its wind farms won’t be ready by the time the data centre is expected to open in late 2027, but company officials said the province’s independent grid operator has produced a study saying existing energy infrastructure can support the operation.

The company plans to build about 200 megawatt-hours of battery storage at the site.

On another front, EverWind confirmed it will pay the full cost of all energy connections, network upgrades and other costs associated with the data centre project so they are not passed on to existing Nova Scotia ratepayers.

EverWind has signed on to the federal government’s responsible data centre principles and says it has agreed to meet provincial conditions as well.

Houston suggested Friday that his government doesn’t plan to legislate new data centre rules, instead pointing to existing environmental and industrial approval processes.

NDP Opposition Leader Claudia Chender issued a statement Friday calling on Houston to protect the public from power rate shocks from data centres.

“The Houston government is supporting this project without any discussion, consultation, legislation or regulations,” Chender said. “The premier is saying people should just trust his word that Nova Scotians will be protected.”

Earlier this year, Houston said it was premature to discuss potential data centres until major projects such as Wind West were completed. He softened that stance last month saying data centres could help create demand and investment cases for energy projects.

The project is the latest in a string of data centre projects popping up across the country.

In March, BCE Inc. announced plans for a 300-megawatt site just outside Regina, which the company increased to 1.2 gigawatts last month. In May, Telus and the federal government announced three data centres in B.C., while Meta, the parent company of Facebook, announced in July a $13-billion, one-gigawatt AI data centre north of Edmonton.

Meanwhile, opposition to data centres has been rising in communities across Canada.

In late June, protesters rallied in Vancouver to protest the opening of AI data centres.

Earlier that month, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew said no to a massive data centre southeast of Winnipeg, citing the sheer size of the project and its potential threat to the environment.

In August, the Alberta Utilities Commission has denied an application to build a 1.4-gigawatt natural gas plant that would have powered a massive data centre complex in the small town of Olds, Alta.

The Ontario communities of Oakville and Mississauga, Ont., recently passed one-year moratoriums on data centre development.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

— By Devin Stevens in Halifax.

EverWind officials declined to disclose the value of the lease with the company, which says the site will power its Claude AI assistant and growing Canadian demand. Anthropic, led by CEO Dario Amodei, said in a press release that Canada is the sixth-largest user of Claude worldwide.

The data centre is scheduled to come online late next year. A 325-megawatt expansion is expected in mid-2028, which would bring the development’s total energy demand to 420 megawatts, the company said.

“Speed matters, and capable partners matter and this is something that we can do,” Vichie told a news conference in Point Tupper. “We can set an example for the rest of the country on how we can bring this industry to Canada and to protect Canadian sovereignty.”

The plan includes $8 billion to build a data centre campus and $2 billion to advance onshore wind energy projects. The company said the project will create 2,000 construction jobs and 215 permanent positions.
Permanent data centre jobs will pay between $135,000 and $185,000 per year, and the project will create millions of dollars in spinoff benefits, the company said.

Vichie, who is based in New York, launched EverWind about four years ago to build wind and green hydrogen projects in Atlantic Canada. He was previously a senior managing director and co-founder at New York alternative investment firm Stonepeak Infrastructure Partners. Prior to that, he was a senior managing director at alternative investor The Blackstone Group and a managing director at Australia’s Macquarie Bank.

stories.title: Liberals announce $258.6M fund for skilled worker training in critical sectors
stories.summary: For the second day in a row, the federal government is announcing plans to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to train more skilled workers in Canada.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
For the second day in a row, the federal government is announcing plans to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to train more skilled workers in Canada.

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu is in her home riding of Thunder Bay today rolling out a plan to spend up to $258.6 million over the next five years to train workers in critical sectors, with annual funding of $50 million in the years to follow.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the creation of a Sectoral Workforce Innovation Fund a little over a year ago and the government opened applications for the program in August.

Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.CA

The fund aims to fill the gaps between workers’ skills and industry requirements in sectors like energy or critical minerals by funding projects that could speed up training or certification.

Hajdu’s announcement comes a day after Ottawa unveiled $430 million in spending to help unions and other organizations cover costs for new training facilities and equipment.

The Liberals have announced billions of dollars in spending to train up to 100,000 new skilled workers over the next half decade to support the government’s ambitious infrastructure agenda.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Blind. Hong Kong dissident. Refugee. And as of Monday, she's a Toronto lawyer
stories.summary: Joy Luk says she is is grateful for the welcome she received in Canada — but dismayed by Ottawa’s push to improve relations with China.
stories.author: Tom Blackwell
stories.content:
Joy Luk can’t leave behind the time she spent on the front lines of Hong Kong’s massive democracy protests in 2019.

Seven years after the movement was crushed, the city’s first and only blind lawyer lives in Toronto as a refugee, and is reminded frequently of her worst moments during the uprising.

Luk says she has nightmares about being struck by police and is startled by a knock at her apartment door, a reminder of the visits to her home from belligerent officers amid a Chinese-government-backed crackdown on opposition.

But the spirit behind her extraordinary role in the Hong Kong protests hasn’t dimmed, even as she’s treated for post-traumatic stress disorder.

The 47-year-old has spoken at vigils here commemorating the anniversary of the Tiananmen Square massacre, given talks on the “criminalization” of dissent and picketed outside China’s Toronto consulate.

A ceremony on Monday, though, will mark what might be Luk’s most impressive accomplishment since arriving in Canada. After obtaining a Global Professional Master of Laws degree at the University of Toronto and passing bar-admission exams made all the more challenging by her lack of sight, she’ll be officially admitted to the profession in Ontario.

“In the very beginning, when I arrived in Canada, I didn’t think I could be a lawyer again,” Luk said in an interview Wednesday. But she says she reminded herself of a favourite message from Apple founder Steve Jobs: “I accept failure, but I do not accept not trying … The worst case is I would not pass.”

She passed, ON her first attempt.

Luk is grateful for the welcome she received in Canada, especially its willingness to provide care for her many health needs even before her refugee application was accepted. That said, she’s dismayed by one issue – the current federal government’s push to improve relations with China as a response to the massive tariffs imposed by the U.S.

She understands the motivation, but worries that Prime Minister Mark Carney is forsaking those whose rights Beijing tramples.

“I guess they are not eager to fight for freedom of the people in Hong Kong and other parts of China under that kind of tyranny,” she said. “Because they want to sell some things to China … We are very disappointed by this.”

The way she tells it, Luk’s own determination to combat injustice started early.

Born almost entirely blind, she said she realized from a young age the law was needed to protect the rights of the disabled. She first dreamt of being a lawyer in kindergarten, Luk says.

She later passed law school and obtained her first Masters degree, in human-rights law, though she began her career practising general law, while also becoming an advocate for the disabled.

Then China began to tighten its grip on the city, and her life changed irrevocably.

The Beijing-loyal Hong Kong government proposed a new law that would allow extradition from Hong Kong to the mainland, raising fears of dissidents and others being dragged into China’s notoriously oppressive justice system.

The legislation sparked historic protests in 2019 that brought as many as a million people into the streets. The demonstrations, generally peaceful though occasionally more unruly, led to violent clashes with the police and finally a crackdown that would erase most of Hong Kong’s political freedoms.

Despite her blindness, Luk put herself in the midst of the maelstrom, offering on-the-spot legal advice to other demonstrators and passing on information about police tactics she gleaned with her acute hearing.

“I had to ask A.I. … ‘Using a blind person’s perspective, describe this picture, this figure, to me and let me know what it’s showing.”

Luk is now working part-time at a law firm in Markham, north of Toronto. But even as her career restarts in a new country, she wants the world to remember what she and thousands of others fought for in Hong Kong seven years ago.

“We believe that after several years, if we do not do anything, then people will forget what happened in 2019,” just like 1989’s Tiananmen massacre, she said. “We have no choice but to do something.”

stories.title: Self-driving taxi company Waymo to launch in Toronto, plans to begin service in 2028
stories.summary: California-based Alphabet subsidiary approved to participate in Ontario’s autonomous vehicle pilot program
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
Waymo, the American self-driving taxi company owned by Alphabet Inc. Googl-Q , is entering Canada and launching a pilot program in Toronto as it seeks to become a first mover in the country’s robotaxi market.

The California-based company announced on Friday that it had received approval from the Ontario government to test its fleet of driverless vehicles through the province’s autonomous vehicle pilot program. It will begin operations in the coming days, with the aim of carrying its first passengers in 2028.

Waymo taxis are already popular in a slew of global cities, including San Francisco, Singapore, Tokyo and London. The company operates a fleet of 4,000 fully autonomous vehicles servicing more than 30 cities, mostly in the United States.

Waymo will partner with Element Fleet Management EFN-T , a Toronto-based logistics company, to organize its operations in Toronto. In a joint press release, the two companies said Waymo’s entry into Canada will create hundreds of jobs, including in fleet maintenance, customer service and testing vehicles.

Waymo will start by mapping the streets of Toronto with trained human drivers behind the wheels, the company said. More than a dozen cars will be part of the company’s initial testing.

Waymo has existing ties to Canada. The Canada Pension Plan Investment Board was one of the company’s earliest investors, participating in two funding rounds in 2020 and 2021 worth more than US$3-billion in total. Magna International MG-T was also one of the company’s early investors and is a key manufacturing partner in the construction of an autonomous vehicle plant in Arizona, which will build Jaguar and Zeekr electric vehicles for Waymo’s fleet.

But the robotaxi giant’s entry to Toronto could prove challenging.

The city’s private transportation market is dominated by ride-hailing companies – Uber and Lyft – that are themselves making big investments in autonomous vehicles with the aim of operating their own fleets. Uber has partnerships with more than 30 autonomous vehicle companies, including Waabi Innovation Inc., a Toronto-based startup that raised US$750-million earlier this year.

In a statement to The Globe and Mail, Laura Miller, Uber Canada’s head of policy and communication, said autonomous vehicles have the potential to make transportation “safer, more accessible and more affordable” but “how we introduce the technology matters.”

She speculated that driverless rides for paying passengers are still at least two years away in Ontario, and urged the government and industry to set safety standards and prepare for the impact on workers.

Uber has said that autonomous vehicles will never fully replace the need for human drivers because people are still required during peak demand hours, for emergencies and in areas where autonomous vehicles cannot operate.

“Combining humans and autonomous vehicles improves reliability while letting autonomous vehicles scale gradually, preserving earning opportunities and giving workers and governments time to adapt,” Ms. Miller said. She declined to respond specifically to a query about when Uber plans to bring driverless taxis to Toronto.

Uber also has a relationship with Waymo, partnering with the company in Austin, Tex., and Atlanta. But there has reportedly been friction between the two Silicon Valley companies. A report in the Financial Times from June said Uber raised concerns about Waymo’s routing and the unavailability of its vehicles during bad weather. The report also speculated that the Uber-Waymo partnership was financially unsustainable.

Both Uber and Waymo did not respond to The Globe and Mail’s request for comment about the nature of the partnership.

Ontario began allowing companies to test autonomous vehicles in 2016, but success stories are limited.

Gatik, a Silicon Valley autonomous vehicle startup, completed a 10-month testing run in Toronto at the end of 2020 and subsequently partnered with Loblaw Inc. to provide autonomous delivery trucks.

Magna began piloting driverless three-wheel delivery devices in Toronto last May, but ended the test early because of technical difficulties. Its vehicles were often confused when encountering construction sites, according to a City of Toronto report from December 2025.

Adam Motaouakkil, one of the co-founders of Technologists for Democracy, a Toronto-based advocacy group, said he is concerned that Waymo’s entry will worsen congestion issues and pose a safety risk.

“Waymo is operating in cities with sprawl, which don’t have massive snow banks or streetcars. Waymo cars in Toronto will have to navigate blizzards, heavy rain and flooding. I’m not sure if the company, or governments, are equipped to address this,” he said.

Waymo spokesperson Amanda Galbraith told The Globe in an e-mail that the company has spent years testing in diverse snowy and icy environments and already operates at below-freezing temperatures in multiple cities, including during frost and hail conditions.

The company began operating in Denver – a city that receives a moderate amount of snow – in September, after a successful pilot project. It also operates in Detroit.

Mr. Motaouakkil said Waymo’s arrival could upend the lives of thousands of Toronto-based gig workers who depend on ride-hailing jobs for extra income, and noted that labour groups’ opposition to Waymo has been growing in multiple American cities.

Waymo paused its testing in New York earlier this year after opposition from the New York Taxi Workers Alliance, a group that has been publicly backed by New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

stories.title: At Toronto event, Margaret Atwood reiterates need for due process in Galloway case
stories.summary: Atwood has written opinion articles, most recently in the Vancouver Sun this week, in support of Galloway.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
By The Canadian Press

Posted October 16, 2026 9:18 am.

As Steven Galloway concluded his testimony in his defamation trial in Vancouver, in Toronto, author Margaret Atwood reiterated her stance as a defender of due process in his case.

Atwood, who was receiving an award at a Journalists for Human Rights event, spoke about her decision to sign an open letter in November 2016 calling for an investigation into how the University of British Columbia handled the Galloway case.

She also referred to Article 10 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which calls for “the right of every human being to a fair, open and impartial trial.”

She lamented the Canadian media’s reluctance to cover the case over the last eight years.

“Finally, the Canadian press is covering it after eight years of mostly not,” she said. “As one of those attacked online, trashed and derided as a due processor for asking for an open investigation with information and evidence from the University of British Columbia, I’m happy to see that.”

Atwood has written opinion articles, most recently in the Vancouver Sun this week, in support of Galloway. She added that legacy media publications face growing pressures and dwindling revenue, which make it difficult to “defend against lawsuits.”

“This has made them more cautious,” she added.

Atwood also worried that social media has made the public more distrustful with a growing tendency to believe anything posted online.

“There’s a youngish place where something resembling news can appear and even be believed by the uncautious,” she said. “As you know, that place is social media.”

Galloway, known for the award-winning novel “The Cellist of Sarajevo,” is in the middle of a defamation trial against several people who he alleges published unproven allegations of sexual assault.

One of the defendants includes a former student, known as A.B., who made sexual assault allegations against him that later spread on social media. Galloway was fired from UBC shortly after rumours of the accusations spread in late 2015.

He was a tenured professor and the former chair of Ubc’s creative writing program.

A report produced by a former judge for the university concluded that the accusations against Galloway were unsubstantiated.

stories.title: Woman faces assault, threats charges after incident outside St. Thomas police headquarters
stories.summary: A 62-year-old St. Thomas woman is facing several charges after an alleged confrontation with a police officer outside St. Thomas Police Service headquarters Thursday evening.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 62-year-old St. Thomas woman is facing several charges after an alleged confrontation with a police officer outside St. Thomas Police Service headquarters Thursday evening.

Police said an officer was leaving headquarters shortly after 6 p.m. at the end of a shift when the officer was confronted by the woman while exiting the parking lot.

According to police, the woman allegedly threatened to kill the officer and raised her fists in an attempt to strike the officer’s vehicle.

Officers attempted to take the woman into custody, but police said she resisted arrest. During the incident, the officer was kicked and scratched while the woman continued to resist.

Police said no injuries or property damage were reported.

The woman, 62, has been charged with:

Uttering threats to cause death

Assaulting a peace officer

Resisting a peace officer

She was taken into custody and is scheduled to appear in court at a later date. Police have not released her name.

stories.title: Owen Sound printing facility to close in 2027, affecting 360 workers
stories.summary: TC Transcontinental says it will close its printing facility in Owen Sound at the end of January 2027 as part of an effort to optimize its national printing network.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
TC Transcontinental says it will close its printing facility in Owen Sound at the end of January 2027 as part of an effort to optimize its national printing network.

The company announced earlier this week that the closure will affect approximately 360 employees.

Patrick Brayley, chief operating officer of TC Transcontinental, said ongoing productivity improvements across the company’s printing network and changes in its product mix have allowed production to be consolidated at other facilities.

“As a result, we have made the difficult decision to close our Owen Sound plant,” Brayley said in a statement.

The facility has been part of TC Transcontinental since 1992.

Brayley said the decision was not made lightly and acknowledged the impact on workers, their families and the Owen Sound community. The company said it will provide support to employees through the transition, including career transition services, and will work with customers as production shifts to other locations.

TC Transcontinental chief executive officer Sam Bendavid said the company continues to adapt to changing market conditions while expanding higher-growth segments of its business, including in-store marketing, specialty services and educational publishing.

Bendavid said the company must continue taking steps to remain competitive while stabilizing its traditional printing operations.

He also thanked Owen Sound employees for their contributions to the company over the years.

Despite the closure, TC Transcontinental said Ontario will remain a key part of its operations, with about 40 per cent of its workforce based in the province.

The company operates facilities in Vaughan, Aurora, Brampton, Paris and Mississauga, and also has operations in British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Quebec and Nova Scotia.

The Owen Sound facility is scheduled to cease operations at the end of January 2027.

Owen Sound mayor pledges support

Owen Sound’s mayor says local officials are working to coordinate support for hundreds of workers affected by TC Transcontinental’s decision to close its printing facility in the city.

In a statement, Mayor Ian Boddy said the facility has been a significant part of the community for decades, noting its roots in Owen Sound date back to 1907.

He called the announcement deeply concerning for the employees, families and local businesses. “On behalf of city council and the City of Owen Sound, I want those impacted to know that your community is behind you.”

Boddy said he has directed the city manager to lead efforts to bring together key partners in response to the closure.

The city said it has already connected with the Ontario government, Grey County, Georgian College and Employment Services Bruce Grey Huron Perth, and has spoken directly with TC Transcontinental.

“Our immediate priority is to understand the situation before determining what further action is needed,” Boddy said.

The mayor said the city is currently gathering information on the effects of the closure and the supports already available to affected workers. The findings will help determine whether additional assistance is required.

stories.title: Snowbirds to perform final air show demonstration
stories.summary: The Royal Canadian Air Force's Snowbirds will perform their final air show with the Tutor jets in Moose Jaw, Sask., Friday, before the iconic aircraft are retired for good.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The Royal Canadian Air Force’s Snowbirds will perform their final air show with the Tutor jets in Moose Jaw, Sask., Friday, before the iconic aircraft are retired for good.

The annual season home closing show is set to be livestreamed online — although there will be one more chance to see the CT-114 Tutors in action before they are sent to Trenton, Ont., for disposal.

The Snowbirds are scheduled to perform a flyover at the Grey Cup game in Calgary on Nov. 15.

The aging Tutor jets are being retired and the Snowbirds will go on hiatus until the team can be trained on the replacement Pilatus aircraft, the CT-157 Siskin.

Captain Philip Rochon, the public affairs officer for the team, says it’s a bittersweet time as the pilots say goodbye to the planes the Snowbirds have flown for nearly six decades.

Rochon says over the summer months, the Snowbirds received an outpouring of support from Canadians across the country, including former pilots.

stories.title: Data centres being built in your backyard, an unlikely housing win and the Home of the Week: Canadian real estate news for the week of Oct. 16
stories.summary: Plus, a controversial solution to homelessness that won over homeowners
stories.author: Moira Wyton
stories.content:
This week: Find out whether a data centre is planned for your backyard, and what $930,000 gets you in Brampton. Plus, a controversial solution to homelessness that won over homeowners, and one property worth a look.

You’ve probably heard the intense debate around building data centres in Canada, but do you know what’s going on in your own backyard? The Globe’s new dashboard lets you see how many centres are active, proposed and under construction near you, whether they power artificial intelligence and the totals across the country. Dexter McMillan, Jason Kirby and Chris Manza created the tool to help Canadians navigate the pressing issue that could affect their neighbourhoods and utility bills.

“These data centres have the potential to be tremendously impactful to the communities they’re in – creating jobs, yes, but also potentially drawing substantial power and water for cooling once they’re operational,” Dexter told me. That’s why, as Jill Mahoney reports from Centre Wellington, Ont. , data centres have become a divisive issue in the upcoming municipal elections.

And you might find an unexpected data-centre-next-door through our dashboard, just like Dexter did when he was researching. “I was surprised to notice that just a few kilometres from my home in Toronto, a big expansion of an already-existing data centre has been planned, increasing the potential energy draw from 10 MW to 70 MW,” he told me. Explore our new tool and how the issue is playing out on your block.

In Brampton, the drop in home values is hitting hard . The median price of a detached home was $1,486,000 at the peak just four years ago in March, 2022, but in September it hit $930,000, according to the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board. That more-than-half-a-million-dollar drop equates to 37.4 per cent, one of the worst decreases in the recent decline of real estate prices.

So what does the city’s median price get you now in Brampton compared to Toronto and Canada’s median prices? From a central four-bedroom likely to go below asking to a relisted home with rental suite potential, Shane Dingman offers a glimpse into the city’s market. And as he reports, the struggles of homeowners looking to sell – even at a loss – mean you can for sure get a lot more house than some other places in the GTA.

Which house do you think is the best value for money? Read about the three options and cast your vote in the poll at the end.

How would you feel if you bought a new condo on a quiet street and then found out the building next door was going to be supportive housing for people dealing with mental health and substance issues? You might have some understandable concerns, like Julia Clisshold and many other residents in Maple Ridge, B.C., did in 2022. But today, Clisshold has become an unlikely champion for the project that initially generated years of acrimony.

As Andrea Woo reports, the fire, noise, safety and disorder concerns Clisshold and many other neighbours had never materialized, and the project has become a case study in how local leaders can help overcome entrenched opposition to supportive housing and create safer communities for everyone.

One key strategy, a community advisory committee, might not seem like a radical proposal. But it made all the difference for the success of the Rivers Reach project. And as Andrea’s story illustrates , it’s an example of how communities can meaningfully address homelessness, a key issue for communities across the province in the upcoming municipal and provincial elections.

The cooler weather has me getting cozy on the couch with a book more often – and also contemplating which design and decor changes I’d like to make at home. It’s natural to think more about your space when you’re spending more time in it, so why not curl up with a design book and get some inspiration this autumn?

Nathalie Atkinson suggests six notable books on all things style and design , including a volume on bold new cabins across Canada that piqued my interest. While not every book is explicitly about home decor, they all illustrate important design concepts with beautiful images and rich colours you’ll want to fall right into.

770 Millgrove Side Rd., Millgrove, Ont. – Full gallery here

In this orchard homestead north of Hamilton, the fruits of a family’s labour aren’t just on the branches. The modern architectural home is an ambitious showpiece that is both beautiful and livable. Graham McNally designed it custom for his aunt and uncle, Wendy and Chris McNally, and the personal touches still shine through.

While it May look like a low-slung country bungalow from certain angles, the 6,571-square-foot home rises like a grand two-storey mansion from others. Inside the double-height great room, clerestory windows tucked under the eaves flood the kitchen, living and dining areas with light. A Douglas-fir clad ceiling appears to almost float above, and off the kitchen, a large limestone-mantled fireplace warms the hearth room. Those natural elements and others – such as solid oak and walnut floors and lime plasterwork walls – were important to the McNallys’ vision of a warm and inviting space.

But the six-bedroom home also welcomes the surrounding nature in. A window wall and doors take you from the great room onto the balcony that runs the length of the home, a large covered gazebo sits just outside the kitchen’s breakfast nook and the primary suite has its own patio that becomes the grand staircase to the pool deck. Tucked underneath the steps, the lower floor has a massive recreation room, full gym, wine storage room and a children’s play area with glass doors to help parents keep a watchful eye.

stories.title: Pundits say B.C. housing policy well meant but failing to deliver
stories.summary: The decree for density is creating the reverse of affordable housing
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
British Columbians have seen a lot of policies aimed at addressing the housing shortage in the past three years: tax measures aimed at reducing speculative demand, towers around transit hubs, and multiplex units on single-family lots. But allowing development doesn’t necessarily deliver housing, say housing professionals.

Former Vancouver planning director Larry Beasley says provincial and local governments are putting too much faith in their ability to deliver housing through legislation.

“They seem to think that their power is stronger than the marketplace, which actually delivers housing,” he said. “And they seem to think the market will do whatever they say through their laws, and if the market doesn’t respond with more housing, the additional numbers alone will lead to lower prices and rents. My experience suggests that they are sadly mistaken.”

He also believes that their policies are creating the reverse of affordable housing, by increasing speculation through mass rezonings and driving up land prices.

Vancouver’s Broadway Plan illustrates the gap between a density plan and construction. Four years after its adoption, only three of the 169 developments in various stages of approval have reached occupancy, according to a July 31 memo to council from Josh White, the city’s general manager of planning, urban design and sustainability. He called the rezoning and development progress “strong,” with about 25,000 residential units in the pipeline, and 90 per cent for rental housing. He said in the memo that there are around 3,800 below-market units in the pipeline compared to about 2,100 units of existing units that are impacted by redevelopment. But only 10 building permits had been issued and 59 rezoning approvals given.

“Meanwhile, hundreds of residents in older apartment buildings live with rezoning signs in their front yards and uncertainty over what might happen to their homes,” said housing commentator, retired architect and real estate consultant Michael Geller.

In advance of B.C.’s civic and provincial elections, Mr. Geller will discuss housing policy at Simon Fraser University on Oct. 14, joined by former Vancouver planning directors Ann McAfee and Mr. Beasley.

The decree for density, Mr. Geller said, has “done more harm than good.” The additional school tax, for example, is a challenge for developers because it applies to vacant residential lots. When it was introduced in 2019, most people thought it was aimed at expensive detached houses. But a developer who isn’t ready to build because of the market downturn will also be facing 0.2 per cent tax on a residential lot with an assessed value of between $3-million and $4-million, and 0.4 per cent on the portion above $4-million. Starting next year, those rates go up to 0.3 and 0.6, respectively.

“With all the projects going onto the back burner, they’re all going to be liable to pay this, and all it’s going to do is add to their costs,” said Mr. Geller, who has been appealing the tax on behalf of a developer client who’s facing the tax because he hasn’t begun construction of a 350-unit apartment building. So far, they’ve paid around $640,000 for that tax alone, he said.

Taken together with Premier David Eby’s recent proposal to tax unsold condo inventory, developer Hani Lammam, executive vice-president of Cressey Development Group, said such policies work against his industry.

“Why would you even start a project, because you get punished for not succeeding? I’m okay with taxing people when they make money; that’s fair. But taxing them for losing money is bizarre.”

Mr. Lammam gave the province a thumbs up for mandating density around transit hubs, which he said was “well intentioned.” That policy, however, became financially challenging when municipalities then mandated affordable housing requirements that added to costs, he added.

“It lacked a team perspective because, really, it allowed the municipalities to say, ‘You can build as big a tower as you want, as long as 20 per cent of it is below market.’ Which means it’s not even that we break even on it, we actually lose money on delivering below market at the level of discount that they were asking for.

“We’ve had actually measurable success over the past 12 months in dealing with municipalities and getting municipalities to adjust their regulations and their demands on our industry. And so that’s been terrific,” added Mr. Lammam.

“But with every little win, we end up with a provincial announcement that counteracts it.”

Mr. Lammam said the federal government should let the foreign buyer ban expire in January and allow foreign investment in Canadian real estate again. He said relatively few from outside the country are buying, anyway.

“The reality is we need foreign capital to grow our economy. We have to be able to attract foreign investment.”

Mr. Beasley said the affordable housing component should have been factored into the rezonings around the transit hubs so that developers could factor the cost into the purchase of the land from the get-go. Otherwise, land prices go up on the expectation of greater density, and speculators stand to benefit from the lift.

“In any rezoning from now on, the affordable parameters have to be built in from the start.”

Former City of Vancouver director of planning Ann McAfee, who speaks at the SFU event, said municipalities are having to pull back on development charges to obtain infrastructure funding, but are still required to pick up a lot of the slack. Until recently, Ms. McAfee served as a member of the National Housing Council.

“Municipalities are being asked to reduce development charges in order to make market housing, pencil out, and just exactly how are municipalities going to provide the variety of services? This is basic infrastructure plus any other community services which support the housing that’s getting built. So that’s one of the big issues,” she said.

“Whether it’s new Canadians coming in, having to be housed and serviced, or whether it’s people who can’t afford rents and are now homeless, all these responsibilities are being picked up by the municipalities.”

Mr. Beasley said the pervasive idea by government that it just needs to remove all obstacles in the way of adding supply is “a highly destructive” myth.

“Prices are not coming down, and most new development is stalled.”

He said government needs to stop mass rezonings, re-engage with the public and collaborate with the private sector.
