“Why would you even start a project, because you get punished for not succeeding? I’m okay with taxing people when they make money; that’s fair. But taxing them for losing money is bizarre.”

Mr. Lammam gave the province a thumbs up for mandating density around transit hubs, which he said was “well intentioned.” That policy, however, became financially challenging when municipalities then mandated affordable housing requirements that added to costs, he added.

“It lacked a team perspective because, really, it allowed the municipalities to say, ‘You can build as big a tower as you want, as long as 20 per cent of it is below market.’ Which means it’s not even that we break even on it, we actually lose money on delivering below market at the level of discount that they were asking for.

“We’ve had actually measurable success over the past 12 months in dealing with municipalities and getting municipalities to adjust their regulations and their demands on our industry. And so that’s been terrific,” added Mr. Lammam.
“But with every little win, we end up with a provincial announcement that counteracts it.”

Mr. Lammam said the federal government should let the foreign buyer ban expire in January and allow foreign investment in Canadian real estate again. He said relatively few from outside the country are buying, anyway.
“The reality is we need foreign capital to grow our economy. We have to be able to attract foreign investment.”

Mr. Beasley said the affordable housing component should have been factored into the rezonings around the transit hubs so that developers could factor the cost into the purchase of the land from the get-go. Otherwise, land prices go up on the expectation of greater density, and speculators stand to benefit from the lift.
“In any rezoning from now on, the affordable parameters have to be built in from the start.”

Former City of Vancouver director of planning Ann McAfee, who speaks at the SFU event, said municipalities are having to pull back on development charges to obtain infrastructure funding, but are still required to pick up a lot of the slack. Until recently, Ms. McAfee served as a member of the National Housing Council.

“Municipalities are being asked to reduce development charges in order to make market housing, pencil out, and just exactly how are municipalities going to provide the variety of services? This is basic infrastructure plus any other community services which support the housing that’s getting built. So that’s one of the big issues,” she said.

“Whether it’s new Canadians coming in, having to be housed and serviced, or whether it’s people who can’t afford rents and are now homeless, all these responsibilities are being picked up by the municipalities.”
Mr. Beasley said the pervasive idea by government that it just needs to remove all obstacles in the way of adding supply is “a highly destructive” myth.
“Prices are not coming down, and most new development is stalled.”
He said government needs to stop mass rezonings, re-engage with the public and collaborate with the private sector.

stories.content:
Council Highlights is an informal summary of selected actions taken by Middlesex County Council or Committee of the Whole at business meetings. The Council Highlights are not an official record of County Council proceedings. To view official agendas and minutes, please visit Council Meetings and Minutes .

Council approves 2026-2031 Middlesex Community Safety and Well-Being Plan (Cswbp)

County Council approved a new Community Safety and Well-Being Plan, aiming to address complex social issues that contribute to crime and public safety challenges through a proactive and collaborative approach. A joint initiative between Middlesex County and the eight local municipalities, the Plan was developed in consultation with community service delivery partners.

The Plan identifies six interconnected priority areas: Housing Stability and Homelessness; Child, Youth and Family Well-Being; Access to Services and Mobility; Economic Well-Being; Mental Health and Addictions; and Violence Prevention. These priorities are supported by a rural lens and an equity, accessibility and cultural safety lens. The Plan will better align existing municipal and community efforts, strengthen coordination, identify gaps and focus collective resources where collaboration can improve community outcomes.

A key feature is a strengthened governance framework bringing together municipalities and community partners to oversee implementation, monitor progress, and respond to emerging challenges. The approach emphasizes leveraging existing partnerships and resources wherever possible, while maintaining local decision-making authority and avoiding unnecessary duplication.

This does not commit municipalities to new spending but provides a framework for future collaborative initiatives that May be considered through normal budget and Council approval processes.

Read the 2026-2031 Middlesex Community Safety and Well-Being Plan (Cswbp) report for more information.

Procedure By-Law Update

The Committee of the Whole recommended updates to the County Procedure By-law, aimed at improving clarity, accessibility and consistency in how Council conducts business.

The proposed changes reflect current practices and align with the County’s broader governance framework. Updates include revisions to inaugural meeting procedures, changes to the agenda structure, new provisions for alternate members of County Council, and the clarification of rules related to reconsidering decisions from previous terms of Council.

Under the proposed By-law, members of the public would be able to register to speak on items appearing on a published agenda up until noon on the day before a meeting, creating a clearer and more accessible process for public participation. The draft also expands and clarifies circumstances where delegations would not be permitted, helping ensure the process supports fair and effective decision-making.

For more information, see the Procedure By-Law Report .

Artificial Intelligence Roadmap to guide AI implementation at the County

Council received an update on the County’s Artificial Intelligence Roadmap, which sets a phased approach for expanding AI tools across County operations, while maintaining strong governance, privacy, security, transparency, and human oversight. Building on the County’s AI Policy , the roadmap outlines four priorities: organizational readiness and governance; Microsoft Copilot deployment and organizational learning; improved internal information access through Laserfiche; and improved internal and public access to Council information through eScribe.

The Roadmap emphasizes a gradual, measured approach that balances innovation with accountability. Early phases will focus on policy review, privacy impact assessments, security reviews, and performance measurement before broader implementation. The pilot projects are intended to improve access to trusted information, increase efficiency and support informed decision-making. The framework also establishes processes for ongoing monitoring, continuous improvement, and collaboration with municipal partners as the County evaluates future AI opportunities.

Read the AI Roadmap Report for more details.

International local leadership program wraps up

County officials and employees recently marked the end of a six-year international initiative focused on strengthening local governance and supporting women’s leadership around the world.

Since joining the Federation of Canadian Federation of Municipalities’ Partnerships for Municipal Innovation – Women in Local Leadership (FCM PMI-Will) project in 2022, County officials and staff have participated in workshops, technical missions, and knowledge sharing programs with municipal partners in Cambodia.

The partnership provided opportunities to share Middlesex County’s municipal expertise and learn from the experiences of local governments operating in different social and economic environments. Participants explored topics such as public engagement, gender-responsive service delivery, leadership development, communications, project management, and community outreach.

The project culminated in a closing knowledge exchange forum that highlighted lessons learned, project achievements, and the value of international collaboration in local government.

Read the FCM Partnerships for Municipal Innovation – Women in Local Leadership (PMI-Will) Project Update report for more information.

Recommendations made by the Committee of the Whole at the October 13, 2026, meeting will be considered by County Council at its next regular meeting on October 27, 2026. The Legislative Services Department maintains the official record for all County government proceedings.

For more information please contact: @email

stories.title: Waymo to launch robotaxis in Toronto under pilot program for self-driving vehicles
stories.summary: Self-driving taxi operator Waymo says it will launch a test phase in Toronto in the coming days, with the goal of carrying its first passengers in 2028.
stories.author: Christopher Reynolds
stories.content:
Self-driving taxi operator Waymo says it will launch a test phase in Toronto in the coming days, with the goal of carrying its first passengers in 2028.

The California-based company says the Ontario government has given it the green light to take part in a provincial pilot program that regulates testing of autonomous cars.

Waymo, a subsidiary of Google parent company Alphabet Inc., says the first phase includes high-definition street mapping and test runs of the robotaxis with a driver behind the wheel, starting this fall.

Skeptics of the technology say autonomous vehicles struggle to handle more complicated environments, including heavy traffic and bad weather, but Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana says the company is committed to safer streets and more accessible mobility.

For its launch in Canada, Waymo is partnering with Toronto-based Element Fleet Management, which will provide maintenance, customer service and other support functions.

Waymo’s distinctive white crossover SUVs will not be the first vehicles to traverse Toronto streets under the provincial pilot program, after California-based Gatik began a rollout of 50 autonomous box trucks for Loblaw in the city last year.

stories.title: A green star has been identified by astronomers for the first time
stories.summary: It is a dense stellar remnant called a white dwarf, situated about 280 light-years from Earth
stories.author: Will Dunham
stories.content:
Astronomers for the first time have identified a green star, documenting a dense stellar remnant called a white dwarf that became a ghostly shade of chartreuse after ingesting rocky debris from planets that once had orbited it.

A star’s colour typically is governed by its temperature, with cooler stars appearing orange, the sun and stars similar to it appearing white, and the hottest ones appearing a pale blue.

But the formula is different for a white dwarf, which is the leftover core of a low- to medium-mass star that burned through its nuclear fuel and blew off its outer layers. Most white dwarfs have colours similar to other stars, and their average colour is white. But changes in their chemistry over time can turn some of them into rarer colours.

The newly identified green one, named WD J1330+6435, is a white dwarf in the Milky Way galaxy that is located about 280 light-years from Earth in the constellation Draco. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, 9.5 trillion km.

“We first became interested in this white dwarf because bits of planetary material have fallen onto its surface, enriching its outer layers in elements including calcium, lithium and, in particular, sodium,” said astrophysicist Mark Hollands of the University of Warwick in England, lead author of the study published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments.

In normal stars, sodium absorbs a very specific wavelength of orange – the same orange that gives sodium street lamps their characteristic colour.

“In this particular white dwarf, however, the density is so high that the sodium atoms are constantly being bombarded by surrounding helium atoms, which alters the sodium atomic energy levels,” Hollands said.

“The end result is that the sodium atoms no longer absorb one very narrow wavelength of orange – they absorb the yellows, oranges and some of the red wavelengths. And what you’re left with is a star that has a beautiful chartreuse green glow, something that wouldn’t be possible for sun-like stars,” Hollands said.

The discovery was part of a project assessing the colour of white dwarfs as human eyes would see them. A white dwarf typically has half the mass of the sun compacted into the size of Earth.

“Because white dwarfs are super-dense stars – they are roughly the size of the Earth, but contain about 165,000 times its mass – even a small amount of sodium blocks out a large amount of the orange light coming out of the star,” University of Warwick astrophysicist and study co-author Boris Gänsicke said.

“In the end, it’s all very similar to the mixing of colours in the palette of a painter. They start with a few basic colours, then mix them together to form any colour they need for their painting. Take away some of the colour going into the mix, and the output will change,” Gänsicke said.

The researchers studied 151 white dwarfs located within about 65 light-years of Earth, with white the average colour.

One showed perhaps the reddest hue of any known star, a salmon pink. Named WD J1011+2845, it is located 48 light-years from Earth in the constellation Leo Minor. This time, it was not sodium that was changing the palette, but carbon.

“Rather than something hitting the star, in this case the carbon comes out from its deep interior,” Gänsicke said.

Data used by the researchers included light spectrum observations from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey using a telescope in New Mexico, as well as white dwarf spectrum models they developed.

They found that white dwarf colours divide into distinct groups based on atmospheric composition. Carbon-rich white dwarfs usually were pink or purple. Those enriched with debris from shattered remnants of planetary systems leaned toward yellow. Lower-temperature white dwarfs with mixed hydrogen and helium atmospheres tended toward a cyan or pale blue hue.

In all, they spanned almost every colour of the spectrum.

While WD J1330+6435 was the first documented example of a green star in the real world, green stars have existed in science fiction, including in the recent comic book movie “Supergirl.”

“It does show that the universe is sometimes just as weird as anything science fiction can conjure up,” Hollands said.

stories.title: A modernist homestead in an orchard
stories.summary: This Millgrove, Ont. home is an architectural showpiece that uses the landscape to play down its ambitious design
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
770 Millgrove Side Rd., Millgrove, Ont.

Asking price: $5,999,000

Land Size: 52.135 acres

Annual Property Taxes: $15,335.49 (2026)

Listing agent: Martinus Geleynse, Corcoran Horizon Realty

On a rural road north of Hamilton sits a modernist architectural showpiece that uses the landscape to play down its ambitious design.

In 2013, Wendy and Chris McNally had removed the nonproducing apple trees from a former orchard they owned and discovered what was left on the 50-acre piece of land were many of the tree species – oak, cherry, walnut – common to the Carolinian forest. It seemed the perfect place to build a custom home that fit their needs as they approached retirement.

“It was the first time we’d built a home from scratch,” said Mrs. McNally, who said in the late 1980s she and her mining engineering husband had bought a lot from a developer, with hopes to get a home with a farmhouse feel. “They came up with a plan, but you didn’t have as much say in what you were getting. There was constrictions working with a developer like that.”

Luckily, this time they had a nephew who was just beginning his career in architecture and who leapt at the challenge to create a home that incorporates ancient styles, natural materials, modern sustainable technology and fits within the land. “I had been working since 2009, but it’s a pretty significant project at that point in my career and also for the firm,” said Graham McNally, one of the principals of Toms + McNally Design.

From the outside, the result appears to be a modest single-storey ranch bungalow, but when viewed from the pool deck or gardens feels like a much grander – even palatial – two-level manse. Seen from above, the floor plan zigs and zags, but it’s all aimed at livability.

“With subdivision houses there’s so little consideration for how people live; it’s all about efficiency for the builder,” said Mr. McNally, who spent a lot of time early on figuring out how his aunt and uncle wanted to spend their time with their still-growing family. “This house, you can tell it’s sort of funny shaped, but it’s all organized around that idea about the way people were going to live in it and how it facilitates their life.”

At the end of the long driveway is a paved courtyard that squares off the space between the attached three-car garage that extends at a 90-degree angle from the main living space.

The formal foyer at the opposite end of the square collects visitors into the bottom corner of the L-shaped living space. Directly ahead is the guest bedroom and primary suite on the short side of the L, and to the left is a long hallway that connects to the great room, dining room, and kitchen. On the other side is an office facing the courtyard and a spacious mud-room/laundry room off the garage. A hallway culminates in what the McNallys call the “hearth room,” a den with a large limestone fireplace mantel wall just off the kitchen.

But the heart of the building is that enormous central volume that is double-height and contains the great room, dining room and kitchen. These spaces are separated by walls that don’t extend all the way to the Douglas-fir clad ceiling that seems to float above the whole space, levitating on a cushion of light from the clerestory windows that wrap around on all four sides.

“Graham did an absolutely marvellous job of giving us the room sizes that we needed for when everyone was there, but still making it feel like an intimate home,” said Mrs. McNally. “You didn’t feel like you were in a big barn of a room when there were just the two of us.”

These clerestory windows, which tuck under the eaves of the home, are a feature of mid-century modern design, but their origins go back to premodern societies in Egypt and Crete, copied down through the ages in Rome and in churches and cathedrals in Europe. They flood the home with light, and on the side facing the old orchard they are met with banks of window walls and doors that open onto the balcony that runs the length of the home above the lower-level patio walkout.

“Graham was the one that guided us to what the house became; he had the vision,” said Mrs. McNally. “We were comfortable with it as long as it had warm elements like the wood; we’re not chrome and glass kind of people. We like real things.”

There is steel in the huge open structure for support, but it’s hidden. And the glass mainly serves to keep sightlines uncluttered. And the natural elements are not only real, they are also substantial: swathes of solid oak and walnut flooring – not engineered hardwood – as well as literal tonnes of limestone from a quarry in Owen Sound, Ont., that clads the outside of the home. The walls are also robust: instead of drywall (when it’s not exposed concrete, tile or stone), the finished surfaces are all lime plasterwork, which Mr. McNally said leaves behind a lot less dust during construction.

Like any design with mid-century-modern influences, the outdoors is in conversation with the indoors. For instance, just beyond the kitchen breakfast nook is a large, covered gazebo. The primary suite at the opposite end of the house opens onto its own patio that transitions into a grand staircase that steps down to the pool deck.

A wall of windows connects an expansive recreation room that anchors the lower level to the patio and pool deck, paired with raised planters and landscaping that climbs toward the second level. Inside is a play area that’s behind glass doors, which help keep the kiddos under the watchful eyes of parents. A built-in entertainment centre on one wall integrates with a fireplace to help program the space.

This level also features a full gym, two more bedrooms with their own ensuite bathrooms, and a wine storage room.

In a house of this scale, there are many places you could choose to settle into, but particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic the McNallys found themselves drawn to the den or hearth room off the kitchen.

“It was just sort of cozy. We had a new grandchild arriving – actually we had three arrive during COVID – and so I would knit,” said Mrs. McNally. Close to the kitchen with access to the outside, the laundry room/utility room and the garage, it was an informal hub for her and her husband.

And it has produced several yards of knitting.

“I try to give each new grandchild like a 40-inch by 40-inch hand-knit blanket,” she said. “The first two grandchildren got double-sided blankets, but I don’t have time for that any more because this one or that one needs a sweater or a hat or something.”

Her own children were gifted hand-knit goods made by her mother-in-law, and she saw how those became treasured items to be passed on to their children. Now she’s added to the pool of knitting, in a tradition Mrs. McNally hopes extends to the next generation: “It’s a labour of love.”

So, too, is hiding an elegantly functional family home inside a modern design masterpiece.

They flood the home with light, and on the side facing the old orchard they are met with banks of window walls and doors that open onto the balcony that runs the length of the home above the lower-level patio walkout.

“Graham was the one that guided us to what the house became; he had the vision,” said Mrs. McNally. “We were comfortable with it as long as it had warm elements like the wood; we’re not chrome and glass kind of people. We like real things.”

There is steel in the huge open structure for support, but it’s hidden. And the glass mainly serves to keep sightlines uncluttered. And the natural elements are not only real, they are also substantial: swathes of solid oak and walnut flooring – not engineered hardwood – as well as literal tonnes of limestone from a quarry in Owen Sound, Ont., that clads the outside of the home. The walls are also robust: instead of drywall (when it’s not exposed concrete, tile or stone), the finished surfaces are all lime plasterwork, which Mr. McNally said leaves behind a lot less dust during construction.

Like any design with mid-century-modern influences, the outdoors is in conversation with the indoors. For instance, just beyond the kitchen breakfast nook is a large, covered gazebo. The primary suite at the opposite end of the house opens onto its own patio that transitions into a grand staircase that steps down to the pool deck.

A wall of windows connects an expansive recreation room that anchors the lower level to the patio and pool deck, paired with raised planters and landscaping that climbs toward the second level. Inside is a play area that’s behind glass doors, which help keep the kiddos under the watchful eyes of parents. A built-in entertainment centre on one wall integrates with a fireplace to help program the space.
This level also features a full gym, two more bedrooms with their own ensuite bathrooms, and a wine storage room.

In a house of this scale, there are many places you could choose to settle into, but particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic the McNallys found themselves drawn to the den or hearth room off the kitchen.

“It was just sort of cozy. We had a new grandchild arriving – actually we had three arrive during COVID – and so I would knit,” said Mrs. McNally. Close to the kitchen with access to the outside, the laundry room/utility room and the garage, it was an informal hub for her and her husband.
And it has produced several yards of knitting.

“I try to give each new grandchild like a 40-inch by 40-inch hand-knit blanket,” she said. “The first two grandchildren got double-sided blankets, but I don’t have time for that any more because this one or that one needs a sweater or a hat or something.”

Her own children were gifted hand-knit goods made by her mother-in-law, and she saw how those became treasured items to be passed on to their children. Now she’s added to the pool of knitting, in a tradition Mrs. McNally hopes extends to the next generation: “It’s a labour of love.”
So, too, is hiding an elegantly functional family home inside a modern design masterpiece.

stories.title: Quebec sovereigntists see fundamental rift with Alberta separatists
stories.summary: With just days before Alberta’s vote on an independence referendum, longtime Quebec sovereigntists are distancing themselves from the Western province's separatists.
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
With just days before Alberta’s vote on an independence referendum, longtime Quebec sovereigntists are distancing themselves from the Western province’s separatists.

Question 10 of 10 on Monday’s referendum ballot asks whether Alberta should remain in Canada or if the government should start the legal process to hold a subsequent, binding referendum on separation.

Advance polls opened Tuesday and run until Saturday.

Quebecers May have a sense of déjà vu after voting on a similar question in 1980, when René Lévesque’s Parti Québécois asked whether the province should begin negotiations to leave Confederation. Nearly 60 per cent of Quebec voters were against Lévesque’s proposal.

A second referendum followed in 1995, narrowly won by the “No” side. But ardent sovereigntists see profound differences in the two movements.

Marie-Anne Alepin, president of the Société St-Jean-Baptiste de Montréal, a prominent Quebec nationalist group, believes Alberta is using the threat of separatism as leverage in negotiations with Ottawa. She sees the referendum as a means of pressure rather than a genuine desire to form a country.

“They want a bigger role within Canada and we want to leave,” she said. “They want more control over their oil and gas … we don’t want pipelines.”

But that hasn’t stopped some leaders in the Alberta separatist movement from claiming common cause.

Quebec elected the PQ — which has promised a third independence referendum — to a minority government on Oct. 5, leading figures in the Alberta separatist movement to rally behind premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and declare him a possible ally.

“Quebec rejected the status quo today,” wrote columnist Cory Morgan — a founding member of the Alberta Independence Party in 2001 — on social media after the PQ’s victory. “Alberta can do the same in two weeks by choosing to send a message with Option 2 on Question 10.”

Alberta separatist Jeffrey Rath also took to social media the day after the provincial election, saying that “for the first time in history, Alberta Independence will have the support of the elected government of Quebec.” He also congratulated St-Pierre Plamondon and “the country of Quebec.”

The two, along with lawyer Keith Wilson, lamented that Quebec’s quest for independence is seen as legitimate while they say Alberta separatists are sneered at.

During a visit to Calgary last year, St-Pierre Plamondon said he would recognize an independent Alberta should the province vote to separate. Rath said he met with the PQ leader during that visit.

But while they believe in the democratic process of a referendum, many Quebec sovereigntists do not identify with the Alberta separatists.

Former PQ leader Jean-François Lisée did not mince words when asked about Monday’s referendum.

“It’s mostly a waste because defeat is certain,” he said. “There’s really nothing much to gain from watching the Alberta independence movement, except maybe negative lessons.”

It’s a feeling shared by other sovereigntists.

Louise Harel, who was a PQ minister during Quebec’s 1995 sovereignty referendum and later served as interim leader of the party, agrees with Lisée. Both say the Quebec and Alberta sovereigntist movements are fundamentally different.

In their view, Quebec sovereigntists are motivated to preserve their cultural and linguistic identity, while Alberta separatists are motivated by the economy and political libertarianism. They also see a desire for Alberta to get closer to the United States, while Quebecers are wary of talk of assimilation.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has repeatedly said she is against secession, while PQ leaders have openly called for sovereignty.

“In Quebec, the idea is to give a unique historical nation in North America, which … has valiantly resisted assimilation, the powers it needs to survive in a globalized world,” said Harel. “But there is no such issue of identity or culture in Alberta.”

While sovereigntist Quebecers also feel economically disadvantaged within Canada, Lisée said, the sentiment isn’t at the core of the movement. He also stressed that Quebec’s sovereigntist parties have historically been social-democrat, while the movement in Alberta seems tied to conservatism.

Daniel Turp, a Université de Montréal law professor who represented both the Bloc Québécois and the PQ, sees differences in the referendum process itself. Quebec’s two independence referendums included a single question on sovereignty.

As a result, there were mass mobilizations from both federalist and sovereigntist factions for weeks.

Public support for independence also varies widely between the two provinces.

On the eve of the 1995 referendum, public opinion was split evenly in the polls. Three days before Quebecers cast their ballots, Canadians from across the country made their way to Montreal to urge them to vote against independence.

Poll aggregator 338Canada shows less than 25 per cent support for Alberta to leave Canada as of Oct. 11.

“There hasn’t been a love-in in Alberta yet,” Turp said. “Maybe we’re not as worried because the polls show the option to remain will win.”

More than 90 per cent of registered voters cast a ballot in the 1995 referendum, which federalists won with 50.58 per cent of the vote.

“That’s the kind of voter turnout you see in countries where voting is mandatory,” said Harel. “I would be extremely surprised if voter turnout in the Alberta referendum were the same.”

But the sovereigntists do not reject the Alberta separatist movement entirely. All four said they sympathize with the desire for autonomy and self-determination.

“If Alberta were to vote yes, and then Ottawa would say, ‘well, you can’t leave,’ we will be on the side of Alberta,” said Lisée.

Harel added that while she does not see ideological similarities between separatists in Quebec and Alberta, the democratic process must be respected. She said that the Alberta referendum can give legitimacy to the one promised by the PQ.

Asked if they worry that a no vote on Monday could affect the PQ’s promised referendum, all four said no.

Alepin believes the two movements are too different for Albertans to influence Quebecers’ appetite for sovereignty.

Meanwhile, Lisée predicts that “the defeat of the yes side in Alberta will be a negative but very insignificant factor in (Quebec’s) referendum debate.”

If Alberta stays within Canada, Turp believes the province May be inspired by Quebec’s approach to negotiating more autonomy with Ottawa.

“And then they can organize a second referendum, like we did,” he added.

But that hasn’t stopped some leaders in the Alberta separatist movement from claiming common cause.

Quebec elected the PQ — which has promised a third independence referendum — to a minority government on Oct. 5, leading figures in the Alberta separatist movement to rally behind premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and declare him a possible ally.

“Quebec rejected the status quo today,” wrote columnist Cory Morgan — a founding member of the Alberta Independence Party in 2001 — on social media after the PQ’s victory. “Alberta can do the same in two weeks by choosing to send a message with Option 2 on Question 10.”

Alberta separatist Jeffrey Rath also took to social media the day after the provincial election, saying that “for the first time in history, Alberta Independence will have the support of the elected government of Quebec.” He also congratulated St-Pierre Plamondon and “the country of Quebec.”
The two, along with lawyer Keith Wilson, lamented that Quebec’s quest for independence is seen as legitimate while they say Alberta separatists are sneered at.
During a visit to Calgary last year, St-Pierre Plamondon said he would recognize an independent Alberta should the province vote to separate. Rath said he met with the PQ leader during that visit.
But while they believe in the democratic process of a referendum, many Quebec sovereigntists do not identify with the Alberta separatists.
Former PQ leader Jean-François Lisée did not mince words when asked about Monday’s referendum.
“It’s mostly a waste because defeat is certain,” he said. “There’s really nothing much to gain from watching the Alberta independence movement, except maybe negative lessons.”
It’s a feeling shared by other sovereigntists.

Louise Harel, who was a PQ minister during Quebec’s 1995 sovereignty referendum and later served as interim leader of the party, agrees with Lisée. Both say the Quebec and Alberta sovereigntist movements are fundamentally different.

In their view, Quebec sovereigntists are motivated to preserve their cultural and linguistic identity, while Alberta separatists are motivated by the economy and political libertarianism. They also see a desire for Alberta to get closer to the United States, while Quebecers are wary of talk of assimilation.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has repeatedly said she is against secession, while PQ leaders have openly called for sovereignty.

“In Quebec, the idea is to give a unique historical nation in North America, which … has valiantly resisted assimilation, the powers it needs to survive in a globalized world,” said Harel. “But there is no such issue of identity or culture in Alberta.”

While sovereigntist Quebecers also feel economically disadvantaged within Canada, Lisée said, the sentiment isn’t at the core of the movement. He also stressed that Quebec’s sovereigntist parties have historically been social-democrat, while the movement in Alberta seems tied to conservatism.

Daniel Turp, a Université de Montréal law professor who represented both the Bloc Québécois and the PQ, sees differences in the referendum process itself. Quebec’s two independence referendums included a single question on sovereignty.
As a result, there were mass mobilizations from both federalist and sovereigntist factions for weeks.
Public support for independence also varies widely between the two provinces.

On the eve of the 1995 referendum, public opinion was split evenly in the polls. Three days before Quebecers cast their ballots, Canadians from across the country made their way to Montreal to urge them to vote against independence.
Poll aggregator 338Canada shows less than 25 per cent support for Alberta to leave Canada as of Oct. 11.
“There hasn’t been a love-in in Alberta yet,” Turp said. “Maybe we’re not as worried because the polls show the option to remain will win.”
More than 90 per cent of registered voters cast a ballot in the 1995 referendum, which federalists won with 50.58 per cent of the vote.
“That’s the kind of voter turnout you see in countries where voting is mandatory,” said Harel. “I would be extremely surprised if voter turnout in the Alberta referendum were the same.”
But the sovereigntists do not reject the Alberta separatist movement entirely. All four said they sympathize with the desire for autonomy and self-determination.
“If Alberta were to vote yes, and then Ottawa would say, ‘well, you can’t leave,’ we will be on the side of Alberta,” said Lisée.

Harel added that while she does not see ideological similarities between separatists in Quebec and Alberta, the democratic process must be respected. She said that the Alberta referendum can give legitimacy to the one promised by the PQ.
Asked if they worry that a no vote on Monday could affect the PQ’s promised referendum, all four said no.
Alepin believes the two movements are too different for Albertans to influence Quebecers’ appetite for sovereignty.
Meanwhile, Lisée predicts that “the defeat of the yes side in Alberta will be a negative but very insignificant factor in (Quebec’s) referendum debate.”
If Alberta stays within Canada, Turp believes the province May be inspired by Quebec’s approach to negotiating more autonomy with Ottawa.
“And then they can organize a second referendum, like we did,” he added.

stories.title: Highway 401 eastbound closed near Woodstock after three-vehicle crash
stories.summary: In a social media update issued shortly after 4 a.m., OPP said all eastbound lanes were shut down as emergency crews responded to the crash.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
The eastbound lanes of Highway 401 are closed at Highway 2 in Woodstock following a three-vehicle collision early Friday morning.

In a social media update issued shortly after 4 a.m., OPP said all eastbound lanes were shut down as emergency crews responded to the crash.

Police said occupants involved in the collision were being assessed for injuries. The extent of any injuries has not been released.

Motorists are being asked to avoid the area and use alternate routes while the closure remains in effect.

No further details about the cause of the collision or the number of people involved were immediately available.

CTV News has reached out to police for more information.

stories.title: Stellantis workers set to vote on strike mandate as bargaining stalls
stories.summary: Unifor, company at an impasse over job security and future of Brampton, Ont., plant
stories.author: Sammy Hudes
stories.content:
Stellantis Stla-N workers in Canada are set to vote this weekend on whether to authorize a strike as their union says contract negotiations with the automaker remain at a standstill.

Unifor is holding the votes on Saturday and Sunday and plans to announce results at the start of next week.

However, the union representing more than 9,000 Stellantis workers in Canada said it is hoping to avoid a potential strike. It said authorization for job action would provide leverage to help reach a negotiated agreement.

“A strike authorization gives the bargaining committee the authority to call a strike if necessary, it does not automatically mean a strike will take place,” said a statement last week signed by Unifor national president Lana Payne and other members of the union’s bargaining committee.

“Strike action remains a last resort, but the ability to strike is an important part of collective bargaining and can help create the conditions for an agreement.”

The previous collective agreement between Stellantis and the union expired Sept. 20 without the two sides coming to terms on a new tentative deal.

Unifor’s bargaining committee and the company are at an impasse over several key issues, including job security and the future of the Brampton, Ont., assembly plant Stellantis wants to sell.

The fate of the Brampton plant, which has been idled since 2023, has been a central issue. Talks came to a standstill on Sept. 11 when Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with defence contractor Roshel for a potential sale of the facility.

Stellantis Canada president and CEO Trevor Longley said in a September letter to employees that “market and trade conditions have directly impacted the original business case” for the plant, but that the move to sell could support future operations at the site.

“Stellantis remains committed to bargaining in good faith and is prepared to continue discussions toward a negotiated agreement that recognizes the contributions of our employees while supporting the long-term competitiveness of our Canadian operations,” the automaker’s spokesperson LouAnn Gosselin in a statement this week.

More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when it halted operations in 2023.

The facility had been slated to be retooled for Jeep production, a process that began early in 2024, before the company paused the plan in early 2025. It later announced it was moving production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois., leaving the plant idled indefinitely.

Unifor has filed a grievance over that move, alleging it violated the previous collective agreement.

For its part, Roshel has said it is willing to consider hiring laid-off workers from the plant as soon as this year “through the federal government’s Light Utility Vehicles procurement program and other automotive and defence opportunities.”

Roshel CEO Roman Shimonov said the company plans to establish a Canadian Centre of Excellence for Defence Manufacturing in Brampton in addition to automotive production, which would involve more than 2,000 jobs.

Payne has written to federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly urging the government to block the potential sale and clarify whether the MOU breached Stellantis’ previous commitments to Ottawa.

Last fall, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he had expressed disappointment during a conversation with the global head of Stellantis over the company moving Jeep Compass production to the United States. At the time, the prime minister said he reminded Stellantis of its commitments to the government under funding deals – such as keeping the Brampton plant – and warned there would be consequences if it failed to meet those obligations.

Joly’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

Contract talks began Sept. 1 in Toronto after Unifor ratified new collective agreements with Ford Motor Co. and General Motors in Canada earlier in the summer, as part of its pattern bargaining process with each of the Detroit Three.

stories.title: Ontario’s Osap pause affects students at ballet and divinity schools, among others
stories.summary: Pause affects all private postsecondary institutions, including private universities, chiropractic and naturopathic medicine colleges, performing arts schools
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
A recent pause on financial assistance payments to private postsecondary institutions in Ontario is affecting divinity schools, Canada’s National Ballet School and many others, with students feeling unfairly swept up in what they describe as a trawling net-like policy.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced last week that the province had tasked Kpmg with auditing Ontario Student Assistance Program usage at career colleges, and that preliminary findings were of such concern that he referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police.

While the audit is ongoing, Quinn said, Osap payments to private postsecondary institutions would be paused. Quinn said he is “working on” securing low-interest loans for affected students at financial institutions, but he has not indicated a timeline.

Many career college students have said they are worried about the pause, with no clear end in sight and with some students relying on that financial aid to cover not just tuition but living expenses while they study.

The broad nature of the pause affects all private postsecondary institutions, including private universities, chiropractic and naturopathic medicine colleges, and performing arts schools such as Canada’s National Ballet School.

Alessia Di Palma is in her last year of the ballet school’s five-year joint teacher training program with York University, and said she does not want to have to leave school when she is so close to finishing, but at the moment doesn’t know how she will pay her rent, even though she works two jobs while going to school.

“I’m heartbroken,” she said. “My heart sunk when I found out because it’s unfair that I’ve had this funding for four years and then the fifth year it’s just gone now because of something that didn’t even have anything to do with me.”

Initial concerns stemmed from activity at a few schools, Quinn’s office says, but evidence of “systemic issues” has come up in recent weeks.

“At this time, we do not have assurances from the audit team that the issues are not more widespread, leaving us with no choice but to pause Osap payments to all private institutions to protect taxpayer dollars and hold bad actors accountable,” spokesperson Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement.

“We understand this is creating uncertainty for students and are working quickly to develop options for low-interest, third-party loans facilitated by financial institutions to help students through this period of transition.”

At the ballet school, programs are mostly at the secondary level, but it does have a postsecondary teacher training program that is affected by the Osap pause. About half of those students rely on that aid to pay their tuition, said executive director John Dalrymple.

The government has chosen the bluntest and most harmful way of dealing with the root of the problem, he said, and it is especially disappointing that Quinn enacted the pause before securing those third-party loans.

“The fact that now all of these students who are working multiple jobs to make ends meet, who are at the very beginning of their career, are now left holding the bag to figure out how to finance something that the government had already assured them they qualified for and they were going to receive, I think is unconscionable,” he said.

Theological schools like McMaster Divinity College, affiliated with McMaster University, are also affected by the pause. Ambrose Thomson, the school’s registrar and director of student services, said students are beside themselves.

About 10 per cent of the non-profit institution’s revenue is dependent on Osap-paid tuition, he said. McMaster Divinity College is relatively well-positioned to weather that storm, Ambrose said, but not all schools are so lucky.

“The impression I get is that the government knows full well what the impacts are,” he said.

“They’re not stupid. All I can assume is that at the highest levels where these decisions were made, they’re actually willing to allow career colleges and other schools to shut their doors ... I think they’re trying to look like they’re doing something in the face of 300-whatever million dollars that they were not smart enough to pay attention to.”

Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request showed large increases in Osap usage at a relatively small number of career colleges from 2020-21 to 2024-25.

The seven career colleges that had the highest Osap usage in 2024-25 received $385-million in provincial grants – the same amount that went to students at all of Ontario’s publicly funded colleges that year.

Career Colleges Ontario has raised concerns since 2023 about what it calls potentially “suspicious activity” with Osap usage at a few schools.

Deanna Hutten, a second-year master’s student in McMaster Divinity College’s counselling and spiritual care program, is borrowing money from family and working 10 more hours per week at her marketing job to make up for her Osap being on hold.

The single mother to a one-year-old daughter who hopes to work in hospital chaplaincy said it is frustrating to be lumped in with some suspected bad actors.

“It definitely feels very unfair,” she said.

“They had known about this since 2023 that there were people kind of [allegedly] fudging the system, and now we as private career – not even career colleges, but private institutions – are kind of being swept into that field or that group of people, even though we’re not a part of that.”

At the Toronto Film School, there is also “tremendous uncertainty and anxiety” for many students, said president Andrew Barnsley. He is calling for prompt reinstatement of Osap for eligible students, or at least a clear, expedited timeline to resolve the pause.

“The Osap pause is deeply disappointing, and our greatest concern is the impact on our students who made significant commitments to their education with the reasonable expectation that financial assistance would be available,” he wrote in a statement.

“Many students have rearranged their lives, reduced or left employment, made child-care arrangements and, in some cases, relocated to Toronto in order to pursue their studies. They need to know whether they can meet their financial obligations, including life essentials like rent or food, and continue the programs in which they have already invested time, money and effort.”

stories.title: An election that ducks B.C.’s dire fiscal reality
stories.summary: Neither the NDP nor the Conservatives have a credible plan to pull the province out of its debt trap
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
The two main parties vying for power in British Columbia’s Oct. 24 election have lots to say about how their rival will make the province’s abysmal fiscal situation even worse.

But the BC NDP and the BC Conservatives are much less forthcoming about what they might actually do to avoid the debt trap that is closing around the province’s finances.

Under NDP Leader David Eby, the province’s debt burden has more than doubled, with taxpayer-supported debt as a percentage of provincial gross domestic product projected to surge to 37.4 per cent in fiscal 2029, from just 15 per cent in fiscal 2023, the year that Mr. Eby became premier.

Without a sharp reduction in the deficit, that ratio will crest 40 per cent by the end of this decade, and will be headed to 50 per cent by the middle of the next. That is a fiscal disaster waiting to happen. To avoid that calamity, the NDP and Conservatives each propose a confection of unaffordable promises, and dreamy revenue projections.

In a meeting with The Globe and Mail editorial board earlier this month, Mr. Eby tried to put a positive shine on his fiscal record, arguing that a massive infrastructure deficit meant that the NDP government needed to take on debt for capital projects. He pushed back on the notion that the debt burden would continue to rise at its current pace, saying that he expected it to stabilize well below 40 per cent of GDP and that he was committed to the deficit declining year over year.

That defence is flimsy. For one, two-thirds of the debt that Mr. Eby’s government expects to take on through to fiscal 2029 is from operations, not from capital projects. And it would take a sustained and substantial decline in the deficit to arrest the growth in B.C.’s debt burden. There is no sign of such a plan in the costed platform that the BC NDP released on Wednesday.

But that projection rests on some questionable assumptions and rosy forecasts. For one, the costing of platform commitments does not include Mr. Eby’s pre-election move to put off an expansion of the provincial sales tax. The party also assumes that its boost to income tax rates for top earners will take in $1-billion by fiscal 2029; economists have said the actual revenue will be lower, perhaps just one-quarter of the Ndp’s projections. And the platform also pencils in hundreds of millions in revenue from “targeted economic growth,” above and beyond the growth forecasts in this year’s budget.

If those rosy forecasts are set aside, the deficit would surge past both the latest projections and the forecasts in the party’s platform. Even the best case scenario in the costed platform would still leave B.C. finances on a disastrous course.

The B.C. Conservatives had not, as of Thursday, released a costed platform. But Leader Lorne Doerkson laid out his fiscal vision in his own meeting with The Globe editorial board earlier this month. Mr. Doerkson rightly criticizes the run-up in provincial debt under the NDP.

But his plan – like that of his rival – fails to come to grips with that fiscal challenge. Like the NDP, the Conservatives would depend on economic growth to shrink the deficit (although they have not yet provided numbers).

Mr. Doerkson did point to some limited cuts he would make in provincial spending, including climate-change expenditures under CleanBC, and he did acknowledge that the ranks of civil servants should be winnowed. But for the most part he has shied away from specifics, beyond promising not to cut services such as health and education and to not raise taxes.

Those measures that have been specific would widen the fiscal gap in B.C., at least in the short term. The Conservative proposals to reduce PST on machinery, equipment and business software has merit as a pro-growth policy. The same cannot be said of a much more expensive promise – estimated to cost upwards of $2.5-billion a year – to increase the basic personal exemption for individual taxpayers. Bluntly speaking, B.C. cannot afford such a tax cut, at least not without spending reductions that not only offset its cost but shrink the existing deficit.

Mr. Doerkson has voiced his intent to reduce the deficit, but has not offered a cohesive plan. Mr. Eby has offered a plan to maintain a status quo but that plan is unrealistic, and in any case, would only lock in a ruinous status quo.

Neither party is dealing with the reality of B.C.’s dire finances. But the next premier will soon find that reality will be dealing with them.

stories.title: Snowbirds’ final air show to be livestreamed, before jets head into retirement
stories.summary: Royal Canadian Air Force is set to livestream the annual season home closer online at 2 p.m. ET on its Facebook page
stories.author: Kyle Duggan
stories.content:
Members of the Royal Canadian Air Force Snowbirds aerial aerobatics team are set to perform their final air show Friday in Moose Jaw, Sask., before their decades-old Tutor jets head into retirement.

The Rcaf is set to livestream the annual season home closer online at 2 p.m. ET on its Facebook page.

There will still be one more chance to see the CT-114 Tutors in action before they are sent to the airbase in Trenton, Ont., for disposal.

The Snowbirds are scheduled to perform a flyover at the Canadian Football League Grey Cup game in Calgary on Nov. 15.

Capt. Philip Rochon, public affairs officer for the Snowbirds, said it’s a bittersweet time for the pilots who are saying farewell to the planes the team has flown for 55 years.

“It’s like saying goodbye to a good friend,” he said.

Rochon said the Snowbirds received an outpouring of support over the summer from Canadians across the country who shared memories of past shows and their encounters with an iconic “piece of Canadiana.”

“At the same time, we’re looking forward to the future with the new aircraft that was announced,” he said. “That will come online hopefully in the next few years. We’re looking forward to seeing what the next chapter of the Snowbirds will be.”

Defence Minister David McGuinty announced in May that the old Tutors will be replaced eventually by the Swiss-made PC-21 Pilatus aircraft, known as the CT-157 Siskin II.

The Rcaf is also acquiring those same aircraft for pilot training.

While the Snowbirds were formed in 1971, the air force obtained the Tutor jets in 1963.

The Snowbirds will go on a multiyear hiatus until the replacement aircraft are delivered and the team can be trained up on the new planes. That could take until the early 2030s but there’s no set timeline.

The decision to ground the team came after planned upgrades to the Tutors’ engines and escape systems meant to keep them in the air until 2030 encountered a range of problems, including parts obsolescence.

Rcaf Commander Lt.-Gen. Jamie Speiser-Blanchet told reporters at the Aero Gatineau-Ottawa air show last month that it’s been “heartwarming” to see how Canadians have responded over the last season.

“The Snowbirds are so much more than just an air demonstration team, obviously, and it evokes so much emotion and we all have such fond strong memories,” she said.

“I really can’t overstate just how significant they are to Canadians and specifically to the Rcaf. The idea that we’d have to take a pause was definitely not an easy one. However, the Tutor aircraft is 63 years old and it is time to move into the future and make sure that we’re doing things for the right reasons.”

She said the demonstration team has been focused solely on finishing the current season. Once that’s done, she said, the Rcaf can “build the right kind of plan” to ensure the pilots don’t get rusty in the meantime.

“We’re looking at things like, can we send an exchange into some of our allied teams, or obviously instructing and working with the PC-21 in Moose Jaw as an option,” she said.

stories.title: ‘Call them out’: AI data centres becoming an Ontario municipal election issue
stories.summary: Stop the Datacentre, a grassroots advocacy group, is looking for more signatories before the municipal elections are held later this month.
stories.author: Trevor Popoff
stories.content:
AI data centres have become an issue in Ontario’s municipal elections, with grassroots groups pressing candidates to support stricter regulations.

Several Greater Toronto Area mayoral and city council candidates have signed a pledge promising to oppose building any data centres that fail to adhere to strict oversight and regulations.

Early signatories include incumbent Mississauga mayoral candidate Carolyn Parrish and incumbent Hamilton council candidates Cameron Kroetsch and Nrinder Nann.

Stop the Datacentre, a grassroots advocacy group, is looking for more signatories before municipal elections are held later this month.

The pledge asks candidates to sign on if they agree with the following conditions:

I will oppose any recommendation to build AI data centres which does not include stringent regulations.

Data centres must not compete with households and businesses for electricity and water.

Residents can’t be asked to accept round-the-clock noise pollution or air pollution.

Data centres must not be eligible for tax relief or economic development incentives.

Community benefits that come with data centres must be binding.

Data centres should not be allowed to operate if their massive computational power is trained to act against the public good.

So far, the pledge has gone out to candidates in Hamilton and Mississauga, two cities that have had heated debates over data centres already.

In September, Mississauga city council approved a one-year moratorium on new data centre approvals after residents raised concerns about a data centre project proposed in northwest Mississauga, outlining fears around energy consumption, strain on the water supply and possible noise pollution.

Hamilton residents similarly pushed back against data centres in their city. But in July, city council voted down a moratorium on construction. Mayor Andrea Horwath and some councillors cited concerns around scaring away tech companies from investing in the city.

Martin Reid, who is running for re-election as Mississauga Ward 9 councillor, has signed the pledge. He was one of the councillors who set in motion the city’s moratorium.

Nick Tsergas, a Hamilton resident, created the pledge. He said he was motivated to hold politicians accountable after seeing the data centre issue take hold across the country.

Tsergas said the pledge is intended to hold signatories accountable to their commitments. If anyone ends up reneging on it, “we can call them out,” he added.

Tsergas was also motivated to start his record-keeping effort because of a lack of clarity from the province about whether data centres will be subject to specific regulatory standards. No legislation on the issue has been passed.

The Ford government released its AI data centre playbook in August, which includes proposed policies on how to govern data centres. But it is an evaluation tool, not binding legislation.

“We don’t know what those rules will look like, or when they arrive,” Tsergas said. “Will they be geared to protecting communities and addressing concerns, or will they be geared towards attracting data centre investment from large U.S. tech companies?”

The government’s playbook proposes prioritizing Canadian companies, community benefits and self-sustaining power systems.

However, Reid argues the proposed data centre that prompted his push for a moratorium does not satisfy several priorities outlined in the province’s playbook.

The project is proposed for a plot of land in the Tenth Line and Argentia Road area. The property was formerly farmland and was acquired by U.S.-based logistics company Prologis for the proposed development.

When the Prologis plans came across his desk, Reid did some digging and realized there was no land use designation for a data centre.

“It’s a warehouse, but it has 14 generators,” he said, alluding to the grey area that data centres fall into.

Tsergas also raised concern with classification, especially for data centres that propose to generate their own power.

“Is it a power plant or a data centre? What’s the noise going to be like? What’s the pollution going to be like?” he asked.

Reid identified safety concerns beyond environmental issues.

“Fire did not have a fire study for a data centre,” Reid said. “We have a building with lithium-ion batteries in it. It could be a ticking time bomb.”

Reid also said that Prologis did not plan on offering any community benefits.

“I went to them at one point and asked them to consider that, but they don’t have to do that from a development perspective. It’s not legislated, and they didn’t offer.”

Global News reached out to Prologis, which said it remains committed to the project at Tenth Line and Argentia, even with the city’s moratorium in place.

Prologis said construction would support 1,600 jobs. Once operational, the company estimates the project would sustain 63 direct, indirect and induced full-time-equivalent jobs.

Prologis also said that it is working with the provincial government to develop the data centre playbook, and that the Mississauga site will generate $1.6 million in annual property tax revenue for the city and region.

Tsergas stressed the purpose of his pledge is to seek clarity on how prospective candidates view the issue.

“We’re not asking people if they like or don’t like AI. We are just asking people if they think rules should exist before a major development goes in, and what at minimum those rules should be.”

stories.title: Canada should sprint to make one of its marathons a World Major race
stories.summary: The Abbott World Marathon Majors represent the world’s best races, bringing people from all over the globe. While many of Canada’s marathons deserve to be among them, Toronto’s is the country’s best bet
stories.author: Ben Kaplan
stories.content:
Ben Kaplan is the author of Feet, Don’t Fail Me Now: The Rogue’s Guide to the Marathon and the owner of iRun magazine.

The best running races in the world are part of a series called the Abbott World Marathon Majors. There are eight in total: three in the U.S. in New York, Chicago and Boston, as well as in Berlin, Tokyo, London, Sydney and Cape Town. These aren’t just races, though: They’re Coachella for runners, Investment Summits for joggers, Davos for the oddballs who bring three pairs of shoes on vacation, none of which are leather or have heels.

In short, they’re amateur running’s Olympics: a way for competitive people with disposable income to achieve a difficult, expensive, but sought-after goal. The Majors are proud markers for the world’s best marathons – and being able to say they’ve performed on the world’s greatest courses is a key reason people run these races.

Canada doesn’t have a race with such a designation – at least, not yet. But as international tourists look to avoid the U.S. under Donald Trump, and as the Majors expand – Sydney and Cape Town became part of the series over the last two years, and the Shanghai Marathon is currently being evaluated – this is a race we can win.

This country has runs that could qualify, including marathons in Vancouver, Ottawa, Calgary and Montreal. These are world-class events with big-budget sponsors, prize money for winners and precisely measured courses, complete with sparkly race expos and throngs of spectators that increase every year.

But the TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon, a World Athletics Elite Label race that’s taking place this weekend and being televised for the first time this year, is the country’s best hope.

Not only does Toronto’s marathon have big-name sponsors like Peloton and Nespresso, and not only is it as loud and colourful as Chicago’s and New York’s, it’s in the conversation with Boston, the running event regarded as the best in the world. The city is a multicultural hub for running clubs, with a major international airport connected by a transit link that makes it easy to get downtown. Unlike marathons in New York and Boston, the starting line for Toronto’s Marathon isn’t in the middle of nowhere – it’s right on Yonge Street. Like Berlin and London, the course is flat and fast, which means marathoners can set records.

It’s high time Toronto became the next World Marathon Major. And such efforts would also have an ace in the hole in the race’s title sponsor, TCS, a billion-dollar IT firm that is already the title sponsor for three Abbott World Majors. With its green policies, network, AI sorcery and long-term vision – TCS signed a five-year sponsorship extension with Toronto this month – the company elevates moderately known races into global sensations with the power of a Taylor Swift.

Sure, Toronto’s marathon has things it needs to work on before it can race onto the world stage. Other Majors feature at least 27,000 marathon runners, and while the full Toronto race weekend counts roughly that many participants overall, only around 7,500 racers compete in its marathon segment. Race weekend would have to hold its 5K and half-marathon on Saturday, then triple its marathon participants on Sunday – no easy feat. But Toronto’s roads can handle the volume; the Sporting Life 10K shuts down Yonge Street for 25,000 runners, and while a 42-kilometre race would require more road closures than 10, race directors work best when working toward a difficult goal.

Transit would also need to open at 4 a.m. on race day, for instance, so runners can get to their start line. Construction on the Gardiner Expressway would have to (finally) end. And the city would probably have to keep its bike lanes as a signal that mental and physical health are important here.

But the Majors designation would make it all worthwhile. When a race becomes a Major, it becomes more valuable as the world’s top runners gather to try to collect each of the Majors’ coveted stars. The 2025 Chicago Marathon added an estimated US$756-million to the local economy and delivered US$47-million to charities, both record-setting figures. Cash like that also buys support from the federal government, which can unlock huge events like the Fifa World Cup or the Olympics.

What makes a World Major also goes beyond the race itself. After Boston’s marathon, there’s a party in Fenway Park. In Berlin, there’s free transit for runners, and the iconic finish runs through the Brandenburg Gate. Asics, the Toronto Marathon’s shoe sponsor, designs a limited-edition sneaker for Tokyo’s marathon every year, and New York stacks its race with celebs. Montreal is more fun than Toronto and has louder sports fans, Calgary’s got pipeline cash, Ottawa’s race weekend is larger and Vancouver’s is better-looking, but Canada’s biggest city has just enough of everything to blow the socks off Boston or Berlin. It doesn’t hurt that the Toronto International Film Festival shows that the city can party.

There’s a real running culture in this country, too. Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow is a runner. Prime Minister Mark Carney runs marathons. And Canada’s best marathon runner, Rory Linkletter, puts up finishing times that compete with the fastest athletes in the world, finishing sixth in Boston in 2025 before getting even faster. Mr. Linkletter winning a World Marathon Major on Canadian soil would be like when the Blue Jays won the World Series at home in 1993.

There’s never been more runners, more attention or more money in marathons. The TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon is a worthy finish line for promoting Canadian marathons – and Canada – all over the world.
paragraphs: Ben Kaplan is the author of Feet, Don’t Fail Me Now: The Rogue’s Guide to the Marathon and the owner of iRun magazine.

The best running races in the world are part of a series called the Abbott World Marathon Majors. There are eight in total: three in the U.S. in New York, Chicago and Boston, as well as in Berlin, Tokyo, London, Sydney and Cape Town. These aren’t just races, though: They’re Coachella for runners, Investment Summits for joggers, Davos for the oddballs who bring three pairs of shoes on vacation, none of which are leather or have heels.

In short, they’re amateur running’s Olympics: a way for competitive people with disposable income to achieve a difficult, expensive, but sought-after goal. The Majors are proud markers for the world’s best marathons – and being able to say they’ve performed on the world’s greatest courses is a key reason people run these races.

Canada doesn’t have a race with such a designation – at least, not yet. But as international tourists look to avoid the U.S. under Donald Trump, and as the Majors expand – Sydney and Cape Town became part of the series over the last two years, and the Shanghai Marathon is currently being evaluated – this is a race we can win.

This country has runs that could qualify, including marathons in Vancouver, Ottawa, Calgary and Montreal. These are world-class events with big-budget sponsors, prize money for winners and precisely measured courses, complete with sparkly race expos and throngs of spectators that increase every year.
But the TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon, a World Athletics Elite Label race that’s taking place this weekend and being televised for the first time this year, is the country’s best hope.

Not only does Toronto’s marathon have big-name sponsors like Peloton and Nespresso, and not only is it as loud and colourful as Chicago’s and New York’s, it’s in the conversation with Boston, the running event regarded as the best in the world. The city is a multicultural hub for running clubs, with a major international airport connected by a transit link that makes it easy to get downtown. Unlike marathons in New York and Boston, the starting line for Toronto’s Marathon isn’t in the middle of nowhere – it’s right on Yonge Street. Like Berlin and London, the course is flat and fast, which means marathoners can set records.

It’s high time Toronto became the next World Marathon Major. And such efforts would also have an ace in the hole in the race’s title sponsor, TCS, a billion-dollar IT firm that is already the title sponsor for three Abbott World Majors. With its green policies, network, AI sorcery and long-term vision – TCS signed a five-year sponsorship extension with Toronto this month – the company elevates moderately known races into global sensations with the power of a Taylor Swift.

Sure, Toronto’s marathon has things it needs to work on before it can race onto the world stage. Other Majors feature at least 27,000 marathon runners, and while the full Toronto race weekend counts roughly that many participants overall, only around 7,500 racers compete in its marathon segment. Race weekend would have to hold its 5K and half-marathon on Saturday, then triple its marathon participants on Sunday – no easy feat. But Toronto’s roads can handle the volume; the Sporting Life 10K shuts down Yonge Street for 25,000 runners, and while a 42-kilometre race would require more road closures than 10, race directors work best when working toward a difficult goal.

Transit would also need to open at 4 a.m. on race day, for instance, so runners can get to their start line. Construction on the Gardiner Expressway would have to (finally) end. And the city would probably have to keep its bike lanes as a signal that mental and physical health are important here.

But the Majors designation would make it all worthwhile. When a race becomes a Major, it becomes more valuable as the world’s top runners gather to try to collect each of the Majors’ coveted stars. The 2025 Chicago Marathon added an estimated US$756-million to the local economy and delivered US$47-million to charities, both record-setting figures. Cash like that also buys support from the federal government, which can unlock huge events like the Fifa World Cup or the Olympics.

What makes a World Major also goes beyond the race itself. After Boston’s marathon, there’s a party in Fenway Park. In Berlin, there’s free transit for runners, and the iconic finish runs through the Brandenburg Gate. Asics, the Toronto Marathon’s shoe sponsor, designs a limited-edition sneaker for Tokyo’s marathon every year, and New York stacks its race with celebs. Montreal is more fun than Toronto and has louder sports fans, Calgary’s got pipeline cash, Ottawa’s race weekend is larger and Vancouver’s is better-looking, but Canada’s biggest city has just enough of everything to blow the socks off Boston or Berlin. It doesn’t hurt that the Toronto International Film Festival shows that the city can party.

There’s a real running culture in this country, too. Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow is a runner. Prime Minister Mark Carney runs marathons. And Canada’s best marathon runner, Rory Linkletter, puts up finishing times that compete with the fastest athletes in the world, finishing sixth in Boston in 2025 before getting even faster. Mr. Linkletter winning a World Marathon Major on Canadian soil would be like when the Blue Jays won the World Series at home in 1993.

There’s never been more runners, more attention or more money in marathons. The TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon is a worthy finish line for promoting Canadian marathons – and Canada – all over the world.
