stories.title: I spent a year visiting ‘world-class’ cities. Here’s how Canada compares on the global stage
stories.summary: When you go to big city after big city for an entire year, you realize the areas where Canada’s world-class obsessed cities struggle to keep up with the rest of the world
stories.author: Justin McElroy
stories.content:
Justin McElroy is a Vancouver-based journalist and author of the new book Searching for the Best Place on Earth: 52 Countries in 52 Weeks .

In October, 2023, a few months before I left Vancouver to travel the world for a year, I was in city hall listening to Mayor Ken Sim argue for increased housing density around rapid transit stations. In response to a question of whether any budgeting or planning had been done, Mr. Sim answered with a sentence that has loomed over the city for more than two generations.

“We’re talking about building a world-class city.”

In many ways, it’s a benign, calorie-free phrase. There’s no real way to quantify what makes a city “world-class,” and there are no tangible benefits if everyone agrees that a city has indeed become that. But at the time, I was about to embark on a quest to visit 52 countries in 52 weeks, focusing mostly on cities, including 44 of the top 50 cities in the annual ranking by Vancouver consulting firm Resonance.

So when Mr. Sim said that phrase, I said to myself, “well, I’m travelling to almost every world-class city on Earth next year. I’ll figure out what one actually is, and see how we measure up.” Instead of just wandering old towns and quirky neighbourhoods, I would consider housing affordability and overtourism and retail diversity. On trains and tubes I could research each city’s transportation system and how well it managed congestion. While going to museums and city squares I could think about how a country expresses its distinct culture and history while trying to remain forward-thinking and vibrant.

Interestingly, the idea of a “world-class” city seems to be a Canadian invention, which began over a very Canadian worry about what others might think about a landmark new building.

“Those who want to believe that Toronto has outgrown the narrow, self-satisfied Hogtown of the past to become a cosmopolitan, world-class city wince at the mention of the tower,” wrote a reporter in the Ottawa Citizen in 1976, the day before the CN Tower opened to the public.

It’s the earliest use of the term that I could find on the website newspapers.com – which has full archives of more than 29,000 newspapers around the world. From there, the phrase started appearing in Canadian newspapers every so often, usually about Toronto.

But it quickly spread around the globe in the 1980s, becoming an aspirational goal used by politicians, marketers, and urban planners to denote what a city could or should be, often tied to building that new megaproject or bringing a global festival to town. Arguably, nowhere has it had more resonance than in Canada’s two biggest English-speaking cities: In both Vancouver and Toronto, “world-class city” has been used seriously and sardonically so many times that it had long lost any meaning to me.

For the record, I did not plan to travel the Earth as a year-long exercise to give meaning to an overused turn of phrase.

Before my trip, I had reported on city politics for a decade, and was fascinated by all the ways that cities come together in a coherent whole or devolve into frustrating paralysis or chaos. But I’d never travelled outside Canada and the U.S. as an adult.

After 149,000 kilometres, 111 trains, 74 nights in hostels, 47 art galleries, six continents, and only one time being scammed by a fake taxi driver, the things I learned about great cities will not surprise most seasoned travellers. In most wealthy countries the city centre is dominated by car-free walkways, bustling town squares and rapid transit stations; in Canada the car still reigns supreme. Patios, plazas and alleyways in much of the rest of the world are filled with public activities and private enterprise that generally get regulated or ticketed out of existence here. Every city is trapped to some degree by its geography, its political culture, and the planning norms of the time when it exploded in population.

There are some areas where Canada’s top cities stood out – Toronto’s incredible diversity has few comparisons, and Vancouver’s endless activities you can do on a mountain or on water become more impressive when you realize just how rare that is in a big city anywhere else on Earth. The virtues of politeness, tolerance and rule of law are embedded in our urban DNA in a way you realize doesn’t happen automatically once you navigate a truly chaotic city like Cairo, a truly autocratic one like Beijing, or a truly techno-class-based one like Dubai.

Generally speaking, though, when you go to big city after big city for an entire year, with each city adding another point of comparison with the rest you’ve visited, you realize the areas where Canada’s world-class obsessed cities struggle to keep up with the rest of the world.

You see it in debates over public space that would seem quaint in much of the world: Toronto’s municipal and Ontario’s provincial governments have feuded over waterfront land, park preservation and bike lanes, while Vancouver’s municipal government has spent four years piloting three different streets to be car-free without committing long-term to any of them.

But nowhere is the discrepancy between world-class ambition and reality more clear than affordable housing. European cities often have huge amounts of publicly owned housing, Eastern Asian cities often have medium and high-rise housing spread across the city, and cities in countries with illiberal governments certainly have faults, yet can also have edicts to ensure virtually all people have a roof over their head regardless of means.

That’s not the case in Toronto, and especially not the case in Vancouver. In the 52 countries I went to, comprising virtually all of the wealthiest countries on Earth, I didn’t see any other neighbourhood with as many clearly struggling unhoused people crammed into one highly accessible place as Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside, just two blocks from the apartment I’ve rented for the past decade.

The longer that reality sat with me, the worse I felt. My city has world-class mountains and world-class sushi and world-class glass towers reflecting a world-class public waterfront. We also have a world-class concentration of human suffering, visible in a way that every other wealthy city on Earth has decided is not how its most vulnerable residents should live.

The population is shrinking in pockets of Vancouver and Toronto. What if we put more housing there?

So after a year of thinking about it, here’s my definition of a world-class city: one where all of its residents can live and get around with reasonable comfort, with a mix of interesting things to experience that are uniquely tied to the city’s culture or geography.

And while both Vancouver and Toronto can – and will – continue to argue whether they’re world-class or not, I can tell you that neither of them is my pick.

After all, there’s a place in this country with a unique culture, plenty of diversity, vibrant public spaces, good transportation options, and with rents significantly more affordable than Vancouver or Toronto.

Montreal hasn’t spent a lot of time in the last 40 years wondering if it’s “world-class.”

But then again, if you truly are, then you probably don’t need to ask.

content_blocks.text: After 149,000 kilometres, 111 trains, 74 nights in hostels, 47 art galleries, six continents, and only one time being scammed by a fake taxi driver, the things I learned about great cities will not surprise most seasoned travellers. In most wealthy countries the city centre is dominated by car-free walkways, bustling town squares and rapid transit stations; in Canada the car still reigns supreme. Patios, plazas and alleyways in much of the rest of the world are filled with public activities and private enterprise that generally get regulated or ticketed out of existence here. Every city is trapped to some degree by its geography, its political culture, and the planning norms of the time when it exploded in population.

content_blocks.text: There are some areas where Canada’s top cities stood out – Toronto’s incredible diversity has few comparisons, and Vancouver’s endless activities you can do on a mountain or on water become more impressive when you realize just how rare that is in a big city anywhere else on Earth. The virtues of politeness, tolerance and rule of law are embedded in our urban DNA in a way you realize doesn’t happen automatically once you navigate a truly chaotic city like Cairo, a truly autocratic one like Beijing, or a truly techno-class-based one like Dubai.

stories.title: The seduction of Hudson Williams
stories.summary: On set in Victoria for the new witchy Canadian series, Yaga, the Heated Rivalry star is steaming up the screen again, this time with a veteran cast
stories.author: Marsha Lederman
stories.content:
The quietly sizzling scene was being shot on a rainy March morning in a grand old house in Victoria, the stately home separated from the street by an expansive lawn. A main-floor living room had been transformed into a set: a dark, old-school university professor’s office. And a seduction was under way.

“I would like to talk to you today about bones,” the character played by Hudson Williams, suddenly one of the hottest stars on the planet, said to the character played by Carrie-Anne Moss.

In the scene, Moss’s Katherine, a professor with deep expertise in bones, is being interviewed for a podcast by Williams’s Henry Park, heir to a fishery fortune in a small coastal town.

“Are you comfortable or would you rather do it on the desk,” Henry asks.

“I think you mean at the desk,” Katherine responds.

It might be raining outside but it is steamy on set. “Prioritize the hot, people,” showrunner Kat Sandler instructs.

The scene appears in episode five of the upcoming series Yaga – a supernatural psychological thriller based on Sandler’s play, Yaga , marking her first move into television.

She has adapted the witchy award-winning play, inspired by the Slavic legend of Baba Yaga, for the screen, expanding it from a two-act play to an eight-part series with more characters (and thus more suspects).

In the first episode, which premieres on Crave on Oct. 23, a private investigator named Rapp (Noah Reid) arrives, hired by the wealthy Park family to investigate Henry’s potential disappearance. Rapp is paired with a local police detective, played by Clark Backo. It’s not long before Rapp, an old friend of Henry’s, becomes intoxicated by the local women, including Moss’s Katherine.

“It is interesting to play someone that is my age that is supposed to be invoking attraction from younger men. That’s a trip,” said Moss, who is now 59.

Growing up in Vancouver, Moss spent parts of her childhood summers in Victoria with an aunt and uncle who lived here. Being here now to shoot the series, she said, evokes a childhood nostalgia. “Just the smell, the weather, the feeling of the place, even though it’s changed so much,” she said. “I think subconsciously, where you come from is in your bones.”

Moss became a breakout star herself as a younger woman, cast as Trinity in The Matrix opposite another Canadian, Keanu Reeves. Given that, I asked if she had any wisdom to offer 25-year-old Williams, who is also from B.C., about rocketing to stardom.

“I don’t think he needs it, you know? I think he’s very grounded,” she answered. “I don’t know if it’s the Canadian thing.”

We were speaking in between takes of her exchange with Williams, a scene Sandler describes as “really sexy.” So hot, I was told, that even during an online read-through of the scene, Williams appeared to be blushing over Zoom.

Not that Williams is any stranger to shooting racy TV scenes, as anyone who has not been in a pop-culture cave since Heated Rivalry took over the discourse is aware. The heat and chemistry between Williams’s Shane Hollander and co-star Connor Storrie’s Ilya Rozanov shot the two young men into the stratosphere since its late 2025 release.

It was in the midst of this phenomenon that Williams joined the cast of Yaga , giving this new Canadian production a boost beyond its creator’s wildest dreams.

“I was, of course, over the moon,” Sandler, who lives in Toronto, told me. “I couldn’t believe it.”

Production was under way at the peak of the Heated Rivalry frenzy, which at that point was still new and strange for Williams. It was early March and over the past three months, he had gone from relative unknown to one of the two most visible stars in the world, along with Storrie, who four days earlier had guest-hosted Saturday Night Live , complete with a Williams cameo.

Life had changed dramatically. A year earlier, Williams was working on some short films, juggling acting classes and his server job at a suburban Old Spaghetti Factory, trying to save up some money for a vacation, he told me.

And now? He’s one of the most recognizable stars in the world.

“I’m doing relatively good. I’m learning all throughout this,” Williams said during an interview that day on set. We were sitting in an improvised green room on the mansion’s top floor, Williams dressed in his character’s crisp white shirt.

“In the beginning, it was really hard during the blow-up. The good moments are absolute highs, but the lows are weird lows that I hadn’t experienced before because it’s foreign territory. The lows don’t feel like regular emotions. The whole Earth feels different.”

“There is nothing that really prepares you for the weird intricacies of celebrity,” he continued. “It feels completely foreign.”

He talked about meeting thousands of people, shaking endless hands, fans throwing themselves at him. “It’s sweet, but it changes how you just walk down the street.” The other day, he told me, he went out for what should have been a five-minute walk and was stopped about twelve times. So many new people but so few chances for true, organic connection.

“But now I feel like I know the muscle that can engage with all these different things is growing and getting better,” he said.

The hype he has brought to Yaga has been palpable. After Williams was announced as a cast member, orders came in from around the world for copies of Yaga , the play . This season in Toronto, the Tarragon Theatre will revive Yaga for its 50th-anniversary season.

“It’s really cool that theatre begets television, that begets more theatre,” said Sandler, who from the beginning has approached her stage productions with a television model. “Let’s make theatre for people who don’t like theatre, who really love HBO.”

Sandler’s enthusiasm is infectious. On set, in a ball cap that says “Bad” and later during an interview in a “Diet Coke” ball cap, she exudes excitement about her play moving to TV, her first foray as showrunner and her top-flight cast.

“I lost my mind when Carrie-Anne said yes. You don’t get people like this to do first-time shows,” said Sandler, rhyming off the show’s “Avengers-level” team of Canadian talent, also including Reid, Backo, Sheila McCarthy and Megan Follows.

And while much of the early buzz about the series focused on its male breakout star, this is very much a female-centric story and a show powered by women: Sandler as showrunner, her friend and creative partner Mackenzie Donaldson as producer, and Moss as star and an executive producer. Half of the episodes, including episode five, are directed by Rachel Talalay.

The story is based on a folkloric witch figure, Baba Yaga, whom Sandler calls “the original bad girl of Eastern-European folklore.” If TV audiences could accept Dexter, Walter White and Tony Soprano, why couldn’t they also fall for a complicated female anti-hero?

“It’s rage and it’s sexy and it’s witchy and it’s mysterious, but it’s fun,” Sandler said of the show, which imagines Baba Yaga as a woman living in contemporary times.

Reid, who, like Williams, became famous playing a gay Canadian – Patrick on Schitt’s Creek – said during an interview on set that day that the show has contemporary relevance. “This kind of repurposing of the myth of Baba Yaga and how she might be useful in today’s society and the sneaky ways that men try to get away with things.”

It had been just over a month since the shocking death of his Schitt’s Creek co-star Catherine O’Hara, and I asked him what he learned working from her that he was able to bring to his other projects, including this one.

“I think about her process all the time,” he told me, after shooting a driving scene with Backo. “I don’t think it’s something that you could replicate, because she was such a pure source of creative energy.”

Reid and the others I spoke to about Williams were excited about the buzz he was bringing to the show, but quick to point out how deserving he is; that he’s a great actor – and a great guy.

“He is just a really lovely human,” said Sandler. “There’s the Hudson thing, but then there’s a really smart actor who just wants to really work.”

Williams, who plays two characters in the series, more than holds his own up against the veteran Moss (and her desk). At the same time, co-starring with her is a personal thrill, he said during the interview. His parents introduced him to The Matrix when he was very young, and he has often been told that Keanu Reeves is his celebrity look-alike.

“She’s just the best person to work with. No B.S., no sort of prima donna nature whatsoever. Just wants to get in there and do the work.”

And no, he was not intimidated by the onscreen intimacy. “Even Heated Rivalry didn’t scare me.”

On set that day, there was much discussion about their scene: the choreography leading up to the kiss, the way certain words should be said, the desire for maximum steam. Williams and Moss pulled apart and high-fived after takes.

At one point, Williams drifted over to the spot known as video village, where the monitors were set up, and talked to creatives and other crew about horror movies and psychological thrillers. He is a huge film buff, “a film and TV nerd” with “a gajillion references” who has seen everything and can impersonate anyone, as Backo describes him.

Now, the encyclopedic cinephile has suddenly found himself part of the world he has studied so ardently as a fan. Given Yaga ’s subject matter, the video village discussion that morning included Black Swan , Halloween , The Texas Chain Saw Massacre and The Ring . Someone mentioned also Scream and Drew Barrymore.

“I just met her,” Williams said – not a boast; more of a ‘can you believe it?’ He was just one of the gang, even if the odd joke was made about his fandom, which someone jokingly called the Hudson Brigade.

Given his sudden superstar status, Williams could have chosen anything for his next project. He said yes to Yaga , to Sandler, to Canada.

“Well, the patriotic person in me kind of said … I’m not going to run to the States. I want to double down and go Canada, back to back, and show that we are making great content,” he said, adding that it was also nice to be shooting a half-hour helicopter ride from Vancouver, where he lives.

“To see that Canada is really taking big swings, I wanted to sort of honour that.”

stories.title: Montreal man fights charges after rescuing baby raccoon ‘Pepper’ that bonded to him
stories.summary: Montreal's Louka Berman found the seven-month-old raccoon, which he named Pepper, injured by a crossbow bolt at a construction site in May and nursed the baby back to health.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Phil Carpenter
stories.content:
A Montreal man who rescued an injured raccoon and nursed it back to health says he is now fighting charges and trying to prevent wildlife authorities from taking the animal.

Louka Berman found the seven-month-old raccoon, which he named Pepper, injured at a construction site in May.

He said the animal and its mother had been shot with a crossbow.

“Someone shot her with a crossbow, and they shot her too. So they thought that they were both dead,” Berman said.

Berman nursed Pepper back to health with the intention of eventually returning her to the wild, but the baby raccoon has other ideas.

Attempts to release the raccoon have been unsuccessful, he said, because Pepper will stay in the wooded area where he leaves her and wait for him to return.

“She’s attached to me,” Berman said with a laugh. “And I’m attached to her too.”

After videos of Berman and Pepper went viral, Quebec’s Environment Ministry came looking for the raccoon, accusing him of keeping the animal in his home.

Authorities did not find Pepper.

In Quebec, a permit is required to possess a raccoon at home. Berman insists he is not keeping Pepper at his residence and says he has instead been hiding her in parks.

“For the past week and still the next week they can just come at anytime to grab her,” he said.

Berman said he fears wildlife authorities May euthanize Pepper.

He also said he is facing an obstruction charge, in addition to a ticket authorities wanted to issue over allegations that he was keeping the raccoon at home.

Berman plans to go to court to fight the charges.

Sophie Gaillard, with the Montreal Spca’s animal advocacy and legal and government affairs team, said the circumstances raise questions about whether Berman is legally in possession of the animal.

“It’s unclear in this situation whether he is actually in possession of the raccoon or not — so it’s a bit of a blurry line,” Gaillard said.

Pepper’s apparent difficulty in returning to the wild could be an indication that the young raccoon has become habituated to people.

“It sounds like a situation where this animal would need to be rehomed in a wildlife sanctuary,” Gaillard said.

She said the case also points to a broader shortage of facilities able to care for injured wildlife in Quebec. Even the Spca does not have the means to care for such animals and cannot always find another organization able to take them in.

“Every year, we experience this issue where we have animals that, unfortunately, we have to euthanize because we can’t find a facility to take them in,” Gaillard said.

An online fundraiser has now been launched in Pepper’s name to help fund a wildlife sanctuary.

For now, Berman and Pepper’s supporters are hoping a home can be found for the raccoon that would allow her to be saved.

“Every year, we experience this issue where we have animals that, unfortunately, we have to euthanize because we can’t find a facility to take them in,” Gaillard said.

stories.title: Crea downgrades home sales forecast for the third time this year
stories.summary: The Canadian Real Estate Association has downgraded its forecast for home sales activity in 2026 for the third straight quarter.
stories.author: Sammy Hudes The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Canadian Real Estate Association has downgraded its forecast for home sales activity in 2026 for the third straight quarter.

Crea now expects a total of 444,530 homes to be sold by the end of this year, representing a 5.2 per cent decrease from 2025.

That’s down from its July forecast of a 1.4 per cent year-over-year decline, which marked a reversal from its April forecast of a one per cent gain. The association had predicted 5.1 per cent growth year-over-year in January.

Crea also projects the national average home price to tick 0.2 per cent higher on an annual basis to $681,681 this year, which is around $5,000 lower than predicted in the summer.

The association said its revised forecast comes amid a “roller-coaster year,” with the global energy crisis fuelling inflation risks and affecting borrowing costs.

It cited higher fixed mortgage rates and ongoing uncertainty around variable rates, adding that the Bank of Canada has adopted “a notably more hawkish tone.” Those factors hurt September’s residential real estate activity, Crea said.

National home sales were down 7.7 per cent compared with the same month last year, while activity also fell 2.3 per cent from August.

“After a four-month run of modestly positive progress on demand, supply, and prices, many of Canada’s housing markets took a step back in September,” said Crea senior economist Shaun Cathcart in a news release.

“This was hardly surprising given the latest jump in fixed mortgage rates, and with the Bank of Canada now widely expected to follow with a rate hike before the end of the year.”

Worries about higher borrowing costs on the horizon led to a “significantly” shorter fall market compared to usual expectations for the season, said Marco Pedri, a broker with Shoreline Realty.

He said many of those considering a home purchase already made their move in the summer or first few weeks of fall “in an effort to lock in a favourable interest rate.”

That’s left remaining sellers in limbo, and they’ll likely have to wait until next year before demand picks up again.

“It’s honestly a game of chicken. It’s about who’s going to cave first,” Pedri said.

“I think lot of purchasers ... are going to try and see what best deal they can get come January, February, March, when these sellers who have had their property on the record for so long May be at a point to just say, ‘Hey, listen, at this point, I just want to sell.’”

In September, the national average sale price fell 1.6 per cent compared with the same month a year earlier to $666,538.

Crea’s own home price index, which aims to represent the sale of typical homes, edged 0.4 per cent lower from August to September, while the index dropped 3.4 per cent on a year-over-year basis.

The number of newly listed properties decreased 1.8 per cent month-over-month. Slightly more than 200,000 properties were listed for sale by the end of the month, up 1.8 per cent from a year earlier.

“While the Canada/U.S. trade war has recently escalated, and inflation concerns likely remain top-of-mind for Canadians, the rise in borrowing costs was probably the prime force behind September’s monthly decline in home sales and average prices,” said TD economist Rishi Sondhi in a note.

“Looking to 2027, we look for weak price growth across most regions next year, with loose supply/demand balances providing an additional drag on prices in B.C. and Ontario.”

Crea said it now forecasts national home sales in 2027 to improve by 4.4 per cent to 464,235. The prediction bakes in slow but positive economic growth, the resumption of higher population growth, and more certainty for borrowers around the path for interest rates.

Crea said the latter should bring more pent-up demand into the market even with higher borrowing costs.

The national average home price is expected to rise 1.2 per cent from 2026 to $689,909 next year.

With housing affordability already stretched, Cathcart said “the big question going forward is how much farther will the (Bank of Canada) have to go to keep a lid on inflation next year?”

“Until that becomes clearer, this fresh round of uncertainty will likely send some buyers back to the sidelines,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

stories.title: Stelco owner Cleveland-Cliffs is playing a classic game of chicken with Ottawa
stories.summary: The Ohio company’s CEO is confusing Canadian collaboration with capitulation
stories.author: Rita Trichur
stories.content:
Cleveland-Cliffs Inc., the American owner of Stelco Inc., is locked in a blustery battle of wills with Ottawa over Canadian job cuts.

The Ohio-based steelmaker, which is waging Washington’s trade war by proxy, is goading Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government to take it to court for violating labour commitments tied to its takeover of Stelco two years ago.

Canadian officials, too, are refusing to back down, floating possible legal action that could result in financial penalties and the forced divestiture of Stelco. But in characteristic Canadian fashion, they have also consistently conveyed a willingness to resolve the conflict in conjunction with the company. You know, the old-fashioned way, by talking face to face.

“Everything is on the table and so therefore, I’m always open to sit down with the company and find a solution, but we’re looking at everything that is possible to keep jobs in Canada,” Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said at The Globe and Mail’s defence summit in Ottawa on Wednesday.

Cleveland-Cliffs’s chairman and chief executive Lourenco Goncalves, who takes credit for influencing Washington’s steel and aluminum tariffs , is confusing classic Canadian collaboration with capitulation, much like his political paladin, U.S. President Donald Trump , did in August. Canadians, though, are in no mood for more American monkeyshines – and Mr. Carney and his cabinet know it.

At stake in this dispute are up to 500 jobs in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., meaning the Stelco layoffs strike at the heart of the province’s manufacturing heartland.

Although Stelco is long past its heyday, its fate is still of strategic importance to Canadians. As Mr. Carney points out, domestic steelmaking is key to Canada’s national security because it is used to make defence products and critical energy infrastructure.

Ms. Joly is insistent that Cleveland-Cliffs made legally binding employment guarantees in exchange for Ottawa’s approval of its $3.4-billion acquisition of Stelco in 2024. Mr. Carney has appropriately called it a betrayal.

Indeed, a government statement from that time makes clear the company promised to “continue to employ at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees” for five years.

But in recent days, Cleveland-Cliffs has denied violating its commitments, contending its undertakings did not include a vow to avoid layoffs at Stelco.

Its executives have engaged in other mental gymnastics by brazenly arguing that its promise to maintain job levels does not apply to every single day of the five years covered by its undertakings with Ottawa. Huh?

They are also claiming the company would call back laid-off Canadian workers once Ottawa reaches a “Fortress America” trade pact with the U.S. – another sign that Mr. Goncalves is carrying water for Washington.

Cleveland-Cliffs announced the Canadian layoffs on Sept. 28, purporting it couldn’t compete in the galvanized steel market because of the trade war with the United States.

Yes, the very trade war that its top executive, Mr. Goncalves, encouraged in the first place, ostensibly because of “trade distortions enabled by foreign countries,” as he said on an investor call in February, 2025, according to a transcript from S&P Global Market Intelligence. Of course, market disruptions caused by the U.S. are acceptable.

“These tariffs are critical to addressing the problem, and we thank the Trump administration to have the courage to implement these tariffs,” he said on the same conference call.

Mr. Goncalves has since clarified that those comments shouldn’t be interpreted as an attack on Canada because he was merely expressing support for Mr. Trump’s policies.

That still doesn’t explain why the company failed to apply for provincial tariff relief if Canadian jobs were at risk.

In a previous interview with The Globe, Mr. Goncalves also mocked an aggrieved Canadian steel customer as a “ walking eagle ” – a euphemism for a bird grounded by the weight of its own excrement.

It’s all a bit rich.

Cleveland-Cliffs telegraphed the potential for broken promises in its 10-K annual report filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Feb. 9, stating that it faces “ongoing risks arising out of the Stelco acquisition.” Those uncertainties, it said, include “our ability to satisfy our operational, employment, environmental, charitable or other undertakings made to the Canadian government.”

In late July, the company signalled again that Canadian jobs could be in jeopardy. “We continue to defend our point of view with the Canadian government officials, asking them to do what is right to protect the steel industry in Canada, just as our American government has done here in the United States,” Mr. Goncalves said on the company’s second-quarter earnings call.

Are Canadians really to believe that Cleveland-Cliffs is a hapless victim of U.S. tariffs?

At least the shenanigans that U.S. Steel Corp. pulled with Stelco years ago were ordinary corporate fecklessness. Cleveland-Cliffs, ON the other hand, is choosing to cheerlead Mr. Trump’s churlish trade war.

stories.title: Researchers find jump in U.S. influence campaigns targeting Alberta referendum as vote looms
stories.summary: Prominent American influencers, podcasts and websites are pushing narratives about the inevitability of Alberta-U.S. integration
stories.author: Grant Robertson
stories.content:
Researchers tracking how online influence campaigns are targeting Monday’s referendum in Alberta have noticed an increase in activity from the United States in the final weeks before the vote.

Online narratives pushing the idea that Alberta has no choice but to sever ties and join the U.S. have become the dominant message being pushed into Canada by American sources, according to the Centre for Artificial Intelligence, Data, and Conflict at the University of Regina.

Since the project began in July, about 80 per cent of suspected foreign influence activity targeting the Alberta referendum – roughly 40,000 items a month – has been linked to Russian bots and content farms, which churn out memes, social-media messages and videos aimed at promoting pro-separatist messages in Canada.

The remaining 20 per cent has been linked to U.S. sources, including influential podcasters, right-wing political pundits and social media influencers.

That ratio remained mostly unchanged until late September, when the U.S. share rose to 24 per cent, and the portion attributed to Russian sources dropped to 76 per cent.

Brian McQuinn, co-director of the centre, said the relatively small jump was significant, indicating the U.S. sources became more active as the referendum approached.

At a time when Ottawa and Washington are embroiled in a trade war , prominent American politicians and members of the U.S. administration have openly mused about Alberta becoming the 51 st state, noting its rich oil resources. That message is being amplified among Maga voices online.

“This stuff is very opportunistic. So they will find whatever is most controversial and pour energy into that,” Dr. McQuinn said.

The latest data follows a Globe and Mail investigation this month that found Republican political operatives from the U.S. travelled to Alberta this year attempting to help the separatists sway the outcome of the referendum.

The online-influence research is being conducted through Cipher AI, a technology developed by Dr. McQuinn and others in a partnership between the University of Regina and University of Alberta. The project is also producing analysis for federal and provincial governments.

Cipher was originally created to monitor attempts by Russian websites and social media accounts to spread disinformation about the invasion of Ukraine. But early this year, the researchers noticed groups were also targeting Alberta.

The analysis tracks U.S. and Russian activity, including Russian content farms that push pro-separatist content into online communities in Canada, and use Canadians to “launder” those messages by sharing such material on their social media feeds, the researchers said.

Much of the Russian content is covert, and can be traced to a pro-Kremlin content farm known as Pravda Network, the researchers found, which has been known by Western governments to target political debates and stoke discord by spreading false or misleading content.

The U.S. activity is more overt, with prominent American influencers, podcasts and websites conspicuously promoting Alberta separation on a variety of platforms including YouTube, Reddit and Rumble.

In August, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith acknowledged the province’s referendum was being targeted by foreign influence campaigns.

“What we’re seeing right now is that there’s nothing out there that has elevated to a level of criminal involvement in our process, but we are seeing influence campaigns,” the Premier said during an interview on Omni Television in Alberta. She said it “is something that does leave us concerned.”

Amid such concerns, U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra has levelled similar accusations at Canada.

He told a podcast this week that the U.S. is “closely watching Canadian activities” for interference ahead of November’s U.S. midterm elections.

He said comments by Canadian politicians about targeting tariffs at certain states and an Ontario government advertisement critical of President Donald Trump’s tariffs that played on American television have raised concerns for the U.S. administration.

“It appears that some of this – from our perspective, in the way we view our elections – could be inferred to be election interference,” Mr. Hoekstra said on The Really Big Show podcast.

“We appreciate foreign-policy leaders coming into the United States and those types of things, but you know, keep your nose out of American politics,” Mr. Hoekstra said.

In Alberta, sovereignty has never achieved sustained support above 30-per-cent support in polling. However, separatist leaders have called on the province to send a message to Ottawa by voting in favour of seeking a formal process for independence.

Dr. McQuinn said the narratives targeting Alberta from Russian and U.S.-linked sources have started to mirror each other in the final days before the referendum.

Previously, Russian-linked sources appeared to focus on the notion that Alberta was being unjustly punished by Ottawa, while U.S.-driven narratives more broadly singled out Canada as a failed state.

The predominant theme now being pushed online by both involves the inevitability of Alberta-U.S. integration, Dr. McQuinn said.

Such themes were identified in 37 per cent of all monitored items, the report said.

Dr. McQuinn said the researchers expect to see narratives pushing the idea that the vote can’t be trusted after next week.

Marcus Kolga, co-author of the research and director of DisinfoWatch, which tracks influence campaigns, said there is no easy fix to Canada being targeted.

“It’s sort of like a chronic condition that you have to manage. There’s no silver bullet to stop it,” Mr. Kolga said.

“We need to be calling out these sorts of operations when we see them,” Mr. Kolga said. “If we do, our democracy will be far more resilient against these sorts of efforts.”

stories.title: In Oak Bay’s debate over density, voters get two elections to speak their minds
stories.summary: Legislation to build more multiplexes weighs heavily on voters behind Greater Victoria’s ‘Tweed Curtain’
stories.author: Gary Mason, Photography by Chad Hipolito
stories.content:
About this series

The Globe is reporting from cities and towns in Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia to hear from residents about the issues affecting their communities and their votes in the municipal elections. Explore the entire series here .

You don’t need to cruise far along Beach Drive to be enthralled by what you see.

Garry oaks, with their glorious, gnarled branches, beseech you to stop and marvel. The waters of the Juan de Fuca and Haro Straits shimmer in the near distance. Turn a corner and you gaze enviously at golfers approaching greens hugging the shoreline at the very photogenic (and very private) Victoria Golf Club. Continue a bit further and you’ll pass large Tudor-style homes and mansions of grey stone hiding behind ivy-covered castle-like walls.

Those who live to the east of Foul Bay Road, and to certain points north and south, call the municipality of Oak Bay home. Downtown Victoria exists four kilometres to the west.

Once upon a time, the road dividing the two communities was known as The Tweed Curtain , a cheeky reference to the haughty, affluent suburb that existed beyond its imaginary flannel border – one that promoted a strong British heritage with its tea rooms and private schools. While times changed elsewhere over the years, Oak Bay was happy to maintain (and closely guard) the status quo. And then Bill 44 came along.

In the fall of 2023, David Eby’s NDP government passed a law permitting small-scale multiunit housing – think laneway houses, secondary suites, multiplexes – on lots previously restricted to single-family or duplex homes. The government also imposed new housing quotas along with it.

The NDP has defended the legislation as a means of tackling the province’s affordable housing crisis. Various forecasts have shown that there is a severe housing shortage in B.C., especially “missing middle” homes that offer more space for young families than many high-rise condos do.

Feedback on the NDP’s density initiative has been mixed. In many jurisdictions, multiplex buildings that have gone up on corner lots or on big pieces of property, and whose character and style have not clashed with existing homes, have been applauded. But there have also been instances where big, ugly four, five and sixplexes have been erected in the middle of city blocks, on small pieces of property, dwarfing smaller, older homes beside them.

Similar complaints have been registered in cities across the country where multiplexes have been proposed to address housing challenges.

Not surprisingly, housing has become a central focus of the current municipal elections in B.C. that happen Saturday and which overlap with a general election that will take place a week later.

The stakes for Oak Bay, an aging community that prides itself on the stately, pristine appearance of many of its neighbourhoods, couldn’t be higher. For many, Bill 44 threatens to undermine the value of the single most important investment they have – their home.

Oak Bay residents will choose their next mayor, six councillors and an area school trustee on Oct. 17. They’ll be back at the polls a week later for the B.C. provincial election.

A son of Oak Bay, Brian Smith became the town’s mayor from 1974 to 1979, a position that launched him into provincial politics and eventually a role as B.C.’s attorney-general under the Social Credit government of the day. As a politician, he was the perfect embodiment of Oak Bay’s upper-crust repute with his crisp Oxford shirts, blue blazers and grey flannel pants. Today, at 92, Mr. Smith remains as informed and as combative as ever, especially when it comes to Bill 44.

“Oak Bay certainly has had a reputation as being anti-development,” he said, sitting in the living room of his Rockland townhome. “But I don’t think that’s the case any more. People accept we need new forms of housing, but they don’t want it jammed down their throats the way the NDP is doing.”

Because of the continuing provincial election, B.C.’s housing ministry said it could not comment on criticisms of Bill 44.

Mr. Smith says some large multiplexes that have been erected have, in some cases, rendered older, existing smaller homes beside them “stranded assets.”

“[The government] says this is all about creating affordable housing,” Mr. Smith continued. “Well, I can tell you right now they won’t be building affordable housing in Oak Bay. Land values are too high. They’re building multiplexes in which the homes can cost more than $2-million. That’s not affordable for a lot of people. Hardly.

“Let’s get off this socialist guilt trip the NDP is trying to put us on – share the pain and all that crap.”

The man who has had responsibility for navigating the real-world effects of the new housing law is nursing a coffee at Ottavio’s in the heart of Oak Bay village. Kevin Murdoch is running for re-election as the town’s mayor after eight years in office.

Mr. Murdoch is all for new forms of housing – in fact, he ran successfully on that very policy in 2018. He’d like to see the community grow. The population currently is about 18,000 and has been roughly that for decades. Mr. Murdoch believes most of his constituents support new housing but not just any housing and not just anywhere.

He prefers to see new multiplex infills go up on corner lots, for instance, where they are less jarring than in the middle of a block. The city has imposed some restrictions that prevent new builds from encroaching on neighbouring properties, although it hasn’t worked perfectly.

The fact is, much of the residential heritage-style architecture in Oak Bay is distinct and charming. Many homes were built decades ago in the Tudor Revival design, with steep gabled roofs and prominent brick chimneys. Some are West Coast contemporary. Others boast deep, Arts and Craft-style overhangs. Plopping an unsightly multiplex monstrosity into that mix is fraught.

Obviously, the provincial government’s strong-arm approach to housing quotas has not gone over well. “We’re seeing a lot of pushback on housing that didn’t exist before,” said the 56-year-old Mr. Murdoch, driving through the streets of his community to show The Globe and Mail where he thinks new multiplex units have worked and where they haven’t.

“They [the province] have made housing a lot more political than it used to be.”

Under Bill 44, introduced in the fall of 2023, Oak Bay is required to build (and have occupied) 664 new housing units by Sept. 30, 2028. At the end of 2024, Oak Bay had completed just 16 new units of its government-imposed quota of 56 for that year. In 2025, the target was 138 new units, Oak Bay built 36 – or 26 per cent. As of June of this year, the community has completed-to-occupancy 73 net new units.

If you don’t think that’s much, consider that between 2019 and 2022, Oak Bay averaged two net new homes a year.

Mayoral opponent Sam Holland said Oak Bay’s housing issues extend beyond new multiplex units going up. There are people living in big homes that have skyrocketed in value, which come with having to pay some of the highest municipal taxes in the province – $10,000 a year for the average household, according to the city. But many are living on small, fixed incomes.

“This has been a problem for years,” Mr. Holland said in an interview. “These people desperately need different types of housing they can downsize to. The city has been late to address this for years. Council has been reactive to their plight instead of proactive.”

Christopher Causton was mayor of Oak Bay from 1997 to 2011. He backs up what Mr. Holland says about the tough financial straits older people in Oak Bay are in. “I call it genteel poverty,” Mr. Causton said in a phone call.

According to the 2021 census, nearly 68 per cent of the community’s population is 65 or older.

Mr. Causton said another recent housing-related move the NDP made that has hurt seniors in the community was changes to the program allowing those 55 and over to defer their property taxes until they sell their home. Previously, people taking advantage of the program paid an interest rate of prime minus 2 per cent. Now, it’s been changed to prime plus 2 per cent, a move the government made to discourage those taking advantage of the program, not out of need but greed.

“There are many seniors in Oak Bay who are furious about this,” Mr. Causton said. “They feel helpless. They see a provincial government using a sledgehammer to hit municipalities with Bill 44 and are now hitting people, many cash poor, with changes to the tax-deferment program.

“These are huge issues in both the municipal election and the provincial election, and I mean huge.”

Kevin Murdoch, meantime, has learned a thing or two in his time as mayor but none greater than the importance that the home holds for people.

“I’ve seen grown people cry at meetings over some issue related to their home in which they feel threatened in some way,” said the mayor. “You realize how important their home is. It’s everything. It’s their single biggest investment so anything that compromises that is serious stuff.”

Those who live to the east of Foul Bay Road, and to certain points north and south, call the municipality of Oak Bay home. Downtown Victoria exists four kilometres to the west.

stories.title: Accused accomplice in Tumbler Ridge shooting appears in court
stories.summary: The Washington resident is charged with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country
stories.author: The Decibel Staff, Menaka Raman-Wilms, Jesse Winter
stories.content:
This past week, a judge in Washington state heard arguments around whether a woman accused of conspiring with the Tumbler Ridge shooter should be released before her tria l. James Cody Bryant – who identifies as a woman and uses she/her pronouns – was arrested by U.S. authorities at the beginning of the month.

Jesse Winter is a reporter and photographer with The Globe. He went to report on Ms. Bryant’s pretrial hearing in person. He explains the specific allegations against her, what the judge ruled regarding whether to keep her in custody and gives an update on the other legal proceedings surrounding the fallout from one of Canada’s worst mass shootings.

stories.title: Former Csis chief warns that China 'will acquire' all information about you in Chinese EVs
stories.summary: The country's former spy chief warned that everything you do in or around one of those cars will be acquired by China.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — As Chinese electric vehicle manufacturers boost exports to Canada, the country’s former spy chief warned that everything you do in or around one of those cars will be acquired by China.

In a rare interview with the BBC last month, former Csis head David Vigneault did not mince his words: China’s theft of Western intellectual property amounts to a “lost generation of prosperity” for Canada. Furthermore, the Chinese government will use Chinese electric vehicles to further harvest data on Canadians and foreigners.

“Not to overhype it, but there is the reality that all of your data, what you say, where you go, with whom you are, who you associate with, everything you do around your car, will be acquired by China,” Vigneault said if had concerns about Chinese electric vehicles.

“It is not a question for me, it is a reality,” added Vigneault, who headed Csis from 2017 to 2024.

Vigneault is not the first current or former Five Eyes intelligence chief to express concerns about Chinese-made electric vehicles. But he is the most high-profile recent Canadian intelligence official to plainly state grave concerns about how the People’s Republic of China (PRC) will use them as intelligence-collecting devices.

The Chinese government has consistently denied any claims that its domestic companies can be used as information-gathering platforms.

Vigneault’s comments come as Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government works to attract joint-venture Chinese EV manufacturing to Canada in a bid to replace fleeing U.S. automakers.

Earlier this year, Carney travelled to China where he announced wide-ranging new deals with PRC President Xi Jinping to boost trade between both countries, including dropping Canadian tariffs to the lowest level for nearly 50,000 Chinese EVs annually.

“To make Canada a leader in electric vehicle manufacturing, we’re working to attract significant new joint-venture Chinese investments,” Carney said in a statement at the time.

Last week, Chinese EV manufacturer Geely Auto — which also owns brands Lynk & Co and Zeekr — announced it would be introducing its vehicles into the Canadian market for the first time next year.

When asked about concerns linked to Chinese tech and espionage, the prime minister has repeatedly said he is entering “eyes wide open” into the new strategic partnership with China.

During the podcast, Vigneault said he understands that Canada “absolutely needs” to do business with the Asian economic behemoth. But “eyes wide open” isn’t quite enough.

“You need to have more than your eyes wide open; you need to also make sure that you’re protecting your wallet in your back pocket,” said the current chief intelligence officer at Strider.

That’s because China’s longtime efforts to steal intellectual property from Western governments, companies and research facilities has cost tens of billions to Canada and its allies, Vigneault told BBC.

Csis and other Canadian intelligence agencies have also warned of increased Chinese efforts to steal Canadian IP, such as vaccine research during the COVID-19 pandemic or information that could be militarized by the Prc’s military.

In the interview, Vigneault suggested most people don’t fully comprehend the scope, value and impact of the Prc’s IP theft.

“The amount… of intellectual property that has been taken away from the West, from Great Britain, from Canada, the U.S. is essentially a lost generation of prosperity,” he said. “It’s not the amount of job losses in our society now, but also in the future.”

“Any new information innovation technology that comes into China is looked through the prism of, ‘Can we industrialize it to make to create jobs and opportunities’, but also, is there a way to weaponize it to essentially give new capabilities to the People’s Liberation Army.”

Vigneault also expressed his concern about the rise of antisemitism across the world, noting that some anti-Jewish terrorists in Canada are radicalized by ignorance.

“With Israel, you can absolutely disagree with policies. Unfortunately, I’ve seen some of the more extreme groups recuperate some of the legitimate angst against those policies and turn that into anti-semitism,” he explained.

“I’ve seen that in terrorist attacks in my country, in Canada, where people who honestly have no idea what they’re talking about, but the radicalization online essentially brings them… to become anti-semite.”

stories.title: Experts say Indigenous communities deserve say John Risley's art collection sale
stories.summary: ST. John's - Indigenous communities should have a say in what happens to cultural objects linked to a debt-laden investment company in Atlantic Canada that is trying to appease its creditors, say several experts in repatriation.
stories.author: Sarah Smellie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - Indigenous communities should have a say in what happens to cultural objects linked to a debt-laden investment company in Atlantic Canada that is trying to appease its creditors, say several experts in repatriation.

A cache of about 30 items described as Indigenous “cultural objects” are among a list of nearly 670 artworks, antiques and other artifacts identified through recent court proceedings involving seafood tycoon John Risley.

The businessman had asked a Nova Scotia court to approve the sale of his company’s assets to a private equity firm in New York. His company, Cffi Ventures, was placed under creditor protection in March after it collapsed under nearly US$1 billion in debt.

The cultural items include baskets, bone carvings, textiles and moccasins. Some are attributed to an Indigenous group — Inuit, Mi’kmaq, Cree — with no known date or artist. Some are simply labelled “Indigenous.” Other items, labelled as textiles or sculptures, have vague labels such as “unidentified artist, Inuit.”

“My mind, immediately, is less about the items themselves, but more about the overarching question of when do and when should Indigenous nations have the right to engage in this process,” said Cody Groat, an assistant professor of History and Indigenous Studies at Western University and Kanyen’kehaka citizen of Six Nations of the Grand River in Ontario.

“The most ethical situation, is seeing these cultural items return to the nations that they belong to,” Groat said in an interview.

Risley said he agrees with the principle of repatriation, but he said those efforts are typically focused on Indigenous items acquired before their cultural significance was understood.

“Our collection would not include any such pieces,” he said recently via text message.

“We would have bought from dealers and auction houses whose inventory would have been subject to a great deal of public scrutiny. As a result, it is highly likely any culturally important items would have been identified well in advance.”

The Canadian Museum Association’s Indigenous Council said dealers, collectors and institutions are generally not equipped to recognize which objects might be culturally significant to Indigenous communities.

Unless records show the item’s community of origin had a free and fair say in its fate, there is a risk its significance was not understood, the council said in an emailed statement.

In a followup text message on Friday, Risley said he agreed that Indigenous people should have a hand in determining what May be significant to them.

He suggested this could start by having art dealers identify major collectors and collections of Indigenous art. Subsequently, he suggested that a trusted third party could begin documenting those objects.

Risley is one of Atlantic Canada’s best-known businessmen, having co-founded Clearwater Seafoods in 1976. The company sold for $1 billion in 2021.

Last month, a Nova Scotia court approved the sale of most of Cffi’s assets to New Tide Capital, an affiliate of New York-based alternative investment firm HPS Investment Partners LLC, which held the majority of Cffi’s debt.

A collection of more than 1,200 artworks and antiques valued at about $8.1 million were part of the assets on sale. The art includes more than 95 paintings by Nova Scotia folk artist Maude Lewis, as well as works by members of the Group of Seven and renowned Inuit artists Jessie Oonark and Irene Avaalaaqiaq Tiktaalaaq.

Details of 669 items in the collection were released during the court process because their ownership was in dispute: Risley said he owned them, not Cffi. A New Tide lawyer told the court it would negotiate an out-of-court deal with Risley about the disputed works.

Neither New Tide nor HPS Investment Partners responded to a request for comment.

Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, which represents Inuit in Canada, said works of Inuit cultural importance should be properly examined by Inuit. If the parties involved “wish to demonstrate good will,” the organization would gladly help return any historically significant pieces to Inuit, said a spokesperson in an emailed statement.

Groat said there is a long history of private collectors or auction houses acquiring Indigenous cultural items through missionaries or agents enforcing Canada’s Indian Act, who May have claimed they were working in the best interests of Indigenous people.

Those looking to return these items face a number of complications, he said. Canada has no national framework guiding the return of such objects and it can be hard to know where to start or who to contact, particularly since Indigenous belongings have often been misclassified and mislabelled, he said.

If details of private Indigenous holdings are revealed through bankruptcy, as they were in the case of the Hudson’s Bay Company, Indigenous communities often don’t have the money to get involved with the proceedings to lay claim to the objects, Groat added.

Lauren Wheeler, executive director of the Canadian Museum Association, said the sparse details about Risley’s collection shows how hard it is to know what Indigenous objects May be held in private collections.

Public museums across Canada currently hold more than six million Indigenous belongings in their collections, and the association produced a guide to help these institutions return culturally significant items to the communities where they belong.

Titled “More Than Giving Back,” it says Indigenous cultural objects have been taken in the past during the forced relocation of communities, or through religious, political and financial coercion.

Items taken under these conditions must be returned and museums must share information about their collections with Indigenous communities, the document says.

The same concerns and practices should apply to private collections, Wheeler said in an email.

“This means engaging with Indigenous communities to identify the communities of origin and beginning Indigenous-led processes for return of the belongings,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

Neither New Tide nor HPS Investment Partners responded to a request for comment.

Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, which represents Inuit in Canada, said works of Inuit cultural importance should be properly examined by Inuit. If the parties involved “wish to demonstrate good will,” the organization would gladly help return any historically significant pieces to Inuit, said a spokesperson in an emailed statement.

Groat said there is a long history of private collectors or auction houses acquiring Indigenous cultural items through missionaries or agents enforcing Canada’s Indian Act, who May have claimed they were working in the best interests of Indigenous people.

Those looking to return these items face a number of complications, he said. Canada has no national framework guiding the return of such objects and it can be hard to know where to start or who to contact, particularly since Indigenous belongings have often been misclassified and mislabelled, he said.

If details of private Indigenous holdings are revealed through bankruptcy, as they were in the case of the Hudson’s Bay Company, Indigenous communities often don’t have the money to get involved with the proceedings to lay claim to the objects, Groat added.

Lauren Wheeler, executive director of the Canadian Museum Association, said the sparse details about Risley’s collection shows how hard it is to know what Indigenous objects May be held in private collections.

Public museums across Canada currently hold more than six million Indigenous belongings in their collections, and the association produced a guide to help these institutions return culturally significant items to the communities where they belong.
Titled “More Than Giving Back,” it says Indigenous cultural objects have been taken in the past during the forced relocation of communities, or through religious, political and financial coercion.
Items taken under these conditions must be returned and museums must share information about their collections with Indigenous communities, the document says.
The same concerns and practices should apply to private collections, Wheeler said in an email.
“This means engaging with Indigenous communities to identify the communities of origin and beginning Indigenous-led processes for return of the belongings,” she said.

stories.title: Alberta is to vote on holding a separation referendum. A timeline on how we got here
stories.summary: Edmonton — Albertans vote Monday in a referendum asking whether they want the province to stay in Canada or to have a second, binding referendum on separating from Canada. Strains of Western alienation go back decades.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Edmonton — Albertans vote Monday in a referendum asking whether they want the province to stay in Canada or to have a second, binding referendum on separating from Canada. Strains of Western alienation go back decades.

Here’s a look at some key events:

1980 — The federal government ignites widespread alienation in Alberta with the National Energy Program, which keeps domestic oil prices below world levels to promote Canadian energy security and increase the federal share of oil revenues. Alberta views it as an unjustified attack and a federal money grab. The issue is later settled, but discontent with Ottawa continues.

1982 — Separatism enjoys a brief heyday. Gordon Kesler of the Western Canada Concept Party wins a provincial byelection in central Alberta on a separatist platform. Later that year in the general election, he loses a spot in the legislature. The party receives 12 per cent of the vote but no seats.

2019 — The anti-Ottawa mood ramps up as the United Conservative Party under Jason Kenney wins power in Alberta, capitalizing on discontent over federal rules and policies deemed to impair Alberta’s ability to create wealth, particularly in oil and gas. Premier Kenney fights for more independence from Ottawa but remains a staunch advocate for the province staying in Confederation.

2022-23 — Kenney is replaced by Danielle Smith, who wins government in the 2023 election on a platform of further asserting independence from Ottawa. Unlike Kenney, Premier Smith, while stressing her preference for a “sovereign Alberta within a united Canada,” refuses to characterize separatists as fringe extremists, saying they have valid grievances that deserve to be aired.

April 28, 2025 — Mark Carney and the Liberals defeat the federal Conservatives to win a minority government.

May 5, 2025 — Smith announces a panel to discuss Alberta’s future in Canada. She says her government won’t itself put separation on a ballot but would honour a successful citizen petition seeking such a vote. At the same time, her government takes steps to eventually pass rules to lower thresholds for citizen-led petitions.

June 2025 — Former Alberta Progressive Conservative deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk launches a “Forever Canadian” petition to affirm the province stays in Canada. It eventually collects more than 400,000 names — enough to validate the petition. But by the spring of 2026, the petition is tied up in a legislature committee as Smith questions whether Lukaszuk gathered the names for a referendum or as a trigger for a vote among legislature members.

January 2026 — Mitch Sylvestre of the separatist Alberta Prosperity Project is given the green light by election officials to launch a petition asking whether Alberta should leave Canada. Months later, the petition is deemed successful, having gathered about 223,000 signatures.

Feb. 19, 2026 — Smith announces nine referendum questions about immigration and constitutional concerns will be put to Albertans in an Oct. 19 referendum.

May 13, 2026 — An Alberta Court of King’s Bench judge quashes the separatist petition, ruling Smith’s government didn’t properly consult First Nations as required in the Constitution. Smith later promises to challenge the ruling, and it remains in legal limbo.

May 21, 2026 — Smith announces a 10th referendum question asking whether Alberta should stay in Canada or hold a binding vote on separation. Smith cites the legal uncertainty of the court decision on the separatist petition as the driving force, saying it unduly deprives thousands of Albertans of having a say. Smith later cites Lukaszuk’s petition, too, as a reason. She says both show hundreds of thousands of Albertans want the issue decided.

Sept. 10, 2026 — The Alberta government launches a $4-million advertising campaign for the referendum and urges citizens to vote to stay in Canada. The move comes as polls suggest a broad majority of Albertans want to stay.

Sept. 14, 2026 — Smith’s UCP loses a byelection to the Opposition NDP in their conservative stronghold of Calgary-Shaw. Critics across the political spectrum say the referendum was a factor in punishing Smith’s UCP. Her office says the party lost due to right-centre vote splitting.

Sept. 16, 2026 — Smith’s government publishes a report it commissioned from the University of Calgary to determine what fiscal challenges and benefits an independent Alberta could see. It estimates an initial five-year price tag of $50 billion to $170 billion, noting that figures could swing sharply depending on factors outside Alberta’s control.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney to bring his pro-Canada campaign to Edmonton with referendum just days away
stories.summary: Edmonton - Prime Minister Mark Carney continues his pro-Canada campaign in Alberta as the clock ticks down to a referendum on whether the province should break up with Confederation.
stories.author: The Canadian Press

Edmonton - Prime Minister Mark Carney wrapped up his two-day, pro-Canada barnstorming tour of Alberta by rallying with thousands of supporters in his hometown on Friday night.

“Alberta’s my home,” Carney said as thousands erupted in cheers in a party-like atmosphere at Edmonton’s Expo Centre.

“I grew up here,” said Carney.

“This city, this province, this country, have given me everything — my family, my education and my values.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney wrapped up his two-day, pro-Canada tour of Alberta by rallying with thousands of supporters in his hometown on Friday night at Edmonton’s Expo Centre. Supporters were dressed in all manner of Maple Leaf gear, and jammed bleachers, danced, waved Canadian flags and cheered a song stipulating Canada will never be the 51st U.S. state. (Oct. 16, 2026)

Supporters were dressed in all manner of Maple Leaf gear. They jammed bleachers, danced, waved Canadian flags and cheered a song stipulating Canada will never be the 51st U.S. state.

The prime minister implored Albertans to vote to keep the province in Canada. “There are some outside our borders who are working to break us so they can own us. Never,” he said.

“A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians.

“Our country and your futures are too precious to play games with.”

There was also dissent. One person shouted at Carney as he talked about Canadians serving in the military. “Please,” said Carney, “(show) some respect for our men and women in service.”

Carney has been meeting with Canadians for two days in Edmonton, Red Deer and Calgary, posing for selfies, shaking hands and spreading the message to keep the country whole.

He made a similar rally speech to thousands a day earlier in Calgary.

On Monday, Albertans will vote on whether to stay in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on quitting Confederation.

Earlier Friday, Carney was at a brewery in Red Deer, halfway between Edmonton and Calgary, with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith. The two tapped a keg, had a beer, sang O Canada and made a last-ditch pitch for the province to stay in Confederation.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre and Premier Danielle Smith encourage Albertans to vote to keep the province in Canada. (Oct. 16. 2026)

It was a Maple Leaf love affair. About 50 people squeezed in and jockeyed for position inside Red Hart Brewing. They wore Canada shirts, hats, sweaters, jerseys and pins. There were mayors, members of Parliament and former Alberta premier Ed Stelmach.

Outside, there were another 100 supporters. Across the street, a lone protester with an Alberta flag strode back and forth.

Smith and Carney praised each other as sharp-eyed, flinty negotiators who fight for their positions but want the best for Canada. They said they’re making progress, including with a proposed fast-tracked oil pipeline from Alberta to the B.C. coast.

“For the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada are walking together,” Smith said.

They are, however, agreeing to disagree when it comes to the rest of Smith’s referendum. The leaving-Canada question is one of 10 on the ballot. Smith wants Albertans to endorse nine other proposals.

Those proposals urge her government to take more control and impose new rules surrounding immigration and to pursue constitutional changes that wrest power from Ottawa. Smith has said she needs that mandate to negotiate a better deal with Ottawa.

Carney is urging Albertans to reject the nine proposals. Smith said she’ll work to change his mind.

As the brewery crowd looked on, Smith handed Carney an explanatory booklet on the questions, adding, “I have bad news for you, prime minister, all of the premiers are interested in talking about immigration and how we might be able to reform it.”

Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre also made a last-minute pitch for unity Friday. In a speech in Calgary at the Canada Strong & Free Network, he said he understands separatist disillusionment with the state of affairs in Canada but said quitting isn’t the answer.

“Quitting is the easy way out — and Albertans are not quitters,” Poilievre said.

“We don’t just take our ball and go home. We don’t walk away. We stand and fight for what we believe in, and we reflect upon all that we have.”

He said he gets how people are unhappy with rising costs and what he characterized as a lax justice system, an out-of-control immigration program and federal policies that curtail resource development. But he urged Albertans to see the bigger picture.

“Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”

Polls have suggested a strong majority of Albertans will vote to stay in Canada, but leaders stress that voter apathy could open the door to a winning vote for separation.

Albertans have been voting by mail and, for the past few days, at advance polls in numbers that suggest the final count could set a record. Elections Alberta said over one million had voted as of Thursday night.

Smith called the referendum earlier this year. She said bubbling discontent with past federal policies recently reached a boiling point with hundreds of thousands signing petitions for and against staying in Confederation. She said a referendum is needed to resolve the issue once and for all.

Critics, however, say Smith isn’t resolving a broad-based existential debate. Instead, they say, she has inflamed and validated latent fringe separatist sentiment, rolling the dice on the future of the country to appease hardliners in her United Conservative Party.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

— with files from Dayne Patterson in Calgary and Catherine Morrison in Ottawa

Note to readers: This is a corrected story. A previous version stated advance polls began last week. In fact, they began Tuesday.

stories.summary: Edmonton — Prime Minister Mark Carney continues his pro-Canada campaign in Alberta today as the clock ticks down to a referendum on whether the province should break up with Confederation.

As the brewery crowd looked on, Smith handed Carney an explanatory booklet on the questions, adding, “I have bad news for you, prime minister, all of the premiers are interested in talking about immigration and how we might be able to reform it.”

Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre also made a last-minute pitch for unity Friday. In a speech in Calgary at the Canada Strong & Free Network, he said he understands separatist disillusionment with the state of affairs in Canada but said quitting isn’t the answer.
“Quitting is the easy way out — and Albertans are not quitters,” Poilievre said.
“We don’t just take our ball and go home. We don’t walk away. We stand and fight for what we believe in, and we reflect upon all that we have.”

He said he gets how people are unhappy with rising costs and what he characterized as a lax justice system, an out-of-control immigration program and federal policies that curtail resource development. But he urged Albertans to see the bigger picture.
“Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”
Polls have suggested a strong majority of Albertans will vote to stay in Canada, but leaders stress that voter apathy could open the door to a winning vote for separation.

Albertans have been voting by mail and, for the past few days, at advance polls in numbers that suggest the final count could set a record. Elections Alberta said over one million had voted as of Thursday night.

Smith called the referendum earlier this year. She said bubbling discontent with past federal policies recently reached a boiling point with hundreds of thousands signing petitions for and against staying in Confederation. She said a referendum is needed to resolve the issue once and for all.

Critics, however, say Smith isn’t resolving a broad-based existential debate. Instead, they say, she has inflamed and validated latent fringe separatist sentiment, rolling the dice on the future of the country to appease hardliners in her United Conservative Party.
