stories.title: National Ballet School, divinity college students among those affected by Osap pause
stories.summary: Toronto - A recent pause on financial assistance payments to private post-secondary institutions in Ontario is affecting divinity schools, Canada's National Ballet School and many others, with students feeling unfairly swept up in what they describe as a trawling net-like policy.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A recent pause on financial assistance payments to private post-secondary institutions in Ontario is affecting divinity schools, Canada’s National Ballet School and many others, with students feeling unfairly swept up in what they describe as a trawling net-like policy.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced last week that the province had tasked Kpmg with auditing Ontario Student Assistance Program usage at career colleges, and that preliminary findings were of such concern that he referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police.

While the audit is ongoing, Quinn said, Osap payments to private post-secondary institutions would be paused. Quinn said he is “working on” securing low-interest loans for affected students at financial institutions, but he has not indicated a timeline.

Many career college students have said they are worried about the pause, with no clear end in sight and with some students relying on that financial aid to cover not just tuition but living expenses while they study.

The broad nature of the pause affects all private post-secondary institutions, including private universities, chiropractic and naturopathic medicine colleges, and performing arts schools such as Canada’s National Ballet School.

Alessia Di Palma is in her last year of the ballet school’s five-year joint teacher training program with York University, and said she does not want to have to leave school when she is so close to finishing, but at the moment doesn’t know how she will pay her rent, even though she works two jobs while going to school.

“I’m heartbroken,” she said. “My heart sunk when I found out because it’s unfair that I’ve had this funding for four years and then the fifth year it’s just gone now because of something that didn’t even have anything to do with me.”

Initial concerns stemmed from activity at a few schools, Quinn’s office says, but evidence of “systemic issues” has come up in recent weeks.

“At this time, we do not have assurances from the audit team that the issues are not more widespread, leaving us with no choice but to pause Osap payments to all private institutions to protect taxpayer dollars and hold bad actors accountable,” spokesperson Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement.

“We understand this is creating uncertainty for students and are working quickly to develop options for low-interest, third-party loans facilitated by financial institutions to help students through this period of transition.”

At the ballet school, programs are mostly at the secondary level, but it does have a post-secondary teacher training program that is affected by the Osap pause. About half of those students rely on that aid to pay their tuition, said executive director John Dalrymple.

The government has chosen the bluntest and most harmful way of dealing with the root of the problem, he said, and it is especially disappointing that Quinn enacted the pause before securing those third-party loans.

“The fact that now all of these students who are working multiple jobs to make ends meet, who are at the very beginning of their career, are now left holding the bag to figure out how to finance something that the government had already assured them they qualified for and they were going to receive, I think is unconscionable,” he said.

Theological schools like McMaster Divinity College, affiliated with McMaster University, are also affected by the pause. Ambrose Thomson, the school’s registrar and director of student services, said students are beside themselves.

About 10 per cent of the non-profit institution’s revenue is dependent on Osap-paid tuition, he said. McMaster Divinity College is relatively well-positioned to weather that storm, Ambrose said, but not all schools are so lucky.

“The impression I get is that the government knows full well what the impacts are,” he said.

“They’re not stupid. All I can assume is that at the highest levels where these decisions were made, they’re actually willing to allow career colleges and other schools to shut their doors ... I think they’re trying to look like they’re doing something in the face of 300-whatever million dollars that they were not smart enough to pay attention to.”

Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request showed large increases in Osap usage at a relatively small number of career colleges from 2020-21 to 2024-25.

The seven career colleges that had the highest Osap usage in 2024-25 received $385 million in provincial grants – the same amount that went to students at all of Ontario’s publicly funded colleges that year.

Career Colleges Ontario has raised concerns since 2023 about what it calls potentially “suspicious activity” with Osap usage at a few schools.

Deanna Hutten, a second-year master’s student in McMaster Divinity College’s counselling and spiritual care program, is borrowing money from family and working 10 more hours per week at her marketing job to make up for her Osap being on hold.

The single mother to a one-year-old daughter who hopes to work in hospital chaplaincy said it is frustrating to be lumped in with some suspected bad actors.

“It definitely feels very unfair,” she said.

“They had known about this since 2023 that there were people kind of (allegedly) fudging the system, and now we as private career – not even career colleges, but private institutions – are kind of being swept into that field or that group of people, even though we’re not a part of that.”

At the Toronto Film School, there is also “tremendous uncertainty and anxiety” for many students, said president Andrew Barnsley. He is calling for prompt reinstatement of Osap for eligible students, or at least a clear, expedited timeline to resolve the pause.

“The Osap pause is deeply disappointing, and our greatest concern is the impact on our students who made significant commitments to their education with the reasonable expectation that financial assistance would be available,” he wrote in a statement.

“Many students have rearranged their lives, reduced or left employment, made child-care arrangements and, in some cases, relocated to Toronto in order to pursue their studies. They need to know whether they can meet their financial obligations, including life essentials like rent or food, and continue the programs in which they have already invested time, money and effort.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

stories.title: 'Goodbye to a good friend': Snowbirds' final show to be livestreamed today
stories.summary: Ottawa - Members of the Royal Canadian Air Force Snowbirds aerial aerobatics team are set to perform their final air show Friday in Moose Jaw, Sask., before their decades-old Tutor jets head into retirement.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Members of the Royal Canadian Air Force Snowbirds aerial aerobatics team are set to perform their final air show Friday in Moose Jaw, Sask., before their decades-old Tutor jets head into retirement.

The Rcaf is set to livestream the annual season home closer online at 2 p.m. ET on its Facebook page.

There will still be one more chance to see the CT-114 Tutors in action before they are sent to the airbase in Trenton, Ont., for disposal.

The Snowbirds are scheduled to perform a flyover at the Canadian Football League Grey Cup game in Calgary on Nov. 15.

Capt. Philip Rochon, public affairs officer for the Snowbirds, said it’s a bittersweet time for the pilots who are saying farewell to the planes the team has flown for 55 years.

“It’s like saying goodbye to a good friend,” he said.

Rochon said the Snowbirds received an outpouring of support over the summer from Canadians across the country who shared memories of past shows and their encounters with an iconic “piece of Canadiana.”

“At the same time, we’re looking forward to the future with the new aircraft that was announced,” he said. “That will come online hopefully in the next few years. We’re looking forward to seeing what the next chapter of the Snowbirds will be.”

Defence Minister David McGuinty announced in May that the old Tutors will be replaced eventually by the Swiss-made PC-21 Pilatus aircraft, known as the CT-157 Siskin II.

The Rcaf is also acquiring those same aircraft for pilot training.

While the Snowbirds were formed in 1971, the air force obtained the Tutor jets in 1963.

The Snowbirds will go on a multi-year hiatus until the replacement aircraft are delivered and the team can be trained up on the new planes. That could take until the early 2030s but there’s no set timeline.

The decision to ground the team came after planned upgrades to the Tutors’ engines and escape systems meant to keep them in the air until 2030 encountered a range of problems, including parts obsolescence.

Rcaf Commander Lt.-Gen. Jamie Speiser-Blanchet told reporters at the Aero Gatineau-Ottawa air show last month that it’s been “heartwarming” to see how Canadians have responded over the last season.

“The Snowbirds are so much more than just an air demonstration team, obviously, and it evokes so much emotion and we all have such fond strong memories,” she said.

“I really can’t overstate just how significant they are to Canadians and specifically to the Rcaf. The idea that we’d have to take a pause was definitely not an easy one. However, the Tutor aircraft is 63 years old and it is time to move into the future and make sure that we’re doing things for the right reasons.”

She said the demonstration team has been focused solely on finishing the current season. Once that’s done, she said, the Rcaf can “build the right kind of plan” to ensure the pilots don’t get rusty in the meantime.

“We’re looking at things like, can we send an exchange into some of our allied teams, or obviously instructing and working with the PC-21 in Moose Jaw as an option,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

stories.title: Bank of Canada set for pair of important data drops ahead of ‘live’ rate decision
stories.summary: Ottawa — The Bank of Canada will get a raft of fresh data to start next week as it weighs what could be a pivotal interest rate decision at the end of the month.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Bank of Canada will get a raft of fresh data to start next week as it weighs what could be a pivotal interest rate decision at the end of the month.

Statistics Canada is set to release its September inflation data on Monday, giving the central bank a look at how energy price pressures are influencing other parts of the consumer basket.

A Reuters poll of economists expects the annual rate of inflation rose to 3.2 per cent in September, up from three per cent in August, according to Lseg Data & Analytics.

RBC assistant chief economist Nathan Janzen said he expects inflation held steady at three per cent last month. Persistently high gasoline prices tied to the ongoing war in Iran will remain the biggest fuel for inflation, he said.

“We know that energy prices are high. What we don’t know yet is the extent that those higher energy prices have or are going to spill over to broader inflation pressures,” Janzen said.

Economists at BMO are in line with the consensus expectations and call for inflation to be two tenths of a point higher in September, matching the fastest rate for inflation since December 2023.

Bmo’s Benjamin Reitzes and Shelly Kaushik said in a note to clients Friday that a 5.8 per cent monthly increase in gas prices and a double-digit hike in heating oil costs will fuel the jump. They expect some softness in travel and shelter prices to offset that increase.

The Bank of Canada signalled at the start of the Middle East conflict last spring that it would look through a temporary rise in energy costs tied to the war. But officials have warned that the longer global oil prices remain high, the greater the risks that inflation spreads past the gas pump.

In that case, the central bank could be forced to raise its policy rate, which has stood for nearly a year at 2.25 per cent. Most economists consider that level to be modestly stimulative to growth.

Reitzes and Kaushik said they’re expecting the Bank of Canada’s preferred core inflation metrics to hold steady in September and are “not anticipating any red flags in this report.”

Janzen said the Bank of Canada’s upcoming decision on Oct. 28 will be a “live” meeting, where the door is open for the central bank to raise its policy rate, but a hike is not his base case scenario.

Even if the September price data shows signs inflationary pressures are spreading past the gas pumps, Janzen said the central bank will be weighing that against signs of softness in the labour market and wider economy.

Statistics Canada reported last week that the economy shed 68,000 jobs in September, a second consecutive month of falling employment. A re-escalating trade dispute with the United States has also hampered growth prospects heading into the fourth quarter.

“Higher energy prices — all else equal — would mean broader inflation pressures would be expected to rise in the future. But if the economy is getting weaker, then there are some offsetting disinflationary forces there as well,” Janzen said.

“It puts (the Bank of Canada) still in a wait-and-see mode — very, very data dependent.”

Financial market odds of a quarter-point rate hike later this month fell after the weak September jobs report. Odds of a hike stood around 34 per cent as of Friday afternoon, according to Lseg Data & Analytics.

Janzen said Rbc’s call is for no rate hikes in 2026, with modest tightening starting next year.

The Bank of Canada will also release its own quarterly surveys of businesses and consumers on Monday, which can give the bank a better sense of whether firms are planning to pass their own rising costs on to consumers.

Janzen said inflation expectations and business confidence will help inform the central bank whether higher prices among producers could be passed on to store shelves in the months to come.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Health ministers say one-year extension of mental health, home care funding not enough
stories.summary: Provincial and territorial health ministers meet in Winnipeg amid mounting strain on hospitals and medical facilities across the country
stories.author: Temur Durrani, Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
Canada’s provincial and territorial health ministers say Ottawa’s one-year extension of funding for mental health, addiction treatment and home care is not enough, and that federal plans would amount to a spending cut that is “the largest in a generation.”

The ministers made the comments on Thursday at the end of their first day of discussions in Winnipeg, where they are meeting this week during a particularly strained period for hospitals and medical facilities across the country.

Late on Wednesday evening, federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel announced on social media that Ottawa plans to extend for a year programs that were set to expire in 2027, which she said would represent $1.2-billion in funding. But her territorial and provincial counterparts said that change is inadequate and comes at the last minute.

“We welcome the important first step from Minister Michel,” said Uzoma Asagwara, Manitoba’s health minister, speaking alongside officials from all 13 provinces and territories.

“However, it is a first step. We are unified in stating very clearly that we need to go much further than that.”

Mx. Asagwara said the ministers are pushing for longer-term commitments on bilateral agreements. Health ministers want the Canada Health Transfer, the federal government’s main funding vehicle for provincial health care, to grow at a minimum of 5 per cent a year, rather than the 3-per-cent growth rate it is expected to reach in 2028, they said.

As part of the Canada Health Act, jurisdictions in the country must be made federal transfer payments on a per-capita basis.

“How do we work with patients and clients and families and communities? How do you plan when you do not know what the federal government’s plans are for – again – what would potentially be the largest cut to health care in a generation?” Mx. Asagwara said.

Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones added that Ottawa’s temporary commitment “does not fill us with a lot of joy.”

She said discussions with Ms. Michel, who is expected to meet with provincial and territorial ministers Friday, will focus on these issues.

“We all have different programs that we have started in our jurisdictions,” Ms. Jones told reporters, adding that many funding streams in Ontario would have to be cut in half without federal support.

The federal budget is expected to be tabled in the House of Commons this fall, though a date has not yet been announced.

Ms. Michel made no further comments on the matter on Thursday. In her announcement, she said she looks forward to Friday’s meeting.

In an interview, Bolu Ogunyemi, president of the Canadian Medical Association, said physicians agree with the provincial and territorial health ministers. He described Ms. Michel’s announcement as “insufficient from a planning perspective.”

“Certainly, we need longer-term, sustainable funding to allow for stability and certainty,” Dr. Ogunyemi said in Winnipeg. “The demographics in our all cities and jurisdictions are changing, and the federal government needs to support that for us to deliver appropriate care.”

The Canadian Federation of Nurses Unions echoed Dr. Ogunyemi’s calls.

MP Gord Johns, health critic for the federal NDP, said he expects more from Ottawa.

In a statement, he said Ms. Michel must apply 6-per-cent annual increases to the Canada Health Transfer, while covering 35 per cent of provincial and territorial health care costs.

stories.title: Ontario is importing U.S. power this winter. Star readers have a lot to say about it
stories.summary: After the province signed a deal to buy electricity from New York state, readers weighed in on planning, politics and where Ontario’s power should come from.
stories.author: Paige Oldfield
stories.content:
When the Star’s climate change reporter Marco Chown Oved reported that Ontario has signed a 600-megawatt contract to import electricity from New York state this winter, only weeks after Premier Doug Ford threatened to cut off power exports to the U.S., readers had plenty to say.

The deal, which starts Nov. 1, comes as the Pickering nuclear plant is offline for a multi-year refurbishment. Many readers questioned the planning behind it, while others debated which energy sources Ontario should rely on. Here’s what you had to say:

stories.title: Why the Bank of Canada says declining immigration is 'reshaping' the economy
stories.summary: “An aging population will change the goods and services we produce,” the BoC says in a recent report.
stories.author: Ghada Alsharif
stories.content:
Canada’s aging population, low birth rate and declining immigration are “reshaping” the Canadian economy, affecting the country’s workforce and demand for goods and services, according to the Bank of Canada.

“In the coming years, fewer new immigrants will arrive. Canadians will also continue to get older. This will affect the size of our workforce, what we buy and how much the economy can produce,” the Bank of Canada said in an analysis published Oct. 8.

“Less immigration will mean fewer workers and weaker demand for other goods and services. The economy won’t grow as fast as a result.”

The report comes as Canada is expected to announce its immigration levels plan for 2027-29 by early November. The plan breaks down the government’s targets for individual permanent and temporary residence programs . In September, Prime Minister Mark Carney suggested in an interview with the New York Times that a “controlled increase” in population could be on the way.

To launch a new series, the Star spoke to temporary residents caught up in a numbers game and butting up against a system that once promised them

The Bank of Canada “May be worried about an upsurge in major anti-immigrant sentiment and is reminding Canadians that immigration has always been crucial and will continue to be crucial to our economic well-being,” said Jim Stanford, economist and director of the think tank Centre for Future Work.

Over the past two years, Canada’s immigration system has undergone a dramatic shift. After a decade of record-high immigration, and ramping up the issuance of study and work permits in the wake of the pandemic, seeking to address labour shortages and attract newcomers, the government reversed course, vowing to “take back control of the immigration system” amid rising anti-immigrant sentiment.

Canada’s population grew by as much as three per cent a year in the early 2020s, which raised the number of workers and “helped ease labour shortages,” according to the Bank of Canada.

But now, not only has Ottawa let in significantly fewer international students and foreign workers since 2024, it has also pulled the rug out from under hundreds of thousands of temporary residents already in Canada. The Liberal government began cutting the number of new permanent and temporary residents it would admit and tightening the rules for those already here.

“The worst way to do immigration is to view immigrants as just-in-time workers who can be brought in when employers need them and kicked out when they’re no longer wanted,” Stanford said. “That is economically disruptive and morally repugnant.”

For several decades, Canada’s birth rate has been below the level needed to replace the population. In 2025, population growth slowed to just 0.5 per cent, the slowest rate of growth in more than a century, the Bank of Canada report noted.

Immigrants and non-permanent residents are often younger and come in as international students, who are more likely to participate in parts of the economy with labour shortages, such as restaurants and agriculture, “while highly skilled immigrants can bring skills and knowledge that are in short supply, in fields such as computer engineering,” the report said.

Their reduced numbers further accelerate the decline in much-needed labour supply amid a rapidly aging population, the report said. In 1971, the average age in Canada was 26; today, it is over 40.

“An aging population will change the goods and services we produce because older people have specific needs,” the bank pointed out.

And because older people spend more of their money on health care, this adds to demand for pharmaceuticals, adaptive living products and supportive home care services. It could also change how much governments spend on hospitals and long-term care, the report said.

Shamira Madhany, managing director for World Education Services Canada, said the focus of immigration has narrowed too much, shifting from long-term nation-building to short-term labour supply. This also means Canada is losing immigrants who study and work here, gain experience but leave because they can’t stay permanently.

Immigration is “about being intentional in planning and knowing who we need, preparing people before they arrive and making sure they can hit the ground running. Our country needs immigrants.”

The Carney government has prioritized developing major infrastructure and industrial projects , but “where is the labour to develop projects coming from, given the number of experienced people leaving?” she added.

stories.title: Canada is about to announce its new immigration targets. How much wiggle room does Carney have?
stories.summary: Targets will be influenced by the stubborn math of a temporary resident population that’s proven challenging to shrink.
stories.author: Nicholas Keung
stories.content:
It was an unexpected remark from Prime Minister Mark Carney , after two years of sweeping cuts to Canada’s immigration system.

In an interview with the New York Times in September , the PM caused a stir when he floated the idea of population growth — a taboo for the Liberals, who have been blamed for the country’s immigration backlash.

“Now the question starts to become, when do we resume some controlled increase in the population, which is the nature of Canada?” Carney told the Times. “So that will happen, and we just want to make sure that we’ve got it under control.”

Canada’s immigration system has undergone a dramatic transformation in the past two years. After a decade of record-high intake targets under Justin Trudeau that deepened a housing crisis, strained health care and eroded public confidence in immigration, Ottawa sharply reversed course.

The government started slashing the number of new permanent and temporary residents it would admit and tightening the rules for those already here. The consequences have rippled across the country, from college campuses starved of international tuition revenue to employers scrambling to fill job vacancies to hundreds of thousands of migrants struggling to stay here.

Carney’s comments are now fuelling debate over Ottawa’s upcoming immigration levels plan for 2027-2029, and what direction it will take. By law, the plan must be tabled on or before Nov. 1. It is a road map released by the federal government each year that sets targets for how many permanent and temporary residents will be welcomed in the next three years.

What Ottawa tables will be shaped by the targets already in play, the promises Carney has made since taking office, and the stubborn math of a temporary resident population that has proven challenging to shrink.

Last year, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab projected the 2027 annual intake of new permanent residents at 380,000 in 2027 and 2028 — the same as 2026. The target for arriving temporary residents, however, would be reduced further from 385,000 in 2026 to 370,000 — 220,000 workers and 150,000 students — in each of the next two years.

The targets are not set in stone and Diab’s predecessor, Marc Miller, did drastically change course in 2024 by slashing both the permanent and temporary resident intakes amid public backlash over high immigration.

A long-term tracking poll by the Environics Institute since 1977 has shown Canadians’ support for immigration had dipped since 2022, hitting bottom in 2024, with a majority of people saying the country has accepted too many newcomers . Last year, Canadians’ views on immigration have become slightly more positive.

Since becoming prime minister, Carney has pledged to reduce the share of temporary workers and international students to five per cent of the population by the end of 2027 while maintaining permanent resident admission to under one per cent of Canada’s population annually beyond 2027.

Currently, the share of temporary resident population still stands at 6.7 per cent of the country’s nearly 42 million population. Meanwhile, Ottawa’s hands are tied in shifting more temporary residents to permanent status if it sticks to Carney’s one per cent commitment, meaning the upper target for permanent residents can’t go over 418,000.

Parisa Mahboubi of the C.D. Howe Institute said the system should focus on welcoming high-skilled, high-wage immigrants over low-skilled, non-agricultural temporary foreign workers.

There is little wiggle room unless Ottawa finds an innovative way to account for the numbers. It has before. Last year, it rolled out two one-time initiatives to grant permanent residence to 115,000 people with protection status and 33,000 foreign workers in small communities over two years, but the groups were counted on top of the 2026 permanent resident target.

“They’re going to be holding at least relatively close to their 380,000 projection,” said Calgary-based immigration lawyer Mark Holthe. “That five per cent temporary resident target is what’s driving a large portion of this plan. They made a campaign promise and they are going to hit it no matter what.”

Last month, the C.D. Howe Institute, a Toronto-based think tank, recommended an annual admission of 380,000 permanent residents in 2027, and further reductions to 350,000 in 2028, and 340,000 in 2029. It said the five per cent target for temporary residents should be treated as a ceiling and come down to three per cent in the medium and long term.

Managing temporary resident population is not straightforward. Officials can cap new study and work permits to control intakes and transition temporary residents to permanent status, but it takes resources to track and remove people with expired permits.

“The government hasn’t been able to reduce this (population) significantly,” said Parisa Mahboubi, an economist who chairs C.D. Howe’s immigration targets council. “We are going to see a large share of transitions from TR to PR … The government has greater control over that.”

Larissa Bezo, president and CEO of the Canadian Bureau for International Education, doubts that Ottawa will need to raise international student intakes since it didn’t even manage to fill the quotas it set.

“The challenge really has shifted from perhaps managing growth to a period of where we are now having to rebuild confidence,” she noted.

“The larger issue from my perspective is what happens several years from now. Fewer students arriving today means fewer graduates, fewer researchers, fewer health-care workers, fewer engineers, fewer entrepreneurs and fewer permanent residents in the future.”

Diab has been clear about her plan to bring in even more French-speaking permanent residents outside Quebec, raising this demographic’s share of the total annual admissions from nine per cent in 2026 to 9.5 per cent in 2027, 10.5 per cent in 2028 and 12 per cent in 2029.

She has also hinted at maintaining the share of permanent residents in economic class at around 64 per cent in 2027 and 2028, while working with provinces and prioritizing talent in key sectors and industries like health care, emerging technologies and skilled trades.

Earlier this year, the Immigration Department held consultations on proposed reforms to the skilled immigration programs as well as the way points are awarded to candidates for their education, work experience and language skills among other factors . It has also asked for public input in setting economic priorities and selection categories for its targeted talent draws.

Stein Monteiro of Signal49 Research said he does not expect drastic changes to immigration policy direction, rather, more fine-tuning of current programs to better align the system with economic needs.

“There’s a lot of other things they’re trying to do aside from the levels,” said Monteiro, lead immigration researcher at the independent research organization, formerly known as The Conference Board of Canada.

“They’re trying to maintain stability by streamlining programs, cutting unnecessary niche programs and then improving on the application process … (which) makes it more predictable for what’s coming out on the other end of the immigration system.”

C.D. Howe’s Mahboubi said immigration is more than just a numbers game; the type of migrants Canada brings in matters. The system should focus on welcoming high-skilled, high-wage immigrants over low-skilled, non-agricultural temporary foreign workers, she noted.

“We want high-quality students and higher-skilled workers to support our economy,” she said. “There are still more reforms and more oversight needed. We are not there yet.”

Over the past year, Ottawa has stopped accepting applications for immigration programs for start-up entrepreneurs, home care workers, privately sponsored refugees for resettlement (Group of Five), and skilled refugees and displaced people. Few expect they will reopen next year.

“Their focus is on high-wage individuals, so any new program that they’re looking at creating or rolling out are going to target those individuals,” said Holthe, the Calgary lawyer. “Our professionals and executives and people making over $100,000 have no pathways to permanent residence. That’s part of the reason why they’re making changes.”

content_blocks.text: “They’re trying to maintain stability by streamlining programs, cutting unnecessary niche programs and then improving on the application process … (which) makes it more predictable for what’s coming out on the other end of the immigration system.”

content_blocks.text: Targeting high-skilled, high-wage immigrants

content_blocks.text: C.D. Howe’s Mahboubi said immigration is more than just a numbers game; the type of migrants Canada brings in matters. The system should focus on welcoming high-skilled, high-wage immigrants over low-skilled, non-agricultural temporary foreign workers, she noted.

content_blocks.text: “We want high-quality students and higher-skilled workers to support our economy,” she said. “There are still more reforms and more oversight needed. We are not there yet.”

content_blocks.text: Over the past year, Ottawa has stopped accepting applications for immigration programs for start-up entrepreneurs, home care workers, privately sponsored refugees for resettlement (Group of Five), and skilled refugees and displaced people. Few expect they will reopen next year.

[](http://london.ca/newsroom/public-service-announcement/daytime-lane-closures-veterans-memorial-parkway-maintenance)

Friday, October 16, 2026

Weather permitting, crews will begin maintenance work on Veterans Memorial Parkway (VMP) on Monday, October 19.

This map shows the work area on Veterans Memorial Parkway between Highway 401 and River Road.

Crews will be removing debris and mowing grass in the centre median, including trimming vegetation around signs and other roadside features. This regular maintenance helps keep the roadway clear, safe and in good condition.

To safely complete the work, the left lane in each direction will be closed in short sections as crews move along Veterans Memorial Parkway between Highway 401 and River Road.

Work will take place between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. to avoid the busiest travel times. Drivers should expect daytime lane closures and possible delays, and are asked to slow down and follow signs around work areas.

The timing of the work may change due to weather or other conditions.

Weather permitting, crews will begin maintenance work on Veterans Memorial Parkway (VMP) on Monday, October 19.
This map shows the work area on Veterans Memorial Parkway between Highway 401 and River Road.

Crews will be removing debris and mowing grass in the centre median, including trimming vegetation around signs and other roadside features. This regular maintenance helps keep the roadway clear, safe and in good condition.
To safely complete the work, the left lane in each direction will be closed in short sections as crews move along Veterans Memorial Parkway between Highway 401 and River Road.

Work will take place between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. to avoid the busiest travel times. Drivers should expect daytime lane closures and possible delays, and are asked to slow down and follow signs around work areas.

stories.title: Families, friendships strained as Alberta’s referendum enters final days
stories.summary: Divides over whether Alberta ought to stay in or leave Canada run deeper than the campaign signs.
stories.author: Stephanie Taylor
stories.content:
Edmonton and RED Deer, Alta. — Vince Flewell didn’t come to see Prime Minister Mark Carney. He showed up so Carney could see him.

Standing across from a local brewery in Red Deer County where Carney dropped in Friday to rally residents and volunteers campaigning for Alberta to remain in Canada, the independence supporter held an “Alberta Strong” flag on a pole resting against his hip.

Across the street, the federalist crowd that had lingered after the event ended in hopes of catching another glimpse of Carney began to dissipate.

“Carry on,” one man said to Flewell as he walked past.

“Oh, don’t even,” a woman shot back after he commented on her enthusiasm for Carney’s visit.

The former oilfield worker was unfazed. He was used to getting middle fingers from passersby when he drives through town in a truck decked out with pro-independence signs and Alberta flags.

“Us independent people, we’re not violent,” he told the Star. “We love Canada, but it’s kinda crazy — I love Alberta more.”

Divides over whether Alberta ought to stay in or leave Canada run deeper than the campaign signs dotting its highways and boulevards. They have opened gulfs between community members, relatives and friends, leaving uncertainty hanging over what those relationships, let alone the province itself, will look like after Monday’s vote.

“Oh my heavens — I’ve unfriended several people off Facebook because I can’t stand their posts,” said Sharon Miller, a lifelong Red Deer resident who turned up to see Carney.

“It’s broken up families, friendships. It’s sad.”

While Miller proudly wore her Canadian pride to see the prime minister, the referendum isn’t an issue she feels she can talk openly about in the community.

“People are polarized. They are either for or against and they’re passionate.”

For those drawn to the cause of keeping Alberta within Canada, the battle over the province’s future is an emotional one, fuelled by existential questions about what it means to belong and call Alberta home.

It is those feelings that Carney has sought to tap into throughout his rapid two-day campaign through the province, making identity and belonging central to his case against separation.

But even while doing so, Carney has acknowledged the grievances that fuelled the separatist movement, pointing in Red Deer to opposition to Alberta’s oil and gas sector and policies he said left Albertans feeling they lacked control over their own resources.

“The threads that linked us as a country, some of them frayed because of that. And, you know, what we’re facing on Monday is part of a reflection of that,” Carney said.

Smith, who appeared alongside Carney in Red Deer, highlighted what she sees as progress under the Carney government, pointing in particular to Ottawa’s backing of the Pacific Link oil pipeline to the West Coast.

“We don’t always agree on everything. We often disagree quite publicly on several things. But today we can all agree that, ON Question 10, we are voting for Option 1: to remain in Canada,” Smith said, referring to the referendum question on whether to hold a future binding vote on Alberta separation.

“This is now a time, a moment in Canadian history, where we are going to be able to work side by side and feel for the first time in a long time Alberta and Canada are walking together,” she said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre and Premier Danielle Smith encourage Albertans to vote to keep the province in Canada. (Oct. 16. 2026)

Hours later in Edmonton, at Carney’s second “Forever Canadian” rally in as many days, the prime minister stressed the gravity of the moment.

“At this pivotal moment, Albertans have a choice: we can build a stronger Alberta and an even greater Canada to leave for our children … or we can burden them with years of deep divisions and great uncertainty,” he told supporters.

In Edmonton, he leaned on his Alberta roots while making the case for unity. He took the stage to a hometown hero’s welcome at the Edmonton Expo Centre from the crowd of more than 5,000.

“I know. Alberta is my home. I grew up here. This city, this province, this country have given me everything: my family, my education, my values,” he told supporters.

And this country, he said, is “a country where you are free to be who you want to be. To speak your mind. To worship as you choose. To live your life as you wish. That is true independence. That is real sovereignty.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney wrapped up his two-day, pro-Canada tour of Alberta by rallying with thousands of supporters in his hometown on Friday night at Edmonton’s Expo Centre. Supporters were dressed in all manner of Maple Leaf gear, and jammed bleachers, danced, waved Canadian flags and cheered a song stipulating Canada will never be the 51st U.S. state. (Oct. 16, 2026)

At the rally the night prior in Calgary, some spoke of how the referendum campaign had nonetheless unearthed deeply personal rifts within the province.

“I see divisions in families,” said Jacqueline Sheridan, a lifelong Calgary resident who was among the crowd of more than 7,000 that listened to Carney speak at the first of two “Forever Canadian” rallies.

“Some of the cousins I can’t talk to because they’re so separatist and they’re not willing to entertain any other point of view.”

Decked out in a hockey jersey with a Canadian flag draped over his back, Robert Gray left little doubt where he stands. Having lived in Alberta for 50 years, he nevertheless described his surprise, even bewilderment, at seeing neighbours and friends support separation.

“It’s unfortunate, I’ve actually … we’ve backed away from each other, for sure,” he said, before adding, “I don’t know if I call them friends anymore.”

‘It’s hard to think of a worse time to have a referendum, or a better time for the province,’

Carney, like speaker after speaker at Thursday’s rally, focused not on the economic arguments against independence but on Alberta as home.

Angela Saclamacis, who was among the first in line to see the prime minister speak, arriving more than three hours before what would be her first political rally, recalled her father’s pride in the country.

“My father came and immigrated to Canada when he was 13, from Greece, and he was always so proud to be able to say that he was Canadian,” she said.

“To think that would go away for our family, it’s really upsetting.”

If concerns about growing divisions and what it would mean to no longer call themselves Canadian have spurred Albertans to campaign for the country, ON Thursday they united around a desire to hear from the prime minister they see as a champion of their cause.

It was a message Carney returned to as he wrapped up his campaign in Edmonton.

“Now is the time to build, not break. Now it’s our turn to stand up for Canada,” he told supporters.

Michelle Senkow spent the winter collecting signatures for the “Forever Canadian” petition drive opposing separation.

Despite having undergone two knee replacements, Senkow waited more than two hours in the front row at Calgary’s BMO Centre to hear Carney speak.

And when he was done, she shook his hand.

“I caught him as he was walking through, and I told him, I said, ‘For our grandkids, Mark,’ and he said, ‘Yes, for our grandkids.’ He said it to me. He looked at me sincerely and said that,” she told the Star.

“We’ve got to preserve Canada for everyone.”

Smith, who appeared alongside Carney in Red Deer, highlighted what she sees as progress under the Carney government, pointing in particular to Ottawa’s backing of the Pacific Link oil pipeline to the West Coast.

“We don’t always agree on everything. We often disagree quite publicly on several things. But today we can all agree that, ON Question 10, we are voting for Option 1: to remain in Canada,” Smith said, referring to the referendum question on whether to hold a future binding vote on Alberta separation.
“This is now a time, a moment in Canadian history, where we are going to be able to work side by side and feel for the first time in a long time Alberta and Canada are walking together,” she said.
Prime Minister Mark Carney, Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre and Premier Danielle Smith encourage Albertans to vote to keep the province in Canada. (Oct. 16. 2026)
Hours later in Edmonton, at Carney’s second “Forever Canadian” rally in as many days, the prime minister stressed the gravity of the moment.

“At this pivotal moment, Albertans have a choice: we can build a stronger Alberta and an even greater Canada to leave for our children … or we can burden them with years of deep divisions and great uncertainty,” he told supporters.
In Edmonton, he leaned on his Alberta roots while making the case for unity. He took the stage to a hometown hero’s welcome at the Edmonton Expo Centre from the crowd of more than 5,000.
“I know. Alberta is my home. I grew up here. This city, this province, this country have given me everything: my family, my education, my values,” he told supporters.

And this country, he said, is “a country where you are free to be who you want to be. To speak your mind. To worship as you choose. To live your life as you wish. That is true independence. That is real sovereignty.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney wrapped up his two-day, pro-Canada tour of Alberta by rallying with thousands of supporters in his hometown on Friday night at Edmonton’s Expo Centre. Supporters were dressed in all manner of Maple Leaf gear, and jammed bleachers, danced, waved Canadian flags and cheered a song stipulating Canada will never be the 51st U.S. state. (Oct. 16, 2026)
At the rally the night prior in Calgary, some spoke of how the referendum campaign had nonetheless unearthed deeply personal rifts within the province.

“I see divisions in families,” said Jacqueline Sheridan, a lifelong Calgary resident who was among the crowd of more than 7,000 that listened to Carney speak at the first of two “Forever Canadian” rallies.
“Some of the cousins I can’t talk to because they’re so separatist and they’re not willing to entertain any other point of view.”

Decked out in a hockey jersey with a Canadian flag draped over his back, Robert Gray left little doubt where he stands. Having lived in Alberta for 50 years, he nevertheless described his surprise, even bewilderment, at seeing neighbours and friends support separation.
“It’s unfortunate, I’ve actually … we’ve backed away from each other, for sure,” he said, before adding, “I don’t know if I call them friends anymore.”
‘It’s hard to think of a worse time to have a referendum, or a better time for the province,’
Carney, like speaker after speaker at Thursday’s rally, focused not on the economic arguments against independence but on Alberta as home.

Angela Saclamacis, who was among the first in line to see the prime minister speak, arriving more than three hours before what would be her first political rally, recalled her father’s pride in the country.
“My father came and immigrated to Canada when he was 13, from Greece, and he was always so proud to be able to say that he was Canadian,” she said.
“To think that would go away for our family, it’s really upsetting.”

If concerns about growing divisions and what it would mean to no longer call themselves Canadian have spurred Albertans to campaign for the country, ON Thursday they united around a desire to hear from the prime minister they see as a champion of their cause.
It was a message Carney returned to as he wrapped up his campaign in Edmonton.
“Now is the time to build, not break. Now it’s our turn to stand up for Canada,” he told supporters.
Michelle Senkow spent the winter collecting signatures for the “Forever Canadian” petition drive opposing separation.
Despite having undergone two knee replacements, Senkow waited more than two hours in the front row at Calgary’s BMO Centre to hear Carney speak.
And when he was done, she shook his hand.

“I caught him as he was walking through, and I told him, I said, ‘For our grandkids, Mark,’ and he said, ‘Yes, for our grandkids.’ He said it to me. He looked at me sincerely and said that,” she told the Star.
“We’ve got to preserve Canada for everyone.”

stories.title: THREATS
stories.summary: London, ON (October 16, 2026) – A London man is facing a criminal charge after a former supervisor received threatening messages that included images of firearms.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 16, 2026) – A London man is facing a criminal charge after a former supervisor received threatening messages that included images of firearms.

On Thursday, October 15, 2026, a man contacted the London Police Service to report receiving a series of concerning messages from a previous employee.

The messages included photographs of what appeared to be firearms.

At approximately 12 p.m., members of the London Police Service Frontline Division, with the assistance of members of the Emergency Response Unit attended a residence in the 300-block of Thames Street in relation to the investigation.

Following negotiations with officers, at approximately 2:30 p.m., the suspect male exited the residence and was arrested without incident.

Members of the LPS Guns and Gangs Section executed a search warrant at the residence and lawfully owned firearms and ammunition were seized.

As a result of the investigation, Amandeep Singh Basanti, 44, of London, has been charged with one count of uttering threats to cause death or bodily harm.

The accused remains in custody and is scheduled to appear in London court today in relation to the charge.

The investigation is ongoing.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 . Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: New temporary road will keep traffic moving during Wellington Road construction
stories.summary: A new temporary road will open to traffic on Monday, October 19, allowing construction crews to replace underground infrastructure beneath We
stories.content:
A new temporary road will open to traffic on Monday, October 19, allowing construction crews to replace underground infrastructure beneath Wellington Road as part of the Wellington Gateway rapid transit project.

The temporary road, called a diversion road, will run between Wellington Crescent and Thomas Janes Drive. It will keep traffic moving through the area while crews work on the existing road and the infrastructure underneath it. The diversion road will remain in place through the winter and into 2027.

In some locations, the underground infrastructure is almost 10 metres deep, roughly the height of a three-storey building. Building the diversion road gives crews the space they need to safely carry out this large-scale excavation and replacement work without closing Wellington Road completely or repeatedly changing traffic configurations.

Traffic restrictions on side streets near Wellington Road will be in place, and pedestrian access will be maintained on the west side of the road. Drivers should follow posted signs and allow extra time when travelling through the area.

Two temporary London Transit (LTC) stops are in place near Emery Street to maintain bus service during construction. Additional road space has been built at both stops to help buses pull in and safely rejoin traffic.

For information about bus stop changes and detours during construction, visit London Transit’s Wellington Road construction updates .

The traffic change is part of Phase 2 of the Wellington Gateway project, which runs along Wellington Road between Wilkins Street and Watson Street. The work is being completed in two parts: Phase 2A, between Wilkins Street and Base Line Road East, and Phase 2B, between Base Line Road East and Watson Street.

Together, these phases will add centre-running rapid transit lanes, new transit stops and a concrete centre median, along with underground infrastructure upgrades and improved walking and cycling connections. Construction on Phase 2A is expected to continue through 2028, with Phase 2B continuing through 2029. Final restoration work will follow.

For construction updates and traffic information, visit the Wellington Gateway project page .

Learn more about why London is building rapid transit .

The Wellington Gateway project is funded in part by the Government of Ontario and the Government of Canada.

stories.title: Pierre Poilievre urges Albertans not to leave their fellow Canadians behind
stories.summary: The Conservative leader encouraged Albertans to “lock arms with Canadians who want to restore the promise of Canada.”
stories.author: Ryan Tumilty
stories.content:
Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre called on his fellow Albertans to fix Canada, not leave it, as he argued against separation Friday, days before the province’s referendum .

“Our real goal should not be separation, it should be restoration. It should not be to tear down our country but to build it up,” Poilievre said while speaking at a political conference in Calgary.

Poilievre, who was born and raised in Calgary and now represents a rural Alberta riding, made the pitch ahead of Monday’s vote, in which Albertans will choose either to remain in Canada or begin the process toward a second binding referendum on leaving the country.

He said that in his youth he saw a province where people could get ahead, and that he understands the frustration of those who feel that promise is slipping away.

“I looked around my neighbourhood at that time and I saw people who were achieving great lives. They worked as electricians, carpenters, plumbers, police officers or in the case of my parents, teachers,” he said. “They were able to earn a great life or own a home and build a future for their kids.”

Poilievre said he understands the frustration many Albertans feel toward a federal government he says is holding back resource development, hurting the provincial economy and making life more expensive, but said leaving is not the answer.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre and Premier Danielle Smith encourage Albertans to vote to keep the province in Canada. (Oct. 16. 2026)

“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation and the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government, it’s a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”

He said Albertans are not quitters and that, rather than leave a country they believe is holding them back, they should help pull it forward.

“My message to Albertans is this: Don’t leave your fellow Canadians behind. Lock arms with them, lock arms with Canadians who want to restore the promise of Canada.”

Premier Danielle Smith is also set to speak to the conference later on Friday, but she stood alongside Prime Minister Mark Carney this afternoon at a stop in Red Deer, Alta., where the two leaders made the case for staying in Canada.

Smith, who long complained about the Trudeau Liberal government, said there is real change from Carney’s government that shouldn’t be discounted.

Divides over whether Alberta ought to stay in or leave Canada run deeper than the campaign signs.

“This is now a time, a moment, in Canadian history where we are going to be able to work side by side,” she said.

While Carney and Smith are aligned on the question of separation, Albertans will also vote Monday on nine other questions, including proposals on immigration and constitutional issues such as changing how judges are appointed and abolishing the federal Senate.

Smith has encouraged people to vote for those changes, but Carney weighed in for the first time Thursday calling for people to vote “no to the nine.” The premier said they can still disagree on some issues, but stressed real progress is being made.

“This is the point, it’s a conversation. We go, we meet, we find areas where we can agree. We work together,” she said.

Public opinion polling has consistently shown the majority of Albertans want the province to remain in Canada, but support for separation is higher among Smith’s United Conservative Party supporters, which has strong overlaps with the federal Conservatives.

The Conservatives have been running their own unity campaign through the Conservatives for Canada group, which has encouraged Albertans to vote to remain.

Elections Alberta requires third-party advertiser groups such as Conservatives for Canada to file regular financial updates. As of Thursday, the group had raised $37,000, placing it 12th among third-party organizations by fundraising.

stories.title: Canada's skilled immigration system, Express Entry, is giving a boost to high-wage workers
stories.summary: Candidates with Canadian work experience or who receive a job offer on the list of qualifying jobs get bonus points.
stories.author: Nicholas Keung
stories.content:
Kitchener—Ottawa is going to prioritize permanent residence for candidates in 186 high-wage occupations to mark the beginning of what’s expected to be a series of changes to Canada’s signature skilled immigration selection system.

Under the updated rules that take effect Nov. 3 , those who have at least one year of Canadian work experience in one of those listed jobs or receive a job offer on that list will be awarded bonus points in the economic immigration scoring system, to give them an edge in competing for the limited number of permanent resident spots yearly.

“Our immigration system will better recognize the attributes our research shows drive strong outcomes for newcomers, and that is Canadian work experience and job offers in high-wage occupations,” Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab told a news conference on Friday.

“These changes are the first practical steps of broader Express Entry reforms,” she added, referring to the scoring system that ranks candidates based on personal attributes such as education achievement, language proficiency and work experience. “More’s coming.”

When asked about the direction of Canada’s upcoming immigration targets and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s recent comment on a “controlled increase” of the population , Diab said the government has an “ambitious” growth agenda that would require people.

“We are driving that agenda, but we also recognize we need people from outside the country to come and fill gaps that we cannot fill for the next decade,” she said. “So, stay tuned to our next immigration level plan.”

The Immigration Department said a high-wage job is one where the typical pay is at least 1.3 times the median Canadian wage of an occupation — regardless of a candidate’s previous or current salary. Jobs in health care, skilled trades, engineering, technology and education are among those that qualify .

The department will maintain the high-wage occupation list, which is built on wage data from the job bank, labour force survey and census from the previous three years. Qualifying candidates can see their ranking scores boosted by as many as 150 points.

While the consultation report on Express Entry reforms , released a day ago, showed general support for rewarding candidates in qualifying high-wage jobs, concerns were raised that this May exclude certain demographics from being selected, such as younger candidates or candidates working in occupations with labour shortages but do not meet the high-wage threshold.

The changes also fail to ensure rights and protections for migrant workers doing essential but underpaid work in care, agriculture, food processing, cleaning and other sectors, said the Migrant Workers Alliance for Change.

While doctors, engineers and electricians deserve permanent residence, said the advocacy group’s executive director, Syed Hussan, so do the women caring for Canadian families and the farmworkers growing food to feed Canadians.

“Which jobs pay more is not simply a reflection of skill or contribution,” said Hussan. “Wages are shaped by decades of racial and gender discrimination that have systematically undervalued work done by women and racialized workers … Now the government is using those wage inequalities to decide who gets permanent residence.”

Diab said candidates already in the Express Entry pool will have their scores automatically updated in the system, but those who wish to receive the bonus points for a qualifying high-wage job offer must update their online profiles with the required documentation before Nov. 3.

In early 2025, concerns over rampant fraud by unscrupulous employers and recruitment agents forced the Immigration Department to remove points awarded for job offers in the score ranking system.

To streamline job offer assessment, Diab said the approval of Employment and Social Development Canada will no longer be required for candidates to receive the new bonus points for high-wage occupations. Instead, verifying whether a job offer is genuine will be solely in the hands of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada.

“To maintain strong verification systems and to prevent fraud, my officials at Ircc will now assess job offers directly,” she told reporters. “We’re cutting red tape, but let me be clear, we are not cutting corners.”

stories.title: Alberta NDP proposes 3-part plan over custody releases in Edmonton’s Chinatown
stories.summary: The provincial government says it is already taking steps to better connect people leaving custody with housing and other supports.
stories.author: Joel Gotlib
stories.content:
Alberta’s Opposition NDP is proposing a three-part plan to address concerns about detainees and offenders being released in Edmonton’s Chinatown.

In recent weeks, surveillance video has surfaced showing Edmonton police and Alberta corrections officers dropping off people who had recently been released from custody in and around Chinatown.

Community member Wai-Ling Lennon said the situation is affecting people’s sense of safety in a neighbourhood she considers an important connection to her heritage.

“This is the part of Edmonton that reminds me of my heritage. This is the place where I feel I belong,” Lennon said.

She said other members of the community, particularly seniors, have told her they are afraid to go out after dark.

“I have also heard the children, adults, seniors who live outside Chinatown, they do not feel safe to come to Chinatown anymore,” Lennon said.

Karl Miu, with the Edmonton Chinatown and Area Business Association, said the drop-offs are continuing and it is time for the provincial government to take action.

At a news conference Thursday, Edmonton-South West MLA Nathan Ip said the situation is affecting both the community and those being released from custody.

“We’ve been left dealing with the consequences of a system that is failing both the community and the businesses and the people being released,” Ip said.

Members of Edmonton’s Chinese community say the problem is not new, and that detainees and offenders have been dropped off in Chinatown for years.

“Now we see this video evidence, we see what is happening in our community, we see how this has expanded and multiplied and it has reached the level that this is a crisis that needs to be addressed,” said NDP MLA David Shepherd, the party’s public safety critic.

The NDP is proposing a three-part plan for the United Conservative government.

“First, an immediate end to detainee releases in Chinatown and anywhere in Alberta by any law enforcement agency unless a direct connection to services has been made in advance and those services are open and accessible,” Shepherd said.

The Opposition is also calling for expanded reintegration supports for people leaving remand custody and for reintegration plans to be required before high-risk and vulnerable people are released.

In a statement to Global News, Arthur Green, press secretary for Alberta’s public safety minister, said the government has met with Chinatown residents and service providers and is taking steps to address their concerns.

“Our government has met with Chinatown residents and providers and have taken their concerns seriously, taking concrete steps to make their community safer,” Green said.

He pointed to the relocation of the Edmonton Remand Centre from Chinatown and said the province is implementing dedicated system navigators in correctional centres to help co-ordinate releases and connect people with housing and other supports.

Green also criticized the Ndp’s record in government, accusing the party of “fearmongering about disorder” after three supervised consumption sites were established in Chinatown during its time in office.

“Albertans don’t need lectures from the NDP about Chinatown’s challenges — in fact, if the NDP had been paying any attention, they would know our government is already taking real action to address them,” Green said.

The government said Edmonton’s Navigation and Support Centre, located in Chinatown, has helped more than 12,000 Albertans access supports and made more than 75,000 connections to services, including affordable housing and identification supports.

Green also said the province announced an investment of more than $30 million this summer to add more than 400 treatment, housing and stabilization beds in the Edmonton area.

Business owners say improving public safety and revitalizing Chinatown’s economy go hand in hand.

Entrepreneur Wilson Wong called on the province to work with the community.

“We’re asking the province to partner with us as an investment in Alberta’s economy, culture and next generation of entrepreneurs,” Wong said.

stories.title: Carney urges Albertans to vote against separating from Canada
stories.summary: In a Calgary speech, the Prime Minister speaks of the country’s strength when united and warns of the consequences of leaving Confederation
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has taken his unity message to Alberta ahead of Monday’s referendum, urging people to vote for the province to remain in Canada and reject Premier Danielle Smith ’s other nine ballot proposals.

In a speech in Calgary on Thursday evening, Mr. Carney spoke of the country’s strength when united and warned Albertans of the consequences of voting against choosing to keep the province wedded to Confederation.

“At this pivotal moment, Albertans have a choice: to build a stronger Alberta and a greater Canada to leave for our children, or to burden them with years of deep division and great uncertainty,” Mr. Carney told a packed house at a downtown Calgary rally.

Prime Minister Mark Carney told thousands rallying in Calgary on Thursday that Albertans should vote to keep the province in Canada.

The Canadian Press

Monday’s referendum will ask voters to weigh in on 10 questions, one of them on whether Alberta should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on separating. The other nine questions, authored by Ms. Smith’s government, deal with limiting some non-permanent residents’ access to social services, charging them fees for health care and education, and numerous constitutional changes such as abolishing the federal Senate.

The Prime Minister has been critical of Ms. Smith’s decision to call the referendum. In May, he described it as a “dangerous bluff,” likening it to Britain’s 2016 vote to leave the European Union. (Mr. Carney was governor of the Bank of England at the time.)

He used similar language on Thursday night: “This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities,” he said in his prepared remarks.

“Our country and your futures are too precious to play games with.”

While the relationship between Mr. Carney and Ms. Smith has thawed over the last year, one of the first signs of conflict between the two emerged earlier in the day as the Prime Minister made several stops in Calgary ahead of his speech. For the first time, he voiced his opinion on the other referendum questions, encouraging Albertans to vote against the Premier’s nine proposals on immigration and constitutional changes.

He told Albertans to vote “no to the nine,” putting him in direct opposition to Ms. Smith, whose government has spent $4-million in advertising to campaign in favour of the proposals.

The Premier says she needs approval on those questions to fortify her mandate, and that they would provide leverage to gain more autonomy within Confederation.

Ms. Smith clapped back at Mr. Carney’s comments later in the day, writing on social media that “it appears that he has yet to fully understand just how damaging the open-border policies of his predecessor were.”

Mr. Carney and Ms. Smith are expected to share a stage on Friday at a pro-federalist rally in Red Deer, Alta.

Mr. Carney has spent much of the referendum campaign on the sidelines, choosing to make his pitch to Albertans indirectly, by demonstrating Ottawa’s willingness to co-operate with the province. This has included dramatic policy shifts, particularly around environmental safeguards, and standing with the Premier as they announced a proposed oil pipeline to the West Coast .

Alberta’s referendum – the first time the province has put a secession question to voters – is occurring at a time of tremendous stress on national unity. While many Albertans prepare to vote on Monday, a newly elected separatist Quebec government will pose challenges for Ottawa, and U.S. President Donald Trump has shown few signs that the continuing tariff war and musings about annexation will end.

On Thursday night, Mr. Carney said that the referendum “comes at the worst possible time,” pointing to what he described as a more dangerous and divided world.

“Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us.”

Mr. Carney’s push alongside Ms. Smith to build a new bitumen pipeline – most recently by designating it a project of national interest – has underscored a desire to blunt many Albertans’ deep frustration with Ottawa’s direction on energy and environmental policy under his predecessor, Justin Trudeau.

“I won’t sugarcoat it: some of those threads have needed to be repaired. The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” Mr. Carney said to applause at the Thursday event, held by Forever Canadian, one of the most prominent federalist groups in the province.

He added that recently, Albertans were made to feel their “energy contributions were running against the tides of history.”

“What should have brought us together began to divide us. Contributing to a half century of politics that have too often pulled us apart,” he said.

Mr. Carney said the pipeline will reduce Canada’s dependence on the United States – a point that drew some of the loudest applause of the evening.

Keith Procter and Elaine Kirby met in the lineup to get in to see Mr. Carney speak, and were two of the estimated 7,000 people to pack the convention centre. Both voted in advance polls to stay in Canada.

Mr. Procter, an IT project manager, understands the tension between Alberta and Eastern Canada, saying that Ontario’s manufacturing sector benefits when energy prices are low and Alberta’s economy booms when they are high. He said the potential complications and costs of separation are too high to justify entertaining the question.

Ms. Kirby, retired, pushed back on the notion that the Prime Minister is late getting involved in the movement to keep Canada united.

“If he had been here six months ago would this crowd have been here?” she said before Mr. Carney spoke.

“I think it was very strategic on all their parts. This didn’t just get on his calendar three days ago.”

It was the second time this week that the Prime Minister had made the case for unity directly to Albertans . On Monday, he released a short video shot in a classroom at St. Francis Xavier Catholic High School in Edmonton, which he attended as a teenager. In the video, he said that Albertans were being asked to decide on what he called “a long and uncertain process” of separation. “We are stronger together,” he said.

But Thursday was the first time he had encouraged Albertans to vote against the Premier’s nine proposals on immigration and constitutional changes.

As he made several stops in Calgary earlier in the day, he told Albertans to vote “no to the nine,” putting him in direct opposition to Ms. Smith, whose government has spent $4-million in advertising to campaign in favour of the proposals.

The Premier says she needs approval on them to fortify her mandate, and that they would provide leverage to gain more autonomy within Confederation.

The Prime Minister is continuing his pro-Canada campaign on Friday in Red Deer, Alta., where he’ll share a stage with Ms. Smith, and attend another Forever Canadian rally in Edmonton in the evening.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is scheduled to give an address on Friday morning in Calgary at the Canada Strong and Free Network conference, a conservative gathering.

Advance voting opened earlier this week. Elections Alberta said in an e-mail on Thursday morning that roughly 815,000 Albertans had so far cast their ballots – about 27 per cent of all eligible voters.

Campaigners have been divided on how Mr. Carney should support the federalist effort and whether Ottawa should bankroll groups fighting to keep Alberta in Canada. (Alberta’s election-finance rules prohibit the federal government from funding referendum advertisers.)

Some have argued that the Prime Minister shouldn’t leave any cards on the table and use his immense popularity in Alberta to his advantage by giving the federalist side a boost. Others have said he should keep his hands out of it, and that circumventing election-finance rules would backfire.

Mr. Carney in September said his government wouldn’t help fund Alberta’s numerous pro-Canada campaigns , which struggled to raise money through the summer.

Federalist groups have since closed the distance on separatist campaigns that were flush with cash early on. Separatist groups have now scooped up about 59 per cent of all donations during the campaign, down from early September when roughly 75 per cent of all contributions were floating to them.

With a report from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Getting out the Indigenous vote for the Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Some First Nations are concerned by the lack of advance polls
stories.author: Willow Fiddler
stories.content:
Some First Nations in Northern Alberta are concerned that their voter turnout could be a challenge in the referendum, an issue that’s been exacerbated by a lack of advance polling stations.

Chief Allan Adam of the Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation said 800 eligible voters from his community haven’t had access to the referendum’s advanced polling, which should have started on Tuesday, because of an Elections Alberta staff shortage.

On Thursday, Elections Alberta told him that advanced polling would be available on Saturday.

“My people want to go out and vote, and there’s no place to vote right now. So where’s our democracy when it comes to these things?”

A Friday afternoon virtual news conference is planned in which Indigenous leaders will demand answers from Elections Alberta, including why First Nations and Metis in the province, who they say are the most opposed to the referendum, have the least access to voting.

Grand Chief Trevor Mercredi from the Treaty 8 Sovereign Nations told The Globe and Mail that 18 out of 22 First Nations in the Northern Alberta treaty territory, are set up with polling stations. And that only five communities had advance polling stations, three of which are expected to be open for the entire five scheduled days.

“It seems to me that Elections Alberta is failing to comply to their own standards due to lack of employees, and they’re actually asking our nations to facilitate that need. And you know it’s not fair to our nations to have to move polling stations, to move them ahead, move them back. All this confusion that’s happening within our territory, ON our nations is unacceptable. And Elections Alberta has to answer for that,” he said.

Elections Alberta did not respond to The Globe’s request for comment. However, The Globe obtained an e-mail sent on behalf of Elections Alberta to the affected First Nations, including Athabasca Chipewyan, late Thursday evening notifying them of the rescheduled advanced polling date for Saturday.

Mr. Mercredi calls the referendum an attack on his people and says voting against a separatist agenda will protect treaty rights that are being threatened in the referendum.

“When we come together, we’re very strong. We have large numbers, and we could have impact on this referendum,” he said in a video message on social media.

While campaign efforts include info graphics explaining what each of the 10 referendum questions mean and possible impacts, it’s the 10th question that has Indigenous people and communities thinking about what a separation referendum would mean for the treaty territories that cover most of the province.

Some are choosing not to vote because the treaties that cover most of the province were signed with the Crown in the late 1800s before Alberta became a province, tabling the proposition of secession as illegitimate.

“It is understandable why many of our people have traditionally chosen not to vote. Provincial elections and referendums are not our systems of governance, and our treaties do not depend on a provincial ballot,” Mr. Mercredi said.

“Voting does not take away our rights. First Nations are voting against separation to ensure treaty rights are protected,” he said.

Doreen Cardinal-Somers is a Haudenosaunee and Cree treaty adviser living in Fort Chipewyan, part of Treaty 8 territory. She won’t be participating in the referendum vote because she says the treaty relationship with the Crown is not up for debate.

“The fact that this province has made it easy to put a question on a ballot that will, or they’re presupposing, will determine what the treaty relationship is going forward is so offensive to me on so many levels. Like our treaties are not provincial policy; they are solemn agreements that were entered into before Alberta even existed, and I think that distinction is really important,” she said.

Tania Cameron, who is running a “Rock the Vote” campaign for the Treaty 8 nations, said the point of voting is to make a political statement that a separation will never happen.

“I think everyone is of the consensus that you can’t undo treaty by separating,” Ms. Cameron said.

She’d like to see 25 per cent more voters turnout in this election than the last federal election when 11,500 Indigenous people voted in Alberta.

Ms. Cameron said a successful “Rock the Vote” campaign would see a 75-per-cent voter turnout for a total of 14,400.
