stories.title: Cyber intelligence agency planning large data centre in Ottawa area
stories.summary: Proposed facility’s 60 MW capacity would be among largest projects currently operating in Canada, but smaller than many other announced projects
stories.author: Bill Curry, Mercedes Stephenson
stories.content:
Canada’s cyber intelligence agency is planning the construction of a large new data centre in the Ottawa area at an estimated cost of up to $1.85-billion.

The new data centre will address growing demands on the operations of the Communications Security Establishment, the federal agency that provides tech security and foreign signals intelligence, as well as fulfill the government’s desire to onshore sovereign data systems, according to two sources with knowledge of the plan.

The federal government recently posted an advance procurement notice alerting the private sector that it intends to post a contracting opportunity early next year for a new data centre on the Ottawa side of the National Capital Region.

The new data centre is planned to be a 60-megawatt facility, placing it among the country’s larger data centres.

A national security source with knowledge of the project said the need for another data centre has been on Cse’s radar for some time. The agency’s capabilities and computing needs have increased in the face of a rapidly changing technological landscape and the proliferation of threats, the source said. Cse’s current data centre was designed over 15 years ago. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the source because they were not authorized to speak publicly about the matter.

The notice does not specify which department would use the data centre, but in an e-mail to The Globe and Mail, a CSE spokesperson said it will be for the agency’s use.

“CSE operates highly specialized systems that support Canada’s national security, foreign intelligence, cyber defence and secure Government of Canada operations. These activities require dedicated infrastructure designed to meet unique security, resilience and performance requirements,” said CSE spokesperson Janny Bender Asselin.

A senior government source, whom The Globe is not naming because they were not authorized to speak on the matter, said there is also a play for greater strategic autonomy.

While the procurement notice does not directly mention data sovereignty, the government has made several pledges over the past year signalling that securing and onshoring data systems is a high priority.

A document published last month by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada said building data centre capacity in Canada “can help strengthen Canada’s digital and economic sovereignty,” and “also help ensure critical computing capabilities and data remain in Canada.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney also referenced digital sovereignty during an announcement related to artificial intelligence in June.

“Where is the government of Canada going to hold your data and our national security data? It is going to hold it in Canada,” he said.

Data centres can be used to support cloud computing and artificial intelligence tools. But their proliferation has faced community pushback in some cases given that they often require substantial resources, including electricity and sometimes water.

The Globe recently published an interactive map of data centres across the country. According to that tool, the proposed CSE facility’s 60 MW capacity would be among the largest projects in Canada that are currently operating, but is smaller than many other announced data centre projects, several of which have a capacity of 200 MW or more.

For context, Meta Platforms Inc. announced in July that it plans to spend $13-billion on a 1-gigawatt data centre facility north of Edmonton.

The CSE data centre plan has not yet received Treasury Board approval.

The precise site for the data centre has not been finalized.

“To protect national security and the integrity of its operations, CSE does not disclose specific operational or technical requirements beyond what is publicly available,” the Cse’s spokesperson said.

The CSE headquarters is located east of Ottawa’s downtown, across the street from the headquarters of Canada’s spy agency, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service.

The two buildings are surrounded by residential neighbourhoods.

The CSE statement linked the planned contract to an announcement last month in which Ottawa launched a new framework for the responsible development of data centres.

The guidelines state that data centres must create lasting local benefits; must not shift electricity costs to Canadians; must minimize water use and environmental impacts; must be transparent about local impacts; and must bring strategic value to Canada.

The national security source told The Globe the data centre project is possible now because of the Carney government’s significant increase in defence spending. The CSE falls under the Department of National Defence.

The source said the CSE project will enhance Canada’s independent intelligence capabilities, but emphasized there is no scenario where Canadian intelligence data would have been processed or stored outside of the country.

The planned procurement will be led by Defence Construction Canada, a federal Crown corporation that provides contracting and construction contract management for Canada’s defence requirements.

With reports from Dexter McMillan in Toronto

stories.title: Morgan pitches shifting roadwork into high gear, Stevenson asks what took so long
stories.summary: “Londoners are frustrated with construction, and so am I,” admitted incumbent mayoral candidate Josh Morgan at the start of a campaign event to unveil his plan to address the impacts of road construction.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
“Londoners are frustrated with construction, and so am I,” admitted incumbent mayoral candidate Josh Morgan at the start of a campaign event to unveil his plan to address the impacts of road construction.

Morgan was flanked behind the podium by incumbent Ward 2 candidate Shawn Lewis and incumbent Ward 3 candidate Peter Cuddy as he detailed his plan.

“When you think about on Highbury Avenue away from the houses, there’s no reason why we can’t contemplate doing some overnight construction in our city in a way that allows us to complete the necessary infrastructure, but do it more efficiently,” he said.

Much of Morgan’s plan focusses on getting roadwork done faster.

If re-elected Morgan committed to:

Expand overnight and 24-hour work on major arterial roads not near homes, and use Artificial Intelligence to better model and sequence roadwork projects to minimize overlap

Make municipal procurement policies better reflect the experience London firms have, so local businesses can compete for local roadwork

Strictly enforce fines on construction projects that finish late, and reward companies that finish projects early with additional funding from the project’s contingency fund

Improve communication so Londoners are informed about how to get around the city during construction

Morgan says utilizing some funding from a project’s contingency as an incentive for firms to complete roadwork early is appropriate, “Using a bit of a carrot and stick approach. I think both are appropriate. It’s one of the ways that we could be more innovative and try something different. We spend our tax dollars (to) incentivize in a lot of different ways.”

Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson questions why Morgan’s solutions are coming years after it was first needed.

“All those things sound great, but he’s been a leader on council for 12 years and we approved a half-a-billion dollar construction project with BRT (Bus Rapid Transit). We could have used this earlier,” Stevenson asserted.

“We’ve tried overnight construction and paving on Wellington (Road). We’ve done some late night paving on Dundas (Street). It’s the novelty, not the norm right now,” Morgan explained. “What we’ve got to do is transition this into being the normal course of business now that we know it works.”

But Stevenson is skeptical, “I don’t know why it’s taking an election and a need for him to be re-elected to get the changes that Londoners deserved years ago.”

Morgan acknowledges similarities to a campaign announcement last month by council candidates Shawn Lewis and Steve Lehman to extend the length of time construction is permitted each day on certain road projects.

“This is what happens when you collaborate on council. You listen to your colleagues, you listen to their ideas, and nobody has a monopoly on good ideas,” he added.

stories.title: Canada must diversify trade away from the U.S. for security reasons: Freeland
stories.summary: Ottawa - Former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland says it's important for national security reasons that Canada do everything it can to diversify trade away from the United States.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland says it’s important for national security reasons that Canada do everything it can to diversify trade away from the United States.

During a discussion at the Council on Foreign Relations in New York on Thursday, Freeland said it’s dangerous to deepen or maintain a close economic relationship with a partner who “openly says they want to take you over.”

“Unfortunately, tragically, that’s where we are today,” she said.

U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly mused about turning Canada into the 51st state and, while he ruled out using military force to annex the country in January 2025, has said he would consider using “economic force.”

Even if the U.S. had a president who believed in free trade with Canada, Freeland said being dependent on any one partner is “not a great idea.”

“About 60 per cent of Canadians live within a hundred miles of the Canada-U.S. border,” said Freeland. “It makes a huge amount of sense for us to trade with you, but I think for national security reasons, we have to keep on doing everything we can to diversify.”

The Liberal government has set out to double non-U. S. exports over the next decade and have boasted of signing more than 20 strategic trade and defence agreements around the world amid trade tensions with the United States.

Freeland said the Canadian desire to diversify is “very, very long-standing.” She added that Canada’s push to deepen its relationship with the Europe is a continuation of Canadian policy, going back to the years when Stephen Harper was in power.

“I think that what you’re seeing now for sure is a desire in Canada and in Europe to make that relationship even closer,” she said. “I think that’s a good thing.”

In a speech to the European Parliament last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was opening the door to negotiating terms for Canada to become the first associate member of the European Union.

A day later, Prime Minister Mark Carney told the EU Parliament that Canada welcomes the goal, though exactly what that entails is still to be determined.

“We welcome this ambition — polling shows an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties,” Carney said in his speech.

Canada and the EU are holding a bilateral summit later this month. Many observers hope that meeting produces details of a proposed new partnership between Canada and the EU.

Freeland’s new book, “Unreliable Boyfriend,” was released this week and is part international analysis about the evolving role of the United States and part political memoir.

Its title is a reference to a comment she made on an American talk show in February, when she said the U.S. is “not a very reliable boyfriend right now.”

Freeland was former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s deputy prime minister for five years before resigning from cabinet in a dramatic split from the prime minister in December 2024, just hours before she was due to deliver the fall economic statement.

She rejoined cabinet under Carney, but resigned from the role late last year and stepped down from Parliament in January, taking up a role as an economic development adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and accepting a job as CEO of the Rhodes Trust.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

— With files from Dylan Robertson and Nick Murray

stories.title: Stevenson questions Morgan’s election compliance, incumbent calls letter ‘desperation’
stories.summary: Susan Stevenson’s campaign team sent a letter to the City Clerk’s office earlier this week, questioning whether several recent actions by incumbent mayoral candidate Josh Morgan complied with the Municipal Elections Act.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Morgan responded by calling the letter a sign of ‘desperation’ by Stevenson’s campaign.

“The intent is just to ensure that taxpayer-funded salaries are appropriately being used, and that there’s fair and clear rules around the use of city logos and premises,” Stevenson told CTV News.

Dated Oct. 14, the letter is titled, “Questions concerning use of City of London resources in the 2026 municipal election”

The four questions as written in the letter:

A screenshot attributed to Josh Morgan’s social-media reel shows the City Hall logo in a frame carrying the words “I’m asking for your vote. Question: Was the logo incidental background or deliberately incorporated into campaign messaging, and were City resources used? Is it ok for the city logo to be featured in this instance?

A comparison of mayorjoshmorgan.CA and joshmorgan.CA shows matching introductory wording. The civic-style site displays the City logo; the other identifies itself as a re-election website. Questions: Who created, maintained and paid for each site? Was City-produced content, photography or staff work used for campaign purposes? Why does the Mayor Josh Morgan website link to re election social media accounts with the same wording?

Concerns have been raised regarding the involvement of Mayor Josh Morgan’s Chief of Staff, John Fyfe-Millar, in re-election campaign activities during regular City business hours. Our campaign has observed and documented his attendance alongside Morgan at campaign-related events during weekday working hours.

These observations raise legitimate questions about whether taxpayer-funded staff time or municipal resources are being used for campaign purposes. While we recognize that employees May participate in political activities while on approved leave, the public deserves clarity about whether appropriate arrangements were in place and whether City and campaign responsibilities have remained separate.

We are calling for transparency regarding these activities and confirmation that municipal employment and resources are not being used to support any candidate’s re-election campaign

CTV interview screenshots show Morgan in apparent City Hall settings discussing tax and homelessness issues raised during the campaign, responding to Stevenson’s campaign announcements. Question: What distinguishes routine official responses to journalists from campaigning using City premises or resources?

Under Ontario’s Municipal Elections Act, municipal resources including staff time, facilities, and city branding cannot be used to support or oppose a candidate.

Morgan defends his campaign, telling CTV News that he has not heard from the City Clerk regarding the letter.

He pushes back against its questions and intent, “It’s not true. This is just desperation at its best! We follow the rules, each and every one of them.”

Stevenson flatly rejects Morgan’s suggestion that the letter implies desperation on the part of her campaign, “Over the course of the last four years, and throughout this campaign, the mayor has continued to throw stones from a very glass house.”

Regarding the use of city hall in the background of his campaign video, and similar content appearing on the two websites he asserts, “She (Stevenson) knows because she’s used city hall as a backdrop. She did it on city property, and I did it across the road. You can use city buildings in the backdrop of different images. You can be on the other side of the sidewalk.”

And in response to his Chief of Staff, John Fyfe-Millar appearing at campaign events during normal working hours, Morgan points to a flexible work schedule that can also include weekends and evenings, “(Staff) are doing what they’ve done the whole term. They’re using their flexible hours. And that’s all being tracked. John manages a great office, but he’s also allowed to volunteer for the campaign when he’s not working for the City of London.”

Morgan also defended being interviewed about the election while inside city hall.

“The media has every right to ask you questions wherever you are, and there’s an obligation in a free and democratic society to answer. And I will just remind Councillor Stevenson that in council chambers, we both answered questions about (a London) Acorn protest from a campaign perspective,” he added, referring to a news story that aired on CTV News last week about a housing protest and included comments from both candidates filmed immediately following a committee meeting.

In an emailed statement, City Clerk Michael Schulthess writes, “The City Clerk’s Office does not comment on potential penalties or enforcement action in specific cases. Generally speaking, the Municipal Elections Act, 1996 includes offence provisions and a broad range of penalties, including but not limited to fines, incarceration, and forfeiture of office. The application of those provisions and penalties falls within the purview of enforcement agencies, prosecutors, and the courts and is determined on a case-by-case basis.”

“We need clear direction from the Clerk’s Office on what is, and what is not allowed, that will be applied equally and fairly across all candidates,” Stevenson said.

Ten other candidates are running to be mayor of London, John Feher, Lawrence-Zachary Howe, Barry Douglas Jacklin, Tariq Khan, Kirsten Krose, Dan Lenart, Bronagh Joyce Morgan, Christine Rosehart, Jeff Yam, and Mustafa Zeboon.

Election Day is Oct. 26.

stories.title: Enigmatic rock lyricist Pye Dubois was the silent fifth member of Max Webster
stories.summary: After the band broke up, he kept writing songs for singer Kim Mitchell and contributed to four tracks recorded by Rush, including Tom Sawyer
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
On June 9, 1977, Max Webster, a band not a man, topped the bill at the city’s venerable Massey Hall for the first time. The stylish Toronto rockers opened the concert with Oh War! , a progressive-rock protest song.

“So, so long, soldier, wash your socks and guns,” frontman Kim Mitchell sang. “And just remember if you don’t see a profit, sell your stocks and run.”

Reviews of the show that ended with three encore sets were universally ecstatic. Trade magazine RPM Weekly, for one, wrote that the band “held the audience on the edge of their seats with a very tight set, both musically and stage-wise.”

Bob Mackowycz of Q107 (Cilq-FM) was particularly impressed with the lyrics: “They’re written by some bizarre character named Dubois. … He writes these surreal crazy songs about things like driving to the moon drunk or meeting a groupie in the washroom. They’re surreal, but the words really express Max Webster’s vision, which I guess is best summed up by the word ‘absurd.’”

The bizarre character was Pye Dubois, the band’s lyricist and non-performing fifth member. He made a rare public appearance at Massey Hall, briefly popping on stage and waving to the audience before Toronto Tontos , a song with bilingual lyrics: “Nous sommes fous/ Put down a little life from a morning cosmic.”

Mr. Dubois was born Paul Woods. (“Dubois” translates to “from the woods.”)

If nothing else, the sighting dispelled any rumours that the invisible songwriter May have been a fanciful creation cooked up by the band’s publicity people and record label. It was, after all, the seventies, a decade in which the mysterious Canadian band Klaatu was initially thought to be the Beatles undercover.

He had a big head of curls and an unapologetic mustache − a stockier Kurt Vonnegut. At Massey Hall, the man wore a white lab coat. Which was appropriate enough for the lyrical mad scientist of Canadian rock ’n’ roll.

Mr. Dubois died on Sept. 15. He was 77 and had been living in London, Ont. No details of his death were provided by the family in the death notice .

He was the chief word supplier for Max Webster, whose eclectic music was once described by Mr. Mitchell as “high-class curiosity rock.” Mr. Dubois wrote obsessively, supplying countless sheets of paper full of poetry and far-out ideas he called “flourishes” that could be edited into singable songs.

“For me, Pye was the most important part of the band,” said Martin Popoff, author of A Million Vacations: The Max Webster Story .

“He was a full creative partner,” author and musician Dave Bidini said. “The band counted on him.”

Mr. Dubois’s death is one of several in the Max Webster world this year. The band’s drummer Gary McCracken and keyboardists Terry Watkinson and Jim Bruton all died in 2026, as did Kim Mitchell’s drummer, Chris (Suds) Sutherland, and songwriting collaborator, Jim Chevalier.

Both Mr. Dubois and Mr. Mitchell hailed from Sarnia, Ont. Their songwriting relationship continued post-Max Webster into Mr. Mitchell’s more commercially successful solo career. Royalties from the co-written mid-eighties hits Go for Soda and Patio Lanterns helped sustain him.

He also contributed to four songs recorded by legendary Canadian prog-rock trio Rush: Force Ten , Between Sun and Moon , Test for Echo and Tom Sawyer . The latter was one of the band’s most enduring hits.

“In my company, Pye was always very friendly and upbeat but remained a rather private person when it came to his life outside music. His background was more of a matter of speculation than fact for those of us outside their band,” Rush singer-bassist Geddy Lee told The Globe. “Adding his voice to our songs gave it a different twist, and twists and turns in our music were what Rush was all about.”

Mr. Dubois was inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2021 with songwriting partner Mr. Mitchell but never picked up his trophy. “I still have it,” Mr. Popoff said. “Pye was a little bit of an enigma. Some people described him as reclusive, but I would characterize him as secretive.”

Mr. Dubois held down a job for years at Toronto’s Clarke Institute of Psychiatry (now part of the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health).

He was a fan of Frank Zappa, Joni Mitchell, Kate Bush and fellow inscrutable persona Captain Beefheart, and was among a unique class of non-performing rock lyricists associated with a particular band: Pete Brown with Cream; Keith Reid with Procol Harum; Robert Hunter and John Perry Barlow with the Grateful Dead.

Despite not being a musician, Mr. Dubois toured with Max Webster, living and documenting the rock ‘n’ roll dream like a war correspondent embedded with troops.

“If I’m not on the road with those guys, songs like The Party and Oh War! and America’s Veins don’t happen,” he once said.

From his spot backstage, he observed the interaction between fans and musicians. On The Party , for example: “We’re all here for a celebration, the madcap scene and the max machine.” The 1979 single Paradise Skies poetically captured the thrill and mystique of live music:

Tonight, inaugurates rock and roll wings

Tonight, we’ll turn the world around

And we’ll hover and we’ll leave the ground

And the magic we need frees the dancer we wanna be

Mr. Mitchell’s 1989 double-Platinum solo album Rockland was co-written with his wordsmith wingman. The biggest hits were Rocklandwonderland and Rock N Roll Duty . The latter song took just a half-hour to come together.

“I had the riff and Pye came over and I started to sing nonsense to the changes, and he just went for writing lines down,” Mr. Mitchell said. “Thirty minutes later it was finished. [It’s] the only song that went that fast.”

The last of Mr. Mitchell’s albums the pair wrote together was 1994’s Itch . “I’m sure they had a complicated relationship,” Mr. Wegner said. “They were making music intensely together for 20 years.”

Though Mr. Dubois’s lyrics could be abstract and free-form, he did consider who would be singing his words. “I remember him telling me that he liked the way “r” sounded on Kim’s voice. So, sometimes to that end he would favour one word over another in a lyric,” said Todd Booth, who also collaborated with Mr. Mitchell.

Mr. Dubois’s last songwriting co-credit was for Rush’s Test for Echo , a biting critique of modern media and the American justice system, which reached the top of Billboard’s mainstream rock airplay chart in 1996. “What a show,” the chorus went. “Vertigo.”

Paul Phillip Woods was born on Oct. 6, 1948. His parents were Sam Woods and Noreen Woods. Part of his upbringing was portrayed in Mr. Mitchell’s 1986 hit Patio Lanterns , a hummable, nostalgic and autobiographical song about middle-schoolers drinking lemonade, listening to Bobby Vinton’s Blue on Blue and working up the nerve to ask for a dance at a patio party in the early 1960s.

Growing up, Sarnia native Mary Ellen Wigle lived behind the Woods family’s house. Because she was years younger than Mr. Dubois and his friends, she could only watch the parties from her bedroom window.

“I vividly remember the backyard with a big tree and the patio lanterns that were there every summer,” she said. “ Patio Lanterns paints a picture of an idyllic time. You’re young, you’re shy and you’re just beginning to have feelings for the opposite sex.”

Mr. Dubois’s upbringing, however, was not altogether idyllic. While attending St. Clair Secondary School (since renamed Great Lakes Secondary School) he left home to stay with a friend’s family.

“I didn’t like my parents and they didn’t like me, so I thought I’d try to survive adolescence on my own,” he said in a 1979 Toronto Sun interview.

He began writing lyrics at the age of 13. Though Mr. Dubois and Mr. Mitchell did not attend the same high schools, they shared the directionless glory of coming of age in small-city Ontario.

“We’d walk the streets and we’d skip high school and be smoking cigarettes out the back,” Mr. Dubois told biographer Mr. Popoff. “I can remember a couple basements we used to go to. The parents would let us go and we’d listen to Zappa’s 200 Motels or something. Someone usually had a joint.”

While enrolled at Lakehead University in Thunder Bay, Mr. Dubois split for Greece, where Mr. Mitchell had landed a steady gig with a crooner. The guitarist recalled the incident in a 1982 interview with Music Express magazine.

“I’m living on one of the Greek islands, no one knows where, and Pye decides to visit me. He flies to Greece, gets a boat to the right island − all of this on instinct − takes a cab to the town and stopped in front of three or four apartment buildings. He picks the one that hasn’t been finished, walks up to the third floor, down the corridor and opens the door to my room, where I’m sleeping. I mean, the guy’s a bit … psychic, I think. Too many things like that have happened.”

The pair would collaborate on all five Max Webster albums, beginning with the band’s 1976 self-titled debut. Their songwriting on Mr. Mitchell’s solo efforts produced the enduring summer rock anthems I Am a Wild Party and Lager & Ale .

“My favourite is Go for Soda , with the line, ‘Might as well go for a soda, nobody drowns and nobody dies,’” said singer-songwriter and Sarnia native Donovan Woods. “It always makes me think of kids jumping off the base of the Blue Water Bridge outside of Sarnia and letting the current haul you down the St. Clair River, which people, including me, often did drunk. Some drowned.”

Though not specifically about the perils of drinking and driving, Go for Soda was adopted as an anthem by Mothers Against Drunk Driving.

“That type of slogan songwriting is kind of amazing,” Mr. Woods said. “When you read the titles, it seems like they’d all run the risk of turning schlockey, but they don’t. There are lots of ideas in all of them.”

Mr. Dubois’s lyrics were typically evocative, whether their meaning was vague or more straightforward. He told the Toronto Sun in 1979 that his function as a lyricist was to show people aspects of reality: “I could never do something as pretentious as persuade them.”

His songwriting partner appreciated Mr. Dubois’s gift for metaphor and symbolism rather than clean narratives. “He built pictures in your mind and images, and that’s what I loved about his stuff,” Mr. Mitchell told The Toronto Star’s Nick Krewen in 2021.

If his lyrics were hard to pin down, so was Mr. Dubois. He kept a low profile after he stopped working with Mr. Mitchell. In Toronto he could be found at the Detroit Eatery, a neighbourhood institution on Toronto’s Danforth Avenue destroyed by fire in 2019. In retirement he divided his time between Florida and Ontario.

“He battled himself a little bit,” Mr. Bidini said. “He would come to see our band, Rheostatics, but then leave before we got on stage. He was a little ghostly in that way. He was there, and then he wasn’t.”

Mr. Dubois leaves his brothers, Dave Woods and Rob Woods.

paragraphs: On June 9, 1977, Max Webster, a band not a man, topped the bill at the city’s venerable Massey Hall for the first time. The stylish Toronto rockers opened the concert with Oh War! , a progressive-rock protest song.
“So, so long, soldier, wash your socks and guns,” frontman Kim Mitchell sang. “And just remember if you don’t see a profit, sell your stocks and run.”

Reviews of the show that ended with three encore sets were universally ecstatic. Trade magazine RPM Weekly, for one, wrote that the band “held the audience on the edge of their seats with a very tight set, both musically and stage-wise.”

Bob Mackowycz of Q107 (Cilq-FM) was particularly impressed with the lyrics: “They’re written by some bizarre character named Dubois. … He writes these surreal crazy songs about things like driving to the moon drunk or meeting a groupie in the washroom. They’re surreal, but the words really express Max Webster’s vision, which I guess is best summed up by the word ‘absurd.’”

The bizarre character was Pye Dubois, the band’s lyricist and non-performing fifth member. He made a rare public appearance at Massey Hall, briefly popping on stage and waving to the audience before Toronto Tontos , a song with bilingual lyrics: “Nous sommes fous/ Put down a little life from a morning cosmic.”
Mr. Dubois was born Paul Woods. (“Dubois” translates to “from the woods.”)

If nothing else, the sighting dispelled any rumours that the invisible songwriter May have been a fanciful creation cooked up by the band’s publicity people and record label. It was, after all, the seventies, a decade in which the mysterious Canadian band Klaatu was initially thought to be the Beatles undercover.

He had a big head of curls and an unapologetic mustache − a stockier Kurt Vonnegut. At Massey Hall, the man wore a white lab coat. Which was appropriate enough for the lyrical mad scientist of Canadian rock ’n’ roll.
Mr. Dubois died on Sept. 15. He was 77 and had been living in London, Ont. No details of his death were provided by the family in the death notice .

He was the chief word supplier for Max Webster, whose eclectic music was once described by Mr. Mitchell as “high-class curiosity rock.” Mr. Dubois wrote obsessively, supplying countless sheets of paper full of poetry and far-out ideas he called “flourishes” that could be edited into singable songs.
“For me, Pye was the most important part of the band,” said Martin Popoff, author of A Million Vacations: The Max Webster Story .
“He was a full creative partner,” author and musician Dave Bidini said. “The band counted on him.”

Mr. Dubois’s death is one of several in the Max Webster world this year. The band’s drummer Gary McCracken and keyboardists Terry Watkinson and Jim Bruton all died in 2026, as did Kim Mitchell’s drummer, Chris (Suds) Sutherland, and songwriting collaborator, Jim Chevalier.

Both Mr. Dubois and Mr. Mitchell hailed from Sarnia, Ont. Their songwriting relationship continued post-Max Webster into Mr. Mitchell’s more commercially successful solo career. Royalties from the co-written mid-eighties hits Go for Soda and Patio Lanterns helped sustain him.

He also contributed to four songs recorded by legendary Canadian prog-rock trio Rush: Force Ten , Between Sun and Moon , Test for Echo and Tom Sawyer . The latter was one of the band’s most enduring hits.

“In my company, Pye was always very friendly and upbeat but remained a rather private person when it came to his life outside music. His background was more of a matter of speculation than fact for those of us outside their band,” Rush singer-bassist Geddy Lee told The Globe. “Adding his voice to our songs gave it a different twist, and twists and turns in our music were what Rush was all about.”

Mr. Dubois was inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2021 with songwriting partner Mr. Mitchell but never picked up his trophy. “I still have it,” Mr. Popoff said. “Pye was a little bit of an enigma. Some people described him as reclusive, but I would characterize him as secretive.”
Mr. Dubois held down a job for years at Toronto’s Clarke Institute of Psychiatry (now part of the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health).

He was a fan of Frank Zappa, Joni Mitchell, Kate Bush and fellow inscrutable persona Captain Beefheart, and was among a unique class of non-performing rock lyricists associated with a particular band: Pete Brown with Cream; Keith Reid with Procol Harum; Robert Hunter and John Perry Barlow with the Grateful Dead.
Despite not being a musician, Mr. Dubois toured with Max Webster, living and documenting the rock ‘n’ roll dream like a war correspondent embedded with troops.
“If I’m not on the road with those guys, songs like The Party and Oh War! and America’s Veins don’t happen,” he once said.

From his spot backstage, he observed the interaction between fans and musicians. On The Party , for example: “We’re all here for a celebration, the madcap scene and the max machine.” The 1979 single Paradise Skies poetically captured the thrill and mystique of live music:
Tonight, inaugurates rock and roll wings
Tonight, we’ll turn the world around
And we’ll hover and we’ll leave the ground
And the magic we need frees the dancer we wanna be

Mr. Mitchell’s 1989 double-Platinum solo album Rockland was co-written with his wordsmith wingman. The biggest hits were Rocklandwonderland and Rock N Roll Duty . The latter song took just a half-hour to come together.

“I had the riff and Pye came over and I started to sing nonsense to the changes, and he just went for writing lines down,” Mr. Mitchell said. “Thirty minutes later it was finished. [It’s] the only song that went that fast.”
The last of Mr. Mitchell’s albums the pair wrote together was 1994’s Itch . “I’m sure they had a complicated relationship,” Mr. Wegner said. “They were making music intensely together for 20 years.”

Though Mr. Dubois’s lyrics could be abstract and free-form, he did consider who would be singing his words. “I remember him telling me that he liked the way “r” sounded on Kim’s voice. So, sometimes to that end he would favour one word over another in a lyric,” said Todd Booth, who also collaborated with Mr. Mitchell.

Mr. Dubois’s last songwriting co-credit was for Rush’s Test for Echo , a biting critique of modern media and the American justice system, which reached the top of Billboard’s mainstream rock airplay chart in 1996. “What a show,” the chorus went. “Vertigo.”

Paul Phillip Woods was born on Oct. 6, 1948. His parents were Sam Woods and Noreen Woods. Part of his upbringing was portrayed in Mr. Mitchell’s 1986 hit Patio Lanterns , a hummable, nostalgic and autobiographical song about middle-schoolers drinking lemonade, listening to Bobby Vinton’s Blue on Blue and working up the nerve to ask for a dance at a patio party in the early 1960s.

Growing up, Sarnia native Mary Ellen Wigle lived behind the Woods family’s house. Because she was years younger than Mr. Dubois and his friends, she could only watch the parties from her bedroom window.

“I vividly remember the backyard with a big tree and the patio lanterns that were there every summer,” she said. “ Patio Lanterns paints a picture of an idyllic time. You’re young, you’re shy and you’re just beginning to have feelings for the opposite sex.”
Mr. Dubois’s upbringing, however, was not altogether idyllic. While attending St. Clair Secondary School (since renamed Great Lakes Secondary School) he left home to stay with a friend’s family.
“I didn’t like my parents and they didn’t like me, so I thought I’d try to survive adolescence on my own,” he said in a 1979 Toronto Sun interview.
He began writing lyrics at the age of 13. Though Mr. Dubois and Mr. Mitchell did not attend the same high schools, they shared the directionless glory of coming of age in small-city Ontario.

“We’d walk the streets and we’d skip high school and be smoking cigarettes out the back,” Mr. Dubois told biographer Mr. Popoff. “I can remember a couple basements we used to go to. The parents would let us go and we’d listen to Zappa’s 200 Motels or something. Someone usually had a joint.”

While enrolled at Lakehead University in Thunder Bay, Mr. Dubois split for Greece, where Mr. Mitchell had landed a steady gig with a crooner. The guitarist recalled the incident in a 1982 interview with Music Express magazine.

“I’m living on one of the Greek islands, no one knows where, and Pye decides to visit me. He flies to Greece, gets a boat to the right island − all of this on instinct − takes a cab to the town and stopped in front of three or four apartment buildings. He picks the one that hasn’t been finished, walks up to the third floor, down the corridor and opens the door to my room, where I’m sleeping. I mean, the guy’s a bit … psychic, I think. Too many things like that have happened.”

The pair would collaborate on all five Max Webster albums, beginning with the band’s 1976 self-titled debut. Their songwriting on Mr. Mitchell’s solo efforts produced the enduring summer rock anthems I Am a Wild Party and Lager & Ale .

“My favourite is Go for Soda , with the line, ‘Might as well go for a soda, nobody drowns and nobody dies,’” said singer-songwriter and Sarnia native Donovan Woods. “It always makes me think of kids jumping off the base of the Blue Water Bridge outside of Sarnia and letting the current haul you down the St. Clair River, which people, including me, often did drunk. Some drowned.”
Though not specifically about the perils of drinking and driving, Go for Soda was adopted as an anthem by Mothers Against Drunk Driving.

“That type of slogan songwriting is kind of amazing,” Mr. Woods said. “When you read the titles, it seems like they’d all run the risk of turning schlockey, but they don’t. There are lots of ideas in all of them.”

Mr. Dubois’s lyrics were typically evocative, whether their meaning was vague or more straightforward. He told the Toronto Sun in 1979 that his function as a lyricist was to show people aspects of reality: “I could never do something as pretentious as persuade them.”

His songwriting partner appreciated Mr. Dubois’s gift for metaphor and symbolism rather than clean narratives. “He built pictures in your mind and images, and that’s what I loved about his stuff,” Mr. Mitchell told The Toronto Star’s Nick Krewen in 2021.

If his lyrics were hard to pin down, so was Mr. Dubois. He kept a low profile after he stopped working with Mr. Mitchell. In Toronto he could be found at the Detroit Eatery, a neighbourhood institution on Toronto’s Danforth Avenue destroyed by fire in 2019. In retirement he divided his time between Florida and Ontario.

“He battled himself a little bit,” Mr. Bidini said. “He would come to see our band, Rheostatics, but then leave before we got on stage. He was a little ghostly in that way. He was there, and then he wasn’t.”
Mr. Dubois leaves his brothers, Dave Woods and Rob Woods.

stories.title: Author Steven Galloway concludes testimony at Vancouver defamation trial
stories.summary: Author and former University of British Columbia creative writing chair Steven Galloway has concluded testifying in his defamation lawsuit trial in Vancouver.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
Vancouver — Author and former University of British Columbia creative writing chair Steven Galloway has concluded testifying in his defamation lawsuit trial in Vancouver.

Galloway, who alleges the defendants defamed him by publishing unproven allegations of sexual assault, took questions from Glynnis Kirchmeier, a defendant in the case who is representing herself and attending the trial remotely.

The former UBC student pressed Galloway about whether he believed she had been involved with an advocacy group for victims of sexual violence and harassment, and had also contacted other defendants, including A.B., another former student who made the allegations against Galloway.

Galloway says he found it “unlikely” Kirchmeier wasn’t involved with the group because she was on one of its fundraising pages, and he recalled becoming nauseated about one of her Tweets, and wondering “why is this person I’ve never met calling me a rapist?”

The court heard during the brief hearing in B.C. Supreme Court on Thursday that the next witness is expected to be Ronna Syed, a producer for the CBC program the “Fifth Estate.”

Galloway, who has been testifying since last week, said earlier in the trial that Syed was the first journalist to call him after the allegations surfaced, and says he told her “no comment.”

Galloway filed the defamation lawsuit in 2018 but several defendants have settled with him and published public apologies.

The author of “The Cellist of Sarajevo” alleges his career was destroyed by the allegations of rape and sexual assault, which he denies and were found unsubstantiated in a report by a former B.C. Supreme Court judge.

The court heard last week that A.B.’s defence no longer includes an assertion she was assaulted by Galloway, but rather that she reported the alleged assaults.

Galloway has testified he felt ashamed at having an affair with A.B., who cannot be named due to a publication ban, but there was no prohibition on sexual relationships between faculty and students at UBC and he knew of “numerous” other examples.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Darryl Greer, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Suspect sought for alleged assault at anti-Israel protest in Toronto turns himself in
stories.summary: Video footage appeared to show the attacker strike the victim from behind, pull him to the sidewalk and punch him repeatedly.
stories.author: Jerusalem News Syndicate
stories.content:
A man surrendered himself to police on Monday after allegedly punching a person repeatedly in the head at an anti-Israel demonstration on Oct. 10 in Toronto.

The Toronto Police Service’s hate crime unit alleges that Martin Salgatar, 20, of Mississauga, was walking in a demonstration near Yonge and Grosvenor Streets when he attacked the victim from behind without provocation.

The blows knocked the victim to the ground, injuring his face and leg, according to police.

A police spokesman told JNS it was a “pro-Palestine event” and that the hate crime unit investigates “any arrests made at demonstrations.”

Video footage that circulated on social media appeared to show the attacker strike the victim from behind, pull him to the sidewalk and punch him repeatedly, as fellow anti-Israel protesters tried to stop him.

The protesters then appear to berate the victim, who is on the ground bleeding from the face, and a man wearing a sweatshirt with an upside-down red triangle—a Hamas terror symbol—seems to curse the victim and accuse him of “trying to pick fights.”

“You f deserve it, you piece of sh,” the man yells.

After a screenshot of the suspect’s face from the video footage circulated on Monday, Salgatar turned himself in.

stories.title: ‘It is very unfortunate’: Winnipeg candidate says election signs vandalized, similar incidents occurring across the country
stories.summary: Nafiya Naso's signs have been spray-painted with negative messaging and inappropriate pictures, with some signs reading “Ur not win” and “Loser.”
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Winnipeg – Nafiya Naso is hoping to become the next city councillor for Winnipeg’s Waverly West district, marking her first run for public office.

With fewer than two weeks until election day, Naso has been busy on the campaign trail.

But amid the demands of campaigning, she is also navigating challenges that she says have taken time and attention away from her bid for city council.

“I’ve had about 45 signs that have been vandalized,” she said. “It is unfortunate.”

Her signs have been spray-painted with negative messaging and inappropriate pictures, with some signs reading “Ur not win” and “Loser.”

She says her signs are being vandalized every day.

“Unfortunately, this has taken a lot of time out of our campaign,” she said.

“I have about five volunteers that drive around and babysit these signs. They’re literally babysitting them because every day we have signs that are being torn off fences. They’re being kicked down. They’re being spray painted. This is literally every single day.”

Naso isn’t the only candidate in the city dealing with this issue.

CTV News recently spoke with Naso’s competitor, Jasmine Brar, who has been dealing with a similar situation.

“It’s pretty disturbing, honestly,” Brar told CTV News on Sept. 26.

“It looks like somebody just went out with a knife or something. They sliced the signs. They did not just break it. So, it’s very intentional.”

Christian Sweryda, who is running for city councillor in the Elmwood East-Kildonan district, recently posted on his social media that his signs were also damaged.

“We have noticed that this is the second major incident of signs being vandalized or stolen,” he wrote on social media. “We are going to keep going with the campaign.”

A spokesperson for the Winnipeg Police Service told CTV News they are aware of these incidents and that investigations are ongoing.

“The WPS take all reports of vandalism seriously and will investigate thoroughly. The public is encouraged to report these incidents so they can be investigated,” said Const. Pat Saydak in a statement.

Incidents across the country

Similar incidents have been reported by candidates in other communities across the country.

Video surveillance captured footage of someone taking a sign off private property in Orangeville, Ont., just northwest of Toronto.

Referendum signs in Fort McMurray, Alta. were also damaged with spray paint earlier this month.

Political science professor Christopher Adams says election sign vandalism is not new, but he believes the behaviour has become more common in recent years.

“I think that’s because people think they have a green light to be out of the proper world of etiquette or of proper behaviour,” said Adams, who works at the University of Manitoba.

“There seems to be a bit of an anger sometimes among voters that seeks to find an outlet, and I think that’s unfortunate.”

He says there are a few reasons these incidents are taking place.

“Social media feeds into extreme views, and I think there are people who feel that their extreme views are acceptable,” he said.

‘Motivates me even more’

As for Naso, she is trying to put all of her energy into running her campaign, instead of letting these incidents distract her.

“Every day I hear one or two signs have been knocked down,” she said.

“It just motivates me even more to work harder and knock on more doors in the evening.”

The Winnipeg civic election is on Oct. 28.

With files from CTV News’ Devon McKendrick

stories.title: Koats for Kids campaign in need of winter clothing donations
stories.summary: Donations are slowly trickling in at the Boys and Girls Club (BGC) of London on Horton Street but organizers say a lot more is needed to keep up with the growing demand for this coming winter.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Donations are slowly trickling in at the Boys and Girls Club (BGC) of London on Horton Street but organizers say a lot more is needed to keep up with the growing demand for this coming winter.

“If people can look in their closets and find any clothing that your kids outgrew, it can help another child during the winter.” said Nafis Ahmed with BGC London.

For more than 35 years the Koats for Kids campaign has helped thousands in our community stay warm during the coldest months of the year.

“We are looking for clothing of any sizes but particularly for small children, boots, hats, mitts and coats,” said Ahmed. “The economy is bad for a lot of people with things being expensive especially for newcomers to Canada and people who can’t afford coats.”

This year the campaign has joined forces with other organizations so they can assist more children.

“We have joined with Western Fair District, Kiwanis Clubs of London and the London Muslim Mosque so we can reach more families in need,” said Ahmed.

There are 20 drop-off locations across the city. The deadline to donate is Nov. 1. For more information visit the BGC London website .

Also if you know a family in need, the clothing will be distributed at the Boys and Girls Club on Horton Street on Saturday, Nov. 7 and then on Saturday, Nov. 14 at the London Muslim Mosque on Oxford Street West.

stories.title: The poll-ar bear results are in, Winnipeg zoo reveals cub’s new name
stories.summary: After a record-setting number of votes, the Assiniboine Park Zoo said it has determined its new polar bear cub's name. His name is an homage to where he was found, Churchill, Man.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The votes are in, and the Assiniboine Park Zoo’s newest polar bear has officially been named “Mantayo,” the zoo said on social media.

A record setting number of votes were cast during the polling process, which opened last week and closed Tuesday, according to the zoo’s post. Four names were on the ballot, all of which were nods to Churchill, Man., where the cub was found and rescued after his mom died.

Mantayo is derived from the Cree name for a large river in Churchill called “Mantayo Seepee” or “Mantayo Sîpî,” the zoo said. In English, that translates to the River of Strangers.

The name beat out three competitors – Duke, Marly and Fletcher.

Duke and Marly honoured the local school that serves students from kindergarten to Grade 12 in Churchill, the Duke of Marlborough School, the zoo said.

Fletcher, like the winner, was also an homage to a northern Manitoba waterway, it added. The suggestion honoured Fletcher Lake, which is in Wapusk National Park – a common place for polar bear mothers to den with their cubs.

stories.title: Canada’s EV sales are growing, but not fast enough: expert
stories.summary: Electric vehicle sales grew substantially in Q3 but one expert says they still are not on pace to reach the federal government’s updated EV and emissions targets.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
New data shows a substantial growth in electric vehicle sales in Canada, but one expert says they still are not on track to reach the federal government’s updated EV and emissions targets.

EV purchases increased 55 per cent in August 2026 compared to the same month last year, newly-released data from Statistics Canada shows.

“It’s a little bit surprising, a little stronger than we would have expected,” Robert Karwell, director of OEM solutions with JD Power, told Global News.

JD Power’s own analysis, conducted with data from automotive dealers, shows that EV sales increased two percentage points in the third quarter of 2026, now making up seven per cent of the market share.

If plug-in hybrids and direct-to-consumer vehicles, like Tesla, are included, Karwell said that number increases to approximately 10 per cent.

The Government of Canada previously set a target of achieving 60 per cent of all new vehicles sold being electric by 2030. By 2035, that share was pledged to be 100 per cent.

In February, the federal government announced a major shift in its national auto strategy, repealing the 2023 standards with new standards that require 75 per cent of vehicles sold to be electric by 2035 and 90 per cent by 2040.

Karwell said that even with the boost in Q3 and the less aggressive target, Canada is still far from achieving it.

“The data right now is telling us no,” he said. “While they’re doing better, they’re not on that path.”

But he said he does think uptake will continue to increase, especially as the cost drops.

“Vehicles, ON average, are getting more expensive by about one and a half percent,” Karwell said. “The interesting thing with EVs is that, and I guess this isn’t surprising considering they’re more popular, is they’re actually getting cheaper to buy on average.”

As technologies continue to evolve, Karwell said the price to go electric will continue to decline, coming closer and closer to the cost of the average gas-powered vehicle. Government incentives will also help to close the gap.

Right now, he said that gap sits at around $7,000.

The gap for hybrid vehicles is around $3,000 to $4,000.

“A lot of Canadians have voted with their feet and their wallets and are purchasing a hybrid vehicle as kind of another option amongst electrified vehicles amongst alternative power trains,” Karwell said, adding that hybrid vehicles make up approximately 17 per cent of the market share.

He said hybrid vehicles are also becoming a more suitable option for many people who May not own their own homes with a place to charge their vehicles.

“Homes are really expensive. If you don’t own a home, where are you going to recharge?” he said.

Challenges associated with charging infrastructure continue to remain an inhibitor to a full adoption of electric vehicles, Karwell added.

In July, the federal government announced $9 million to install nearly 400 chargers across Canada.

stories.title: B.C.'s Eby says proposed Indigenous land transfer legislation is about saving money
stories.summary: British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby is defending draft plans by his previous government to limit the compensation of forest companies when land is transferred to First Nations.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A forest industry leader would like to cut down a plan by the previous government to limit the compensation of forest companies when land is transferred to First Nations, but British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby has defended the proposal.

Kim Haakstad, president of the Council of Forest Industries, said it was unfair for government to ask businesses to absorb the costs.

“But particularly right now, this is one more way that the government is making it hard for forest products manufacturing companies to continue to operate in British Columbia,” Haakstad said.

The province compensated companies in 2003, when it took about 20 per cent of tenures to create BC Timber Sales. “I believe the same principle should apply,” she said.

Confidential documents published in the Northern Beat, an online publication, said Eby’s government had previously committed to transferring about 400 parcels of Crown land to First Nations, while limiting compensation for companies with timber rights on the land.

Eby said the transfers reflected existing treaties and other commitments under the process of reconciliation, some of them dating back decades, and the proposed legislation was about reducing costs for taxpayers.

The documents said the current law requires the government to compensate forestry firms, but “given ongoing fiscal constraints,” that would create substantial barriers to completing land returns.

A spokesperson for the Eby campaign said the draft legislation would limit compensation, and if a land transfer affected less than five per cent of the annual allowable cut for a license, the holders would not receive any compensation at all.

The briefing notes, dated Sept. 10, were revealed just days before the provincial election on Oct. 24.

The New Democrat platform doesn’t mention the plans, while forest companies had to sign non-disclosure agreements if they wanted to see them.

Eby said such agreements are standard, and he rejected suggestions of secrecy.

“It’s not a new thing, and what it does, it provides a little bit of relief in terms of cost for taxpayers for these agreements, some of which are historic with First Nations,” he said during an unrelated campaign announcement in Surrey, B.C.

Asked how the proposed legislation would help forest companies avoid job losses during a time of economic difficulties, Eby said transfers of tenure to local groups and First Nations help the industry by keeping logs and jobs in communities.

“To characterize it as something that obstructs forestry is actually the complete opposite of what’s happening here,” he said. “It’s about minimizing the impact on taxpayers of these kinds of agreements.”

A spokesperson for the campaign said cabinet approved engagement with stakeholders in July, but the proposal was draft, not final legislation. The engagement was considering adjustments to how compensation works in a limited number of cases where transfers affect land on which there are forest licenses.

The B.C. Conservatives issued a statement Thursday saying the plans constituted “more secret dealings” by Eby’s NDP.

“As is usually the case, David Eby is refusing to be upfront and honest with British Columbians,” the party said.

Haakstad, meanwhile, said more than 20 mills have closed in B.C. since 2023 and others continue to operate below full capacity.

“It’s not just the duty and tariff environment all the time,” but also the “homegrown challenges that we have created,” she said.

Haakstad said she hopes the New Democrats will reconsider the proposal if they are re-elected to form government.

“They need to have a budget for how they fund the agreements that they make with (First Nations) and I support many of the agreements,” she added.

Forest companies support the work of reconciliation, she said, and have many significant partnerships with First Nations.

But if government commits to costs, it needs to pay for those costs, she said. “Asking forest companies to absorb that is generally unfair.”

Companies haven’t been at the table for the proposal, she said. “We know there are 400 parcels of land, but we have no idea where those parcels are. We have little information about what the likely impacts, and I think that is a troubling pattern.”

Haakstad said she was not convinced that non-disclosure agreements were needed in the situation, but her organization nonetheless signed one.

She could not say how many other industry groups or companies did the same.

“We had concerns at Cofi about NDAs, but when we sign them, we respect, and we work with legal counsel … because I don’t want to break an NDA.

“Somebody has done that,” she added. “I wouldn’t have. I would have respected it. But elections make for interesting times, right?”

Conservatives said in their 2024 election platform that returning land to First Nations was critical for achieving economic self-sufficiency.

The party said at the time it was “committed to the strategic and collaborative return of land to First Nations, enabling bands to forge their own economic future.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: B.C. Conservatives cut ties with candidate over posts about the Holocaust and Hitler
stories.summary: The party distanced itself from Vancouver-Strathcona candidate Jordan McIntosh after posts about the Holocaust and Hitler were brought to light
stories.author: J.J. Adams
stories.content:
The B.C. Conservative party has cut ties with Vancouver-Strathcona candidate Jordan McIntosh after he was accused of tweeting about Hitler and downplaying the Holocaust.

Within hours of NDP candidate Callista Ryan posting screenshots on X of what she claimed were McIntosh’s posts, the Conservative party deleted McIntosh from its website and said he wouldn’t sit with the caucus if elected.

It’s the second time in as many weeks that Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson has dropped a candidate over offensive social media posts. Joachim Agou, the former Tory candidate in the Victoria-Beacon Hill riding, was turfed from the party after he posted comments praising violence against pro-Palestine protesters.

Agou, in a now-deleted social media post, had commented on a video of a car crashing into a crowd of pro-Palestine protesters in Lausanne, Switzerland, last year, saying: “He should have reversed too!”

In that case, Agou said he would continue to run as an independent, and, in an apology posted to Facebook, took responsibility for his comments.

“Taken on their own, my words could be read as supporting violence. I should have expressed myself more clearly and calmly,” he wrote.

McIntosh hasn’t said if he will continue to run as an Independent in the strongly NDP-leaning riding.

In Wednesday night’s debate among party leaders, Doerkson alleged there was an antisemitic faction within the NDP, pointing at the departure of former cabinet minister Selina Robinson, who resigned from cabinet in 2024 after being caught up in a controversy for saying Israel was founded on “a crappy piece of land with nothing on it.”

stories.title: RCMP won’t reveal toxicology results in crash that killed 2, including Roughrider Captain
stories.summary: The Saskatchewan RCMP has concluded its collision reconstruction investigation into a crash outside of Regina that killed a 22-year-old man and a Roughriders linebacker.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Results of the toxicology report of Jayden Dalke , the Saskatchewan Roughrider who was involved in a fatal collision this summer, will not be shared publicly according to RCMP.

Two people, Bhishma Rajyaguru, 22, and 30-year-old Dalke, died in the collision on Highway 11 between Lumsden and Regina on July 18. Almost three months later, the Saskatchewan RCMP said in a news release Thursday its collision reconstruction investigation has concluded.

The details communicated Thursday confirmed the information that was previously shared by Mounties, including that the silver SUV Dalke was driving was in the southbound lane heading northbound on the highway.

The reconstruction investigation also affirmed alcohol and cannabis were in the linebacker’s vehicle, the RCMP said. Whether Dalke had ingested those intoxicants remains unclear, as police are not releasing his toxicology report, claiming it is personal health information.

“The (Saskatchewan) Coroner’s Service has advised the RCMP they will not be releasing this information publicly,” it added, noting consultations were conducted with the RCMP’s Information Management Team and the families involved.

Police said it did not locate cannabis or alcohol in the black SUV Rajyaguru was driving.

Further information regarding the circumstances of the fatal collision will not be shared publicly, as it will never be presented in court, according to police.

stories.title: Manitoba government says it will use crypto levy to reduce hydro rates
stories.summary: Winnipeg - The Manitoba government says it plans direct revenue from a levy on crypto operations to reducing hydro rates.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Winnipeg - The Manitoba government says it plans direct revenue from a levy on crypto operations to reducing residential hydro rates.

Finance Minister Adrien Sala said Thursday that the government expects the measure to bring in about $20 million based on current crypto operations, which would translate into $50 a year in savings per ratepayer household.

stories.title: The Canadian Press celebrates 75th anniversary of its French services
stories.summary: Montreal - The Canadian Press is celebrating the 75th anniversary of its French-language service, which sent out its first dispatches on Sept. 30, 1951.
stories.author: Pierre Saint-Arnaud The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The Canadian Press is celebrating the 75th anniversary of its French-language service, which sent out its first dispatches on Sept. 30, 1951.

Until then, The Canadian Press, founded in 1917, had been sending English-language dispatches to French-language newspapers, which then translated them.

By launching a French-language service, The Canadian Press became the world’s first bilingual news agency.

In the early years, The Canadian Press’s French service was mostly a writing and translation service, with very little on-the-ground reporting except on Parliament Hill in Ottawa and in Quebec City, where it had its own correspondents.

Established as a cooperative, the PC — as it is often referred to in the news industry — produced 30,000 words a day for the nine newspapers in Quebec and Le Droit in Ottawa.

In 1954, the Évangéline, based in Moncton, N.B., became the 11th member to join the cooperative, and the Action catholique in Quebec City joined two years later.

Over the years, The Canadian Press’s French service established itself as a true national news organization with its own field reporters and correspondents. News dispatches, originally transmitted by telegraph, were then sent via teletype, increasing the transmission speed from 66 words per minute to 300.

When The Canadian Press switched to satellites, its transmission speed rose to 19,200 words per minute. Computerization and the advent of the internet in the late 1990s eliminated transmission limitations.

Canadian Prime Minister Louis St-Laurent flips the switch to turn on the teletype machine, officially inaugurating the French-language service of The Canadian Press. From left to right: Mr. St-Laurent, Roy H. Thomson, president of the Canadian Press, and Hervé Major, president of La Presse Canadienne. This launch on October 3, 1952—one year after the inauguration—confirmed the permanent establishment of the French Service.LA Presse Canadienne.

The company ultimately abandoned the cooperative model and became a private corporation owned equally by the daily newspaper La Presse, The Globe and Mail and Torstar.

Over the course of its 75-year history, the PC’s staff has distinguished itself in its coverage of major events, including numerous federal and provincial elections, referendums, and countless landmark moments in Quebec, Canada, or abroad.

The Canadian Press, with its reporters in the field and journalists assigned to various news desks, has always distinguished itself by its speed in responding to events without sacrificing the accuracy of the information.

Among these historic moments, The Canadian Press’s French service provided comprehensive coverage, notably during: the October Crisis (1970), the Montreal Olympics (1976), the shooting of Corporal Denis Lortie at the National Assembly (1984), the Montreal flood (1987), the death of René Lévesque (1987), the Polytechnique tragedy (1989), the Oka Crisis (1990), the Canadiens’ last Stanley Cup victory (1993), the Saguenay flood (1996), the Éboulements tragedy (1997), the ice storm (1998), the Maple Spring (2012), the Lac-Mégantic train derailment (2013), the attack on the Grand Mosque of Quebec City (2017), the pandemic (2020–2022), the attack on a daycare centre in Laval (2023), and the truck-ramming attack in Amqui (2023).

The PC also sent journalists to cover the Olympic Games around the world, stationed correspondents in Afghanistan when Canada had troops there, and provided its members and subscribers with coverage of the extraordinary funerals of Maurice Richard, Pierre Elliott Trudeau, and Guy Lafleur, held in Montreal.

These examples of the French service’s coverage are just a tiny sample of the agency’s work that enables all French-language media outlets that are members or subscribers to its services to inform their audiences about events taking place outside their own coverage areas.

All major French-language media outlets employ journalists who once worked at The Canadian Press, which also boasted a few famous writers in the very early days of its French Service. These include the poets Alfred DesRochers and Olivier Marchand, the essayist Jean Lemoyne, the columnist Guy Fournier, comedian and screenwriter Carl Dubuc, and journalist Michel Roy, who would eventually hold executive positions at Le Devoir and La Presse.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Three dead after fiery transit bus crash in Calgary, police say
stories.summary: Police report several injuries and one officer hospitalized as two buses collide in city’s northeast
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Three people died Thursday when a transit bus set off a chain-reaction crash on a busy Calgary road and rear-ended another bus to ignite an explosion

Officials said the three killed were on one of the buses, and more than a dozen others were injured in the crash involving eight vehicles.

Staff Sgt. Andy Woodward said one officer was also hurt and taken to hospital after she ran toward a bus just as the fire erupted.

He said investigators were trying to figure out how it all happened.

“Our collision reconstruction [staffers] have arrived on scene and they will try to piece together what has occurred,” Woodward told reporters.

The crash happened shortly after 1 p.m., when one bus slammed into a car and hit other vehicles in the city’s northeast, near the airport.

Woodward said the bus then bounced from that crash through the intersection and hit the second bus parked at a bus stop, setting off the fireball.

One of the buses was powered by compressed natural gas.

Police Staff Sgt. Andy Woodward said it appears to have begun after a transit bus slammed into a car that then hit other vehicles.

The Canadian Press

The impact saw flames quickly envelop the entire roof of one bus, lifting aloft thick clouds of ashy-black smoke. The force of that crash also propelled the second bus into three more vehicles.

The front end of the other bus was left crumpled and smashed, its steering wheel hanging out.

Crews from a nearby firehall quickly extinguished blazes on both buses. The area was scattered with bits of metal and debris.

“I’ve been a police officer for 36 years, and I think this is probably the biggest scene I’ve worked on in relation to the collision we’ve got here,” Woodward said.

Emergency Medical Services spokesperson Adam Loria said 19 people were injured in all. Ten were taken to hospital by ambulance.

“It was a very busy scene,” Loria said.

Mike Mahar, the head of Calgary’s transit union, said one bus driver was able to quickly escape, but the other bus driver had to be extracted by emergency crews. He was transported to hospital but Mahar said his condition is unknown.

Mahar called it a “horrific event” and a tragedy for everyone impacted.

“Our thoughts obviously go out for our members and the environment that they find themselves in today, but also for the passengers and all the families that are affected,” he said in an interview.

He said it appears that at some point the natural gas-powered bus lost control.

Mahar added that it’s not clear why the fire was so extreme and that generally natural gas buses are safe.

“It’s very unusual for this level of damage and the number of fatalities in a transit accident,” he said.

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas said he’s heartbroken over the deaths and injuries.

“There will be a full investigation into what happened,” Farkas said on social media.

Later Thursday at a Forever Canadian rally in the city with Prime Minister Mark Carney ahead of the province’s referendum, Farkas called the crash horrific and commended a first responder.

“In the middle of the chaos, one brave Calgary police officer ran into a burning bus to save the life of a child,” he said.

Carney, in remarks at the rally, also commended the first responders who risked their lives to help those in the crash.

“Tonight doctors and nurses are treating the wounded, and friends, family and neighbours are consoling the bereaved. Because in Calgary, in Alberta, in Canada, we take care of each other,” he said to cheers.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith shared condolences online earlier in the day. “My sincere thoughts are with the families of those who died and with everyone injured,” she said.

Calgary Transit says on its website that it has nearly 250 compressed natural gas-powered buses, representing about 20 per cent of its fleet.

It says it first acquired this type of bus in 2014 and since then the fleet’s emissions have reduced significantly.

The website says the city plans to buy 153 more natural gas buses this year to replace diesel buses.

Editor’s note: A previous version of this story incorrectly stated that one of the buses was powered by liquid natural gas. The bus was powered by compressed natural gas.

stories.title: Joni Mitchell says she became U.S. citizen to vote but will never stop being Canadian
stories.summary: Alberta-born folk legend says she has no intention of giving up her Canadian passport
stories.author: Alex Nino Gheciu
stories.content:
Joni Mitchell May have just become an American citizen, but she insists she’ll never stop being Canadian.

The Alberta-born folk legend says her decision to obtain U.S. citizenship after more than six decades living south of the border was motivated by a desire to vote, and that she has no intention of giving up her Canadian passport.

“I became a citizen so I could vote. I didn’t give up my Canadian citizenship, and I never will,” Mitchell said Thursday in a statement.

“I’m a proud Canerican like Neil Young.”

The 82-year-old also shared the message on her Instagram story, offering some clarity after her naturalization announcement earlier this week prompted questions about her Canadian citizenship.

Mitchell broke the news Tuesday by posting a photo and video from her citizenship ceremony, showing her smiling and holding an American flag in front of U.S. and Department of Homeland Security flags.

“A journey that began 62 years ago,” read her caption.

Mitchell now joins fellow Canadian music icon Neil Young as a dual citizen. Young, who was born in Toronto, became an American citizen in 2020 after living in the United States for decades.

On Thursday, Mitchell also announced News , a new book featuring 23 of her paintings that take aim at relentless news cycles and offer her response to “the world as she sees it today,” according to a release.

“In the current climate, I felt a need to express my concern,” said Mitchell in a statement. “It is an artist’s duty to speak up.”

The book is set for release Nov. 4.

Born Roberta Joan Anderson in Fort Macleod, Alta., in 1943 and raised in Saskatoon, Mitchell moved to Toronto in 1964 before relocating to Detroit with her then-husband and fellow musician Chuck Mitchell.

Following their divorce, she moved to New York, releasing her debut album Song to a Seagull in 1968 and her breakthrough second album, Clouds , the following year.

She currently resides in Santa Barbara, Calif., and maintains a second residence on British Columbia’s Sunshine Coast.

Mitchell publicly lamented her inability to vote in the 2024 U.S. presidential election.

During an Oct. 2024 concert at the Hollywood Bowl, she delivered a profane, two-word rebuke of Donald Trump before urging the audience to cast their ballots.

“This is an important one,” she told the crowd. “I wish I could vote – I’m Canadian. I’m one of those lousy immigrants.”

stories.title: Province “reconsidering” safety improvements following Kincardine crash
stories.summary: Motorists speed past Kincardine Township-Tiverton Public School, along Highway 21, ON the edge of Kincardine. On Tuesday it was the site of a violent crash, where four vehicles collided, sending three people to hospital with serious, life-threatening injuries.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Motorists speed past Kincardine Township-Tiverton Public School, along Highway 21, ON the edge of Kincardine. On Tuesday it was the site of a violent crash, where four vehicles collided, sending three people to hospital with serious, life-threatening injuries.

“There has been too many collisions, and unfortunately the most recent collision has caused big injuries and critical conditions. So we want the community and the students to be safe. And this is one way to do it,” said local parent, Melissa Jackson.

Kincardine Township-Tiverton Public School officials, and the Municipality of Kincardine have been pushing the province to lower the speed limit along Highway 21, through Kincardine, from 80 km/h to 60 km/h, as well as install a northbound left-hand turn lane, to allow school buses, teachers, and parents, to safely turn into Kincardine Township-Tiverton Public School, which is what one of the most seriously injured motorists was doing when they were struck from behind by multiple vehicles, said Jackson.

A 2025 traffic study recommended a speed reduction and a turn lane, but the Ministry of Transportation, said no.

“At the end of the day, the M.T.O evaluated and put up some signs that say Community Safety Zone. But, we didn’t get the speed reduction that we needed, and we didn’t get the left turn that we needed to keep people safe. When we’re traveling through town, we go past four school locations at 80 kilometres an hour. And, there’s no reason why it should be that fast. A left turn lane lets people come up and safely enter the school, with a decreased risk of being rear ended by someone coming along at a high speed,” said Kincardine’s Councillor at Large, and incoming Deputy Mayor, Rory Cavanagh.

Following Tuesday’s violent crash in front of the school, which teachers and parents jumped in to assist before paramedics arrived, Kincardine parents and councillors bombarded Premier Doug Ford with more than 13,000 emails and texts, imploring the province to make the requested safety upgrades.

It appears, it worked. Cavanagh says he’s been told the M.T.O is actively reconsidering it’s position, and has committed to reducing the speed limit along Highway 21 from North Line to Bruce Avenue very shortly, and will accelerate plans to install a turn lane in front of Kincardine Township-Tiverton Public School.

While appreciated, parents and councillors say they’ll believe the changes once they see them.

“I attended this school. Back in primary days, it was a concern then. In the past 15 plus years, it has really gotten worse and it’s more of a concern. And Tuesday’s accident is showing that this needs to happen now. The change needs to happen now,” said Jackson, who is also President of the Kincardine Township-Tiverton Public School Home and School Association.

“I am going to keep pushing and pushing until we actually see the items up here on the ground in person. It’s easy to promise something. It’s much harder to deliver,” said Cavanagh, who has been acclaimed as Kincardine’s incoming Deputy Mayor.

At their council meeting on Wednesday night, the Municipality of Kincardine passed a motion imploring the province to make immediate safety improvements to the section of Highway 21, flowing through Kincardine.
