When we’re traveling through town, we go past four school locations at 80 kilometres an hour. And, there’s no reason why it should be that fast. A left turn lane lets people come up and safely enter the school, with a decreased risk of being rear ended by someone coming along at a high speed,” said Kincardine’s Councillor at Large, and incoming Deputy Mayor, Rory Cavanagh.

Following Tuesday’s violent crash in front of the school, which teachers and parents jumped in to assist before paramedics arrived, Kincardine parents and councillors bombarded Premier Doug Ford with more than 13,000 emails and texts, imploring the province to make the requested safety upgrades.

It appears, it worked. Cavanagh says he’s been told the M.T.O is actively reconsidering it’s position, and has committed to reducing the speed limit along Highway 21 from North Line to Bruce Avenue very shortly, and will accelerate plans to install a turn lane in front of Kincardine Township-Tiverton Public School.
While appreciated, parents and councillors say they’ll believe the changes once they see them.

“I attended this school. Back in primary days, it was a concern then. In the past 15 plus years, it has really gotten worse and it’s more of a concern. And Tuesday’s accident is showing that this needs to happen now. The change needs to happen now,” said Jackson, who is also President of the Kincardine Township-Tiverton Public School Home and School Association.

“I am going to keep pushing and pushing until we actually see the items up here on the ground in person. It’s easy to promise something. It’s much harder to deliver,” said Cavanagh, who has been acclaimed as Kincardine’s incoming Deputy Mayor.

At their council meeting on Wednesday night, the Municipality of Kincardine passed a motion imploring the province to make immediate safety improvements to the section of Highway 21, flowing through Kincardine.

stories.title: Officials close road, respond to two transit buses on fire in northeast Calgary
stories.summary: Calgary - Police have closed a road in northeast Calgary following a fiery crash involving transit buses.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - Three people died Thursday when a transit bus set off a chain-reaction crash on a busy Calgary road and rear-ended another bus to ignite an explosion

Officials said the three killed were on one of the buses, and more than a dozen others were injured in the crash involving eight vehicles.

Staff Sgt. Andy Woodward said one officer was also hurt and taken to hospital after she ran toward a bus just as the fire erupted.

He said investigators were trying to figure out how it all happened.

“Our collision reconstruction (staffers) have arrived on scene and they will try to piece together what has occurred,” Woodward told reporters.

The crash happened shortly after 1 p.m., when one bus slammed into a car and hit other vehicles in the city’s northeast, near the airport.

Woodward said the bus then bounced from that crash through the intersection and hit the second bus parked at a bus stop, setting off the fireball.

One of the buses was powered by compressed natural gas.

The impact saw flames quickly envelop the entire roof of one bus, lifting aloft thick clouds of ashy-black smoke. The force of that crash also propelled the second bus into three more vehicles.

The front end of the other bus was left crumpled and smashed, its steering wheel hanging out.

Crews from a nearby firehall quickly extinguished blazes on both buses. The area was scattered with bits of metal and debris.

“I’ve been a police officer for 36 years, and I think this is probably the biggest scene I’ve worked on in relation to the collision we’ve got here,” Woodward said.

Emergency Medical Services spokesperson Adam Loria said 19 people were injured in all. Ten were taken to hospital by ambulance.

“It was a very busy scene,” Loria said.

Mike Mahar, the head of Calgary’s transit union, said one bus driver was able to quickly escape, but the other bus driver had to be extracted by emergency crews. He was transported to hospital but Mahar said his condition is unknown.

Mahar called it a “horrific event” and a tragedy for everyone impacted.

“Our thoughts obviously go out for our members and the environment that they find themselves in today, but also for the passengers and all the families that are affected,” he said in an interview.

He said it appears that at some point the natural gas-powered bus lost control.

Mahar added that it’s not clear why the fire was so extreme and that generally natural gas buses are safe.

“It’s very unusual for this level of damage and the number of fatalities in a transit accident,” he said.

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas said he’s heartbroken over the deaths and injuries.

“There will be a full investigation into what happened,” Farkas said on social media.

Later Thursday at a Forever Canadian rally in the city with Prime Minister Mark Carney ahead of the province’s referendum, Farkas called the crash horrific and commended a first responder.

“In the middle of the chaos, one brave Calgary police officer ran into a burning bus to save the life of a child,” he said.

Carney, in remarks at the rally, also commended the first responders who risked their lives to help those in the crash.

“Tonight doctors and nurses are treating the wounded, and friends, family and neighbours are consoling the bereaved. Because in Calgary, in Alberta, in Canada, we take care of each other,” he said to cheers.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith shared condolences online earlier in the day. “My sincere thoughts are with the families of those who died and with everyone injured,” she said.

Calgary Transit says on its website that it has nearly 250 compressed natural gas-powered buses, representing about 20 per cent of its fleet.

It says it first acquired this type of bus in 2014 and since then the fleet’s emissions have reduced significantly.

The website says the city plans to buy 153 more natural gas buses this year to replace diesel buses.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

— With files from Lisa Johnson and Jack Farrell in Edmonton

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version said the crash was in northwest Calgary and that a bus was powered by liquid natural gas.

stories.title: Parti Québécois caucus members swear allegiance to ‘the people of Quebec’ — not the King
stories.summary: Quebec’s Lieutenant-Governor Manon Jeannotte was nowhere in sight during the swearing-in ceremony.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Ottawa — Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and the 58 members of the Parti Québécois caucus did not pledge allegiance to King Charles III at the swearing-in ceremony for the incoming PQ government on Thursday.

Instead, they pledged their loyalty to “the people of Quebec” — something that is technically possible to do under a provincial law that was adopted four years ago in the National Assembly of Quebec, but that constitutional lawyers remain skeptical about.

St-Pierre Plamondon entered the red room of the legislature to thunderous applause from his caucus and guests who were chanting for Quebec to become a country only moments before. The premier-elect looked visibly emotional.

“I, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, solemnly declare that I will be loyal to the people of Quebec and that I will perform my duties as a Member of the National Assembly with honesty and justice, in accordance with the Constitution of Quebec,” he said.

One by one, members of his caucus repeated the same phrase to be sworn in as MNAs.

Quebec’s Lieutenant-Governor Manon Jeannotte was nowhere in sight during the swearing-in ceremony. St-Pierre Plamondon has vowed to strip her office’s funding, instead dedicating those funds to fight homelessness in the province.

The National Assembly adopted a law in December 2022 that made swearing an oath to the King optional after the PQ members — including St-Pierre Plamondon — were temporarily barred from taking their seats in the legislature for refusing to do just that.

Philippe Lagassé, a professor at the Norman Paterson School of International Affairs at Carleton University who is an expert in the Westminster system, said the constitutionality of the act remains “unclear” but is being challenged in court.

Last week, Lawrence David, a professor at the University of Ottawa’s faculty of law and president and founder of the Public Interest Litigation Institute, filed an application in Quebec Superior Court for an injunction to force MNAs to swear the oath to the King.

How the separatist Parti Québécois took back power in Quebec

Who is Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, Quebec's new separatist premier?

David and the Public Interest Litigation Institute had already filed a lawsuit seeking to restore the oath in August. But given the urgency of the situation with a PQ government promising to abolish the monarchy, he sought an injunction the day after the election.

The hearing is expected to be held sometime between Oct. 19 and Nov. 9.

David claims that MNAs who do not take the oath to the King are not constitutionally authorized to sit in the National Assembly or to pass any laws.

Lagassé noted that the federal Department of Justice seems to have accepted the constitutionality of the Quebec law prima facie, as has its provincial government.

“However, we don’t know if that is the case yet, since it has not been tested before the courts. And I would say that there is a strong view amongst experts of the Constitution that this is likely not constitutional,” said the professor.

Even Governor General Louise Arbour has expressed skepticism, in recent public comments made to Radio-Canada , about MNAs refusing to swear allegiance to the monarchy, saying that Canada operates within a constitutional framework.

She added that St-Pierre Plamondon, as a lawyer, is well-aware of this reality.

Constitutional or not, the option to swear to the King or not crosses party lines. Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard told FM93 radio that he does not intend to swear allegiance to the King while saying he does not want a “monarchical crisis” in Canada.

The swearing-in ceremonies for opposition MNAs should take place next week, as will St-Pierre Plamondon’s swearing-in as premier and of his members of cabinet.

Lagassé said the PQ’s decision to cast aside the lieutenant-governor will be even more interesting when forming cabinet, since members of the Executive Council — the Quebec equivalent of the Privy Council — are effectively advisors to the Crown.

“So, it’ll be interesting to see if they go out of their way to have a separate public ceremony, and then secretly do all their oaths with the lieutenant-governor behind closed doors. It’s entirely possible,” he said.

Lagassé said there are lots of things the incoming PQ government can do to reduce the symbolism of the lieutenant-governor’s office such as kicking her out of her office or cutting her budget, but the federal government can always swoop in to help.

Lagassé said he doesn’t think a PQ government would necessarily object to that, because they still need the lieutenant-governor to do certain things like sign bills into law.

“But if, symbolically, they don’t want to fund it, but then the federal government comes and backfills it and allows them to have an office somewhere and allows them to still have a small office, in a way they’d be able to have their cake and eat it too.”

— With files from Kalina Laframboise, Montreal Gazette

Last week, Lawrence David, a professor at the University of Ottawa’s faculty of law and president and founder of the Public Interest Litigation Institute, filed an application in Quebec Superior Court for an injunction to force MNAs to swear the oath to the King.

Who is Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, Quebec's new separatist premier?

David and the Public Interest Litigation Institute had already filed a lawsuit seeking to restore the oath in August. But given the urgency of the situation with a PQ government promising to abolish the monarchy, he sought an injunction the day after the election.
The hearing is expected to be held sometime between Oct. 19 and Nov. 9.
David claims that MNAs who do not take the oath to the King are not constitutionally authorized to sit in the National Assembly or to pass any laws.
Lagassé noted that the federal Department of Justice seems to have accepted the constitutionality of the Quebec law prima facie, as has its provincial government.

“However, we don’t know if that is the case yet, since it has not been tested before the courts. And I would say that there is a strong view amongst experts of the Constitution that this is likely not constitutional,” said the professor.

Even Governor General Louise Arbour has expressed skepticism, in recent public comments made to Radio-Canada , about MNAs refusing to swear allegiance to the monarchy, saying that Canada operates within a constitutional framework.
She added that St-Pierre Plamondon, as a lawyer, is well-aware of this reality.

Constitutional or not, the option to swear to the King or not crosses party lines. Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard told FM93 radio that he does not intend to swear allegiance to the King while saying he does not want a “monarchical crisis” in Canada.
The swearing-in ceremonies for opposition MNAs should take place next week, as will St-Pierre Plamondon’s swearing-in as premier and of his members of cabinet.

Lagassé said the PQ’s decision to cast aside the lieutenant-governor will be even more interesting when forming cabinet, since members of the Executive Council — the Quebec equivalent of the Privy Council — are effectively advisors to the Crown.

“So, it’ll be interesting to see if they go out of their way to have a separate public ceremony, and then secretly do all their oaths with the lieutenant-governor behind closed doors. It’s entirely possible,” he said.

Lagassé said there are lots of things the incoming PQ government can do to reduce the symbolism of the lieutenant-governor’s office such as kicking her out of her office or cutting her budget, but the federal government can always swoop in to help.
Lagassé said he doesn’t think a PQ government would necessarily object to that, because they still need the lieutenant-governor to do certain things like sign bills into law.

“But if, symbolically, they don’t want to fund it, but then the federal government comes and backfills it and allows them to have an office somewhere and allows them to still have a small office, in a way they’d be able to have their cake and eat it too.”

stories.title: B.C. Conservatives cut ties with candidate accused of Hitler remarks
stories.summary: Vancouver-Strathcona candidate Jordan McIntosh is no longer a Conservative candidate, party says
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The British Columbia Conservatives have dumped a teenage candidate in the provincial election after he was accused of posting “offensive” remarks online about the Holocaust and Hitler.

The party said Thursday that Jordan McIntosh was no longer the Conservative candidate in Vancouver-Strathcona and if elected he would not sit in the caucus.

The Conservatives announced his removal from the slate less than an hour after NDP candidate Callista Ryan, who is running in Vancouver-Quilchena, posted screenshots on social media platform X showing what she said were McIntosh’s remarks.

One post under the username “DeathNight” said Hitler “May have not intended death” during the Holocaust, and that “lots of Jews died” not because Hitler “hated them specifically” but because there were so many of them.

An Apple Music artist profile for a musician called “DeathNight” listed Jordan Zheng McIntosh as their lyricist, composer and producer.

Jordan Zheng McIntosh is the full name of the former Conservative candidate, according to Elections BC.

McIntosh’s LinkedIn profile shows he graduated from high school last year.

Ryan said in her post that it appeared McIntosh thought he could use a “nameless Twitter account to say many awful, offensive things.”

She said in an interview on Thursday that she identified McIntosh through a photo on Twitter and cross-referenced the social media account with a music account.

McIntosh declined to comment when reached by phone on Thursday, saying only that he would call back.

Ryan said she wanted to hear an apology showing that McIntosh understood his mistakes.

“We haven’t heard anything from him, but really it’s about the leadership of the B.C. Conservatives and doing the right thing, even when it’s inconvenient, because they’re not dropping other candidates like Heather Maas for saying hateful comments as well.”

Ryan was referring to 2022 comments from Maahs about the Sogi 123 program. The Conservative legislator said during a podcast that the program was “not just sex education that has gone too far” but May even be a form of grooming.

“It’s for sure grooming,” she added. “It desensitizes kids, and it’s all under the name of Lgbtq because it’s boy on boy.”

McIntosh’s removal comes after interim Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson said during Wednesday’s leaders’ debate that he would “stand against hate” and raised concerns about what he called “antisemitic behaviour” within the NDP caucus.

Doerkson had come under fire from NDP Leader David Eby in the debate over whether he tolerated “hateful” views.

Eby said online posts about Islam by Conservative campaign director Katy Merrifield were “like the worst corners of the dark web.”

Doerkson countered by asking Eby if antisemitic behaviour in his caucus qualified as hate, in reference to former New Democrat legislator Selina Robinson, who left the party in March 2024 citing antisemitism and indifference towards the problem.

Eby responded by saying that he asked Robinson to step down from cabinet in February 2024 after she made what he called “some unfortunate comments” about Palestine at a media event. Robinson had called pre-1948 Palestine a “crappy of piece of land.”

Doerkson was asked during a post-debate media availability about what he would do if his caucus members made remarks he considered hateful.

“I am absolutely committed to serving British Columbians in a respectful way ... and with dignity,” he said. “I will not allow those kinds of actions in our caucus going forward for certain and I will be absolutely committed to that.”

Doerkson declined to comment about allegations from CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko, who is openly gay and said Maahs had called her immoral over her sexual orientation.

McIntosh’s ejection also comes a week after the Conservatives kicked out another candidate, Joachim Agou, for online comments saying the driver of a car that rammed a pro-Palestinian protest group in Switzerland should have “reversed too.”

The party said if Agou won the seat in Victoria-Beacon Hill, he would not sit in the Conservative caucus.

Agou issued a statement the next day saying he was “truly sorry” and while he took responsibility for his words, he rejected NDP accusations of racism.

He said in a social media post on Oct. 9 that he should have expressed himself “more clearly and calmly,” adding that demonstrations “should not bring a city to a standstill or put lives at risk.”

stories.title: Property crime a key issue for Winnipeggers in upcoming election
stories.summary: Property crime is a key issue many Winnipeggers say they want to see the next mayor and council take action on.
stories.author: Marney Blunt
stories.content:
Property crime is an issue many Winnipeggers say they want to see the next mayor and council take action on.

It’s a concern for North Kildonan resident Chris Grabski.

“Lots of door handle checking, we’ve had people rifle through our vehicles, we’ve had one instance where somebody came to our door tried to get in. I had somebody come in my backyard,” he said.

He says he has also heightened home security measures.

“It’s frustrating because I felt like we picked a quiet neighbourhood to raise our kids,” Grabski said.

“But it’s not surprising. Frustrating, but not surprising.”

Crystal Watson moved to the Centennial neighbourhood in the city about a year ago.

“I’ve never seen this much crime,” she said.

Her backyard is now kept locked up after a rash of property crime and suspicious activity.

“We had someone going through our backyard when no one was home, my child was home, and no one did anything. It took two and a half hours for the cops to come. We didn’t know if he was going to break in or not,” Watson said.

She has also installed security cameras around her house, and put plywood boards on top of the backyard fence to deter people from climbing in.

“We paid for the security cameras and…. I will say, I have a bat by my door now.”

According to data from the Winnipeg Police Service , property crime is down slightly this year, dropping 0.2 per cent from July 2025 to June of this year. But in some areas, like the William Whyte neighborhood, it’s up 46 per cent over the three year average.

“People feel very unsafe and they are fed up,” William Whyte Neigbourhood Association president Darrell Warren told Global News.

“People want to feel safe when they are in our yards and in our homes. And unfortunately, that’s not happening. And it’s not just my area. It’s city-wide.”

Warren says lengthy police response times to reports of property crimes sometimes deters residents from reporting the crime at all.

“Lots of door handle checking, we’ve had people rifle through our vehicles, we’ve had one instance where somebody came to our door tried to get in. I had somebody come in my backyard,” he said.

“It’s frustrating because I felt like we picked a quiet neighbourhood to raise our kids,” Grabski said.
“But it’s not surprising. Frustrating, but not surprising.”

“I’ve never seen this much crime,” she said.

stories.title: ‘The price just dropped for every home in town’: St. Thomas receives funding to reduce development charges
stories.summary: With the rapid rise of big industry at St. Thomas’s Yarmouth Yards industrial park, so comes the demand for housing.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
With the rapid rise of big industry at St. Thomas’s Yarmouth Yards industrial park, so comes the demand for housing. It’s something Mayor Joe Preston knows all too well. “The price just dropped for every home in town. Because normally the development charge would have been tacked on to the new build,” he said.

Preston was on hand in a new section of the Shaw Valley subdivision, as federal and provincial officials announced more than $19.6 million in funding to help cover development charges over three years. “There are a lot of new locates to the area,” explained Russell Higgins, President, MacPherson Builders.

“So, the addition of rental housing stock is key for the time being. Ultimately these people will move to home ownership,” he explained. The funding is from the Development Charge Reduction Program (Dcrp). For single detached homes and multi-unit housing, the city has committed to a 30 per cent reduction on development charges.

For other types of housing, 50 per cent. “When you combine with HST relief, and the Dcrp reduction, here in St. Thomas it can be anywhere from $80 to $135,000 off the price of one of these new homes,” said Elgin-Middlesex-London MPP Rob Flack, who serves as Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing.

“There’s a housing crisis, and this is what we need in this moment. And it’s really great to see all levels of government working together,” remarked London West MP, Arielle Kayabaga. The program will fund the development charges for more than 3,700 new homes.

For many would-be homeowners, hidden costs, such as development charges, are what’s standing in the way of home-ownership. “Anything we can do to promote sales, i.e., dropping the price of a house while still making an acceptable margin to build the houses, we’re going to pass it through to the homeowners,” said Higgins.

The program is in effect for three years, from March 30, 2026 to March 31, 2029.

stories.title: ‘A show of confidence’: Ottawa invests $100M in Nova Scotia offshore wind
stories.summary: It was a blustery day on the Dartmouth, N.S. waterfront as the federal government announced a $100 million investment to advance offshore wind development in Nova Scotia.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Skye Bryden-Blom
stories.content:
It was a blustery day on the Dartmouth, N.S. waterfront as the federal government announced a $100 million investment to advance offshore wind development in Nova Scotia.

The money will be used to collect wind, ocean and seafloor data for the Wind West project. Wind West is part of the Atlantic Energy Strategy, which was referred to the federal Major Projects Office in September 2025 .

Premier Tim Houston called it an “incredible” day for Nova Scotia.

“I’m incredibly excited about what the future holds for our province,” he told reporters.

“(The funding) will shave years off (the project). It will bring us closer to the jobs, closer to the realities. We’re really appreciative of the $100 million. It means a lot. It means a lot for Nova Scotians. It’s a show of confidence in what we have.”

According to the provincial government, Nova Scotia has some of the best, and consistently-fast, wind speeds in the world. The province also sits on a “large continental shelf with vast areas of relatively shallow water that are ideal for floating and fixed wind platforms.”

“Nearly 30 countries are ahead of Canada in developing offshore wind and it’s time to change that,” said federal Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson, who was on hand to deliver the news.

As a first step, Hodgson says $5 million will go toward the development of tools to measure wind speeds and ocean conditions. He anticipates the call for bids will be issued this winter.

“This data will help developers better understand the unique conditions off Nova Scotia’s coast and design offshore wind projects that are safe, that are efficient and built for long-term success,” he said.

Nearly $3 million is being committed to expand transmission modelling and marine survey work.

This work is expected to help lay the foundation for Wind West and support Nova Scotia’s goal of licensing up to five gigawatts of offshore wind energy by 2030.

“Just this five (gigawatts) could be $40 billion of private investment, $50 billion, $60 billion. It’s a big, big number. It means jobs, it means opportunity,” said Houston.

Provincial officials have said Wind West could generate up to 60 gigawatts of electricity if all phases are built.

“When you can take $100 million of public money and leverage it to unlock tens of billions of dollars of private money, that is a good use of public capital,” said Houston.

“Imagine what our province looks like when we have all of that 60 (gigawatts). It’s an incredible opportunity.”

Houston has also suggested the excess electricity could be used to supply 27 per cent of Canada’s total demand. Quebec and Massachusetts have already shown interest in buying electricity from the proposed project.

A Canadian Renewable Energy Association (CanREA) poll released this week found 33 per cent of Canadians ranked affordability as a top priority for new electricity supply — ahead of reliability, how quickly new supply can be built, economic growth and energy security.

“Electricity demand in Canada is expected to increase between 26 to 85 per cent by 2050 as the economy grows and electrifies,” said Eddie Oldfield, the association’s director of policy for the Maritimes.

“Canadians need more electricity. They’ve told us they want it to be affordable. Wind, solar and storage are among the top new sources of energy that can provide affordable, reliable electricity in Canada.”

He points out that Wind West would be the first time offshore wind would be introduced on Canadian shores and calls it “an incredible opportunity.”

Official Opposition Leader Claudia Chender says her party supports the expansion of the ocean science and technology sector, but adds that it’s “vitally important” to understand how projects like Wind West ultimately help people afford power bills and “secure our energy future.”

“What people are concerned about when we talk about power is being able to pay their power bills. And so we would like to see federal investment in our transmission and distribution,” the NDP leader said.

Oldfield agrees transmission to get that power to markets is something that needs to be discussed and addressed.

“And that might require a regional framework with clear rules, timelines that investors can count on, (as well as) real partnerships with the Mi’kmaq, Indigenous communities, fisheries and coastal communities to ensure that benefits accrue locally as they develop these great resources,” he said.

— with files from Global News’ Heidi Petracek and The Canadian Press.

stories.title: Vancouver officer denies giving 'lopsided' account of fatal fight with Myles Gray
stories.summary: Vancouver - A Vancouver police officer involved in the deadly arrest of Myles Gray in 2015 says he doesn't agree that he has given a "lopsided" account of the altercation by describing Gray as "the Hulk" or a "charging bull."
stories.author: Darryl Greer The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - A second Vancouver police officer involved in the violent arrest that ended in the death of Myles Gray says he had never previously encountered someone in such a state that he believed was a medical situation known as “excited delirium.”

Const. Beau Spencer is among seven Vancouver officers facing a public hearing by British Columbia’s Police Complaint Commissioner into whether they committed misconduct during the fatal confrontation in 2015.

Spencer said Thursday he had been trained about excited delirium and that it could include making animalistic sounds and an inability to comprehend surroundings.

“Once the amount of time that had gone by with him fighting, it started to become more apparent that (excited delirium) might be a possibility,” he said of Gray.

The officer told the hearing he had been trained to regard excited delirium as a medical emergency, not a crime.

No charges have been laid over Gray’s death, which a 2023 coroner’s inquest ruled was a homicide, a term that does not assign legal blame.

A pathologist told the earlier coroners’ inquest that it had been thought “so-called excited delirium syndrome” could result independently in death, but analysis of the published data suggests that’s “quite unlikely.”

Spencer’s lawyer, Claire Hatcher, said in introductory remarks at the public hearing that during a lucid moment by Gray, the officer told him he would be OK, and he was “reassured by a professional police officer who was concerned about his well-being.”

She said Spencer’s role in the arrest had to be “considered distinctly” from those of other officers, since he arrived “after the fight had been ongoing for several minutes.”

Hatcher said Spencer “delivered three or four closed fist strikes, punches” to the shoulder of Gray to get his arm behind his back so he could be handcuffed during the arrest on a lawn.

“I expect Const. Spencer will testify that he and (other) officers then moved Mr. Gray further out from the tree to an open area on the lawn,” she said. “The adjudicator will hear that this is the whole of the force Const. Spencer used.”

She also addressed allegations that Spencer might have neglected his duties by not making notes immediately after the incident.

Hatcher said the hearing would be told that officers in the arrest had gathered at Vancouver police headquarters for a meeting after Gray’s death, where a “union representative or representatives instructed the members, Constable Spencer in particular, not to take any notes, and not to write anything on a computer while the IIO (independent Investigations Office) investigation was underway.”

Spencer’s testimony at the hearing in Vancouver on Thursday came after that of Const. Eric Birzneck, who said he did not agree he had given a “lopsided” account of the altercation by likening Gray to “the Hulk” or a “charging bull.”

Birzneck also denied trying to hide the fact that another officer had punched Gray as they tried to subdue him when the counsel for the commission, Brock Martland, asked him if he was trying to “protect a fellow officer.”

Martland asked Birzneck about his account of the attempt to arrest Gray, questioning whether his evidence omitted certain facts or minimized things to avoid creating problems for the others involved in the confrontation.

Birzneck disagreed and told the hearing his memories had been jogged over time with “pieces of the puzzle” coming together afterward.

paragraphs: Vancouver - A second Vancouver police officer involved in the violent arrest that ended in the death of Myles Gray says he had never previously encountered someone in such a state that he believed was a medical situation known as “excited delirium.”

Const. Beau Spencer is among seven Vancouver officers facing a public hearing by British Columbia’s Police Complaint Commissioner into whether they committed misconduct during the fatal confrontation in 2015.
Spencer said Thursday he had been trained about excited delirium and that it could include making animalistic sounds and an inability to comprehend surroundings.
“Once the amount of time that had gone by with him fighting, it started to become more apparent that (excited delirium) might be a possibility,” he said of Gray.
The officer told the hearing he had been trained to regard excited delirium as a medical emergency, not a crime.
No charges have been laid over Gray’s death, which a 2023 coroner’s inquest ruled was a homicide, a term that does not assign legal blame.

A pathologist told the earlier coroners’ inquest that it had been thought “so-called excited delirium syndrome” could result independently in death, but analysis of the published data suggests that’s “quite unlikely.”

Spencer’s lawyer, Claire Hatcher, said in introductory remarks at the public hearing that during a lucid moment by Gray, the officer told him he would be OK, and he was “reassured by a professional police officer who was concerned about his well-being.”
She said Spencer’s role in the arrest had to be “considered distinctly” from those of other officers, since he arrived “after the fight had been ongoing for several minutes.”
Hatcher said Spencer “delivered three or four closed fist strikes, punches” to the shoulder of Gray to get his arm behind his back so he could be handcuffed during the arrest on a lawn.

“I expect Const. Spencer will testify that he and (other) officers then moved Mr. Gray further out from the tree to an open area on the lawn,” she said. “The adjudicator will hear that this is the whole of the force Const. Spencer used.”
She also addressed allegations that Spencer might have neglected his duties by not making notes immediately after the incident.

Hatcher said the hearing would be told that officers in the arrest had gathered at Vancouver police headquarters for a meeting after Gray’s death, where a “union representative or representatives instructed the members, Constable Spencer in particular, not to take any notes, and not to write anything on a computer while the IIO (independent Investigations Office) investigation was underway.”

Birzneck said Thursday that he believed Gray was “arrestable” at the time, with no lawful right to repel officers’ use of force against him.

stories.title: Stelco negotiations still on the table, Joly says amid layoffs
stories.summary: Joly said she is still reviewing a letter from the company that was sent in response to her own letter, dated Oct. 5, in which she gave Stelco five days to respond to an ultimatum.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said she is willing to negotiate if Stelco wants to come back to the table after the company announced layoffs of up to 500 workers .

At an unrelated announcement Thursday in Peterborough, Ont., Joly said she is still reviewing a letter from the company that was sent in response to her own letter, dated Oct. 5, in which she gave Stelco five days to respond to an ultimatum.

Joly said the federal government would be using the “full force of the law” if jobs are not preserved.

A copy of the letter from Stelco, dated Oct. 9, was obtained by Global News. The letter, written by Stelco’s president, Paul Simon, detailed the consequences that U.S. tariffs have had on the company.

The Ontario-based steel manufacturer announced last month that pressure from U.S. tariffs forced it to concentrate steel production at its Lake Erie Works plant in Haldimand, and halt production at its plant in Hamilton. Some employees would be offered transfers, but many would be out of work.

“Our early September meetings with several senior government officials, including representatives from your office, led Stelco to believe that the government understood the market realities confronting Stelco’s Hamilton Works finishing lines,” the letter said.

It also said that the government’s representation that Stelco’s planned layoffs cause it to breach its undertakings is “false.”

“The CEO has been clear, he has been advocating for the imposition of U.S. tariffs on steel and steel makers here in Canada,” Joly said Thursday.

She said her offices are willing to continue conversations with Stelco, but reiterated her position from the day prior that financial penalties or a forced sale of assets could be imposed if the company continues to lay off workers.

Approximately 90 workers received notices last week, and the first layoffs took effect Sunday, the president of United Steelworkers local 1005 previously told Global News.

The remainder of the layoffs are expected to roll out over the course of three weeks.

“We’ve hired the best lawyers in Canada to help us to deal with that, and we will fight to keep the jobs in Hamilton,” Joly said.

She said the government is willing to take the matter to the courts, but did not say when that process would begin.

– With files from Global News’ Ariel Rabinovitch

stories.title: A new AGO exhibition explores the evolution of Black style, starting with the tradition of ‘Sunday best’
stories.summary: One of the first major North American exhibitions on the African diaspora, the show explores more than a century of self-fashioning, power and resistance
stories.author: Santanae Luzige
stories.content:
Walking through Sunday Best: The Power And The Glory of Black Style at the Art Gallery of Ontario, it’s immediately clear that one visit isn’t enough to fully absorb the expansiveness of what’s on display.

Spanning from the 1880s to the present day, the exhibition features historical and high-fashion garments, contemporary art, ephemera, accessories and photographs by artists from Canada, the U.S., the U.K. and the Caribbean that reveal the instrumental role of fashion in shaping African diasporic identities.

A concept born out of the transatlantic slave trade, when enslaved people were given only a small allotment of coarse cloth to make their own garments, “Sunday best” refers to clothes reserved for church or special occasions. Across the African diaspora, this ritualized approach to dressing has endured as a form of resistance, community-building and self-fashioning, which refers to the way that one creates an identity and public persona to reflect cultural standards and social codes. Above all, it was a crucial exercise in autonomy – a form of rebellion when so much else was systematically stripped away.

For co-curators Julie Crooks and Jason Cyrus, an exhibition of this magnitude has been nine years in the making.

As for the timing, Crooks pointed toward a broader cultural shift. With the Victoria and Albert Museum’s Africa Fashion exhibition touring globally and the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Superfine: Tailoring Black Style in the cultural orbit, she explained, “We felt that this was a moment to build on those exhibitions and ideas but tell a different story that fits within an African diasporic perspective.”

The goal, according to Cyrus, was to capture Black style’s “myriad manifestations, moving between the historic and contemporary, the personal and communal, the everyday and the couture.” To do that, the show is organized into five thematic sections: Origins, Church, Migration, Liberation, and Call and Response. The curators collaborated with architect and artist Jayden Ali of UK-based JA Projects on the exhibition design.

Ali described the spatial layout as bookended by the motif of the spotlight. The opening sequence features the signature tailcoat and top hat of abolitionist Frederick Douglass, alongside a recreation of the wedding dress worn by his first wife, Anna Murray Douglass, crafted in plum-coloured silk by Harlem designer Cassandra Bromfield.

Then, Ali notes, in the finale, “the matte silk ball gown by Christopher John Rogers occupies its own pool of light.” As Cyrus explains, the Black, queer designer from Louisiana takes the antebellum Gone with the Wind silhouette – a shape historically designed for white Southern women to take up space and project plantation wealth – and reimagines it. In striking contrast to those small allotments of coarse cloth forced upon his ancestors, Rogers uses yards of vibrant fuchsia silk to actively reclaim that physical and cultural space. He uses joy as resistance, honouring his Southern roots without letting them define him.

Between those moments, the two largest galleries in the exhibition continue to play with the qualities of light. “We situate the garments beneath the skylights of Frank Gehry’s architecture, congregated together at the centre of the room,” Ali said. “That idea of congregation is itself a nod to the curatorial sections Origins and Church, while also speaking to togetherness: holding space for oneself and holding space for each other.”

That space holds an extraordinary amount of talent. The exhibition brings together the roots of contemporary Black style, housing the dramatic cape of late fashion editor André Leon Talley – displayed on a mannequin moulded in his likeness, alongside his signature Manolo Blahniks – and the eclectic onstage wardrobe of Toronto transgender soul icon Jackie Shane, as well as 1970s Ebony magazine issues from actor Linda V. Carter’s collection. It puts them in dialogue with recent designs by Diotima and Proenza Schouler creative director Rachel Scott and powerful visual artworks by Sasha Huber.

Yet this celebration of Black style isn’t confined behind museum glass. The AGO has partnered with Canadian label Greta Constantine to present a live fashion show celebrating Black style and sartorial innovation. Led by Kirk Pickersgill, the brand’s designer, Greta Constantine marks its 20th anniversary on Oct. 16 with the special event, accompanied by a live soundtrack from Toronto-based vocal group Echo Collective.

For Pickersgill, the runway presentation is anything but a standard retrospective. “This couldn’t feel nostalgic; it had to foster a sense of hope and opportunity, aligning with the exhibition itself,” he said. To achieve that, Pickersgill selected pieces that highlight the label’s signature DNA – voluminous, structural and expertly constructed – designed entirely in white, a considered choice meant to convey purity and peace. Between the DJ and the choir, he noted, the music also bridges two distinct worlds, helping champion Black arts and culture in all of its forms.

As a Black designer and the son of Jamaican immigrants, Pickersgill feels a profound significance in being part of the Ago’s first major fashion exhibition. “This exhibition is a reminder of where I’ve come, hardships and challenges included, and a reminder of what can be achieved with discipline, hard work and creativity.”

When the choir’s voices fill the museum, the runway echoes the core themes of Sunday Best, proving that self-fashioning remains an active, ongoing symbol of hope and resilience.

Sunday Best: The Power and The Glory of Black Style runs until Feb. 28, 2027

He uses joy as resistance, honouring his Southern roots without letting them define him.

Between those moments, the two largest galleries in the exhibition continue to play with the qualities of light. “We situate the garments beneath the skylights of Frank Gehry’s architecture, congregated together at the centre of the room,” Ali said. “That idea of congregation is itself a nod to the curatorial sections Origins and Church, while also speaking to togetherness: holding space for oneself and holding space for each other.”

That space holds an extraordinary amount of talent. The exhibition brings together the roots of contemporary Black style, housing the dramatic cape of late fashion editor André Leon Talley – displayed on a mannequin moulded in his likeness, alongside his signature Manolo Blahniks – and the eclectic onstage wardrobe of Toronto transgender soul icon Jackie Shane, as well as 1970s Ebony magazine issues from actor Linda V. Carter’s collection. It puts them in dialogue with recent designs by Diotima and Proenza Schouler creative director Rachel Scott and powerful visual artworks by Sasha Huber.

Yet this celebration of Black style isn’t confined behind museum glass. The AGO has partnered with Canadian label Greta Constantine to present a live fashion show celebrating Black style and sartorial innovation. Led by Kirk Pickersgill, the brand’s designer, Greta Constantine marks its 20th anniversary on Oct. 16 with the special event, accompanied by a live soundtrack from Toronto-based vocal group Echo Collective.

For Pickersgill, the runway presentation is anything but a standard retrospective. “This couldn’t feel nostalgic; it had to foster a sense of hope and opportunity, aligning with the exhibition itself,” he said. To achieve that, Pickersgill selected pieces that highlight the label’s signature DNA – voluminous, structural and expertly constructed – designed entirely in white, a considered choice meant to convey purity and peace. Between the DJ and the choir, he noted, the music also bridges two distinct worlds, helping champion Black arts and culture in all of its forms.

As a Black designer and the son of Jamaican immigrants, Pickersgill feels a profound significance in being part of the Ago’s first major fashion exhibition. “This exhibition is a reminder of where I’ve come, hardships and challenges included, and a reminder of what can be achieved with discipline, hard work and creativity.”
When the choir’s voices fill the museum, the runway echoes the core themes of Sunday Best, proving that self-fashioning remains an active, ongoing symbol of hope and resilience.

content_blocks.text: Spanning from the 1880s to the present day, the exhibition features historical and high-fashion garments, contemporary art, ephemera, accessories and photographs by artists from Canada, the U.S., the U.K. and the Caribbean that reveal the instrumental role of fashion in shaping African diasporic identities.

content_blocks.text: A concept born out of the transatlantic slave trade, when enslaved people were given only a small allotment of coarse cloth to make their own garments, “Sunday best” refers to clothes reserved for church or special occasions. Across the African diaspora, this ritualized approach to dressing has endured as a form of resistance, community-building and self-fashioning, which refers to the way that one creates an identity and public persona to reflect cultural standards and social codes. Above all, it was a crucial exercise in autonomy – a form of rebellion when so much else was systematically stripped away.

stories.title: CFB Kingston failed environmental compliance inspection on refrigerants: memo
stories.summary: Ottawa — Environment and Climate Change Canada warned National Defence earlier this year that the CFB Kingston base had broken federal environmental regulations by failing to test air conditioners for refrigerant leaks.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Environment and Climate Change Canada warned National Defence earlier this year that the CFB Kingston base had broken federal environmental regulations by failing to test air conditioners for refrigerant leaks.

After inspecting a building on the base last year, an enforcement officer alleged in a January letter that National Defence had violated federal halocarbon regulations under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.

Halocarbons are a category of chemicals widely used as refrigerants that qualify as greenhouse gases associated with both ozone depletion and climate change.

The Environment Department warned National Defence in January the base had failed to conduct and log leak tests on five rooftop air conditioning units in 2023, according to National Defence documents from March obtained through Access to Information law.

The Kingston base “experienced three large … halocarbon releases” of over 100 kilograms within the past two years, according to a memo signed by Peter Hammerschmidt, the assistant deputy minister for infrastructure and environment at National Defence

“The non-compliance stemmed from limited maintenance resourcing and under use of Defence Resource Management Information System for scheduling and record-keeping,” the memo said.

While breaking the federal regulations can lead to fines, the memo suggests no fines would be issued in this case because the problem was fixed.

The memo said while this is the only warning received by CFB Kingston in the past decade, other National Defence establishments were hit with 37 such “enforcement measures” over the last decade, “primarily for similar administrative or maintenance deficiencies.”

The memo says an influx of federal government spending on defence has enabled the department to address some of its maintenance shortcomings.

“With the recent increase in Defence funding, DND is implementing a real property compliance framework which includes halocarbon containing systems and expanding resources where required,” the memo said.

“At CFB Kingston, an additional position is being created to support local compliance activities, and new contracting initiatives are underway to enhance system maintenance, though reducing maintenance backlog will take time.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government hiked last year’s defence budget by $9 billion and plans to spend tens of billions of dollars more on defence over the coming years as Ottawa scrambles to meet its Nato commitments.

CBC recently reported previously planned cuts to the department’s operations are also going ahead at the same time.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Sunnybrook hospital parts ways with worker filmed using ‘racist language’ on public transport
stories.summary: Hospital says it recognizes the harm the incident caused to the organization’s Black staff, patients and supporters
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A Toronto hospital says it has parted ways with an employee who used “racist language” while riding public transit in a standoff caught on camera.

Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre says the worker is no longer employed at the hospital after it conducted an investigation into a video that circulated on social media.

The hospital, home to Canada’s largest trauma centre, says it recognizes the harm the incident has caused especially for the organization’s Black staff, patients and supporters.

Sunnybrook adds the former employee’s behaviour is inconsistent with its values.

The hospital did not say which video prompted the investigation, but footage filmed on a Toronto subway and shared on social media showed a person wearing a Sunnybrook sweater being confronted by other subway riders after they used derogatory language against Black people.

The video concludes with the person, who identifies themselves as a Sunnybrook employee, appearing to knock the camera out of the hands of the rider recording them.

stories.title: Myles Gray not lawfully entitled to repel police during arrest, Vancouver officer says
stories.summary: Const. Eric Birzneck is testifying at a public hearing into Gray’s death
stories.author: Darryl Greer
stories.content:
A second Vancouver police officer involved in the violent arrest that ended in the death of Myles Gray says he had never previously encountered someone in such a state that he believed was a medical situation known as “excited delirium.”

Const. Beau Spencer is among seven Vancouver officers facing a public hearing by British Columbia’s Police Complaint Commissioner into whether they committed misconduct during the fatal confrontation in 2015.

Spencer said Thursday he had been trained about excited delirium and that it could include making animalistic sounds and an inability to comprehend surroundings.

“Once the amount of time that had gone by with him fighting, it started to become more apparent that (excited delirium) might be a possibility,” he said of Gray.

The officer told the hearing he had been trained to regard excited delirium as a medical emergency, not a crime.

No charges have been laid over Gray’s death, which a 2023 coroner’s inquest ruled was a homicide, a term that does not assign legal blame.

A pathologist told the earlier coroners’ inquest that it had been thought “so-called excited delirium syndrome” could result independently in death, but analysis of the published data suggests that’s “quite unlikely.”

Spencer’s lawyer, Claire Hatcher, said in introductory remarks at the public hearing that during a lucid moment by Gray, the officer told him he would be OK, and he was “reassured by a professional police officer who was concerned about his well-being.”

She said Spencer’s role in the arrest had to be “considered distinctly” from those of other officers, since he arrived “after the fight had been ongoing for several minutes.”

Hatcher said Spencer “delivered three or four closed fist strikes, punches” to the shoulder of Gray to get his arm behind his back so he could be handcuffed during the arrest on a lawn.

“I expect Const. Spencer will testify that he and (other) officers then moved Mr. Gray further out from the tree to an open area on the lawn,” she said. “The adjudicator will hear that this is the whole of the force Const. Spencer used.”

She also addressed allegations that Spencer might have neglected his duties by not making notes immediately after the incident.

Hatcher said the hearing would be told that officers in the arrest had gathered at Vancouver police headquarters for a meeting after Gray’s death, where a “union representative or representatives instructed the members, Constable Spencer in particular, not to take any notes, and not to write anything on a computer while the IIO (independent Investigations Office) investigation was under way.”

Spencer’s testimony at the hearing in Vancouver on Thursday came after that of Const. Eric Birzneck, who said he did not agree he had given a “lopsided” account of the altercation by likening Gray to “the Hulk” or a “charging bull.”

Birzneck also denied trying to hide the fact that another officer had punched Gray as they tried to subdue him when the counsel for the commission, Brock Martland, asked him if he was trying to “protect a fellow officer.”

Martland asked Birzneck about his account of the attempt to arrest Gray, questioning whether his evidence omitted certain facts or minimized things to avoid creating problems for the others involved in the confrontation.

Birzneck disagreed and told the hearing his memories had been jogged over time with “pieces of the puzzle” coming together afterward.

He told the hearing earlier this week that Gray displayed incredible strength and appeared “impervious to pain” as police tried to subdue him near the boundary between Burnaby and Vancouver on Aug. 13, 2015.

Birzneck said Thursday that he believed Gray was “arrestable” at the time, with no lawful right to repel officers’ use of force against him.

The seven officers involved in the fatal altercation with Gray are named as respondents in the public hearing, called under the Police Act.

paragraphs: A second Vancouver police officer involved in the violent arrest that ended in the death of Myles Gray says he had never previously encountered someone in such a state that he believed was a medical situation known as “excited delirium.”

Const. Beau Spencer is among seven Vancouver officers facing a public hearing by British Columbia’s Police Complaint Commissioner into whether they committed misconduct during the fatal confrontation in 2015.
Spencer said Thursday he had been trained about excited delirium and that it could include making animalistic sounds and an inability to comprehend surroundings.
“Once the amount of time that had gone by with him fighting, it started to become more apparent that (excited delirium) might be a possibility,” he said of Gray.
The officer told the hearing he had been trained to regard excited delirium as a medical emergency, not a crime.
No charges have been laid over Gray’s death, which a 2023 coroner’s inquest ruled was a homicide, a term that does not assign legal blame.

A pathologist told the earlier coroners’ inquest that it had been thought “so-called excited delirium syndrome” could result independently in death, but analysis of the published data suggests that’s “quite unlikely.”

Spencer’s lawyer, Claire Hatcher, said in introductory remarks at the public hearing that during a lucid moment by Gray, the officer told him he would be OK, and he was “reassured by a professional police officer who was concerned about his well-being.”
She said Spencer’s role in the arrest had to be “considered distinctly” from those of other officers, since he arrived “after the fight had been ongoing for several minutes.”
Hatcher said Spencer “delivered three or four closed fist strikes, punches” to the shoulder of Gray to get his arm behind his back so he could be handcuffed during the arrest on a lawn.

“I expect Const. Spencer will testify that he and (other) officers then moved Mr. Gray further out from the tree to an open area on the lawn,” she said. “The adjudicator will hear that this is the whole of the force Const. Spencer used.”
She also addressed allegations that Spencer might have neglected his duties by not making notes immediately after the incident.

Hatcher said the hearing would be told that officers in the arrest had gathered at Vancouver police headquarters for a meeting after Gray’s death, where a “union representative or representatives instructed the members, Constable Spencer in particular, not to take any notes, and not to write anything on a computer while the IIO (independent Investigations Office) investigation was under way.”

Spencer’s testimony at the hearing in Vancouver on Thursday came after that of Const. Eric Birzneck, who said he did not agree he had given a “lopsided” account of the altercation by likening Gray to “the Hulk” or a “charging bull.”

Martland asked Birzneck about his account of the attempt to arrest Gray, questioning whether his evidence omitted certain facts or minimized things to avoid creating problems for the others involved in the confrontation.
Birzneck disagreed and told the hearing his memories had been jogged over time with “pieces of the puzzle” coming together afterward.

He told the hearing earlier this week that Gray displayed incredible strength and appeared “impervious to pain” as police tried to subdue him near the boundary between Burnaby and Vancouver on Aug. 13, 2015.

stories.title: Supreme Court to take on B.C. Aboriginal title case after province appeals
stories.summary: Indigenous rights and territorial claims are at the fore of public debate as the province gears up for election
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada on Thursday agreed to hear an Aboriginal title case from British Columbia, where the provincial government is challenging the amount of land awarded to a small First Nation.

In 2024, the Nuchatlaht won Canada’s second-ever declaration of Aboriginal title on Nootka Island, ON the Western edge of Vancouver Island. But the lower court in B.C. at the time granted title to only a small portion of the Nuchatlaht’s claim.

In April this year , the B.C. Court of Appeal ruled the declaration of Aboriginal title applied to the Nuchatlaht’s entire claim: 201 square kilometres – more than a third of Nootka Island.

The Supreme Court’s decision to take the case comes amid a provincial election in British Columbia this month during which the array of Indigenous court cases involving Aboriginal title and other rights have vaulted such legal questions to the fore of public debate.

The new case also lands as judges on the top court are saying yes to twice as many appeal applications than they had this decade. There had been criticism in the legal profession that the Supreme Court was not hearing enough cases.

On Thursday, the Nuchatlaht appeal was one of five the court agreed to hear, increasing the total of new cases this year to 48, the most since 2017.

A hearing on the Nuchatlaht case has not yet been scheduled and likely wouldn’t happen before next spring or possibly next fall.

The Nuchatlaht case centres around questions of what amounts to sufficient Indigenous occupation of land in the mid-1800s to establish Aboriginal title, when the British asserted sovereignty in the region, and how to delineate the geographic breadth of a claim if occupation of the land was variable.

The case will feature arguments over how courts apply the Supreme Court’s landmark Aboriginal title judgment in 2014, the Tsilhqot’in Nation ruling that marked the country’s first declaration of Aboriginal title to land in northwestern B.C.

In the B.C. government’s application to the Supreme Court to have its appeal of the Nuchatlaht ruling heard, the province cited a “time of intensifying Aboriginal title litigation in British Columbia and beyond” that urgently requires the consideration of the country’s top court.

The provincial government argued that the B.C. Court of Appeal’s backing of the full Nuchatlaht claim to 201 square kilometres amounted to a “loosening of the test for Aboriginal title” and that the original declaration to about 11 square kilometres should be restored.

Jack Woodward, counsel for the Nuchatlaht, said in an interview on Thursday that B.C.’s decision to appeal could backfire if the Supreme Court reaffirms the appellate-court ruling.

Mr. Woodward, who was one of the Tsilhqot’in Nation’s lawyers in 2014, also called on the next provincial government to pull out of the Supreme Court case and allow the B.C. Court of Appeal declaration of Aboriginal title to stand. The incumbent NDP is contesting a tight election against the opposition B.C. Conservative Party. The final day to vote is Oct. 24.

“There’s no reason to continue with this,” Mr. Woodward said. “I would encourage a re-elected NDP government or the new government to think hard of whether they want to do this.”

The B.C. government declined to comment on Thursday, citing the election campaign and a government in caretaker mode with communication limited to critical health and safety information.

The Nuchatlaht is a small First Nation, with about 160 members. Its case for Aboriginal title did not include land claimed by other Indigenous groups or private land.

This is a contrast to last year’s Cowichan Tribes ruling at the trial court in B.C., which recognized Aboriginal title over about 800 acres of land in the Vancouver suburb of Richmond and sparked worries over implications for private-property ownership. There are multiple appeals planned in the Cowichan case for the B.C. Court of Appeal.

After the Nuchatlaht’s initial victory in 2024, winning Aboriginal title to a portion of their claim, the B.C. provincial government quietly gave up a portion of Nuchatlitz Park on the northwestern tip of Nootka Island as a result of that ruling.

In the B.C. Court of Appeal ruling this year, the judgment noted that the province’s Forest Act and Park Act no longer applied to the 201 square kilometres to which the Nuchatlaht won a declaration of Aboriginal title. That means public access to the park is no longer assured.

stories.title: Why Trump is reviving 51st state rhetoric with midterms in less than 3 weeks
stories.summary: During a campaign rally in Arizona on Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump revived his rhetoric on wanting Canada to be '51st state' of the United States.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump is hitting the campaign trail as Republican candidates across the country face tough races in the midterm elections , and he has fallen back on a familiar target – Canada.

During a campaign rally in Arizona on Wednesday, Trump revived his rhetoric on wanting Canada to be “51 st state” of the United States.

“They’ll end up being the 51st state, because that’s the only way it works,” Trump told the crowd at his rally.

“We don’t need them, but they need us,” Trump said, adding that Canada would be “doing something just like Greenland.”

This was an apparent reference to an Arctic security agreement Trump signed with Denmark and Greenland last month, paving the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and easing tensions over his repeated calls for the vast island to become part of the United States.

Trump’s comments came as U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference ahead of pivotal midterm elections next month.

“Keep your nose out of American politics,” Hoekstra said during a podcast interview.

Hoekstra was referring to an anti-tariff ad paid for by the Ontario government and Industry Minister Melanie Joly’s comments that Canada’s counter-tariffs would target specific U.S. states.

Speaking to reporters Wednesday, Joly denied the claims that Canada was attempting to interfere in American politics.

“We’ll never do that and we’ll never accept that also being done to us in Canada,” she said.

Polling shows Republicans trailing in several key races, including in states bordering Canada where Trump’s trade war with Ottawa has become an election issue.

“Canada is being put on the table,” said University of Ottawa political science professor Emily Regan Wills.

Nowhere is that more evident than in Michigan, the heart of the American auto manufacturing sector, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers narrowly in most polls in their U.S. Senate race.

Rogers has attempted to put some distance between themselves and Trump’s trade policies, urging an end to the trade war with Canada.

He said in his debate with El-Sayed that he’d urged the White House privately to reach a trade deal with Canada and end the president’s tariffs. Canada is Michigan’s largest trading partner, as it is for many Great Lakes and Midwestern states.

Days before, Rogers unveiled a new ad in which he said, “We know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end the tariff war — now.”

That’s a noticeable departure from Rogers’ earlier, less specific statements praising Trump’s “America First” economic agenda while saying tariffs are not a “one-size-fits-all” solution.

“Americans in border states are used to being able to interact with Canada,” Wills said.

“Visiting, vacationing, shopping, that’s all being profoundly disrupted at this moment.”

In Maine, another state hit hard by Canada’s retaliatory tariffs, veteran Republican Susan Collins is trailing narrowly in most polls behind Democrat Troy Jackson.

During a debate, Collins touted her ability to remove certain items from Trump’s trade war with Canada, including pulp, concrete and road salt. Jackson pushed back by quipping “we can’t eat road salt.”

While prominent Republicans in tight races seek to distance themselves from his rhetoric, Trump is doubling down.

“I truly think this is psychological, this is not strategic. Donald Trump’s response to being told ‘no’ is to go harder,” Wills said.

For Republicans, Trump’s rhetoric might do more harm than good in border states.

“It would be great for other Republicans if he would stop talking about it. The issue is that nobody has yet discovered how to get Donald Trump to stop talking about something he wants to talk about,” she said.

“He doesn’t really have an ‘off’ button or ‘maybe that’s an inside thought’ button,” Wills added.

Trump’s own approval rating was at 37 per cent on Thursday, remaining steadily low for several months leading up to the midterms.

Trump’s renewed rhetoric around Canada’s sovereignty is likely intended to create a “rally around the flag” effect that is “supposed to make Americans feel embattled,” she said.

Whether that works is less clear.

The comments also come as U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gasoline and many other goods and services became more expensive. The consumer price index rose 3.7 per cent in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 3.4 per cent in August.

Some experts suggest Trump May be trying to shift the burden of high prices from himself to other targets, including Canada, but it May not connect with the voters as it has in the past.

“The American people are paying more and getting less because of the choices of Donald Trump,” said Todd Belt, professor of political management at George Washington University.

“You can’t out-message the economy. People get angry when you tell them that things are good and they know how much money they have at the end of the month,” he added.

stories.title: 7 times Trump reignited '51st state' rhetoric, suggesting 'that's the only way it works' for Canada
stories.summary: Donald Trump has reignited his "51st state" rhetoric, despite his administration warning Canada against getting involved in U.S. politics.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump has reignited his rhetoric around Canada becoming the “51st state,” shortly after his administration warned Canadian politicians against getting involved in U.S. affairs.

In a podcast appearance on Tuesday, U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said America is “closely watching Canadian activities” for election interference, referencing comments from Canada’s Industry Minister, ⁠Mélanie Joly, about retaliatory tariffs. “Keep your nose out of American politics,” he said.

Joly has hit back against his claims, saying: “We never do that, and we never accept that also being done to us in Canada,” while speaking to reporters in Ottawa on Wednesday. “What I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments…and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Later that day, Trump reiterated his ongoing stance that Canada should become the 51st U.S. state at a campaign rally in Arizona. Here are seven key occasions the U.S. president has suggested annexing Canada.

On Wednesday, Trump listed a number of grievances he has with Canada in his speech at Laughlin/Bullhead International Airport, adding: “They’ll end up being the 51st state, because that’s the only way it works.”

He said: “Canada treats us very badly. They always have. Not anymore. It’s a whole different ball game now that Trump is in town.”

The U.S. president also suggested Canada will “be doing something just like Greenland,” adding that it “just adds to our beautiful plate,” referring to the U.S.

He made the comments the same day Hoekstra warned Canadian politicians against engaging in behaviour that could be inferred as election interference.

After almost a year of silence from Trump on the 51st state topic, the U.S. president renewed the rhetoric after Canada entered a technical recession in June this year.

In a post on Truth Social , Trump wrote “51st state!” with a link to a Bloomberg report about the technical recession. Hoekstra then shared the post on his X account just hours before the Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and chief trade negotiator Janice Charette were due to meet with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Washington, D.C.

In September 2025, Trump referenced his desire for Canada to become the 51st state during his address to U.S. military officials in Virginia.

In the speech, he claimed work on the “Golden Dome Missile Defence Shield” was proceeding and that Canada had recently contacted him to say “they want to be a part of it.”

“To which I said, ‘Well, why don’t you just join our country? You become the 51st state and you get it for free,” he suggested.

On April 28, 2025, the day of Canada’s federal election, Trump told Canadians to “elect the man” who will let Canada become the 51st state in a Truth Social post.

“Elect the man who has the strength and wisdom to cut your taxes in half, increase your military power, for free, to the highest level in the World, have your Car, Steel, Aluminum, Lumber, Energy, and all other businesses, Quadruple in size, With Zero Tariffs OR Taxes, if Canada becomes the cherished 51st,” the post read.

He added: “America can no longer subsidize Canada with the Hundreds of Billions of Dollars a year that we have been spending in the past. It makes no sense unless Canada is a State!”

The post came just a few days after Trump sat down for an interview with Time magazine ’s senior political correspondent Eric Cortellessa and editor-in-chief Sam Jacobs.

“You’ve talked about acquiring Greenland, taking control of the Panama Canal, making Canada the 51st state,” Cortellessa said. “Maybe you’re trolling a little bit on that one. I don’t know.”

Trump’s answer was short: “Actually, no, I’m not.”

Trump’s comments in the Time interview doubled down on statements he made earlier that month in an interview that aired during the Super Bowl pre-show.

When asked whether his talk of annexing Canada is “a real thing,” Trump told Fox News Channel’s Bret Baier: “Yeah, it is.”

“I think Canada would be much better off being the 51st state because we lose $200 billion a year with Canada. And I’m not going to let that happen,” he said. “Why are we paying $200 billion a year, essentially a subsidy to Canada?”

Trump has repeatedly claimed that the U.S. loses hundreds of billions of dollars a year to Canada during his second term as president. But according to the Office of the United States Trade Representative , the U.S. goods trade deficit with Canada was US$48.3 billion in 2025, a 21 percent decrease ($12.9 billion) over 2024 and far less than Trump has claimed.

In January 2025, before the inauguration for his second term, Trump threatened to use “economic force” to make Canada the 51st state and called the border between the two countries an “artificially drawn line.”

“You get rid of that artificially drawn line and you take a look at what that looks like, and it would also be much better for national security,” he said at a news conference at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida. “And don’t forget, we basically protect Canada.”

Then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau responded with a post on X, in which he said: “There isn’t a snowball’s chance in hell that Canada would become part of the United States.”

Trump first floated the idea of Canada becoming the 51st state during a dinner with then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau at Mar-a-Lago in November 2024.

A few days later, in December that year, Trump called Trudeau “governor.” In a Truth Social post on Dec. 10, 2024, the U.S. president said it was a pleasure to have dined “with Governor Justin Trudeau of the great state of Canada” and that he looked forward to seeing “the governor again soon” to continue their “in-depth talks on tariffs and trade.”

It was the start of a long-running commentary from Trump on the annexation of Canada, which has now lasted almost two years.

content_blocks.text: ‘Join our country and you get it for free’
In September 2025, Trump referenced his desire for Canada to become the 51st state during his address to U.S. military officials in Virginia.

content_blocks.text: In the speech, he claimed work on the “Golden Dome Missile Defence Shield” was proceeding and that Canada had recently contacted him to say “they want to be a part of it.”
“To which I said, ‘Well, why don’t you just join our country? You become the 51st state and you get it for free,” he suggested.
Election Day comments
On April 28, 2025, the day of Canada’s federal election, Trump told Canadians to “elect the man” who will let Canada become the 51st state in a Truth Social post.

content_blocks.text: “Elect the man who has the strength and wisdom to cut your taxes in half, increase your military power, for free, to the highest level in the World, have your Car, Steel, Aluminum, Lumber, Energy, and all other businesses, Quadruple in size, With Zero Tariffs OR Taxes, if Canada becomes the cherished 51st,” the post read.
He added: “America can no longer subsidize Canada with the Hundreds of Billions of Dollars a year that we have been spending in the past. It makes no sense unless Canada is a State!”
The post came just a few days after Trump sat down for an interview with Time magazine ’s senior political correspondent Eric Cortellessa and editor-in-chief Sam Jacobs.
content_blocks.html: The post came just a few days after Trump sat down for an interview with TIME magazine’s senior political correspondent Eric Cortellessa and editor-in-chief Sam Jacobs.

content_blocks.text: “You’ve talked about acquiring Greenland, taking control of the Panama Canal, making Canada the 51st state,” Cortellessa said. “Maybe you’re trolling a little bit on that one. I don’t know.”
Trump’s answer was short: “Actually, no, I’m not.”
Super Bowl interview
Trump’s comments in the Time interview doubled down on statements he made earlier that month in an interview that aired during the Super Bowl pre-show.
When asked whether his talk of annexing Canada is “a real thing,” Trump told Fox News Channel’s Bret Baier: “Yeah, it is.”

“I think Canada would be much better off being the 51st state because we lose $200 billion a year with Canada. And I’m not going to let that happen,” he said. “Why are we paying $200 billion a year, essentially a subsidy to Canada?”

Trump has repeatedly claimed that the U.S. loses hundreds of billions of dollars a year to Canada during his second term as president. But according to the Office of the United States Trade Representative , the U.S. goods trade deficit with Canada was US$48.3 billion in 2025, a 21 percent decrease ($12.9 billion) over 2024 and far less than Trump has claimed.

content_blocks.text: The artificially drawn line

In January 2025, before the inauguration for his second term, Trump threatened to use “economic force” to make Canada the 51st state and called the border between the two countries an “artificially drawn line.”
