content_blocks.text: “You get rid of that artificially drawn line and you take a look at what that looks like, and it would also be much better for national security,” he said at a news conference at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida. “And don’t forget, we basically protect Canada.”
Then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau responded with a post on X, in which he said: “There isn’t a snowball’s chance in hell that Canada would become part of the United States.”
‘Governor Justin Trudeau’
Trump first floated the idea of Canada becoming the 51st state during a dinner with then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau at Mar-a-Lago in November 2024.

A few days later, in December that year, Trump called Trudeau “governor.” In a Truth Social post on Dec. 10, 2024, the U.S. president said it was a pleasure to have dined “with Governor Justin Trudeau of the great state of Canada” and that he looked forward to seeing “the governor again soon” to continue their “in-depth talks on tariffs and trade.”

stories.title: Inquest into death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet hears and sees woman's final moments
stories.summary: Toronto - A coroner's inquest into the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet has watched and listened to some of the 29-year-old woman's final moments before she fell to her death from a 24th-floor balcony.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Regis Korchinski-Paquet expressed difficulty breathing and reported losing control in a fight with her family in a series of agitated 911 calls shortly before she fell to her death from a 24th-floor balcony while police were inside her home, a coroner’s inquest heard Thursday.

Some of the 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman’s final moments were laid bare as jurors watched a compilation video that overlaid the recordings of five 911 calls and two police microphones with Cctv footage from the hallway outside her home and video from a police cruiser on May 27, 2020.

The calls made to 911 over roughly half an hour late that afternoon, including three by Korchinski-Paquet herself, brought six police officers and two paramedics to the west Toronto building in short succession.

Korchinski-Paquet’s mother, Claudette Beals, was the first to call at 5:13 p.m., telling the operator she needed police immediately because her son and daughter were fighting. Shouting could be heard in the background as Beals paced in the hallway.

Over the course of the 12-minute call, which overlapped with some of the others, Beals knocked on a neighbour’s door, shouted at her children that police were coming, and eventually told the operator that the siblings had an argument and “a fight broke out.”

“My daughter had a seizure this morning, and so this is how basically it all started,” she said.

“I just want the both of them out of my house. I don’t want no contact with neither one of them again.”

Meanwhile, Korchinski-Paquet made her first call to 911 at 5:15 p.m., breathing heavily as she told the operator she was being attacked and needed police immediately.

“I can’t breathe!” she shouted, prompting the operator to tell her to catch her breath and explain what happened.

“My brother just attacked me,” she said before the call was transferred to the paramedic service. The call ended shortly after the operator confirmed emergency crews were on the way.

In two more calls at 5:22 p.m. and 5:30 p.m., Korchinski-Paquet said her brother and mother attacked her after she told her brother to turn down the TV.

“My brother just jumped up and started punching me in my head and choked me, and my mom jumped in and started attacking me as well,” she said in the earlier of the two calls. When asked if they had weapons, she said the pair “pulled out knives” but couldn’t say where the knives were now.

“I broke two bottles because I got so angry that I threw them at them in the hallway. I could not control myself,” she said.

Korchinski-Paquet, who paced up and down the hallway in the security footage, also told the operator she had epilepsy, had experienced a seizure and wasn’t feeling well.

Her brother, Reece Korchinski, called 911 at 5:17 p.m. as he took refuge in the stairwell by the apartment.

Korchinski told the operator his sister started the fight but that he defended himself and managed to get the knives out of her hands before leaving the home and getting his fiancée and their children to do the same.

“My mom was trying to control me and my sister from arguing, but obviously once my sister pulled out the knife, there’s no controlling that,” he said.

He noted his sister’s epilepsy several times, adding she’d had two seizures that day and had “clearly” not calmed down afterward.

“My sister, she doesn’t know what she’s doing, because tonight she’ll apologize to me if I don’t end up going to jail for trying to protect myself and my family,” he said.

An agreed narrative read at the inquest earlier this week said Korchinski-Paquet had a history of seizures from epilepsy and often experienced confusion, “physically and verbally abusive behaviour,” and temporary amnesia in their wake. She had two seizures the morning of the day she died, inquest counsel said.

A neurologist who examined Korchinski-Paquet’s records after her death testified that in the years before her death, she showed symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium or postictal psychosis on several occasions. Both are mental states that can follow seizures.

Dr. Julien Hébert, who also watched the video as part of his review, said Korchinski-Paquet sounded distressed and repetitive in the recordings, as though she couldn’t remember her earlier calls.

Inquest counsel Roger Shallow warned jurors Thursday that the recordings would be difficult to see and hear, as he offered sympathies to Korchinski-Paquet’s grieving family.

“I take no shame in sharing with you that, in compiling this and watching it once it came together, I wept, and I’ll probably weep again tonight,” he said.

“To the family of Regis: This video is going to depict your daughter, your sister, your auntie, your loved one in the few final moments before this tragedy occurred, both in visual and in sound. My heart bleeds at the thought of the agony viewing this might cause you.”

Const. Brian VandenBrink was the first to arrive at the building at 5:20 p.m. and was told to wait for backup, according to the narrative. Const. Shane Beaudoin was second, and the two went up together at 5:29 p.m. Const. Brian Villeneuve followed suit about a minute later.

Constables Glenn Weddell and Frances Mallinger arrived at 5:31 p.m. and both had wireless microphones that captured heavily muffled and distorted audio from the scene. Two paramedics, Jessica Smitheram and Ronald Warzek, got there around the same time. Const. Christopher Beninger was the last at the scene at 5:36 p.m.

On the Cctv video, the officers can be seen arriving in waves, with the first few appearing to talk to Korchinski-Paquet and her mother by the elevators sometime before Korchinski-Paquet’s third call to 911. There was no sound in that portion of the video.

Another conversation appeared to take place once Villeneuve arrived after her third call.

Korchinski-Paquet went into the apartment at 5:35 p.m., and several first responders went in and out between then and 5:41 p.m., as did her mother and brother.

At one point, a voice can be heard saying Korchinski-Paquet reported experiencing seizures. “She’s quite hard to reason with,” the voice said as shouting could be heard in the background. “She’s a little erratic.”

Korchinski-Paquet fell from the balcony around 5:39 p.m., the narrative said.

Around that time on the video, a radio called for an ambulance, “Asap.”

Soon after, Korchinski-Paquet’s mother yelled “No!” then repeatedly sobbed “oh my God” as she came out of the apartment and walked up and down the hallway, at one point appearing to pound on the neighbour’s door.

A voice can be heard urging her to sit down and catch her breath before saying, “I got you.”

Korchinski-Paquet’s death, which came days after the police killing of George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, shook the city. Thousands of protesters took to Toronto’s streets to demand change to policing in the weeks that followed.

Ontario’s police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, eventually cleared Toronto police of wrongdoing in Korchinski-Paquet’s death, finding it happened as she was trying to move from her apartment balcony to the one next door.

The inquest will not look into the investigations conducted by various watchdog organizations, but its scope includes how police and first responders are informed about epilepsy.

A Toronto police employee is set to continue testifying Friday on the logistics of 911 call centres.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Carney stumps for unity as Alberta referendum approaches
stories.summary: Prime Minister urges supporters to vote to stay in Confederation and reject nine other questions put on ballot by Alberta Premier
stories.author: Bill Graveland and Dayne Patterson
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has taken his unity message to Alberta ahead of Monday’s referendum, urging people to vote for the province to remain in Canada and reject Premier Danielle Smith ’s other nine ballot proposals.

In prepared remarks ahead of a speech in Calgary on Thursday evening, Mr. Carney spoke of the country’s strength when united and warned Albertans of the consequences of voting against choosing to keep the province wedded to Confederation.

“At this pivotal moment, Albertans have a choice: to build a stronger Alberta and a greater Canada to leave for our children, or to burden them with years of deep division and great uncertainty,” Mr. Carney was set to tell a packed house at a downtown Calgary rally.

Monday’s referendum will ask voters to weigh in on 10 questions, one of them on whether Alberta should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on separating. The other nine questions, authored by Ms. Smith’s government, deal with limiting some non-permanent residents’ access to social services, charging them fees for health care and education, and numerous constitutional changes such as abolishing the federal Senate.

The Prime Minister has been critical of Ms. Smith’s decision to call the referendum. In May, he described it as a “dangerous bluff,” likening it to Britain’s 2016 vote to leave the European Union. (Mr. Carney was governor of the Bank of England at the time.)

He used similar language for his speech on Thursday night: “This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities,” he said in his prepared remarks.

“Our country and your futures are too precious to play games with.”

Mr. Carney has spent much of the referendum campaign on the sidelines, choosing to make his pitch to Albertans indirectly, by demonstrating Ottawa’s willingness to co-operate with the province. This has included dramatic policy shifts, particularly around environmental safeguards, and standing with the Premier as they announced a proposed oil pipeline to the West Coast .

Alberta’s referendum – the first time the province has put a secession question to voters – is occurring at a time of tremendous stress on national unity. While many Albertans prepare to vote on Monday, a newly elected separatist Quebec government will pose challenges for Ottawa, and U.S. President Donald Trump has shown few signs that the continuing tariff war and musings about annexation will end.

On Thursday night, Mr. Carney was set to say that the referendum “comes at the worst possible time,” pointing to what he described as a more dangerous and divided world.

“Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us.”

Mr. Carney’s push alongside Ms. Smith to build a new bitumen pipeline – most recently by designating it a project of national interest – has underscored a desire to blunt many Albertans’ deep frustration with Ottawa’s direction on energy and environmental policy under his predecessor, Justin Trudeau.

“I won’t sugarcoat it: some of those threads have needed to be repaired. The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” Mr. Carney was expected to say at the Thursday event, held by Forever Canadian, one of the most prominent federalist groups in the province.

He added that recently, Albertans were made to feel their “energy contributions were running against the tides of history.”

“What should have brought us together began to divide us. Contributing to a half century of politics that have too often pulled us apart,” he said in his prepared remarks.

It was the second time this week that the Prime Minister had made the case for unity directly to Albertans . On Monday, he released a short video shot in a classroom at St. Francis Xavier Catholic High School in Edmonton, which he attended as a teenager. In the video, he said that Albertans were being asked to decide on what he called “a long and uncertain process” of separation. “We are stronger together,” he said.

But Thursday was the first time he had encouraged Albertans to vote against the Premier’s nine proposals on immigration and constitutional changes.

As he made several stops in Calgary earlier in the day, he told Albertans to vote “no to the nine,” putting him in direct opposition to Ms. Smith, whose government has spent $4-million in advertising to campaign in favour of the proposals.

The Premier says she needs approval on them to fortify her mandate, and that they would provide leverage to gain more autonomy within Confederation.

Ms. Smith clapped back at Mr. Carney’s comments later in the day, writing on social media that “it appears that he has yet to fully understand just how damaging the open-border policies of his predecessor were.”

The Prime Minister is continuing his pro-Canada campaign on Friday in Red Deer, Alta., where he’ll share a stage with Ms. Smith, and attend another Forever Canadian rally in Edmonton in the evening.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is scheduled to give an address on Friday morning in Calgary at the Canada Strong and Free Network conference, a conservative gathering.

Advance voting opened earlier this week. Elections Alberta said in an e-mail on Thursday morning that roughly 815,000 Albertans had so far cast their ballots – about 27 per cent of all eligible voters.

Campaigners have been divided on how Mr. Carney should support the federalist effort and whether Ottawa should bankroll groups fighting to keep Alberta in Canada. (Alberta’s election-finance rules prohibit the federal government from funding referendum advertisers.)

Some have argued that the Prime Minister shouldn’t leave any cards on the table and use his immense popularity in Alberta to his advantage by giving the federalist side a boost. Others have said he should keep his hands out of it, and that circumventing election-finance rules would backfire.

Mr. Carney in September said his government wouldn’t help fund Alberta’s numerous pro-Canada campaigns , which struggled to raise money through the summer.

Federalist groups have since closed the distance on separatist campaigns that were flush with cash early on. Separatist groups have now scooped up about 59 per cent of all donations during the campaign, down from early September when roughly 75 per cent of all contributions were floating to them.

With a report from The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘We are stronger together’: Carney rallies for pro-Canada side in Calgary ahead of Monday referendum
stories.summary: Ahead of Monday's referendum, Mark Carney encouraged Albertans to vote to stay in Canada. He also urged voters to 'say no to the nine.'
stories.author: Payton Delisle-Miller
stories.content:
With the vote on Alberta’s future in Canada days away, Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Calgary on Thursday to rally support for keeping Alberta in Confederation, while also making clear where he stands on the other nine referendum questions.

Carney started his day with a visit to Cinnamon Indian Cuisine and Bar to enjoy some pakoras, before heading to Bridgeland Riverside Community Association Park to meet with Public Interest Alberta volunteers, a non-partisan organization that’s been campaigning against separation.

While speaking to a crowd of volunteers and supporters, Carney encouraged door-knockers to get Albertans voting on every question.

“Make sure everyone’s out there marking their ballots by Monday, including no to the nine,” Carney said.

Speaking to Public Interest Alberta executive director Brad Lafortune, Carney emphasized that it is not the time for division, but rather unity and Canadian generosity.

“There couldn’t be a worse time for this referendum. It’s a dangerous and divided world, and it’s time for us to come together and stand up for ourselves and to take care of each other,” he said. “This is an opportunity to do both.”

Carney also pointed to Alberta’s long-standing connections to the country. One of his examples was how firefighters come from across Canada during wildfire season to give Alberta a helping hand, with Albertan firefighters doing the same in other parts of the country.

and Canada is worth fighting for,” he said. “And fighting is about showing up, showing up to vote. Polls don’t vote, people vote.”

Lafortune echoed the prime minister’s call for unity, arguing that the province is stronger because of its diversity.

“Everyone comes from somewhere. Let’s build this country and this province together,” he said.

In an interview with Global News Morning Calgary, Carney said Canada is stronger in part because of Alberta, pointing to key announcements made in the province in recent months, such as the Pacific Link pipeline and the deepening of the Ukraine defence partnership .

“These big projects ultimately need private capital to be behind them. There’s huge interest, sort-of a step-change in investment in Alberta from private capital,” Carney said. “But on the expectation that Alberta’s gonna be moving forward, not endlessly debating its future within this country but taking advantage of a great future in the world.”

Another reason to keep Alberta a part of Canada, Carney said to volunteers, is the country’s rising global status. Carney said that since the start of this year, exports of grain, canola and beef have risen by 80 per cent, as an increasing number of countries make trade deals with Canada, creating opportunities across the country.

“We’re making ourselves more independent, we’re making ourselves stronger as a county, stronger as Albertans. Why? So we can live our lives as we want.

“We can have the diversity in this province if we take care of each other and we build together,” Carney said. “To do that, for the youth of this great province, we need to get people out to vote.”

In the same Global News interview, Carney also noted the work his government has done to lower immigration numbers. He said temporary foreign workers are down by 60 per cent, while foreign students are down 80 per cent.

He added that he’s also increased collaboration with provinces on immigration selections, making some questions on the ballot unnecessary.

“To be candid, I don’t need a referendum to tell us to co-operate more with the provinces on immigration. I think that’s where we’re headed,” he said.

Carney wrapped up his Bridgeland visit with a walk around the area, popping into stores and speaking with locals. He will attend Forever Canadian’s rally tonight at the BMO Centre before heading off to Edmonton tomorrow.

stories.title: Sunnybrook hospital parts ways with worker caught on video using 'racist language'
stories.summary: Toronto - A Toronto hospital says it has parted ways with an employee who used "racist language" while riding public transit in a standoff caught on camera.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - A Toronto hospital says it has parted ways with an employee who used “racist language” while riding public transit in a standoff caught on camera.

By The Canadian Press

Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre says the worker is no longer employed at the hospital after it conducted an investigation into a video that circulated on social media.

The hospital, home to Canada’s largest trauma centre, says it recognizes the harm the incident has caused especially for the organization’s Black staff, patients and supporters.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Sunnybrook adds the former employee’s behaviour is inconsistent with its values.

The hospital did not say which video prompted the investigation, but footage filmed on a Toronto subway and shared on social media showed a person wearing a Sunnybrook sweater being confronted by other subway riders after they used derogatory language against Black people.

The video concludes with the person, who identifies themselves as a Sunnybrook employee, appearing to knock the camera out of the hands of the rider recording them.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Fifty-nine Parti Québécois members swear oath at provincial legislature
stories.summary: representatives elected in the Oct. 5 general election are being sworn in at the provincial legislature.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A room full of Parti Québécois supporters chanted “Quebec, a country” as the party’s 59 elected officials lined up to get sworn in at the Quebec City legislature on Wednesday.

PQ leader and premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon had tears in his eyes as the new and returning members of the national assembly each swore their oath to the people of Quebec.

St-Pierre Plamondon said in his speech that it marked the first year a governing party did not swear an oath to the monarchy.

“We will work for Quebec and only for Quebec,” he said.

Members of the national assembly are no longer required to swear an oath to the King since the legislature changed its rules in 2022, when PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon refused to pledge his allegiance to the reigning monarch of Canada.

St-Pierre Plamondon noted how a number of MNAs previously swore the oath to the monarch with their fingers crossed behind their backs, or mumbled through it, before the change.

“Behind closed doors, everyone was criticizing and calling out the odious nature of the process,” he said.

The new MNAs instead swore to uphold the laws of Quebec.

St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to hold a referendum on Quebec sovereignty after 2029, when U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House.

The sovereigntist party fell short of the 64 seats needed to form a majority in the Oct. 5 election, but could get closer to that threshold after requesting recounts in two ridings where it came second.

St-Pierre Plamondon reminded the party rank-and-file that after the 2022 election, only three PQ members were sworn in. The party won four more seats in subsequent byelections before forming a minority government.

“We will be masters in our own home … as is our destiny,” St-Pierre Plamondon said.

Most the officials sworn in have no experience at the national assembly.

St-Pierre Plamondon emphasized the importance of a strong government and said former premier Pauline Marois and Jean Royer, previously a chief of staff to former premier Jacques Parizeau, would help train the new MNAs.

The party has some returning veterans. Joël Arseneau and Pascal Bérubé, both re-elected, held the PQ’s two other seats after the 2022 election. Nicolas Marceau, who won his seat in the Marie-Victorin riding in the Montérégie, served as finance minister under Marois. Alain Therrien is also returning to the national assembly after serving as a member of Parliament for the Bloc Québécois.

St-Pierre Plamondon said his government would work to ensure it can keep its promises — which includes cutting government spending, tackling the cost of living, improving the education system and protecting Quebec culture — despite its minority.

“We’re going to reach out to the opposition because Quebecers want their legislature to work,” he said.

Liberal, Conservative and Québec solidaire representatives will be sworn in next week.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard said in a radio interview on Tuesday that he has “no intention” to swear an oath to the King.

St-Pierre Plamondon is scheduled to unveil his cabinet and officially form a government on Oct. 21.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Calgary Stampeders need help to reach CFL playoffs
stories.summary: The Calgary Stampeders will be playing for much more than the season series with the B.C. Lions on Saturday night.
stories.author: n The Canadian Pressn
stories.content:
Toronto – The Calgary Stampeders will be playing for much more than the season series with the B.C. Lions on Saturday night.

Calgary (8-9) visits B.C. (10-6) with the two teams having split their previous two contests this season. The Lions can cement a home playoff game with a victory.

Calgary doesn’t control its playoff fate. It can neither clinch a post-season berth with a victory nor be eliminated from contention with a loss, thanks to last week’s 33-28 setback to the Winnipeg Blue Bombers.

That loss gave Winnipeg the season series with Calgary 2-1. The Bombers split their series with Saskatchewan 1-1 but have a better point differential in those two contests, giving them the tiebreaker with the Riders.

If Calgary beats B.C., there exists the possibility of a tie among three teams at 9-9 in the West Division. The tiebreaker would be combined head-to-head records involving the tied teams.

Winnipeg would get third based upon a 3-2 record, Saskatchewan would be fourth (2-2) while Calgary (2-3) would finish fifth and out of the playoffs.

If the Stampeders and Riders were to end the season with identical records, Calgary would finish ahead of Saskatchewan on point differential. The Stamps outscored the Riders 74-71 in their head-to-head contests.

Calgary could still reach the playoffs with a loss to B.C., so long as Saskatchewan (8-8) drops both of its final two regular-season games. But a Riders victory — either Saturday versus Montreal or versus Edmonton on Oct. 24 — would eliminate the Stampeders from playoff contention.

Either a Calgary loss or a Winnipeg win over Edmonton (12-4) on Friday would clinch a playoff berth for the Bombers.

Edmonton can clinch first in the West — and home field for the division final Nov. 7 — with a win over Winnipeg next week over Saskatchewan. The Elks would also cement top spot if the Lions were to lose either of their final two regular-season contests.

If Edmonton cements first, B.C. can secure second — and host the West semifinal Oct. 31 — with one more victory or a Winnipeg loss.

The Bombers still have an outside chance of capturing second if they finish tied with the Lions at the end of the season, but would need to beat B.C. by 17 points in the final week of the season.

B.C. won the first meeting of the teams 35-19 at Princess Auto Stadium on July 30.

The East Division playoff picture is settled. The Toronto Argonauts (9-7) will host the West’s fourth-place finisher in the semifinal contest Oct. 31, with the winner visiting Montreal (13-3) on Nov. 7.

The Grey Cup will be held Nov. 15 at Calgary’s McMahon Stadium.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Sophie Grégoire Trudeau didn't see Justin Trudeau as a PM: 'I knew it was his job, but come on'
stories.summary: talked about the pitfalls of allowing public perception to influence once self-image.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
During her time as Canada’s unofficial first lady, Sophie Grégoire Trudeau said she never saw her “former partner as a prime minister.”

“I knew it was his job, but come on,” the soon-to-be 52-year-old told Talia Bronfman and Jessica Green, hosts of Canadian podcast Built For This , in a recent episode.

“Like snap out of every role you’re in, because if you believe it for half a second you’re doomed, and including celebrity.”

Grégoire Trudeau and former prime minister Justin Trudeau have been separated since August 2023 after 18 years of marriage and three children together — Xavier, 18, Ella-Grace, 17, and Hadrien, 12. Trudeau, 54, has been in a heavily publicized romantic relationship with American pop star Katy Perry since the summer of 2025.

Grégoire Trudeau recounted keeping herself and her ex grounded when ordinary people they would encounter in their official capacity started “losing it.”

“Right away I’m like, ‘No, no, no, no, no. This is not going to happen. Look into my eyes right now. We belong to each other. We’re doing this for each other. So, let’s put all the titles and the accolades and the lighting aside and let’s just come back to like we’re walking each other home,’” she explained.

Those were the only mentions of Trudeau during their nearly hour-long conversation posted on Oct. 10, World Mental Health Day, and focused largely on Grégoire Trudeau’s debut self-help book, Closer Together: Knowing Ourselves, Loving Each Other. Grégoire Trudeau is a long-time mental health advocate and the first national volunteer for the Canadian Mental Health Association .

But she did discuss the realities of political life, which is both an “incredible opportunity” and often quite trying.

“People still think politics is like glamorous and it’s champagne and I’m like ‘Oh my goodness, if people only knew the sacrifices that you make in your life. Like your time is not yours anymore. Your family is almost not yours anymore,” she explained.

“So to be honest, if people would ask me today, would you tell anybody to go into public service? I would say if you don’t have little kids, yes.”

To keep herself grounded, she said she avoided most articles written about her because “it was already a situation in which the physical and psychological safety” of her loved ones “was at play every single day.

“I can’t even tell you as a mother what that does to your nervous system, “ she said. “So my main work was to keep that calm so that when they came back … they could feed from somebody who was grounded.”

The podcast was recorded in Montreal, where Grégoire Trudeau returned to live this year in a rented home about four streets from where she spent most of her youth. She has mixed feelings about returning to her hometown now, most of it “melancholy.” Trudeau, who also grew up in the Quebec city, bought a $4.26 million home in Outremont earlier this year.

“I’m in a period of life that there’s been a lot of years of sadness and tears because so much shedding, so much letting go, so much deconstructing what I thought my life would be like, and when you’re a separated mother and you coming into an empty home… ” she said, fighting back tears, “I’m still not used to it and I’m not built for that. So, I’m learning non-stop.”

Grégoire Trudeau said she’s not sure what chapter comes next in her life, but she did allude to a potential romantic partner when questioning out loud why she moved back to Montreal.

“And I’m like, why am I back here? Is he here? Is he waiting for me,” she asks, giving the female hosts knowing looks and drawing equally knowing replies.

Earlier in the show, she divulged that her second book — a children’s “emotional literacy” book — will be published in 2027 and will feature illustrations inspired by her childhood growing up in nature with her parents.

During the rapid-fire question round, she said her go-to karaoke track is the Four Non Blondes’ What’s Going On?, she’d recommend Little Italy for anyone looking to dine out in Montreal and once accidentally ran over a baby mouse on the road that she’d stopped to help.

stories.title: Flintstones vitamins, Aleve and Claritin tablets hit in new recall
stories.summary: Bottles of Flintstones Complete Multivitamins and Minerals tablets and 10 mg Claritin Allergy Tablets have been recalled due to distribution errors.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Bottles of Flintstones vitamins, Claritin and Aleve have been recalled due to distribution errors.

Flintstones Complete Multivitamins and Minerals tablets, 10 mg Claritin Allergy Tablets and 200 mg Aleve tablets were recalled after customer-returned products were mistakenly reintroduced into saleable inventory and redistributed across wholesale markets, according to the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia).

The Cfia is encouraging consumers to check with the recalling firm if their product is affected.

All three products are produced by the pharmaceutical company Bayer Inc.

The Cfia also said that any health product related side effects should be reported to Health Canada.

stories.title: Nova Scotia premier defends changing his stance on welcoming data centre proposals
stories.summary: Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston is defending his decision to change his stance on when data centres might be considered for approval to operate in the province.
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong
stories.content:
Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston is defending his decision to change his stance on when data centres might be considered for approval to operate in the province.

In June, the premier said it was too soon to turn his government’s full attention to the matter.

He said data centres wouldn’t receive approval until the province could supply their considerable energy demands.

At the time, the premier said discussions about data centres would have to wait until the province had completed major energy generation projects, including the ambitious Wind West offshore wind farms.

Late last month, however, Houston softened his position, saying data centres are becoming critical pieces of Canadian infrastructure.

He said he became more open to considering data centre proposals after Ottawa rolled out new rules for the sector.

Houston said today the federal government’s focus on data sovereignty played a role in changing his mind.

Data centres, used in artificial intelligence and other high-tech industries, are massive operations that require an immense amount of electricity to run and cool off computer servers.

stories.title: Nova Scotia premier defends change of his stance on data centre proposals
stories.summary: Halifax - Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston is defending his decision to change his stance on when data centres might be considered for approval to operate in the province.
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston is defending his decision to change his stance on when data centres might be considered for approval to operate in the province.

In June, the premier said it was too soon to turn his government’s attention to the matter, and that it would not be discussed until far into the future.

A few months later, he softened that stance, opening a door to consider proposals from the sector.

“A lot has happened … in the world, geopolitics, all kinds of situations there,” Houston told reporters Thursday.

“When you look at some of the positioning of the federal government around data sovereignty, around the regulations that would be required, (they) definitely were thoughtful and had an impact on me.”

The premier had previously said discussions about data centres would have to wait until the province had completed major energy generation projects, including the ambitious Wind West offshore wind farms.

“We’re going to generate significant amounts of energy … (and) at that point in time, that would be a more appropriate discussion,” he said on June 18.

At the time, the premier said the discussion about data centres “is so far out in the future … but there wouldn’t be a commitment to a data centre unless we could fully supply the energy without any risk to Nova Scotians.”

Late last month, however, Houston said data centres are becoming increasingly critical pieces of infrastructure, adding that Canada can’t rely on other countries to store its data. He said he became more open to considering data centre proposals after Ottawa rolled out its new rules.

“I think the sentiment of that (June) statement was that we wouldn’t allow an impact on ratepayers,” Houston said Thursday. “We’re not going to drive up the rates to let another user, any type of industrial use, have their power while households and Nova Scotians pay more. That sentiment remains.”

Data centres, used in AI and other high-tech industries, are typically massive operations that require immense amounts of electricity to run and cool off computer servers.

EverWind Fuels, the company planning a large-scale green hydrogen project in Cape Breton to be powered by onshore wind, says it’s exploring setting up a data centre at an existing industrial site at Point Tupper, N.S.

The proposed data centre “would form part of the broader Point Tupper Energy Hub and complement EverWind’s clean energy projects across Nova Scotia,” company spokesperson Claire Parsons said in an email Thursday.

Parsons declined to say if the proposed data centre would be used for artificial intelligence.

Official Opposition Leader Claudia Chender called Houston’s changed stance on data centres a “stunning reversal.”

“When the premier said not long ago that we were not considering AI data centres, not today, not tomorrow … people took him at his word as they watched these debates play out in other places,” Chender, the NDP leader, told reporters Thursday.

Last month, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew rejected plans for a massive AI data centre southeast of Winnipeg. Kinew said the project’s size, energy use and community impact outweighed its limited gains. He said he was also skeptical of the long-term demand for centres of this scale given advances in computing.

Meanwhile, Bell Canada intends to quadruple the size of its planned data centre project in Saskatchewan, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying last month the project is expected to bring in more than $50 billion in capital investment.

Alberta has also embraced data centre development. Electricity generator TransAlta Corp. announced plans in February to power a new data centre west of Edmonton. This came after the provincial technology minister said in 2024 that province was hoping to see $100 billion worth of artificial intelligence data centres under construction over five years.

Environmental advocates have raised concerns about the massive volume of energy and water used by data centres. They’ve also warned about the potential for chemical pollution.

A recent United Nations University report says the environmental footprint of data centres globally already rivals some of the world’s largest countries. The report also predicts their water and energy use and pollution will double in just four years as use of artificial intelligence grows.

Chender and interim Liberal leader Iain Rankin both said Thursday they have serious concerns about the potential environmental impacts and water use tied to a data centre.

Houston said Thursday a data centre in Nova Scotia would have to go through an approval process that could exceed federal requirements. This means the process would need to consider the impact on the environment and ratepayers.

Both opposition leaders said these protections should be built into legislation.

“It’s one thing to say that water and environmental concerns and ratepayers will be protected, but it’s not a fact that the premier’s word is stronger than regulations or legislation,” Rankin said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Police investigating ‘suspicious’ fire at abandoned Toronto building
stories.summary: Crews arrived and found a "fully involved" fire that was quickly upgraded to a three-alarm blaze, said Fire Capt. Bill Papakonstantinou.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Toronto police are treating a three-alarm overnight blaze at an abandoned building as suspicious after crews spent Wednesday night battling heavy smoke and flames that resulted in the temporary shut down of the nearby Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway.

Fire crews said they responded to reports of a commercial building on fire at Matilda and Munro streets at around 9:30 p.m. Wednesday.

Crews arrived and found a “fully involved” fire that was quickly upgraded to a three-alarm blaze, said Toronto fire Capt. Bill Papakonstantinou.

A male in his 30s was taken to the hospital around 9:45 p.m. with non-life-threatening injuries in connection to the fire, Toronto paramedics said.

Roads, including the highways, reopened around 3 a.m. Thursday, the city said on social media. By 7 a.m., the fire was completely extinguished but the “structural integrity” of the building is a concern, said Papakonstantinou.

Toronto building inspectors are on scene for a structural assessment, he said. As of Thursday afternoon, Toronto fire has remained on scene.

Toronto police told Global News the fire is being treated as suspicious.

stories.title: Cohere announces plan to buy European AI cybersecurity startup Aisle
stories.summary: Toronto company aims to bolster its AI models with Aisle’s systems that detect and address software vulnerabilities
stories.author: Joe Castaldo
stories.content:
Cohere Inc. is acquiring European startup Aisle to bolster its cybersecurity capabilities as the artificial intelligence industry grapples with the technology’s potential to both defend against threats and conduct more sophisticated hacks if used by bad actors.

Toronto-based Cohere said on Thursday that it had signed a letter of intent to acquire Aisle, which is based in Prague. Financial terms were not disclosed. Aisle was founded in 2024 and has built AI systems that detect and help address vulnerabilities in software.

Aisle said it had found more than 500 previously unknown vulnerabilities in more than 100 code bases in the past year, and said its platform has matched or outperformed competing systems.

“Aisle has been focused on defending the critical infrastructure of the open source ecosystem, and it’s done that better than many of the more well known efforts,” Cohere chief executive officer Aidan Gomez wrote on LinkedIn.

In a blog post, Cohere said that it will combine Aisle’s autonomous security research with its AI models. “The capabilities of a foundation model and the specialized system built around it can reinforce each other,” the company said.

Cohere also said it will make a substantial investment in Prague to expand Aisle’s existing presence and establish the city as its global hub for AI cybersecurity systems.

Aisle is not Cohere’s first acquisition. In May, it announced the purchase of biopharma company Reliant AI, which has operations in Montreal and Berlin. Cohere also announced a deal to combine with German AI company Aleph Alpha this year, which still requires regulatory approval.

The Globe and Mail previously reported that Cohere is in talks to raise upwards of US$3-billion, including funds from the Canadian and German governments that would value the company at US$20-billion.

The cybersecurity risks of AI have been heightened ever since Anthropic announced its Mythos model earlier this year, which the company said was adept at finding software vulnerabilities. Anthropic initially limited access to a select group of companies to shore up their defences, and has since made it available to qualifying security professionals.

More recently, businesses, governments and regulators have become deeply concerned about instances of AI agents breaking free of testing sandboxes to access the internet. Agents from OpenAI, for example, have infiltrated the systems of the Australian government and AI company Hugging Face, while an Anthropic agent submitted a false homicide tip to the Philadelphia police.

“You might think, ‘Oh, this is a renaissance for cyber attackers. They have these models that just exploit systems,’” Cohere co-founder Ivan Zhang said in an interview. But companies engaged in cyber defense have an advantage, he continued. “It’s actually easier to patch vulnerabilities than it is to discover them and chain them together to attack a target.”

Aisle co-founder Ondrej Vlcek will become senior vice-president of Cohere Cyber, a newly established division. Fellow co-founder Jaya Baloo will assume the role of Cohere’s chief information security officer, while Stanislav Fort will become vice-president of AI security.

The three co-founders have previously worked at Google DeepMind, Anthropic and Czech cybersecurity company Avast.

Mr. Vlcek wrote on LinkedIn that Cohere and Aisle began talking earlier this year and realized that combining would be a “natural fit.”

The companies are also pitching the deal as a sign of the deepening ties between Canada and Europe, when relations with the United States are frayed and the AI industry is dominated by American tech giants.

“I’ve been hearing how Europe is behind in AI, and how Canada is behind in AI,” Mr. Vlcek wrote. “We can either keep complaining about it, or do something about it.”
paragraphs: Cohere Inc. is acquiring European startup Aisle to bolster its cybersecurity capabilities as the artificial intelligence industry grapples with the technology’s potential to both defend against threats and conduct more sophisticated hacks if used by bad actors.

Toronto-based Cohere said on Thursday that it had signed a letter of intent to acquire Aisle, which is based in Prague. Financial terms were not disclosed. Aisle was founded in 2024 and has built AI systems that detect and help address vulnerabilities in software.
Aisle said it had found more than 500 previously unknown vulnerabilities in more than 100 code bases in the past year, and said its platform has matched or outperformed competing systems.

“Aisle has been focused on defending the critical infrastructure of the open source ecosystem, and it’s done that better than many of the more well known efforts,” Cohere chief executive officer Aidan Gomez wrote on LinkedIn.

In a blog post, Cohere said that it will combine Aisle’s autonomous security research with its AI models. “The capabilities of a foundation model and the specialized system built around it can reinforce each other,” the company said.
Cohere also said it will make a substantial investment in Prague to expand Aisle’s existing presence and establish the city as its global hub for AI cybersecurity systems.

Aisle is not Cohere’s first acquisition. In May, it announced the purchase of biopharma company Reliant AI, which has operations in Montreal and Berlin. Cohere also announced a deal to combine with German AI company Aleph Alpha this year, which still requires regulatory approval.

The Globe and Mail previously reported that Cohere is in talks to raise upwards of US$3-billion, including funds from the Canadian and German governments that would value the company at US$20-billion.

The cybersecurity risks of AI have been heightened ever since Anthropic announced its Mythos model earlier this year, which the company said was adept at finding software vulnerabilities. Anthropic initially limited access to a select group of companies to shore up their defences, and has since made it available to qualifying security professionals.

More recently, businesses, governments and regulators have become deeply concerned about instances of AI agents breaking free of testing sandboxes to access the internet. Agents from OpenAI, for example, have infiltrated the systems of the Australian government and AI company Hugging Face, while an Anthropic agent submitted a false homicide tip to the Philadelphia police.

“You might think, ‘Oh, this is a renaissance for cyber attackers. They have these models that just exploit systems,’” Cohere co-founder Ivan Zhang said in an interview. But companies engaged in cyber defense have an advantage, he continued. “It’s actually easier to patch vulnerabilities than it is to discover them and chain them together to attack a target.”

Aisle co-founder Ondrej Vlcek will become senior vice-president of Cohere Cyber, a newly established division. Fellow co-founder Jaya Baloo will assume the role of Cohere’s chief information security officer, while Stanislav Fort will become vice-president of AI security.
The three co-founders have previously worked at Google DeepMind, Anthropic and Czech cybersecurity company Avast.
Mr. Vlcek wrote on LinkedIn that Cohere and Aisle began talking earlier this year and realized that combining would be a “natural fit.”

The companies are also pitching the deal as a sign of the deepening ties between Canada and Europe, when relations with the United States are frayed and the AI industry is dominated by American tech giants.
“I’ve been hearing how Europe is behind in AI, and how Canada is behind in AI,” Mr. Vlcek wrote. “We can either keep complaining about it, or do something about it.”

The federal agency says customer-returned bottles of Flintstones Complete Multivitamins and Minerals were inadvertently reintroduced into saleable inventory and distributed to wholesalers. The recalled products bear the lot number Naaexkw. “Consult your healthcare pr…
stories.author: John Marchesan
stories.content:
Health Canada has issued a recall of Flintstones multivitamins due to a distribution error.

The federal agency says customer-returned bottles of Flintstones Complete Multivitamins and Minerals were inadvertently reintroduced into saleable inventory and distributed to wholesalers.

The recalled products bear the lot number Naaexkw.

“Consult your healthcare provider prior to discontinuing use of the affected product, or for any health concerns,” read a statement from Health Canada.

stories.title: Fanshawe College Unveils New Simulator Centre to help with Ptsd
stories.summary: Fanshawe College has opened a new extended reality training Centre designed to prepare students for hig...
stories.author: Ben McFadden
stories.content:
XR Opening at WSIB Centre of Excellence (Photo: Benjamin McFadden, XFM News)

Fanshawe College has opened a new extended reality training Centre designed to prepare students for high-stress situations they could encounter in frontline careers, students will use headsets to get a glimpse into pivotal scenarios they will experience in the field.

The Centre of Excellence was announced in partnership with the Workplace Safety & Insurance Board (WSIB) following an investment of $20 million coming from the board as part of a broader initiative which includes London’s Police and Firefighters launched by WSIB.

Construction began two years ago after t he WSIB announced its partnership with Fanshawe and London’s emergency services.

Located on the college’s main campus, the Centre uses extended reality (XR) technology to simulate high-stress, real-world situations before students encounter them in their careers. The software developed will simulate scenarios about fires, shootings, and emergency room operations.

College officials said the Centre is designed to improve preparedness and support mental health outcomes among future frontline workers. “By using XR technology, we are pushing everything on the cutting edge,” said Pedro Nuez a professor with the Video Game Development program at Fanshawe.

WSIB Centre of Excellence, Respiratory Nursing students training (Photo: Benjamin McFadden, XFM News)

“I’ve always felt drawn toward something that can make actual change for people,” said Yeva Makhankova, a junior technical artist for the XR program, and a graduate of Fanshawe’s Game Development program.

This unique program is offered to the Police and Firefighting Foundations as well as Respiratory Nursing programs and will soon be available to other similar courses provided at Fanshawe.

“PTSD is a real problem, especially in emergency services. It makes life harder for them, their families and even the people they help every day,” said Makhankova. With students seeing these circumstances in a virtual setting, it will prepare them mentally for witnessing them on the job.

As the doors open students and working professionals alike will be able to further train their skills when the time comes to act in the real world.

WSIB Centre of Excellence, respiratory student (Photo: Benjamin McFadden, XFM News)

stories.title: Dozens of drivers went wrong way on Highway 401 since Gordie Howe bridge opened: OPP
stories.summary: Ontario Provincial Police are urging drivers to pay closer attention to traffic signs when approaching the Gordie Howe International Bridge in Windsor, Ont., after dozens of cars were seen driving the wrong way on the nearby stretch of Highway 401.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontario’s Ministry of Transportation said it will add more signage near Gordie Howe International Bridge in Windsor, after provincial police said dozens of cars were seen driving the wrong way on the nearby stretch of Highway 401.

“We are working closely with the Ontario Provincial Police and the Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority to add additional signage throughout the area to alert drivers of the border crossing,” Dakota Brasier, spokesperson for Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria, said in a statement Thursday.

stories.title: Fisheries sector fund gets $300 million extension from Ottawa, Atlantic provinces
stories.summary: Ottawa and the four Atlantic provinces are extending a multimillion-dollar fund aimed at supporting the region's fish and seafood sector amid global economic headwinds.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
Ottawa and the four Atlantic provinces are extending a multimillion-dollar fund aimed at supporting the region’s fish and seafood sector amid global economic headwinds.

Federal Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson announced Thursday a five-year renewal of the Atlantic Fisheries Fund , which will result in $300 million worth of investments in industry research, infrastructure and other areas.

Ottawa will provide 60 per cent of the cash while Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, P.E.I. and Newfoundland and Labrador will contribute the rest.

The fund was introduced in 2017 and has since provided more than $370 million for more than 1,300 projects.

The new money will also be used to help the sector find new markets through advertising, industry branding and market research.

The federal Fisheries Department says improved marketing will make the sector more resilient to global trade disruptions.

Thompson says she wants to see Canadian harvesters and growers expand their markets.

“When Atlantic seafood sells to more of the world, we build Canada strong,” Thompson said in a statement.

stories.title: Competition Bureau says Quebec real estate board violated abuse of dominance rules
stories.summary: The Competition Bureau says it has reached a settlement with Quebec's real estate industry association to loosen data-sharing restrictions that violated the Competition Act.
stories.author: Sammy Hudes
stories.content:
The Competition Bureau says it has reached a settlement with Quebec’s real estate industry association to loosen data-sharing restrictions that violated the Competition Act.

The watchdog said the Quebec Professional Association of Real Estate Brokers and its subsidiary, Société Centris, broke abuse of dominance rules by refusing to provide members with a real estate data feed, while also restricting how such data could be used.

The bureau said lack of access to that data was likely meant to “impede innovation and limit competition in the real estate brokerage services market.”

As part of a consent agreement reached with the association, it will now provide its members with a real estate data feed containing information about sale prices, listing history and property characteristics.

The bureau said data feeds could help real estate brokers create property comparison tools, market valuation or data visualization services, along with platforms offering consumers more detailed information.

“Real estate data is crucial to some of the most important decisions Quebecers make when purchasing a property,” said Jeanne Pratt, interim commissioner of competition, in a statement.

“This agreement will promote innovation, enhance competition, and help consumers make informed choices by providing more complete access to this data.”

In a news release, Qpareb said it would implement all measures outlined in the settlement over the next year.

It said the agreement ensures that real estate agencies will have automated access to the data. Agencies would then be able to provide that data to clients, typically via a secure website.

“It is the result of several years of efforts so that the Qpareb can implement a solution tailored to the Quebec reality, especially given that Quebec’s laws are more restrictive than those in the rest of Canada, particularly with regard to the protection of personal information,” said Pierre-Olivier Simard, president of the Qpareb board of directors, in a statement.

The bureau launched its investigation into Qpareb’s data-sharing practices in 2023. It previously obtained a Federal Court order requiring the association to hand over information related to the effects of its restrictions and the reasons for them.

The watchdog has been keen in recent years to ensure that limited public access to real estate data doesn’t contribute to market dominance or ward off innovation within the sector.

During a previous case against the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board, the bureau challenged rules that prevented brokers in that region from sharing certain real estate data with their clients through secure online platforms.

It had claimed Trreb’s grip on multiple listing service (MLS) data was so tight it constituted anticompetitive behaviour. The bureau sought to make the data publicly accessible on brokers’ websites, but Trreb fought back, claiming the publication of such data posed privacy and copyright concerns.

The Competition Tribunal, and later the Federal Court of Appeal, sided with the bureau, before the Supreme Court of Canada refused to hear the case in 2018.

The Supreme Court’s refusal cleared the way for MLS data to appear on other websites, which must be password-protected and are typically open to an agent’s clients or site subscribers.

paragraphs: The Competition Bureau says it has reached a settlement with Quebec’s real estate industry association to loosen data-sharing restrictions that violated the Competition Act.

The watchdog said the Quebec Professional Association of Real Estate Brokers and its subsidiary, Société Centris, broke abuse of dominance rules by refusing to provide members with a real estate data feed, while also restricting how such data could be used.
The bureau said lack of access to that data was likely meant to “impede innovation and limit competition in the real estate brokerage services market.”

As part of a consent agreement reached with the association, it will now provide its members with a real estate data feed containing information about sale prices, listing history and property characteristics.

The bureau said data feeds could help real estate brokers create property comparison tools, market valuation or data visualization services, along with platforms offering consumers more detailed information.
“Real estate data is crucial to some of the most important decisions Quebecers make when purchasing a property,” said Jeanne Pratt, interim commissioner of competition, in a statement.
“This agreement will promote innovation, enhance competition, and help consumers make informed choices by providing more complete access to this data.”
In a news release, Qpareb said it would implement all measures outlined in the settlement over the next year.
It said the agreement ensures that real estate agencies will have automated access to the data. Agencies would then be able to provide that data to clients, typically via a secure website.

“It is the result of several years of efforts so that the Qpareb can implement a solution tailored to the Quebec reality, especially given that Quebec’s laws are more restrictive than those in the rest of Canada, particularly with regard to the protection of personal information,” said Pierre-Olivier Simard, president of the Qpareb board of directors, in a statement.

The bureau launched its investigation into Qpareb’s data-sharing practices in 2023. It previously obtained a Federal Court order requiring the association to hand over information related to the effects of its restrictions and the reasons for them.
The watchdog has been keen in recent years to ensure that limited public access to real estate data doesn’t contribute to market dominance or ward off innovation within the sector.

During a previous case against the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board, the bureau challenged rules that prevented brokers in that region from sharing certain real estate data with their clients through secure online platforms.

It had claimed Trreb’s grip on multiple listing service (MLS) data was so tight it constituted anticompetitive behaviour. The bureau sought to make the data publicly accessible on brokers’ websites, but Trreb fought back, claiming the publication of such data posed privacy and copyright concerns.
The Competition Tribunal, and later the Federal Court of Appeal, sided with the bureau, before the Supreme Court of Canada refused to hear the case in 2018.
The Supreme Court’s refusal cleared the way for MLS data to appear on other websites, which must be password-protected and are typically open to an agent’s clients or site subscribers.
The bureau used some documents related to its fight with Trreb in its application seeking information from Qpareb.

stories.title: Canada cautions Canadians against travel to Saudi Arabia after airports targeted
stories.summary: Global Affairs Canada has issued an advisory cautioning against travel to Saudi Arabia and specific airports that have been targeted during the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Global Affairs Canada has issued an advisory cautioning against travel to Saudi Arabia and specific airports that have been targeted during the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

The advisory, issued by Canada’s embassy in the kingdom, notes the airports in Riyadh and Dammam have been targeted in recent days and the Riyadh airport remains closed.

Saudi authorities have attributed the Oct. 10 attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport to a Houthi missile strike.

The advisory encourages Canadians in the region to book travel through neighbouring countries like Bahrain and Qatar and offers information on ground transport options to those locations.

The advisory says Canadians with expiring visitor visas should arrange to leave Saudi Arabia as soon as possible and warns the embassy will not be able to help with visa extensions or fines for overstaying.

It says travellers should keep a close eye on their flight status because flights can be disrupted by attacks with little or no warning.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Suspect arrested after catalytic converters stolen from food charity's trucks
stories.summary: Toronto - Toronto police say they have arrested and charged a 29-year-old man accused of breaking into a charity's parking lot over Thanksgiving weekend and stealing several catalytic converters from their trucks.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Toronto police say they have arrested and charged a 29-year-old man and are looking for at least one more suspect accused of breaking into a charity’s parking lot over Thanksgiving weekend and stealing several catalytic converters from the organization’s trucks.

Police say they arrested the man after executing a search warrant at an Oakville residence on Wednesday and charged him in connection with the thefts at Second Harvest, a charity that rescues food en route to landfills and redistributes it to people in need.

stories.title: As bond yields rise, how to pick between a variable or fixed rate mortgage?
stories.summary: Canada is currently in the midst of the largest wave of mortgage renewals, with more than a million households either renewing or close to renewing their mortgages this year.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Whether you’re in the market for a new mortgage or are looking to renew, you’re likely paying attention to rising bond yields across the world, including here in Canada.

The turbulence in the bond market may be changing how Canadians shop for their mortgages, some experts say. Historically, Canadians have preferred for the stability of monthly costs that a fixed-rate mortgage offers.

However, rising bond yields have left some wondering if a variable rate mortgage might be a better bet for families trying to save money in the short term.

Canada is currently in the midst of a significant wave of mortgage renewals, with more than one million households either renewing or close to renewing their mortgages this year.

While variable mortgages are driven directly by the Bank of Canada’s overnight rate, your fixed-rate mortgages respond to bond yields as well.

Over the last few months, bond markets around the world have been volatile amid global uncertainty and high levels of government debt, with multi-year highs in bond yields around the world, including the 10-year Treasury bond yield in the U.S. and bond yields here in Canada.

Canada’s 10-year government bond yield hit 3.85 per cent on Thursday. The five-year yield, typically the benchmark for fixed-rate mortgages, was up to 3.55 per cent.

This has meant that the gap between fixed-rate mortgages and variable-rate mortgages is widening in Canada. As of Thursday, the lowest available rate for the five-year fixed-rate mortgage – the most popular mortgage in Canada – was 4.34 per cent, according to Ratehub.ca. This was almost an entire percentage point higher than the lowest variable rate mortgage at 3.43 per cent.

“That difference can have a significant impact on monthly mortgage payments,” said Jamie David, vice president of mortgages at RateHub.

This has made variable rates more attractive to Canadian borrowers who are looking to reduce their monthly costs, she said.

“This year, we’re seeing a significant shift in borrower interest towards variable-rate mortgages,” she said.

Inquiries for variable-rate mortgages accounted for 36 per cent of all inquiries on RateHub between January and September, up from 10 per cent during the same period in 2025, David added.

However, fixed is still king for most borrowers, said Rates.ca mortgage and real estate expert Victor Tran.

“Variable rates haven’t moved up the way fixed rates have so borrowers who can handle some movement are asking about them more. But it’s not a flood of people switching,” he said.

“Most still want the certainty of fixed, particularly if they’re renewing or buying with a tight budget,” Tran added.

While variable rates can offer lower costs right now, it is important to understand your risk tolerance and financial goals before you make a decision, David said.

“Assess whether your household budget can comfortably absorb higher payments if interest rates rise during your mortgage term, rather than focusing entirely on today’s rate,” she said.

Most lenders offer the option of converting a variable mortgage to a fixed during their term without a prepayment penalty, but you would have to switch to your lender’s available fixed rate at the time, she added.

On the other hand, fixed-rate mortgages may cost more now but they offer certainty of monthly costs.

“Fixed is simple. Payments don’t change, which makes budgeting easier. The downside is you may pay more if rates come down and breaking the mortgage early can be costly,” Tran said.

Shorter-term fixed mortgages, like a two-year or three-year fixed mortgage, can offer a compromise for borrowers who want certainty of monthly payments but don’t want to commit to a five-year fixed mortgage with today’s rising bond yields, David said.

“If you believe that rates will go down within the next two to three years, then this might be a good option for you,” she said.

However, the tradeoff is that if the rates are higher when your term ends, you might end up paying more when it comes time to renew.

Canadians should expect continued volatility in the bond market and fixed-rate mortgage rates in the coming days, David said.

“If the Bank of Canada signals a potential rate hike at its Oct. 28 announcement or inflation remains elevated due to high energy prices, yields could climb further, pushing fixed mortgage rates even higher,” she said.

“However, if inflation eases or economic conditions weaken due to ongoing tariff uncertainty, yields could pull back.”

stories.title: AI firm Cohere to buy cybersecurity company Aisle
stories.summary: Toronto - Canadian artificial intelligence firm Cohere says it has signed a letter of intent to purchase a cybersecurity business.
stories.author: Tara Deschamps The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Cohere’s acquisition target is Aisle, a company split between San Francisco and Prague that has developed AI systems capable of uncovering and remediating vulnerabilities in software.

Cohere did not immediately reveal the value or structure of the deal, as well as its expected closing date.

Article continues below

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Image 9Image 10Image 11

Cohere framed the proposed transaction as a way to further develop sovereign AI and invest in Europe, the home of its recent acquisitions Aleph Alpha and Reliant AI.

Aisle was started last year by Ondrej Vlcek, the ex-chief executive of Avast, a Czech antivirus provider.

Vlcek and his two fellow co-founders will take on leadership roles at Cohere, which has promised to make a substantial long-term investment in Prague to further expand Aisle.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2025.

stories.title: Ottawa cautions Canadians against travel to Saudi Arabia after airports targeted
stories.summary: Ottawa - Global Affairs Canada has issued an advisory cautioning against travel to Saudi Arabia and specific airports that have been targeted during the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Global Affairs Canada has issued an advisory cautioning against travel to Saudi Arabia and specific airports that have been targeted during the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

The advisory, issued by Canada’s embassy in the kingdom, notes the airports in Riyadh and Dammam have been targeted in recent days and the Riyadh airport remains closed.

stories.title: Show us your favourite Halloween costumes from years past
stories.summary: You never forget dressing a baby in their first pumpkin outfits or a couple’s costume with your partner
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
Halloween is just around the corner, but anyone worth their weight in candy is already working on their costumes.

Whether you’re going out partying, entering a themed contest or forcing your child to add a snowsuit or rain jacket on top, costumes are an intrinsic part of the Halloween experience. Parents never forget dressing their babies in their first pumpkin outfits, and couples look fondly on their first matching sets.

This year, the Globe wants know about your favourite costume that you wore in years past. Was it something you made from scratch? Did it take months of planning, or was it a last-minute scrounge? Why did it mean so much to you?

Share your story and pictures in the box below, or send us an e-mail at audience@globeandmail.com with “Halloween costumes” in the subject line.

stories.title: Western electrochemists found silicon inside nuclear fuel before it ever entered a reactor
stories.summary: Discovery of silicon in nuclear fuel before it enters reactor May change usage and fabrication
stories.author: Jeff Renaud
stories.content:
Professor Samantha Gateman and her team at Western University use highly localized electrochemical techniques to see how corrosion starts and evolves at the microscopic level.

Their research focuses on how nuclear fuel and reactor materials change over time, and how those changes could affect the containers and components used to safely store and dispose of them for millennia.

So, when Gateman, Western’s Nwmo Chair in Radiation Induced Chemistry, and postdoctoral researchers Soroosh Hakimian and Shamim Pourrahimi were given tiny Triso (tri-structural isotropic) particles – poppy seed-sized nuclear fuel kernel surrounded by four protective layers – to characterize, they approached them the way they approach many unfamiliar materials.

First, figure out what is there. Then, determine how it behaves.

To their surprise, they found small regions of silicon inside the Triso fuel kernel, and that silicon was already there before the particle ever entered a reactor.

Triso is among the most robust nuclear fuel designs ever developed, with each tiny fuel kernel surrounded by multiple layers designed to contain radioactive fission products.

Researchers had previously found silicon inside irradiated, or used, Triso fuel that had been exposed to extreme temperatures and radiation. It was generally attributed to silicon migrating inward from the surrounding silicon-carbide protective layer during reactor operation.

Gateman, Hakimian and Pourrahimi have now shown that some silicon is present before the fuel ever enters a reactor, giving researchers a new baseline for understanding what happens to the material during reactor operation and raising new questions about how the material entered the fuel kernel in the first place.

“It was like we were detectives on an episode of CSI ,” said Gateman, a chemistry professor in Western’s Faculty of Science . “At first, we saw the silicon and thought, ‘okay, that’s interesting. It’s a little weird that it’s there, but let’s keep going.’ We had other things we wanted to understand about this material. But then we started asking where that silicon came from, and that’s when the investigation really began.”

The result, published in the Journal of Nuclear Materials , offers a new clue for understanding one small but important feature of Triso nuclear fuel.

Each Triso particle contains a tiny uranium oxycarbide fuel kernel roughly 300 to 400 micrometres across, about the size of a poppy seed, surrounded by layers of carbon and silicon carbide. Hundreds of thousands, potentially millions, of these particles can be packed into a nuclear reactor.

In her lab, Gateman was studying the Triso fuel particles as part of a larger project to characterize their chemistry for future safe disposal and eventually examine how they May dissolve electrochemically. Before those experiments could begin, her team needed to know exactly what they were working with.

Much of the detective work fell to Hakimian and Pourrahimi, who examined the tiny particles and helped identify the chemical signatures that led to the silicon discovery.

“It was really the carefully detailed research of Soroosh and Shamim that allowed us to follow that trail and figure out the silicon was already there,” said Gateman.

Critical to their process was examining fuel that had never been irradiated. By looking at the material before it entered a reactor, the researchers could separate what was present in the fuel kernel from the start, from what might develop during reactor operation.

Samantha Gateman (Christopher Kindratsky/Western Communications)

“We found silicon in the fuel kernel before it had ever been inside a reactor. That means when we see silicon inside irradiated fuel, we can’t automatically assume it migrated there from the silicon-carbide coating,” said Gateman.

That distinction sent the team back to the fuel-making process.

Triso fuel kernels are produced through a process called sol-gel fabrication, in which uranium-containing material is formed into tiny spheres in a hot silicone-oil bath before undergoing additional thermal processing and receiving their protective coatings.

“The surprising part was realizing the silicon could be connected to the way the fuel is made,” said Gateman. “From a chemistry perspective, the composition of the oil matters because the material is interacting with it as the fuel kernel is being formed.”

The researchers had an unusual opportunity to test that idea because they had access to Triso particles at different stages of fabrication. They could examine the bare kernels, as well as fully coated particles. Silicon was present at both stages.

“We found that the silicon present is not a consequence of the subsequent coating process,” said Gateman. “It’s already there as you make the kernel.”

The findings are particularly interesting because Triso fuel is not new technology. The concept dates back to the 1950s, and the fuel has been studied for decades. What has changed is the ability to see and chemically characterize materials at increasingly fine scales.

“Silicon inside Triso kernels had been reported before for fuel that had been used during reactor operation. But we couldn’t find a detailed measurement of the fuel before it went into the reactor that told us how much silicon was there to begin with,” said Gateman. “Now we have the tools to see much more clearly what’s actually in these tiny fuel particles. That baseline is important, because if we want to understand what happens to these materials in a reactor, we need to know what they looked like chemically before they went in.”

Fully ceramic microencapsulated (FCM) fuel pellets contain Triso fuel particles (Usnc)

The finding has already generated interest among researchers working on Triso fuel.

At an international Triso fuel workshop this summer, Hakimian and Pourrahimi met authors of earlier work describing silicon-rich phases inside irradiated fuel. Those researchers told Gateman’s team they had gone back to their original data and had not found silicon in their samples before irradiation. They continue to believe silicon can migrate into the kernel from the surrounding silicon-carbide layer.

Gateman does not dispute that possibility. Instead, her lab’s work adds another piece to the puzzle.

“If we want to know how much is moving during reactor operation, we need to know how much is there in the first place,” she said.

Whether the manufacturing process for Triso fuel should eventually be changed is a different question. Previous research found silicon-rich regions in irradiated fuel could potentially influence gas buildup and pressure within the fuel particle.

“We don’t know yet what effect these silicon-rich phases have on fuel performance, but there are some interesting possibilities,” said Gateman. “The first step is recognizing they’re there and making sure we account for them when we study how the fuel behaves.”
