stories.title: More than a third of young nurses in Canada do not renew licences, says think tank
stories.summary: Montreal - A new report says more than a third of the registered nurses in Canada under the age of 35 in 2023 did not renew their licences the next year.
stories.author: Katrine Desautels The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - A new report says more than a third of the registered nurses in Canada under the age of 35 in 2023 did not renew their licences the next year.

The Montreal Economic Institute compiled the numbers in the report using the latest data available from the Canadian Institute for Health Information.

The health information organization’s numbers are based on licence applications from provincial and territorial nursing regulatory bodies.

It reveals that for every 100 nurses under the age of 35 who were registered to practise in Canada in 2023, 34 did not renew their registration in 2024.

The numbers suggest an improvement from the previous year, when 40 per cent of nurses did not renew their licences.

The Montreal-based think tank has promoted more private sector involvement in the health care system to improve services.

Gabriel Giguère, a public policy analyst at the think tank and co-author of the report, said the report shows Canada still has work to do to persuade nurses to remain in the profession.

“This sends a very clear message about the retention rate of young nurses, and it’s a bad one,” he told The Canadian Press.

The report notes how recent survey responses suggest factors such as excessive overtime, poor working conditions, high stress and the risk of extreme fatigue on the job May be contributing to the exodus of some nurses.

The think tank also suggests in the report that provinces could help encourage more nurses to remain in the profession if they had additional opportunities in the private sector that offered more flexibility, such as in travel nurse agencies, private clinics or telehealth companies.

It also notes how some provinces such as Quebec have programs that pair novice nurses with colleagues who have more experience.

“British Columbia has job swapping pools, which allow nurses to trade shifts without needing approval from administrators,” the report said. “Union contracts should also be renegotiated to reward skills and competence over seniority.”

The report also highlights that, countrywide, the proportion of nurses under the age of 35 rose from 27.7 per cent in 2014 to over 30 per cent in 2017 and has remained between 30 per cent and 31 per cent since then.

The number of unfilled positions — which stood at more than 27,000 in 2025 — has declined from its peak of approximately 41,000 unfilled positions in 2023.

“When you look at it year by year, it’s obviously a good thing to have fewer job openings,” said Giguère, nuancing that the 10-year trend is not moving in the same direction.

In 2016, there were just over 9,000 job openings, three times fewer than today.

stories.title: Petrolia mayor welcomes benefits of MP in governing party at funding announcement
stories.summary: Brad Loosely, who is not seeking re-election, commented at an infrastructure announcement alongside Sarnia-Lambton-Bkejwanong MP Marilyn Gladu.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Petrolia’s mayor concedes that having an MP in the governing party is good news for his Lambton County community.

Brad Loosely, who is not seeking re-election, commented at an infrastructure announcement alongside Sarnia-Lambton-Bkejwanong MP Marilyn Gladu.

Gladu shocked many in her community in April, after she crossed the floor from the Conservatives to the Liberals.

“The idea of having a local MP that is involved with the government in power, that certainly has its advantages, maybe... The federal government and Marilyn have been great to help support this community,” said Loosley, who added Gladu has been helpful no matter which party banner she wears.

His comments came as Gladu announced $300,000 in funding to replace one kilometre of sidewalks in Petrolia.

The project is part of a larger investment to replace more than three kilometres of walkways to improve accessibility and safety.

Gladu, who has made multiple funding announcements in the last week, expects more are coming.

“Sarnia-Lambton needs about seven new stormwater and wastewater systems. We need an upgrade here at the Victoria Playhouse Petrolia for accessibility,” she added.

“So, I meet with each of the mayors and got their wish lists for various types of infrastructure, buildings and affordable housing. Affordable housing is a priority for Lambton County. So, all of these things are on the ask, and on a weekly basis, I’m on the phone with the minister’s office asking, ‘Is our funding available yet?”

stories.title: ‘It’s time we talk’: Black Londoners open up about issues at town hall
stories.summary: Around 100 Black Londoners with different backgrounds gathered Tuesday to discuss "interconnected issues affec...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Around 100 Black Londoners with different backgrounds gathered Tuesday to discuss “interconnected issues affecting their lives,” at the city’s first Black community town hall.

The town hall took place at the Innovation Works building on King Street and was designed as an opportunity for African, Caribbean and Black community members to share experiences on a range of issues, including health-care access, food insecurity and racism, said Mystery Furtado, founder of Type Diabeat-It, which was one of three groups that organized the event.

“An hour or two can’t erase decades of fear and trauma, but we can definitely find solutions,” said Furtado.

Mystery Funtado Founder and CEO of Type Diabeats It (Credit: Daniel Thuss XFM)

“Were looking for coming together of a community, having conversations in the city that go silent. We’re here to learn what’s happening. There’s so much happening but a lot of our community members fall through the gaps.”

Type Diabeat-It is a charity that helping with food literacy, and sovereignty, exercise, and type 2 diabetes management. The group organized Tuesday’s town hall with the London Black Heritage Council and FilAfrik Inc.

Aluel Nhial (credit: Daniel Thuss XFM)

“These organization helps us to be heard, for people to express there need, and we can get the help we need that we don’t get outside of this community,” said Aluel Nhial a mother of 10.

Nhial said her kids sometimes face stereotypes, and it was good to gather with other Black Londoners to share concerns.

“It’s a great way where you can see your loved one, sister or brother,” she said.

Several Londoners at the event shared issues they have faced in London, including food scares, property disagreements and health care challenges. Participants were also asked to answer a survey on how they felt and how they responded during certain situations.

“This is a big important event to help us with funding and to grow as a community” said Patrick Tennant is a volunteer that helps out at London’s Wean Community Centre, he stated he was very excited to be apart of it.

During the meeting, Furtado recalled how she was told her son was losing his vision when it turned out his eyes were simply a different colour. She said it’s important to share stories and numbers. According to the 2021 census, there were more than 20,000 Black community members living in London and surrounding areas.

About 32 per cent of Black Canadians, experience food insecurity, she said, and Black adults experience diabetes about four times the rate of white adults.

The anti-Black racist action plan that was approved by London council in November of 2024 included 61 different recommendations for the city.

“How can we help?” said Furtado “How can we make these commitments and make them possible?”

Pastor Philip Omondi speaking. (Credit: XFM Daniel Thuss)

stories.title: Carney says he expects nations, including U.S., to stay out of Alberta vote
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says Ottawa has made it 'absolutely clear' to foreign governments, including U.S., not to meddle in domestic votes.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada’s expectations that foreign governments, including the United States, will stay out of Alberta’s referendum are “absolutely clear.”

Speaking to Global News in Calgary Thursday morning, Carney said that it’s “fundamental” for Canada to ensure the integrity of elections at all levels of government — including the Oct. 19 referendum that will decide if Alberta will hold a vote on separating.

“Our expectation is, to be absolutely clear, ON foreign governments, United States included, is we don’t get ourselves involved in their elections, they don’t get themselves in our elections,” Carney said.

“ Fundamental point: the way to ensure there’s no foreign interference in an election is to get out and vote in the election, and let’s have the voices of Albertans heard.”

The prime minister was in Alberta ahead of the Oct. 19 vote, which includes a question on whether Albertans want to begin the legal process to hold a binding referendum on separation from Canada.

The issue has dominated Albertan politics for more than a year, and been tinged with concerns about foreign actors supporting the separatist cause.

Leading figures in the separatist movement has claimed to have traveled to the U.S. to appeal for assistance from the State Department.

Trump’s treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has openly mused about Alberta being a “natural partner” for the U.S. and Howard Lutnik, Trump’s commerce secretary, has accused Carney of collapsing trade talks to somehow gain “leverage” over the separatist movement.

Carney told Global News that Canada’s national security agencies are actively watching for covert foreign interference in the referendum, but said he could not speak to specifics.

“It’s fundamental to ensure the integrity of all our elections, whether it’s municipal, this referendum, national, provincial elections … Our national security agencies are very active in monitoring potential foreign interference,” Carney said.

“Ultimately … there’s a limit to what I can say, given the codes, but there’s active involvement in that.”

Carney appealed directly to Albertans to vote against a formal separation referendum, talking up his government’s recent announcements of federal projects — including a new pipeline, the Pacific Link, to the B.C. coast — in the province.

Carney also pointed to the aftermath of the Brexit referendum — which took place while he was governor of the Bank of England — as something Alberta should want to avoid.

“It wasn’t clear what Brexit meant at the time people made that vote. And for the next few years, while that was being determined, there was huge uncertainty, investments stopped, the economy started to underperform,” Carney said.

“Now the economy is at least 10 per cent lower than it would otherwise be. We’re taking thousands and thousands of dollars of earnings that people are giving up, higher taxes, higher debt on the government.”

Instead, Carney said Alberta has an opportunity to “boldly move forward” as a province within Canada.

“The world’s opening up to Canada. Let’s take advantage of it. Or take another path, which is not the one I recommend, which is (to) subject ourselves to uncertainty, slower economy, higher debt, higher taxes, and missed opportunity,” Carney said.

“Our expectation is, to be absolutely clear, ON foreign governments, United States included, is we don’t get ourselves involved in their elections, they don’t get themselves in our elections,” Carney said.
“ Fundamental point: the way to ensure there’s no foreign interference in an election is to get out and vote in the election, and let’s have the voices of Albertans heard.”
The prime minister was in Alberta ahead of the Oct. 19 vote, which includes a question on whether Albertans want to begin the legal process to hold a binding referendum on separation from Canada.
The issue has dominated Albertan politics for more than a year, and been tinged with concerns about foreign actors supporting the separatist cause.
Leading figures in the separatist movement has claimed to have traveled to the U.S. to appeal for assistance from the State Department.

Trump’s treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has openly mused about Alberta being a “natural partner” for the U.S. and Howard Lutnik, Trump’s commerce secretary, has accused Carney of collapsing trade talks to somehow gain “leverage” over the separatist movement.
Carney told Global News that Canada’s national security agencies are actively watching for covert foreign interference in the referendum, but said he could not speak to specifics.

“It’s fundamental to ensure the integrity of all our elections, whether it’s municipal, this referendum, national, provincial elections … Our national security agencies are very active in monitoring potential foreign interference,” Carney said.
“Ultimately … there’s a limit to what I can say, given the codes, but there’s active involvement in that.”

Carney appealed directly to Albertans to vote against a formal separation referendum, talking up his government’s recent announcements of federal projects — including a new pipeline, the Pacific Link, to the B.C. coast — in the province.
Carney also pointed to the aftermath of the Brexit referendum — which took place while he was governor of the Bank of England — as something Alberta should want to avoid.

“It wasn’t clear what Brexit meant at the time people made that vote. And for the next few years, while that was being determined, there was huge uncertainty, investments stopped, the economy started to underperform,” Carney said.

“Now the economy is at least 10 per cent lower than it would otherwise be. We’re taking thousands and thousands of dollars of earnings that people are giving up, higher taxes, higher debt on the government.”
Instead, Carney said Alberta has an opportunity to “boldly move forward” as a province within Canada.

“The world’s opening up to Canada. Let’s take advantage of it. Or take another path, which is not the one I recommend, which is (to) subject ourselves to uncertainty, slower economy, higher debt, higher taxes, and missed opportunity,” Carney said.

stories.title: Toronto police to update catalytic converter theft that disabled 7 Second Harvest trucks
stories.summary: Toronto police will provide an update Thursday morning on the theft and vandalism of seven trucks belonging to Second Harvest.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Toronto police will provide an update Thursday morning on the theft and vandalism of seven trucks belonging to Second Harvest.

Acting Supt. Jeff Bangild will speak to reporters at 11:30 a.m., a day after police said officers were searching for one or more suspects allegedly behind the theft at the food rescue organization.

Over the Thanksgiving weekend, Second Harvest said suspects broke into its Toronto yard , cut through the exhaust systems of seven trucks and stole their catalytic converters.

All seven trucks were rendered out of service. The charity had been preparing for its previously advertised Thanksgiving turkey giveaway. Only two trucks were able to operate Sunday, and the organization said it was worried how it would meet demand in the coming week.

Repairs are expected to cost approximately $80,000 and take two to three weeks, CEO Lori Nikkel said. She announced Wednesday that Aurora Importing had donated $60,000 to help cover some of the costs.

Police have released images of a black, four-door Infiniti G25 with black rims that investigators allege was used to flee the scene.

stories.title: Second career college court challenge reveals concerns about 'bona fide studies'
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario's colleges and universities ministry is alleging it could not "reliably determine bona fide studies" at two of the career colleges it barred from student financial aid — a decision those schools are now challenging in court.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Ontario’s Colleges and Universities Ministry is alleging it could not “reliably determine bona fide studies” at two of the career colleges it barred from student financial aid — a decision those schools are now challenging in court.

Two campuses of Citi College of Canadian Careers are among six schools the province blocked from the Ontario Student Assistance Program in May for the 2026-27 year, alleging “high-risk admissions” practices and other concerns.

They have filed an application in Divisional Court asking for a judicial review of that decision, similar to a court challenge by three Academy of Learning locations affected by the May order.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn did not base his decision on a “rational chain of analysis” connecting evidence to the ministry’s conclusions, and the order does not refer to any specific instances of alleged non-compliance, Citi College wrote in its court challenge.

“In making the decision, the minister reached findings regarding ‘compromised participation,’ ‘inadequate attendance tracking,’ and ‘inability to reliably determine bona fide studies’ that are not justified, transparent, or intelligible, having regard to the ministry’s own prior approvals ... and the systems and safeguards Citi College had previously implemented,” the school wrote.

Citi College had been approved to administer Osap in each of the preceding 20 years, they wrote, and two audits by the ministry last year “concluded without adverse findings.” The ministry’s allegations have not been tested or proven in court.

Quinn’s decisions to bar the six schools from receiving Osap this year come after Career Colleges Ontario had been warning for years about possible “suspicious” Osap activity at a small number of schools.

His spokesperson said the government has taken targeted actions, including inspections at certain schools, since receiving an increased number of complaints.

“As part of the province’s work to monitor compliance at private career colleges, corrective action was taken to issue notices of non-renewal to six campuses, including Citi College of Canadian Careers who have since had their Osap eligibility suspended,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement.

The minister announced last week that Kpmg started an audit in August of Osap at career colleges and he referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police based on “serious concerns” uncovered in the audit’s preliminary findings. He did not name the colleges that were the subject of the concerns referred to police.

Citi College is not aware of being subject to any issues raised by Kpmg or the OPP referral, its lawyer said.

A January 2025 letter from Career Colleges Ontario to the government highlights what it calls concerning increases in Osap usage at 10 schools, including one school that saw a nearly 2,700 per cent increase in two years. The letter was filed as part of the Academy of Learning court challenge, and all of the schools listed except for Academy of Learning are redacted, so it is not known if Citi College was included.

Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request earlier this year shows that Citi College’s two campuses had about 133 people on Osap in 2021-22, and three years later that rose to 1,754 students, an increase of about 1,200 per cent.

A lawyer for Citi College said in a statement Wednesday to The Canadian Press about the judicial review application that the school “continues to maintain compliance with its regulatory obligations and support its existing students in completing their programs.”

Harris Rosen also wrote in a previous statement about the Osap increases that a more accurate calculation would use a pre-pandemic figure and rely on a compound annual growth rate, in which case Citi College would have been at about 38 per cent per year.

“The percentage increase you’ve cited appears substantial largely because it is calculated from a relatively low 2021–22 base,” Rosen wrote.

“When that figure is considered alongside the expansion of online education, broader geographic accessibility, and the relatively short duration of my client’s programs, Citi does not believe the growth is as unusual as the percentage alone May suggest.”

In the court application, Citi College argues that the minister unfairly assessed the school based on new “technological and monitoring expectations” that weren’t previously communicated to them.

Those included continuous webcam participation, long-term IP retention, forensic IP analytics, and VPN prohibitions, Citi College wrote.

When Quinn announced last week that he had referred concerns to the OPP, he said many had centred around online-only programs. This fall, the government will introduce legislation to exclude predominantly online programs at private career colleges from Osap eligibility.

In the meantime, Quinn has also paused Osap payments at all private post-secondary institutions.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Saskatchewan seeks higher immunization rates with campaign launch
stories.summary: The Saskatchewan government has launched its 2026-27 immunization campaign for free influenza and COVID-19 vaccines.
stories.author: Grace Miller
stories.content:
The Saskatchewan government has launched its 2026-27 immunization campaign for free influenza and COVID-19 vaccines.

The provincial government is hoping to see an increase in the number of people vaccinated in Saskatchewan. While Saskatchewan’s case count is considered low so far, Saskatchewan Health Authority (SHA) medical health officer Dr. Vivian Onaemo said getting vaccinated will help reduce transmission.

“They’re also very protective, not only for yourself, but for your family (and) for your community. So we all have a shared responsibility, that all of us roll up our sleeves, check with our health-care provider, whether it’s a nurse closest to you,” said Onaemo.

The federal government’s figures so far show a decline in confirmed COVID-19 cases compared to the previous year, though flu cases are higher in comparison.

Since September, the country has seen two flu-related deaths and 24 COVID-19-related deaths. Saskatchewan has seen one flu and one COVID-19 death in the same period.

“It’s a sobering reminder that COVID-19 and influenza can cause serious illness,” said Onaemo.

Onaemo estimates that last year, 20 per cent of the province received the flu vaccine and fewer people had the COVID-19 vaccine.

“We do have room for improvement,” said Onaemo. “We don’t have many people taking the vaccination at the provincial level, so we’re hoping that more would get the vaccine and protect people around them.”

Flu shots are free and available in some walk-in clinics or can be booked online or by phone through the SHA .

stories.title: ‘We’re ready to expand’: RCMP Heritage Centre pushes for national museum status
stories.summary: There are nine official national museums across the country, seven in the Ottawa area, the Immigration Museum at Pier 21 in Halifax and the Human Rights Museum in Winnipeg.
stories.author: Raygan Johnson
stories.content:
It’s already an international destination that tens of thousands visit every year to learn about the RCMP’s history.

Sam Karikas views the RCMP Heritage Centre as a place to recognize part of Canada’s intricate past.

But despite that reputation among history buffs, the Regina-based Heritage Centre isn’t recognized as a national museum in Canada.

There are nine official national museums across the country, seven in the Ottawa area, the Immigration Museum at Pier 21 in Halifax and the Human Rights Museum in Winnipeg.

Now the Centre, backed by a petitions and surveys with the support of over 10,000 Canadians, is going to the capital to push to become the 10th.

Karikas said national designation could increase the centre’s annual operating support from approximately $3.5 million to nearly $10 million and significantly expand its programming and reach.

“We are we’re ready to expand … because we have done all the planning and have done all the thinking,” Karikas said.

There is progress with the Centre being listed in federal budget commitments and ministerial documents dating back to 2019. Federal representatives are working with the Centre’s CEO to move towards national museum designation.

“We just need one person to make the decision,” Karikas said.

stories.title: Supreme Court will rule on Ottawa's single-use plastics ban
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada says it will hear an appeal of Ottawa’s ban on single-use plastics.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Supreme Court of Canada says it will hear an appeal of Ottawa’s ban on single-use plastics.

The Federal Court of Appeal overturned a lower court decision in January, allowing the federal government to keep the ban in place.

A 2023 Federal Court decision in a case brought by the plastics industry said Ottawa had overstepped by designating all “plastic manufactured items” as toxic.

But in a unanimous decision in January, the three-judge appellate panel ruled the federal government’s decision to list plastic manufactured items as toxic was reasonable.

Ottawa used that designation to issue a ban on the manufacturing and importing of six types of single-use plastics, including straws, grocery bags, stir sticks and the six-pack rings used to hold soda and beer cans.

The government said it chose those items because they were commonly found in litter and had known and accessible alternatives.

This report from The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

stories.title: B.C. Conservatives maintaining two-point lead less than two weeks from provincial election: poll
stories.summary: At present, 42 per cent of decided voters support the Conservatives, compared to 40 per cent who support the NDP.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
The Conservatives are holding a narrow two-point lead among decided voters, the Leger data suggests. Meanwhile, there is growing support for the two leading parties, but a significant share of voters are open to changing their minds before they go to the polls on Oct. 24.

At present, 42 per cent of decided voters support the Conservatives, compared to 40 per cent who support the NDP. Support for the Green party has dropped, falling 13 per cent in September to 9 per cent in October. That said, 26 per cent of British Columbians polled by Leger say they are likely to switch their vote, especially among voters 18 to 34 years-old.

Notably, 56 per cent of B.C. residents believe the province is heading in the wrong direction. That compares with 34 per cent who believe it is moving on the right track.

Since Leger’s September poll , Conservative support has climbed three points, while NDP support has increased by four points. With just two points separating the parties, neither has established a clear lead as the campaign enters its final weeks.

NDP support is concentrated on Vancouver Island. It holds a narrow advantage in Metro Vancouver. The Conservatives, meanwhile, are stronger in the rest of the province. Leger contemplates that the regional differences could be important in determining how the province-wide race translates into individual riding results.

The choices for voters supporting smaller parties could become important in ridings where their preferred party is not running a candidate. According to Elections BC’s official candidate list , not all parties are fielding candidates in every riding. Among supporters of smaller parties, 29 per cent say they will vote for the NDP if their preferred party does not have a candidate in their riding, while 21 per cent will vote Conservative. Another 22 per cent would vote for a party other than the NDP or Conservatives.

Block after block of death and despair. This is Vancouver's Downtown Eastside, where all hope is now lost

B.C. Conservatives have five-point lead over NDP as voting day nears: survey

Green supporters May be the most open to reconsidering their choice, says Leger. More than one-third (37 per cent) indicate they are likely to switch parties, compared with 23 per cent of Conservative supporters and 20 per cent of NDP supporters.

Turning to the leaders, 39 per cent say their opinion of David Eby has worsened over the past week. Only 13 per cent report an improvement. Nearly half (47 per cent) of B.C. voters say their opinion of Eby remained unchanged.

For Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson, 20 per cent of voters say their opinion of him has declined, with 23 per cent reporting an improved opinion.A majority (56 per cent) report no change in their view of Doerkson.

Leger says that these differences should also be viewed in the context of each leader’s present position, with Eby as the incumbent premier possessing an established governing record, while Doerkson is relatively new to leadership and voters still forming their views of him.

With neither party holding a commanding lead, the remaining lead-up to the vote leaves room for shifts in support, particularly among voters who are not firmly committed, suggest the Leger survey results.

This online survey was conducted from Oct. 9 to 12, 2026, among1,000 British Columbia residents aged 18 or older. A margin of error cannot be associated with a non-probability sample. For comparison purposes, a probability sample of 1,000 respondents would have a margin of error of no greater than ±3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: Saskatoon youth group delivers food, supplies after Prairie Harm Recovery closure
stories.summary: The Red Bear Party is making noise around the city by getting involved in their community and calling for a change. Every Thursday they hand out essentials to those that need them
stories.author: Ashley Beherns
stories.content:
Christen Carter-Red Bear is seeing the need for change in Saskatoon, particularly in the wake of the closure of Prairie Harm Recovery.

Now he and a group of youth calling themselves “The Red Bear Party” are taking the initiative themselves.

“We pull up into a parking lot and people know they’re going to get fed,” said Carter-Red Bear. “The closure of PHR was definitely a big reason why we started this. … There were our people dying out here. People dying, you know, my direct relatives. I have relatives I meet every day that I didn’t know I’m related to via blood.”

Carter-Red Bear is motivated by his own upbringing, growing up homeless on Saskatoon’s west side himself.

“I’ve always experienced the effects of assimilation… I’m the first generation in my family that didn’t attend a residential school. Both my mom and dad did. They both qualified for a level five trauma settlement.”

And after digging a little deeper into his family history from the Lakota Region, he acted.

“My dad’s side always told me that we did come from a long line of medicine men, but I didn’t look into that until the last few years,” said Carter-Red Bear. “Definitely tapping into that as of recent. Learning the power I get from having this strong ancestral background and yeah, it’s definitely been a process breaking these cycles.”

The Red Bear Party gets together every week on Thursday to pack food and other essential supplies to hand out.

They work out of the Gabriel Dumont Local 11 kitchen and have supports from Nestor’s Bakery and Wholesale Club, for baked goods and produce. Volunteers help make the meals.

“We like to have at least four people here every week so that we have a good team running. We reach out for volunteers on social media. We meet people at the events that we do who express their want to volunteer,” said Jenna Straf, a Red Bear Party co-founder.

Furthermore, the team is making noise around the city with rallies and getting involved in their community.

“If no one will show up for these relatives, we’re forming the foundation for that. We’re forming teams to help kids with literacy. If no one’s going to show up for those kids, we’re going to show for those kids.”

Carter-Red Bear wants others on First Nations across the province to do the same.

“Growing up with those hardships, growing up with family and addiction, deep in addiction, I’ve always wanted to find a way to provide for them. Doing this kind of allows me to do my due diligence as an indigenous man, inherited right to take care of my people as an Indigenous man.”

A sell-off for artificial-intelligence stocks is hitting Wall Street again after whipping around the world on worries about how much longer the AI frenzy will last.

The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent early Thursday, and the Nasdaq composite 1.2 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 269 points. Among tech stocks, Nvidia fell 3.2 per cent and Advanced Micro Devices lost 5.4 per cent. South Korea’s Kospi index sank 7.6 per cent.

The losses came as another report signaled inflation has worsened by even more in the United States than economists expected. Wholesale inflation jumped last month, driven by a big increase in energy costs.

Tech stocks appeared to be headed for another sell-off before the bell with inflation anxiety hammering that high-growth sector ahead of the U.S. earnings season.

Artificial intelligence stocks were down again after taking a beating a day earlier.

CoreWeave, which offers AI computing power to customers over the cloud, fell another 3.8 per cent early after tumbling 15.5 per cent a day earlier, its worst day since February. GE Vernova, which is hoping to electrify power-hungry data centres, dropped 3.2 per cent after a 6.2 per cent decline on Wednesday and Oracle sank 1.6 per cent, adding to its nearly nine per cent loss in the previous session.

Chipmaker and AI darling Nvidia fell 1.6 per cent in early trading, as did Broadcom, while Advanced Micro Devices retreated 3.1 per cent.

The yield on 10-year bonds eased to 5.09 per cent from 5.32 per cent, but remains elevated. Higher bond yields that have made borrowing more expensive could make it more difficult for companies to raise cash to build data centres and fill them with AI chips.

The latest inflation figures showed Wednesday that prices remain well above the Federal Reserve’s two per cent target, putting in play another potential interest rate hike before the end of the year, which also puts pressure on the equities market.

The government’s latest report on wholesale prices, the producer price index, arrives Thursday along with another trove of corporate earnings reports.

Canada’s main stock index, the Toronto Stock Exchange, fell 0.2 per cent early Thursday, with shares in Canadian tech giant Celestica falling close to seven per cent.

In Asia, South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index lost 7.6 per cent to 5,554.22. It plummeted more than 16 per cent over the past month and was well below the 9,000 mark that it crossed in June at its all-time high driven by optimism over the global artificial intelligence frenzy.

Samsung Electronics slid 9.5 per cent and South Korean memory chipmaker SK Hynix plunged 11.1 per cent.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 tumbled 4.9 per cent to 64,425.95. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group lost 9.3 per cent. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron dropped 7.8 per cent, and memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings lost 12.3 per cent.

Taiwan’s Taiex, which also benefited from the AI boom, fell 3.4 per cent. Its leading chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., or Tsmc, dropped two per cent ahead of its earnings report. Tsmc reported on Thursday another record profit for the latest quarter, which was better than what analysts had expected, and the company said AI demand remains very strong.

“The problem for heavily technology-weighted markets such as Korea and Taiwan, to a lesser extent Japan, is that any risk to perceived AI spending growth May lead to slower demand growth for chips and equipment,” said Lorraine Tan, director of equity research for Asia at Morningstar.

“The key issue is a possible mismatch between the market’s growth expectations for the tech sector and what May eventuate,” she said.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped one per cent to 24,062.72. The Shanghai Composite index slipped 1.6 per cent to 3,707.48.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 edged down 0.1 per cent to 8,719.70.

At midday in Europe, Britain’s Ftse 100 rose 0.7 per cent, France’s CAC 40 gave back 0.3 per cent and Germany’s DAX was down 0.4 per cent.

Oil prices fell as tensions and uncertainties surrounding global oil supply and the situation in the Middle East dragged on. Brent crude, the international standard, declined more than one per cent to US$104.91 per barrel. That’s still elevated compared with the approximately $72 per barrel level before the start of the Iran war in late February.

U.S. crude was up 23 cents a barrel to $95.32.

– with a file from Global News’ Ariel Rabinovitch

stories.title: Supreme Court of Canada to hear appeal of First Nation's Nootka Island claim
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Supreme Court of Canada will hear a case about a First Nation's claim to title over a swath of Nootka Island.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Nuchatlaht First Nation brought a claim for Aboriginal title to about 200 square kilometres of the island, which lies off the west coast of Vancouver Island.

The trial judge found the Nuchatlaht had established title over only portions of the claimed area.

Article continues below

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

The First Nation challenged the decision in the British Columbia Court of Appeal.

In April, the Court of Appeal found the trial judge used an “arbitrary boundary” to determine title.

A three-judge panel of the Appeal Court said the Nuchatlaht identified territory it exclusively occupied and used for hunting, fishing and gathering activities, and presented other evidence that established its “strong presence on or over the land claimed.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Supreme Court to rule on Ottawa’s single-use plastics ban
stories.summary: The Federal Court of Appeal overturned a lower court decision in January, allowing the federal government to keep the ban in place
stories.author: Nick Murray
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada said Thursday it will hear an appeal that will determine if Ottawa’s ban on single-use plastics can stay in place.

In 2022, Ottawa phased in a ban on the manufacture and sale of six single-use plastic items, including straws, stir sticks, cutlery, takeout containers and the six-pack rings used to hold soda and beer cans.

The government said at the time it chose those items because they were commonly found in litter and had known and accessible alternatives.

In order to introduce the ban, the federal government listed “plastic manufactured items” as toxic under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, following a scientific assessment.

In 2023, the Federal Court said that listing was too broad, in part because the federal government had failed to demonstrate that all plastic items harm human health or the environment.

The Federal Court of Appeal overturned the lower court’s decision in January, allowing the government to keep the ban in place. The three-judge panel unanimously ruled the decision to list plastic manufactured items as toxic was reasonable.

They argued the lower court had erred by viewing as one step what was actually a two-step process: designating plastics as toxic and regulating individual plastic items.

The initial decision to list all plastics as toxic was challenged by a group representing companies in Canada’s plastics industry, along with three chemical companies which manufacture plastics.

The plastics industry argued, among other things, that a lack of testing to determine which plastics are harmful made Ottawa’s decision unreasonable.

The Court of Appeal dismissed that argument in January.

“To put the matter bluntly … the chemical content of (plastics) is irrelevant to the sea otter choking on a plastic straw. The problem is the plastic item itself, not its chemistry,” the judges wrote.

Karen Wirsig, senior program manager for plastics at Environmental Defence, said Ottawa should maintain the ban pending the Supreme Court decision.

“It is rare for appeals to be granted so we were not particularly expecting it. However, it does open the opportunity for a stronger precedent for the listing from the Supreme Court of Canada,” Wirsig told The Canadian Press.

The office of Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said the plastics ban will stay in place until the Supreme Court rules on it.

“Canadians understand the importance of reducing pollution and waste,” Dabrusin’s press secretary Amy Falkner said in a statement.

“The government will continue to work with all partners to reduce plastic waste and pollution.”

In a statement posted to their website, the group representing plastics companies said it welcomes the opportunity to bring the case to the Supreme Court.

stories.title: SeatGeek Canada faces two more fines from Ontario over ticket resale violations
stories.summary: Province’s consumer beware website shows the new fines issued to the ticket resale website earlier this month total $22,500 collectively
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value.

The province’s consumer beware website shows the new fines issued to the ticket resale website earlier this month total $22,500 collectively.

The website says the first of the two fines amounts to $15,000 and is for allegedly making a ticket available for sale or facilitating a sale of a seat beyond the resale price limit.

The second fine is for $7,500 and is for allegedly failing to disclose the total price of a ticket when a seat was purchased from a primary seller.

The province and SeatGeek Canada did not immediately respond to questions about what events the fines stem from or whether the reseller will fight the penalties.

The province previously issued $25,000 in fines to the company in August for similar offences.

stories.title: Ontario fines SeatGeek Canada $22,500 more over ticket resale violations
stories.summary: Toronto - SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value.
stories.author: Tara Deschamps The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value.

The province’s consumer beware website shows the new fines issued to the ticket resale platform earlier this month total $22,500 collectively.

The website says the first of the two fines amounts to $15,000 and is for allegedly making a ticket available for sale or facilitating a sale of a seat beyond the resale price limit.

The second fine is for $7,500 and is for allegedly failing to disclose the total price of a ticket when a seat was purchased from a primary seller.

SeatGeek Canada did not answer questions about what events the fines stem from or whether it will fight the penalties.

“We are doing our best to comply but we have yet to receive meaningful direction from the government on how to do so,” spokesperson Cameron Papp said Thursday in an email.

Giulia Paikin, a spokesperson for the Ontario Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery Stephen Crawford, also did not answer questions about the nature of the penalties.

However, she sent a statement that repeated nearly verbatim what the province has previously said about anyone responsible for price cap violations facing fines of up to $250,000.

“We will not hesitate to hold bad actors who break the rules accountable,” an email from Paikin said.

SeatGeek’s new fines stem from legislation the province implemented earlier this year, after fans complained about resale prices for tickets to Taylor Swift’s Eras tour in 2024 and last year’s playoff run by the Toronto Blue Jays.

The legislation was meant to keep people from reselling seats to Ontario events for well beyond face value and tamp down on scalpers profiting off their ability to scoop up tickets to hot concerts and shows.

After the legislation came into effect, the province issued $25,000 in fines to SeatGeek in August for similar offences.

A $20,000 fine for fellow resale website StubHub Canada followed in September.

When SeatGeek was given its first round of fines, it told The Canadian Press it had notified third-party sellers on its platform about the new law but was still seeking guidance from the province around how to comply with the regulations.

The platform argued it is challenging to confirm the original value of tickets because many sellers don’t have access to that information. Sometimes seats have changed hands several times before they wind up on a resale site and if tickets were bought as part of a broader package, like a season’s seat arrangement, it can be hard to break down the value of a single ticket.

To address these issues, SeatGeek said it has asked Ontario to define what counts as acceptable proof of a ticket’s original price and for guidance around how a marketplace is expected to validate the cost of seats.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Death toll unknown after intense fire in fatal Highway 401 crash: OPP
stories.summary: Ontario Provincial Police say an intense fire has prevented investigators from determining how many people died in a multi-vehicle crash on Highway 401 Tuesday.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Ontario Provincial Police say an intense fire has prevented investigators from determining how many people died in a multi-vehicle crash on Highway 401 Tuesday.

OPP said officers were called around 4:03 p.m. on Oct. 13 to the eastbound lanes of Highway 401 near Mill Road in the Township of Southwold for reports of a multi-vehicle crash.

Police said traffic had slowed because of an earlier collision in the eastbound lanes of Highway 401 near Colonel Talbot Road in Middlesex County. A second crash then occurred west of the initial scene and involved two transport trucks and a passenger vehicle.

The vehicle and one of the transport trucks caught fire and quickly became engulfed in flames, police said.

Police described the collision as fatal but said investigators had not determined the total number of occupants or deaths because of the intense fire involving the passenger vehicle.

“The driver of the transport truck was able to exit the vehicle and was not injured. The second transport driver was taken to hospital to be treated for minor injuries,” police said in a news release Wednesday.

Highway 401 was closed for approximately 11 hours while emergency crews investigated.

The investigation remains ongoing.

stories.title: Canada aims for India trade deal by year-end, minister says
stories.summary: The two countries exchanged $30.4 billion of goods and services last year, according to Canadian government data.
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
Canada is looking to conclude a trade deal with India by the end of the year as the two countries look to strengthen economic ties and diversify partnerships amid growing global uncertainty.

Negotiators from India and Canada began a fifth round of talks from Oct. 5, building on discussions that concluded last month. Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to visit Canada in December and sign a completed trade deal.

“The momentum is there, the energy is there to get it done,” Canadian International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said in an interview with Bloomberg’s Haslinda Amin. “Hopefully we will get it done this year. That is the focus.”

The push to deepen economic ties with India comes as Canada faces rising trade tensions with the US following the breakdown of negotiations between the two countries. India, meanwhile, is contending with fresh tariff threats from a new law that gives Donald Trump the power to impose levies of as much as 100% on countries that purchase Russian oil and gas.

Canada sees opportunities to deepen ties with India in mining and food security, while also identifying infrastructure investment and nuclear energy as areas for deeper cooperation.

“The business community wants to see this happen,” Sidhu said of the trade deal.

Trade between Canada and India is currently small. The two countries exchanged $30.4 billion of goods and services last year, according to Canadian government data.

“The leaders have set an ambitious target to go from $30 billion to $70 billion,” Sidhu said. “How are we going to get there? Many of the conversations I’ve had in Mumbai with some of the conglomerates is we want to do more on energy. We know we want to do more in critical minerals.”

He signaled Ottawa’s interest in participating in India’s expansion plans.

“As India grows, Canada grows. We want to support India,” Sidhu said. “We can help India build all the supply chains. Negotiations are always tough but we are going to do what is best for our businesses.”

Nuclear energy is another potential area of cooperation. India is opening up its tightly controlled nuclear industry to private companies as it seeks to rapidly expand atomic power generation.

That could create opportunities for Canada, which has some of the world’s largest uranium resources as well as nuclear technology and expertise, to supply fuel and participate in new projects.

—With assistance from Anup Roy and Shruti Srivastava.

stories.title: St. Thomas police reach 20,000 calls for service at earliest point on record
stories.summary: The St. Thomas Police Service says it has reached 20,000 calls for service earlier than ever before, highlighting what officials describe as growing demand for policing in the city.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
The St. Thomas Police Service says it has reached 20,000 calls for service earlier than ever before, highlighting what officials describe as growing demand for policing in the city.

Police announced they recorded their 20,000th call for service on Oct. 13, more than two weeks earlier than last year, when the milestone was reached on Oct. 31.

According to the service, this marks the earliest date on record that officers have surpassed the 20,000-call threshold.

The date has been steadily moving earlier in recent years, reflecting a rise in calls for service. The milestone was reached on Dec. 12 in 2022, Nov. 12 in 2023, Nov. 3 in 2024, Oct. 31 in 2025 and Oct. 13 this year.

Police said the impact of higher call volumes extends well beyond the initial response to incidents.

“Many calls require follow-up investigations, court preparation, disclosure processing and administrative work, creating additional demands across the organization, including communications, frontline patrol, investigative units, court services, information technology and administrative staff,” read a statement from police.

St. Thomas police did not provide a breakdown of the types of calls contributing to the increase.

stories.title: Canada has not interfered in the U.S. midterm elections, former diplomat says
stories.summary: A former Canadian diplomat has dismissed U.S. allegations of Canadian interference in the upcoming midterms elections as “noise.”
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
A former Canadian diplomat has dismissed U.S. allegations of Canadian interference in the upcoming midterms elections as “noise.”

“I don’t think that it deserves much response,” Colin Robertson, a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, told CTV’s Your Morning on Thursday.

Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada, suggested in an interview with “The Really Big Show” podcast released earlier this week that the actions of several Canadian politicians could amount to interference in the midterms, which will be held on Nov. 3.

He pointed to an advertising campaign run by Ontario Premier Doug Ford last year that featured a clip of former U.S. president Ronald Raegan talking about the benefits of free trade.

“Did that constitute any kind of interference? No, I think that’s advocacy,” Robertson said.

Hoekstra also criticized Industry Minister Melanie Joly for stating that Canadian counter-tariffs were designed to target certain states.

“Again, that’s quite justified,” Robertson said, as retaliatory action against the U.S. tariffs. “All of which international trade law recognizes.”

Having petitioned U.S. lawmakers in the past to advance Canada’s interests, Robertson said Canadian politicians are now trying to encourage American businesses to advocate against the trade war, ON their behalf.

“We’re seeing this now ... Republican candidates are going out and saying, ‘well we shouldn’t be applying these tariffs.’ So they’re breaking with the president,” the former diplomat said.

“That’s Americans talking to Americans. That’s exactly what we want to see.”

Robertson said he wouldn’t be surprised if Trump blames Canada should Republicans lose the midterms.

“With Donald Trump, you’re never sure of anything,” he said. “And he’s of course made very clear that if he doesn’t win these midterms, it’s not his fault.”

Trump, after losing the 2020 presidential election, accused his opponent Joe Biden of election fraud .

On Wednesday, Trump told a crowd of supporters during a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Ariz., that Canada will “end up being the 51st state.”

“I don’t think that it deserves much response,” Colin Robertson, a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, told CTV’s Your Morning on Thursday.

Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada, suggested in an interview with “The Really Big Show” podcast released earlier this week that the actions of several Canadian politicians could amount to interference in the midterms, which will be held on Nov. 3.
He pointed to an advertising campaign run by Ontario Premier Doug Ford last year that featured a clip of former U.S. president Ronald Raegan talking about the benefits of free trade.
“Did that constitute any kind of interference? No, I think that’s advocacy,” Robertson said.

stories.title: Rosemead House hotel helps guests discover a stylish side of Victoria
stories.summary: The splashy boutique hotel in Esquimalt just went through a vibrant, maximalist refresh
stories.author: Adrienne Matei
stories.content:
Victoria is well-known for its quaint, British-inflected downtown core. But across the Johnson Street Bridge, just west of the city centre, are the equally pretty Victoria West and the township of Esquimalt. The area’s sense of community, lush waterfront parks, charming old houses and thriving small businesses are all easily accessible from Rosemead House, a splashy boutique hotel owned by developer Lenny Moy.

For years, this property was known as the Old English Inn, a storied, time-worn institution that Moy bought in 2016. Since then, he has invested $25 million into a vibrant, maximalist refresh. Think reams of technicolour William Morris wallpaper, claw-foot tubs and thousands of antiques. Most have been purchased by Moy himself at auctions of goods from British hotels the Dorchester and the Savoy, including everything from minibars to writing desks to light fixtures. “We buy pieces, have them shipped here, and then do refurbishment,” says Moy, who maintains a nearby warehouse to stash his luxurious loot.

As the hotel’s entry gates make clear, there’s nothing West Coast Modern about the place. They’re Buckingham Palace replicas nabbed from the set of the Crown. “Purposefully, we wanted colours to pop, we didn’t want anything subtle,” he says of design elements like plush upholstery in red, pink and blue geometric motifs. Overall, the feeling is extravagance or bust, an ethos that extends to creature comforts like deluxe mattresses from the Swedish company Duxiana.

From the hotel, it’s easy to access Esquimalt’s gourmet destinations. Grab a complimentary e-bike or your walking shoes and head to Fry’s Bakery. Owner Byron Fry comes from a Canadian baking legacy dating back to the late 1800s; today, the bakery uses historic methods to craft its many varieties of sourdough. Locally, Fry’s is known for its pretzels, sausage rolls and weekly specials. “We have a long-standing tradition of turning the bakery into a pizza shop every Sunday,” Fry says.

A five-minute walk from Fry’s is the Market Garden, which is best described as what it would look like if Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland author Lewis Carroll opened a boutique grocer. A labyrinth of rooms is packed with whimsical products: imported, ladybug-shaped marzipans; a cabinet of glacé fruit; a non-alcoholic wine cellar. Stock up on truffle chips and candied orange peel while, ON weekends, a live pianist serenades shoppers. The store’s owners recently opened Sabayons grocer in the former Bay Centre in downtown Victoria.

For lunch, try a home-cooked Syrian meal at Syriana, which founder Safaa Naeman opened in 2023 after moving to Esquimalt as a refugee and becoming a farmers’ market star with pastries like cheese fatayer . “This is such a warm, close, friendly community,” Naeman says of her decision to put down roots. This season, she will debut a second location focusing on coffees and desserts near the Esquimalt Gorge Park Pavilion.

Driftwood Brewery’s sunny patio is an excellent spot for an afternoon beer and a snack. Local business Dumpling Drop runs a kitchen out of the brewery, meaning crispy dumplings and steamed baos come at you hot and fresh. Rosemead House’s own restaurant, Janevca, offers a dinner menu of wood-fired meats, pizza and Pacific seafood in a dining room festooned with a seasonally changing artificial tree canopy. Complete your meal with pastry chef Brian Bradley’s trompe l’oeil Peach Melba, served on plates from the Savoy, where the dessert originated.

To caffeinate, stop by either of Esquimalt Roasting Company’s two locations on a Wednesday and breathe in the delicious smell of toasting coffee. Sampler packs of its single-origin beans make an energizing souvenir. Hide + Seek coffee, a little gem tucked right next to the Market Garden, has a hip and homey atmosphere, lovely for lingering with an espresso and accompanying glass of seltzer.

Or take a stroll down the West Bay Walkway to visit Marina Bay Cafe, where owner Maria Tanjaoui has intentionally “created a space without voices and without music,” for an environment that “respects visual communication and Deaf culture,” she writes in an email. The Turtle Latte, with caramel, hazelnut, chocolate and a pinch of salt is a customer favourite, and you can get a Birthday Matcha topped with rainbow sprinkles any day of the year.

There are many scenic paths in Esquimalt and Vic West. Just a couple of blocks from Rosemead House, amble by the maritime meadows and abandoned navy barracks of Macaulay Point Park (Esquimalt is home to a Royal Canadian Navy base).

North America’s oldest Japanese garden can be found in Esquimalt Gorge Park. Learn about the Kishida and Takata families, who built this garden and a long-gone tea house near the turn of the 20th century and suffered its loss when they were forced to move to an internment camp in 1942.

Today, the township has restored the park with a serene ornamental stream, Japanese bridge, and traditional torii welcome gate. From June to late September, the Gorge Park Pavilion hosts Monday evening markets, a one-stop shop for feeling immersed in Esquimalt’s festive energy.

Stays from $399/night through rosemeadhouse.CA

stories.title: Canadians split on how much power Ottawa should have in ending labour strikes: poll
stories.summary: Labour groups are opposed to legislation that puts conditions on the use of Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to end strikes.
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
Most Canadians believe the federal government should be able to end a labour strike but are divided over how it should be done, as Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to entrench a controversial power used by the labour minister to intervene in some disputes.

A poll conducted by Nanos Research Group on behalf of Bloomberg News found 32 per cent of Canadians support giving the federal labour minister the power to end strikes that are believed to be against the national interest, while 36 per cent said the government should have to pass back-to-work legislation to do so. Meanwhile, 25 per cent of respondents said the government should not be allowed to end strikes at all.

Labour groups have pushed back against proposed Carney government legislation that puts conditions on the use of Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to end strikes. In recent years, labour ministers have invoked the provision to direct a quasi-judicial body to resolve disputes involving flight attendants, postal workers and rail and port employees — without having to go through the politically fraught process of passing back-to-work legislation.

The government has said that the proposed changes will raise the bar for ending strikes using Section 107, while several unions have argued that the government is doubling down on a power it should not have by enshrining it in law.

Business groups have long called on the government to play a more active role in ending labour disputes, arguing that strikes carry significant economic costs and cause uncertainty, both of which could discourage investment.

Nik Nanos, the founder of Nanos Research, said the poll results suggest the government’s solution is not a “slam dunk” politically. That means it will have to put in work to win over Canadians on the issue, he said.

Young people between the ages of 18 and 24 were the least likely to support giving the labour minister the power to end a strike and the most likely to say that the government should not be allowed to play a role.

The poll was conducted between Sept. 27 and 29 with 1,057 respondents, as is considered accurate within three percentage points, 19 times out of 20.
paragraphs: Most Canadians believe the federal government should be able to end a labour strike but are divided over how it should be done, as Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to entrench a controversial power used by the labour minister to intervene in some disputes.

A poll conducted by Nanos Research Group on behalf of Bloomberg News found 32 per cent of Canadians support giving the federal labour minister the power to end strikes that are believed to be against the national interest, while 36 per cent said the government should have to pass back-to-work legislation to do so. Meanwhile, 25 per cent of respondents said the government should not be allowed to end strikes at all.

Labour groups have pushed back against proposed Carney government legislation that puts conditions on the use of Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to end strikes. In recent years, labour ministers have invoked the provision to direct a quasi-judicial body to resolve disputes involving flight attendants, postal workers and rail and port employees — without having to go through the politically fraught process of passing back-to-work legislation.

The government has said that the proposed changes will raise the bar for ending strikes using Section 107, while several unions have argued that the government is doubling down on a power it should not have by enshrining it in law.

Business groups have long called on the government to play a more active role in ending labour disputes, arguing that strikes carry significant economic costs and cause uncertainty, both of which could discourage investment.

Nik Nanos, the founder of Nanos Research, said the poll results suggest the government’s solution is not a “slam dunk” politically. That means it will have to put in work to win over Canadians on the issue, he said.

Young people between the ages of 18 and 24 were the least likely to support giving the labour minister the power to end a strike and the most likely to say that the government should not be allowed to play a role.

stories.title: Claims that Canada interfered in U.S. midterms are ‘noise,’ former diplomat says
stories.summary: A former Canadian diplomat has dismissed U.S. allegations of Canadian interference in the upcoming midterms elections as “noise.”
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
A former Canadian diplomat has dismissed U.S. allegations of Canadian interference in the upcoming midterms elections as “noise.”

“I don’t think that it deserves much response,” Colin Robertson, a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, told CTV’s Your Morning on Thursday.

Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada, suggested in an interview with “The Really Big Show” podcast released earlier this week that the actions of several Canadian politicians could amount to interference in the midterms, which will be held on Nov. 3.

He pointed to an advertising campaign run by Ontario Premier Doug Ford last year that featured a clip of former U.S. president Ronald Raegan talking about the benefits of free trade.

“Did that constitute any kind of interference? No, I think that’s advocacy,” Robertson said.

Hoekstra also criticized Industry Minister Melanie Joly for stating that Canadian counter-tariffs were designed to target certain states.

“Again, that’s quite justified,” Robertson said, as retaliatory action against the U.S. tariffs. “All of which international trade law recognizes.”

Having petitioned U.S. lawmakers in the past to advance Canada’s interests, Robertson said Canadian politicians are now trying to encourage American businesses to advocate against the trade war, ON their behalf.

“We’re seeing this now ... Republican candidates are going out and saying, ‘well we shouldn’t be applying these tariffs.’ So they’re breaking with the president,” the former diplomat said.

“That’s Americans talking to Americans. That’s exactly what we want to see.”

Robertson said he wouldn’t be surprised if Trump blames Canada should Republicans lose the midterms.

“With Donald Trump, you’re never sure of anything,” he said. “And he’s of course made very clear that if he doesn’t win these midterms, it’s not his fault.”

Trump, after losing the 2020 presidential election, accused his opponent Joe Biden of election fraud .

On Wednesday, Trump told a crowd of supporters during a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Ariz., that Canada will “end up being the 51st state.”

He then listed a longstanding number of grievances that the U.S. held with Canada including Canadian tariffs on milk, car companies moving their factories to the U.S. and renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

“They’ll end up being the 51st state, because that’s the only way it works,” he said. “We don’t need them, but they need us.”

stories.title: How these book publishers balance business risk and personal security
stories.summary: It’s important for entrepreneurs to draw lines around their business wealth and their personal wealth
stories.author: Nickie Shobeiry
stories.content:
When it comes to the economics of book publishing, Jack David doesn’t mince words: “It’s a terrible business.”

Mr. David is the co-founder of ECW Press, a Toronto-based independent publisher. The company, now over 50 years old, has published over 3,500 books and hit about $5-million in annual revenue. However, profit margins in publishing can be as narrow as two per cent. After acquiring a book, a publisher May spend 18 months editing, designing and printing, followed by another several months waiting to collect revenue after the book hits the stores.

To help cover expenses, Mr. David has often dipped into his personal finances. When to mingle personal and business assets and when to keep them apart is a common challenge for entrepreneurs. Mr. David says he has been putting his own money into ECW since “day two”, including borrowing against the home he shares with his wife, Sharon, a retired veterinarian.

Because the property is jointly owned, she was required to receive independent legal advice before agreeing to put their home on the line. Her lawyer walked her through what Mr. David jokingly calls the “80 bad things” that could happen: “Is he ever going to be able to pay this off? What if he goes bankrupt?”

Sharon chose to back her husband, but the couple drew some lines around their personal wealth. For example, when they came into an inheritance, they invested the money rather than put it into ECW. They also own Toronto real estate and a cottage, diversifying their assets.

That separation is important for entrepreneurs. “You can’t put all your eggs in one basket,” says Catherine Metzger-Silver, a financial advisor with Edward Jones in Kentville, Nova Scotia. “There’s so much risk management involved.”

Today, ECW is one of Canada’s biggest trade and academic publishers, but getting there has been marked by financial uncertainty. In 2001, both its Canadian and American distributors went bankrupt, leaving the company without money it was owed.

Around that time, Mr. David took a gamble on a manuscript by Neil Peart, drummer for the band Rush, scraping together the money for the advance fee. The band went on tour, which helped promote the book Ghost Rider: Travels on the Healing Road . It has sold roughly 250,000 copies to date.

“You get enough of those hits, you get new books you want to publish,” Mr. David says. “That’s what keeps me involved – apart from the fact that my mortgage is on the line.”

Ms. Metzger-Silver often hears entrepreneurs say, “my business is my retirement”. But if an entrepreneur can’t find a buyer, or the company sells for less than expected, they May have little to fall back on in their later years. She says that makes it especially important to build wealth throughout their career.

David Caron, part of Ecw’s next generation of ownership, is walking the same tightrope between investing in the business and protecting personal finances. He joined the company in 2004 when he was in his mid-30s with two children, aged six and three, and is now co-publisher with Mr. David.

No matter how ECW performed, Mr. Caron and his wife set a minimum amount of household income that needed to be protected, covering their living expenses, mortgage, their children’s post-secondary education and their own retirement contributions. “We’re equal partners in this, that’s my rule of thumb,” he says.

At ECW, Mr. Caron pays himself a salary. “The idea of me taking a dividend – I just keep thinking about the other people at the company,” he says. “You’re constantly reinvesting everything else back into the company.”

Mr. Caron plans to stay in publishing for years to come, but is already planning his eventual exit. His experience buying ECW and, more recently, buying majority ownership of Annick Press has shown him that a well-planned succession can take a decade. “If I want to think about somebody taking things on when I’m in my late 60s, the time is now,” he says.

When selling a business, Ms. Metzger-Silver recommends allowing plenty of runway. “The day you open your business is the day you plan the exit. You never know where life will take you.”

stories.title: Pressure builds on former MP Raj Grewal amid fraud allegations
stories.summary: Father-in-law says 'I am a victim of the fraud' as Peel Regional Police and Ontario legal regulator circle law firm founded by former MP.
stories.author: Tom Blackwell
stories.content:
Former Ontario MP Raj Grewal is facing a dramatic new wave of legal pressure, with police asking for help investigating alleged fraud and other wrongdoing by the lawyer and his colleagues, Ontario’s legal regulator moving to take over the law firm Grewal founded — and even his own father-in-law accusing him of multi-million-dollar fraud and forgery.

The impact of the affair on Grewal’s family is particularly striking.

Father-in-law Kailash Kasal said in an affidavit last month he’s struggling to preserve good relations with his lenders based on “the fact that I have no connection to this fraud perpetrated by Raj Grewal and others and that I am a victim of the fraud.”

The businessman confirmed that his daughter and her husband are estranged, but said he had held off asking Grewal about allegedly tainted funds that appeared in one of his companies’ accounts.

stories.title: Fry and Sim face off in Vancouver, but other mayoral candidates reject spoiler label
stories.summary: Interest in the Vancouver race appears high. The City of Vancouver says more than 103,000 people have voted in advance, up 60 per cent from roughly 65,000 voters in 2022.
stories.author: Marissa Birnie
stories.content:
Vancouver mayoral candidates Ken Sim and Pete Fry view each other as their main rival in the battle for City Hall.

But while recent polling suggests the mayoral race is indeed a faceoff between incumbent Sim and two-term Green Councillor Fry, there are three other big-name candidates who reject the label of spoiler.

Kareem Allam — Sim’s former chief of staff turned litigation adversary — is running with the Vancouver Liberals, which is not affiliated with the federal party.

“The pollsters don’t always get it right. Municipal government is also the hardest level to poll. It’s got its tricks and nuances, especially in an at-large system,” he said in an interview Tuesday.

The Vancouver race culminates Saturday, when municipalities across British Columbia go to the polls.

Interest in the Vancouver race appears high. The City of Vancouver says more than 103,000 people have voted in advance, up 60 per cent from roughly 65,000 voters over five advance days in 2022.

Sim, who is campaigning for a second term as mayor with the right-of-centre ABC Vancouver, said while he would be the first to admit he didn’t get everything right during his tenure, he believes he can lead the city in the right direction.

“We’ve gotten some pretty significant things done, but there’s way more work to do,” he said in an interview Wednesday.

Other candidates include Rebecca Bligh, a two-term councillor who helped get Sim elected with ABC Vancouver in 2022 and is now running with Vote Vancouver, and Team candidate Colleen Hardwick, a former councillor.

Allam, Hardwick and Bligh all rejected the notion their candidacies could split the centre or centre-right vote.

“The question is not left or right. The question is about who we are serving at city hall,” Hardwick said Tuesday.

Bligh said she was running to govern for Vancouver’s ignored middle class, and polling did not change how she campaigned.

“It’s anyone’s race,” she said in an interview Wednesday.

Fry, son of longtime Liberal MP Hedy Fry, has acknowledged benefiting from the narrowing of the progressive field, after the withdrawals of William Azaroff from OneCity Vancouver and Stephanie Allen for Cope Vancouver.

After ending his candidacy, Azaroff appeared at City Hall with Fry, who praised him for running a serious campaign that “raised real issues” such as housing, small business and affordability.

“I think folks are excited to be able to talk up a viable alternative to Ken Sim as the mayor of Vancouver and really reset,” Fry said in an interview Tuesday.

He added that Azaroff’s withdrawal was recognition that he was the person best suited to defeat Sim.

Bligh said she’s a progressive candidate with a centrist platform. Meanwhile, Allam said he believed he was taking votes from Sim and Fry equally.

The candidates’ platforms all emphasize quality-of-life issues, including affordability and public safety. Sim’s promises include a zero per cent property tax increase.

The election ballot also includes two plebiscite questions on public safety.

The non-binding questions ask voters if they’re in favour of the city “strengthening its laws to forbid open-air hard drug use in public spaces,” which is already illegal in B.C. The other asks if the city should ask the province to convert portions of the old St. Paul’s hospital into a “secure medical facility” with 100-plus involuntary care beds.

Hardwick called the questions a “populist election tactic,” while other critics said they aren’t realistic.

Sim said strengthening the city health bylaw — regulating conduct such as smoking in common areas — would allow officers to issue tickets or confiscate drugs without arrests. The involuntary care question, he said, is about asking the province to fulfil its accountability to people who pose a risk to their own safety or others.

Fry said he supports managing drug use in public spaces, but differs from Sim in believing that people should be diverted to supervised consumption sites or shelters.

His platform focuses on housing, transportation and the economy. “Folks should be able to have a good life in this city, he said.

Bligh said Sim’s property tax freezes protect wealthy landowners and undercut critical services. She said she would work with the federal government to leverage city-owned land and provide free transit for youth.

Hardwick said the key to livability in Vancouver is effective city planning. She said she wanted to repeal the city’s official development plan and re-establish neighbourhood planning offices

Allam said he wants to bring youth back to Vancouver by improving affordability through jobs and housing, and investing in parks and community centres.

He said his platform cuts across ideologies, and distanced himself from Sim, who filed a lawsuit in May 2025 alleging Allam falsely accused him of drinking and driving.

Sim faces his own defamation lawsuit from councillor Sean Orr, filed after falsely accusing Orr of distributing illegal drugs in comments to Chinese-speaking reporters.

Trials in both cases are far off.

For now, the focus is on the ballot box.

“I think people will be surprised at the results,” Allam said.
