The non-binding questions ask voters if they’re in favour of the city “strengthening its laws to forbid open-air hard drug use in public spaces,” which is already illegal in B.C. The other asks if the city should ask the province to convert portions of the old St. Paul’s hospital into a “secure medical facility” with 100-plus involuntary care beds.
Hardwick called the questions a “populist election tactic,” while other critics said they aren’t realistic.

Sim said strengthening the city health bylaw — regulating conduct such as smoking in common areas — would allow officers to issue tickets or confiscate drugs without arrests. The involuntary care question, he said, is about asking the province to fulfil its accountability to people who pose a risk to their own safety or others.
Fry said he supports managing drug use in public spaces, but differs from Sim in believing that people should be diverted to supervised consumption sites or shelters.
His platform focuses on housing, transportation and the economy. “Folks should be able to have a good life in this city, he said.

Bligh said Sim’s property tax freezes protect wealthy landowners and undercut critical services. She said she would work with the federal government to leverage city-owned land and provide free transit for youth.
Hardwick said the key to livability in Vancouver is effective city planning. She said she wanted to repeal the city’s official development plan and re-establish neighbourhood planning offices
Allam said he wants to bring youth back to Vancouver by improving affordability through jobs and housing, and investing in parks and community centres.
He said his platform cuts across ideologies, and distanced himself from Sim, who filed a lawsuit in May 2025 alleging Allam falsely accused him of drinking and driving.
Sim faces his own defamation lawsuit from councillor Sean Orr, filed after falsely accusing Orr of distributing illegal drugs in comments to Chinese-speaking reporters.
Trials in both cases are far off.
For now, the focus is on the ballot box.
“I think people will be surprised at the results,” Allam said.

stories.title: Health ministers meet in Winnipeg after Ottawa announces funding extension
stories.summary: Federal government announced it would extend funding for mental health, addictions and home care by one year
stories.author: Ian Bickis
stories.content:
Canadian health ministers meet in Winnipeg today after the federal government announced it would extend funding for mental health, addictions and home care by one year.

Federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel made the announcement on social media late Wednesday, saying the extension represents $1.2-billion in funding.

The existing funding was set to expire next year.

Manitoba Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara is to host provincial and territorial counterparts today, and Michel is to co-chair Friday’s meeting.

Provincial health ministers had said they were worried about “profound and negative” effects on patients and health-care jobs if the federal funding agreements weren’t renewed in this year’s budget.

Provinces and territories also raised concerns about the future of the Canada Health Transfer as the federal budget states the minimum growth rate will drop to three per cent from five per cent in 2028.

Asagwara says they spoke with Michel about the unanimous concerns of health ministers and are keen to hear more on federal health funding.

“I am thrilled to be able to say that I feel Minister Michel has been listening,” Asagwara said Wednesday.

“I look forward to hearing some news from the minister on this, we all do.”

Linda Silas, president of the Canadian Federation of Nurses Unions, said funding commitments should be a priority.

She said the federal government can’t lose sight of the importance of health care as it ramps up spending on defence and other priorities.

“There has to be a just balance, and we have to see our health-care system as an investment, as a human rights issue, and as proud Canadians, it’s the core of our fabric, and we need to hear our prime minister speak more loudly about it.”

The Canadian Medical Association said in a release Wednesday that the meeting is an important opportunity for the federal government to provide certainty on funding to provinces and territories.

The association said strong and reliable federal funding to maintain universal health care is foundational to growing Canada’s economy.

stories.title: Burnaby school district says cyberattack May have leaked student, parent info
stories.summary: The Burnaby School District says in a notice that the ransomware attack it suffered on Sept. 21 affected school websites and portals, internal network services and phone lines.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Public school officials in Burnaby, B.C., say hackers May have obtained student and parental information in a recent cyberattack.

The Burnaby School District says in an online notice that the ransomware attack it suffered on Sept. 21 affected school websites and portals, internal network services and phone lines.

The notice says hackers copied and stole files that May have contained lists of parent, guardian and student names and contact information, as well as birthdates, grades and school names.

It says the hackers May also have obtained registration forms, kindergarten assessment notes and detailed lists of students on specialized learning plans.

The school district says the matter is in the hands of the RCMP and B.C.’s privacy commissioner, adding that its system security is being evaluated to prevent further breaches.

It says staff, students and their families have been offered registration with TransUnion’s fraud alert service and encourages them to be wary of any suspicious communications.

“We understand that incidents of this nature are concerning and we remain committed to keeping the Burnaby Schools community updated throughout this process, as the investigation proceeds and additional information becomes available,” the notice says.

stories.title: ‘Hardly surprising’ many Alberta business leaders staying mum on separation: expert
stories.summary: The silence from many Alberta business leaders on the upcoming provincial referendum comes as no surprise to one corporate leadership expert.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
The silence from many Alberta business leaders on the upcoming provincial referendum comes as no surprise to one corporate leadership expert.

Monday’s vote includes 10 questions: one on whether Alberta should remain in Canada or move toward a binding separation referendum; five on immigration and four on constitutional matters.

Richard Leblanc, a professor of governance, law and ethics at York University, says there’s a tradition in Canada for CEOs to stay in their lanes and not risk alienating shareholders or employees by taking a political stand.

But Leblanc says there May be times a company’s board of directors agrees that a CEO should speak out on a matter that affects the well-being of the business, as Alberta taking steps toward a potential split from Canada arguably would.

A handful of leaders at big, publicly traded companies are among the more than 70 signatories to an open letter from the Calgary Chamber of Commerce warning of the economic fallout of separation, while the top brass at many prominent firms have stayed mum.

A few top executives have made their views known: Imperial Oil’s John Whelan has spoken in favour of Alberta and Canada sticking together while Atco Ltd.’s Nancy Southern has warned of the disruption a split would cause.

“It’s hardly surprising that a majority of CEOs are not speaking up,” Leblanc said. “There’s more to be lost than gained, generally, by speaking up about a political matter.”

Some corporations have former prime ministers, premiers and cabinet ministers as directors on their boards, who can advise on when and how to weigh in on politics, Leblanc noted.

Atco’s board includes former Alberta premier Jason Kenney, who has been a fervent voice in favour of the province staying in Confederation, as well as former federal cabinet minister Rona Ambrose.

Leblanc said customers and employees May have “legitimate expectations” that a CEO take a public stand on something that could affect the business, though getting board sign-off on the message is no easy feat.

“Sometimes the risk of not doing something can be far greater than doing something and dealing with the blowback.”

stories.title: U.S. watching for Canadian ‘interference’ in midterms, Hoekstra says
stories.summary: During an interview on a podcast, Hoekstra said political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference ahead of pivotal midterm elections next month.

During an interview on “The Really Big Show” podcast that was posted last week, Hoekstra said political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.

U.S. President Donald Trump ended trade talks with Canada in October 2025 after Ontario aired an ad during the World Series using clips of former U.S. president Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs and supporting free trade.

Hoekstra also cited recent comments by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and former prime minister Justin Trudeau and suggested they also could amount to interference.

Hoekstra went on to warn Canadian politicians to keep their “nose out” of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.

Trudeau criticized the Trump administration during a discussion at Brown University on Sept. 22.

“There is a pattern here of doing things that are driving up prices for your consumers and not necessarily making anything better for America, by fighting with one of your oldest and best allies,” Trudeau said during the conversation.

In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at “politically sensitive states.”

Joly pushed back Wednesday, telling reporters Canada would never engage in election interference and would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says Canada would never interfere in U.S. elections. Her comments came after U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra said Canadians should keep their noses out of American politics during the congressional midterms. (Oct. 14, 2026)

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.

The ambassador declined a request from The Canadian Press for an interview.

Tension between the United States and Canada has increased since Trump won the presidential election in 2024, and began threatening to turn Canada into the 51st state.

That threat, and his attacks on Canada, have become a focal point of his stump speeches as he actively campaigns in battleground states ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which could end Republican control over Congress.

At a rally in Bullhead City, Ariz., ON Wednesday, Trump went after Canada again, listing grievances over dairy sector trade and repeating his claim that Canada treats the United States “very badly.”

He said Canada will end up being the 51st state because “that’s the only way it works.”

“We don’t need them, but they need us,” he said.

The Republicans are under heavy pressure ahead of the midterms, when the entire House of Representatives and one-third of U.S. Senate seats will be contested. While the Republicans currently hold a majority of seats in both chambers, polls suggest the Democrats could win control of both.

Peter Navarro, one of Trump’s trade advisers, warned Ottawa last month against interfering in the midterms and berated Canada over its successful lobbying efforts in the past.

Speaking at the American Growth Summit in Washington, he told the audience that any Canadians in the room intent on lobbying the U.S. government should “get the hell out of our country.”

“The problem you have is you lobby this country, and you’ve been successful in the past and you think you can keep doing that. Memo to Canada: You cannot keep doing that,” Navarro said.

“That game is up and if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan, you will pay even more dearly.”

The Globe and Mail reported recently that Republican political operatives were on the ground in Alberta earlier this year to help the separatist campaign. It also reported that some Alberta separatists went to Washington to lobby for U.S. government support.

In August, Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered the Canadian negotiating team to call off trade talks with the U.S. after accusing the Americans of making unreasonable demands.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre was in Detroit on Tuesday to make a case for tariff-free trade in the auto sector.

Poilievre appeared on CNN, where he continued to pitch the benefits of tariff-free trade.

“We have a 200-year-old relationship, there’s always going to be grievances on both sides of the border,” he said. “We have our grievances with the United States even predating this most recent trade dispute, but I would focus on what we can do together.”

Peter Navarro, one of Trump’s trade advisers, warned Ottawa last month against interfering in the midterms and berated Canada over its successful lobbying efforts in the past.

“The problem you have is you lobby this country, and you’ve been successful in the past and you think you can keep doing that. Memo to Canada: You cannot keep doing that,” Navarro said.
“That game is up and if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan, you will pay even more dearly.”

stories.title: Supreme Court hears challenge of law clearing path for Ontario Place redevelopment
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada plans to hear arguments from a coalition challenging the constitutionality of legislation that smooths the way for major changes at Ontario Place.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada plans to hear arguments Thursday from a coalition challenging the constitutionality of legislation that smooths the way for major changes at Ontario Place.

The case unfolding in Canada’s top court could reverberate far beyond the Toronto waterfront park that opened in 1971.

Over the years, the theme park featured a spherical theatre that showed movies on a huge screen, children’s play areas, a revolving concert stage and several pavilions suspended above the water.

The provincial government wants to redevelop Ontario Place to include an elaborate spa operated by a private company, a relocated Ontario Science Centre, revamped play and shoreline areas, a parking facility and a provincial police detachment.

The coalition Ontario Place Protectors challenged the province’s Rebuilding Ontario Place Act on the basis that it insulates state action from scrutiny by the courts and therefore violates the Constitution.

The coalition also argued that exemptions from environmental and heritage laws and municipal noise regulations amount to a breach of public trust.

An Ontario judge dismissed the application in 2024 and a challenge of the ruling in the provincial Court of Appeal was also unsuccessful.

Writing on behalf of a unanimous Court of Appeal, Justice Grant Huscroft said there was no doubt that the provincial government’s decision to redevelop Ontario Place is strongly opposed by a number of concerned citizens and organizations.

Political opposition to the plan has not swayed the government and the coalition has turned to the court in an effort to stop it, Huscroft said.

“But there is no basis for the court to do so. The court is not an alternative forum for resolving political grievances. The only legitimate question for the court is whether the impugned provisions of Ropa violate the law or the Constitution,” he wrote.

“They do not, and the appeal must be dismissed.”

In January, the Supreme Court agreed to hear the Ontario Place Protectors’ case.

The coalition says provincial superior courts have historical and inherent jurisdiction to review laws and government actions protected under section 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867, and to provide effective remedies when governments do not respect the limits on their powers.

The coalition says the Rebuilding Ontario Place Act’s scope is unprecedented and appears to violate section 96 by removing the essential core powers of the courts.

It argues the legislation severely limits or entirely eliminates the ability of courts to hold Crown officials accountable through declaratory actions, damage awards and injunctions when they have acted beyond their powers.

The coalition is also seeking to have the doctrine of public trust acknowledged as an unwritten constitutional principle rooted in English common law and inherited by Canada.

It argues the doctrine of public trust maintains that natural and cultural assets are essential to public welfare and must be safeguarded by the state in its role as trustee.

Margie Zeidler, the daughter of Ontario Place architect Eberhard Zeidler, remembers visiting the park as a child.

“It was extraordinary. It was a public place,” she said in an interview. “You could have a picnic in the forest. You could watch films at Cinesphere. You could watch any musical performance at the forum.”

Zeidler, a member of the Ontario Place Protectors coalition, says the provincial government’s actions have made the fight about more than just the historic theme park. “It became more, not about Ontario Place, but about, wait a minute, what democracy are we living in here?” she said. “I didn’t know governments could do that.”

In their written submission to the Supreme Court, the Crown and the Ontario attorney general say the case should be dismissed.

The immunity provided by the provincial legislation does not go as far as the coalition alleges, the submission says: “(The act) does not make Ontario Place a lawless zone.”

Rather, it immunizes the Crown, its servants and agents from civil causes of action arising from specific circumstances, the submission says.

The Crown and attorney general also urge the court to reject the claim that the legislation is invalid because of the doctrine of public trust.

“The novel doctrine articulated by the Appellant is not an unwritten constitutional principle, and even if such a doctrine existed in law, which is denied, there is no evidence in the record that could warrant applying this far-reaching new doctrine to Ontario Place,” the submission says.

The case has attracted submissions from interveners, including several provinces, First Nations, civil liberties groups and environmental organizations.

The Supreme Court often reserves its decisions until a later date, meaning a ruling in the case might not come until next year.

stories.title: Health ministers set to meet in Winnipeg after Ottawa announces funding extension
stories.summary: Winnipeg — Canadian health ministers meet in Winnipeg today after the federal government announced it would extend funding for mental health, addictions and home care by one year.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Winnipeg — Provincial and territorial health ministers are still pushing for clarity on federal funding despite a one-year extension on some programs, Manitoba Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara said Thursday.

Speaking as host of the meeting of ministers in Winnipeg, Asagwara said federal confirmation of the extension is a first step but nothing more.

“We are unified in stating very clearly that we need to go much further than that,” they said.

“We have been asking very consistently for full clarity on all of the bilateral agreements and the Canada Health Transfer, and we remain unified in that ask.”

Federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel announced an extension of funding on social media late Wednesday. She said it represents $1.2 billion in funding for mental health, addictions and home care.

The existing funding was set to expire next year.

The funding doesn’t add any new programming and doesn’t provide the certainty needed to plan long-term, said Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones.

“Respectfully, I would say that a one-year extension of an existing 10-year (agreement) about to expire does not fill us with a lot of joy.”

Michel said in her letter confirming the extension that it provides stability as the federal government works to strengthen the health-care system.

She said she looks forward to collaborative discussions Friday, when she meets with provincial and territorial counterparts in Winnipeg.

Asagwara said provinces and territories could continue to ask for long-term commitments on bilateral agreements and push for the Canada Health Transfer to grow at a minimum of five per cent, rather than the three per cent it’s set to drop to in 2028.

“We are all in the same boat here that we are still facing an enormous fiscal cliff,” they said.

“We do not have clarity, and in every single jurisdiction, every single minister here can tell you stories about how these potential cuts would affect real Canadians, would affect real families, real services, real jobs and would have very real consequences.”

Groups, including the Canadian Medical Association and the Canadian Federation of Nurses Unions, have also been pushing for more reliable federal funding, saying health-care funding is a foundational investment.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Ian Bickis, The Canadian Press

stories.title: All the ways the Alberta referendum could result in an October surprise
stories.summary: Support for remaining in Canada is in the high 60s, while the leave side is in the low 20s. But pollsters have been wrong before.
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
With just days to go before Albertans vote on whether to pursue independence, polls suggest residents who want to stay in Canada have a safe lead. Support for remaining is in the high 60s, while the leave sentiment is in the low 20s. But it could go differently. Pollsters have been wrong before, even on separatist votes. The National Post’s Joseph Brean surveys various possibilities for how this referendum on a referendum could turn out to be an October surprise.

This is a question of confidence, both in the polls and in the broader issue. Confidence is a subjective attitude, shifting and hard to measure or predict. If turnout is low, public opinion polling could be a less reliable guide to the actual results.

“Fervent separatists will crawl across broken glass to make their vote count,” said remain campaigner and former Alberta deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk in a recent speech. The danger, he meant, is that a pro-Canada majority will think they have it in the bag and stay home.

In 1980, Quebec’s sovereignty movement under a Parti Québécois government soundly lost a referendum that would have given it a mandate to “negotiate a new constitutional agreement with the rest of Canada, based on the equality of nations.” In 1995, however, the PQ came within a single percentage point of a vote to leave. Turnout of over 90 per cent is thought to have boosted the remain numbers such that projections of a leave victory by a few points turned out to be wrong. Now, another vote seems likely, and is at least promised by the newly elected PQ government.

In Scotland, separatists lost their referendum in 2014 by fully 10 percentage points, with voter turnout at more than 80 per cent.

Alberta’s voter turnout in the last provincial election was 60 per cent, and in the last federal election 67 per cent, but this is obviously a different sort of ballot question.

Curiously, the referendum is not a simple “Yes/No” question. It is a rambling offer of two numbered options. You can almost ignore the setup and get straight to the options, which are clear enough on their own without the wordy question, which reads: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”

Still here? Did you drift off a bit at “commence the legal process”? Did you need to be told “the Constitution” is “Canadian”? Did you already assume the “legal process” would be “required”? This referendum has more words than it needs.

Eventually, it gets to the key parts: “Option 1: Alberta should remain a province of Canada. Option 2: The Government of Alberta should commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.”

It is a referendum, but the ballot reads like a lawyer’s letter. There are also nine other questions, all of which are yes/no, ON things like immigration control, immigrant access to social services, voter identification, judicial appointments and provincial-federal relations. How and even if people read through all that could have measurable impact on the emotionally charged central question among an electorate with a wide spectrum of interests and motivations.

“There’s a lot of people who want to send a message,” said Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Oct. 7. “There’s a lot of people who think voting for Option 2 will give leverage. If those are your reasons, I would say there is a better way to send a message or to give leverage. And that is to give us a mandate on the other nine questions.”

Scotland was more concise, not troubling voters with too much windup or alternative messages. “Should Scotland be an independent country?” the 2014 referendum asked. The answer was no, according to 55 per cent of Scots.

Another way the true will of Albertans could be misrepresented in referendum results is by invalidation of good faith ballots.

More than 3,000 ballot packages have been invalidated for reasons such as missing declaration forms or problems with identification, though there remains time to fix those problems.

All ballots are to be counted by hand. Question 10, the central one about a referendum on separating, will be counted and reported first, followed by the other nine, with a deadline of 48 hours, according to Elections Alberta.

Quebec sovereigntists have marched farther along the road to separatism, and their history offers cautionary tales for Alberta sovereigntists. But with a new Quebec government seeking the same goal, they also offer inspiration.

The idea that Canada is broken has lately had a run as a political slogan. The idea that it is actually breaking up is a less familiar notion, not exactly new, but surging to unprecedented levels of public interest with two provincial sovereignty movements campaigning simultaneously. So the successes of one could boost the fortunes of the other, even without actual cooperation.

As separatist advocate and leader of the Alberta Prosperity Project Mitch Sylvestre said after a cordial meeting with Paul St-Pierre Plamondon prior to his election as Quebec’s new premier, according to Rick Bell of the Calgary Herald, “You know, we both agreed, and this came out of Paul’s mouth not mine. He said the only level of government neither of us needs is at the federal level.”

The folk wisdom is that bad weather lowers turnout. It has even been measured in the U.S. at one percentage point per inch of rain, and half a point per inch of snow. In Canada, University of Ottawa researchers found that from the 2004 to 2015 federal elections, “each millimeter of precipitation decreases turnout by more than 0.1 percentage points.”

Higher temperatures boost turnout, they found, but only in spring, summer and fall elections. In the winter 2006 election victory for Stephen Harper, warmer temperatures “triggered lower turnout, in particular, when there was also high precipitation.”

This is the October surprise, in which U.S. President Donald Trump could say or do something provocative, or perhaps offer something like the $5,000 payment he has offered American voters if Republicans win the midterm elections. In Alberta’s referendum, he could see some usefulness to his side in the wider trade war.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, therefore, is in a tricky strategic position, needing to both advocate for the Albertan remain side while managing his chaotic conflict with Trump, who is on record as coveting not only Alberta, but all of Canada.

Carney’s play was a Thanksgiving video, posed in a classroom at his Edmonton high school with a world map behind him, ON a long-weekend holiday that was thematically useful.

“It is a chance to give thanks for Canada,” he said. “This year, Thanksgiving is a bit different. A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future, whether to remain part of Canada, or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada.”

His voice lilted on “could,” a little rhetorical emphasis on the inherent risk of Option 2, in contrast to his pitch for Option 1.

“I’m back home a lot these days, because we are building big things again in Alberta, thousands of new homes, high-speed rail, a new pipeline to the West Coast that will create lasting opportunity and prosperity,” he said. “Canada’s working. Truth is, we can’t achieve any of this if we’re divided. We can’t build big things on fault lines.”

Of all the referendum results that few saw coming, Brexit, Britain’s vote to leave the European Union in 2016, stands out as maybe the most shocking.

It cost Prime Minister David Cameron his leadership, and was a failure of sorts also for Carney, who as Governor of the Bank of England had warned Brexit would cause a recession. He then agreed to extend his term to help avert one.

One immediate political winner was Boris Johnson, the now former prime minister whose appeal was to seem “shambolic,” as the British say, clownish, chaotic, disruptive, but massively likeable, like the earlier Torontonian archetype, the former mayor Rob Ford, who died a few months before Brexit.

A few months after Brexit came the equally momentous surprise first election of Donald Trump, who took that same archetype to new extremes of political power.

Britain still labours under the consequences of that political sea change. So does their Conservative Party’s revolving leadership of less charismatic figures. So, indeed, does the rest of the world, including Alberta.

The tech titan does not have a perfect track record for sage prediction of domestic affairs in other countries, such as Britain where he once said civil war is “inevitable.” But he does take an interest. And, as in Germany, he can speak influentially in support of a populist right-wing movement on its way from the fringe to the mainstream of power, such as the Alternative for Germany.

This is a question of confidence, both in the polls and in the broader issue. Confidence is a subjective attitude, shifting and hard to measure or predict. If turnout is low, public opinion polling could be a less reliable guide to the actual results.

“Fervent separatists will crawl across broken glass to make their vote count,” said remain campaigner and former Alberta deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk in a recent speech. The danger, he meant, is that a pro-Canada majority will think they have it in the bag and stay home.

In 1980, Quebec’s sovereignty movement under a Parti Québécois government soundly lost a referendum that would have given it a mandate to “negotiate a new constitutional agreement with the rest of Canada, based on the equality of nations.” In 1995, however, the PQ came within a single percentage point of a vote to leave. Turnout of over 90 per cent is thought to have boosted the remain numbers such that projections of a leave victory by a few points turned out to be wrong. Now, another vote seems likely, and is at least promised by the newly elected PQ government.
In Scotland, separatists lost their referendum in 2014 by fully 10 percentage points, with voter turnout at more than 80 per cent.
Alberta’s voter turnout in the last provincial election was 60 per cent, and in the last federal election 67 per cent, but this is obviously a different sort of ballot question.

Curiously, the referendum is not a simple “Yes/No” question. It is a rambling offer of two numbered options. You can almost ignore the setup and get straight to the options, which are clear enough on their own without the wordy question, which reads: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”

Still here? Did you drift off a bit at “commence the legal process”? Did you need to be told “the Constitution” is “Canadian”? Did you already assume the “legal process” would be “required”? This referendum has more words than it needs.

Eventually, it gets to the key parts: “Option 1: Alberta should remain a province of Canada. Option 2: The Government of Alberta should commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.”

It is a referendum, but the ballot reads like a lawyer’s letter. There are also nine other questions, all of which are yes/no, ON things like immigration control, immigrant access to social services, voter identification, judicial appointments and provincial-federal relations. How and even if people read through all that could have measurable impact on the emotionally charged central question among an electorate with a wide spectrum of interests and motivations.

“There’s a lot of people who want to send a message,” said Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Oct. 7. “There’s a lot of people who think voting for Option 2 will give leverage. If those are your reasons, I would say there is a better way to send a message or to give leverage. And that is to give us a mandate on the other nine questions.”

Scotland was more concise, not troubling voters with too much windup or alternative messages. “Should Scotland be an independent country?” the 2014 referendum asked. The answer was no, according to 55 per cent of Scots.
Another way the true will of Albertans could be misrepresented in referendum results is by invalidation of good faith ballots.
More than 3,000 ballot packages have been invalidated for reasons such as missing declaration forms or problems with identification, though there remains time to fix those problems.

All ballots are to be counted by hand. Question 10, the central one about a referendum on separating, will be counted and reported first, followed by the other nine, with a deadline of 48 hours, according to Elections Alberta.

Quebec sovereigntists have marched farther along the road to separatism, and their history offers cautionary tales for Alberta sovereigntists. But with a new Quebec government seeking the same goal, they also offer inspiration.

The idea that Canada is broken has lately had a run as a political slogan. The idea that it is actually breaking up is a less familiar notion, not exactly new, but surging to unprecedented levels of public interest with two provincial sovereignty movements campaigning simultaneously. So the successes of one could boost the fortunes of the other, even without actual cooperation.

As separatist advocate and leader of the Alberta Prosperity Project Mitch Sylvestre said after a cordial meeting with Paul St-Pierre Plamondon prior to his election as Quebec’s new premier, according to Rick Bell of the Calgary Herald, “You know, we both agreed, and this came out of Paul’s mouth not mine. In Alberta’s referendum, he could see some usefulness to his side in the wider trade war.

“It is a chance to give thanks for Canada,” he said. “This year, Thanksgiving is a bit different. A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future, whether to remain part of Canada, or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada.”
His voice lilted on “could,” a little rhetorical emphasis on the inherent risk of Option 2, in contrast to his pitch for Option 1.

“I’m back home a lot these days, because we are building big things again in Alberta, thousands of new homes, high-speed rail, a new pipeline to the West Coast that will create lasting opportunity and prosperity,” he said. “Canada’s working. Truth is, we can’t achieve any of this if we’re divided. We can’t build big things on fault lines.”

stories.title: In Brampton, the house value decline bites hard
stories.summary: The median price of a detached home in Brampton hit $930,000 in September, dropping 37.4 per cent from March, 2022
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
In recent years, Brampton, Ont., has played a major role in the Toronto-area housing market as one of the fastest-growing municipalities in the sprawling metro area. It is also among the areas hardest hit by the decline in real estate prices since the 2022 peak.

According to the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board, the median price of a detached home in Brampton hit $930,000 in September, a 37.4 per cent drop from March, 2022, when median prices were $1.486-million.

Brampton’s struggles provide plenty of shocking anecdotes of value destruction. One Reddit thread, entitled “HouseSigma blunders” cited the example of the detached home at 79 Templehill Rd., purchased for $1.875-million in late February, 2022, and sold in late September, 2026, for $1.135-million – a $740,000 change of fortune and a 39.5 per cent loss.

So, what kind of house can you find for prices almost 40 per cent less than four years ago?

Despite its list price, this updated four-bedroom house in the city’s centrally located Peel Village is probably going to sell for less than the city’s median price.

“These guys, they are selling for loss,” said Nav Takkar, a broker with Re/Max President Realty. “They bought this house last year; it looks like it will sell for less than asking price.”

Mr. Takkar is blunt about the reality facing sellers in much of the city. Mortgage costs, falling rents and economic worries are keeping prices depressed, he said. However, for these sellers, there is also opportunity. With good incomes, he said they can afford to take advantage of the situation and are looking to upgrade to a newer, larger home, one with more than 3,500 square feet of living space.

A few years ago, what they are looking for would have cost close to $2.5-million. Today? “The prices in those areas, they are listing for $1.8 to $1.9-million, but actually selling for $1.5 to $1.6-million,” Mr. Takkar said.

Brampton’s larger neighbours – Toronto and Mississauga – also saw median detached prices fall about 25 per cent, but from a higher level and not quite as far: from $1.6-million to $1.2-million. In that price range, inside Brampton, you get a lot more house than you do in Toronto, but it’s also hard to find a buyer for those houses.

Take the example of 22 Oldham, which listing agent Sumit Sharda with Re/Max Realty Services Inc. is selling for the second time this year.

“It sold in July, and the buyer failed to close. So we had to relist it,” he said. Just a few months after that offer for just under $1.2-million fell through, Mr. Sharda is finding the market decidedly slow.

The home has some real assets: A large lot next to a park and an in-ground pool. “The outside of that property is spectacular,” said Mr. Sharda. “Inside it’s kind of dated.” However, he notes the upstairs has 2,200 square feet of living space, with another 2,200 square feet on the lower level that has a walkout at grade. If a buyer could get a basement suite legalized, there might be potential for rental income.

Brampton’s decline has been nearly twice as rapid as the fall of the median detached price across Canada in the same period, according to data from the Canadian Real Estate Association. In March, 2022, the national median price for a detached house was $932,900. It has since fallen 21 per cent to just over $730,000.

There are houses in Brampton at the national median, though at that price there can be demerits caused by curb appeal, according to Bradley Mayer-Harman, with Century 21 Millennium Inc.

“I will be frank, this street is a bit more high-density,” he said, describing the neighbourhood as a solidly middle-class area, one with lots of hard-working people living in it. “There are a lot of townhomes and semis on the street. If your house is one of the largest ones on the street, you’re likely to be on the lower average of similar size homes.”

Mr. Mayer-Harman started working in real estate 16 years ago, and has recently spent a lot of time knocking on doors as he runs for town council in Mono, Ont. According to him, the mood of many homeowners is dark and getting darker.

“People had unbridled confidence that market values were always going to go up. Now it’s interesting to see how vividly that confidence has been shaken,” he said. “I’ve never experienced so many people moving based on fear rather than opportunity. Scared for their kids, scared of AI; it’s unbelievable. There’s a level of anxiety that goes beyond rational.”

stories.title: Pierre Poilievre’s impossible Alberta balancing act
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses how vital a Tory voice could be in the referendum, and whether or not decided-Albertans could be swayed either way.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
In less than a week, Albertans will head to the polls to vote on a series of 10 referendum questions, one of which brings the province’s sovereignty into focus. For the past several months, support for separation has dwindled, as both former and current politicians continue to plead with Albertans to reconsider thoughts of separation.

Among the current names that have stayed out of the spotlight for the most part, however, is Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre. Other than a handful of speaking events, he hasn’t been as loud as other figures in making the case for federalism.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Duane Bratt, a political scientist with Mount Royal University to discuss how vital a Tory voice could be at this point, and whether or not decided-Albertans could be swayed either way.

stories.title: Cyberattack May have leaked student and parent information, Burnaby school district says
stories.summary: Ransomware attack it suffered on Sept. 21 affected school websites and portals, internal network services and phone lines
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Public school officials in Burnaby, B.C., say hackers May have obtained student and parental information in a recent cyberattack.

The Burnaby School District says in an online notice that the ransomware attack it suffered on Sept. 21 affected school websites and portals, internal network services and phone lines.

The notice says hackers copied and stole files that May have contained lists of parent, guardian and student names and contact information, as well as birthdates, grades and school names.

It says the hackers May also have obtained registration forms, kindergarten assessment notes and detailed lists of students on specialized learning plans.

The school district says the matter is in the hands of the RCMP and B.C.’s privacy commissioner, adding that its system security is being evaluated to prevent further breaches.

It says staff, students and their families have been offered registration with TransUnion’s fraud alert service and encourages them to be wary of any suspicious communications.

“We understand that incidents of this nature are concerning and we remain committed to keeping the Burnaby Schools community updated throughout this process, as the investigation proceeds and additional information becomes available,” the notice says.

stories.title: The right to know about Tumbler Ridge
stories.summary: Canadians are still waiting for answers, and officials in this country seem just fine with that
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
Justice officials recently released some important information about the Tumbler Ridge massacre, including allegations gathered by police about where the killer got their weapons. Unfortunately, this did not come from the officials in Canada.

The shooting left eight Canadians dead, including six children. Canadians should be kept fully up to date about the investigation – by the federal government, or the provincial government, or the RCMP. Instead, these details came from the United States. While it’s good that the information is now public, how it emerged is part of a troubling trend of secrecy in Canada.

This is a problem that goes beyond the police. Too often in Canada, the default assumption among officials is that the public has no right to know. For years The Globe and Mail has been exposing this kneejerk reticence in a project dubbed Secret Canada .

Because of the importance of law enforcement and the justice system – which are crucial both to public safety and to the public’s perception of safety – secrecy from them has a particularly corrosive effect.

In 2020, during the mass shooting that began in Portapique, Nova Scotia, the RCMP did not alert the public for 12 hours that the killer was disguised as a police officer. The Mass Casualty Commission, which examined the incident, found that “the RCMP public communication, sent by Twitter during the evening of April 18, seriously understated the threat presented by the perpetrator and the associated risks to the public.”

More recently, Mounties in Saskatchewan went beyond controlling what they reveal and tried to encourage the media to hold back as well. The police there warned journalists that the act of journalism – specifically, talking to witnesses and publishing what they say – can be dangerous. The police helpfully offered to advise media on how to do their jobs.

This tendency toward secrecy is not unique to the RCMP. In the wake of a synagogue shooting in the eastern Ontario community of Belleville, local police did not reveal that the gunman did not have a firearm licence.

It’s good that a source close to the investigation was willing to share that information with The Globe and Mail. Every extra detail about the shooting helps give Canadians a fuller understanding of what happened. But it’s bad that the information was, officially, deemed secret.

While reasonable people can disagree on which investigative details can be released without jeopardizing an investigation, two aspects of these recent shootings are worth remembering.

First, in both cases the killer is dead. While there could be prosecutions of accomplices, and the U.S. information about Tumbler Ridge was released in relation to a person in that country being charged, the central perpetrator is beyond the reach of justice. Their prosecution cannot be put into danger.

Second, the very fact that the Tumbler Ridge information was released by U.S. officials and not Canadian ones highlights that there are differing views on what must be kept secret. That two different institutions came to two different conclusions shows that the Canadian instinct towards secrecy is not inherently correct – or required.

According to a criminal complaint filed against an accused co-conspirator, Canadians now know a number of allegations related to the Tumbler Ridge shooting. The person charged in the U.S. reported that Jesse Van Rootselaar claimed to have stolen firearms from the family gun safe, convinced someone to buy ammunition for them and possessed a device that U.S. police believed would convert a rifle into a machine gun.

Why does this matter? At the most basic, it May reveal gaps in Canada’s gun-safety regime. But it also helps paint a picture of how an unspeakable tragedy was able to unfold.

There remain many unanswered questions in Tumbler Ridge. Were warning signs missed? Did people deliberately, or inadvertently, help make the crime happen? And beyond this particular tragedy, are there broader vulnerabilities that need to be addressed? Canadians don’t know the answers, and officials in this country seem just fine with that.

The principle of “need to know” is common in security and intelligence jobs. This limits information to those who require it. But officials must remember that the public is not party to any such policy. The public has a default right to know – that’s fundamental to a free and open society.

stories.title: Nan’s House (still) slated for demolition
stories.summary: There will be no last-minute reprieve by London city council for the heritage home at 100 Stanley St. that was unofficially dubbed “Nan’s House” after its last owner Nan Finlayson.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
There will be no last-minute reprieve by London city council for the heritage home at 100 Stanley St. that was unofficially dubbed “Nan’s House” after its last owner Nan Finlayson.

On Wednesday, Council considered the engineering department’s request to demolish the small yellow-brick heritage home to accommodate work to widen Wharncliffe Rd. under the CN Rail tracks just north of Horton Street.

The four-lane arterial road narrows to just three lanes beneath the aging rail overpass.

Finlayson sat and watched council debate the fate of her former home from the public gallery.

Starting in 2016, a public campaign fought to stop the city from taking Finlayson’s home, but she eventually she agreed to sell in 2020.

“I do believe that there is an opportunity to save this building. We don’t need to rush into making decisions right now,” Coun. Anna Hopkins told council colleagues.

A report to the Planning and Environment Committee had stated, “the proposed construction method for the CN Bridge has changed, reducing the original justification for the removal of the heritage house from the protected heritage property at 100 Stanley St.”

“The cost of preservation is going to far exceed the cost of demolition,” Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis countered, “The city is growing and we need to move a major transportation bottleneck out of the way to keep people going.”

Kelly Scherr, Deputy City Manager of Environment and Infrastructure told council that it is highly unlikely that alternative construction methods could prevent the house from being severely damaged during the replacement of the rail overpass and road widening.

“While we could spend a great deal of money doing so and exploring that, the only way to find out is to go to a tender process, see what is proposed by a contractor, and then make a decision,” Scherr told council. “At that point, we’re going to be substantially down the road with respect to investing costs into a design.”

A motion to refer the matter to a future meeting was defeated, and the demolition request was approved.

No firm date has been set for the demolition to begin.

Citing steep increases in cost estimates, council previously removed the widening project from the 2024-2027 multi-year budget.

Scherr said the demolition would ensure the project is “shovel-ready” in the event funding from senior levels of government is made available.

stories.title: Ken Sim and Pete Fry face off in Vancouver mayoral race
stories.summary: Kareem Allam, Rebecca Bligh and Colleen Hardwick are three other big-name candidates who reject the label of spoiler
stories.author: Marissa Birnie
stories.content:
Vancouver mayoral candidates Ken Sim and Pete Fry view each other as their main rival in the battle for City Hall.

But while recent polling suggests the mayoral race is indeed a faceoff between incumbent Sim and two-term Green Councillor Fry, there are three other big-name candidates who reject the label of spoiler.

Kareem Allam – Sim’s former chief of staff turned litigation adversary – is running with the Vancouver Liberals, which is not affiliated with the federal party.

“The pollsters don’t always get it right. Municipal government is also the hardest level to poll. It’s got its tricks and nuances, especially in an at-large system,” he said in an interview Tuesday.

The Vancouver race culminates Saturday, when municipalities across British Columbia go to the polls.

Interest in the Vancouver race appears high. The City of Vancouver says more than 103,000 people have voted in advance, up 60 per cent from roughly 65,000 voters over five advance days in 2022.

Sim, who is campaigning for a second term as mayor with the right-of-centre ABC Vancouver, said while he would be the first to admit he didn’t get everything right during his tenure, he believes he can lead the city in the right direction.

“We’ve gotten some pretty significant things done, but there’s way more work to do,” he said in an interview Wednesday.

Other candidates include Rebecca Bligh, a two-term councillor who helped get Sim elected with ABC Vancouver in 2022 and is now running with Vote Vancouver, and Team candidate Colleen Hardwick, a former councillor.

Allam, Hardwick and Bligh all rejected the notion their candidacies could split the centre or centre-right vote.

“The question is not left or right. The question is about who we are serving at city hall,” Hardwick said Tuesday.

Bligh said she was running to govern for Vancouver’s ignored middle class, and polling did not change how she campaigned.

“It’s anyone’s race,” she said in an interview Wednesday.

Fry, son of longtime Liberal MP Hedy Fry, has acknowledged benefiting from the narrowing of the progressive field, after the withdrawals of William Azaroff from OneCity Vancouver and Stephanie Allen for Cope Vancouver.

After ending his candidacy, Azaroff appeared at City Hall with Fry, who praised him for running a serious campaign that “raised real issues” such as housing, small business and affordability.

“I think folks are excited to be able to talk up a viable alternative to Ken Sim as the mayor of Vancouver and really reset,” Fry said in an interview Tuesday.

He added that Azaroff’s withdrawal was recognition that he was the person best suited to defeat Sim.

Bligh said she’s a progressive candidate with a centrist platform. Meanwhile, Allam said he believed he was taking votes from Sim and Fry equally.

The candidates’ platforms all emphasize quality-of-life issues, including affordability and public safety. Sim’s promises include a zero per cent property tax increase.

The election ballot also includes two plebiscite questions on public safety.

The non-binding questions ask voters if they’re in favour of the city “strengthening its laws to forbid open-air hard drug use in public spaces,” which is already illegal in B.C. The other asks if the city should ask the province to convert portions of the old St. Paul’s hospital into a “secure medical facility” with 100-plus involuntary care beds.

Hardwick called the questions a “populist election tactic,” while other critics said they aren’t realistic.

Sim said strengthening the city health bylaw – regulating conduct such as smoking in common areas – would allow officers to issue tickets or confiscate drugs without arrests. The involuntary care question, he said, is about asking the province to fulfill its accountability to people who pose a risk to their own safety or others.

Fry said he supports managing drug use in public spaces, but differs from Sim in believing that people should be diverted to supervised consumption sites or shelters.

His platform focuses on housing, transportation and the economy. “Folks should be able to have a good life in this city, he said.

Bligh said Sim’s property tax freezes protect wealthy landowners and undercut critical services. She said she would work with the federal government to leverage city-owned land and provide free transit for youth.

Hardwick said the key to livability in Vancouver is effective city planning. She said she wanted to repeal the city’s official development plan and re-establish neighbourhood planning offices

Allam said he wants to bring youth back to Vancouver by improving affordability through jobs and housing, and investing in parks and community centres.

He said his platform cuts across ideologies, and distanced himself from Sim, who filed a lawsuit in May 2025 alleging Allam falsely accused him of drinking and driving.

Sim faces his own defamation lawsuit from councillor Sean Orr, filed after falsely accusing Orr of distributing illegal drugs in comments to Chinese-speaking reporters.

Trials in both cases are far off.

For now, the focus is on the ballot box.

“I think people will be surprised at the results,” Allam said.

stories.title: ‘Being forced out of business’: Niagara wine industry sees mixed fortunes as harvest begins amid U.S.-Canada trade war
stories.summary: The harvest, one of the most important periods of the year for Ontario's wine sector, comes after months of escalating trade tensions.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By David Zura and Lucas Casaletto

Posted October 15, 2026 6:05 am.

As grape harvest season gets underway across Niagara wine country, growers and wineries are taking stock of a year marked by trade upheaval, shifting consumer habits and sharply different fortunes across the industry.

The harvest, one of the most important periods of the year for Ontario’s wine sector, comes after months of escalating trade tensions between Canada and the United States . The industry has weathered a series of tariffs, retaliatory measures and, most recently, a near-total U.S. import ban on Canadian wine , forcing producers to adapt to a dramatically altered marketplace.

For some, strong domestic demand has more than offset the loss of access to the American market.

“The last couple of years, we have seen demand for our product skyrocket,” said Kevin Watson, chair of the Grape Growers of Ontario and a grower in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

Watson said Canadian consumers have stepped up in a significant way, helping absorb supply that might otherwise have been destined for export markets.

“Three years ago, we had about 5,000 metric tons of grape surplus. In the last couple of years, we have been short on grape. It’s a seller’s market,” he said. “That’s how much the Canadian consumer has helped our industry.”

The shift comes as many Canadian shoppers have increasingly sought out domestic products following months of trade disputes and restrictions affecting wine sales between the two countries.

At Pelham Family Estate Winery, owner Paul Speck said both consumer support and a healthy crop are contributing to optimism about the sector’s future.

“The crop’s coming in nicely, so I’m very, very confident and bullish about the next couple of years,” he said.

Speck added that some international customers are also turning to Canadian wines amid changing global purchasing patterns.

“We’re hearing from our Belgium and Denmark customers that people are, instead of buying American wines, buying Canadian.”

While many growers and wineries are benefiting from the changing market dynamics, others are struggling to adapt.

For John Kocsis, who owns Atlantis Niagara Wines with his wife, the past several years have been marked by one challenge after another.

Kocsis, whose business specializes in tourism-focused experiences and premium products such as ice-wine, said sales had finally begun recovering in 2024 after pandemic-related setbacks. That momentum, he said, was derailed by tariffs and trade restrictions introduced in 2025.

Operating in Niagara since 2018, Kocsis said his business relies heavily on tourists visiting the region and purchasing wine to take home. With uncertainty surrounding cross-border sales and travel-related purchases, he fears the business May not survive.

“We’re basically being forced out of business.”

Kocsis said he sees little opportunity to pivot after years of investing heavily in the operation.

“I’ve got everything that we have tied up in this already. The damage that’s been done is just, for us, so embedded into the business now.”

Watson acknowledged that adapting business models in the wine sector can be difficult, particularly for smaller operators.

“It’s very difficult,” he said.

Despite those challenges, vineyards across Niagara remain focused on bringing in this year’s crop. Growers say harvest conditions have generally been favourable, with grapes continuing to come off the vine through the fall.

The 2026 harvest is expected to continue into November, offering the industry’s strongest performers hope for another successful vintage, even as some wineries face an increasingly uncertain future.

stories.title: Freeland's book reveals Chrétien's power play, crying in cabinet and Trudeau's lecture about using the word 'crazy'
stories.summary: Nearly two years after her shocking resignation that shook the halls of power in Ottawa, Freeland is telling her side of the story.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Ottawa — Nearly two years after her shocking resignation from cabinet that shook the halls of power in Ottawa, Chrystia Freeland is telling her side of the story of how she was about to get dumped by Justin Trudeau as finance minister.

Her new book “Unreliable Boyfriend” is in part a political memoir and in part a reflection of Donald Trump’s America. But it also contains so-far undisclosed details of why she chose to resign from Trudeau’s cabinet the day she was supposed to present the fall economic statement — thus precipitating Trudeau’s own departure weeks later.

Freeland writes that while she thinks history will be kind to Trudeau because he stood up to Trump and implemented social programs such as childcare, she thinks she probably left Trudeau’s cabinet “a year, or maybe two years, too late.”

Here are a few revelations from Freeland’s new book.

Freeland said while many were encouraging her to leave cabinet in her final six months in Trudeau’s cabinet, the pivotal moment was when she was drinking chardonnay with former prime minister Jean Chrétien at his Ottawa home in November 2024.

Chrétien, she writes, started the conservation with a “healthy dose of flattery” — calling her a “very good finance minister” and said she had been “unfailingly loyal” to Trudeau which was “admirable.”

But the tone of the conversation took a turn when Chrétien said Freeland had a responsibility not only to Trudeau, but to the Liberal party and to Canada.

“As long as you support him, he will stay on as PM. And he will lose the next election,” she recalls the former prime minister saying.

He added that Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre would become prime minister, the Liberal Party would be devastated, and she would be partly to blame for that.

“After the gentle caress of Mr. Chrétien’s earlier compliments, those words felt like a slap in the face, or, since we’re Canadian and winter was coming, like stepping out from a warm house into forty-below weather,” she wrote.

Freeland said she did not go back to her hotel room that evening planning to step down from Trudeau’s cabinet, but she did go to bed with “a new and horrible understanding” that she would be partly at fault if Trudeau led the Liberals into the next election.

Despite having served as one of Trudeau’s top ministers for nearly a decade, Freeland said she could count on the fingers of one hand the number of times she met with the prime minister alone. That was about to change in the days prior to her departure.

At the end of a meeting in his office on Dec. 2, 2024, she said that Trudeau called her aside for “a few rare private minutes” to tell her he wanted her to continue serving as his finance minister until the next election, which would happen in less than a year.

Six days later, ON Dec. 8, 2024, Trudeau invited her to his home at Rideau Cottage.

“It was probably the longest time I have spent alone with him,” she wrote.

Freeland said they drank glasses of water and Trudeau mused about his determination to lead the Liberals into the next election. He then made a surprising statement.

“At one point, apropos of nothing, he told me he believed that one day I would become prime minister, and that I would do a good job,” she wrote.

Later that week, Trudeau and his team removed $12 billion in spending cuts she had pushed for in the fall economic statement. The Globe and Mail also reported that Trudeau was again trying to convince Mark Carney to replace her as finance minister.

On Dec. 13, 2024, Trudeau and Freeland had their infamous one-on-one Zoom call.

Trudeau said she would be shuffled out of the finance portfolio the day after presenting the fall economic statement. When she asked who would replace her, Trudeau said with a “half-proud, half-defiant smile” that it would be Carney.

“The Zoom call with Trudeau had taught me that I simply couldn’t trust the PM — and that he had decided not to trust me. I had to leave.”

Trudeau took a lot of heat for correcting a woman who used the word “mankind” instead of “peoplekind” in a town hall meeting in 2018 — but it turns out cabinet ministers also had to mind their language in private, according to Freeland.

In one cabinet meeting, Trudeau apparently took issue with “a very progressive female colleague” casually referring to something as “crazy.”

“That earned her a long, harsh public scolding from Trudeau, who informed her that using ‘crazy’ as a derogatory adjective was insulting to people with mental health issues,” wrote Freeland.

Trudeau suggested they instead use the word “bananas” which was less offensive.

Freeland said that while she has always bristled at accusations of “wokeness” and “political correctness,” she said that “linguistic-purity tests” can also be off-putting to regular people who struggle with which words are okay or not to use.

“And they can give people the sense — and rightly so — that their leaders are more focused on the performance of virtue than on actually improving people’s lives.”

“Crying was routine at cabinet meetings. There were always boxes of Kleenex on hand, and really sad colleagues would sometimes get a hug from the PM,” Freeland wrote.

Yet what troubled her the most about the crying and the lectures “was that it sometimes went along with what seemed like bullying,” she added.

Freeland did not go into detail about the alleged bullying but said one of Trudeau’s “favourite homilies” to cabinet and caucus was talking about the necessity of eating “shit sandwiches” from time to time.

He would also instruct his ministers to stay on message until they “wanted to vomit a little bit in our mouth.”

“By the time he stepped down, PM Trudeau had been so thoroughly caricatured as a woke poser that it was easy to forget that one of the things that had captivated Canadians when he first burst onto the scene was his macho charisma,” she wrote.

Freeland referred to one of his early breakthrough moments as the charity boxing match against Senator Patrick Brazeau, a member of the Algonquin Nation.

In a controversial interview with the Rolling Stone, Trudeau boasted about his wager with Brazeau that the loser of the fight would be required to have his hair cut in the lobby of the House of Commons.

Brazeau apparently resisted as long hair carries deep spiritual significance in many First Nations cultures. Trudeau said that is why he proposed that bet. “When a warrior cuts his hair, it’s a sign of shame, so it’s very apropos,” he told the magazine.

In one cabinet meeting, Trudeau apparently took issue with “a very progressive female colleague” casually referring to something as “crazy.”
“That earned her a long, harsh public scolding from Trudeau, who informed her that using ‘crazy’ as a derogatory adjective was insulting to people with mental health issues,” wrote Freeland.
Trudeau suggested they instead use the word “bananas” which was less offensive.

Freeland said that while she has always bristled at accusations of “wokeness” and “political correctness,” she said that “linguistic-purity tests” can also be off-putting to regular people who struggle with which words are okay or not to use.
“And they can give people the sense — and rightly so — that their leaders are more focused on the performance of virtue than on actually improving people’s lives.”
There was some crying in cabinet — and sometimes some bullying too
“Crying was routine at cabinet meetings. There were always boxes of Kleenex on hand, and really sad colleagues would sometimes get a hug from the PM,” Freeland wrote.
Yet what troubled her the most about the crying and the lectures “was that it sometimes went along with what seemed like bullying,” she added.

Freeland did not go into detail about the alleged bullying but said one of Trudeau’s “favourite homilies” to cabinet and caucus was talking about the necessity of eating “shit sandwiches” from time to time.

content_blocks.text: He would also instruct his ministers to stay on message until they “wanted to vomit a little bit in our mouth.”

“By the time he stepped down, PM Trudeau had been so thoroughly caricatured as a woke poser that it was easy to forget that one of the things that had captivated Canadians when he first burst onto the scene was his macho charisma,” she wrote.
Freeland referred to one of his early breakthrough moments as the charity boxing match against Senator Patrick Brazeau, a member of the Algonquin Nation.

In a controversial interview with the Rolling Stone, Trudeau boasted about his wager with Brazeau that the loser of the fight would be required to have his hair cut in the lobby of the House of Commons.

Brazeau apparently resisted as long hair carries deep spiritual significance in many First Nations cultures. Trudeau said that is why he proposed that bet. “When a warrior cuts his hair, it’s a sign of shame, so it’s very apropos,” he told the magazine.

stories.title: Kenora residents applaud ‘fantastic’ move to permanent daylight time
stories.summary: The provincial government announced Tuesday that northwestern Ontario communities west of the 90th meridian would stop the twice-annual clock changes.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Whether it’s watching NHL games, appointment scheduling or just less confusion, some residents of Kenora, Ont. say permanent daylight saving time is a “fantastic” move.

Scott Green, owner and operator of Lake of the Woods Marina and Service Centre, said Wednesday he loves that the community will stick to the same time zone as Manitoba going forward.

“I love it as long as we’re still matching with Winnipeg and Manitoba,” he said in an interview with Global News.

Green added his marina also has a restaurant and bar that hosts Winnipeg Jets watch parties during the season. He said with the permanent change, watching the game “just times out better.” He added it will also make it easier if travelling to Winnipeg for a Jets game.

The Ontario government announced Tuesday that northwestern Ontario communities west of the 90th meridian would stop the twice-annual clock changes and stay on daylight time year-round.

Kenora, along with communities like Dryden, Sioux Lookout and Pickle Lake, currently observe Central daylight time, the same time zone observed by Manitoba.

That means come Nov. 1, it will be the same time in Manitoba and all of Ontario. But when the clocks tick forward an hour in March for much of Ontario, people in the province’s northwest and Manitoba won’t have to adjust their time.

Tuesday’s announcement from the Ontario government came after what MPP for Kenora-Rainy River Greg Rickford says was “unanimous consensus” across the region.

“Through the collective efforts of communities and First Nations across the northwest, we’ve led a process to build consensus the right way, with detailed and nuanced considerations,” said Rickford in a news release on Tuesday.

Several communities conducted surveys from residents to see if there was support for a change.

In Kenora, about 6,000 of its approximately 16,000 residents responded to the survey and Mayor Andrew Poirier told Global News 93 per cent supported keeping daylight time.

“So we listened to the people of Kenora and we stand by what we did as a council to pass a resolution that we would look at aligning ourselves with Manitoba, and so did lots of our neighbouring communities, which was very important in this whole process,” Poirier said Wednesday.

The mayor said though in Ontario, Kenora is “much more linked” to Winnipeg or Manitoba.

He said whether during much of summer or winter, travel between the Ontario and Manitoba communities is “like the 401” highway that runs through Toronto.

“That’s how much economic activity, tourism, visiting back and forth occurs between the two jurisdictions,” Poirier said.

But it’s not just economic activity, it’s also logistical aspects like medical appointments or tourist bookings.

“So when somebody makes an appointment for a boat taxi or a tour and we are on the same page for a time frame (or) often Zoom meetings if people are calling out of Toronto you have to definitely make sure that you’re on the same time,” said Green. “So this will really make things efficient and a lot easier for bookings and communications.”

Northwestern Ontario is not the only region to observe a different timezone than the majority of the province it is in.

The Kootenay Region in B.C. is on Mountain Time, Nunavik and Lower North Shore in Quebec are on Atlantic Time and parts of Labrador are also on Atlantic Time unlike the rest of Newfoundland and southeastern Labrador.

Golden, B.C., Coun. Wesley Routley said his community last month originally planned to shift to Mountain standard time permanently on Nov. 1, but after hearing from hundreds of residents, council reversed course.

He said people felt they wanted to be aligned with other communities like the Regional District of East Kootenay to the south and other communities on Mountain daylight time.

He added a large share of visitors to Golden are from Alberta, so it could limit confusion for people visiting the community.

British Columbia, Alberta and Manitoba have each announced they will remain on daylight time starting Nov. 1, with Saskatchewan having observed central standard time year-round. The remaining provinces have said in recent months no changes are expected though discussions and analyses are ongoing.
