stories.title: Five takeaways from the B.C. leaders’ debate
stories.summary: Leaders of B.C.’s three main parties clashed over health care, the province’s finances and Dripa in only televised debate ahead of the Oct. 24 election
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
The leaders of British Columbia’s three main political parties squared up on Wednesday in the only televised debate leading up to the Oct. 24 provincial election.

NDP Leader David Eby , interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson and Green Leader Emily Lowan clashed over affordability, health care, the province’s finances and Indigenous rights for nearly two hours in a debate that grew testy at times. Shachi Kurl, president of the Angus Reid Institute, moderated.

The polls show the Conservatives narrowly continuing to lead the NDP, with the Greens in distant third.

Here are five takeaways from the leaders’ debate.

Mr. Eby opened the debate by laying out his rationale for calling a snap election two years ahead of schedule, saying he needed a strong mandate to meet the “existential moment” the province finds itself in.

“When you have a one-seat majority, after you appoint a speaker, it’s tough,” Mr. Eby said. “Every vote potentially could bring down the government.”

Mr. Doerkson, asked why voters should trust a leader who was an “unknown entity in B.C. politics one month ago,” deflected. He accused Mr. Eby of calling the snap election because he saw an opportunity for himself and said he instead sees an opportunity for British Columbians.

Ms. Lowan described Mr. Eby’s NDP as a party of broken promises and recycled ideas, and the official opposition as “opaque” on what it would cut to fund its various promises. Ms. Lowan, 26, noted she is roughly half the age of elected representatives in the legislature and said her youth is an asset in today’s politics, which have seen a “huge generational rift.”

Mr. Eby acknowledged a need to improve health care services, including the need to hire more medical professionals and reduce wait times. A re-elected NDP government would increase taxes on income of more than $190,000 which would go to fund health care services, he said.

Mr. Doerkson called Mr. Eby’s tax proposal an “attack on doctors.” Mr. Eby countered by saying that B.C. has the second-lowest tax rate in Canada on incomes of $250,000, and that his party is being “up front with British Columbians” about how it plans to pay for its promises.

The interim Conservative leader said his party would fully fund health care, never cutting from the front lines, but has yet to fully explain how it would do so while honouring other promises, including to freeze income taxes across the board. Mr. Doerkson said a Conservative government would cut red tape and bureaucracy within health care and “supercharge the economy.”

Ms. Lowan said her party would tax the ultra wealthy , with funds going to public services.

Mr. Eby acknowledged that the province has faced a couple of challenging court decisions related to the province’s Indigenous rights legislation but said the legislation has also enabled partnerships with Indigenous people that have paved the way for major projects, including LNG Canada Phase 2.

The Cowichan Tribes decision, which was brought under Section 35 of the Constitution Act, has further added to debate over how Aboriginal title claims intersect with private property rights and B.C.’s laws, including Dripa, the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act. Mr. Eby said the NDP is appealing certain court decisions to protect private property rights and ensure that major projects are not mired in litigation.

Mr. Doerkson reiterated that a Conservative government would repeal Dripa.

“There has to be a better path forward, and that is to respect relations and certain partnerships with First Nations in this province,” he said. “And I’m absolutely committed to that.”

Ms. Lowan accused Mr. Eby’s party of sowing uncertainty with his government’s handling of the issue, and Mr. Doerkson’s of “constantly pushing misinformation and blatant fearmongering.”

A Green government would follow the advice of First Nations leaders who have been unequivocal in saying that B.C. must do the work of implementing the legislation, she said.

Some of the testiest moments of the debate came as the leaders attacked controversial figures in each other’s caucuses. Mr. Doerkson was asked about Conservative members with extreme views, including a candidate whom the leader dropped last week after racist social media posts surfaced, and others who remain in the party.

“There there have been challenges on both sides of our chamber, and there have been many challenges online,” Mr. Doerkson said. “I will lead with an absolute commitment to respect and dignity going forth. I’ll expect it from my caucus.”

Mr. Doerkson then turned the question on Mr. Eby, asking about former cabinet minister Selina Robinson, who left the NDP in 2024 , citing antisemitism in the caucus.

The debate also heard video messages from CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko and OneBC Leader Dallas Brodie. Ms. Sturko described her party as “socially progressive, environmentally pragmatic and fiscally responsible,” saying it would ensure a strong centrist voice in Victoria.

Ms. Brodie vowed to “fight against these land back giveaways that are being done by the current government” and “stop the greed and corruption of the reconciliation industry.”

stories.title: Key quotes from the British Columbia leaders' debate ahead of Oct. 24 election
stories.summary: Vancouver - Three of British Columbia's provincial party leaders debated Wednesday on issues such as health care, seniors housing, public safety, Indigenous relations, housing and government financing.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Three of British Columbia’s provincial party leaders debated Wednesday on issues such as health care, seniors housing, public safety, Indigenous relations, housing and government financing.

Here are some key quotes from Wednesday’s televised debate:

NDP Leader David Eby, when asked why he called an election two years early:

“This was not a government that was able to deliver the big swings that you and your family need government to be taking for you. We need a government with representatives from every part of the province that are focused on your priorities, not on culture wars, not on repealing the human rights code, but on the real issues that matter to you and your family.”

Eby to Interim B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson on online posts about Islam by his campaign director, Katy Merrifield:

“Her Twitter feed at points reads like the worst corners of the dark web, and you stand here today, in the face of a call from national Muslim organizations and say, ‘hey, we need to feel safe in this province.’ And she’s gonna continue as your campaign director.”

Doerkson, ON Merrifield’s posts:

“I will always stand up against hate. I want to just refer to the woman that you’re referring to just for a moment, because this is a woman who survived sexual violence and she acted out in a moment of trauma. She removed the post and from there, I think she has been very apologetic.”

Green Party Leader Emily Lowan:

“If the Greens held the balance of power, it would be my top priority to advocate for a better voting system. A voting system where we’re not caught between lesser evils, where we are choosing between broken promises or service cuts. And I think we can find that system in proportional representation.”

Lowan, after an exchange between Eby and Doerkson on hateful comments by candidates:

“I have to say this feels like déjà vu of the 2024 race. Our politics haven’t advanced. We have a Conservative party that is yet again being divided, ripped up from the inside with candidates making abhorrent comments and an interim leader. And we see the same failing status quo, a managed decline under David Eby.”

Doerkson, ON Eby’s record:

“The challenge that I think British Columbians have is that you continue to refer to a decade ago. The reality is Mr. Eby you’ve been running this province for a decade and nothing is better than it was years ago.”

Doerkson, ON when he will provide his costed election platform:

“I do not want to introduce a platform that I break promises on.”

Eby, when asked if he could work with the B.C. Conservatives in order to prevent another election:

“I struggle to know what areas we have in common. I believe in being honest with the voters about how we’re going to pay for things, what we’re gonna pay for. When we make difficult decisions, look, I’m not perfect, but I will always act in the best interests of British Columbians, and that’s my commitment to you and your family. ”

Lowan on Eby’s LNG “gamble.”

“But you’re betting everything on fracked gas projects that are owned by American corporations, backed by equity firms and (U.S. President Donald) Trump’s inner circle. So, how can we expect British Columbians to believe you? And how dare you gamble our economy on LNG when we are looking at every forecast that B.C.‘s projects could be sold at a loss.”

CentreBC leader Elenore Sturko, in video remarks:

“I’m not asking British Columbians to pretend that CentreBC will form government. I’m asking them a different question. Who will hold the next government accountable? CentreBC is a socially progressive, environmentally pragmatic, and fiscally responsible party. Divisiveness and extremes on the left and on the right aren’t helping British Columbian.”

OneBC leader Dallas Brodie, in video remarks:

“We will push for a 25 per cent income tax cut for both individuals and corporations, and we will push a two per cent cut in the PST. As well, we will fight against these land back giveaways that are being done by the current government. We will read the treaties and let you know what is going on. We will stop the greed and corruption of the reconciliation industry in British Columbia, and put B.C. back in the hands of British Columbians.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Canada Child Benefit payments go out next week
stories.summary: Oct. 20. Here’s who qualifies, how much families can receive and when the remaining 2026 payments are scheduled.
stories.author: Adshayah Sathiaseelan; Matthew Daldalian
stories.content:
The next Canada Child Benefit (CCB) payments are set to go out next week on Oct. 20.

The tax-free monthly payment from the Canada Revenue Agency helps millions of families across the country with the cost of raising kids. Here’s what you need to know about the benefit, including who qualifies, how much you could receive and when payments are issued.

To be eligible for the Canada Child Benefit, you need to live with a child under 18 and be primarily responsible for their care and upbringing, including supervising their daily activities, and attending to their health and child care needs.

You must also be a resident of Canada for income tax purposes. You or your spouse or common-law partner also needs to be a Canadian citizen, permanent resident, protected person, eligible temporary resident or registered under the Indian Act.

Temporary residents generally must have lived in Canada for the previous 18 months and hold a valid permit in the 19th month.

For parents who share custody, each typically receives 50 per cent of what they would receive with full custody, calculated based on their respective family incomes.

To estimate your amount, use the child and family benefit calculator . Your payment depends on your adjusted family net income from your previous year’s tax return, the number of children in your care and their ages. Payments are recalculated every July.

For payments from July 2026 through June 2027, the CRA uses adjusted family net income reported for 2025. Benefit amounts are recalculated each July.

Families with adjusted net income below $38,237 receive the maximum benefit for each eligible child. Payments gradually decrease as income rises, with further reductions for families earning more than $82,847.

The CCB increased in July, with maximum annual payments rising by $160 for children under six and $135 for children aged 6 to 17.

If your child is eligible for the disability tax credit, you May also be eligible for the child disability benefit. For the July 2026 to June 2027 period, eligible families can receive up to an additional $3,480 per year or $290 per month for each child. The CRA automatically calculates this payment and adds it to the CCB payment.

You should apply for the CCB as soon as you or your spouse or common-law partner meet the eligibility criteria and any of the following occurs: your child is born, a child begins to live with you or returns to live with you, you gain custody or a child or your shared custody arrangement changes.

New parents in most provinces and territories, including Ontario, can apply for the CCB when registering their newborn’s birth using the Automated Benefits Application. You can also apply online through your CRA account or by mail using Form RC66, Canada Child Benefits Application.

Applicants using a CRA account or applying by mail May also have to provide proof of the child’s birth if the CRA has never previously paid benefits for that child.

To continue receiving the CCB, you and your spouse or common-law partner, if applicable, must file a tax return every year, even if one or both of you had no income.

CCB payments can be deposited directly into a bank account or sent by cheque.

The CRA recommends direct deposit as the fastest way to receive benefit payments. People who already receive CRA payments by direct deposit will generally receive the CCB the same way. If a direct deposit cannot be completed, the CRA says it will mail a cheque instead.

Recipients can check their upcoming payment date, payment amount and payment status through their CRA account.

If your total CCB entitlement for the year is less than $240, the CRA does not issue monthly payments. Instead, the amount is paid as one lump sum in July.

CCB payments are generally issued once a month.

The next payment is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 20. The remaining 2026 payments are scheduled for Nov. 20 and Dec. 11.

While payments often fall on the 20th of the month, dates can shift when the usual payment date falls on a weekend or holiday. In 2026, for example, the June and September payments were issued early, while the December payment is scheduled for Dec. 11.

If a payment does not arrive on the scheduled date, the CRA advises recipients to wait five working days before contacting the agency.

stories.title: Ontario signs contract to import electricity from U.S.
stories.summary: The contract, to import oil- and gas-fired electricity, comes after Doug Ford threatened to cut Ontario-generated power to the States.
stories.author: Marco Chown Oved
stories.content:
Only weeks after Premier Doug Ford threatened to cut off electricity exports to the United States as retaliation in the ongoing trade war , Ontario has signed a contract to import electricity from New York state through the winter.

The 600-megawatt contract starting Nov. 1 will provide power to compensate for “facility maintenance,” the Independent Electricity System Operator said in its announcement of the deal, without being more specific.

The Pickering nuclear plant was shut down in September for a multi-year refurbishment and this contract will partially replace its emissions-free electricity with carbon-intensive power from oil- and gas-fired plants.

There was no price mentioned in the announcement.

“This deal just increases our dependency on Donald Trump’s America to keep our lights on,” said Jack Gibbons, chair of the Ontario Clean Air Alliance and a former Toronto Hydro commissioner. “It’s absolutely the wrong way to go because it means more pollution, higher electricity bills and it means that we’re more vulnerable to attack.”

In March 2025, Ford imposed a 25 per cent tax on power exports to the U.S. before backtracking and lifting them the next day . In August of this year, he threatened to reimpose the surcharges , saying “everything is on the table.”

Just over a month later, the province’s power grid operator, the IESO, announced a contract with Alpha Generation, a company that runs fossil-fuel power plants in the U.S. northeast and California, including the Oswego oil-fired generator north of Syracuse, N.Y.

Energy Minister Stephen Lecce’s office referred the Star to the IESO for comment as decisions around energy supply and import contracts are made without input from the ministry.

“Ontario’s electricity system remains reliable, and securing additional short-term capacity provides greater flexibility,” wrote IESO spokesperson Michael Dodsworth. “This also provides additional safeguards through the winter months, as the IESO prepares for higher winter peak demand.”

Last year, U.S. power imports made up only one per cent of electricity demand and the province exported nearly seven times more, Dodsworth said.

Earlier this year, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the Trump Administration, which has imposed tariffs on key Canadian industries like auto manufacturing and steelmaking, wants to collaborate on energy and critical minerals. His office did not respond to a request for comment.

Ontario previously signed a much smaller deal with Oswego for the winter of 2024-25, providing one-quarter 1/4 of power secured by the current contract. The province also has an existing contract with Quebec that imports and exports up to 600 megawatts of power when either province needs it.

Alpha Generation is partly owned by the Canadian Pension Plan, which announced a $1.4-billion investment in the company last year.

Premier Doug Ford has quietly changed the rule that used to mean Ontario ratepayers would only start paying for new generation once it was completed.

“In a weird twist, not only are Ontarians paying an American fuel oil plant to pollute, that same money is being used to generate returns for the CPP,” said Patrick DeRochie, senior manager of Shift Action for Pension Wealth and Planet Health, a non-profit that works to protect pensions and the climate.

Energy analysts say this new deal represents a departure from the past 18 years when Ontario did not import much power from the U.S. Prior to 2008, Ontario imported significant amounts of electricity, far more than this contract represents.

Energy analysts say this new deal represents a departure from the past when Ontario could reliably generate its own power and only needed to import and export small amounts during short periods.

“The era of long-term capacity surpluses in Ontario is officially over,” wrote Brendan Callery and Brady Yauch, analysts with Power Advisory, in a report on Ontario’s power procurement. This import contract “is the latest sign of an increasingly tight supply/demand balance.”

In addition to the Pickering nuclear plant going offline, the Darlington reactors, which completed their own years-long refurbishment in February, are being taken back offline for additional maintenance next spring, creating more power shortfalls, they wrote.

Ontario was unable to procure all the electricity it wanted for this winter in its most recent capacity auction, which drove up the wholesale price paid to generators to $725 per megawatt per business day, which is the “the highest ever capacity price in Ontario,” the Power Advisory analysts wrote.

Mike Marcolongo, associate director of Environmental Defence, says the import contract is likely the result of a hard lesson learned last winter: that Ontario’s gas plants can’t be relied upon during big winter storms.

“In January 2026’s winter storm Fern, 2,400 megawatts of natural gas went offline. That’s not just one or two, it’s multiple gas plants across the province that couldn’t produce power because the gas was routed away from Canada and to the U.S,” he said.

In a public presentation from last spring, the IESO said multiple gas plants “had issues securing gas,” during last winter’s coldest months. Fortunately, Ontario’s 800 megawatts of battery storage “performed really well,” allowing the province to avoid blackouts.

Gibbons says Ontario’s push to increase nuclear generation by building new reactors and repairing old ones has been carried out at the expense of cheaper options like renewables and battery storage and has left the province short on power.

“Six hundred megawatts is a substantial amount of power. It’s larger than one of the Pickering nuclear station’s reactors,” he said. “And we need it to keep the lights on this winter.”

“This problem has arisen because we’re too dependent on high-cost and slow-to-deploy nuclear power and we’re not investing enough in energy efficiency and load shifting and battery storage.”

The Ford government has introduced a suite of energy efficiency programs that offer rebates for home renovations, payments to households for the ability to remotely turn down air conditioning and to industry for curbing demand during peak periods. The Energy Ministry says these programs collectively represent the biggest investment in energy efficiency in the country, and are projected to save ratepayers $12.2 billion over the next 24 years.

A national poll conducted for the Canadian Renewable Energy Association found affordability was Canadians’ top priority for new generation, with solar power the most popular choice, ahead of hydro, nuclear, wind and natural gas.

“The most affordable energy in the world right now is renewables,” said Vittoria Bellissimo, president and CEO of CanREA. “Ontario should be building as much solar, wind and storage as possible.”

The Ford government, which was elected on a platform overtly hostile to renewable energy, and spent $231 million to cancel more than 700 renewable projects. In recent years, faced with increasing demand for power, the government has held several rounds of procurements, contracting new solar and wind projects at significantly lower prices than the ones that were cancelled and making the province the Canadian leader in battery storage .

“Ontario is still moving forward with wind, solar and storage,” Bellissimo said. “It would serve customers better if it did more.”

The Ford government, which was elected on a platform overtly hostile to renewable energy, and spent $231 million to cancel more than 700 renewable projects. In recent years, faced with increasing demand for power, the government has held several rounds of procurements, contracting new solar and wind projects at significantly lower prices than the ones that were cancelled and making the province the Canadian leader in battery storage .
“Ontario is still moving forward with wind, solar and storage,” Bellissimo said. “It would serve customers better if it did more.”

stories.title: Ryan Wedding was just a happy-go-lucky kid. How did he become ‘a modern-day Pablo Escobar’?
stories.summary: Read on for the origin story of alleged drug kingpin Ryan Wedding. And scroll down to access The Most Wanted Olympian, a new podcast series about his alleged drug network
stories.author: Calvi Leon
stories.content:
The tall blond-haired rich kid lived in an upscale pocket of this northwestern Ontario city, ON a sprawling lot with a backyard tennis court. He was gifted at school and, as the first-born in a family of skiers, spent much time at his grandparents’ ski hill, learning what it takes to become a successful athlete.

If this were the origin story of a Canadian Olympic hero, this bucolic starting point on Whitegates Drive would make sense. But Ryan Wedding isn’t famous because he ultimately did compete in the 2002 Olympics .

He’s famous because he was allegedly one of Canada’s most prolific — and murderous — criminals. The hulking ex-athlete is accused of running a billion-dollar cocaine empire for Mexican cartels, and arranging to kill anyone who stood in his way, even innocents . The man some U.S. officials have labelled a “modern-day Pablo Escobar .”

This is the origin story of that guy — an alleged larger-than-life criminal who, until his arrest , was considered the Fbi’s most wanted fugitive and a top public safety threat to Canada.

As the 44-year-old sits in a California jail awaiting trial for his alleged crimes, the Star visited his hometown and interviewed more than half a dozen childhood friends, neighbours and old teammates to get some answers. What emerged is the clearest picture yet of his life before he became a narco.

How did a small town Canadian boy allegedly become a narco kingpin? In a new podcast from the Toronto Star and CBC, host Michelle Shephard and journalist Calvi Leon trace Ryan Wedding’s descent into a violent criminal underworld. Listen to all the episodes .

On its own, it’s a portrait of an intelligent, happy-go-lucky kid who was practically destined for the Olympics since birth. There were no signs of trouble early on; certainly nothing to suggest the little boy who tinkered with toy cars and excelled at draftsmanship would grow into the violent criminal authorities describe . But knowing the logistical skills, confidence and grit required to build a drug operation of massive scale and sophistication, the precursors to his alleged success were all there.

Wedding was born in Thunder Bay in September 1981, just months after the death of Terry Fox. Fox was forced to end his historic run across Canada just outside the city. His cancer had spread aggressively to his lungs, causing chest pain and compromising his ability to breathe.

Back then, Thunder Bay was still a bustling industrial hub, pumping out pulp and paper and grain across Canada and into global markets. A large chunk of the population worked jobs that supported these sectors: at the mills, in transportation and railway manufacturing, or at the grain elevators and docks along the waterfront.

Wedding’s dad, Rene, didn’t work in the mills, but he did work in industry. A mechanical engineer — the kind of professional who worked on big projects, for big businesses, travelling all over the world.

The eldest of three and the only son, Wedding grew up in a red brick bungalow with a U-shaped driveway, in a sought-after neighbourhood on the southwestern edge of the city. The semirural pocket is full of mid-to-high-end homes. It’s not Thunder Bay’s Bridle Path, but Whitegates is comfortable — large homes on deep lots studded with towering pine trees.

Today, the exterior of Wedding’s childhood house looks much the same as it would have in the 1980s, save for the Weddings’ tennis court, with big floodlights his parents installed after they bought the property. It’s long been replaced by a backyard pool.

Rene and Karen Wedding, a registered nurse, married in 1977. Both were longtime skiers in a city where it was almost unusual not to be a part of the local hockey culture. Thunder Bay is famous for churning out elite hockey players — from modern-day stars like the Staal brothers to Hall of Famers like Alex Delvecchio with the Detroit Red Wings — but Wedding was not going to be one of them.

Rene was a varsity skier at the University of Toronto, where he earned his engineering degree, while Karen hailed from a family of skiers who were fixtures in the local skiing community.

Her parents, Laurence “Larry” and Marlyn Spiess, ran the Mount Baldy ski club north of town. They bought it in the late 1960s and kept it running for decades before their son, Craig Spiess, took over the business. (Karen also had shares in the ski hill.)

Craig started as a local instructor and after 12 seasons working at a prominent ski instruction and training program in New Zealand, he returned to Canada to coach some of Ontario’s best alpine racers. Eventually, he became a coach with the national alpine ski team. Throughout the late ‘80s and into the ‘90s, Wedding would’ve watched his uncle train some of the best female athletes in the sport, including 1992 Olympic gold medallist Kerrin Lee-Gartner. To date, she remains the only Canadian to win the downhill ski event.

Larry would start his day with a cup of coffee and a crossword, then jet off to the ski club with four sets of keys to ensure the lights were on and the hills were groomed. It was “his personal paradise,” his family wrote in an obituary. Marlyn was the friendly face greeting patrons at the ticket office and gear shop.

By all accounts, the two adored their five grandchildren. Larry spoiled Wedding, his first grandson, teaching him how to drive before his feet could reach the pedals, and after Wedding’s sister was born, he painted the club purple and pink because those were her favourite colours.

Rene and Karen had Wedding on skis and in a training harness by the age of two. By age nine, he could carve down the slopes on just one ski, as if it was a snowboard.

Childhood friend Rudi Phillion remembers that well. The few times they hit the slopes together, Wedding would drop a ski to challenge himself.

“That way, he and I would go at more or less the same speed,” he said.

Mount Baldy is still a mom-and-pop ski club, but with new owners. The Kardas brothers — the sons of two-time Olympic ski jumper and national coach Slavomir Kardas — bought it in 2016. The trio, Jason, Kristoff and Daniel, were all once on the national ski jumping team.

When the Star visited on a recent Saturday, Daniel and a team of workers were making improvements to the roof of the chalet. Aside from necessary upgrades and renovations, he said the ski club is largely the same as when Wedding was a kid.

It’s no Whistler or Chamonix; it’s far more modest than Blue Mountain — but Mount Baldy is more than enough to foster a love of the sport.

The hill features 14 runs for all skill levels and a terrain park with rails and jumps. At the base, patrons are hit with a cosy cabin smell as soon as they step into the chalet. It’s three levels with large windows facing the slopes, a stone fireplace and an interior finished with the classic tongue and groove wood. The walls are adorned with old racing bibs, photographs and vintage signage.

At the canteen and bar, patrons can grab craft beer and comfort food, including pizza and what Daniel describes as world-class poutine. Cheese curds from the Thunder Oak Cheese Farm. Potatoes from Breukelman’s Potato Farm. “We try to use everything local.”

At the top of the hill, a lookout point offers expansive views of Lake Superior and the famous Sleeping Giant, a land formation resembling a giant lying on its back in the water. Nearby, ON a different run, a plaque bearing the name of Wedding’s grandfather, Larry Spiess, is mounted into the ground.

“Larry taught us that it is not what you have in life but what you do that counts,” it reads, detailing his legacy of hard work. “This is Larry’s spot.”

Ryan Wedding, the man

Those who spoke to the Star in Thunder Bay struggle to comprehend the tall, baby-faced Wedding they once knew is the same hulking, aggressive person accused of leading an international drug ring aligned with the Sinaloa Cartel.

For his alleged victims, however, that concept is all they know.

Authorities claimed Wedding ran a drug ring that moved more than a billion dollars worth of cocaine into Canada each year from Mexico and orchestrated multiple murders.

It’s hard not to believe his love of fast things came from his dad, Rene.

In 2025, Mexican authorities confiscated Wedding’s rare collection of 62 racing motorcycles, including many MotoGP bikes once belonging to famous riders like Valentino Rossi and Jorge Lorenzo.

As a kid, friends say, he was obsessed with his father’s Kawasaki Ninja. He’d boast about it to peers. “He thought it was the coolest,” recalled childhood friend Neil MacEachern.

Rene was a confident, earnest man who spoke fluent German and worked long hours for an engineering company before starting his own firm the year after Wedding was born. He played various sports, could ski barefoot on the lakes, according to one neighbour, and had a taste for fast, high-end motor vehicles, such as the Corvette he drove.

The Weddings had more money than most in this lunch-bucket town, but to MacEachern’s memory, his old friend never came across as flashy or spoiled. Confident, sure, but not showy, he said.

His family’s wealth only came through in the occasional brag about his dad’s stuff or when he had friends over to play the latest video games or use high-tech gadgets, such as the LaserDisc player in their basement recreation room.

At Mother Theresa elementary school, Wedding was in French immersion and, in Grade 4, he joined a small cohort of students in the gifted program. Among the others were Phillion, MacEachern and his twin sister. Once a week, they would be bused to another school across town.

Phillion and MacEachern recalled science and art projects, geography games, creative-thinking prompts such as listing as many uses for a pencil as possible, and short presentations on topics they’d researched.

Wedding was uninhibited as a kid — not particularly warm, but not mean-spirited or bombastic, MacEachern said. “He had a forceful presence, a strong presence, but he wasn’t a bully.”

The fact his dad was an engineer was something MacEachern didn’t know. Looking back, it made perfect sense, he said. “Ryan was a natural draftsman.”

Sometimes in class, he’d be drawing mechanical things, like cars or bikes, rather than paying attention to the teacher. Like MacEachern, Wedding was also interested in assembling plastic model kits. The boys spent hours at a time piecing together a German Second World War submarine that his parents bought for him.

With human figures, however, his skills wavered. One day, MacEachern recalled, Wedding had nudged him to look over at a sketch — a woman fellating a man.

MacEachern was caught off guard. While it wasn’t the best quality, the illustration was clear enough.

How a nine-year-old would’ve learned about fellatio in the early ‘90s, MacEachern has no clue. Perhaps a pornographic magazine or satellite TV.

A new province and newfound passion

In 1991, during the Grade 4 school year, Wedding and his family moved to Coquitlam, B.C., then a rapidly growing suburb east of Vancouver, for Rene’s work. The family’s youngest child, and second daughter, was born soon after.

MacEachern and Phillion were sad to see their friend go. They stayed in touch over the next few years and each visited him in B.C. and Wedding came back to Thunder Bay a handful of times, too.

“Dear Rudi,” he wrote in a letter dated July 15, 1991. “I miss you very much,” he said, pivoting to the news about his new baby sister. “She was nine pounds and 52 cm when she was born.”

He told his friend he wasn’t yet in his new school’s gifted program because he came too late in the school year.

In another letter, Wedding said he tried his hand at football. He wasn’t great but was getting better, he said. “I’ve made 20 touchdowns since school started.”

At home, he now had a room for “my Lego, model building and my train,” he told Phillion, and had recently gone biking with his dad on the logging roads nearby.

When you look down the side of the mountain, “all you see is clear cut almost strait down,” he said, misspelling a few words. The view “makes M. Baldy look like an ant hill, it’s very scary.”

It didn’t take long for the young Wedding to discover snowboarding. The sport was exploding in popularity. At age 10, he hopped on a board and was instantly hooked.

A few years later, he was recruited to train with the national snowboard team. The tall, excitable teenager who knocked back energy drinks was now hanging with the pros.

In high school, Wedding trained regularly and competed overseas while also attending class and playing on the rugby team. By 17, he was a multi-time provincial champion, and had just won bronze in the parallel giant slalom at the world junior championships.

At 20, as the youngest member on Canada’s snowboard team at the 2002 Olympics in Salt Lake City, Wedding had tons of potential. He was no wide-eyed young kid, there just for the experience. He qualified as one of the best talents on a loaded men’s team that was expected to medal.

But it was over quickly. A hasty start out the gate — or bad conditions, depending on who you ask — wasn’t enough to get him to the qualifying round. He placed 24th.

As for what happened after Wedding quit snowboarding, from running a massive illicit cannabis operation to his first cocaine bust and fleeing Canada, that’s a longer story — a path that the Star and the CBC have spent the last year uncovering in a new podcast series released Thursday.

Called “The Most Wanted O lympian ,” the six-episode series details the sprawling FBI and RCMP case against Wedding and his alleged drug network, as well as the victims left in its wake.

A large chunk of the population worked jobs that supported these sectors: at the mills, in transportation and railway manufacturing, or at the grain elevators and docks along the waterfront.

Wedding’s dad, Rene, didn’t work in the mills, but he did work in industry. A mechanical engineer — the kind of professional who worked on big projects, for big businesses, travelling all over the world.

The eldest of three and the only son, Wedding grew up in a red brick bungalow with a U-shaped driveway, in a sought-after neighbourhood on the southwestern edge of the city. The semirural pocket is full of mid-to-high-end homes. It’s not Thunder Bay’s Bridle Path, but Whitegates is comfortable — large homes on deep lots studded with towering pine trees.

Today, the exterior of Wedding’s childhood house looks much the same as it would have in the 1980s, save for the Weddings’ tennis court, with big floodlights his parents installed after they bought the property. It’s long been replaced by a backyard pool.

Rene and Karen Wedding, a registered nurse, married in 1977. Both were longtime skiers in a city where it was almost unusual not to be a part of the local hockey culture. Thunder Bay is famous for churning out elite hockey players — from modern-day stars like the Staal brothers to Hall of Famers like Alex Delvecchio with the Detroit Red Wings — but Wedding was not going to be one of them.
Rene was a varsity skier at the University of Toronto, where he earned his engineering degree, while Karen hailed from a family of skiers who were fixtures in the local skiing community.

Her parents, Laurence “Larry” and Marlyn Spiess, ran the Mount Baldy ski club north of town. They bought it in the late 1960s and kept it running for decades before their son, Craig Spiess, took over the business. (Karen also had shares in the ski hill.)

Craig started as a local instructor and after 12 seasons working at a prominent ski instruction and training program in New Zealand, he returned to Canada to coach some of Ontario’s best alpine racers. Eventually, he became a coach with the national alpine ski team. Throughout the late ‘80s and into the ‘90s, Wedding would’ve watched his uncle train some of the best female athletes in the sport, including 1992 Olympic gold medallist Kerrin Lee-Gartner. To date, she remains the only Canadian to win the downhill ski event.

Larry would start his day with a cup of coffee and a crossword, then jet off to the ski club with four sets of keys to ensure the lights were on and the hills were groomed. It was “his personal paradise,” his family wrote in an obituary. Marlyn was the friendly face greeting patrons at the ticket office and gear shop.

By all accounts, the two adored their five grandchildren. Larry spoiled Wedding, his first grandson, teaching him how to drive before his feet could reach the pedals, and after Wedding’s sister was born, he painted the club purple and pink because those were her favourite colours.
Rene and Karen had Wedding on skis and in a training harness by the age of two. By age nine, he could carve down the slopes on just one ski, as if it was a snowboard.
Childhood friend Rudi Phillion remembers that well. The few times they hit the slopes together, Wedding would drop a ski to challenge himself.
“That way, he and I would go at more or less the same speed,” he said.

Mount Baldy is still a mom-and-pop ski club, but with new owners. The Kardas brothers — the sons of two-time Olympic ski jumper and national coach Slavomir Kardas — bought it in 2016. The trio, Jason, Kristoff and Daniel, were all once on the national ski jumping team.

When the Star visited on a recent Saturday, Daniel and a team of workers were making improvements to the roof of the chalet. Aside from necessary upgrades and renovations, he said the ski club is largely the same as when Wedding was a kid.
It’s no Whistler or Chamonix; it’s far more modest than Blue Mountain — but Mount Baldy is more than enough to foster a love of the sport.

The hill features 14 runs for all skill levels and a terrain park with rails and jumps. At the base, patrons are hit with a cosy cabin smell as soon as they step into the chalet. It’s three levels with large windows facing the slopes, a stone fireplace and an interior finished with the classic tongue and groove wood. The walls are adorned with old racing bibs, photographs and vintage signage.

At the canteen and bar, patrons can grab craft beer and comfort food, including pizza and what Daniel describes as world-class poutine. Cheese curds from the Thunder Oak Cheese Farm. Potatoes from Breukelman’s Potato Farm. “We try to use everything local.”

At the top of the hill, a lookout point offers expansive views of Lake Superior and the famous Sleeping Giant, a land formation resembling a giant lying on its back in the water. Nearby, ON a different run, a plaque bearing the name of Wedding’s grandfather, Larry Spiess, is mounted into the ground.
“Larry taught us that it is not what you have in life but what you do that counts,” it reads, detailing his legacy of hard work. “This is Larry’s spot.”
Ryan Wedding, the man

Those who spoke to the Star in Thunder Bay struggle to comprehend the tall, baby-faced Wedding they once knew is the same hulking, aggressive person accused of leading an international drug ring aligned with the Sinaloa Cartel.
For his alleged victims, however, that concept is all they know.
Authorities claimed Wedding ran a drug ring that moved more than a billion dollars worth of cocaine into Canada each year from Mexico and orchestrated multiple murders.
It’s hard not to believe his love of fast things came from his dad, Rene.
In 2025, Mexican authorities confiscated Wedding’s rare collection of 62 racing motorcycles, including many MotoGP bikes once belonging to famous riders like Valentino Rossi and Jorge Lorenzo.
As a kid, friends say, he was obsessed with his father’s Kawasaki Ninja. He’d boast about it to peers. “He thought it was the coolest,” recalled childhood friend Neil MacEachern.

Rene was a confident, earnest man who spoke fluent German and worked long hours for an engineering company before starting his own firm the year after Wedding was born. He played various sports, could ski barefoot on the lakes, according to one neighbour, and had a taste for fast, high-end motor vehicles, such as the Corvette he drove.
The Weddings had more money than most in this lunch-bucket town, but to MacEachern’s memory, his old friend never came across as flashy or spoiled. Confident, sure, but not showy, he said.

His family’s wealth only came through in the occasional brag about his dad’s stuff or when he had friends over to play the latest video games or use high-tech gadgets, such as the LaserDisc player in their basement recreation room.

At Mother Theresa elementary school, Wedding was in French immersion and, in Grade 4, he joined a small cohort of students in the gifted program. Among the others were Phillion, MacEachern and his twin sister. Once a week, they would be bused to another school across town.

Phillion and MacEachern recalled science and art projects, geography games, creative-thinking prompts such as listing as many uses for a pencil as possible, and short presentations on topics they’d researched.
Wedding was uninhibited as a kid — not particularly warm, but not mean-spirited or bombastic, MacEachern said. “He had a forceful presence, a strong presence, but he wasn’t a bully.”
The fact his dad was an engineer was something MacEachern didn’t know. Looking back, it made perfect sense, he said. “Ryan was a natural draftsman.”

Sometimes in class, he’d be drawing mechanical things, like cars or bikes, rather than paying attention to the teacher. Like MacEachern, Wedding was also interested in assembling plastic model kits. The boys spent hours at a time piecing together a German Second World War submarine that his parents bought for him.
With human figures, however, his skills wavered. One day, MacEachern recalled, Wedding had nudged him to look over at a sketch — a woman fellating a man.
MacEachern was caught off guard. While it wasn’t the best quality, the illustration was clear enough.
How a nine-year-old would’ve learned about fellatio in the early ‘90s, MacEachern has no clue. Perhaps a pornographic magazine or satellite TV.
A new province and newfound passion

In 1991, during the Grade 4 school year, Wedding and his family moved to Coquitlam, B.C., then a rapidly growing suburb east of Vancouver, for Rene’s work. The family’s youngest child, and second daughter, was born soon after.
MacEachern and Phillion were sad to see their friend go. They stayed in touch over the next few years and each visited him in B.C. and Wedding came back to Thunder Bay a handful of times, too.
“Dear Rudi,” he wrote in a letter dated July 15, 1991. “I miss you very much,” he said, pivoting to the news about his new baby sister. “She was nine pounds and 52 cm when she was born.”
He told his friend he wasn’t yet in his new school’s gifted program because he came too late in the school year.
In another letter, Wedding said he tried his hand at football. He wasn’t great but was getting better, he said. “I’ve made 20 touchdowns since school started.”
At home, he now had a room for “my Lego, model building and my train,” he told Phillion, and had recently gone biking with his dad on the logging roads nearby.
When you look down the side of the mountain, “all you see is clear cut almost strait down,” he said, misspelling a few words. The view “makes M. Baldy look like an ant hill, it’s very scary.”
It didn’t take long for the young Wedding to discover snowboarding. The sport was exploding in popularity. At age 10, he hopped on a board and was instantly hooked.
A few years later, he was recruited to train with the national snowboard team. The tall, excitable teenager who knocked back energy drinks was now hanging with the pros.

In high school, Wedding trained regularly and competed overseas while also attending class and playing on the rugby team. By 17, he was a multi-time provincial champion, and had just won bronze in the parallel giant slalom at the world junior championships.

At 20, as the youngest member on Canada’s snowboard team at the 2002 Olympics in Salt Lake City, Wedding had tons of potential. He was no wide-eyed young kid, there just for the experience. He qualified as one of the best talents on a loaded men’s team that was expected to medal.
But it was over quickly. A hasty start out the gate — or bad conditions, depending on who you ask — wasn’t enough to get him to the qualifying round. He placed 24th.

As for what happened after Wedding quit snowboarding, from running a massive illicit cannabis operation to his first cocaine bust and fleeing Canada, that’s a longer story — a path that the Star and the CBC have spent the last year uncovering in a new podcast series released Thursday.
Called “The Most Wanted O lympian ,” the six-episode series details the sprawling FBI and RCMP case against Wedding and his alleged drug network, as well as the victims left in its wake.

Thursday, October 15, 2026

The City of London has released the draft of its new zoning by-law, giving Londoners an opportunity to explore what is being proposed across the city, learn what it could mean for different areas, ask questions and provide feedback before the proposed by-law goes to Council for approval.

Public engagement will continue throughout October and November, with Londoners invited to review the draft, explore proposed zoning for their property, neighbourhood or other areas of interest, and ask questions and provide feedback until November 20.

The draft zoning by-law supports the planning direction set out in The London Plan(London’s Official Plan). It sets out the rules for how properties can be used and developed across London.

“Modernizing our zoning by-law is an important part of the City’s ongoing work to make it easier to build and invest in London. By updating our zoning, streamlining approvals and creating a clearer, more predictable regulatory framework, we can provide more opportunities for housing of all types while also supporting new and growing businesses across the city,” said Scott Mathers, Deputy City Manager Housing and Community Growth.

“We know there’s a lot of information to take in when it comes to zoning,” said Heather McNeeley, Director of Planning & Development. “Our goal is to make it easier for Londoners to learn about zoning, explore what’s being proposed for their property and neighbourhood, and understand what it could mean. We want people to feel comfortable asking questions and have the information they need to provide informed feedback.”

Londoners can use theReThink Zoning interactive map to find their property or neighbourhood, see the proposed zoning and learn more about what the proposed zoning could allow. Plain-language information, videos and FAQs are also available to help Londoners understand the proposed changes.

Opportunities to ask questions and provide feedback

There will be several opportunities throughout October and November for Londoners to learn more about the draft zoning by-law and speak with City Planning staff.

In-person drop-in sessions are planned at:

South London Community Centre on October 22 from 6:30 - 8 p.m.

Sherwood Library branch on October 27 from 6:30 - 8 p.m.

Beacock Library branch on November 3 from 6:30 - 8 p.m.

Bostwick Library branch on November 6 from 1:30 - 3 p.m.

Covent Garden Market Pop-Up Booth on October 27 and November 3 from 11:30 a.m. - 1:30 p.m.

A Community Information Session will also be held at Goodwill Industries (Horton Street) on Tuesday, November 24, from 7 to 9 p.m. The session will include a formal presentation and an opportunity to ask questions.

More details about these engagement opportunities are available on theReThink Zoning webpage.

After the engagement period, the City will share what it heard, identify common themes and explain changes made where applicable.

The draft zoning by-law, interactive map, educational resources, FAQs and information about engagement opportunities are available atgetinvolved.london.ca/rethink-zoning.

The proposed zoning by-law is part of the City’s work to modernize Zoning By-law Z.-1 and create an updated regulatory framework that supports the planning direction established through The London Plan, London’s official plan.

Through the ReThink Zoning engagement initiative, the City is providing information and tools to help Londoners understand the draft zoning by-law and what it could mean for their property and neighbourhood.

Zoning sets out what uses and forms of development may be permitted on a property. The proposed zoning does not mean development will automatically happen. Other regulations, approvals and requirements may apply to individual development proposals.

Thursday, October 15, 2026

The City of London has released the draft of its new zoning by-law, giving Londoners an opportunity to explore what is being proposed across the city, learn what it could mean for different areas, ask questions and provide feedback before the proposed by-law goes to Council for approval.

Public engagement will continue throughout October and November, with Londoners invited to review the draft, explore proposed zoning for their property, neighbourhood or other areas of interest, and ask questions and provide feedback until November 20.
The draft zoning by-law supports the planning direction set out in The London Plan(London’s Official Plan). It sets out the rules for how properties can be used and developed across London.

“Modernizing our zoning by-law is an important part of the City’s ongoing work to make it easier to build and invest in London. By updating our zoning, streamlining approvals and creating a clearer, more predictable regulatory framework, we can provide more opportunities for housing of all types while also supporting new and growing businesses across the city,” said Scott Mathers, Deputy City Manager Housing and Community Growth.

“We know there’s a lot of information to take in when it comes to zoning,” said Heather McNeeley, Director of Planning & Development. “Our goal is to make it easier for Londoners to learn about zoning, explore what’s being proposed for their property and neighbourhood, and understand what it could mean. We want people to feel comfortable asking questions and have the information they need to provide informed feedback.”

Londoners can use theReThink Zoning interactive map to find their property or neighbourhood, see the proposed zoning and learn more about what the proposed zoning could allow. Plain-language information, videos and FAQs are also available to help Londoners understand the proposed changes.
Opportunities to ask questions and provide feedback
There will be several opportunities throughout October and November for Londoners to learn more about the draft zoning by-law and speak with City Planning staff.
In-person drop-in sessions are planned at:

items: South London Community Centre on October 22 from 6:30 - 8 p.m.
Sherwood Library branch on October 27 from 6:30 - 8 p.m.
Beacock Library branch on November 3 from 6:30 - 8 p.m.
Bostwick Library branch on November 6 from 1:30 - 3 p.m.
Covent Garden Market Pop-Up Booth on October 27 and November 3 from 11:30 a.m. - 1:30 p.m.

content_blocks.text: A Community Information Session will also be held at Goodwill Industries (Horton Street) on Tuesday, November 24, from 7 to 9 p.m. The session will include a formal presentation and an opportunity to ask questions.
More details about these engagement opportunities are available on theReThink Zoning webpage.
After the engagement period, the City will share what it heard, identify common themes and explain changes made where applicable.
The draft zoning by-law, interactive map, educational resources, FAQs and information about engagement opportunities are available atgetinvolved.london.ca/rethink-zoning.

The proposed zoning by-law is part of the City’s work to modernize Zoning By-law Z.-1 and create an updated regulatory framework that supports the planning direction established through The London Plan, London’s official plan.

Through the ReThink Zoning engagement initiative, the City is providing information and tools to help Londoners understand the draft zoning by-law and what it could mean for their property and neighbourhood.

Zoning sets out what uses and forms of development may be permitted on a property. The proposed zoning does not mean development will automatically happen. Other regulations, approvals and requirements may apply to individual development proposals.

stories.title: Missing Person – Layla Hart
stories.summary: London, ON (October 15, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 15-year-old Layla Hart, of London.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 15, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 15-year-old Layla Hart, of London.

The missing person is described as female, White, approximately 5’5”, medium build, long black and red hair, a piercing on the left side of her nose, and blue eyes. She was last seen wearing a black sweater, grey shorts, black shoes and glasses.

The missing person was last seen on October 13, 2026, at approximately 9 a.m., and was in the area of Wonderland Road S and Southdale Road West. She was reported missing on October 14, 2026.

Family and police are concerned for her welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

stories.title: London researchers explore outcomes for patients with high potassium
stories.summary: While the condition is asymptomatic, high potassium in the blood can lead to fatal heart complications. High levels of potassium in the blood, common in people on certain medications or with kidney…
stories.content:
Uncategorized October 15, 2026

While the condition is asymptomatic, high potassium in the blood can lead to fatal heart complications . High levels of potassium in the blood, common in people on certain medications or with kidney disease, often come with no symptoms, but can be deadly in severe cases.

Because people with hyperkalemia, or high potassium, often “feel normal,” their treating physicians must determine whether their condition can be safely managed outside the hospital or requires more urgent treatment in the emergency department.

Researchers at Western University and London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (Lhscri) have shown that the risk of death was significantly lower among patients who were able to get to an emergency department within 24 hours of an abnormally high potassium reading. The study was recently published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal .

“The challenge is patients with hyperkalemia can feel completely fine, even when their potassium is at a dangerously high level. It can be difficult for patients to understand why they need to get to the emergency department right away,” said Dr. Michael Chiu, professor at Western’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry and scientist at Lhscri.

Potassium is a normal electrolyte found in the body, but for people with certain kidney conditions or on some blood pressure medications, the body’s ability to flush the potassium is impaired, leading to a build-up in the blood. Because potassium is a key player in the electrical activity of the heart, elevated levels can trigger abnormal heart rhythms and potentially fatal cardiac arrest.

Using population health data from the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences , the researchers explored patients who weren’t already admitted to hospital to determine how many went to the emergency department and how that correlated with their risk of dying.

“It was the first study to investigate if patients with diagnosed high potassium were going to the emergency department or not, and for those who went, what their outcomes were,” said Chiu. “When people are admitted to hospital or seen in the emergency department, there are medications we can give that help protect the heart. There are also intravenous medications that can lower potassium levels quickly by moving it into cells or helping remove it from the body. These emergency treatments can only be done in a hospital setting.”

The team hopes to use this as a starting point to develop a clinical decision-making tool for health-care providers to consider patient characteristics like age and other chronic conditions, as well as laboratory values, when managing patients with a high outpatient potassium value and making a determination about whether or not they need in-hospital care.

“One of the reasons we wanted to do this research is that if we get a call in the middle of the night from a lab saying a patient has high potassium, we have to decide whether the patient needs to go to the emergency department and convince the patient why it is important to do so,” he said. “We also need to ensure that patients who May not benefit from in-hospital treatment, aren’t making an unnecessary trip to the emergency department.”

stories.title: Mark Carney tells Calgary that ‘polls don’t vote, people vote’ as he campaigns against separation referendum
stories.summary: "It's hard to think of a worse time to have a referendum, or a better time for the province," the prime minister said in Calgary on Thursday.
stories.author: Stephanie Taylor; Alex Ballingall
stories.content:
Calgary — Prime Minister Mark Carney blitzed through Calgary on Thursday as part of a whirlwind trip through Alberta days before the province’s referendum on separation, telling a packed evening rally of federalist supporters that only a decisive result would settle the issue.

With advance voting underway, Carney capped a day of campaigning alongside federalist groups with a speech to thousands gathered at a “Forever Canadian” rally.

Mark Carney was in Calgary for a Forever Canadian Rally just days ahead of a vote in Alberta on whether there should be a referendum on separation.

On a stage before a swelling crowd, Carney outlined the stakes in Monday’s vote.

He laid out that residents face a choice of whether to “build a stronger Alberta and an even greater Canada” for future generations or, he warned, “we can burden them with years of deep division and great uncertainty.”

“What we need is a decisive result on Monday to settle this question,” Carney said to thunderous applause. He later urged Albertans to “lead, not leave.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney was met with well-wishers Thursday as he toured through Calgary to rally the pro-Canada vote ahead of Monday’s referendum on separation. Carney urged Albertans to not only vote for Confederation, but to also reject the nine other questions on the ballot involving immigration and the Constitution.

He urged Albertans not only to vote, but to show their Canadian pride by wearing red and displaying the maple leaf, as many in the crowd did Thursday evening.

“Don’t let anyone tell you that this is already decided,” Carney said. “Turnout will determine the outcome.”

He also pushed back against the argument advanced by independence leaders that Albertans need not support separation to vote for “Option 2,” the label attached to the proposal on the ballot, and could instead use it to express frustration with Ottawa.

“This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and for Canada,” Carney said.

He nevertheless acknowledged that Ottawa had to repair its relationship with Alberta. Carney drew on his own experience growing up in Edmonton, where he recalled residents being made to feel like its resources “weren’t our own.”

Carney said the frustrations felt by Albertans were “real,” arguing they had shaped decades of provincial politics and contributed to the divisions on display today.

The prime minister’s appearance at the rally led to a crowd exceeding what his team had been expecting. Thomas Lukaszuk, the former deputy premier in the province who launched the “Forever Canadian” federalist group, told the crowd on stage that more than 7,000 people showed up.

Throughout multiple public appearances Thursday, Carney emphasized that with four days remaining before the vote, federalists could not let up.

He told one gathering of federalist volunteers earlier in the day that “polls don’t vote, people vote.”

At the same stop, he for the first time endorsed efforts urging voters to say “no to the nine” referendum questions accompanying the independence question, which deal with immigration and constitutional reform.

Speaking to volunteers with Public Interest Alberta’s campaign for Alberta to remain in Canada, Carney said, “We need to get people out to vote,” before urging them to also vote “no to the nine.”

He went further in an interview with a South Asian broadcaster when asked how Albertans should vote on proposals to abolish the Senate and change access to certain provincial services for residents without citizenship or permanent residency, including by allowing the province to charge a premium.

“We don’t need a referendum to make progress on taking control on immigration,” Carney told Red FM Calgary.

“We’ve taken control on immigration.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith responded on X, saying that while the pair have found “common ground on many things over the last 18 months,” he was failing “to fully understand just how damaging the open-border policies of his predecessor were.”

Carney has defended his government’s reductions to immigration levels, a shift first set in motion by former prime minister Justin Trudeau during his final months in office after years of increases following the COVID-19 pandemic.

Smith’s comments come as she urges Albertans to vote to remain in Canada while also saying “yes to the rest” of the questions on immigration and constitutional change, arguing they would give her a mandate to push for greater provincial sovereignty.

While polling suggests support for separation remains a minority view in Alberta, federalists say a strong turnout is key to putting the issue to rest.

The outlook for the immigration-related questions, however, appears less clear.

Grace Guan is an immigrant who has lived in Calgary for 16 years. She said she decided to get involved with the Public Interest Alberta’s campaign because she believes the questions blame immigrants for the province’s problems.

“I feel I should stand up,” Guan said.

Cesar Cala, a prominent advocate in Calgary’s Filipino community, said many temporary residents in Alberta are fearful of the proposed changes.

“I work with a lot of people who work here but have temporary permits,” he said. “They’ve been invited to help build Alberta, especially during COVID, and they put themselves in the line of danger, right? Front-line workers, workers in “the food industry and so on — they have temporary permits but their impact is permanent.”

Smith has argued Alberta needs greater control over immigration, saying population growth has strained the province’s ability to deliver services.

Throughout his stops on Thursday, Carney repeated his often-used line about Alberta’s referendum being staged as the country finds itself in a “more dangerous and divided world.”

His decision to visit the province did not go unnoticed by separatist leaders.

“I think they must be worried,” said Mitch Sylvestre, who leads the Alberta Prosperity Project.

ByEdward Keenan Columnist

Good morning. This is the Thursday, Oct. 15 edition of First Up, the Star’s daily morning digest. Sign up to get it earlier each day, in your inbox.

Today is the “ides of October.” No one ever says to beware it. But it does mean that Thanksgiving is over and you can start hauling your Halloween decorations out of storage.

Here are six things to know this Thursday morning:

The federal government wants to give police forces across the country — including in Toronto and the GTA — the power to disrupt radiocommunication signals.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Stelco could be forced to sell its Canadian assets.

The provincial government started removing the bike lanes on Bloor Street West Wednesday morning.

A new report predicts GTA home prices will drop even further before the end of the year.

The Backstreet Boys residency at the Rogers Centre next year will extend to 12 shows (doubling up Taylor Swift’s record).

Alright! Let’s get into it.

He grew up in Thunder Bay and seemingly had it all, spending his days on tennis courts and ski hills. He would go on to become an Olympian. He is also alleged to have become one of Canada’s most prolific criminals, accused of running a billion-dollar cocaine empire for Mexican cartels, and arranging to kill anyone who stood in his way. The Star visited his hometown and interviewed more than half a dozen childhood friends, neighbours and old teammates to get the origin story of one of Canada’s most notorious accused criminals.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Listen: “The Most Wanted Olympian,” a new podcast from reporters Calvi Leon and Michelle Shephard, goes from Thunder Bay to Toronto to Mexico to get the story behind the man the FBI also compared to El Chapo.All episodes are now available to Star subscribers here.

Mayoral candidates Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford each met with the Star’s editorial board Wednesday. Here are the tough questions they faced.

People using our Vote Compass tool find housing and taxation to be the biggest issues — but voters’ top concerns lead to different candidates.

Three Canadian Armed Forces members are among seven men facing more than 80 charges after a cryptocurrency exchange owner was allegedly kidnapped.

“I thought he was a sharp kid”: Self‑described financially savvy real‑estate developer tells jurors he funnelled more than $3.6 million into “Crypto King” Aiden Pleterski’s enterprise.

Doug Ford said Donald Trump has “permanently” changed the U.S.-Canada relationship, in a speech laying out Ontario’s financial challenges.

U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra warns Canada: “Keep your nose out of American politics.”

Liberal critic says thousands of students are unable to pay rent or buy groceries because the Ford government was “asleep at the switch” over abuse of the OSAP system.

Toronto-area condos are being sold in bulk at discounts as high as 45 per cent. Anastasia Blosser reports how regular investors can now get in on the action.

I went out to the area near Bloor and Islington Tuesday night, trying to see the scheduled removal of bike lanes. Apparently, I missed the confrontation between protestors and construction crews, but I saw the result: plenty of cyclists hanging out, no lane-removal crews anywhere. (The crews were back on Wednesday, though.)

While there, I thought of the day Mayor Rob Ford removed the Jarvis bike lanes. And I thought of what happened next, which may not be remembered as well: the day Ford cut the ribbon to open Toronto’s first separated bike lanes.

Given his “war on the car” persona, it is easy to forget that the late Ford was a champion of routes for cyclists separated from car traffic. As Dave Meslin, the founder of Cycle Toronto, wrote in an op-ed in the Star in 2011, Ford advocated early and often for bike lanes built into suburban boulevards, or at the edge of widened sidewalks beside the road.

So after he took out the Jarvis bike lanes, he and his public works commissioner, Denzil Minnan-Wong, cut the ribbon on separated lanes on Sherbourne Street. And then built separated lanes on Wellesley Street. And installed the cycle tracks on Richmond and Adelaide Streets. “I think this is the first step in having an integrated bike lane system down here, and that’s what the people want downtown,” Rob Ford said at the Sherbourne ribbon-cutting. No more “swimming with the sharks.”

Research shows that this type of lane makes the street safer not just for cyclists, but for pedestrians and people in cars too. And indeed, once people saw the Rob Ford-style lanes, Toronto never looked back. We carried on building an “integrated network” on Bloor and University and Yonge, and so many other streets. That’s what Doug Ford is now determined to rip out.

I’ve mentioned before that no one at any level has ever won an election campaigning against the Bloor bike lanes in Etobicoke. Past polls have shown overwhelming support for such lanes, even among drivers and suburbanites. Still, in a poll commissioned by Citytv this week, 62 per cent of Torontonians support Premier Ford’s removal plan. Yet 64 per cent in another poll say decisions about bike lanes should be left to the city, rather than the province. Public opinion is clear as mud.

But what is your opinion? Did you know that Rob Ford was the pioneer of this network of separated bike lanes? Do you think his brother Doug is justified in removing the ones he thinks are messing with traffic? Or do you think, as opponents have argued, that it’s a step back that won’t even improve car travel times? Let us know in the comments section here.

ADAM RADWANSKI:The upcoming federal budget is a good time for Mark Carney to think small.

STEPHEN MARCHE:Donald Trump is on a rampage with no clear objectives. That gives Canada, and our allies, one big advantage.

BARBARA YAFFE:Next week’s Alberta referendum could decide more than the question of separation. It may well determine Danielle Smith’s future as premier.

The Raptors 905 tryout lures the best local basketball players every year. The Star’s Libaan Osman gave it a shot — and says he barely survived.

Chris Tanev is essential to the Leafs’ defence. Nick Kypreos looks at what his injury means to the team.

Millennial optimism isn’t dead. Lena Dunham’s hit TV show “Girls” is returning. Briony Smith reminisces about what the show meant for young people in the 2010s.

“A Fine Balance” has become the most successful show in Crow’s Theatre history — and it will get an extended life in a new home next year.

Thursday marks the first joint appearance for Prince Harry and Meghan Markle since they returned to live in the U.K. How’s their new British life faring?

Stelco blamed U.S. tariffs for its planned layoffs in Hamilton. Now Ottawa is mulling a lawsuit. That definitely got your attention:

“These layoffs are a direct result of the tariffs. This was always going to be the end result for those industries subjected to the 50 per cent tariffs. The federal government should assist those that are laid off for a certain amount of time.” — D.

A reader pointed out that Canada is in the midst of rebranding itself and Stelco could be part of that move:

“Nationalize the company now and take the hit financially for the next five years while the company resets its commercial goals.” — Orville

Before you go, spare a thought for a little dog named Luna who had been on the lam in Yellowstone National Park for more than a month. Folks trying to get her home safe before winter set in finally successfully captured her on Wednesday. Luckily, while she is underweight, she is otherwise in good condition.

Thanks for starting your day with us. If you enjoy First Up, please share it with a friend. And let us know what you think of the changes we’ve made, and what you’d like to see. Email firstup@thestar.ca. I’ll see you back here tomorrow morning.

content_blocks.text: THE CONVERSATION
Revisiting Rob Ford’s bike lane legacy

I went out to the area near Bloor and Islington Tuesday night, trying to see the scheduled removal of bike lanes. Apparently, I missed the confrontation between protestors and construction crews, but I saw the result: plenty of cyclists hanging out, no lane-removal crews anywhere. (The crews were back on Wednesday, though.)

While there, I thought of the day Mayor Rob Ford removed the Jarvis bike lanes. And I thought of what happened next, which may not be remembered as well: the day Ford cut the ribbon to open Toronto’s first separated bike lanes.

Given his “war on the car” persona, it is easy to forget that the late Ford was a champion of routes for cyclists separated from car traffic. As Dave Meslin, the founder of Cycle Toronto, wrote in an op-ed in the Star in 2011, Ford advocated early and often for bike lanes built into suburban boulevards, or at the edge of widened sidewalks beside the road.

So after he took out the Jarvis bike lanes, he and his public works commissioner, Denzil Minnan-Wong, cut the ribbon on separated lanes on Sherbourne Street. And then built separated lanes on Wellesley Street. And installed the cycle tracks on Richmond and Adelaide Streets. “I think this is the first step in having an integrated bike lane system down here, and that’s what the people want downtown,” Rob Ford said at the Sherbourne ribbon-cutting. No more “swimming with the sharks.”

Research shows that this type of lane makes the street safer not just for cyclists, but for pedestrians and people in cars too. And indeed, once people saw the Rob Ford-style lanes, Toronto never looked back. We carried on building an “integrated network” on Bloor and University and Yonge, and so many other streets. That’s what Doug Ford is now determined to rip out.

I’ve mentioned before that no one at any level has ever won an election campaigning against the Bloor bike lanes in Etobicoke. Past polls have shown overwhelming support for such lanes, even among drivers and suburbanites. Still, in a poll commissioned by Citytv this week, 62 per cent of Torontonians support Premier Ford’s removal plan. Yet 64 per cent in another poll say decisions about bike lanes should be left to the city, rather than the province. Public opinion is clear as mud.

But what is your opinion? Did you know that Rob Ford was the pioneer of this network of separated bike lanes? Do you think his brother Doug is justified in removing the ones he thinks are messing with traffic? Or do you think, as opponents have argued, that it’s a step back that won’t even improve car travel times? Let us know in the comments section here.
