stories.title: One Alberta under God: Inside a Christian push for Alberta independence
stories.summary: That battle casts Alberta's struggle as one of good versus evil, led by those who see independence as a chance to reform a nation that has lost its way.
stories.author: Stephanie Taylor
stories.content:
Calgary — On an evening in February, Tim Stephens stood before a crowd and asked them to picture something.

“I want you to imagine with me,” the Calgary pastor said, “the possibility, and I believe it is a possibility, to see abortion banned in the province of Alberta, in an independent Alberta.”

The audience applauds as Stephens broadens the argument, acknowledging that abortion is not the only issue he believes mainstream political parties will not touch. The same, he said, is true of “transgenderism and homosexuality.”

Abortion is not “going to be broached in Ottawa,” he told the crowd, “but it could be an issue here in the nation of Alberta.”

Just as David Cameron lost a Brexit vote he never supported, then had to resign as UK leader, the same thing looks poised to happen in Alberta.

While economic grievances over equalization payments, federal government spending and regulations governing Alberta’s natural resources form the basis of the decades-long alienation that has fuelled the push for the province to separate, a moral dimension also exists to the fight.

That battle casts Alberta’s struggle as one of good versus evil, featuring Christian leaders who see independence as a chance to reform a nation they believe has lost its way and to build Alberta into its own city on a hill.

These leaders are looking not only to influence the hearts and minds of Albertans heading to the polls on Oct. 19, but also the independence movement itself.

And while these figures represent only one strand of opinion within Alberta’s faith communities, the idea that Alberta independence could open the door to a cultural rewind has garnered the support of one of the United States’ most influential evangelical voices.

“I think that Albertans are getting a raw deal from the Ottawa government,” said Doug Wilson, the Idaho pastor and leading figure in the American Christian nationalist movement, who has been invited to pray at venues including the Pentagon by U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.

While talk of values and prayer is commonplace at many events staged by independence leaders across the province, one of the movement’s most prominent activists is blunt that the grassroots push to leave is driven more by economics than religion.

“I don’t think that the independence movement is actually primarily driven by Christians,” David Parker told the Star.

“There’s a lot of Christians in it, but it’s actually more of an economic movement than it is a religious movement.”

Parker, who was raised as the home-schooled son of a pastor, approaches politics through a world view shaped by his faith. At events, online and on podcasts, that perspective is reflected in language steeped in Christian concepts, from equating voter indifference to a “sin” to describing political involvement as a form of “repentance.”

He describes his role in the separation push as that of a “cheerleader.” Elections Alberta is investigating allegations that a voting identification initiative he launched earlier this year relied on an improperly obtained electors’ list , resulting in the province’s largest privacy breach. Parker declined to comment on those matters.

He nevertheless predicts that, should the independence movement fail, the lack of focus on cultural issues “will be a large reason why.”

Seated in his office at Fairview Baptist Church in south Calgary, Stephens suggests that more pastors support of independence than are willing to speak about it.

Many of those who attend events like the ones he has hosted in Calgary and elsewhere in the province, he says, are Christians who are “curious about what the Bible says about these political issues” but May not hear those issues addressed by their own pastors.

Stephens was arrested during the pandemic for holding church services that violated the province’s COVID-19 restrictions. That decision drew more attention to his congregation and his own teachings and preaching. He estimates upwards of 400 people fill his church’s pews on Sundays.

Some in his congregation assisted in collecting the 300,000 signatures that helped trigger the referendum. He is encouraging people to vote for the option that sets the province down the potential path of secession, even though he doubts the separatists will get 50 per cent of the vote .

Through his thinking about independence, Stephens says what he found was a “longing” people had for a return to the “values that our country and nation was built upon.”

While the divides between Central Canada and Alberta are often framed in economic terms, Stephens sees them as running along deeper fault lines shaped by the province’s social conservatism and evangelical heritage.

“In my mind, we’re going away from our Christian heritage and the values that we had as a country,” he said.

As Stephens and others like him see independence as an off-ramp from the cultural shifts of the past decade around the legalization of assisted deaths or Lgbtq-related issues, Wilson agrees it creates an opening.

“It does create the opportunity for activist Christians to make their voice heard in a more significant way,” he told the Star.

Wilson, whose mother hailed from Alberta, supports independence in part because he believes it would bring decision-making closer to home.

His views are controversial. His version of Christian nationalism calls for an end to same-sex marriage, and a repeal the U.S. Constitution’s 19th Amendment — which protects women’s voting rights — in favour of household voting.

He suggests that a cultural shift is underway in the U.S. and Canada, with more people “willing to hear radical things from conservative Christians than they were willing to before, because radical leftism is being jammed down their throats.”

Within his denomination, the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches, which includes at least three congregations in Alberta, Wilson says he has spoken to Canadian pastors about “how they live under an impressive anti-Christian government.”

That concern over religious freedom is echoed by Stephens.

“The biggest moral issue that is tied directly to independence is the freedom issue,” he said.

Among the laws most frequently targeted by independence leaders and their supporters is Bill C-9, the anti-hate law that removed a long-standing exemption for religious defences to hate speech from the Criminal Code. The federal government has defended the change as having no impact because freedom of religion remains protected under the Constitution’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Shawn Hamm says COVID changed him. He counts Artur Pawlowski, one of the pastors jailed for violating pandemic rules, among his friends.

In February 2022, Hamm founded his own church ministry in Red Deer, Alta., which he says opened its doors to people who were attracted to the fact that he was a leader “standing for freedom and standing for truth.”

He has since spoken at independence events wearing a T-shirt emblazoned with the words “Trust in God, not government,” and has been invited to speak about Bill C-9. His pitch to audiences is that “Jesus was political.”

Hamm embraces leading a congregation of between 60 and 100 people with a distinctly political message. He is unafraid of being viewed as offensive or controversial, defending public comments he has made about Islam as not being “hateful” but instead taking issue with what he sees as a “false religion.”

For the past two Sundays, independence has been his focus. Recently, he led a room of congregants in prayer for the separatist movement, asking God to “raise up a godly leader.”

“If things in our country are going the wrong way, pastors need to speak up about it,” he said. “Christians need to speak up about it. We’re called to do that.”

stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
Update - London, ON (October 17, 2026) -A previously reported missing 15-year-old female has been located and is safe. We would like to thank the public for sharing the information. We kindly ask that all photographs of the missing person be removed from publication.

Original - London, ON (October 15, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 15-year-old Layla Hart, of London.

The missing person is described as female, White, approximately 5’5”, medium build, long black and red hair, a piercing on the left side of her nose, and blue eyes. She was last seen wearing a black sweater, grey shorts, black shoes and glasses.

The missing person was last seen on October 13, 2026, at approximately 9 a.m., and was in the area of Wonderland Road S and Southdale Road West. She was reported missing on October 14, 2026.

Family and police are concerned for her welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers.

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Court hears of intense campaign for public influence in Galloway case
stories.summary: Award-winning authors came to his defence, while others considered a boycott against his book publisher
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Both Steven Galloway and the former University of British Columbia student who accused the bestselling author of sexual assault and harassment worked behind-the-scenes to curry sympathy amid a national firestorm over the allegations, B.C. Supreme Court heard Wednesday.

Mr. Galloway, who is suing the woman known as A.B. due to a publication ban and three others for defamation, testified that after he was fired as chair of the university’s creative writing program in June, 2016, he was asked by fellow CanLit star and UBC alumna Madeleine Thien to read a draft of her letter to their alma mater excoriating it for the university’s treatment of Mr. Galloway.

He testified Tuesday that he had also seen a copy of the controversial ‘UBC Accountable letter’ calling for the university to open an independent investigation into his firing before it was published. The letter was signed by dozens of prominent writers, including Margaret Atwood.

During cross-examination Wednesday, Aria Laskin, counsel for defendant Mandi Gray, presented Mr. Galloway with a private e-mail involving her client from the days following Mr. Galloway’s suspension.

In that e-mail, court heard, Ms. Gray, an author based in Toronto, discussed the idea of launching a boycott against Mr. Galloway’s book publisher Penguin Random House.

In the e-mail, Ms. Gray notes A.B. agreed with the idea.

“She seems to support it as long as it’s not tied to her in any way,” Ms. Laskin read from the e-mail while questioning Mr. Galloway. The court did not hear who Ms. Gray was corresponding with.

Wednesday’s revelations showed how Mr. Galloway and A.B., who had an extramarital affair from 2011 to 2013, were privy to some of the efforts from allies to sway public perception after the allegations surfaced in late 2015 to torpedo Mr. Galloway’s career.

Mr. Galloway testified Wednesday that Ms. Thien only asked him to look at her letter beforehand to verify its accuracy and he ended up sending along a few minor suggestions.

“Madeleine Thien does not need me editing her work,” he said.

He agreed with Ms. Laskin that Ms. Thien’s letter, the UBC Accountable letter, his own interview with The Globe and Mail in 2018 and his other efforts to publicly defend himself against the original sexual assault allegations didn’t help his public image.

Ubc’s announcement of a formal investigation of “serious allegations” involving Mr. Galloway in 2015 led to an online firestorm over Mr. Galloway’s right to due process versus the rights of his alleged victim.

A retired judge hired by UBC to investigate A.B.’s claims found he had sexually harassed her and found other instances of misconduct leading to his firing, but did not find that he sexually assaulted the woman.

The school fired Mr. Galloway in 2016 without severance, but two years later, an arbitrator awarded him more than $220,000 in two separate awards for violating his privacy during the process of suspending and dismissing him.

He was never charged with a crime and in 2018 he launched his defamation suit, arguing the defendants repeated claims online that he had sexually assaulted a student.

A.B. is not testifying and, at the start of the trial, her lawyer Arden Beddoes told the court that she was withdrawing her defences of truth and fair comment – but not admitting that she spread lies about her former romantic partner. Mr. Beddoes said she had tried to kill herself twice in recent months because of the stress of the ordeal.

Defendant Glynnis Kirchmeier, a former UBC student who is now studying law and representing herself in the trial, spent the end of Wednesday cross-examining Mr. Galloway.

Justice Neena Sharma began Wednesday’s hearing by denying a request from the defendants the day before to gain access to an unredacted version of Mr. Galloway’s dismissal letter. On Tuesday, Mr. Galloway testified that university’s administration provided him with a “laundry list” of reasons for his dismissal in 2016, but apart from the extramarital affair with the student in his creative-writing program, those reasons remain secret.

The trial, which has gone on for seven days and was initially scheduled to last a further 13, continues Monday with other witnesses.

stories.title: Toronto police arrest three reservists, seize allegedly stolen ammunition in crypto-kidnapping investigation
stories.summary: Probe into abduction of cryptocurrency exchange owner evolved as firearms, ammunition and illicit drugs uncovered, police chief says
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
Toronto police have seized more than 2,500 rounds of ammunition allegedly stolen from the Canadian Armed Forces as part of an investigation into the July abduction of the owner of a cryptocurrency exchange that has led to the arrests of seven people, including three military members.

Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw said Wednesday that what started as a kidnapping investigation evolved into something “much larger” as the force uncovered firearms, ammunition and illicit drugs. Police say the abduction reflects an increasingly sophisticated brand of crime targeting digital assets.

“Criminals continue to adapt their methods and identify new opportunities for financial gain,” Joe Matthews, chief superintendent of detective operations with the Toronto Police Service, said during a press conference. “In this case, the victim was allegedly targeted because of his access to cryptocurrency assets.”

The Department of National Defence said it is investigating the matter and is working to improve oversight of ammunition holdings. “Canadians rightly expect the Canadian Armed Forces to manage ammunition and explosives safely, securely, and responsibly,” said spokesperson Andrée-Anne Poulin in an e-mailed statement.

“While the Canadian Armed Forces maintains extensive controls and oversight mechanisms for ammunition and explosives, we recognize the need to put more safeguards in place.”

Ms. Poulin did not respond to questions about how the alleged theft of military ammunition could have taken place, and when the CAF became aware of the issue.

Three of the accused – Talarambage Fernando, 22, James Moreau, 29, and Jack Miley, 24 – are enrolled as reservists in the 7 th Toronto Regiment, Ms. Poulin confirmed Wednesday. She said they have been removed from military duties, and have had their access to facilities and equipment restricted since their arrests in August and September. “They remain members of the CAF pending the outcome of an administrative review,” she added.

The three men are facing charges of kidnapping for ransom and forcible confinement, as well as various gun-related offences. Mr. Moreau has also been charged with two counts of drug possession for trafficking.

The Toronto police investigation began after officers responded to a reported abduction in North York on July 25. They say the victim was targeted as he approached his vehicle, then abducted at gunpoint, handcuffed and assaulted. He was later released after being warned not to contact police, according to the force.

Chief Supt. Matthews said the victim suffered minor injuries, but has recovered. His identity has not been made public.

Two suspects were arrested on July 26, with an additional five arrests made in August and September. Search warrants executed during the investigation led to the seizure of a shotgun, two 3D-printed handguns, two silencers and a large quantity of illicit drugs, including methamphetamine and cocaine. Police also seized more than 2,700 rounds of ammunition, including live ammunition and blanks, the bulk of which had allegedly been stolen from the Canadian military.

“What started as an abduction investigation quickly unfolded into a much larger operation,” said Chief Supt. Matthews. He said the Canadian Armed Forces didn’t reveal whether they were already aware of the theft before it was reported to them by the Toronto police.

In total, the seven people accused of participating in the abduction are facing 82 charges related to kidnapping as well as firearm and drug offences.

Chief Supt. Matthews said police have not yet uncovered a connection to a larger organized crime group and are still trying to work out how the seven suspects knew each other, but said the investigation remains open. The alleged involvement of CAF members is worrisome, he said.

“Their training that they had received through the military is quite concerning, not only to the victims of this type of violence, but also to our officers who May encounter them,” he said. “These are highly trained individuals with access to firearms.”

This is not the first kidnapping incident involving cryptocurrencies in Toronto. In 2024, for example, The Globe and Mail confirmed that Dean Skurka, the chief executive officer of cryptocurrency company WonderFi Technologies Inc., was allegedly abducted and held for ransom.

Defence Minister David McGuinty did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Globe.

The Toronto police investigation began after officers responded to a reported abduction in North York on July 25. They say the victim was targeted as he approached his vehicle, then abducted at gunpoint, handcuffed and assaulted. He was later released after being warned not to contact police, according to the force.
Chief Supt. Matthews said the victim suffered minor injuries, but has recovered. His identity has not been made public.

Two suspects were arrested on July 26, with an additional five arrests made in August and September. Search warrants executed during the investigation led to the seizure of a shotgun, two 3D-printed handguns, two silencers and a large quantity of illicit drugs, including methamphetamine and cocaine. Police also seized more than 2,700 rounds of ammunition, including live ammunition and blanks, the bulk of which had allegedly been stolen from the Canadian military.

“What started as an abduction investigation quickly unfolded into a much larger operation,” said Chief Supt. Matthews. He said the Canadian Armed Forces didn’t reveal whether they were already aware of the theft before it was reported to them by the Toronto police.
In total, the seven people accused of participating in the abduction are facing 82 charges related to kidnapping as well as firearm and drug offences.

Chief Supt. Matthews said police have not yet uncovered a connection to a larger organized crime group and are still trying to work out how the seven suspects knew each other, but said the investigation remains open. The alleged involvement of CAF members is worrisome, he said.

“Their training that they had received through the military is quite concerning, not only to the victims of this type of violence, but also to our officers who May encounter them,” he said. “These are highly trained individuals with access to firearms.”

This is not the first kidnapping incident involving cryptocurrencies in Toronto. In 2024, for example, The Globe and Mail confirmed that Dean Skurka, the chief executive officer of cryptocurrency company WonderFi Technologies Inc., was allegedly abducted and held for ransom.
Defence Minister David McGuinty did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Globe.

stories.title: Chinese businessman faces deportation hearing over war crimes allegations
stories.summary: Chinese army veteran denies he misrepresented his military record to Canadian immigration authorities
stories.author: Marie Woolf
stories.content:
A Chinese businessman who served in the People’s Liberation Army in the 1980s is facing a deportation hearing at Canada’s immigration tribunal amid allegations that he May have misrepresented his military record when applying to live in Canada.

Rong Xiang Yuan, also known as “Tiger” Yuan, has been referred by Canada’s border security agency to the Immigration and Refugee Board, which will consider whether he should be allowed to remain in Canada. The tribunal will look at whether he May have committed war crimes while serving in China’s army during a conflict with Vietnam.

Mr. Yuan, who was born in China and emigrated to Canada in 2008, is the former owner of a gun store in British Columbia.

Since arriving in Canada, Mr. Yuan has spoken at community events in B.C. promoting relations between China and Canada, and was a director of the Canada-China Association For Promoting Friendly Relations, a non-profit.

The Canada Border Services Agency, which is responsible for border security and has its own intelligence division, can request the IRB undertake proceedings to consider whether a foreign national or permanent resident who is believed to have contravened the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act should be allowed to stay in the country. Such requests over alleged war crimes are rare.

The IRB said, in a statement, that it had “received a referral from the Cbsa in the matter of Rong Xiang Yuan for an admissibility hearing under paragraphs 35(1)(a) and 40(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and that a hearing date has not yet been scheduled.”

The first paragraph of the immigration law cited by the IRB relates to foreign nationals or permanent residents being deemed inadmissible to Canada because they engaged in crimes against humanity, war crimes, or gross human rights violations.

The second paragraph cited is about there being grounds for deportation if a foreign national or permanent resident is found to have been “misrepresenting or withholding material facts relating to a relevant matter” that could induce an error in the approval of an immigration application.

Mr. Yuan’s lawyer, Daniel Reid, strenuously denied that his client had any involvement in war crimes or “improper conduct” while serving in China’s military.

“Mr. Yuan denies, in the strongest terms, having violated Canadian or international law during his service in the Chinese armed forces or, decades later, during his immigration to Canada,” he said in a statement on Wednesday. “Mr. Yuan was discharged from the military in 1991 following a serious injury, for which he was awarded the Citation for Merit. He subsequently immigrated to Canada where he has contributed extensively to Canadian and Chinese Canadian communities.”

Mr. Yuan was born in China in 1962 and joined the People’s Liberation Army as a mortar operator after leaving high school, according to an affidavit he filed in the B.C. Supreme Court as part of a defamation suit against another media outlet.

After graduating from a military academy, he was promoted to second lieutenant and led an army platoon. In 1987, his unit was dispatched to the Sino-Vietnamese border where it fought Vietnamese forces until late 1988, according to the affidavit.

His platoon was sent multiple times behind the lines of the Vietnamese army, including for close-quarters fighting, the affidavit Mr. Yuan provided to the B.C. court said. It adds that he was wounded nine times, including in the head, and had been hit by the butt of a gun, stabbed in the abdomen by a bayonet, and hit by landmines and shells. He was admitted to military hospital and fell into a coma on one occasion. He was awarded a citation for valour in battle.

After leaving the army, Mr. Yuan, according to the affidavit, used his discharge fee to start a business, trading in cars, car parts, coal, grains and timber. His businesses thrived and he became a wealthy and successful businessman.

Mr. Yuan, 64, who does not have Canadian citizenship, travelled between B.C. and China until about 2019, the affidavit said. He is a gun and classic car enthusiast with a private collection of vehicles and guns, including historic firearms from the First and Second World Wars, the Korean War and the American Civil War. He said in his affidavit that he was formerly a gambling addict who had gambled at casinos in Singapore, Malaysia, South Korea, Germany, Australia and the United States, as well as in Canada, running up millions of dollars in losses here.

The Cbsa declined to comment. The IRB said it does not comment on individual cases before the tribunal.

stories.title: Canadians urged to check their cheese after several brands hit with recall
stories.summary: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency has issued a nation-wide recall for various brands of cheese due to the presence of Listeria monocytogenes.
stories.author: Aarjavee Raaj
stories.content:
A nationwide recall for various brands of cheese has been issued due to the presence of Listeria monocytogenes.

According to a food recall warning posted to Health Canada Wednesday, the following products from Farm Boy, L’Ancêtre and Life Smart have been recalled from the marketplace:

Farm Boy Organic Swiss Cheese – 190 g

Farm Boy Organic Medium Cheddar Cheese – 200 g

Farm Boy Organic Old Cheddar Cheese – 200 g

Farm Boy Organic Extra Sharp Cheddar Cheese – 200 g

Farm Boy Organic 3-Year-Old Cheddar Cheese – 195 g

L’Ancêtre Organic Swiss Cheese – 200 g

L’Ancêtre Organic Cheddar Cheese - Shredded Old – 2 kg

L’Ancêtre Organic Mozza - Cheddar Shredded Cheese Blend – 200 g

L’Ancêtre Organic Mozzarella Cheese - Shredded Partially Skimmed – 1 kg

L’Ancêtre Organic Swiss Cheese - Shredded – 1 kg

Life Smart Organic Part Skim Mozzarella Cheese - 200 g

“There have been no reported illnesses associated with the consumption of these products,” the recall said.

The federal agency advised customers to check if they are in possession of the recalled products and not consume, serve, use, sell or distribute them. Instead, customers are being asked to discard or return the recalled products to the location of purchase.

“Food contaminated with listeria monocytogenes May not look or smell spoiled but can still make you sick,” the recall notice said. “Symptoms can include vomiting, nausea, persistent fever, muscle aches, severe headache and neck stiffness.”

The notice also warned that pregnant women, the elderly and people with weakened immune systems are “particularly at risk.”

“Although infected pregnant women May experience only mild, flu-like symptoms, the infection can lead to premature delivery, infection of the newborn or even stillbirth,” the recall read. “In severe cases of illness, people May die.”

The recall was triggered due to test results by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) and a food safety investigation is underway which could lead to more recalls, the notice said. The Cfia is also verifying that all recalled products are being removed from the marketplace.

Life Smart Organic Part Skim Mozzarella Cheese - 200 g
“There have been no reported illnesses associated with the consumption of these products,” the recall said.

The federal agency advised customers to check if they are in possession of the recalled products and not consume, serve, use, sell or distribute them. Instead, customers are being asked to discard or return the recalled products to the location of purchase.

“Food contaminated with listeria monocytogenes May not look or smell spoiled but can still make you sick,” the recall notice said. “Symptoms can include vomiting, nausea, persistent fever, muscle aches, severe headache and neck stiffness.”
The notice also warned that pregnant women, the elderly and people with weakened immune systems are “particularly at risk.”

“Although infected pregnant women May experience only mild, flu-like symptoms, the infection can lead to premature delivery, infection of the newborn or even stillbirth,” the recall read. “In severe cases of illness, people May die.”

The recall was triggered due to test results by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) and a food safety investigation is underway which could lead to more recalls, the notice said. The Cfia is also verifying that all recalled products are being removed from the marketplace.

stories.title: The Last Word: Councillors Pribil and Hillier offer parting thoughts at final meeting
stories.summary: A pair of London city councillors who are not seeking re-election were given time at the end of Wednesday’s meeting at city hall to reflect on their time in office.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
A pair of London city councillors who are not seeking re-election were given time at the end of Wednesday’s meeting at city hall to reflect on their time in office.

Ward 14 Coun. Steve Hillier has served two terms on council representing southeast London since 2018.

Ward 5 Coun. Jerry Pribil has spent the last four years serving as the representative for neighbourhoods in northcentral London.

“I have seen everything from this seat,” explained Hillier. “I have seen backstabbing, and I have seen support. We are a family, and like all families we don’t always get along. But the one thing we do is we talk.”

He added, “I want Londoners to know this group works together. Whether or not we seem to agree, we do work together.”

Both used the opportunity to express their gratitude to city staff and recognize the contributions of their colleagues.

“Bottom line is, thank you to all of you. Thank you to the staff we really have a lot of expertise here,” Pribil remarked.

Pribil also offered advice to the next council with regards to the 35 per cent increase to base pay that comes into effect next month, “With the changes we made with the stipend, that is really is going to be for all fifteen people a full-time job because Londoners do deserve it, (and) they do need it.”

The next city council will be elected on Oct. 26.

Both Pribil and Hillier remain in their elected roles until London’s next council is sworn-in at its inaugural meeting on Nov. 17.

stories.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge conspirator indicted by grand jury in U.S.
stories.summary: James Bryant alleged to have offered advice to Jesse Van Rootselaar while broadcasting shooting on internet
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A grand jury in Washington state has indicted an alleged co-conspirator in the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooting.

The indictment of 30-year-old James Bryant for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country means there is probable cause for prosecutors to pursue the case.

Emily Langlie, a spokeswoman for the U.S. Attorney’s Office, said last week that an indictment would mean a preliminary hearing in the case scheduled for Oct. 20 would be eliminated.

Bryant, whose lawyer says she goes by “Melody” and uses female pronouns, was denied bail a day ahead of Wednesday’s indictment.

A statement issued by the U.S. Department of Justice says the indictment “details several overt acts that Bryant took to further the school shooting conspiracy.”

Eight victims were shot dead in Tumbler Ridge by 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar in February, including five pupils and a teacher at a secondary school.

Among the alleged acts the indictment of Bryant, who’s a resident of Bellingham, Wash., lists are that she agreed to record the shooting and broadcast it over the internet, offered the shooter advice on where to attack and what weapons to use, and sent Van Rootselaar money to buy a lighter for use in an improvised explosive device.

The Justice Department’s statement says conspiracy to murder in a foreign country is punishable by up to life in prison.

It cautions that the accusations against Bryant remain unproven, and says the case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Todd Greenberg with help from the Justice Department’s National Security Division.

Van Rootselaar shot herself dead at the school on Feb. 10 as police closed in.

stories.title: Fsin launches legal action over Ottawa’s $12.4M audit claim
stories.summary: The Fsin says it rejects Indigenous Services Canada’s final forensic audit decision and has launched legal action over $12.4 million in disputed spending.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta
stories.content:
The Federation of Sovereign Indigenous Nations (Fsin) says it has launched legal action after rejecting Indigenous Services Canada’s (ISC) final decision in a long-running dispute over millions of dollars in spending.

In a statement released Wednesday, the Fsin said it does not accept the federal government’s conclusion or its claim that close to $12.4 million in expenditures are ineligible.

“ISC May have concluded its process, but this matter is not concluded for the Fsin,” Chief Bobby Cameron said in the statement.

The decision marks the latest development in a dispute that earlier this year saw Indigenous Services Canada identify $28.7 million in ineligible and unsupported expenses between April 2019 and March 2024.

That figure stemmed from a forensic audit conducted by Kpmg that reviewed the Fsin’s use of federal funding for compliance with funding terms, conditions and accountability standards.

The Fsin, which represents 74 First Nations in Saskatchewan, has consistently disputed the findings and defended its spending.

In its latest statement, the organization said it participated fully in the federal review and held extensive line-by-line discussions with a negotiation team appointed by Indigenous Services Canada.

The Fsin said the two sides had substantially narrowed the amount in dispute by June 12.

According to the Fsin, federal representatives had confirmed that all purchases of personal protective equipment, accounting for almost $8 million of the current $12.4-million claim, were substantiated as purchased and delivered and had been removed from the list of ineligible or questionable expenditures.

The organization said it was surprised those expenses were subsequently added back to the amount being claimed.

The Fsin said the remaining approximately $4.4 million is mainly related to administration fees, and alleged Indigenous Services Canada has failed to provide policies supporting its position.

The dispute over pandemic-related spending has been a major part of the audit process. In March, Indigenous Services Canada identified more than $23.2 million in COVID-19-related expenditures among unsupported costs, saying at the time there was insufficient documentation to validate purchases of personal protective equipment and their delivery and distribution to First Nations.

The Fsin disputed that position, saying it had documentation supporting the rollout, including sign-offs from chiefs on deliveries. Cameron said at the time that the organization believed it had followed appropriate financial procedures.

“We fully believe that we don’t have to repay a dime,” Cameron said in March.

In Wednesday’s statement, Cameron said Fsin staff had co-operated with the federal government and provided the requested records.

“We remain confident that when this matter is subjected to a fair and independent review, that all expenditures will be proven eligible and the allegations proven false,” Cameron said.

Indigenous Services Canada confirmed the letter to Global News but did not provide a comment.

–with files Vanessa Tiberio

stories.title: London politicians hope the legacy of Irene Mathyssen will be carried on
stories.summary: There was a moment of silence in the council chambers at London City Hall on Wednesday afternoon as councillors reflected on the passing of longtime politician Irene Mathyssen.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
There was a moment of silence in the council chambers at London City Hall on Wednesday afternoon as councillors reflected on the passing of longtime politician Irene Mathyssen.

A tearful Hadleigh McAlister, the Councillor for Ward 1 stood up and said, “A lasting memory for me will be on election night four years ago, she gave me a big hug and said I’m so proud of you, now go out there and do some good.”

Moments later the Councillor for Ward 12 Elizabeth Peloza spoke of Irene and her daughter saying, “When the seat for London-Fanshawe changed from Irene to Lindsay that was a first in Canadian history for politics with a daughter succeeding her mother,” she said. “There’s a lot of work that she started and we will carry on.”

As a member of the New Democratic Party, Irene was a part of London’s political landscape over a three decade period. She first served as MPP from 1990 until 1995 and then as MP from 2006 until 2019.

Her daughter Lindsay would then hold on to the seat of London Fanshawe until 2025.

“Even here at 300 Dufferin Avenue, she never served municipally but she certainly has a legacy in this building,” said Shawn Lewis, the deputy mayor who also worked in her constituency office for 12 years before getting into politics himself.

“Irene May have been small in stature but she was a giant in this community touching thousands of lives,” said Lewis. “The work she did in Parliament on different pieces of legislation is immeasurable, for example she fought for eight years to get the HST taken off of feminine hygiene products.”

Before getting into politics, Irene was an English teacher and Lewis says she never really left that profession behind saying “I would not be here today without her influence.”

Another politician she mentored was Edmonton Strathcona MP Heather McPherson.

“Irene was an incredible force in our movement as a New Democrat,” said McPherson. “I learned so much from Irene and she would be available anytime, day or night whenever you had any questions.”

Over the past several months she had been battling cancer until it took her life over the long weekend.

The Mathyssen family is expected to have a celebration of life for Irene at a later date.

“She will be dearly missed by all of the people who loved her,” said Lewis.

McPherson added “I really cherished the time with her, I just wish it would have been longer and it should have been longer for all of us.”

Irene Mathyssen was 75 years of age.

stories.title: Céline Dion gets her own Barbie inspired by iconic 1998 Oscars look
stories.summary: A new Céline Dion Barbie recreates the Quebec superstar’s memorable 1998 Oscars look, complete with a navy gown and blue diamond necklace.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Felicia Parrillo
stories.content:
Céline Dion is joining the ranks of some of the world’s most recognizable names in miniature form, with a new Barbie inspired by one of her most memorable performances.

Mattel has created a collectible doll modelled after the Quebec-born superstar’s look at the 1998 Oscars, where Dion performed “My Heart Will Go On” in a navy blue gown and a blue diamond necklace from the movie Titanic.

The doll recreates the signature look, offering fans a miniature tribute to one of the singer’s most memorable moments on stage.

“It’s about time,” one fan said at Montreal’s Barbie Expo. “We have Cher right here, we have Beyoncé, we have a bunch of people, but we don’t have the greatest singer in the world?”

Dion joins a growing lineup of celebrity singers and fashion-inspired dolls, many of which are on display at the downtown Montreal exhibit.

For fans in Quebec, however, Dion’s addition to the collection hits particularly close to home.

“It looks a lot like her. It’s really, really accurate,” one teenage girl told Global News. “It’s really beautiful. I think it’s a great thing because Céline Dion deserves it.”

The doll comes as the 58-year-old singer makes her long-awaited return to the stage. Last month, Dion launched a sold-out residency in Paris, marking her first full-length concert in six years after revealing she had been diagnosed with stiff-person syndrome, a rare disorder that affects her mobility.

Fans say the collectible offers another way to celebrate the woman behind the music.

“It’s her work ethic that I really admire,” one fan told Global News. “She really works hard at what she does, and she deserves it.”

Organizers at the Barbie Expo say they do not yet know if or when the Dion doll will become part of their collection.

Fans can buy the doll online for $92.

stories.title: Politics Insider: Joly vows to hold Stelco owner accountable if layoffs go ahead
stories.summary: Plus, Anand meets India’s PM and B.C. leaders debate
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. Let’s look at what happened today.

Stelco Inc. owner Cleveland-Cliffs could face a forced divestment of assets or financial penalties if it proceeds with hundreds of layoffs in Canada, says the federal Industry Minister.

Stelco, which is owned by U.S. steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs, said on Sept. 28 that it was laying off up to 500 workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., saying it couldn’t compete in the galvanized steel market as a result of the trade war with the United States.

Mélanie Joly has said these layoffs are a breach of the commitments the steelmaker made when it acquired Stelco. Earlier this month, she warned she would invoke the “full force of the law” if the company didn’t comply with the agreement.

When the federal government approved Cliffs’s $3.4-billion acquisition of Stelco in 2024, it imposed legally binding conditions, including maintaining at least the same number of unionized employees in Canada for five years, as well as the vast majority of non-unionized workers.

Steven Chase and Niall McGee report that today the Industry Minister told reporters she’s not backing down and that she expects Stelco to uphold its commitments.

Joly spoke after a fireside chat at The Globe and Mail’s defence summit in Ottawa.

“Right now, a business decision or even a change in market conditions cannot be used to not follow the commitment,” Joly said, adding that Ottawa is reviewing the letter.

Defence leaders, policy makers and industry experts have gathered in Ottawa today for The Globe’s Welcome to National Defence: Mapping Canada’s growth strategy event .

. It is available exclusively to our digital subscribers. You can sign up for more than 20 other newsletters on

U.S. officials `closely watching’ for Canadian interference in midterm elections, Hoekstra says: During a recent interview on the The Really Big Show podcast, Pete Hoekstra said political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.

What about Alberta’s nine other referendum questions: Premier Danielle Smith is asking voters to consider policies that would upend immigration and require reopening the Constitution .

B.C. party leaders to face off in only debate of snap provincial election: NDP Leader David Eby, interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson and Green Leader Emily Lowan are scheduled to debate from 6:15 p.m. to 8 p.m. PT.

On our radar

Commons break: The House of Commons is on a break this week.

Prime Minister’s Day: In Ottawa, Mark Carney chaired a virtual meeting of the federal cabinet.

Party Leaders: In Toronto, Green Party Leader Elizabeth May attended the KAIROS Canada 25th anniversary celebration. No schedules released for other party leaders.

Ministers on the Road:

In New Delhi, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand , on an official visit, met with Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

In Fredericton, Energy Minister Tim Hodgson announced an investment of up to $50 - million to establish the New Brunswick Strategic Innovation Centre in Digital Forestry.

In Winnipeg, Health Minister Marjorie Michel and provincial Health Minister, Uzoma Asagwara, announced up to $6-million in federal funding to bring more family doctors into the health care system.

Political lives, Helen Branswell: The late Canadian medical journalist lauded for her coverage of infectious diseases was remembered by the director general of the World Health Organization for her “unwavering commitment to evidence, science and truth.”

Irene Mathyssen: The longtime MP, who served the London, Ont., region both provincially and federally under the NDP banner, has died at the age of 75.

How many Parti Québécois premiers has Quebec had?

Scroll to the bottom of this newsletter for the answer.

Perspectives

First past the post sets Canada up for secession threats

The separatists have never once, in 16 provincial elections and 11 federal elections, won a majority of the vote in Quebec. Provincially, they have averaged just less than a third of the vote. Yet they have governed the province six times since 1976, twice using their “majorities” to put the province, and the country, through the agonies of a referendum. — Andrew Coyne, Columnist

The cost of a mass exodus from Alberta if it goes independent

Albertans should weigh all these significant migration consequences carefully before voting on Question 10 next week. A majority vote to start the secession process, even without a widespread desire to see it go all the way, will have significant negative consequences for the Alberta economy. — Christopher Worswick is a professor of economics at Carleton University and a research fellow of the C.D. Howe Institute.

Canada to the Palestinian Authority; Stop, before we say stop again

If the Palestinian Authority is allowed to ignore its commitments, and Canada simply expresses its regret – sorry, deep regret – then why should any future commitment, by the PA or anyone else, ever be honoured? — The Globe and Mail Editorial Board

Got a news tip that you’d like us to look into? E-mail us at tips@globeandmail.com . Need to share documents securely? Reach out via SecureDrop .

The answer to today’s question: Six between René Lévesque in 1976 and Pauline Marois, who served from 2012 to 2014. Lévesque, Pierre Marc Johnson, Jacques Parizeau, Lucien Bouchard, Bernard Landry and Marois. Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, the current premier elect of the province, is also a member of the PQ.

stories.title: Major projects CEO faces B.C. First Nations’ frustrations over lack of consultations
stories.summary: First Nations in B.C. are calling on Ottawa to set national standards for Indigenous consultations on major projects, saying they were given limited time to review the proposal.
stories.author: Nick Murray and Alessia Passafiume
stories.content:
Major Projects CEO Dawn Farrell told First Nations in B.C. on Wednesday that the frustrations expressed over a lack of consultation on the Pacific Link pipeline made her feel like Canada is “never going to work,” but her office is determined to try to be better.

Farrell was addressing the B.C. Assembly of First Nations at its annual general meeting in Vancouver. Media were asked to leave the room before Farrell’s appearance, but the meeting continued to be publicly streamed on the B.C. Assembly of First Nations YouTube channel.

First Nations in B.C. are calling on Ottawa to set national standards for Indigenous consultations on major projects. They say they were given just 11 working days to review and engage on whether the proposed Pacific Link pipeline should be designated as a project of national interest.

The standard, they say, should include “minimum procedural protections,” including protected timelines for consultations before decisions are made.

The proposed pipeline from Alberta to B.C. was named a project in the national interest on Oct. 1 by Prime Minister Mark Carney alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

The designation does not eliminate the requirement for the government to consult with First Nations on the impact of the project itself. Rather, the goal is to complete the required reviews and consultations over the next year so construction can begin next September.

Tkʼemlúps te Secwépemc Chief Rosanne Casimir, who presented the call for a national consultation standard, said the current process expects First Nations to review thousands of documents under tight timelines and with limited funding.

“Even in your presentation initially starting off, you shared that there was excessive amounts of papers and documents. Well, we’re receiving that after the fact,” Casimir said, referring to an anecdote Farrell shared about having two binders of 1,200 pages on her coffee table.

“Meaningful consultation is difficult when nations, communities, are still trying to understand the project while decisions are continuing to move forward. For the (Pacific Link) oil pipeline, we raised process concerns, and Canada took nearly a month to respond and only 11 working days remained for the review and engagement.”

Farrell said she agrees with the concept of national consultation standards but she wondered how such standards would work alongside the government’s accelerated timelines for project approvals.

“I hear your pleas and I hear your discussions and I hear, you know, sort of a disbelief that it’s ever going to change, and a cynicism. And I feel like, ‘Oh my God, we can never get this country to work. Like it’s never going to work. We’ll never make it,'” Farrell said.

She added that staff in her office have “very, very big scars” from working on projects like the Trans Mountain pipeline that didn’t have the depth of Indigenous consultation the Pacific Link pipeline “has after two months.”

“Because we’re all committed in our office to try to do it better. Now, what does doing it better look like? It’s really hard to sit here and actually lay out what a day looks like and what the work looks like, and really, you’re not going to believe us at all,” Farrell said.

“No amount of presentation that I’m going to give … is going to give you a sense of what we’re trying to accomplish. The only thing that will give you that sense of it is if we actually do, in action, get to a different place.

“The best I can do is the best I can do. Our office is working hard to try to accommodate all the concerns you brought here today. And I totally get that you will not believe us until we deliver. And so we’ll mostly spend all of our time delivering, and maybe next year when we come back we’ll have some examples of how we try to deliver.”

The federal government initially planned to hold consultations for one month on whether to designate the pipeline as a project in the national interest under the Building Canada Act. That was extended to two months after Indigenous leaders raised concerns about the tight timeline.

A summary of those consultations posted online by the federal government says Indigenous groups decried a lack of information about the project, which they said prevented them from fully assessing its impact.

On Wednesday, Farrell acknowledged adequate consultation was key for seeing a project be successful.

“The projects that we have to deliver out of our office have to achieve your rights. We have to make sure that we go through your processes,” Farrell said.

“We can’t just make stuff up. The courts will just come and overturn the projects and we’ll be like Canada’s always been, 10, 15 years, dragging stuff around in the ditch and not getting it done and wasting time and money and resources, and your time and your people’s resources. We can’t keep doing that.”

Farrell faced criticism at the meeting over the federal government’s push to move quickly on approving major projects.

“Our concern is not efficiency itself. It’s whether the speed and certainty for proponents are being advanced equivalent protection for Aboriginal title and rights, our governance and the lands and waters that sustain our people,” said Shana Thomas, hereditary chief of the Lyackson First Nation.

“Consultation is something you do. We are a partner at this table and we need to be part of the decision-making process. What we have to say is not something that you can then evaluate and make your own decision based on what you think about what we said. We have to be at the table as equal partners.”

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak has said staff in the Major Projects Office do not understand how to work with First Nations communities and that “junior staffers” aren’t helping to build relationships.

She also said Farrell has been unavailable to meet with leadership, including at Assembly of First Nations gatherings.

Farrell said in the closed-door meeting Wednesday the only way she knows how to do her work is “to not talk very much.”

“They can’t get me on planes to go anywhere because I feel a huge responsibility to make sure that these projects that we’re working on hit the standards that you’re talking about today,” she said.

In an emailed statement last week, the Privy Council Office said the Major Projects Office works closely with Indigenous communities and that senior officials make themselves available to meet with communities when asked.

First Nations in B.C. also passed a resolution at Wednesday’s meeting calling on Prime Minister Mark Carney to halt the advance of the Building Canada Act and to repeal Bill C-39 if it passes through Parliament.

The legislation would fast-track approvals for major projects, cut their review times and create zones of “national interest” to pre-approve certain types of projects.

First Nations chiefs have warned the government it risks ending up in court if it approves and builds projects without their free, prior and informed consent, as outlined in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

Chiefs are set to meet with Carney and the country’s premiers in Ottawa later this month, and major projects are expected to be a major topic of debate.

stories.title: Fatal crash on Highway 401 near London
stories.summary: A fatal multi-vehicle collision south of London closed the eastbound lanes on Highway 401 for 11 hours Tuesday.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
A fatal multi-vehicle collision south of London closed the eastbound lanes on Highway 401 for 11 hours Tuesday.

There were two collisions on the eastbound side of the highway.

The first collision was at about 2:15 p.m. near Colonel Talbot Road and involved approximately three vehicles.

Just after 4 p.m. OPP responded to a second collision involving a transport truck and passenger vehicle, further down the highway near Union Road.

The transport truck collided with the rear of a passenger vehicle, that according to OPP was stopped in traffic. The vehicle burst into flames.

Highway 401 was closed between Colonel Talbot Road and Iona Road.

OPP is investigating the number of deceased individuals.

stories.title: Danielle Smith votes to stay in Canada, urges support for other 9 questions
stories.summary: Smith said in a video on social media about Monday's referendum that it's not the time to give up hope on the country, saying she voted to stay.
stories.author: Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says she has voted at an advance poll for the province to stay in Canada.

Smith says in a video on social media about Monday’s referendum that it’s not the time to give up hope on the country.

She says she knows many Albertans are frustrated with Ottawa but that the province is starting to see progress with major projects, including a proposed new oil pipeline.

The premier says if Albertans want to send a message to the federal government then they should vote in support of nine proposals also on the ballot that deal with immigration and constitutional reform.

Elections Alberta says nearly 175,000 voters trekked to the polls Tuesday for the first day of advance voting, suggesting interest remains high for the historic referendum.

The key question asks voters if they want Alberta to remain in Canada or if there should be a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi was among those who voted Tuesday, and is encouraging Albertans to reject the United Conservative Party government’s nine proposals and vote to stay in Canada.

St.Amant receives $5M provincial funding boost for autism programming

Doug Ford says Republicans might ‘pull the carpet’ under Trump if midterms are lost

Elections Alberta says nearly 175,000 voters trekked to the polls Tuesday for the first day of advance voting, suggesting interest remains high for the historic referendum.
The key question asks voters if they want Alberta to remain in Canada or if there should be a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

stories.title: Alberta's Smith casts vote to stay in Canada, urges support for other nine questions
stories.summary: Edmonton - Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says she has voted at an advance poll for the province to stay in Canada.
stories.author: Jack Farrell The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - ‘Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says she has officially marked her ballot in the provinces separation referendum — and it’s a vote for a united Canada.

“We have seen great progress lately in addressing the unfair laws and policies that have hurt Alberta,” Smith said in a video posted Wednesday to social media announcing she had voted earlier in the day.

She said she knows many Albertans are frustrated with the federal government, but said the province is starting to see headway with major projects, including a proposed new oil pipeline to the B.C. coast.

Smith encouraged fellow Albertans to vote to stay. She has long said she would vote for the province to remain in Confederation.

“Canada can still work,” she said. “We just need to make some changes.”

Monday is the official polling day but advance polls are open this week.

Smith has put 10 questions on the ballot, including one that asks whether Albertans want to stay in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on quitting Confederation.

The other nine questions deal with proposals Smith has put forward for immigration and constitutional reform. Her government seeks approval from Albertans to seek more control over immigration, along with new rules and fees for newcomers.

They also seek approval from Albertans to pursue working with other provinces to change the Constitution and devolve more power to provinces.

Smith again urged Albertans to vote yes to those nine questions.

“Voting yes to questions one through nine is how we send a message to Ottawa that provinces need more autonomy and respect if Canada is going to be stronger and unified,” she said.

Advance voting began Tuesday and ends Saturday. Elections Alberta said the first day was a busy one, with close to 175,000 voters trekking to the polls.

Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi was among those who voted Tuesday. He encouraged Albertans to reject the United Conservative Party government’s nine proposals and vote to stay in Canada.

Michelle Gurney, a spokesperson for the agency, said Tuesday’s turnout was higher than the daily average of nearly 152,000 people seen during the advance voting period in the 2023 provincial election.

Gurney said a few advance polling stations stayed open late Tuesday to accommodate those who were in line before 8 p.m., including one that kept the lights on for three hours after it was supposed to close.

Technology issues at 17 polling stations meant some also stayed late to make up for delayed openings.

Issues also came up Wednesday, when severe winds caused afternoon power outages at two rural polling stations north of Edmonton.

Elections Alberta has said it’s expecting record voter turnout for the referendum, and it saw unprecedented interest in mail-in ballot requests last month.

Gurney said Wednesday that nearly two thirds of the roughly 658,000 special ballots requested have now been returned ahead of Friday’s 5 p.m. deadline.

Polls have suggested a strong majority of Albertans want to remain in Canada, but the debate has at times been acrimonious, dividing families and neighbours.

In Coutts — a tiny village on the U.S. border that became ground zero in the anti-government COVID-19 protests — the sign wars rage.

Several pro-Canada signs and Canadian flags were present on many people’s lawns Wednesday, counterweight to an equal number of signs urging Alberta to move on from Confederation.

One home proudly had a Republic of Alberta flag beside a Montana state flag.

Coutts made headlines in early 2022 as part of the broader “Freedom Convoy” movement that erupted across Canada in protest of COVID-19 vaccine mandates and public health restrictions. Trucks and vehicles blocked the U.S. access point for two weeks, tying up traffic and disrupting trade.

Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney has said that after the pandemic, the protesters’ focus morphed into separatism.

Jim Willett, 78, the mayor of Coutts during the trucker blockade, agrees.

“They just changed flags. Separationists that are local are the ones that buy into the conspiracy theories and all of that,” said Willett, who sports a Forever Canadian lawn sign and two Canadian flags in his front yard.

Willett, who grew up in Texas, said he understands the feeling of alienation.

“I know what it’s like to live in an area where you were a Texan first and you were an American second,” he said. “You didn’t like being told what you had to do and I can understand it here.”

Scott MacCumber, the current mayor of Coutts, declined a request for an interview.

William Harty, 72, has operated the Double Tree Motel in the village for a quarter century, and said he supports the decision to hold a vote. But he said he doesn’t support Alberta leaving Canada.

“I believe it’s a good deal to send a message, but I want to stay in Canada,” he said.

“If we separate, (U.S. President Donald) Trump May come in and take us over.”

He said having the vote might be what’s needed to get Ottawa’s attention.

“They’re getting a lot more money out of Alberta,” he said.

“Be a little more fair.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

— With files from Bill Graveland in Coutts, Alta.

stories.title: New Brunswick government says it was late to report inmate death
stories.summary: The New Brunswick government says it should have notified the public sooner about the death of a provincial jail inmate on Oct. 10.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
The New Brunswick government says it should have notified the public sooner about the death of a provincial jail inmate on Oct. 10.

The Department of Justice and Public Safety released details about the death four days later.

The department has a policy of informing the public of deaths in custody within 12 hours.

Bruce Macfarlane, a provincial government spokesperson, says the department is reviewing the matter and will take steps to lower the risk of future delays.

The department says Pierre Dartiguenave, 50, was found unresponsive in his cell at the Saint John Regional Correctional Centre on Oct. 7 and later died in hospital on Oct. 10.

The department also noted in a news release that staff attempted to resuscitate Dartiguenave and provide medical assistance as emergency services were called.

Macfarlane says Dartiguenave was on life support for days following his medical emergency.

Dartiguenave’s family was notified, Macfarlane told The Canadian Press on Wednesday. He did not say what caused the delay.

stories.title: Media executive Salah Bachir was a singular figure of bedazzled benevolence
stories.summary: He built a highly successful career working in movie magazines, was also a philanthropist who helped artistic organizations, 2SLGBTQ+ causes and other underserved communities
stories.author: Josh O’Kane
stories.content:
Salah Bachir crashed into Canadian culture with a singular verve, imprinting his generous vision across massive swaths of the country’s arts and queer communities. He breathed life into Canada’s film magazines while brushing elbows with the people who bring life onto the screen. He sought out the stories that made those people relatable, while his own style brought a flashy rebelliousness to corporate Canada. He was outspoken about his own queerness and chose brooches over neckties – “he was too busy putting jewellery on,” his husband, the visual artist Jacob Yerex, said.

In spite of his stylistic flair, Mr. Bachir did not necessarily enjoy the spotlight , so he directed it elsewhere. At the galas he hosted – an endless stream, according to his friends – he shone it on causes he deemed important and people whom he mentored and befriended.

For Mathieu Chantelois, the executive vice-president of communications and strategy with the Canada Media Fund, this became almost like a father-son relationship.

“Salah introduced me to two prime ministers, two premiers, two mayors, two governors-general, to Elton John, to k.d. lang, to Valentino – but what he really did was he introduced me to his wonderful circle of friends,” said Mr. Chantelois, who first came under Mr. Bachir’s wing while editing the Quebec edition of his Famous Players magazine a quarter-century ago, and would later become executive director of Pride Toronto. “He was surrounded by incredible people – people that were advocating for queer rights in this country, people that were fighting for newcomers, for immigrants, for social justice.”

This included Mr. Bachir’s work with The 519, the storied community centre for 2SLGBTQ+ people in Toronto’s Gay Village. Two decades ago, he led a capital campaign to renovate and expand The 519’s building; a wing now bears his name. He also led its annual fundraising gala for years. “Salah helped make The 519’s future possible,” said Maura Lawless, its executive director. “He understood that queer communities needed a place to gather, organize, celebrate and receive care – and that such a place deserved ambition and investment.”

Mr. Bachir racked up an extraordinary amount of accolades: he was a member of the Order of Canada and the Order of Ontario; he served as chancellor of Ocad University; he received five honorary doctorates; he served twice as grand marshal of the Toronto Pride parade. (“I always felt Salah was pretty much the grand marshal of everything he got involved with,” said his friend, filmmaker Atom Egoyan.)

Gallery spaces and community centres across Toronto bear Mr. Bachir’s name, including at the 519 and the Art Gallery of Ontario. Stephan Jost, the gallery’s director and chief executive, said Mr. Bachir was “always the life of a party – he loved art and people and smart conversation that connected all of the threads. He lived surrounded by art and immersed himself in a world of artists, thinkers, and creators.”

The film executive, philanthropist and merry gala-runner received medical assistance in death on Oct. 8 after years of kidney problems, which were followed by a compromised immune system, an inability to walk or stand, and what he told friends was relentless pain. He was 71.

Salah John Bachir was born on Oct. 3, 1955, in Kfar Hatta, Lebanon, and moved to Canada with his family at the age of 10, settling in the Toronto-area suburb of Rexdale. He studied at the University of Waterloo, where his time in student journalism gave him an affection for salesmanship. Selling newspaper ads helped him understand the importance of relationships in getting things done.

This was profoundly helpful when, after working at his brother George’s early video-rental store , the pair launched the magazine Videomania in 1982, focused on the fast-rising world of home video. Mr. Bachir rarely rested – in fact, friends say he rarely slept at all – and soon after he launched Premiere Magazine and the Focus on Video trade show, which helped him build his wealth and a bustling network of film-industry bigwigs.

“He was a success because he was fun to do business with,” said Cathy Prowse, who worked closely with Mr. Bachir for three decades across numerous ventures.

As the industry shifted, so did Mr. Bachir, moving on from the home-video world to the cinema world, but his focus on advertising remained. His ability to maintain relationships extended well beyond his life in business, she said: It helped him build a network of people to tap when raising money for causes he believed in.

Mr. Bachir rallied around causes that helped underserved communities, including Lgbtq organizations, and the artistic world, in which he deeply immersed himself. He earned the half-joking nickname “Gala Salah” for the dozens of fundraising galas he hosted to raise money.

“If you had Salah on your side and he believed in what you were trying to do, he was a magician,” said Chris Abraham, artistic director of Crow’s Theatre in Toronto, for which Mr. Bachir raised a “significant amount of money” in the past decade.

This endless stream of fundraising galas allowed Mr. Bachir to develop a series of rules for success, which his husband, Mr. Yerex, can recount from memory: “Short speeches. He talked Lebanese food with Marlon Brando; he had regular check-in calls with filmmaker Norman Jewison .

Even Mr. Bachir’s wedding in 2015 reflected his gala strategy. Mr. Bachir spent much of his later life struggling with health problems. He lived with HIV and Type 1 diabetes, and spent the 2010s struggling with his kidneys; he needed dialysis for seven years until 2019, when he received a transplant. (He made sure to thank his donor, Tracey Agnew, in his self-written obituary.) It was through this process that he became a patron of St. Joseph’s Health Centre; both of its dialysis centres are named after him and Mr. Yerex, and the couple also arranged for lights to illuminate the hospital’s exterior over the winter.

In fact, he purchased a literal truckload of lights as a surprise, said Maria Dyck, president and CEO of the St. Joseph’s Health Centre Foundation. “I got a call from our shipping and receiving department – ‘Maria, your UPS truck is here,’” she recalled. “He then raised the funds for the installation and started a tradition of the hospital lighting up over the holidays.

“Through his care, Salah came to know and deeply value the contributions of St. Joe’s physicians, nurses and staff, and he thought the hospital’s dark exterior didn’t reflect the warmth and care within.”

He told friends that complications from the transplant, however, only furthered his decline in health, leading to his decision to receive medical assistance in dying this month at his home in Toronto.

Mr. Bachir leaves Mr. Yerex; his stepdaughter, Ivy Yerex; siblings, Anissa Beale, George Bachir and Ziad Bachir; and an extended family that includes eight nieces and nephews, eight grandnieces and grandnephews, and 15 godchildren.

For his funeral service, at the Turner & Porter Yorke chapel in Toronto’s west end on Thursday at 11 a.m., he insisted that those in attendance wear vibrant colours – and that his favourite colour, black, be banned.

stories.title: London teen creates ‘digital passport’ designed to make volunteering easier for students
stories.summary: Angela Kalopisis, 17, noticed significant challenges while completing the mandatory 40 volunteer hours required to graduate high school, one of them being schools are still using paper volunteer sheets.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
Angela Kalopisis, 17, noticed significant challenges while completing the mandatory 40 volunteer hours required to graduate high school, one of them being schools are still using paper volunteer sheets.

“For me, verifying these hours and submitting to my school is sometimes difficult because I’ll forget the paper,” said Kalopisis. “Even after getting assigned, it’s very easy to lose.”

Kalopisis said she wanted to create a system that was more practical for students.

“I wanted to create the digital passport to create a long-standing digital record that can be transferred across schools, scholarships, and anything needing volunteer recognition,” she said.

The passport is available through My Volunteer Platform (MVP), a website designed by Kalopisis.

She said the platform is aimed at connecting volunteers with organizations looking for support.

“The volunteers come to the website and take a look at all the opportunity listing cards,” said Kalopisis. “From there, they can apply and organizations decide whether to approve or deny.”

Emma Aldred, volunteer coordinator with the London Food Bank said she thinks it is a “fantastic” idea.

“It’s great to have lots of different people in the community that are looking to be change makers and looking to encourage other people to volunteer,” said Aldred.

“To hear especially that our youth are sharing that passion as well as having the same mindset of finding different ways to give back but then encouraging and making it easier for people to find those opportunities,” said Aldred. “I think it is a great thing.”

MVP currently has 70 volunteers and 16 registered organizations.

“It’s a nice way to stay involved in your community and give back to the programs we have all benefitted from,” said Kalopisis. “I hope to continue working on this project after high school.”

stories.title: Mastermind of Toronto airport gold heist testifies that Ptsd, prison conditions have robbed him of his memory
stories.summary: The prosecutor at the trial of Parmpal Sidhu quickly became frustrated as Arsalan Chaudhary said he could not recall names, dates and places
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
One of the admitted masterminds behind Canada’s largest gold heist who has been ordered to testify in court against a co-accused — and against his will — said his memory is fried because of Ptsd from being kidnapped, poor treatment in prison and a lack of sleep.

Arsalan Chaudhary, who previously pleaded guilty for his role orchestrating the Toronto airport gold heist, was subpoenaed by Crown prosecutors to be the star witness at the trial of Parmpal Sidhu, a former Air Canada employee in the cargo warehouse from where the crate of gold and cash, worth more than $22 million, was stolen in 2023 shortly after it arrived on a flight from Switzerland.

On Tuesday, he told a dramatic story of being one of two key organizers of the successful plot to steal the loot and then of losing his 30 per cent share to kidnappers in Pakistan, where he fled after the heist. The kidnappers, he said, were members of the Pakistani police, who grabbed him and tortured him until he revealed where the gold was hidden. His captors used contacts in Canada to secure the gold before releasing him.

He said the ordeal left him psychologically scarred and suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder.

By midday Tuesday, the first day of Chaudhary’s testimony, Crown prosecutor Jelena Vlacic was already appearing increasingly frustrated by Chaudhary’s answers.

He said he could not recall important names, dates and places.

He said he did not know whether a phone that police seized from his apartment where he lived alone was his, nor could be recall his phone number, or if messages police extracted from the phone were from him, to him, or anything to do with him. She led him through a 34-page print out of text messages, and chats using the encrypted messaging apps Signal and WhatsApp, none of which he said were familiar to him.

Vlacic asked him about a WhatsApp group chat extracted from the phone called “Let’s Roll” from the time of the gold heist.

“Does that group chat name mean anything to you?”

“Do any of those participant names mean anything to you?”

He was also asked about two debt lists seized by police that appear to be breakdowns of how the heist profits were divided. He said the lists were make-believe, one just to satisfy his kidnappers in Pakistan.

“It was just a bunch of names that I put on, whatever. It didn’t mean anything,” he said.

Vlacic asked about the name “Hulk” appearing both as a contact name on the phone, in the group chat, and on the debt list.

“I don’t know, ma’am,” he said. “I can’t recall this chat, ma’ am.”

What he did recall about the people who had been charged for the gold heist by Peel Regional Police, he told court, is that most of them didn’t know anything about the plan to steal gold.

Vlacic said she planned to ask for permission to cross-examine the witness, a court process that would allow her to challenge her own witness’s testimony.

Judge Gordon Cudjoe said they weren’t at that stage yet and told Vlacic to try again.

All of that preceded Wednesday’s hearing. The day started with little promise of revelations.

Just a few minutes into questioning by Vlacic, Chaudhary interrupted.

“Last night I couldn’t sleep well because I had Ptsd from what I’ve gone through,” he said. “My memory is very vague and I have locked out a lot of stuff from my memory.

“If you’d been through that trauma that I’ve been through and been shocked and had bruises, you would probably understand where I’m coming from… Even talking about all of this, you can probably hear from my voice right now. Last night, I couldn’t sleep. I had terrors, night terrors. I couldn’t eat.

“So that’s why I’m not able to help you, but I would like to.”

After a break, Vlacic tried again, but Chaudhary seemed even further from answering.

He said he had been moved from his federal prison of Collins Bay, near Kingston, Ont., to a provincial facility, Maplehurst Correctional Complex, in Milton, Ont., to be closer to court for his testimony. He said he has been at Maplehurst for nearly three weeks and is not getting his medication.

“It has been messing with my memory, especially last night, so I’m not in a very good state of mind to help you remember stuff.

“I’ve been in Maplehurst, living with three people in a cell by a toilet, and I’ve been getting no medical attention. I’ve asked for it. So I’m not in the right state of mind to remember stuff you’re asking me.”

He was asked what would help him settle his state of mind.

“I’m not a doctor, ma’am. I don’t know,” he said. But he did have some ideas: a transfer back to Collins Bay where he could take his meds, and where all of his belongings are, and perhaps allow him to testify by video link instead of in person.

Court took another break.

Afterwards, the judge issued an order for Chaudhary to be returned to Collins Bay, where he could take his medication and get better sleep and then be brought directly to court on Monday to continue his testimony.
