stories.title: Roughriders hitting tough spell at end of season
stories.summary: These are difficult times for quarterback Trevor Harris and the Saskatchewan Roughriders.
stories.author: Dan Ralph
stories.content:
These are difficult times for quarterback Trevor Harris and the Saskatchewan Roughriders.

The defending Grey Cup champions have dropped four straight games. And matters don’t get any easier Saturday when Saskatchewan (8-8) hosts Montreal (13-3) to complete a home-and-home series.

The Alouettes took last week’s contest 44-24 at Molson Stadium, the first meeting between the two teams since last year’s Grey Cup game.

But Saskatchewan would punch its playoff ticket with a win over Montreal and a loss by either Calgary or Winnipeg loss. The Blue Bombers (8-8) visit the Edmonton Elks (12-4) on Friday night while the Stampeders (8-9) host the B.C. Lions (10-6) on Saturday night.

Neither Saskatchewan nor Calgary can host a playoff contest. Edmonton can clinch first in the West — and host the division final Nov. 7 — with either a win over Winnipeg or a B.C. loss.

The Lions can clinch a home playoff game with a win or Winnipeg loss. The Bombers can secure a post-season berth with a victory or Calgary loss.

The East is set with Montreal having clinched first. The Toronto Argonauts (9-7) will finish second and host the division semifinal Oct. 31 versus the West crossover squad.

Last week, Montreal starter Davis Alexander threw for 403 yards with five touchdowns and an interception versus Saskatchewan. The Alouettes also converted 13-of-21 second-down opportunities and accumulated 524 net offensive yards.

Alexander leads the CFL in passing yards (5,247), TDs (35) and completion percentage (72.1).

Harris completed 23-of-33 passes for 243 yards with two TDs and an interception.

There is a question of how much Alexander and Montreal’s other starters will play. The Alouettes enter action tops in offensive points scored (33.8 per game) and second overall in net offence (430.6 yards) and passing (334.4) while also averaging 106.1 yards rushing per contest.

Conversely, Saskatchewan is fourth in passing (320.8 per game), fifth in both offensive points (27.5 per game) and net offensive yards (401.6) but a distant seventh in rushing (89.8 yards).

Montreal also leads the CFL in 30-plus yard completions (37) and is second in fewest 30-plus yard passes allowed (16, one behind Hamilton). Canadian Tyson Philpot needs 228 receiving yards over the Als’ final two games to break Allen Pitts’s single-season record of 2,036.

Despite Saskatchewan’s struggles, Harris stands second overall in passing (5,117) and sports a solid 70.1 per cent completion average. While Harris has 31 TD tosses, his 14 interceptions are tied for second-most by a CFL starter.

Saskatchewan is 5-3 at home and should be the more desperate team.

Pick: Saskatchewan.

Toronto Argonauts vs. Ottawa Redblacks (Friday night)

At Ottawa, Chad Kelly is expected to start for Toronto, which comes off a bye week. Kelly (right hand) didn’t play in the Argos’ 24-17 home loss to B.C. on Oct. 3 but practised fully this week. How much he and other starters play remains unclear. Newcomer Bryson Barnes starts for Ottawa (0-16) and is expected to do so for its regular-season finale in Hamilton on Oct. 24. The six-foot-one, 213-pound Barnes has been used mostly in short-yardage situations, having scored nine rushing TDs. He has completed 10-of-13 passes for 110 yards with an interception.

Pick: Toronto.

Winnipeg Blue Bombers vs. Edmonton Elks (Friday night)

At Edmonton, the Elks look to sweep the three-game season series. More importantly, the Elks are chasing first place in the West Division. The Alberta club has won two straight and six of its last seven games overall. Veteran starter Zach Collaros made a triumphant return last week for Winnipeg, passing for 349 yards and two TDs in the 33-28 win over Calgary after missing two games with a head injury. The Bombers are 6-4 with Collaros under centre, but CFL rushing leader Brady Oliveira (1,307 yards) should get more than the eight carries (40 yards) he had against Calgary.

Pick: Edmonton.

B.C. Lions vs. Calgary Stampeders (Saturday night)

At Calgary, B.C. has won four straight and nine of its last 10. Nathan Rourke threw for 360 yards and three TDs in last week’s 41-20 home win over Ottawa. Zander Horvath ran for 89 yards and two TDs, giving him 18 rushing scores and 21 overall. He needs one more rushing touchdown to tie Mike Pringle’s single-season record and two more TDs to tie Milt Stegall’s overall mark. The Stampeders (8-9) missed a chance last week to clinch a playoff spot by losing to Winnipeg. Vernon Adams Jr. had 284 passing yards and a TD while rushing for 38 yards on five carries. If the Stamps drop this, they’ll need Saskatchewan to lose out to reach the playoffs.

Last week: 3-1.

Overall: 50-23.

stories.title: Doug Ford says Republicans might ‘pull the carpet’ under Trump if midterms are lost
stories.summary: As the mid-term elections draw closer, Ford is dipping a toe into American politics, stating that the Democrats might be able to flip the Senate and House of Representatives.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford is predicting that Republicans might “pull the carpet out from underneath” U.S. President Donald Trump if the party loses the midterm elections in November, but warns that little would change for Canadians impacted by tariffs.

During a speech and fireside chat at the Empire Club, Ford also appeared to hold back his views on American politics and expressed concerns that Trump might use his comments to retaliate against its northern neighbour.

In recent months, as the trade war between the two countries escalated, Ford and Trump took multiple verbal swipes at one another.

In August, Ford called Trump a “loser,” the “king of bankruptcies,” and told him to “kiss my ass” while Trump called Ford the “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, (former Toronto Mayor) Rob Ford”.

The war of words ended with the White House renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America, and Ford erecting a $25,000 sign asserting the correct name.

As the mid-term elections draw closer, however, Ford is once again dipping a toe into American politics, offering new hope that the Democrats might be able to flip the Senate and House of Representatives on Nov. 3.

“President Trump is not going to last forever. He has a couple more years,” Ford told the audience.

“I spent 20 years of my life in the U.S. If he loses the Senate and the House, the Republicans are just going to pull the carpet out from underneath him. He has about a 30 per cent base (support), but that’s even being dwindled down as well,” he said.

Ford’s comments come amid a warning from U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra to Canadian politicians to “keep your nose out of American politics”

During an appearance on The Really Big Show podcast, Hoekstra said Ford’s infamous 2025 Ronald Reagan commercial amounted to “election interference” and said the Trump administration is “closely watching Canadian activities.”

“We’re monitoring it, we’re evaluating it, and if some of it becomes election interference then we’ll respond to it.”

When asked during the fireside chat whether Trump could be “weakened by his own party” after the midterms, Ford said: “I got to pick my words here.”

“He’ll change another lake on me if I say anything else.”

stories.title: Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturer Pharmaline setting up shop in London’s Innovation Park
stories.summary: London’s pharmaceutical industry is about to expand. The city has attracted Mississauga-based manufacturer Pharmaline.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
London’s pharmaceutical industry is about to expand. The city has attracted Mississauga-based manufacturer Pharmaline.

It’s the latest addition to a growing sector of London industry based around pharmaceutical and medical manufacturers.

“We have a really mature and robust industrial land development strategy, and we’ve got Ledc (London Economic Development Corporation) going out there and selling us to the world,” exclaimed London Mayor Josh Morgan.

The company is described as a pharmaceutical and nutraceutical contract manufacturer.

It plans to build a new 90,000 sq. ft. facility on five acres of land at London’s Innovation Park next to Veteran’s Parkway and Highway 401.

London City Council approved the deal in a closed-door session Wednesday.

“And at a time when the unemployment rate is high. At a time when we’re facing significant headwinds internationally, every single job we can create here in this community is a long-term, good-paying job that helps with that,” said Morgan.

The Ledc says the facility will introduce advanced manufacturing technologies for tablets, capsules, powders, gummy, and softgel products.

The facility is designed to support 300 products.

Ledc President and CEO Kapil Lakhotia says up to 70 skilled jobs will be created.

“This includes a lot of different occupations, in quality-control testing, R&D new product development. Because it’s a regulated environment, there’s a lot of attention to detail. A lot of different scientific work being done there,” he explained.

Lakotia says the company’s decision to set up shop in London has to do, in part, with reducing reliance on imports, and strengthening the domestic supply chain.

“Well that is certainly top of mind for this company, to increase its Made In Canada footprint,” he said.

“And pharmaceutical companies are companies that aren’t going to go away. So, once they make an investment, they’re here for the long haul,” added Morgan.

The value of investment by Pharmaline has not been released. Construction is expected to begin within the next year.

stories.title: Alberta’s referendum draws 174K ballots in the 1st day of advance polls
stories.summary: 'When polling indicates that you’re on the winning side, complacency sets in. We saw that with Brexit, we saw that in elections,' Lukaszuk said.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
More than 174,500 Albertans cast their ballots in the province’s referendum on the first day of advance polls Monday, as both separatist and pro-Canada groups focus on getting their supporters out in a campaign where experts say turnout will be critical.

Elections Alberta said Tuesday that a total of 174,532 people voted on the first of five advance polling days ahead of the Oct. 19 vote. For context, advanced polls in the 2023 provincial general election saw an average of 151,727 Albertans vote per day.

With the roughly 418,000 mail-in ballots already approved by Elections Alberta, early turnout for the Oct. 19 referendum — which includes a question on whether the province should begin the process to hold a vote on separating from Canada — looks to be strong.

For both separatist and pro-Canada campaigners, the focus has shifted from attempting to persuade voters to their side and is now increasingly on getting their supporters to the polls.

Thomas Lukaszuk, the former Alberta cabinet minister who has been spearheading the Forever Canadian campaign, said they have approximately 18,000 volunteers working to get out the vote ahead of Oct. 19.

“Albertans are very passionate about being Canadian … so I’m not surprised that Albertans are lining up to cast their votes, because they’re quite angry that they’re being put through this, that they have to prove to someone how proud they are to be Canadian,” Lukaszuk said in an interview.

“And I think they want to send a strong message to (Premier) Danielle Smith, to the rest of Canada … and frankly to the world that Alberta is not going to be the weak link in our confederation.”

Still, Lukaszuk allowed that the separatist voters are very motivated — suggesting they’d “crawl over broken glass” to cast their ballot. But Lukaszuk said the Forever Canadian organization was “laser focused” on identifying voters and making sure they cast their ballot.

Albertans aren’t actually voting on whether to separate, but on whether they want to begin the legal process to hold a second binding referendum on independence.

An Ipsos poll conducted between Sept. 18 and 22 exclusively for Global News found that 70 per cent of Albertan respondents wanted to remain part of Canada, while just 20 per cent said they wanted an independence referendum.

The current referendum has a total of 10 government-initiated questions, mostly to do with immigration and constitutional issues. Only one question is on the possibility of an independence referendum.

Ipsos found that a strong majority of respondents (76 per cent) were aware that there were multiple questions on the ballot, and that 62 per cent intended to vote on all 10 questions.

The Ipsos findings also suggest that there May be more Albertans willing to provoke an independence referendum than there are who actually want the province to separate. While 20 per cent said they’d vote to hold a binding referendum, just 14 per cent said they’d actually vote to leave.

There is a sense in Alberta that voters are also not viewing the referendum in isolation, according to Andrew MacKendrick, a former political staffer who has worked both for the Alberta NDP and the federal Liberals.

MacKendrick said the risk of a binding independence referendum at a time of geopolitical and economic instability is also a motivating factor to get Albertans to the ballot box.

“We have daily updates of whatever Trump is saying about Canada, we have companies all over the country talking about layoffs because of tariffs. And I think the risk factor is so large right now that the frustration (of the referendum) gets combined with, ‘There’s a big risk if I don’t participate,’” MacKendrick said in an interview.

“I think there’s a much higher combined motivation-risk vote that hopefully most folks will pick up on.”

For Lukaszuk’s part, he said he’s not taking anything for granted.

“When polling indicates that you’re on the winning side, complacency sets in. We saw that with Brexit, we saw that in elections,” he said.

“The last part of the campaign is the most important one.”

With the roughly 418,000 mail-in ballots already approved by Elections Alberta, early turnout for the Oct. 19 referendum — which includes a question on whether the province should begin the process to hold a vote on separating from Canada — looks to be strong.
For both separatist and pro-Canada campaigners, the focus has shifted from attempting to persuade voters to their side and is now increasingly on getting their supporters to the polls.

Thomas Lukaszuk, the former Alberta cabinet minister who has been spearheading the Forever Canadian campaign, said they have approximately 18,000 volunteers working to get out the vote ahead of Oct. 19.

“Albertans are very passionate about being Canadian … so I’m not surprised that Albertans are lining up to cast their votes, because they’re quite angry that they’re being put through this, that they have to prove to someone how proud they are to be Canadian,” Lukaszuk said in an interview.
“And I think they want to send a strong message to (Premier) Danielle Smith, to the rest of Canada … and frankly to the world that Alberta is not going to be the weak link in our confederation.”

Still, Lukaszuk allowed that the separatist voters are very motivated — suggesting they’d “crawl over broken glass” to cast their ballot. But Lukaszuk said the Forever Canadian organization was “laser focused” on identifying voters and making sure they cast their ballot.
Albertans aren’t actually voting on whether to separate, but on whether they want to begin the legal process to hold a second binding referendum on independence.

An Ipsos poll conducted between Sept. 18 and 22 exclusively for Global News found that 70 per cent of Albertan respondents wanted to remain part of Canada, while just 20 per cent said they wanted an independence referendum.

The current referendum has a total of 10 government-initiated questions, mostly to do with immigration and constitutional issues. Only one question is on the possibility of an independence referendum.
Ipsos found that a strong majority of respondents (76 per cent) were aware that there were multiple questions on the ballot, and that 62 per cent intended to vote on all 10 questions.

The Ipsos findings also suggest that there May be more Albertans willing to provoke an independence referendum than there are who actually want the province to separate. While 20 per cent said they’d vote to hold a binding referendum, just 14 per cent said they’d actually vote to leave.

There is a sense in Alberta that voters are also not viewing the referendum in isolation, according to Andrew MacKendrick, a former political staffer who has worked both for the Alberta NDP and the federal Liberals.
MacKendrick said the risk of a binding independence referendum at a time of geopolitical and economic instability is also a motivating factor to get Albertans to the ballot box.

“We have daily updates of whatever Trump is saying about Canada, we have companies all over the country talking about layoffs because of tariffs. And I think the risk factor is so large right now that the frustration (of the referendum) gets combined with, ‘There’s a big risk if I don’t participate,’” MacKendrick said in an interview.
“I think there’s a much higher combined motivation-risk vote that hopefully most folks will pick up on.”
For Lukaszuk’s part, he said he’s not taking anything for granted.
“When polling indicates that you’re on the winning side, complacency sets in. We saw that with Brexit, we saw that in elections,” he said.
“The last part of the campaign is the most important one.”

stories.title: One arrested as cyclists attempt to block Toronto bike lane removal
stories.summary: Ontario presses ahead with plan to overhaul up to 19 kilometres of city’s protected bike lane network
stories.author: Jordan Omstead
stories.content:
Demonstrators trying for a second day to block roadwork to remove Toronto bike lanes were met by police on Wednesday afternoon, deepening a faceoff between Premier Doug Ford’s government and cycling advocates.

The work comes as the province pressed ahead with its plan to overhaul up to 19 kilometres of the city’s protected bike lane network, starting on the premier’s home turf in Etobicoke. The province has framed it as a traffic relief measure, but critics say it’s an example of provincial overreach that will make streets less safe, and no less congested.

A protest Tuesday night ended peacefully when construction crews were escorted from Bloor Street by police and demonstrators chanted “get home safe” to the workers in trucks carrying stacks of pylons.

But at Wednesday afternoon’s protest, at least one demonstrator in a green bike helmet was led away in handcuffs by two police officers. Nearby, a worker in high-visibility vests took down a bike lane sign.

Police confirmed a 25-year-old demonstrator from Hamilton was arrested and charged with mischief and obstructing a peace officer.

The work along a roughly one-kilometre stretch of Bloor between Islington Avenue and Royal York Road took place despite efforts by the city to propose alternatives that would keep bike lanes while restoring a lane of traffic, the mayor’s spokesperson has said, a compromise already used further west along Bloor.

In a statement after Tuesday’s protest, Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said, “make no mistake: these bike lanes are coming out”.

The minister’s spokesperson did not respond to questions Tuesday about the cost of the work, or whether it would keep a bike lane intact.

Michael Longfield, executive director of Cycle Toronto, said in an interview ahead of Wednesday’s demonstration that he expected protests to continue “until further notice.”

“It’s not about addressing traffic congestion and very disappointingly, it seems like rather than, you know, try to find those win-win solutions, they’re just doubling down on spite,” said Longfield, executive director of Cycle Toronto, in an interview earlier Wednesday.

An engineering report commissioned by the province found any congestion benefits from taking out bike lanes would be negligible or short-lived. The same report, surfaced in a court challenge of the plan, found bike lanes were predicted to reduce crashes among all road users by between 35 and 50 per cent.

The latest construction between Islington and Royal York was expected to run through Nov. 17, according to a notice on the city’s website. The work was to take place overnight, the notice suggests, but advocates had caught wind after Tuesday’s protest of plans for the construction crews to return daytime Wednesday.

Cycle Toronto is one of the parties to a constitutional challenge of the province’s bike lane plan. A lower court initially blocked the plan as an unconstitutional safety risk, but the Appeal Court overturned that decision and said the trial judge had overstepped into the legislature’s policy-making and political purview.

The group announced Tuesday it would ask the Supreme Court to hear the case.

Mayor Olivia Chow, who is campaigning for re-election, linked bike lanes to other issues where the province has sought to override the city’s position, including the island airport expansion and the removal of automated speed cameras.

“It’s a gigantic waste of money, and it’s trampling on local democracy. It’s unacceptable and it’s outrageous,” Chow said of the bike lanes plan.

Brad Bradford, her main challenger in the race, has supported removing the Bloor bike lanes in Etobicoke, citing the frustration of some local businesses, but left open the question about what to do with the other targeted lanes.

“The people who live and work there decide, street by street, with their city. Not from a podium, and not from the provincial legislature,” Bradford said in a statement.

The city pegged the cost to remove all targeted bike lanes on Bloor, Yonge Street and University Avenue at $48-million, a figure disputed by the province, which has yet to provide its own. Sarkaria has said earlier work that restored a lane of traffic but kept a bike lane on a stretch of Bloor from Kipling Avenue to Islington would cost $750,000.

Last month, the province put out a bid request to study and design options to restore vehicle traffic on bike lane sections of the affected roads, and said the successful bidder would be expected to look for ways to retain or reconfigure bike lanes, “where they make sense and do not make gridlock worse.”

stories.title: Canada would never interfere in U.S. elections, Joly says after ambassador’s accusation
stories.summary: Pete Hoekstra tells podcast that Canada could be interfering in U.S. midterms
stories.author: Steven Chase, Laura Stone
stories.content:
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is rejecting an accusation by U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra that Canada might be interfering in the coming U.S. midterm elections.

In a recent interview on a Canadian podcast, Mr. Hoekstra referenced the actions of several Canadian politicians, including Ms. Joly, and said the U.S. is “closely watching Canadian activities” right now.

“It appears that some of this – from our perspective, in the way we view our elections – could be inferred to be election interference,” the U.S. ambassador told The Really Big Show podcast in an episode that was published this week .

“You have Minister Joly talking about, ‘Of course we are going to target retaliatory tariffs in politically sensitive states,’ ” he said.

As another example, Mr. Hoekstra mentioned an Ontario government TV ad that ran in the United States last year that criticized U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods.

“We appreciate foreign-policy leaders coming into the United States and those types of things, but you know, keep your nose out of American politics,” Mr. Hoekstra said.

“We’re monitoring it, we’re evaluating it, and if some of it becomes election interference, you know, then America will respond to it.”

The U.S. embassy in Canada posted a clip from the interview on its X account Wednesday saying their envoy was speaking “about political interference in U.S. elections.”

Ms. Joly said Canada is not interfering in U.S. politics and said it’s “absolutely not” fair of Mr. Hoekstra to suggest that.

We “would never do that,” she told reporters in Ottawa, and said Canada would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says Canada would never interfere in U.S. elections. Her comments came after U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra said Canadians should keep their noses out of American politics during the congressional midterms.

The Canadian Press

She summarized her recent trips to the United States, saying she has met with business people and political leaders from both Democrats and Republicans to attract new investment to Canada.

“I’ve been to Boston, engaging with the governor there. I’ve been also to Illinois and also engaging with the governor, JB Pritzker, there,” the minister said. “I’ve been also to Nasa in Florida,” she said.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” Ms. Joly said, adding that she hopes to soon announce “good news of investments by different American companies” in Canada.

She said her job is to persuade foreign investors to put their capital in Canada.

“That’s exactly what I’m doing, and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Ms. Joly spoke to reporters after a fireside chat at The Globe and Mail’s defence summit in Ottawa.

Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump again belittled Canada Wednesday, saying that the country will “end up being the 51st state.”

“Canada treats us very badly. They always have. Not any more. It’s a whole different ball game now that Trump is in town,” he said during a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Ariz.

Mr. Hoekstra’s talk of Canadian political interference follows similar accusations last month by Trump adviser Peter Navarro, who told Canadian lobbyists to “get the hell out” of the U.S. and warned Canada against interfering in U.S. midterm elections.

Prime Minister Mark Carney was later asked about Mr. Navarro’s comments and laughed at a reporter’s question, saying he had “no response” to the adviser’s caution.

The comments from two U.S. figures connected to the Trump administration come as the Republicans face difficult midterm election races in which the cost of living and U.S. tariffs on foreign goods have been prominent political issues.

Meanwhile, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Wednesday that Canada’s relationship with the U.S. has “changed permanently.”

He also said Canada needs to act as though tariffs are here to stay.

“Next month will mark two years since President Trump was re-elected. It has been two years of crisis, chaos from the White House. Ripped up trade deals, tariffs, threats of annexation and economic force,” said Mr. Ford, speaking to a crowd of about 1,200 people at an Empire Club of Canada luncheon in downtown Toronto.

“We can no longer depend on this being the most durable, prosperous and secure economic partnership the world has ever known. … We need to plan as if tariffs are here for good. We need to ensure that Canada’s future is in Canadian hands, now and always.”

The Ontario Premier, speaking during a question-and-answer session with former Newfoundland and Labrador premier Andrew Furey, also predicted that Mr. Trump could lose control of Congress, which includes the House of Representatives and the Senate, in November’s midterms.

“We need to continue building relationships because President Trump is not going to last forever,” Mr. Ford said.

“If he loses the Senate and the House, the Republicans are just going to pull the carpet out from underneath him.”

Still, he added “you never know” what Mr. Trump will do, adding that he has to choose his words carefully or Mr. Trump “will change another lake on me if I say anything else,” a reference to the U.S. President’s decision to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America amid the trade dispute.

Mr. Ford’s office did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday about Mr. Hoekstra’s remarks.

Ms. Joly said Canada is not interfering in U.S. politics and said it’s “absolutely not” fair of Mr. Hoekstra to suggest that.
We “would never do that,” she told reporters in Ottawa, and said Canada would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says Canada would never interfere in U.S. elections. Her comments came after U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra said Canadians should keep their noses out of American politics during the congressional midterms.
The Canadian Press
She summarized her recent trips to the United States, saying she has met with business people and political leaders from both Democrats and Republicans to attract new investment to Canada.

“I’ve been to Boston, engaging with the governor there. I’ve been also to Illinois and also engaging with the governor, JB Pritzker, there,” the minister said. “I’ve been also to Nasa in Florida,” she said.
“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” Ms. Joly said, adding that she hopes to soon announce “good news of investments by different American companies” in Canada.
She said her job is to persuade foreign investors to put their capital in Canada.
“That’s exactly what I’m doing, and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”
Ms. Joly spoke to reporters after a fireside chat at The Globe and Mail’s defence summit in Ottawa.
Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump again belittled Canada Wednesday, saying that the country will “end up being the 51st state.”
“Canada treats us very badly. They always have. Not any more. It’s a whole different ball game now that Trump is in town,” he said during a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Ariz.

Mr. Hoekstra’s talk of Canadian political interference follows similar accusations last month by Trump adviser Peter Navarro, who told Canadian lobbyists to “get the hell out” of the U.S. and warned Canada against interfering in U.S. midterm elections.
Prime Minister Mark Carney was later asked about Mr. Navarro’s comments and laughed at a reporter’s question, saying he had “no response” to the adviser’s caution.

The comments from two U.S. figures connected to the Trump administration come as the Republicans face difficult midterm election races in which the cost of living and U.S. tariffs on foreign goods have been prominent political issues.
Meanwhile, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Wednesday that Canada’s relationship with the U.S. has “changed permanently.”
He also said Canada needs to act as though tariffs are here to stay.

“Next month will mark two years since President Trump was re-elected. It has been two years of crisis, chaos from the White House. Ripped up trade deals, tariffs, threats of annexation and economic force,” said Mr. Ford, speaking to a crowd of about 1,200 people at an Empire Club of Canada luncheon in downtown Toronto.

“We can no longer depend on this being the most durable, prosperous and secure economic partnership the world has ever known. … We need to plan as if tariffs are here for good. We need to ensure that Canada’s future is in Canadian hands, now and always.”

The Ontario Premier, speaking during a question-and-answer session with former Newfoundland and Labrador premier Andrew Furey, also predicted that Mr. Trump could lose control of Congress, which includes the House of Representatives and the Senate, in November’s midterms.
“We need to continue building relationships because President Trump is not going to last forever,” Mr. Ford said.
“If he loses the Senate and the House, the Republicans are just going to pull the carpet out from underneath him.”

Still, he added “you never know” what Mr. Trump will do, adding that he has to choose his words carefully or Mr. Trump “will change another lake on me if I say anything else,” a reference to the U.S. President’s decision to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America amid the trade dispute.
Mr. Ford’s office did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday about Mr. Hoekstra’s remarks.

stories.title: New immersive technology centre opens at Fanshawe College to improve workplace safety
stories.summary: A new state-of-the-art facility intended to advance workplace safety has opened at Fanshawe College.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
A new state-of-the-art facility intended to advance workplace safety has opened at Fanshawe College. “Two years ago, this was a dream,” said Jeff Lang, Workplace Safety and Insurance Board (Wsib) President and CEO. “Now it’s a real space that will change lives, and save lives too, especially for our first responders.” The Wsib Centre of Excellence in Immersive Technologies Simulation for Workplace Safety is a facility which will use extended reality (XR) and artificial intelligence (AI) to develop immersive training and therapeutic simulations to help public safety personnel prepare for high-pressure scenarios, strengthen decision-making skills, and support recovery and return-to-work outcomes after a mental stress injury.

“It’s a critical problem that first responders are facing, especially in policing,” said Chief Thai Truong of the London Police Service. “This partnership means a great deal. It’s about protecting the officers, getting them ready to come back and having it backed by research.

This partnership is not just about the officers that are currently suffering right now, but it’s actually preparing the future.” Driven by a transformational invest of $20 million in 2024 from the Wsib, this facility will develop innovative training and therapeutic simulations designed to address some of the most pressing challenges facing the public safety sector today.

“First responders pay a heavy psychological price for everything they see in the line of duty. I see that price every day in the data,” said Lang. “Mental stress claims are the fastest growing types of claims that we deal with at the Wsib and mental stress injuries among first responders is a key driver in that growth, and the numbers are not slowing down.

But that’s the volume story. Then there’s the story of pain, the psychological struggle that each of our heroes deal with every single day.” Lang continued, “The impact to their families, their friendships, their coworkers.

And when that pain becomes so intense, so unmanageable and overwhelming that that person decides to take their life. Even if that happens once, it’s once too much, once too many. No one should ever have to pay that price to respond to keep our communities safe.

And quite frankly, neither should their loved ones, their coworkers, nor their communities.”

stories.title: Major projects CEO faces B.C. First Nations frustrated over lack of consultation
stories.summary: Ottawa - Major Projects CEO Dawn Farrell told First Nations in B.C. today that the frustrations expressed over a lack of consultation made her feel like Canada is "never going to work," but her office is determined to try.
stories.author: Nick Murray and Alessia Passafiume The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Major Projects CEO Dawn Farrell told First Nations in B.C. on Wednesday that the frustrations expressed over a lack of consultation on the Pacific Link pipeline made her feel like Canada is “never going to work,” but her office is determined to try to be better.

Farrell was addressing the B.C. Assembly of First Nations at its annual general meeting in Vancouver. Media were asked to leave the room before Farrell’s appearance, but the meeting continued to be publicly streamed on the B.C. Assembly of First Nations YouTube channel.

First Nations in B.C. are calling on Ottawa to set national standards for Indigenous consultations on major projects. They say they were given just 11 working days to review and engage on whether the proposed Pacific Link pipeline should be designated as a project of national interest.

The standard, they say, should include “minimum procedural protections,” including protected timelines for consultations before decisions are made.

The proposed pipeline from Alberta to B.C. was named a project in the national interest on Oct. 1 by Prime Minister Mark Carney alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

The designation does not eliminate the requirement for the government to consult with First Nations on the impact of the project itself. Rather, the goal is to complete the required reviews and consultations over the next year so construction can begin next September.

Tkʼemlúps te Secwépemc Chief Rosanne Casimir, who presented the call for a national consultation standard, said the current process expects First Nations to review thousands of documents under tight timelines and with limited funding.

“Even in your presentation initially starting off, you shared that there was excessive amounts of papers and documents. Well, we’re receiving that after the fact,” Casimir said, referring to an anecdote Farrell shared about having two binders of 1,200 pages on her coffee table.

“Meaningful consultation is difficult when nations, communities, are still trying to understand the project while decisions are continuing to move forward. For the (Pacific Link) oil pipeline, we raised process concerns, and Canada took nearly a month to respond and only 11 working days remained for the review and engagement.”

Farrell said she agrees with the concept of national consultation standards but she wondered how such standards would work alongside the government’s accelerated timelines for project approvals.

“I hear your pleas and I hear your discussions and I hear, you know, sort of a disbelief that it’s ever going to change, and a cynicism. And I feel like, ‘Oh my God, we can never get this country to work. Like it’s never going to work. We’ll never make it,’” Farrell said.

She added that staff in her office have “very, very big scars” from working on projects like the Trans Mountain pipeline that didn’t have the depth of Indigenous consultation the Pacific Link pipeline “has after two months.”

“Because we’re all committed in our office to try to do it better. Now, what does doing it better look like? It’s really hard to sit here and actually lay out what a day looks like and what the work looks like, and really, you’re not going to believe us at all,” Farrell said.

“No amount of presentation that I’m going to give … is going to give you a sense of what we’re trying to accomplish. The only thing that will give you that sense of it is if we actually do, in action, get to a different place.

“The best I can do is the best I can do. Our office is working hard to try to accommodate all the concerns you brought here today. And I totally get that you will not believe us until we deliver. And so we’ll mostly spend all of our time delivering, and maybe next year when we come back we’ll have some examples of how we try to deliver.”

The federal government initially planned to hold consultations for one month on whether to designate the pipeline as a project in the national interest under the Building Canada Act. That was extended to two months after Indigenous leaders raised concerns about the tight timeline.

A summary of those consultations posted online by the federal government says Indigenous groups decried a lack of information about the project, which they said prevented them from fully assessing its impact.

On Wednesday, Farrell acknowledged adequate consultation was key for seeing a project be successful.

“The projects that we have to deliver out of our office have to achieve your rights. We have to make sure that we go through your processes,” Farrell said.

“We can’t just make stuff up. The courts will just come and overturn the projects and we’ll be like Canada’s always been, 10, 15 years, dragging stuff around in the ditch and not getting it done and wasting time and money and resources, and your time and your people’s resources. We can’t keep doing that.”

Farrell faced criticism at the meeting over the federal government’s push to move quickly on approving major projects.

“Our concern is not efficiency itself. It’s whether the speed and certainty for proponents are being advanced equivalent protection for Aboriginal title and rights, our governance and the lands and waters that sustain our people,” said Shana Thomas, hereditary chief of the Lyackson First Nation.

“Consultation is something you do. We are a partner at this table and we need to be part of the decision-making process. What we have to say is not something that you can then evaluate and make your own decision based on what you think about what we said. We have to be at the table as equal partners.”

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak has said staff in the Major Projects Office do not understand how to work with First Nations communities and that “junior staffers” aren’t helping to build relationships.

She also said Farrell has been unavailable to meet with leadership, including at Assembly of First Nations gatherings.

Farrell said in the closed-door meeting Wednesday the only way she knows how to do her work is “to not talk very much.”

“They can’t get me on planes to go anywhere because I feel a huge responsibility to make sure that these projects that we’re working on hit the standards that you’re talking about today,” she said.

In an emailed statement last week, the Privy Council Office said the Major Projects Office works closely with Indigenous communities and that senior officials make themselves available to meet with communities when asked.

First Nations in B.C. also passed a resolution at Wednesday’s meeting calling on Prime Minister Mark Carney to halt the advance of the Building Canada Act and to repeal Bill C-39 if it passes through Parliament.

The legislation would fast-track approvals for major projects, cut their review times and create zones of “national interest” to pre-approve certain types of projects.

First Nations chiefs have warned the government it risks ending up in court if it approves and builds projects without their free, prior and informed consent, as outlined in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

Chiefs are set to meet with Carney and the country’s premiers in Ottawa later this month, and major projects are expected to be a major topic of debate.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

She added that staff in her office have “very, very big scars” from working on projects like the Trans Mountain pipeline that didn’t have the depth of Indigenous consultation the Pacific Link pipeline “has after two months.”

“Because we’re all committed in our office to try to do it better. Now, what does doing it better look like? It’s really hard to sit here and actually lay out what a day looks like and what the work looks like, and really, you’re not going to believe us at all,” Farrell said.

“No amount of presentation that I’m going to give … is going to give you a sense of what we’re trying to accomplish. The only thing that will give you that sense of it is if we actually do, in action, get to a different place.

“The best I can do is the best I can do. Our office is working hard to try to accommodate all the concerns you brought here today. And I totally get that you will not believe us until we deliver. And so we’ll mostly spend all of our time delivering, and maybe next year when we come back we’ll have some examples of how we try to deliver.”

The federal government initially planned to hold consultations for one month on whether to designate the pipeline as a project in the national interest under the Building Canada Act. That was extended to two months after Indigenous leaders raised concerns about the tight timeline.

A summary of those consultations posted online by the federal government says Indigenous groups decried a lack of information about the project, which they said prevented them from fully assessing its impact.
On Wednesday, Farrell acknowledged adequate consultation was key for seeing a project be successful.
“The projects that we have to deliver out of our office have to achieve your rights. We have to make sure that we go through your processes,” Farrell said.

“We can’t just make stuff up. The courts will just come and overturn the projects and we’ll be like Canada’s always been, 10, 15 years, dragging stuff around in the ditch and not getting it done and wasting time and money and resources, and your time and your people’s resources. We can’t keep doing that.”
Farrell faced criticism at the meeting over the federal government’s push to move quickly on approving major projects.

“Our concern is not efficiency itself. It’s whether the speed and certainty for proponents are being advanced equivalent protection for Aboriginal title and rights, our governance and the lands and waters that sustain our people,” said Shana Thomas, hereditary chief of the Lyackson First Nation.

“Consultation is something you do. We are a partner at this table and we need to be part of the decision-making process. What we have to say is not something that you can then evaluate and make your own decision based on what you think about what we said. We have to be at the table as equal partners.”

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak has said staff in the Major Projects Office do not understand how to work with First Nations communities and that “junior staffers” aren’t helping to build relationships.
She also said Farrell has been unavailable to meet with leadership, including at Assembly of First Nations gatherings.
Farrell said in the closed-door meeting Wednesday the only way she knows how to do her work is “to not talk very much.”
“They can’t get me on planes to go anywhere because I feel a huge responsibility to make sure that these projects that we’re working on hit the standards that you’re talking about today,” she said.

In an emailed statement last week, the Privy Council Office said the Major Projects Office works closely with Indigenous communities and that senior officials make themselves available to meet with communities when asked.

First Nations in B.C. also passed a resolution at Wednesday’s meeting calling on Prime Minister Mark Carney to halt the advance of the Building Canada Act and to repeal Bill C-39 if it passes through Parliament.
The legislation would fast-track approvals for major projects, cut their review times and create zones of “national interest” to pre-approve certain types of projects.

First Nations chiefs have warned the government it risks ending up in court if it approves and builds projects without their free, prior and informed consent, as outlined in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
Chiefs are set to meet with Carney and the country’s premiers in Ottawa later this month, and major projects are expected to be a major topic of debate.

stories.title: OPP focus on commercial vehicles with Project Safe Haul
stories.summary: Provincial police have launched a three-week campaign to find unsafe commercial vehicles and prevent crashes a...
stories.author: Georgia Chambers
stories.content:
Provincial police have launched a three-week campaign to find unsafe commercial vehicles and prevent crashes across southwestern Ontario.

Project Safe Haul started Wednesday and runs to Nov. 1.

During the blitz, OPP and commercial vehicle inspectors will check brakes, tires, cargo securement and steering components, police said.

“Anytime that we May locate an unsafe vehicle, commercial motor vehicle, obviously the driver is spoken to, there’s a thorough inspection completed by trained commercial motor vehicles inspectors, and I can tell you that that vehicle is taken off the roadway until such time that vehicle is properly repaired.”

Ali Alkhatib, program manager of licensing and compliance at Fanshawe College’s Corporate Training Solutions, says safety starts before the truck even goes into traffic.

Inspections before leaving the lot help drivers find problems in truck cabs and around the vehicle and regular maintenance can catch mechanical issues or wear down before they become serious, Alkhatib said.

Truck drivers work under very demanding conditions and carry heavy loads, making these checks extremely important.

“It doesn’t rest with one person. Drivers, employers, and maintenance teams, they all have a role to play. It’s a team effort,” said Akhatib.

Fanshawe’s commercial drivers training works on inspection before, during and after trips.

“Through commercial driver education and training, we emphasize that safety begins with preparation. It continues with proper vehicle inspection and it depends on sound decisions every time a driver gets behind a wheel,” he said.

Alkhatib said campaigns like Project Safe Haul bring back that training and draw more attention to serious road hazards.

The OPP says updates and results will be shared throughout the campaign.

stories.title: Joly says 'everything is on the table' but still no court filing against Stelco layoffs
stories.summary: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said "everything is on the table" when it comes to her government's response to layoffs at Stelco.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said “everything is on the table” when it comes to her government’s response to layoffs at Stelco but stopped short of announcing any legal action against the steelmaker.

“We expect Stelco to follow the undertakings that they’ve committed to…the Government of Canada,” Joly told reporters in Ottawa on Wednesday.

“And right now, a business decision or even a change in market conditions cannot be used to not follow the commitment,” she added.

Joly was referring to the commitments made by American-based Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. when it acquired Stelco in 2024.

Joly’s predecessor approved the purchase, following a review under the Investment Canada Act (ICA), which included a commitment to maintain the same amount of unionized employees for a period of five years.

The union representing steelworkers at the Stelco plant in Hamilton has confirmed layoffs are now underway. Layoffs are also expected to take place at Stelco’s Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont. Stelco has cited U.S. tariffs as the main reason for the “temporary” job cuts.

Last week, the industry minister threatened the “full force of the law” if Cleveland-Cliffs failed to comply with its undertakings that it agreed to when it purchased the steelmaker.

On Wednesday, Joly said she is “always open to sit down with a company and find a solution, but we’re looking at everything that is possible to keep jobs in Canada.”

On Oct. 5, Joly sent a letter to Stelco’s president, and a legal team is reviewing the response from the company, which was received on Friday.

Joly said she has been in contact with the unions and called the layoffs “unacceptable.”

On Tuesday, NDP Leader Avi Lewis and Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles called for Stelco to be nationalized.

The Conservative opposition has urged Joly to sue Stelco over the layoffs and noted the minister should have already taken action.

“The hundreds of workers being laid off don’t have 10 months to wait,” said Conservative MP Ned Kuruc, who represents the riding of Hamilton East—Stoney Creek, in a statement Wednesday.

“Their mortgage payment is at the end of the month, their grocery trip is this weekend, and Christmas planning is happening right now,” he added.

Joly cited Section 40 of the ICA which could lead to a few possible outcomes from a court process, including financial penalties towards the company, forcing them to abide by the commitment, and forced divestiture.

On Sunday, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves disputed the government’s claims and told CBC News he was prepared to fight Canada in court.

Notably, this is not the first time Stelco plants have idled due to bad market conditions. U.S. Steel, which acquired Stelco in 2007, began layoffs at the company following the 2008 financial crisis.

The federal government filed a lawsuit against U.S. Steel in 2009 for failing to meet their job commitments when they made the Stelco purchase. The lawsuit resulted in an out-of-court settlement in 2011, with commitments to keep production going by U.S. Steel.

However, U.S. Steel filed for creditor protection and severed ties with its Canadian operations, before those pledges could be followed through on.

stories.title: Foreign student enrolment at Atlantic Canada universities fell by nearly 50% since 2024, data show
stories.summary: East Coast schools that used to rely on tuition paid by international students continue to struggle, survey shows
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
The number of foreign students studying at universities in Atlantic Canada has dropped by nearly 48 per cent since 2024, a steeper decline than the federal government intended and a reflection of the body blow Canada’s reputation has suffered on the international education market.

There were 13,775 full-time visa students enrolled in undergraduate and graduate programs at universities in the four Atlantic provinces as of Oct. 1, an 18-per-cent reduction from 16,795 at the same time last year, according to new data released Wednesday.

The Association of Atlantic Universities’ annual enrolment survey offers one of the first looks at postsecondary education trends in Canada for the 2026-27 academic year. This fall’s survey – much like last year’s – shows that East Coast schools that used to rely on high tuition paid by foreign students continue to struggle.

“Atlantic Canada is the most severe example of a huge challenge we see across the country, which is our universities are fighting to make Canada competitive again in the race for international talent,” said Gabriel Miller, president and chief executive officer of Universities Canada, which represents postsecondary institutions nationwide.

“That’s taking an enormous amount of work and a lot of time because of the damage that was done by radical changes made by the previous federal government.”

In January of 2024, the Liberal government of Justin Trudeau began capping the number of international study permits it would grant annually.

The policy change was one of several Ottawa made in the ensuing months and years to curb an international student program that had grown so large it sparked a public backlash over temporary residents competing for housing, jobs and health care.

Canada’s international student cap helped lower rents. But will it bring colleges and universities down as well?

But many in Canada’s higher-education sector say the pendulum has swung too far in the opposite direction, in part because the changes have created uncertainty for applicants who once would have considered the country’s postsecondary system to be straightforward to access.

The federal government’s target is to receive 155,000 new international students this calendar year. As of the end of July, only 28,200 had arrived .

“I will go as far as to say that if we don’t have population growth in the Atlantic region, it could jeopardize some of the big programs that the prime minister has announced in national defence [and] in energy,” said David Dingwall, the president of Cape Breton University and a former Liberal cabinet minister. “You need people. You need intelligent people, and without that, we are in a very difficult situation in the Atlantic.”

Cape Breton University has seen the most precipitous decline in foreign students of any university in the Atlantic region, according to the preliminary enrolment survey.

In 2023-24, when international enrolment was at its peak, nearly 7,000 full-time visa students studied at the institution in Sydney, N.S. This year, 1,388 full-time visa students are enrolled at Cape Breton University.

International student enrolment has also declined at some of the largest universities in Eastern Canada, including Dalhousie University in Halifax, the University of New Brunswick and Memorial University of Newfoundland.

Ava Czapalay, chief executive officer of the Association of Atlantic Universities, said fewer overseas students are applying because of Canada’s tarnished reputation and because they fear visa requirements might change again. The unpredictability is turning international students off Canada, she added.

“In speaking with the federal government, we have tried to emphasize the hit that Canada’s reputation has taken globally by having opaque rules,” Mr. Czapalay said. When foreign students realize they could invest significant time and money applying to a Canadian university or college only to be denied a study permit, “they’re going to go to a country where they feel like they’re going to be more welcome.”

On top of that, Ms. Czapalay said federal visa officers are rejecting international students bound for Atlantic universities at rates higher than for universities in larger provinces.

“We don’t know why that is,” Ms. Czapalay said, “since our universities offer a great program, great experience, great value for money.”

In a March report on international student program reforms, federal Auditor-General Karen Hogan noted that smaller provinces were “disproportionately impacted” by lower study permit approvals, although colleges were hit harder than universities.

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, the department that processes visa applications, told The Globe and Mail by e-mail Wednesday that it recently provided a list of best practices to designated colleges and universities about what they can do to improve the quality of study permit applications.

“Designated learning institutions are responsible for their own recruitment and enrolment practices, which affect study permit approval rates,” spokesperson Jeffrey MacDonald said.

He also said policy changes designed to raise the share of international students in higher-level programs “have shown promising initial results,” with university students accounting for 40 per cent of new study permit holders in 2025, up from 30 per cent the year before.

Despite the decline in numbers of international students at Atlantic Canadian universities, there was some encouraging news for those institutions in the new data. Overall enrolment among full-time, first-year students was up by 3.4 per cent across the 16 universities in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland and Labrador.

“We think that is a positive sign because our universities offer an exceptional first-year experience for undergraduate students,” Ms. Czapalay said.

stories.title: Veteran bookseller Ben McNally wins Toronto International Festival of Authors Ivy Award
stories.summary: McNally is the first bookseller to win the prize, which has typically been awarded to executives at major publishing companies
stories.author: Josh O’Kane
stories.content:
Long-time bookseller Ben McNally has won the Toronto International Festival of Authors Ivy Award, given each year to a major contributor to the Canadian publishing sector.

McNally, 77, has been selling books across the festival’s home city since 1970 – at his namesake downtown shops since 2007, but also at Nicholas Hoare Books, Book City, Coles and more.

He’s the 15th winner of the award, which is administered by the writing fest’s International Visitors Programme. The program helps members of the Canadian book sector build relationships with international partners and expand the global reach of the country’s books.

McNally is also the first bookseller to win the prize, which has typically been awarded to publishing executives such as HarperCollins Canada’s Iris Tupholme, Simon & Schuster Canada’s Nicole Winstanley and Kegedonce Press’s Kateri Akiwenzie-Damm.

“It’s nice, as a bookseller, to be representing all the booksellers in the country for all that we do,” McNally said in an interview. After all, he said, the business of getting Canadian stories into the world is not strictly a top-down affair. “We really need authors, like authors need us, and we really need publishers, and publishers need us. And the general public needs us more than anybody else.”

This has been a particularly strong year for the publishing industry’s recognition of the entrepreneurs who get books in front of Canadian readers, he added. The Giller Prize, which has undergone significant changes after a boycott earlier this decade over past sponsors’ ties to Israel’s war in Gaza, appointed an all-indie-bookseller jury this year. The jurists include Rupert McNally and Danielle McNally, his children who now run his shop’s day-to-day operations.

Festival director Roland Gulliver said that the Ivy Award has always celebrated the people who champion Canadian publishing, and that booksellers are a key part of the sector. “Ben has been such a stalwart of the literary community,” Gulliver said. “This felt like the point to honour his work for many, many decades.”

Bookselling has undergone numerous transformations since McNally began slinging hardcovers and paperbacks fresh out of school at the turn of the seventies. Independent bookstores have struggled to survive the sector’s consolidation of power, including the amalgamation of book chains that resulted in today’s physical-store domination by Indigo Books and Music, and the subsequent encroachment of Amazon on all booksellers. Today, he says, real-estate costs only add to the difficulties for independents in Canada.

But, McNally said, “If we were not optimists, we wouldn’t be in this business in the first place.” He and other booksellers have found new ways to get voracious readers in their doors, especially with author speaking events. “In the old days, nobody thought about doing that.”

The Professional Association of Canadian Literary Agents, in conjunction with the festival, also announced that McClelland & Stewart executive editor Anita Chong would be named its Person of the Year. Chong acquires and edits fiction and memoir with a focus on under-represented voices, and has worked on award-winning titles such as Souvankham Thammavongsa’s How to Pronounce Knife , Michael Christie’s Greenwood and Eleanor Catton’s Birnam Wood .

The Toronto International Festival of Authors, recently separated from its long-time home at the city’s Harbourfront Centre, will run from Oct. 28 to Nov. 1 at the University of Toronto’s Victoria University. Dave Eggers, Ann-Marie MacDonald, Patrick deWitt, Vivek Shraya, Canisia Lubrin and Téa Mutonji are among this year’s participating authors.

The festival’s International Visitors Programme helps Canadian authors, publishers and agents to find buyers for books’ international rights and has run since 2008. It routinely appoints global publishing leaders as fellows to attend the festival to deepen connections with Canada’s literary scene.

The Ivy Award will be officially awarded on Oct. 28 alongside a keynote conversation between Barnes & Noble chief executive officer James Daunt and Craig Swinwood, CEO of Harlequin & HarperCollins Canada.
paragraphs: Long-time bookseller Ben McNally has won the Toronto International Festival of Authors Ivy Award, given each year to a major contributor to the Canadian publishing sector.
McNally, 77, has been selling books across the festival’s home city since 1970 – at his namesake downtown shops since 2007, but also at Nicholas Hoare Books, Book City, Coles and more.

He’s the 15th winner of the award, which is administered by the writing fest’s International Visitors Programme. The program helps members of the Canadian book sector build relationships with international partners and expand the global reach of the country’s books.

McNally is also the first bookseller to win the prize, which has typically been awarded to publishing executives such as HarperCollins Canada’s Iris Tupholme, Simon & Schuster Canada’s Nicole Winstanley and Kegedonce Press’s Kateri Akiwenzie-Damm.

“It’s nice, as a bookseller, to be representing all the booksellers in the country for all that we do,” McNally said in an interview. After all, he said, the business of getting Canadian stories into the world is not strictly a top-down affair. “We really need authors, like authors need us, and we really need publishers, and publishers need us. And the general public needs us more than anybody else.”

This has been a particularly strong year for the publishing industry’s recognition of the entrepreneurs who get books in front of Canadian readers, he added. The Giller Prize, which has undergone significant changes after a boycott earlier this decade over past sponsors’ ties to Israel’s war in Gaza, appointed an all-indie-bookseller jury this year. The jurists include Rupert McNally and Danielle McNally, his children who now run his shop’s day-to-day operations.

Festival director Roland Gulliver said that the Ivy Award has always celebrated the people who champion Canadian publishing, and that booksellers are a key part of the sector. “Ben has been such a stalwart of the literary community,” Gulliver said. “This felt like the point to honour his work for many, many decades.”

Bookselling has undergone numerous transformations since McNally began slinging hardcovers and paperbacks fresh out of school at the turn of the seventies. Independent bookstores have struggled to survive the sector’s consolidation of power, including the amalgamation of book chains that resulted in today’s physical-store domination by Indigo Books and Music, and the subsequent encroachment of Amazon on all booksellers. Today, he says, real-estate costs only add to the difficulties for independents in Canada.

But, McNally said, “If we were not optimists, we wouldn’t be in this business in the first place.” He and other booksellers have found new ways to get voracious readers in their doors, especially with author speaking events. “In the old days, nobody thought about doing that.”

The Professional Association of Canadian Literary Agents, in conjunction with the festival, also announced that McClelland & Stewart executive editor Anita Chong would be named its Person of the Year. Chong acquires and edits fiction and memoir with a focus on under-represented voices, and has worked on award-winning titles such as Souvankham Thammavongsa’s How to Pronounce Knife , Michael Christie’s Greenwood and Eleanor Catton’s Birnam Wood .

stories.title: Canada's economic ambitions face skilled workforce challenges, Liberal MPs warn
stories.summary: Two Liberal MPs responsible for supporting Ottawa's labour and industry agendas say Canada's plan to fast-track major projects is putting mounting pressure on a workforce already struggling to meet demand.
stories.author: Brett Bundale The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canada’s plan to fast-track major projects is putting mounting pressure on a workforce already struggling to meet demand, two Liberal MPs responsible for supporting Ottawa’s labour and industry agendas said Wednesday.

Leslie Church, parliamentary secretary to the minister of jobs, said the federal government’s push to develop key nation-building projects is making long-standing weaknesses in Canada’s labour force harder to ignore.

“We are out there trying to build — build quickly,” Church said during a panel discussion at a conference hosted by the Future Skills Centre in Toronto.

“We’re trying to energize an economy that is under threat, diversify to new markets, open up supply chains, invest in transportation (and) build the housing that is at the core of a strong economy,” she said. “All of this creates this incredible pressure and strain on the workforce.”

Church added: “Who does the building?”

She said the issue is not new to Canada but rather one that has been compounding for years amid growing industrial and technological transformation and is becoming increasingly urgent.

“This is a crucial challenge for us right now,” Church said.

She said there is also a disconnect between workers looking for jobs and the industries struggling to find workers, including a mismatch of skills, training barriers and other challenges.

“We are ships in the night in Canada,” Church said. “We have a lot of people looking for work, or with a certain set of skills, but we have all these industries that are also looking for labour, and it’s almost like the two never meet.”

Church said the government is aiming to close that gap through investments in apprenticeships and training to accelerate workforce development, while employers and schools also need to work together to ensure training and labour needs are aligned.

The federal government has made developing major infrastructure and industrial projects a centrepiece of its economic agenda.

The push is aimed at boosting economic growth, attracting investment and reducing Canada’s reliance on the United States.

Yet Canada has an enduring shortage of skilled trades, gaps in worker training and a mismatch between the skills jobseekers have and those employers need.

It’s those labour force issues that could intensify as Ottawa looks to accelerate construction of major projects.

Karim Bardeesy, parliamentary secretary to the industry minister, said one of the issues is that Canadian employers have lagged on workforce skills development.

“There’s historic underinvestment in training by employers in Canada ... compared to other Oecd countries,” he said during the panel talk.

Bardeesy said federal apprenticeship incentives are aimed at helping develop a more skilled workforce but that employers still have a role to play in on-the-job training.

He said employers are also grappling with gaps in workers’ interpersonal skills, which he called a lingering effect of the pandemic.

“The COVID hangover as it relates to soft skills is real,” Bardeesy said.

Meanwhile, he said universities and colleges need to move beyond small, incremental improvements in order to keep pace with rapid technology advancements and the changing circumstances of students.

“The innovations on the margins are not going to be enough,” Bardeesy said.

“It doesn’t mean rushing to the latest labour market or industrial fad. It just means attending to the fundamentals of very quickly changing technology and very quickly changing student needs.”

stories.title: Quebec Court of Appeal hears case on granting tenants the right to have pets
stories.summary: MONTRÉAL - The Quebec Court of Appeal is hearing arguments on whether the right to have pets should be protected by law.
stories.author: Pierre Saint-Arnaud The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The Quebec Court of Appeal is deliberating after hearing arguments on Wednesday on whether the right to have pets should be protected by law.

Last March, housing tribunal Judge Suzanne Guèvremont ruled that lease clauses banning pets violate Charter rights to liberty and privacy.

Guèvremont also argued in her decision that the evolution of animal protection laws, which recognize the bond between humans and their pets, required case law to evolve as well.

Amilis, the company that owns the building in which the complainant lives, appealed the decision.

The case was brought to court after a tenant, identified as M Desjardins, had taken over a lease that included a clause banning pets. However, it had been established at the time that Desjardins’ pets — a dog and a cat — were not causing any problems and that other pets in the building were tolerated.

But a new company, Amilis, purchased the building and enforced the no-pet clause.

The company’s lawyer, Damarys Pineda, argued that the judge had gone beyond her authority by acting as a substitute for the legislature, which is responsible for no-pet clauses.

The lawyer also argued that the no-pet clause is intended to protect the well-being of all tenants in a building and that it would be unreasonable to force landlords to allow pets in their buildings if they do not want them.

While landlord-tenant agreements are possible, she argued that any tenant can now contest a no-pet clause by invoking the Charter.

Desjardin’s lawyer, Kimmyanne Brown, stressed that Guèvremont’s decision only applied to Desjardins.

Court documents indicate Desjardins needed pets for animal-assisted therapy due to anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress. She added that the court cannot rule on issues not raised in the initial case, such as the protection of others who May be allergic or afraid of animals.

The Spca also intervened in the case.

Marie-Claude St-Amant, the lawyer representing the Spca, argued that the legislature now allows pets to be considered members of the family and that as a result Desjardins’s rights had been violated.

She also said she asked the office of the Attorney General of Quebec if it wished to intervene in the case, which it declined. St-Amant argued the response is proof that Guèvremont did not overstep her authority.

After the hearing, Spca spokesperson Julie Gaillard said she expected a series of appeals in this case, which could eventually reach the Supreme Court.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Hoekstra tells Canada ‘keep your nose out of American politics’ ahead of midterms
stories.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra warned Canadian politicians to "keep your nose out of American politics" in a podcast appearance.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra has warned Canadian politicians to “keep your nose out of American politics” in a podcast appearance ahead of the U.S. midterms.

“We are closely watching Canadian activities because it appears that some of this, from our perspective, and the way that we view our elections, could be inferred to be election interference,” he said in an appearance on The Really Big Show , a Canadian news podcast.

“Keep your nose out of American politics,” he added, warning that “America will respond to it,” if the behaviour of Canadian politicians is deemed to be election interference.

Joly has previously been open about the fact that Canadian counter-tariffs were in part designed to “target states” and “put political pressure” on the Trump administration after 50 per cent tariffs were imposed on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods.

When asked about the breakdown in trade negotiations between Canada and the U.S., Hoekstra said: “We thought we had a deal in August … it’s the best deal that any country in the world has received.”

He added that U.S. negotiators thought they had the deal “ironed out,” until Prime Minister Mark Carney called his negotiating team back to Ottawa and suspended talks.

Hoekstra’s warning comes as Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre made a trip to Detroit, Michigan, to pitch a tariff-free auto pact between Canada and the U.S.

Michigan has become a crucial battleground in the upcoming U.S. midterm elections and is currently considered a toss-up for the Senate race by The Cook Political Report . It’s one of the states hit hardest by the trade war between the two countries, due to its automakers ​relying on integrated cross-border supply chains.

Meanwhile, Hoekstra isn’t the only U.S. politician who is accusing Canada of interference in America. Last month, President Donald Trump’s trade adviser Peter Navarro told Canadian lobbyists to “get the hell out of our country” and warned that “if you interfere in our elections in Maine and Michigan, you will pay even more dearly.”

Neither Navarro nor Hoekstra offered any evidence that Canadian lobbying or retaliatory tariffs amounted to election interference.

The Democrats need to gain four more seats to win back the Senate majority in the upcoming mid-term elections on Nov. 3.
