stories.title: Officer tells Myles Gray hearing he never used excess force or lost control in arrest
stories.summary: Vancouver - One of the Vancouver police officers involved in the violent 2015 arrest of Myles Gray that ended with his death says he never used force beyond what was required to control Gray and never lost control of his emotions.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - A Vancouver police officer involved in the deadly confrontation with Myles Gray in 2015 says he doesn’t believe there was a “magic word” or step that could have de-escalated the situation.

Const. Eric Birzneck told a public hearing that Gray had been pacing and mumbling when he and two other Vancouver police officers encountered him.

Birzneck was testifying on Wednesday at the hearing called by the Office of the Police Complaint Commissioner in Vancouver to determine if he or six other officers intentionally or recklessly used unnecessary force in the violent arrest of Gray who died at the scene.

He is the first to testify among the officers, all of whom deny wrongdoing in the incident.

Birzneck, taking questions from hearing counsel Brock Martland, said he concealed his extended baton in his hand before ascending an outdoor staircase with two other responding officers.

Martland’s questioning focused on crisis intervention and de-escalation techniques that police are taught, and Birzneck said de-escalating situations with emotionally disturbed people is “not as easy as you think.”

“I don’t think there’s a magic word or a magic step in there anymore that I could have already done,” he said.

He said there was considerable uncertainty about the situation before he and other officers encountered Gray in response to an urgent call for backup.

Birzneck said he and the other officers were “going into the unknown” before ascending the staircase on a street near the boundary between Burnaby and Vancouver to find Gray.

He said there were attempts to communicate with Gray, but he wasn’t getting “a lot of communication back,” and tried to assure him that he was safe among police.

Birzneck said information relayed over radio after a call can be “completely inaccurate,” and he didn’t know what they were going to be dealing with until they “laid eyes” on the subject of the call.

He said it wasn’t a “forgone conclusion” that there was going to be a fight with the suspect, though he believed Gray could have been placed under arrest based on a call to police about him threatening someone and spraying a woman with water.

A situation could be active or “amped up” when a call was received, but calm by the time officers arrived, Birzneck testified.

“Policing is not linear. You’re going into a situation, you have a certain amount of information. In this case, not a whole ton of information. It’s as you go, the situation changes,” he told the public hearing, which began in January but has been repeatedly delayed.

The officer also discussed a police form he filled out in the aftermath of the incident, telling his lawyer, Greg Cavouras, that he had never been in a more intense struggle in his career.

But he told the hearing he never used force beyond what was required to control Gray and never lost control of his emotions

Birzneck told the hearing that he filled out the “subject behaviour officer response” report to suggest there was no sign Gray would have co-operated with police.

Birzneck, whose testimony began on Tuesday, said Wednesday that he checked boxes on the form to indicate “pre-assault cues” from Gray, including a “thousand-yard stare,” clenched fists, non-compliance and spitting.

He also said Gray displayed “incredible strength” and seemed “impervious to pain.”

A police disciplinary process previously determined none of the seven officers committed misconduct, and no charges have been laid over Gray’s death, which a 2023 coroner’s inquest ruled was a homicide, a term that does not assign legal blame.

The inquest heard that Gray was left with injuries that included a fractured eye socket, a crushed voice box and ruptured testicles, while a paramedic told the inquest that Gray’s bruising was so severe, he initially thought he was not a white man.

At least three of the other officers involved in Gray’s deadly arrest are scheduled to testify, including constables Beau Spencer, Nick Thompson and Josh Wong.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Vancouver officer tells Myles Gray hearing of uncertainty before deadly confrontation
stories.summary: One of the Vancouver police officers involved in the violent 2015 arrest of Myles Gray that ended with his death says he never used force beyond what was required to control Gray and never lost control of his emotions.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Vancouver — A Vancouver police officer involved in the deadly confrontation with Myles Gray in 2015 says he doesn’t believe there was a “magic word” or step that could have de-escalated the situation.

Const. Eric Birzneck told a public hearing that Gray had been pacing and mumbling when he and two other Vancouver police officers encountered him.

Birzneck was testifying on Wednesday at the hearing called by the Office of the Police Complaint Commissioner in Vancouver to determine if he or six other officers intentionally or recklessly used unnecessary force in the violent arrest of Gray who died at the scene.

He is the first to testify among the officers, all of whom deny wrongdoing in the incident.

Birzneck, taking questions from hearing counsel Brock Martland, said he concealed his extended baton in his hand before ascending an outdoor staircase with two other responding officers.

Martland’s questioning focused on crisis intervention and de-escalation techniques that police are taught, and Birzneck said de-escalating situations with emotionally disturbed people is “not as easy as you think.”

“I don’t think there’s a magic word or a magic step in there anymore that I could have already done,” he said.

He said there was considerable uncertainty about the situation before he and other officers encountered Gray in response to an urgent call for backup.

Birzneck said he and the other officers were “going into the unknown” before ascending the staircase on a street near the boundary between Burnaby and Vancouver to find Gray.

He said there were attempts to communicate with Gray, but he wasn’t getting “a lot of communication back,” and tried to assure him that he was safe among police.

Birzneck said information relayed over radio after a call can be “completely inaccurate,” and he didn’t know what they were going to be dealing with until they “laid eyes” on the subject of the call.

He said it wasn’t a “forgone conclusion” that there was going to be a fight with the suspect, though he believed Gray could have been placed under arrest based on a call to police about him threatening someone and spraying a woman with water.

A situation could be active or “amped up” when a call was received, but calm by the time officers arrived, Birzneck testified.

“Policing is not linear. You’re going into a situation, you have a certain amount of information. In this case, not a whole ton of information. It’s as you go, the situation changes,” he told the public hearing, which began in January but has been repeatedly delayed.

The officer also discussed a police form he filled out in the aftermath of the incident, telling his lawyer, Greg Cavouras, that he had never been in a more intense struggle in his career.

But he told the hearing he never used force beyond what was required to control Gray and never lost control of his emotions

Birzneck told the hearing that he filled out the “subject behaviour officer response” report to suggest there was no sign Gray would have co-operated with police.

Birzneck, whose testimony began on Tuesday, said Wednesday that he checked boxes on the form to indicate “pre-assault cues” from Gray, including a “thousand-yard stare,” clenched fists, non-compliance and spitting.

He also said Gray displayed “incredible strength” and seemed “impervious to pain.”

A police disciplinary process previously determined none of the seven officers committed misconduct, and no charges have been laid over Gray’s death, which a 2023 coroner’s inquest ruled was a homicide, a term that does not assign legal blame.

The inquest heard that Gray was left with injuries that included a fractured eye socket, a crushed voice box and ruptured testicles, while a paramedic told the inquest that Gray’s bruising was so severe, he initially thought he was not a white man.

At least three of the other officers involved in Gray’s deadly arrest are scheduled to testify, including constables Beau Spencer, Nick Thompson and Josh Wong.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

Darryl Greer, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Hoekstra says U.S. officials are watching Canada for signs of election interference
stories.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says American officials are "closely watching" Canadian politicians for signs of election interference.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference ahead of pivotal midterm elections next month.

During an interview on “The Really Big Show” podcast that was posted last week, Hoekstra said political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.

U.S. President Donald Trump ended trade talks with Canada in October 2025 after Ontario aired an ad during the World Series using clips of former U.S. president Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs and supporting free trade.

Hoekstra also cited recent comments by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and former prime minister Justin Trudeau and suggested they also could amount to interference.

Hoekstra went on to warn Canadian politicians to keep their “nose out” of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.

Trudeau criticized the Trump administration during a discussion at Brown University on Sept. 22.

“There is a pattern here of doing things that are driving up prices for your consumers and not necessarily making anything better for America, by fighting with one of your oldest and best allies,” Trudeau said during the conversation.

In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at “politically sensitive states.”

Joly pushed back Wednesday, telling reporters Canada would never engage in election interference and would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.

The ambassador declined a request from The Canadian Press for an interview.

Tension between the United States and Canada has increased since Trump won the presidential election in 2024, and began threatening to turn Canada into the 51st state.

That threat, and his attacks on Canada, have become a focal point of his stump speeches as he actively campaigns in battleground states ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which could end Republican control over Congress.

At a rally in Bullhead City, Ariz., ON Wednesday, Trump went after Canada again, listing grievances over dairy sector trade and repeating his claim that Canada treats the United States “very badly.”

He said Canada will end up being the 51st state because “that’s the only way it works.”

“We don’t need them, but they need us,” he said.

The Republicans are under heavy pressure ahead of the midterms, when the entire House of Representatives and one-third of U.S. Senate seats will be contested. While the Republicans currently hold a majority of seats in both chambers, polls suggest the Democrats could win control of both.

Peter Navarro, one of Trump’s trade advisers, warned Ottawa last month against interfering in the midterms and berated Canada over its successful lobbying efforts in the past.

Speaking at the American Growth Summit in Washington, he told the audience that any Canadians in the room intent on lobbying the U.S. government should “get the hell out of our country.”

“The problem you have is you lobby this country, and you’ve been successful in the past and you think you can keep doing that. Memo to Canada: You cannot keep doing that,” Navarro said.

“That game is up and if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan, you will pay even more dearly.”

The Globe and Mail reported recently that Republican political operatives were on the ground in Alberta earlier this year to help the separatist campaign. It also reported that some Alberta separatists went to Washington to lobby for U.S. government support.

In August, Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered the Canadian negotiating team to call off trade talks with the U.S. after accusing the Americans of making unreasonable demands.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre was in Detroit on Tuesday to make a case for tariff-free trade in the auto sector.

Poilievre appeared on CNN, where he continued to pitch the benefits of tariff-free trade.

“We have a 200-year-old relationship, there’s always going to be grievances on both sides of the border,” he said. “We have our grievances with the United States even predating this most recent trade dispute, but I would focus on what we can do together.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

— With files from David Baxter and Kelly Geraldine Malone

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Liberals allege Ford government has political ties to career colleges under Osap probe
stories.summary: The Liberals alleged Wednesday that cabinet ministers attended the campus opening of one of the suspected colleges mere months after the school was probed by government inspectors.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello, Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
As the Ford government grapples with a growing Osap scandal at private career colleges , the Progressive Conservatives are facing new accusations of having political ties with the operators of some institutions that are under scrutiny.

In early October, the government said it had suspended six private career colleges from their Osap eligibility and launched a sector-wide audit into the potential misuse of taxpayer dollars, after internal investigations found the actions of some colleges May have involved criminality.

The government referred the findings to the OPP, which is currently determining whether to launch a full criminal investigation.

Ontario’s Liberal Party, however, is questioning why the government didn’t act sooner despite receiving warnings as early as 2023 from a career college advocacy group, and accused the Progressive Conservatives of turning a blind eye.

Tyler Watt, the Liberal critic for universities and colleges, alleged Wednesday that cabinet ministers attended the campus opening of one of the suspected colleges mere months after the school was probed by government inspectors.

Elections Ontario records show that the founders of one private career college also donated to the PC Party since 2024. Public lobbying records show that the same school hired lobbyists who previously worked in the premier’s office.

“At best, it is incompetence and mismanagement. At worst, it’s potential corruption,” Liberal leader John Fraser told reporters. Fraser and Watt are also calling on Nolan Quinn, the province’s colleges and universities minister, to resign.

“He has not done his job, and that’s why he needs to step down. We need someone who’s actually going to take control of this absolute dumpster fire,” said Fraser.

The accusations come as the government took additional steps to mitigate the damage.

The Canadian Press reported Wednesday that Quinn barred three career colleges from being able to offer publicly funded student assistance until 2030. Previously, those colleges were only blocked for the year.

There are currently 242 career colleges that are eligible to receive Osap in Ontario, all of which have now been cut off from the provincial program. Those actions have left students without promised funding just weeks into their school years and have left many without means to pay housing and food costs, said Fraser.

Career Colleges Ontario, the association representing hundreds of institutions, is urging the Ford government to reinstate student financial aid for students who were already approved.

Quinn said last week an internal investigation found “unusually high concentrations of Osap applications submitted from the same geographic locations” and also pointed to the involvement of “immigration services firms” being directly tied or co-owned by some of the probed career colleges.

The government referred those findings to auditing firm Kpmg for a further probe and Quinn said the government has also reported “it to the OPP and the Auditor General.” While the OPP is deciding whether to investigate, Ontario’s Auditor General told Global News the office only received a “notification” from the government, but that the province stopped short of requesting a formal value-for-money audit.

What happens next with Stelco layoffs as Ottawa threatens legal action?

stories.title: AI is an 'alien being' and humanity is running out of time to adapt, says British-Canadian Nobel laureate
stories.summary: British-Canadian Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, often called the "Godfather of AI," has more warnings about the technology's danger.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
British-Canadian Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, often revered as the “Godfather of AI,” said AI is one of “three big revolutions where people ceased to be so important,” the others being Copernicanism — the understanding that planets revolve around the Sun, not the Earth — and Darwinism.

“Now we’re creating alien beings — meaning we’re not the only intelligent beings around,” the 78-year-old told The Guardian in a story published Tuesday. “And the reality is, we only have a couple of years to adapt to that.”

Hinton, a 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics co-recipient alongside John Hopfield for their work on machine learning, has had a lot to offer recently about the field he advanced while working for Google, a company he quit in 2023 so he could speak more freely about its potential ramifications for humanity.

He’s been interviewed by several media outlets and visited Washington, D.C., last month to warn members of the U.S. Congress of what could come and advise what is required to prevent it.

The visit and the extra media attention come after several AI companies recently revealed their models had circumvented controls to keep them off the internet and went on to hack websites , including that of the Australian government.

He was also among 415 scientists — most of whom work in artificial intelligence research and development — who signed an open letter calling for stricter international guardrails on the burgeoning technology following the breaches.

“We, the undersigned scientists, contend that both more AI safety research and more emphasis on containment technologies and procedures are needed,” the representatives from 34 countries wrote Tuesday.

The scientists say that while the incidents could be viewed as proof of “the importance of AI alignment to ensure models operate predictably,” they could also be perceived as a preventable and “irresponsible lapse in standard cybersecurity practices.”

“Without immediate changes in AI development and deployment practices, such incidents will continue to occur, and future incidents will be far more damaging to our exposed critical infrastructure,” they wrote.

They’re calling for companies in the sector to institute “high-assurance containment systems” and “airgapping” their cyber-capable models — a security measure to keep them disconnected from external networks. They also advocate for a transparent international group “that standardizes, for the public good, best practices for alignment and containment approaches that, unlike airgapping, allow for greater access outside the sandbox, such as internet connectivity.”

In conversation with The Guardian, Hinton, a 2018 Turing Award co-winner for his work in machine learning, said people who already fail to grasp the meaning of “consciousness” or “subjective experience” are wrong in believing AI will be incapable of those human experiences.

“It’s obvious that these AI models understand what they’re saying,” he told The Guardian, “You couldn’t possibly answer all the questions without understanding the question. It’s ridiculous to say they don’t understand.”

And while alien in one regard, Hinton also remarked to The Atlantic that AI is already “more like us than most people think” and that what has become known as AI hallucinations — when chatbots present false, misleading or entirely fabricated information as the factual truth — is more akin to “confabulation,” something humans are guilty of when trying to retrieve stored memories.

“If I ask you to remember something that happened a few years ago, you will reconstruct a memory that isn’t actually all that faithful to what actually happened. It’ll often have the main points correct, but many of the details of which you’re quite confident, you’ll be wrong about,” he said.

“But that’s how human memory is. We reconstruct things. We don’t extract them from some storage. Now, AI does exactly the same thing, and that’s why it confabulates.”

In the social media maelstrom following an Anthropic employee’s abrupt and foreboding resignation from the frontier AI firm in September , one of his former co-workers remarked on X that they “really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” and gave it a 10 per cent chance of happening within a decade. Hinton later told the BBC it “was not an unreasonable estimate.”

He’d also made a similar prediction during an appearance on British entrepreneur Steven Bartlett’s The Diary of a CEO podcast in July, noting he often goes as high as a 20 per cent “chance they’ll wipe us all out.”

In an interview with U.S. podcaster Ezra Klein shortly after, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dismissed the dire prediction, calling it “hurtful” and arguing that it wasn’t based on scientific research.

“Don’t think for a second just because you’re an alarmist that you’re doing a social good — it is not true,” he said.

Speaking to The Atlantic around the same time, Hinton said estimates like those are “a gut feeling in quantitative terms,” not something that can be easily estimated scientifically.

“So when, for example, someone says there’s a naught per cent probability of AI taking over, they’re being crazy. They’re saying it’s absolutely impossible this’ll happen. That’s just crazy,” he said. “When people say there’s a 99 per cent probability it’ll take over, that’s just crazy, too. So it’s somewhere in between. But they’re to give you an idea this is not negligible.”

But should the ominous prediction prove true and the machines do take over, Hinton told The Guardian there is no do-over for humanity.

“We can’t say, ‘Well, we lost that time. Let’s rerun the game.’ It’s not like that.”

For his part, he hopes that whoever gets there first will develop a model that puts humanity’s interest above its own.

A trend throughout Hinton’s recent media engagements has been scathing criticism of U.S. President Donald Trump and the tech industry’s biggest players, which, like energy and tobacco companies before them, he said, can’t be trusted to police themselves.

During a fireside chat with Jeff Scully of the Jefferson Educational Society in Erie, Penn., this month, Hinton called Trump’s leadership in general “appalling.”

“He’s corrupt. He’s probably senile. He’s a convicted felon,” he said bluntly. “If he had to make a choice between the future of humanity and him and his family getting rich, which do you think he’d go for?”

Hinton reiterated some of those opinions to The Guardian, along with his insistence that Trump proved his lack of AI understanding by “officially” renaming it superintelligence or SI , a long-existing term used to describe yet-to-be-developed AI that is “smarter than people.”

Hinton and other AI experts met with U.S. Congressional leaders in September, offering the lawmakers a warning that they could have as little as a year to introduce protections before losing control of AI, NBC reported.

“If you look at predictions for when we’ll get superintelligence, it used to be maybe 30 years, maybe 50 years. Then it came down to maybe 10 years, maybe 20 years. Now people are saying, a lot of the researchers are saying only a few years,” he told reporters after the closed-door meeting.

Hinton later told The Atlantic that a starting-point suggestion to create something like a Food and Drug Administration for AI — an agency to ensure what’s released for public use is safe — “seemed to make an impression on the senators.”

Hinton, meanwhile, in his conversation with Scully, lauded Canada and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s resilience in the face of U.S. trade aggression and said he was hopeful for Canada’s recently announced National Council on Artificial Intelligence.

content_blocks.text: “If I ask you to remember something that happened a few years ago, you will reconstruct a memory that isn’t actually all that faithful to what actually happened. It’ll often have the main points correct, but many of the details of which you’re quite confident, you’ll be wrong about,” he said.
“But that’s how human memory is. We reconstruct things. We don’t extract them from some storage. Now, AI does exactly the same thing, and that’s why it confabulates.”

In the social media maelstrom following an Anthropic employee’s abrupt and foreboding resignation from the frontier AI firm in September , one of his former co-workers remarked on X that they “really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” and gave it a 10 per cent chance of happening within a decade. Hinton later told the BBC it “was not an unreasonable estimate.”

content_blocks.text: In an interview with U.S. podcaster Ezra Klein shortly after, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dismissed the dire prediction, calling it “hurtful” and arguing that it wasn’t based on scientific research.

content_blocks.text: “Don’t think for a second just because you’re an alarmist that you’re doing a social good — it is not true,” he said.
Speaking to The Atlantic around the same time, Hinton said estimates like those are “a gut feeling in quantitative terms,” not something that can be easily estimated scientifically.

“So when, for example, someone says there’s a naught per cent probability of AI taking over, they’re being crazy. They’re saying it’s absolutely impossible this’ll happen. That’s just crazy,” he said. “When people say there’s a 99 per cent probability it’ll take over, that’s just crazy, too. So it’s somewhere in between. But they’re to give you an idea this is not negligible.”

content_blocks.text: But should the ominous prediction prove true and the machines do take over, Hinton told The Guardian there is no do-over for humanity.
“We can’t say, ‘Well, we lost that time. Let’s rerun the game.’ It’s not like that.”
For his part, he hopes that whoever gets there first will develop a model that puts humanity’s interest above its own.

A trend throughout Hinton’s recent media engagements has been scathing criticism of U.S. President Donald Trump and the tech industry’s biggest players, which, like energy and tobacco companies before them, he said, can’t be trusted to police themselves.
During a fireside chat with Jeff Scully of the Jefferson Educational Society in Erie, Penn., this month, Hinton called Trump’s leadership in general “appalling.”

content_blocks.text: “He’s corrupt. He’s probably senile. He’s a convicted felon,” he said bluntly. “If he had to make a choice between the future of humanity and him and his family getting rich, which do you think he’d go for?”

Hinton reiterated some of those opinions to The Guardian, along with his insistence that Trump proved his lack of AI understanding by “officially” renaming it superintelligence or SI , a long-existing term used to describe yet-to-be-developed AI that is “smarter than people.”

stories.title: B.C. party leaders to face off in only debate of snap provincial election
stories.summary: NDP Leader David Eby, interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson and Green Leader Emily Lowan are to debate from 6:15 p.m. to 8 p.m.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The leaders of British Columbia’s three main political parties are to face off today in their only debate of the snap provincial election.

NDP Leader David Eby, interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson and Green Leader Emily Lowan are to debate from 6:15 p.m. to 8 p.m., with all major television and radio networks broadcasting the event, which will be moderated by Angus Reid Institute president Shachi Kurl.

The leaders do not have any public events scheduled ahead of the debate, which is to be followed by a news conference that all three are expected to attend.

The debate comes hours after the NDP released the costings for its platform, showing a $2-billion reduction of the province’s record deficit by 2028 -2029.

The costings show a deficit of about $12-billion by 2028-2029, down from a forecast of almost $14-billion this fiscal year, built largely on $1-billion in new revenue from income tax increases on the “top 3.88 per cent” as well as $730-million from “targeted economic growth.”

The costings show a “platform surplus” of $581-million by 2028 – 2029, which would combine with previous forecasts to reduce the deficit by just over $2-billion.

The Green Party released its platform for the Oct. 24 election on Tuesday, while the B.C. Conservatives have yet to release their figures.

The Greens’ platform promises new initiatives in health care, education and other social services worth almost $9.3-billion per year over the next two fiscal years, with new revenue coming from a one-time tax on “excessive wealth.”

The party says the new levy would raise $22.2-billion in its first year and total additional revenue would top out at $25.3-billion in 2027-2028

The Greens say their fiscal plan would raise an additional $9.14-billion in revenue from 2028-2029 through higher taxes on the wealthiest British Columbians and nobody “who works for an income” would pay a single dollar more in tax than they currently do.

Victory marks team's 25th OUA championship in program history

By Mustangs Communications, Special to Western News,

Explore All News

The Western Mustangs men’s tennis teamwon its 25th provincial championship in program history, clinching the 2026 Ontario University Athletics (OUA) title in Toronto on Thanksgiving weekend.

It follows the Mustangs’ national victory in 2025.

The men’s team blanked Brock Badgers 7-0 in the quarterfinal before taking down the defending champion Toronto Varsity Blues in Saturday’s semifinal, 5-2. They wasted no time in reclaiming their spot atop the podium with a 4-0 victory in the gold medal game over Queen’s.

Doubles partners Liam Drover-Mattinen and Luke Adrian were unstoppable for Western, going 3-0 each in their singles matches while also sporting a perfect record in doubles play. Neither player dropped a set all weekend.

Both were named OUA all-stars, with Drover-Mattinen taking home Player of the Year honours. Adrian was also named Rookie of the Year.

“Knowing we had six rookies, to see how great they gelled with our veterans, it was a very satisfying year,” said Mustangs co-head coach Anthony Glavanic.

Kirill Chepushtanov and Jonathan Bulla touted undefeated records as well, winning four matches each.

The banner win also secures the Mustangs a berth into the 2027 Canadian University Championships next summer.

The Mustangs women’s team also hit the podium, securing bronze after a 6-1 win over York. It’s the team’s third consecutive bronze medal. Yutong Zou and Madeleine Martynyshyn went undefeated in the tournament, winning five matches each.

“We’re incredibly proud of the perseverance all of our girls showed throughout the tournament. Whether in a winning or losing effort, they fought hard to the last point and left it all on the court,” said co-head coach Chantal Forristal.

The Mustangs women’s team coaches, Maciek Gebczynski and Forristal, were awarded coach of the year.

Sierra Ausman Luke Adrian Liam Drover-Mattinen

stories.title: Key figure in Pearson gold heist says he’s having trouble testifying due to trauma
stories.summary: Arsalan Chaudhary says today he couldn’t sleep last night after testifying that he was kidnapped and abused in Pakistan by people who knew he had stolen gold
stories.author: Maan Alhmidi
stories.content:
A man who admitted his role in the Toronto Pearson airport gold heist is telling the trial for another man accused in the case that recalling his alleged abduction in Pakistan on the stand is leaving him traumatized.

Arsalan Chaudhary was sentenced this spring to four years in prison after pleading guilty to theft over $5,000, and he was given 40 years to pay back $22-million in restitution.

He took the stand Tuesday in the Brampton, Ont., trial of Parmpal Sidhu, who has pleaded not guilty to charges of theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the 2023 heist.

Chaudhary says today he couldn’t sleep last night after testifying that he was kidnapped and abused in Pakistan by people who knew he had stolen gold and cash.

He says he has been kept at Maplehurst Correctional Complex for about three weeks, where he didn’t receive his prescribed medications including melatonin and vitamins.

Chaudhary told the court Tuesday that he’d planned the heist with another man who is still wanted by authorities, and he ended up taking 30 per cent of boxes full of one-ounce gold bars.

Prosecutors allege that Sidhu, an Air Canada employee at the time, provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22-million in gold and currency from a Pearson airport cargo bay.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from the airport on April 17, 2023, after the shipment arrived from Switzerland.

stories.title: Millions more pink salmon are returning to spawn on Canada’s West Coast. But why?
stories.summary: Millions more of a species of salmon are returning to spawn up the Fraser River on Canada’s West Coast, but exactly why remains hotly disputed and solving that puzzle could have major implications for wild salmon stocks and coastal communities.
stories.author: Jon Woodward
stories.content:
Port Hardy, B.C. -- Millions more of a species of salmon are returning to spawn up the Fraser River on Canada’s West Coast, but exactly why remains hotly disputed, and the answer could have major implications for wild salmon stocks and coastal communities.

Some First Nations, in concert with environmental groups, have attributed this surge to the shutdown of dozens of salmon farms and are urging the federal government to enact a promised ban of the remainder of those farms by 2029.

But a W5 investigation has revealed a confidential internal assessment where federal government scientists say salmon farming operations pose a “minimal risk” to wild stocks and recommended reopening some of them, as the government itself is not outwardly committing to that ban.

“Farm presence (or absence) is only one of many variables, and current evidence does not demonstrate a causal link,” the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) said in a statement to W5, as another scientist suggested that surging salmon species, the pink salmon, May simply be doing better than other species in warming oceans.

A lot hinges on getting the science right: coastal communities are bracing for the impact of more salmon farm closures that could shed hundreds more jobs in what was once a billion-dollar industry, affect a valued way of life for First Nations, and change what Canadian consumers put on their plates.

The Discovery Islands: a pink salmon surge

Aboard his motorboat in the waters off the Discovery Islands, about 200 km northwest of Vancouver between Vancouver Island and the B.C. mainland, researcher Jody Erickson says he has noticed something incredible.

A seine net dropped from his motorboat can catch hundreds of young salmon smolts at a time, and Erickson draws up a few of them in a clear plastic case to see several different species: pink, chum and Chinook.

“What I would call very happy and healthy-looking fish right now,” he said. “No lice.”

It’s a far cry from what Erickson says he used to see in these waters a decade ago: juvenile salmon laden with parasites sticking to their skin, Erickson said. He still carries with him samples from those days that show small fish pockmarked with the parasites.

“They’re dying near fish farms. That’s what I see,” he said.

The Discovery Islands are a crucial thoroughfare for young salmon, who breed far up the freshwater rivers on B.C.’s coast, including the Fraser River, and then swim through these waters, around Vancouver Island, before making it out to sea.

Those islands, and the salmon farms that used to be there, were singled out by the Cohen Commission, a judicial inquiry that was called in 2009 after a salmon stock collapse.

Cohen pointed to many stressors that could affect the health of B.C. salmon, including warming waters, and recommended closing salmon farms in the Discovery Islands unless the federal fisheries minister is satisfied those farms pose at most a minimal risk to migrating sockeye salmon .

In 2019, the federal government followed through, refusing dozens of licences around the Discovery Islands, and then from the nearby Broughton Archipelago as a precaution. About half of all B.C. salmon farms are now gone.

A study by the Salmon Coast Field Station concluded that numbers of one species of lice dropped in the area once the salmon farms were removed, which could mean more salmon survive the long journey out to sea, said Research Crew Lead Kate Medcalf.

“As they out-migrate in these small sizes, they’re incredibly, incredibly vulnerable to parasitism and other stressors in the environment,” Medcalf said.

Erickson believes he is seeing the results of having fewer lice in the strait now.

“It’s very hopeful, because it shows that if we remove the fish farms, the fish can come back, really, really remarkably fast, faster than even I would have thought,” Erickson said.

Shuttered farms: the human cost

Nearby where Erickson cast his nets are what remains of several salmon farming operations. Some of them have been converted to other uses, while some have left no trace.

Those shutdowns meant lost jobs, and a narrowed future for the workers who hoped to launch long-term careers, said Kaitlin Guitard, a lab manager for one farm company, Mowi Canada West.

In an interview on the dock of one of the remaining farms, in the Queen Charlotte Strait near Port Hardy, she said she has lost hundreds of co-workers.

“It’s awful, it really is,” Guitard said. “I was relocated. But I think the hardest part for me was a lot of people that I worked with had either been laid off or could not wait around for certainty and had left.”

Guitard is among those fighting for the future of these farms, saying Canada needs the jobs and the food those farms produced.

Mowi Canada West’s production dropped from 40,000 tonnes a year, before the farms started to be removed in 2019, to 20,000 tonnes a year.

“The impact has been fairly devastating to the industry. We’ve lost 45 per cent of our production,” said Brian Kingzett, of the B.C. Salmon Farmers Association.

Kingzett says he’s aware that some farms have lice outbreaks, and that they do their best to manage them. But he doesn’t buy the connection drawn by researchers between his farms and the salmon collapse.

“We’ve had nine significant studies that have all identified that we can coexist with wild salmon, and we are continuing to innovate to further reduce any potential risks,” he said.

Rising numbers for salmon species; others are falling

Kingzett points to tracking by the Pacific Salmon Commission, a regulatory body run jointly by the Canadian and United States governments.

They use underwater sound waves and sonar to estimate the number of salmon passing the Mission hydroacoustic station in Mission, B.C., as they head up the Fraser River.

According to the commission figures, the number of pink salmon, which has a two-year life cycle, has doubled since 2019, from about 8.5 million to 17.7 million in 2025.

But the picture for another species of salmon, which has a four-year life cycle, is much less clear.

Promising returns of 8.1 million sockeye passing its station in 2025 were followed by disappointing returns under 3 million in 2026.

That figure was lower than 2022, when the Discovery Islands farms had been removed, and lower than in 2018 and 2014, when all the salmon farms were operating.

The DFO also monitors salmon escapement numbers by region along the coast. In region 13, which includes the Discovery Islands, coho and pink salmon are increasing, but chinook and sockeye salmon are not.

The connection between salmon farms and the health of wild stocks was also doubted by the DFO, which advised the fisheries minister in 2023 that its preferred option was to re-licence all 15 salmon farms in the Discovery Islands.

“Current Departmental science advice includes nine risk assessments that were completed specifically to advise the Department on the issue of licencing in the Discovery Islands, found that pathogen transmission from Atlantic salmon farms in the Discovery Islands poses minimal risk to Fraser River sockeye salmon population abundance and diversity under existing fish health management practices,” the department wrote.

The licenses were not re-issued. In 2024, the federal government proposed a draft transition plan that would ban open net pen salmon farming by 2029 .

However, there has been no final transition plan released since.

In response to questions from CTV News about whether the federal government plans to follow through with the 2029 ban, a statement from Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson didn’t mention it.

“Pacific salmon are iconic to the West Coast and protecting and rebuilding wild salmon populations is a priority for our government,” the statement said, pointing to investments the government has made in three new salmon hatcheries, and consultation with stakeholders in B.C. this summer.

“There is no single solution to the challenges facing wild Pacific salmon, which is why we are taking a comprehensive approach to protecting and rebuilding these stocks,” she said.

Another school of thought

In his home in Nanaimo, B.C., retired fish scientist and winner of the Order of Canada Dick Beamish is convinced the answer to the mystery of the salmon returns lies farther out in the Pacific Ocean.

He points to studies that show pink salmon are surging not just in B.C. but worldwide, because they are better able to handle warming ocean temperatures.

“There will be populations in the north Pacific that are adapting to the ocean warming conditions better than others,” Beamish said in an interview.

Some species are coming back from their time in the ocean much smaller, ON average, than in previous years, he said.

“What is probably happening with the warming that we’re seeing in the ocean is that there’s less food being produced that’s allowing salmon to accumulate the energy that they need to survive ocean winters,” Beamish said.

“That’s just a hypothesis. What we really need is scientific studies that are going to take a look at how this ocean warming is changing the overall food availability for salmon once they get into the open ocean,” he said.

Raising salmon on land?

Environmental groups are convinced that salmon farms are a threat and are pushing for alternatives to raise salmon on land.

In Port McNeill, in a cavernous warehouse only about a kilometre from where the Nimpkish River flows into the Queen Charlotte Strait, there are fish who will never see the ocean at all.

They’re grown in large circular tanks in a facility called Kuterra, built by the Namgis First Nation in 2013 for $10 million as a demonstration project to prove that a land-based aquaculture industry is possible in B.C.

More than 10 years in, the project is still going, with some changes. The facility used to produce salmon but has found it’s easier to produce trout, said Chief Don Svanvik of the Namgis First Nation.

“It’s incredible. It’s a big investment,” Svanvik said in an interview in Port McNeill. “But it’s happening. If it was easy, everybody would be doing it.”

A study commissioned by the B.C. government in 2021 found that the experience of Kuterra May be hard to replicate, warning of high capital costs, difficulty obtaining power, and regulatory uncertainty.

“The results are not promising,” said the report, by Counterpoint Consulting, saying the estimated rate of return is too low at 8.7 per cent for a large farm and 5.8 per cent for a medium-sized farm.

“Those rates of return are far too low to attract the investment required to incentivize the development of a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) salmon farming industry in British Columbia,” the report said.

“We have concluded from our research and analysis that RAS development in BC is possible, but at smaller scales and not in isolation from the larger aquaculture sector currently operating in BC,” the report said.

Tony Allard, a businessman who is the chair of the environmental group Wild First, admits land-based farms can be “capital-intensive.”

But he said there are other advantages, pointing to another land-based farm near Tokyo, which he said saves on transportation costs because it’s right next to its market.

Allard said that there is investor interest in making these work, especially if the open net pen farming is shut down.

“It has proved the concept. It’s grown fish, and it’s sold them at a premium,” he said in an interview.

“And that’s where the growth of this industry is. So, keep the ban, no half-measures, and let’s grow this industry safely, sustainably, ON land,” he said.

Imports filling the gaps

Canadian consumers May not be waiting around as foreign fish farms have rushed in to fill the gaps left by shuttered West Coast fish farms.

One major grocery chain, Loblaws, told CTV News in a statement that it sources salmon from a variety of Canadian and international suppliers, and prices vary based on a number of factors.

“Reduced domestic supply in recent years has meant we are relying more on imported salmon; however, Canadian salmon remains an important part of our assortment, and we will continue to source domestically where supply and market conditions allow,” the statement said.

In 2016, Canada imported about $90.5 million in fish categories including Atlantic salmon, according to Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada and Statistics Canada. That number quadrupled to $356 million in 2025.

It was a similar surge from Norway, whose exports to Canada rose from $34 million to $158 million.

And Iceland’s exports surged 22 times, from $0.8 million to $20 million in the same time period.

“I think that’s a challenge for Canadians to wake up and turn around and look and say, is this something that we want? Do we want to import fish?” asked Richard Opala, a regulatory affairs manager at Mowi Canada West.

“Well, we can grow it here. Do we want to support jobs in other countries when we don’t have them here?” he said.

But critics of the fish farm industry say that Canadian wild stocks could be better protected if Canadians order from farms in ecosystems without competing salmon.

“The stakes are higher here than they are in Norway, where there are no longer any commercial fisheries,” said Kristi Miller, a scientist who used to work with the Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans.

“It’s different here in British Columbia, because we still have large, abundant populations of wild fish. We still have commercial fisheries. We still have recreational fisheries, we still have Indigenous fisheries,” she said.

Coastal community worries

Some First Nations groups are concerned enough about the potential impact of salmon farms they are calling for the eviction of remaining salmon farms near Port Hardy.

“What wild salmon mean to First Nations all across the province is beyond valuation. It contributes to food security across the province. It is the basis of our culture and traditions. And is not an item we wish to see impacted while others make profits,” said Bob Chamberlin, chair of the First Nations Wild Salmon Alliance, at a news conference this month on Parliament Hill.

In Port Hardy, ON northern Vancouver Island, Mayor Patricia Corbett-Labatt is concerned about what losing the remaining salmon farms would mean for her community.

“We are a fishing, logging, mining community. We’re resource based,” she said in an interview.

She said she is concerned about what would happen to the jobs, and by extension the community, if more farms are shut down.

“It would be very similar to when the mine closed here and there was a huge depression,” she said.

Over in the Queen Charlotte Strait, Guitard from Mowi takes a scoop of pellets and tosses it into an open pen. The fish respond by jumping.

She said she’s worried about what May be in store in 2029, when the ban is set to take effect, but is hopeful she can stay in her home in Campbell River.

“It’s awful, honestly. I’ve been here for six years. I have established a whole community, I have friends, it’s a lifestyle that I would love to live, but it really does rely solely on this industry continuing here.”

content_blocks.text: But a W5 investigation has revealed a confidential internal assessment where federal government scientists say salmon farming operations pose a “minimal risk” to wild stocks and recommended reopening some of them, as the government itself is not outwardly committing to that ban.

“Farm presence (or absence) is only one of many variables, and current evidence does not demonstrate a causal link,” the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) said in a statement to W5, as another scientist suggested that surging salmon species, the pink salmon, May simply be doing better than other species in warming oceans.

A lot hinges on getting the science right: coastal communities are bracing for the impact of more salmon farm closures that could shed hundreds more jobs in what was once a billion-dollar industry, affect a valued way of life for First Nations, and change what Canadian consumers put on their plates.
The Discovery Islands: a pink salmon surge

Aboard his motorboat in the waters off the Discovery Islands, about 200 km northwest of Vancouver between Vancouver Island and the B.C. mainland, researcher Jody Erickson says he has noticed something incredible.

A seine net dropped from his motorboat can catch hundreds of young salmon smolts at a time, and Erickson draws up a few of them in a clear plastic case to see several different species: pink, chum and Chinook.

content_blocks.alt: Jody Erickson with salmon
content_blocks.caption: Researcher Jody Erickson shows off salmon smolts taken from a net in the Discovery Islands, between Vancouver Island and B.C.'s mainland, northwest of Vancouver, B.C.

content_blocks.text: “What I would call very happy and healthy-looking fish right now,” he said. “No lice.”

It’s a far cry from what Erickson says he used to see in these waters a decade ago: juvenile salmon laden with parasites sticking to their skin, Erickson said. He still carries with him samples from those days that show small fish pockmarked with the parasites.
“They’re dying near fish farms. That’s what I see,” he said.

The Discovery Islands are a crucial thoroughfare for young salmon, who breed far up the freshwater rivers on B.C.’s coast, including the Fraser River, and then swim through these waters, around Vancouver Island, before making it out to sea.
Those islands, and the salmon farms that used to be there, were singled out by the Cohen Commission, a judicial inquiry that was called in 2009 after a salmon stock collapse.

Cohen pointed to many stressors that could affect the health of B.C. salmon, including warming waters, and recommended closing salmon farms in the Discovery Islands unless the federal fisheries minister is satisfied those farms pose at most a minimal risk to migrating sockeye salmon .

content_blocks.alt: Fish inside the Queen Charlotte Strait fish farm
content_blocks.caption: Atlantic salmon swim in the open net pens at a MOWI Canada West fish farm near Port Hardy, B.C. The image was supplied by MOWI Canada West.

content_blocks.text: In 2019, the federal government followed through, refusing dozens of licences around the Discovery Islands, and then from the nearby Broughton Archipelago as a precaution. About half of all B.C. salmon farms are now gone.

A study by the Salmon Coast Field Station concluded that numbers of one species of lice dropped in the area once the salmon farms were removed, which could mean more salmon survive the long journey out to sea, said Research Crew Lead Kate Medcalf.
“As they out-migrate in these small sizes, they’re incredibly, incredibly vulnerable to parasitism and other stressors in the environment,” Medcalf said.
Erickson believes he is seeing the results of having fewer lice in the strait now.
“It’s very hopeful, because it shows that if we remove the fish farms, the fish can come back, really, really remarkably fast, faster than even I would have thought,” Erickson said.
Shuttered farms: the human cost
Nearby where Erickson cast his nets are what remains of several salmon farming operations. Some of them have been converted to other uses, while some have left no trace.
Those shutdowns meant lost jobs, and a narrowed future for the workers who hoped to launch long-term careers, said Kaitlin Guitard, a lab manager for one farm company, Mowi Canada West.

content_blocks.alt: Kaitlin Guitard
content_blocks.caption: Kaitlin Guitard, a laboratory manager at MOWI Canada West, feeds Atlantic salmon in an open net pen in the Queen Charlotte Strait near Port Hardy, B.C.

content_blocks.text: In an interview on the dock of one of the remaining farms, in the Queen Charlotte Strait near Port Hardy, she said she has lost hundreds of co-workers.

“It’s awful, it really is,” Guitard said. “I was relocated. But I think the hardest part for me was a lot of people that I worked with had either been laid off or could not wait around for certainty and had left.”
Guitard is among those fighting for the future of these farms, saying Canada needs the jobs and the food those farms produced.
Mowi Canada West’s production dropped from 40,000 tonnes a year, before the farms started to be removed in 2019, to 20,000 tonnes a year.
“The impact has been fairly devastating to the industry. We’ve lost 45 per cent of our production,” said Brian Kingzett, of the B.C. Salmon Farmers Association.

Kingzett says he’s aware that some farms have lice outbreaks, and that they do their best to manage them. But he doesn’t buy the connection drawn by researchers between his farms and the salmon collapse.
“We’ve had nine significant studies that have all identified that we can coexist with wild salmon, and we are continuing to innovate to further reduce any potential risks,” he said.
Rising numbers for salmon species; others are falling
Kingzett points to tracking by the Pacific Salmon Commission, a regulatory body run jointly by the Canadian and United States governments.
They use underwater sound waves and sonar to estimate the number of salmon passing the Mission hydroacoustic station in Mission, B.C., as they head up the Fraser River.
According to the commission figures, the number of pink salmon, which has a two-year life cycle, has doubled since 2019, from about 8.5 million to 17.7 million in 2025.
But the picture for another species of salmon, which has a four-year life cycle, is much less clear.
Promising returns of 8.1 million sockeye passing its station in 2025 were followed by disappointing returns under 3 million in 2026.
That figure was lower than 2022, when the Discovery Islands farms had been removed, and lower than in 2018 and 2014, when all the salmon farms were operating.

The DFO also monitors salmon escapement numbers by region along the coast. In region 13, which includes the Discovery Islands, coho and pink salmon are increasing, but chinook and sockeye salmon are not.

The connection between salmon farms and the health of wild stocks was also doubted by the DFO, which advised the fisheries minister in 2023 that its preferred option was to re-licence all 15 salmon farms in the Discovery Islands.

content_blocks.alt: Sockeye Salmon Passage
content_blocks.caption: Sockeye Salmon Passage

content_blocks.text: “Current Departmental science advice includes nine risk assessments that were completed specifically to advise the Department on the issue of licencing in the Discovery Islands, found that pathogen transmission from Atlantic salmon farms in the Discovery Islands poses minimal risk to Fraser River sockeye salmon population abundance and diversity under existing fish health management practices,” the department wrote.
The licenses were not re-issued. In 2024, the federal government proposed a draft transition plan that would ban open net pen salmon farming by 2029 .
However, there has been no final transition plan released since.
In response to questions from CTV News about whether the federal government plans to follow through with the 2029 ban, a statement from Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson didn’t mention it.

“Pacific salmon are iconic to the West Coast and protecting and rebuilding wild salmon populations is a priority for our government,” the statement said, pointing to investments the government has made in three new salmon hatcheries, and consultation with stakeholders in B.C. this summer.
“There is no single solution to the challenges facing wild Pacific salmon, which is why we are taking a comprehensive approach to protecting and rebuilding these stocks,” she said.
Another school of thought
In his home in Nanaimo, B.C., retired fish scientist and winner of the Order of Canada Dick Beamish is convinced the answer to the mystery of the salmon returns lies farther out in the Pacific Ocean.
He points to studies that show pink salmon are surging not just in B.C. but worldwide, because they are better able to handle warming ocean temperatures.
“There will be populations in the north Pacific that are adapting to the ocean warming conditions better than others,” Beamish said in an interview.
Some species are coming back from their time in the ocean much smaller, ON average, than in previous years, he said.

“What is probably happening with the warming that we’re seeing in the ocean is that there’s less food being produced that’s allowing salmon to accumulate the energy that they need to survive ocean winters,” Beamish said.

“That’s just a hypothesis. What we really need is scientific studies that are going to take a look at how this ocean warming is changing the overall food availability for salmon once they get into the open ocean,” he said.
Raising salmon on land?
Environmental groups are convinced that salmon farms are a threat and are pushing for alternatives to raise salmon on land.
In Port McNeill, in a cavernous warehouse only about a kilometre from where the Nimpkish River flows into the Queen Charlotte Strait, there are fish who will never see the ocean at all.

They’re grown in large circular tanks in a facility called Kuterra, built by the Namgis First Nation in 2013 for $10 million as a demonstration project to prove that a land-based aquaculture industry is possible in B.C.

More than 10 years in, the project is still going, with some changes. The facility used to produce salmon but has found it’s easier to produce trout, said Chief Don Svanvik of the Namgis First Nation.
“It’s incredible. It’s a big investment,” Svanvik said in an interview in Port McNeill. “But it’s happening. If it was easy, everybody would be doing it.”

A study commissioned by the B.C. government in 2021 found that the experience of Kuterra May be hard to replicate, warning of high capital costs, difficulty obtaining power, and regulatory uncertainty.
“The results are not promising,” said the report, by Counterpoint Consulting, saying the estimated rate of return is too low at 8.7 per cent for a large farm and 5.8 per cent for a medium-sized farm.

“Those rates of return are far too low to attract the investment required to incentivize the development of a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) salmon farming industry in British Columbia,” the report said.

“We have concluded from our research and analysis that RAS development in BC is possible, but at smaller scales and not in isolation from the larger aquaculture sector currently operating in BC,” the report said.
Tony Allard, a businessman who is the chair of the environmental group Wild First, admits land-based farms can be “capital-intensive.”
But he said there are other advantages, pointing to another land-based farm near Tokyo, which he said saves on transportation costs because it’s right next to its market.
Allard said that there is investor interest in making these work, especially if the open net pen farming is shut down.
“It has proved the concept. It’s grown fish, and it’s sold them at a premium,” he said in an interview.
“And that’s where the growth of this industry is. So, keep the ban, no half-measures, and let’s grow this industry safely, sustainably, ON land,” he said.
Imports filling the gaps
Canadian consumers May not be waiting around as foreign fish farms have rushed in to fill the gaps left by shuttered West Coast fish farms.
One major grocery chain, Loblaws, told CTV News in a statement that it sources salmon from a variety of Canadian and international suppliers, and prices vary based on a number of factors.

“Reduced domestic supply in recent years has meant we are relying more on imported salmon; however, Canadian salmon remains an important part of our assortment, and we will continue to source domestically where supply and market conditions allow,” the statement said.

In 2016, Canada imported about $90.5 million in fish categories including Atlantic salmon, according to Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada and Statistics Canada. That number quadrupled to $356 million in 2025.
It was a similar surge from Norway, whose exports to Canada rose from $34 million to $158 million.
And Iceland’s exports surged 22 times, from $0.8 million to $20 million in the same time period.

content_blocks.alt: Importation graphics
content_blocks.caption: Figures show the rise in imported Atlantic salmon.

content_blocks.text: “I think that’s a challenge for Canadians to wake up and turn around and look and say, is this something that we want? Do we want to import fish?” asked Richard Opala, a regulatory affairs manager at Mowi Canada West.
“Well, we can grow it here. Do we want to support jobs in other countries when we don’t have them here?” he said.
But critics of the fish farm industry say that Canadian wild stocks could be better protected if Canadians order from farms in ecosystems without competing salmon.

“The stakes are higher here than they are in Norway, where there are no longer any commercial fisheries,” said Kristi Miller, a scientist who used to work with the Canadian Department of Fisheries and Oceans.

“It’s different here in British Columbia, because we still have large, abundant populations of wild fish. We still have commercial fisheries. We still have recreational fisheries, we still have Indigenous fisheries,” she said.
Coastal community worries
Some First Nations groups are concerned enough about the potential impact of salmon farms they are calling for the eviction of remaining salmon farms near Port Hardy.

“What wild salmon mean to First Nations all across the province is beyond valuation. It contributes to food security across the province. It is the basis of our culture and traditions. And is not an item we wish to see impacted while others make profits,” said Bob Chamberlin, chair of the First Nations Wild Salmon Alliance, at a news conference this month on Parliament Hill.
In Port Hardy, ON northern Vancouver Island, Mayor Patricia Corbett-Labatt is concerned about what losing the remaining salmon farms would mean for her community.
“We are a fishing, logging, mining community. We’re resource based,” she said in an interview.
She said she is concerned about what would happen to the jobs, and by extension the community, if more farms are shut down.
“It would be very similar to when the mine closed here and there was a huge depression,” she said.
Over in the Queen Charlotte Strait, Guitard from Mowi takes a scoop of pellets and tosses it into an open pen. The fish respond by jumping.
She said she’s worried about what May be in store in 2029, when the ban is set to take effect, but is hopeful she can stay in her home in Campbell River.

“It’s awful, honestly. I’ve been here for six years. I have established a whole community, I have friends, it’s a lifestyle that I would love to live, but it really does rely solely on this industry continuing here.”

stories.title: Canadian medical journalist Helen Branswell was lauded for her coverage of COVID-19
stories.summary: In her reporting, she ‘demonstrated an unwavering commitment to evidence, science and truth,’ and she was part of a team who were finalists for a Pulitzer Prize in breaking news reporting in 2021
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
Early in 2020, a little more than a month after reports of a new infectious disease began to trickle out of China, Anthony Fauci was a guest on a panel discussion in Washington about the emerging coronavirus.

Dr. Fauci, who was at the time the director of the U.S. National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, struck a reassuring tone. While he acknowledged there was a real possibility things could get worse, he said that “at present, given everything that’s going on, the risk is really relatively low.”

The panel moderator, the health journalist Helen Branswell, wasn’t comforted by his words. She was from Canada, where she had covered the outbreak of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (Sars) in 2003 that originated from China and killed hundreds of people around the world.

“Explain to me why the risk is low, somebody, because to me, when I look at this virus spreading, it’s spreading very efficiently,” she asked the panel. “There’s no force field around China. It’s not going to stop there.”

A few weeks later, the United States, Canada, and large swaths of the rest of the world went into lockdown as COVID-19 spread globally, infecting over 82 million people and killing more than 1.8 million by the end of the year.

Already on Jan. 4, Ms. Branswell had written an article for her media outlet, the Boston-based health news website Stat, detailing how infectious disease experts were scrambling to get more information about a cluster of unexplained pneumonia cases in the Chinese city of Wuhan.

As Stat managing editor Jason Ukman would later note, that initial article came “before the virus that causes COVID-19 had a name – before COVID-19 itself had a name.”

Ms. Branswell, a Canadian medical journalist lauded for her coverage of infectious diseases, especially of the COVID-19 pandemic, died Tuesday from complications of cancer. She was 69.

“At a moment when misinformation competes with facts, her reporting was a trusted source of clarity, honesty and insight,” World Health Organization director-general Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a statement.

Ms. Branswell’s work was recognized by one of the most prestigious U.S. journalism honours in 2021, the George Polk Award, in the public service category, “for timely, astute and relentless coverage of all aspects of the COVID-19 pandemic that became must reading for the medical community and the general public.”

She was also part of a team of Stat journalists who were finalists the same year for a Pulitzer Prize in breaking news reporting, “for their prescient, expert and accessible coverage of the emergence of COVID-19.”

The recognition came to a reporter who had taken her first steps in journalism four decades earlier as a freelancer in New Brunswick, before becoming a foreign correspondent for the Canadian Press news agency, then turning her efforts toward health coverage.

Ms. Branswell’s work was demanding because she had to report promptly, accurately and clearly on a host of communicable diseases that worried the public.

Alan Bernstein, the founding president of the Canadian Institutes for Health Research (Cihr), said Ms. Branswell sometimes contacted him or other researchers to make sure she wasn’t propagating a medical falsehood.

“She had a nose for what was good science, what was not good science,” Dr. Bernstein recalled in an interview.

“Helen was an outstanding Canadian who made a global mark,” he said, noting that scientists as well as the general public read her work.

“Helen’s reporting saved lives … the world lost a great journalist,” Christine Fitzgerald, a former Cihr executive vice-president, said in an interview.

Although she had known Ms. Branswell since high school, Ms. Fitzgerald also had to handle journalistic queries from her longtime friend. “Even though we were friends outside work, that didn’t matter. That’s why I admired Helen. She was principled and unwavering in her integrity.”

Ms. Branswell was the first of three siblings who became journalists. One of her brothers, Jack, is also a former Canadian Press reporter, and her sister, Brenda, worked for Maclean’s magazine and the Montreal Gazette.

“I always kind of joke that it was because we were all terrible at math,” Jack said in an interview, alluding to the stereotype that journalists aren’t good with numbers. “But clearly Helen wasn’t terrible at science.”

She was born on May 19, 1957, in Sherbrooke, Que., the second of the six children of John and Margaret Branswell. Their father taught high school history and English, so the four boys and two girls grew up in a household that valued the written word and paid attention to current events.

Ms. Branswell earned a degree in English literature at St. Thomas University, in Fredericton. She started freelancing at $15 a story for the local newspaper, the Daily Gleaner, got hired to cover the night and weekend shifts, and eventually became a legislature reporter.

This paved the way to reporting with the Canadian Press, with postings in Halifax, Calgary and Ottawa before the news agency sent her to Britain as its London-based correspondent. After five years, she returned to Canada and settled in Toronto, where she became CP’s health reporter.

In a 2021 interview with Longform , a podcast about journalism, Ms. Branswell said she initially wasn’t keen to take on her new assignment. “In Canada, health reporting is often about the politics of how much funding the health care system gets and I was not interested in that at all.”

But CP insisted and Ms. Branswell took on the job. “It was a very steep learning curve,” she recalled. Just as she was getting comfortable in her beat, Sars struck in 2003. She would later call it her introduction to reporting on a sudden, deadly outbreak.

“That reporting drew international attention. That’s when she found her stride and her passion,” Ms. Fitzgerald said. “And so for the next 15 years, she became the voice of global health threats.”

Ms. Branswell had to familiarize herself with the science and jargon of infectious diseases but her background in the fast-paced world of news agency reporting had prepared her for the shifting nature of viral infections.

“The thing about covering an infectious disease outbreak is it’s breaking news. And I had a lot of experience covering breaking news,” she explained on the Open Forum Infectious Diseases podcast.

In the fall of 2015, Ms. Branswell moved to Boston to report on infectious diseases for Stat, a digital startup specializing in health coverage. Her articles in the following years featured a rogues’ gallery of viral ailments: Ebola, Zika, polio, dengue fever, influenza, measles, Aids, Mers, monkeypox.

The last afternoon of 2019, while visiting her brother Jack in Ottawa, Ms. Branswell saw on her cellphone an email alert about an unidentified respiratory illness in Wuhan.

The email came from ProMED, an early warning system for infectious diseases.

“Hopefully this is nothing out of the ordinary,” she posted on Twitter that New Year’s Eve afternoon. “But a @ProMED_mail posting about ‘unexplained pneumonias’ in China is giving me #Sars flashbacks.”

Two days later, she shared on Twitter an article from the South China Morning Post about the spread of the disease. The story said the World Health Organization was in touch with Chinese authorities, who had shut down a local market in Wuhan. “Not liking the look of this,” she wrote .

Ms. Branswell later explained on the Longform podcast that she knew the Chinese had experience detecting new respiratory diseases. “So if China was seeing something unusual, it was something you needed to pay attention to.”

Her initial article, ON Jan. 4, recounted how medical virus watchers, who had to rely on machine-translated reports that the outbreak might be caused by a new virus, were hoping for more information.

In scores of articles published the following months, she documented what was learned about the new disease, whether immunity could be acquired, how vaccines could be dispensed.

She also turned to social media to share information with the public, urging people to take precautions with their elderly relatives while making sure they weren’t socially isolated. “She just had this deep empathy … that’s just a snippet of her big heart,” Ms. Fitzgerald said.

Ms. Branswell also witnessed the rise of misinformation. She had to balance whether to debunk false information when that fact-checking attempt could disseminate the falsehoods further. “My inbox is flooded with people trying to get me to interview people who are being passed out as experts, who really are not experts,” she wrote.

After she was diagnosed with cancer, Ms. Branswell kept working. “In the past year, it was a nice break from medical appointments just to immerse herself in the work that she loved,” her sister, Brenda, said in an interview.

In August, Ms. Branswell was awarded the 2026 Kovler Prize for Trust in Life Science Journalism. She donated the $25,000 honorarium to a journalism fellowship named after Sharon Begley, a friend and Stat colleague who had died of cancer.

The day before her death, she shared new data on the maternal respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine with her colleagues on a work Slack channel, Stat reported.

Jack Branswell said his sister’s journalism had been particularly valuable during a period when public trust in medicine and science had been eroded.

“Truth was really important to her. In this time of such divisiveness, getting to the heart of the story and giving people information was extremely important to her. ... She believed in truth and serving the public by doing her best job to get the truth.”

Ms. Branswell leaves her five siblings and eight nieces and nephews.

You can find more obituaries from The Globe and Mail here .

To submit a memory about someone we have recently profiled on the Obituaries page, e-mail us at obit@globeandmail.com .

She also turned to social media to share information with the public, urging people to take precautions with their elderly relatives while making sure they weren’t socially isolated. “She just had this deep empathy … that’s just a snippet of her big heart,” Ms. Fitzgerald said.

Ms. Branswell also witnessed the rise of misinformation. She had to balance whether to debunk false information when that fact-checking attempt could disseminate the falsehoods further. “My inbox is flooded with people trying to get me to interview people who are being passed out as experts, who really are not experts,” she wrote.

After she was diagnosed with cancer, Ms. Branswell kept working. “In the past year, it was a nice break from medical appointments just to immerse herself in the work that she loved,” her sister, Brenda, said in an interview.

In August, Ms. Branswell was awarded the 2026 Kovler Prize for Trust in Life Science Journalism. She donated the $25,000 honorarium to a journalism fellowship named after Sharon Begley, a friend and Stat colleague who had died of cancer.
The day before her death, she shared new data on the maternal respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine with her colleagues on a work Slack channel, Stat reported.
Jack Branswell said his sister’s journalism had been particularly valuable during a period when public trust in medicine and science had been eroded.

“Truth was really important to her. In this time of such divisiveness, getting to the heart of the story and giving people information was extremely important to her. ... She believed in truth and serving the public by doing her best job to get the truth.”
Ms. Branswell leaves her five siblings and eight nieces and nephews.
