stories.title: Anti-Zionist group hosting event to 'populate Wikipedia entries honouring martyred Palestinian artists'
stories.summary: The purpose of the event is "to populate Wikipedia entries honouring martyred Palestinian artists."
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
An anti-Zionist group is hosting an event in Toronto to flood Wikipedia with entries to honour what it refers to as “martyred” Palestinians.

Stop Art Washing describes itself as an organization of “art workers across so-called-Canada demanding cultural institutions divest from settler colonialism and genocide.” It is hosting “a Wikipedia 101 session” with “hands-on editing” on Oct. 22 at an undisclosed location, according to its Instagram account.

The purpose of the event is “to populate Wikipedia entries honouring martyred Palestinian artists and exposing the Canadian, Zionist backers of genocide.”

This goes against Wikipedia’s own policy that says the platform should not be used as “a soapbox, a battleground, or a vehicle for propaganda, advertising, and showcasing.” It also says that all content should be written from a neutral point of view .

Wikipedia did not respond to National Post’s request for comment.

A page on the website dedicated to Wikipedia and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict says that since Oct. 7, 2023, the volume of edits on the topic “has surged significantly.” Coverage of the conflict on Wikipedia has faced “criticism from advocates on both sides for perceived bias,” it says.

In an interview with PBS , Wikipedia co-founder Jimmy Wales was asked specifically about an entry on the “Gaza genocide” that described it as an “ongoing, intentional and systematic destruction of the Palestinian people in the Gaza Strip carried out by Israel.”

Wales called it “one of the worst Wikipedia entries” he’s seen in a long time and said he was shocked by it.

Damaged wires, red paint: Group says it targeted Ontario facility because of ties to Israel

“It needs to change. I think it’s just terrible. It doesn’t live up to our standards of neutrality, and I think it’s very problematic,” he said.

An analysis of a Wikipedia page about South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice was published by National Post in 2024. It found there were 27 highly active editors who contributed “significantly” to the page. Some would make changes such as removing neutral language from a section that included a response from Israel, while others would change article titles to include emotionally charged terminology.

Researchers identified “patterns of anti-Israel bias among power-user editors, highlighting how personal viewpoints can seep into supposedly neutral content.”

The analysis revealed “alarming patterns of bias that can cascade through the digital information ecosystem, infecting everything from search engine results to academic citations to social media posts and even AI training data.”

Wikipedia is a free online encyclopedia founded in 2001. Its entries are written by hundreds of thousands of volunteer editors. It is available in more than 300 languages.

stories.title: Adam Gopnik reflects on friendship with photographer Richard Avedon
stories.summary: Longtime staff writer for The New Yorker talks about their first meeting, working together and applying Avedon’s wisdom
stories.author: Martha Schabas
stories.content:
The longtime New Yorker staff writer Adam Gopnik was on assignment for GQ Magazine in 1985 when he first visited Richard Avedon’s Upper East Side studio. The two men started a heartfelt conversation that day that would last the next 20 years, until Avedon’s death in 2004.

Over the years, Gopnik has shared little about his treasured friendship with the legendary American photographer. But lately, sensing Avedon’s presence and personality recede further into the past, he feels an unexpected urgency to discuss his old friend’s work.

It was in this valedictory spirit that I found Gopnik on a September morning at Toronto Metropolitan University’s Image Centre, where a new exhibition – Richard Avedon Immortal: Portraits of Aging 1951-2004 – is on display until Dec. 5. The exhibition features nearly 100 black-and-white portraits of some of the most important cultural and political figures of the latter half of the 20th century, including Samuel Beckett, the Dalai Lama, Ronald Reagan, Truman Capote and Toni Morrison.

Do you remember much about the first time you and Avedon met?

I remember it clearly. I was a young pipsqueak fresh off the bus from Montreal. I’d always loved his work and we hit it off. It was just one of those things that happens two or three times in a lifetime when you’re engaged with someone despite all of the differences in age, which were large, and differences in stature, which were even larger. Professional stature. In fact, one of the funny things about us was we were exactly the same size and build. If I had a fancy dinner, I would call a Dick and say, “Can I borrow a suit?” He had all of these beautiful handmade suits, and I was the only other person they fit.

I imagine the friendship really solidified when Avedon joined you at The New Yorker.

If anything, I was a little reluctant about having him come to The New Yorker , because it was my home and Dick was a very powerful, passionate figure and he had a very paternal role in my life. Tina [Brown] wanted there to be photography in the magazine, which was breaking an ancient tradition, and I knew that Dick was the one person who could do it because of the elegance of his style – its brevity, its minimalism at times, its eloquence.

What did he share about his process and his guiding ideas on photography?

Dick said to me once, “I can teach you everything I know about the technique of photography in 20 minutes.” He was technically virtuosic, his printing would take literally 30 or 40 different proofs before he was satisfied, but he didn’t care about F stops and panoramic views. He said, “Everything that I do is about my relationship with the person I’m photographing.”

Did he offer wisdom about his work that you were able to apply to your writing?

He would always say “go deeper.” He wanted me to be more audacious in my judgment, less constrained in my approach. Dick never wanted to make a flattering portrait of anybody. He didn’t understand why anybody would want to minimize their frailty, their vulnerability, their intelligence, their age. And I’ve learned the same with my own work. Now when I’m going to do a profile of someone, I say to them before, I would love to write about you, because you really intrigue me, but there’s going to be something in the piece that you’re going to hate.

Tell me about his self-portrait in the collection?

It’s a beautiful picture of Dick’s delicacy and integrity, but it isn’t at all what he was like as a man. He was a rambunctious, delightful, funny, warm and welcoming human being – if he liked you. Dick was mischievous, and he loved nothing more than a great game or a wonderful surprise to play on people. The last thing Dick ever was was quiet and introspective.

What do you think he would make of the current era of online photography, such as Instagram and everything that’s happening with AI?

He was resolutely non-nostalgic. He embraced the new with absolute avidity. I think he’d be disturbed by the homogeneous nature of what goes on now – this endless, unlimited ribbon of imagery, which rises, we watch for 30 seconds, disappears, and is replaced by something else. But I actually think that he would have loved the immediacy and spontaneity. He died just as the iPhone was invented, but I am certain he would have had his iPhone out. He loved taking snapshots. He loved that casual and omnivorous relationship to imagery.

What’s your favourite portrait in the exhibition?

Auden in the snow (W.H. Auden, poet, St Mark’s Place, New York, March 3, 1960). Dick gave it to me for my 30th birthday; it hangs in our hallway at home. I think it’s one of the most beautiful and poetic portraits there is. It’s very typical of Dick’s work – it looks like a snapshot but everything is choreographed. He woke up one morning and it was snowing hard and he had this image of W.H. Auden walking in the snow. It captures Auden’s seriousness, his Olympian qualities, his comic qualities, his Chaplin-esque side. It’s a great example of Avedon’s poetry of contradiction: Here’s this great poet who had seen everything and said everything, who’s also this slightly comic old crotchety man walking down Second Avenue in slippers.

stories.title: Fairfax buys controlling stake in India’s Idbi Bank for $5.6-billion
stories.summary: Deal was announced as Canadian delegation in India for trade mission
stories.author: Andrew Willis
stories.content:
Fairfax Financial Holdings Ltd. FFH-T is taking on another bank turnaround by acquiring control of India’s Idbi Bank for US$5.6-billion, the largest foreign investment ever made in the South Asian country’s financial services sector.

Toronto-based Fairfax is buying a 60.72-per-cent stake in Idbi Bank from the government of India, according to a press release on Wednesday from the federal Department of Investment and Public Asset Management.

“This transaction represents a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to purchase a majority interest in a bank in one of the world’s fastest growing economies,” Fairfax chief executive officer Prem Watsa said in a press release.

“We assure the Government of India that we are committed to building the world’s finest financial institution from India,” Mr. Watsa said.

Idbi ranks among the 10 largest banks in India by market capitalization and is in the top 15 by assets. Its retail division, the bank’s dominant business, includes teams dedicated to serving doctors, small-business owners and farmers. Idbi also owns an investment bank that finances infrastructure projects.

Fairfax plans to expand Idbi by combining the bank with its 49-per-cent stake in Go Digit General Insurance Ltd. and its holding in investment bank and wealth manager Iifl Capital Services Ltd.

Founded in 2017, Bangalore-based Go Digit offers car, motorbike, health, fire and property insurance through an online platform and has roughly 80 million customers. In last year’s annual report, Fairfax valued its holding in the company at US$1.3-billion.

The Indian government and state-owned Life Insurance Corp. of India, known as LIC, took control of Mumbai-based Idbi in 2019 after it ran up significant loan losses. Four years ago, the government launched a process to sell its stake as part of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s strategy to attract more private capital to the banking sector.

The government of India announced the Fairfax investment as Canada’s federal Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu leads a trade mission in the country.

Fairfax has previously made significant profits by taking stakes in troubled banks in Ireland, Greece and India, then fixing their balance sheets and expanding their services in fee-generating sectors such wealth management.

In 2014, Fairfax began investing in Athens-based Eurobank and ultimately committed €1.2-billion ($1.9-billion) to the lender. In its most recent annual report, the asset manager showed it has earned a 15-per-cent annual return on the investment. Fairfax has sold part of its holding and still owns a Eurobank stake worth €4-billion.

In 2011, after the global financial crisis, Fairfax led a consortium that recapitalized the Bank of Ireland. Fairfax tripled its investment when it sold the position in 2017, making a €566-million profit.

As part of the sales process at Idbi, the Indian government obtained valuations on the bank from two independent advisers. The government then used the average of the prices its advisers submitted – 75.99 rupees for each Idbi share – as the benchmark price for potential bidders. Fairfax won the auction with a bid of 81 rupees per share.

Five financial companies initially took part in the Idbi auction, according to the government. Two bidders – which Reuters identified as Fairfax and Dubai’s Emirates NBD – made final offers, the government said.

Last year, Emirates NBD acquired a stake in private lender RBL Bank for US$3-billion as part of Mr. Modi’s campaign to boost domestic lenders’ balance sheets.

The government of India and LIC are each selling just over 30 per cent of Idbi to Fairfax. After the sale, the government will hold a 15-per-cent interest in the bank and LIC will retain a 19-per-cent stake. Government and LIC directors stepped down from the Idbi board, which makes it easier for both investors to sell their remaining shares.

In 2018, Fairfax bought a stake in CSB Bank Ltd., which is also based in India. Government regulations on the Idbi investment require Fairfax to either merge or exit its 40-per-cent stake in CSB Bank over the next two years.

CSB Bank is a relatively small, regional lender that ranks outside India’s top 20 banks by assets.

Mr. Watsa was born in Hyderabad, India, and earned a degree in chemical engineering before immigrating to Canada in the 1970s. He paid for an MBA at Western University by selling furnaces and air conditioners door-to-door. In 1985, he launched Fairfax by starting an asset manager and acquiring a truck insurance business, then investing with a value-based approach.

Fairfax is now one of Canada’s largest financial services companies, with a US$51.2-billion market capitalization. The company stock price has more than tripled in the past five years, with Fairfax shares up 340 per cent on the Toronto Stock Exchange.

stories.title: Ontario announces permanent daylight saving time for northwestern parts of the province
stories.summary: Keeping northwestern Ontario aligned with Manitoba will "avoid unnecessary disruptions" in Ontario’s central time zone, says AG Doug Downey.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Ontario says the recently announced change for northwestern Ontario will keep that region aligned with Manitoba, avoiding disruption for businesses, families and Indigenous communities in Ontario’s central time zone.

“Maintaining alignment with Manitoba would help businesses operate more efficiently across provincial boundaries, while making it easier for residents and service providers to coordinate activities such as health-care appointments and travel,” says the Ontario government in its Oct. 13 press release.

“Providing certainty and predictability is essential to supporting strong communities and a competitive economy,” states Attorney General Doug Downey in the release. “By keeping this part of the province aligned with Manitoba, our government is taking a practical … approach to avoid unnecessary disruptions and ensure economic stability in communities that reside in Ontario’s central time zone.”

This move follows considerable engagement with communities throughout northwestern Ontario, including Indigenous leaders. These consultations came in the wake of Manitoba’s move and revealed substantial support for maintaining alignment with Manitoba.

“Through the collective efforts of communities and First Nations across the northwest, we’ve led a process to build consensus,” Greg Rickford, Minister of Indigenous Affairs and First Nations Economic Reconciliation, said in the statement. “What has emerged is unanimous support across the region to move to permanent daylight saving time.”

U.S. House of Representatives votes to move America to permanent daylight savings time. Will Canada follow suit?

Alberta MLAs will again debate moving to permanent daylight time, Danielle Smith says

Under the proposed change, affected communities in northwestern Ontario that currently change their clocks seasonally would not need to turn them back on Nov. 1. The affected communities in Ontario’s Central Time Zone, include Kenora, Dryden, Fort Frances, Sioux Lookout, Red Lake and Rainy River.

Communities in the Eastern Time Zone, such as Thunder Bay, will continue to fall back one hour on November 1st. That’s in line with the rest of Ontario, which is in the Eastern Time Zone.

Generally, daylight saving time has occurred during March to November, when clocks are moved one hour ahead of the standard time to increase evening daylight hours. Ontario has considered the switch to permanent daylight saving time for the entire province in The Time Amendment Act, 2020 . But that legislation is not yet in force. For that to happen, Ontario says neighbouring Quebec and New York would have to make the change too.

stories.title: Irene Mathyssen, longtime London NDP MP, dies at 75
stories.summary: She was elected provincially in 1990 and served as Ontario’s tourism minister, elected to represent London federally in 2006
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Longtime member of Parliament Irene Mathyssen, who served the London, Ont., region both provincially and federally under the NDP banner, has died at the age of 75. She had been battling cancer.

Former NDP MP Lindsay Mathyssen announced her mother’s passing on social media on Tuesday.

“To Londoners and Canadians, she was known for her public service, her dedication to her community, and her commitment to the people and causes she believed in,” she said in a statement on Facebook.

“She believed that our responsibility is to leave this world a better place than we found it. That belief is part of her legacy and I will do my best to honour it throughout my life.”

Mathyssen was first elected provincially in 1990 and served as Ontario’s tourism minister.

She was elected to represent London federally in 2006 and held her seat of London–Fanshawe until her retirement from politics in 2019.

During her time as MP, Mathyssen notably led a successful effort to remove the federal portion of the sales tax from menstrual products.

NDP Leader Avi Lewis said she will be remembered as someone “who fought relentlessly for our movement, and for a Canada that upholds the dignity of every person.”

“In calling for a housing bill of rights, the expansion of EI for workers, and fighting for women’s liberation, Irene pushed to make life better for people on every front,” Lewis said in a statement.

Conservative London-area MP Andrew Lawton said in a media statement that Mathyssen was “a tireless advocate for her values and her constituents and was always generous with her time when I was working in radio.

“My thoughts are with Keith [Irene’s husband] and Lindsay.”

Peter Fragiskatos, Liberal MP for London Centre, called her a “profoundly important” community voice.

“She spoke up for those who had been forgotten and ignored and always approached her work with kindness, humility and dedication. This was a true public servant,” he said in a media statement.

Mathyssen was succeeded in the House of Commons by her daughter Lindsay, who held the seat of London–Fanshawe until 2025.

“In calling for a housing bill of rights, the expansion of EI for workers, and fighting for women’s liberation, Irene pushed to make life better for people on every front,” Lewis said in a statement.

Conservative London-area MP Andrew Lawton said in a media statement that Mathyssen was “a tireless advocate for her values and her constituents and was always generous with her time when I was working in radio.
“My thoughts are with Keith [Irene’s husband] and Lindsay.”
Peter Fragiskatos, Liberal MP for London Centre, called her a “profoundly important” community voice.
“She spoke up for those who had been forgotten and ignored and always approached her work with kindness, humility and dedication. This was a true public servant,” he said in a media statement.

stories.title: Military members charged in Toronto abduction probe that recovered ammunition stolen from CAF
stories.summary: Police say 2,500 rounds of ammunition, about half of them blanks, were allegedly stolen from the military
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Three military members have been arrested for their alleged roles in an abduction for ransom, Toronto police said Wednesday, expanding on an investigation they say uncovered hundreds of ammunition rounds allegedly stolen from the Canadian Armed Forces.

What started as an abduction investigation eventually “became much larger,” said Chief Myron Demkiw.

“Whether you are a member of the military or a member of police service or a public official, no one is above the law,” said Demkiw, who has been managing the fallout from the service’s Project South corruption scandal.

The three military members arrested are among seven accused in what police described as an active investigation. Police allege 2,500 rounds of ammunition, about half of them blanks, and five over-capacity magazines were stolen from the military.

The Department of National Defence confirmed earlier this month that two members of the Canadian Armed Forces had been arrested on charges related to kidnapping and firearms theft.

Both accused, Talarambage Sachintha Fernando and James Moreau, were bombardiers with the 7 Toronto Regiment who were removed from duties and had their access restricted since their Aug. 11 arrest, DND said.

Police now say a third military member, 24-year-old Jack Miley, was arrested on Sept. 24. Police did not comment on his rank and DND did not immediately return a request for comment Wednesday.

Police say the investigation began on July 25, when officers responded to a reported abduction near Finch Avenue East and Bayview Avenue.

They allege the victim, who was targeted for his cryptocurrency, was taken at gunpoint, handcuffed and assaulted before the suspects tried to gain access to his digital money.

Police say the victim was later released and threatened not to contact authorities. Within 24 hours, police say a suspect vehicle had been identified and two suspects were arrested.

Multiple search warrants in the Greater Toronto Area turned up two 3D-printed handguns, a shotgun, two silencers and illicit drugs, police said. All but one of the seven accused is charged with kidnapping for ransom.

Of the 82 charges laid in the investigation, Fernando faces the most of any of the accused, with 20 mostly gun-related offences. Moreau is the only one of the three arrested military members to face a drug-related charge: two counts of possession for trafficking.

stories.title: Interim Indigenous languages commissioner's term extended
stories.summary: Ottawa - The interim commissioner of Indigenous languages will serve in the role for another month as the Canadian Heritage department continues to search for a permanent replacement.
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The interim commissioner of Indigenous languages will serve in the role for another month as the Canadian Heritage department continues to search for a permanent replacement.

Candice St-Aubin, a former senior assistant deputy minister of strategic policy with Indigenous Services Canada, was supposed to serve in the role for 90 days or until a new commissioner was appointed.

A cabinet order dated Oct. 7 extends her appointment for another 31 days, or until she is no longer needed in the role. The order is effective as of Oct. 12.

The term of Ron Ignace, the previous commissioner, ended in July, along with the terms of the office’s directors.

The Canadian Heritage Department said in a media statement the process to appoint a new commissioner was launched in February. It said St-Aubin’s term is being extended “to ensure stability and leadership for the office while the selection process is finalized.”

The Canadian Press reported earlier this year an audit is being conducted on the office, which is tasked with helping to preserve at-risk Indigenous languages.

Half a dozen sources, including former employees, told The Canadian Press that over the five years of its existence, the commissioner’s office has failed to move the needle on strengthening Indigenous languages and supporting research.

Instead, they said, the office has focused on extensive travel and hosting one big conference in Ottawa that cost $10 million. They also allege a toxic work environment, bullying and uncompleted projects, as well as staff quitting in frustration.

The Canadian Press agreed not to name the sources because they feared reprisals.

In a media statement at the time, Ignace said the office has faced challenges but “we succeeded in laying the foundation for an office capable of carrying forward this significant work.”

Canadian Heritage Minister Marc Miller described allegations against the office as serious.

“But part of holding people to account is giving people the benefit of the doubt, and that includes making sure the due process is respected,” he said earlier in June.

In a July interview with The Canadian Press, St-Aubin said she knows her office has work to do on rebuilding trust with Indigenous communities, and she is participating fully in the audit.

“Having seen the reporting coming in, my eyes were wide open. Financial stewardship is something that is ingrained in me, much like ethics and codes of conduct, but also managing people,” St-Aubin said.

St-Aubin said she wants the next commissioner and directors to start their mandates knowing the office is functioning.

She said Indigenous communities also want to see demonstrable results from the office’s work.

“We’ve got to build trust by showing [our work], by talking about it, by engaging in conversations, continued conversations, even if it’s uncomfortable,” St-Aubin said, adding she wants young people to have more of a say in the work the office does.

“There’s a whole lot of great innovation happening there. And I think if we can demonstrate that and show folks what’s going on, we’ll go a long way.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

article_images.alt: Ammo stolen from military recovered in Toronto abduction probe, 3 CAF members charged

stories.title: Ammo stolen from military recovered in Toronto abduction probe, 3 CAF members charged
stories.summary: Toronto - Toronto police say three military members have been charged in an abduction investigation that uncovered hundreds of ammunition rounds allegedly stolen from the Canadian Armed Forces.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Three military members have been arrested for their alleged roles in the abduction of a cryptocurrency exchange owner, Toronto police said Wednesday, expanding on an investigation they say uncovered hundreds of ammunition rounds allegedly stolen from the Canadian Armed Forces.

The trio are among seven arrested in what police described as an active investigation. What began in July as an alleged abduction probe eventually became “much larger,” said Chief Myron Demkiw.

Police allege 2,500 rounds of ammunition, about half of them blanks, and five over-capacity magazines were stolen from the military. That ammunition had not been reported stolen to the service before it was seized in the investigation, police said.

“Whether you are a member of the military or a member of police service or a public official, no one is above the law,” said Demkiw, who has been managing the fallout from the service’s Project South corruption scandal.

The arrested military trio were removed from their duties and their access was “restricted,” but they remain members of the Armed Forces pending the outcome of a formal review, the Department of National Defence said in a statement Wednesday. Military police are also investigating and co-operating with Toronto police, it said.

“Canadians rightly expect the Canadian Armed Forces to manage ammunition and explosives safely, securely, and responsibly,” said the statement.

“While the Canadian Armed Forces maintains extensive controls and oversight mechanisms for ammunition and explosives, we recognize the need to put more safeguards in place, and we remain firmly committed to addressing any identified deficiencies in a timely and decisive manner.”

DND confirmed earlier this month that two of its members, 22-year-old Talarambage Sachintha Fernando and 29-year-old James Moreau, had been arrested in August on charges related to kidnapping, organized crime and firearms theft.

Jack Miley, 24, was the third member arrested on Sept. 24, police said Wednesday.

“These are highly trained individuals with access to firearms and that creates a lot of concern for not only our community but our officers,” said Chief Supt. Joe Matthews, with the service’s detective operations.

A connection between the accused and a larger organized crime group has not been established, though investigators were still combing through cellphones, Matthews said. Dnd’s initial statement earlier month suggested the charges were related to organized crime.

The investigation began on July 25, when officers responded to a reported abduction near Finch Avenue East and Bayview Avenue, police say.

They allege the victim, the owner of a cryptocurrency exchange, was approaching his vehicle when he was taken at gunpoint, handcuffed and assaulted. The suspects tried to gain access to his “cryptocurrency assets and business-related security systems,” a news release said.

Police said the victim was later released and threatened not to contact authorities. He had minor injuries, said police, who declined to elaborate further on the abduction, citing the ongoing court cases.

Within 24 hours, police say a suspect vehicle had been identified and two suspects were arrested.

Multiple search warrants in the Greater Toronto Area turned up two 3D-printed handguns, a shotgun, two silencers and illicit drugs, among other items, police said. All but one of the seven accused is charged with kidnapping for ransom.

Of the 82 charges laid in the investigation, Fernando faces the most of any of the accused, with 20 mostly gun-related offences. Moreau is the only one of the three arrested military members to face a drug-related charge: two counts of possession for trafficking.

Police said they were working to determine how the military members May have known the other accused.

All three accused Armed Forces members are with the 7th Toronto Regiment, a reserve unit, the DND statement said. Moreau and Fernando are bombardiers, a rank used in artillery regiments equivalent to corporal, and Miley is a master bombardier.

Moreau enrolled in the army as a reservist in 2018 and was deployed in 2020 to the pandemic-response Operation Laser. Miley enrolled as a reservist in 2025 and deployed on Operation Reassurance, Canada’s largest international mission to deter Russian aggression in Europe. Fernando joined as a reservist in 2020 and has not deployed.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

“While the Canadian Armed Forces maintains extensive controls and oversight mechanisms for ammunition and explosives, we recognize the need to put more safeguards in place, and we remain firmly committed to addressing any identified deficiencies in a timely and decisive manner.”

DND confirmed earlier this month that two of its members, 22-year-old Talarambage Sachintha Fernando and 29-year-old James Moreau, had been arrested in August on charges related to kidnapping, organized crime and firearms theft.
Jack Miley, 24, was the third member arrested on Sept. 24, police said Wednesday.

“These are highly trained individuals with access to firearms and that creates a lot of concern for not only our community but our officers,” said Chief Supt. Joe Matthews, with the service’s detective operations.

A connection between the accused and a larger organized crime group has not been established, though investigators were still combing through cellphones, Matthews said. Dnd’s initial statement earlier month suggested the charges were related to organized crime.
The investigation began on July 25, when officers responded to a reported abduction near Finch Avenue East and Bayview Avenue, police say.

They allege the victim, the owner of a cryptocurrency exchange, was approaching his vehicle when he was taken at gunpoint, handcuffed and assaulted. The suspects tried to gain access to his “cryptocurrency assets and business-related security systems,” a news release said.

Police said the victim was later released and threatened not to contact authorities. He had minor injuries, said police, who declined to elaborate further on the abduction, citing the ongoing court cases.
Within 24 hours, police say a suspect vehicle had been identified and two suspects were arrested.

Multiple search warrants in the Greater Toronto Area turned up two 3D-printed handguns, a shotgun, two silencers and illicit drugs, among other items, police said. All but one of the seven accused is charged with kidnapping for ransom.

Of the 82 charges laid in the investigation, Fernando faces the most of any of the accused, with 20 mostly gun-related offences. Moreau is the only one of the three arrested military members to face a drug-related charge: two counts of possession for trafficking.
Police said they were working to determine how the military members May have known the other accused.

All three accused Armed Forces members are with the 7th Toronto Regiment, a reserve unit, the DND statement said. Moreau and Fernando are bombardiers, a rank used in artillery regiments equivalent to corporal, and Miley is a master bombardier.

Moreau enrolled in the army as a reservist in 2018 and was deployed in 2020 to the pandemic-response Operation Laser. Miley enrolled as a reservist in 2025 and deployed on Operation Reassurance, Canada’s largest international mission to deter Russian aggression in Europe. Fernando joined as a reservist in 2020 and has not deployed.

stories.title: Cycling protest blocks Toronto bike lane removal work along Bloor Street stretch
stories.summary: Toronto - A cycling advocate is vowing to keep up a protest of Toronto bike lane removals after demonstrators successfully blocked the first night of Ontario's latest planned work along a stretch of Bloor Street.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Demonstrators trying for a second day to block roadwork to remove Toronto bike lanes were met by police on Wednesday afternoon, deepening a faceoff between Premier Doug Ford’s government and cycling advocates.

The work comes as the province pressed ahead with its plan to overhaul up to 19 kilometres of the city’s protected bike lane network, starting on the premier’s home turf in Etobicoke. The province has framed it as a traffic relief measure, but critics say it’s an example of provincial overreach that will make streets less safe, and no less congested.

A protest Tuesday night ended peacefully when construction crews were escorted from Bloor Street by police and demonstrators chanted “get home safe” to the workers in trucks carrying stacks of pylons.

But at Wednesday afternoon’s protest, at least one demonstrator in a green bike helmet was led away in handcuffs by two police officers. Nearby, a worker in high-visibility vests took down a bike lane sign.

Police confirmed a 25-year-old demonstrator from Hamilton has been arrested and charged with mischief and obstructing a peace officer.

The work along a roughly one-kilometre stretch of Bloor between Islington Avenue and Royal York Road took place despite efforts by the city to propose alternatives that would keep bike lanes while restoring a lane of traffic, the mayor’s spokesperson has said, a compromise already used further west along Bloor.

In a statement after Tuesday’s protest, Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said, “make no mistake: these bike lanes are coming out.”

The minister’s spokesperson did not respond to questions Tuesday about the cost of the work, or whether it would keep a bike lane intact.

Michael Longfield, executive director of Cycle Toronto, said in an interview ahead of Wednesday’s demonstration that he expected protests to continue “until further notice.”

“It’s not about addressing traffic congestion and very disappointingly, it seems like rather than, you know, try to find those win-win solutions, they’re just doubling down on spite,” said Longfield, executive director of Cycle Toronto, in an interview earlier Wednesday.

An engineering report commissioned by the province found any congestion benefits from taking out bike lanes would be negligible or short-lived. The same report, surfaced in a court challenge of the plan, found bike lanes were predicted to reduce crashes among all road users by between 35 and 50 per cent.

The latest construction between Islington and Royal York was expected to run through Nov. 17, according to a notice on the city’s website. The work was to take place overnight, the notice suggests, but advocates had caught wind after Tuesday’s protest of plans for the construction crews to return daytime Wednesday.

Cycle Toronto is one of the parties to a constitutional challenge of the province’s bike lane plan. A lower court initially blocked the plan as an unconstitutional safety risk, but the Appeal Court overturned that decision and said the trial judge had overstepped into the legislature’s policy-making and political purview.

The group announced Tuesday it would ask the Supreme Court to hear the case.

Mayor Olivia Chow, who is campaigning for re-election, linked bike lanes to other issues where the province has sought to override the city’s position, including the island airport expansion and the removal of automated speed cameras.

“It’s a gigantic waste of money, and it’s trampling on local democracy. It’s unacceptable and it’s outrageous,” Chow said of the bike lanes plan.

Brad Bradford, her main challenger in the race, has supported removing the Bloor bike lanes in Etobicoke, citing the frustration of some local businesses, but left open the question about what to do with the other targeted lanes.

“The people who live and work there decide, street by street, with their city. Not from a podium, and not from the provincial legislature,” Bradford said in a statement.

The city pegged the cost to remove all targeted bike lanes on Bloor, Yonge Street and University Avenue at $48 million, a figure disputed by the province, which has yet to provide its own. Sarkaria has said earlier work that restored a lane of traffic but kept a bike lane on a stretch of Bloor from Kipling Avenue to Islington would cost $750,000.

Last month, the province put out a bid request to study and design options to restore vehicle traffic on bike lane sections of the affected roads, and said the successful bidder would be expected to look for ways to retain or reconfigure bike lanes, “where they make sense and do not make gridlock worse.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Six puppies ‘in distress’ rescued by police in Hamilton
stories.summary: Officers arrived and located eight puppies that "appeared severely undernourished." Several were unresponsive and one was dead.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Police in Hamilton say they’ve rescued six puppies after responding to a “concerning animal welfare incident” on the east Hamilton Mountain.

They say on Tuesday at around 1:30 p.m., police responded to a residence after a worker removing a tree nearby saw “several puppies in distress” inside an outdoor cage.

Officers arrived and located eight puppies that “appeared severely undernourished.” Several were unresponsive and one was dead.

Police say officers provided water to the surviving puppies and contacted Animal Control and Provincial Animal Welfare Services (Paws).

In total, seven puppies, including one who had died, were transferred to an emergency veterinary clinic. The six surviving puppies received veterinary care.

The homeowner was contacted by police and officers say they have been “cooperative.” Paws has taken over the investigation.

stories.title: Longtime London MP Irene Mathyssen dies at age 75
stories.summary: Ottawa — Longtime member of Parliament Irene Mathyssen, who served the London, Ont., region both provincially and federally under the NDP banner, has died at the age of 75. She had been battling cancer.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Longtime member of Parliament Irene Mathyssen, who served the London, Ont., region both provincially and federally under the NDP banner, has died at the age of 75. She had been battling cancer.

Former NDP MP Lindsay Mathyssen announced her mother’s passing on social media on Tuesday.

“To Londoners and Canadians, she was known for her public service, her dedication to her community, and her commitment to the people and causes she believed in,” she said in a statement on Facebook.

“She believed that our responsibility is to leave this world a better place than we found it. That belief is part of her legacy and I will do my best to honour it throughout my life.”

Mathyssen was first elected provincially in 1990 and served as Ontario’s tourism minister.

She was elected to represent London federally in 2006 and held her seat of London—Fanshawe until her retirement from politics in 2019.

During her time as MP, Mathyssen notably led a successful effort to remove the federal portion of the sales tax from menstrual products.

NDP Leader Avi Lewis said she will be remembered as someone “who fought relentlessly for our movement, and for a Canada that upholds the dignity of every person.”

“In calling for a housing bill of rights, the expansion of EI for workers, and fighting for women’s liberation, Irene pushed to make life better for people on every front,” Lewis said in a statement.

Conservative London-area MP Andrew Lawton said in a media statement that Mathyssen was “a tireless advocate for her values and her constituents and was always generous with her time when I was working in radio.

“My thoughts are with Keith (Irene’s husband) and Lindsay.”

Peter Fragiskatos, Liberal MP for London Centre, called her a “profoundly important” community voice.

“She spoke up for those who had been forgotten and ignored and always approached her work with kindness, humility and dedication. This was a true public servant,” he said in a media statement.

Mathyssen was succeeded in the House of Commons by her daughter Lindsay, who held the seat of London—Fanshawe until 2025.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Former CP health reporter Helen Branswell remembered as excellent journalist and loving person
stories.summary: Toronto - Helen Branswell, the former Canadian Press health reporter known for her award-winning infectious disease coverage, died Tuesday from complications from cancer. She was 69 years old.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Helen Branswell, the former Canadian Press health reporter known for her award-winning infectious disease coverage, died Tuesday from complications from cancer. She was 69 years old.

Branswell spent nearly 30 years at The Canadian Press, beginning as a general assignment reporter before eventually landing on the health and medical beat, where she established herself as an essential source of information through her dogged reporting, including of the 2003 Sars outbreak.

Later, while working at the Boston-based health news outlet Stat, her exhaustive coverage of the COVID-19 pandemic proved prescient and garnered her acclaim as she emerged as an authoritative voice on the virus.

“She leaves behind a very significant record as a journalist, an excellent journalist,” said Jack Branswell, her younger brother. “But we just also knew her as our sister and somebody who really cared and loved people.”

Branswell joined the wire in 1986, first working as a reporter-editor out of the Halifax bureau. In the following years, she spent time in Calgary, Ottawa and London, England. She covered a range of stories and topics, including politics, foreign affairs and sports.

In 2000, Branswell moved to the Toronto bureau, and it was there that she discovered her passion for health and medical reporting.

She spearheaded coverage of the 2003 Toronto Sars outbreak. Branswell became a fixture at daily news briefings, never shying away from asking probing questions that helped readers better understand the emerging medical threat.

“Her work was absolutely stellar,” said former CP health reporter Sheryl Ubelacker. “She developed all kinds of sources and she was really on top of the story and probably led everybody on that particular epidemic. She did wonderful work.”

At CP, Branswell also covered bird flu, polio and Ebola and demonstrated a relentless dedication to the demands of the health beat. She wrote science-backed stories with precision and accuracy, Ubelacker said, but did so in a way that the average reader or listener could comprehend.

“After she realized how much she loved medical reporting, it became a calling,” Ubelacker said. “And she was going to do the very best job she could ever do.”

Following her time at CP, Branswell joined Stat when it launched in 2015. There, she continued to report on infectious diseases and global health until the time of her death.

In January 2020, she published a detailed report on an emerging outbreak believed to be caused by a coronavirus when there wasn’t much reliable information in the U.S. about what would later become known as COVID-19. According to a 2021 news release from Stat, the veteran reporter, citing experience covering Sars, recognized the dangerous potential of the virus early when she saw an alert about four unexplained pneumonia cases in China in December 2019.

Branswell became an authority on the pandemic and COVID-19 through her continued coverage, leading to multiple accolades including winning the George Polk Award for Public Service in 2021. That same year, Branswell and her colleagues were finalists for the Pulitzer Prize for pandemic reporting.

“She was already on her way to becoming a legend and that story made her a legend in my estimation,” said Gerry Arnold, the former executive editor of The Canadian Press and longtime friend of Branswell. “The Canadian Press has turned out many, many, many great journalists over the years and Helen would be near the very, very top of that list of the greats.”

Branswell was born in Sherbrooke, Que., as one of six children. Her brother said she would say “she fell into” her career as a reporter. After graduating with a bachelor’s degree in English literature from St. Thomas University in Fredericton, she freelanced for the local newspaper, The Daily Gleaner, before working there full time.

Arnold first met Branswell in Halifax while she worked for the wire and he reported for a local newspaper. Later, when Arnold joined the wire service, they worked together on Parliament Hill during the early 1990s.

Then, Arnold said, he and Branswell were part of a tight-knit friend group who held dinner parties for those who didn’t have family close by. Arnold described Branswell as the person who “made every dinner party she attended better,” making sure the music was playing and the wine was cold. She was always quick to laugh, too, he said.

“She was a fabulous friend to so many people and the life of the party,” Arnold said. “I’ll never forget those Ottawa dinner parties.”

Her brother said she often would check in on people, especially if they were experiencing difficult things in their lives, but never wanted to take credit for her kindness.

“She did a lot of things quietly and in the background and she was a wonderful, wonderful human being,” Jack said.

As for her reporting, Arnold said what made Branswell stand out was her fearlessness.

“She was never intimidated by power or the pretension of power,” he said. “It didn’t bother her to stand up in a crowded news conference and ask an awkward question of somebody in a position of power that she knew might make waves or might make them feel uncomfortable. She didn’t care about that. She was there to get the story.”

Jack said his sister approached her work as a public service to keep people informed.

“A lot of people have reached out and said, ‘Your sister was kind of a light and a beacon at the start of the pandemic when we all had no information,’” he said.

Following news of her death, the director-general of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said in a statement posted to X that Branswell was a journalist with “integrity and professionalism”

“Throughout her career, Helen demonstrated an unwavering commitment to evidence, science and truth, helping the public understand some of the most complex and consequential health challenges of our time. At a moment when misinformation competes with facts, her reporting was a trusted source of clarity, honesty and insight,” the statement read.

During her career, Branswell earned numerous awards and honours, including the Victor Cohn Prize for Excellence in Medical Science Reporting and an honorary degree from Ottawa’s Carleton University in recognition of her outstanding career.

She also received several fellowships, including the Southam Fellowship at the University of Toronto and the Nieman Global Health Fellowship at Harvard University, focusing on polio eradication. As a CDC Knight Fellow in 2004, she embedded at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for three months.

Her brother said he looked up to Branswell, and followed in her footsteps to pursue journalism along with their sister, Brenda. He said he hoped people remember Helen always sought to bring truth out into the world as a reporter and that “aside from being a fantastic journalist, that she was just such a loving and caring person.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Halifax’s beloved 104-year-old tortoise is recovering after a successful surgery
stories.summary: Believed the be the oldest living gopher tortoise, Gus underwent a procedure to remove a bladder stone on Tuesday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax’s beloved 104-year-old gopher tortoise, Gus, is recovering after a successful surgery.

Believed the be the oldest living gopher tortoise, Gus underwent a procedure to remove a bladder stone on Tuesday.

The Nova Scotia Museum of Natural History, where Gus lives, says he is now resting comfortably in private and will remain with a veterinary care team for 48 hours.

Gus’s many fans will have to wait up to 10 weeks before they can see him in public.

The museum says it will continue to share updates on his recovery.

In the two weeks since the museum first shared news of Gus’s surgery, he has received hundreds of letters, get-well cards and pieces of art.

Meanwhile, the museum’s social media accounts have received thousands of messages from around the world.

stories.title: Father receives life sentence in New York for murder of Montreal girl
stories.summary: A Montreal man has been sentenced to life in prison for killing his nine-year-old daughter and leaving her in a marsh in rural New York.
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
A Montreal man has been sentenced to life in prison for killing his nine-year-old daughter and leaving her in a marsh in rural New York.

The sentence comes two months after a jury in Essex County Court convicted Luciano Frattolin of second degree murder and concealment of a human corpse in the death of Melina Frattolin.

Judge Tatiana Coffinger delivered the sentence after rejecting a motion to set aside the guilty verdict.

Frattolin would not be eligible for parole before 25 years.

The defence issued a notice of appeal following the sentence.

The girl had been living in Montreal with her mother and had gone on a road trip to the U.S. with her father in July 2025.

On the night they were scheduled to return home, Luciano Frattolin called police, reporting she had been kidnapped after he had stopped the car he was driving on the side of the road.

During the three-week-long trial, the defence tried to argue that local police had not adequately investigated Frattolin’s claims that his daughter was kidnapped.

The prosecution called several police officers and experts over the trial who used car location data, cellphone data and surveillance camera footage to recreate Frattolin’s movements on the day his daughter died and prove his story was false.

The jury spent an hour deliberating on Aug. 10 at the end of the trial, before concluding that Frattolin was guilty.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: A tough housing market could revive multigenerational homes, poll suggests
stories.summary: More than half (53 per cent) of respondents looking to buy a home within the next two years said they would consider living in a multi-generational home, a new poll said.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canadians shopping for a home say they are willing to live with mom and dad just to be able to afford a home, a new poll by the Royal Bank of Canada has found.

More than half (53 per cent) of respondents looking to buy their next or first home within the next two years said they would consider living in a multi-generational home, the RBC Home Ownership Poll found.

However, the enthusiasm for multi-generational living is not necessarily matched by mom and dad. In contrast to prospective homebuyers, 35 per cent of current homeowners say they would sell their home and buy one with their children to help them get into the market.

Driving this trend is the high cost of housing, the poll found. Among prospective buyers, 34 per cent said multi-generational living is becoming more common because of housing affordability, while 32 per cent said it was a “smart way” for families to manage housing costs.

However, it is still not the preferred choice for many as more than a quarter (26 per cent) said they would only consider a multi-generational home out of necessity, not choice.

Conventional homebuying wisdom says a new entrant should buy a starter home before moving on to a bigger house. But many homebuyers today are skipping the starter home altogether.

The average prospective buyer feels they will be 41 when they buy their first home, while current homeowners said they were 29 when they first bought theirs.

Instead of a starter home, nearly three-quarters (74 per cent) said they would rather purchase a home within the next two years that they can stay in longer, rather than one they will outgrow.

“We look at what a larger purchase does to the monthly payment against what moving up in five years would cost. For some, the bigger first home is the better decision. For others it isn’t, and it’s worth knowing which of those two scenarios fits your situation before you start looking,” said Brad Evjen, senior mortgage specialist at RBC.

stories.title: Lotto Max hits $90M, biggest lottery prize in Canadian history
stories.summary: There were a number of winners of Maxmillions, Maxplus and Encore in Tuesday's draw, but no one has yet to snag the big Lotto Max jackpot.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
The upcoming Friday Lotto Max jackpot has hit $90 million, the largest lottery prize ever offered in Canada.

The latest prize pot comes after the previous prizes of $80 million last Friday and $85 million Tuesday saw no winning ticket.

It’s not just the $90 million prize up for grabs this Friday either, with 18 Maxmillions worth an estimated $1 million each and 90 Maxplus prizes worth $100,000 also available.

In total, the value of top prizes in Friday’s draw total $117 million.

According to the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation, though the Lotto Max jackpot wasn’t won, there were still some very lucky Ontarians celebrating a win.

Two Maxmillions worth $1 million were sold in Whitby and Hamilton, with two people from Toronto and Mississauga sharing a third Maxmillion to receive a total of $500,000 each.

Some Ontarians also walked away with $100,000 each with 12 Maxplus winning tickets sold. Three other people shared a $50,000 Maxplus prize, with one sharing their winning numbers with someone from British Columbia.

A person in York Region and another in Willowdale also were winners of the Lotto Max second prize, each receiving $81,541.10.

Encore saw a few winners in Ontario as well, with people in Stouffville and Ajax and a third who bought their ticket online set to receive $100,000.

Lottery players are reminded to check their tickets to see if they won and visit OLG.CA to claim their prize. If you purchased online, you can visit your account and visit the lottery ticket history where you’ll be prompted to complete a claim declaration form.

Winners who received under $1,000 will either be automatically added to your OLG cash balance if you purchased online, or you can claim your prize at a lottery retailer.

stories.title: 3 people suffer life-threatening injuries in Kincardine crash
stories.summary: Police, along with Kincardine Fire and Emergency Services, were called to the scene shortly after 3 p.m. on Tuesday.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Three people suffered life-threatening injuries, following a crash near Kincardine.

The collision happened shortly after 3 p.m. on Tuesday, ON Highway 21, in front of Kincardine Township-Tiverton Public School, just north of Kincardine.

Police say four vehicles were involved.

A section of Highway 21 was closed for several hours, as police investigated the cause of the crash.

Anyone with information regarding this incident is asked to contact the Ontario Provincial Police at 1-888-310-1122. Should you wish to remain anonymous, you May call Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 where you May be eligible to receive a cash reward of up to $2000.

stories.title: London Knights draft picks helping St. Thomas Stars to best start in decades
stories.summary: With a red-hot goaltender and four London Knights draft picks on the roster, the St. Thomas Stars are off to an 8-1 start.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
With a red-hot goaltender and four London Knights draft picks on the roster, the St. Thomas Stars are off to an 8-1 start. Goaltender Dylan Durno said he cannot remember a stretch in which he has played as well as he is now.

The reigning Gohl goalie of the month is 8-0 this season with a 1.48 goals-against average. “I think it’s just starts in practice and then competing with these boys out here, it just makes you better than it transitions to the game,” said Durno a London, Ont. native in his second season with the Stars.

It’s been so long since they’ve had a start like this, the league’s website doesn’t even go back that far. Practices at the Joe Thornton Community Centre in St. Thomas look a little different these days. The second-place Stars are young, fast and full of confidence.

“They bring a lot of talent, they bring some jump and they bring some pep,” said head coach Jason Williams. This season, the club has expanded its partnership with the London Knights. London rookies Ryan Beaulieu, Ryker Kesler and Graham Littlejohn are all playing for the Stars and injured goalie Charlie Weiss will also play.

“They’re also with us for practice and video and all the extra development off ice, but it’s shown it to be a really good blend between both leagues, and to be able to have that relationship with St. Thomas is a great thing.

“There’s lots of guys like Jarred Woolley, Easton Cowan and my dad [Josh Beaulieu] just bunch of great hockey players who just developed here [in the Gohl] going into their draft year and it’s just a great spot to be,” said Beaulieu.

“The main goal is next year being in our draft year, obviously I want to get drafted to NHL. So just to come here to develop and Graham and I were together last year too, so it’s just unreal.” Williams is thrilled to have these young talented players and understands his job is to get them back to the Ontario Hockey League “Sometimes this isn’t the spot where they want to necessarily be,” said Williams.

“Actually being here, getting the minutes and getting the puck touches is so crucial for their development. [Knights owners] Mark [Hunter] and Dale [Hunter] have done this for years and have had a lot of success with moving players on to the NHL.

I’m not going to question what they’re what they’re thinking but the fact that we get these guys, I’m excited.” The early season success is starting to create a buzz around the city, both for the fans and the players. “The guys are starting to get really close in the room and we’re starting to be with the fans more in the city and going out to events,” said Durno.

“It’s been really good and super happy for this group of guys.” Simpson, who scouts many Gohl games understands that having high profile draft picks in the league can translate to more fans in the stands. “Their fans can come watch a first rounder, a second rounder, and Weiss was a pick a couple of years ago and Littlejohn this year,” said Simpson.

“It’s always exciting when you can see players early and then you’ll see how they translate into the OHL.”

stories.title: Citytv launches Canadian edition of Dateline, Diana Swain to host
stories.summary: The inaugural episode will revisit the disappearance of Elizabeth Bain, a University of Toronto student who vanished in Scarborough in 1990
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Citytv is bringing the internationally known Dateline franchise to Canada for the first time with a new investigative news special focused on one of the country’s most enduring unsolved cases.

Dateline Canada will premiere Nov. 26 at 8 p.m. ET/PT, marking the first international expansion of Nbc’s long-running Dateline newsmagazine franchise. The two-hour special will air on Citytv and Citytv+ and will be led by award-winning journalist Diana Swain.

The inaugural episode will revisit the disappearance of Elizabeth Bain, a University of Toronto (U of T) student who vanished in Scarborough in 1990. More than three decades later, the case remains one of Canada’s most high-profile unsolved mysteries.

“I’m proud to bring this story to Canadian audiences,” Swain said in a statement. “With Dateline Canada, we have an opportunity to re-examine a complex story through a fresh lens, connect pieces that May have been overlooked, and bring viewers a deeper understanding of the events that shaped this case and investigation.”

The two-hour special will air on Citytv and Citytv+ and will be led by award-winning journalist Diana Swain. Photo: Diana Swain Strategies/website.

The program will explore several aspects of the Bain case, including the wrongful conviction of Robert Baltovich, subsequent reviews of the evidence and newly uncovered information identified through extensive examination of police records.

“Dateline” first aired in 1992 on NBC as a general interest program, but eventually evolved to focus primarily on true crime investigations.

“I’m not sure there is anything else that would have pulled me out of what I was doing,” Swain told The Canadian Press. Notably, she worked on the investigative team during her tenure at CBC before leaving to start her own communications consulting firm in 2024.

“I was happily winding down my professional life, but it’s ‘Dateline’ and it’s the legacy of that program. It’s the power of that program and it is the chance to tell a story in a fulsome way.”

Baltovich, Bain’s former boyfriend, was convicted of second-degree murder in 2000. However, the conviction was later overturned, and prosecutors ultimately chose not to proceed with a retrial. Bain’s disappearance remains unsolved.

“For more than three decades, Dateline has been telling stories that resonate with audiences,” longtime NBC correspondent Keith Morrison said in a statement. “To see the franchise expand with Diana Swain leading the new Canadian edition is an exciting evolution for the broadcast.”

Morrison was born in the Alberta-Saskatchewan provincial border city of Lloydminster and got his start working in local news before landing national roles with CTV and CBC. He joined “Dateline” in 1995 and has been a fixture on the series since.

“I’ve always been a Canadian and I will remain a Canadian until I die,” Morrison told The Canadian Press. “That’s what my blood is and that’s how I feel about things, so to be associated with this makes me very happy.”

stories.title: How a Bay Street legend taught Ryan Bushell to make clients his priority
stories.summary: The CEO of New Haven Asset Management walks us through his investment strategy
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
On his first day at an investment firm, Ryan Bushell expected career advice from his then-boss. Instead, he got a lesson about fancy and ordinary office chairs that still shapes how he manages money.

Today, Ryan is chief executive officer and portfolio manager at New Haven Asset Management in Toronto, where he continues to put his distinctive investing philosophy into practice. He and Brenda discuss the mentor who changed his approach to wealth management, the challenges of starting over in his thirties and why he steers clear of investing in technology stocks.

stories.title: Toronto police to give update on 2 Canadian soldiers facing 49 charges
stories.summary: Sachintha Fernando, 22, and James Moreau, 29, were arrested on Aug. 11 and face a total of 49 charges, including kidnapping for ransom and forcible confinement.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Toronto police will hold an update Wednesday regarding an investigation centred around two Canadian Armed Forces members facing dozens of charges.

Chief Myron Demkiw and Supt. Joe Matthews are set to speak to reporters at 11 a.m. ET, just over a week after the arrests of Bombardiers Sachintha Fernando and James Moreau were announced.

Fernando, 22, and Moreau, 29, were arrested on Aug. 11 and face a total of 49 charges, including kidnapping for ransom, forcible confinement and use of a firearm during the commission of an indictable offence.

Fernando was also charged with multiple firearms-related offences, including unauthorized possession of a prohibited device, possession of property obtained by crime and careless storage of ammunition, a police spokesperson told Global News on Oct. 6.

Fernando and Moreau are members of the 7th Toronto Regiment, a spokesperson for the Department of National Defence told Global News last week.

Moreau enrolled in the Canadian Army as a reservist in March 2018 and Fernando enrolled in the Canadian Army as a reservist in January 2020, the spokesperson said.

Fernando has not been deployed on a CAF operation, whereas Moreau served on Operation Laser in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Both soldiers were removed from military duties after their arrests, and their access to military equipment, facilities and bases was restricted, the defence spokesperson said.

They remain members of the military pending the outcome of an administrative review, a formal process used to assess matters that May affect a member’s continued service while providing procedural fairness.

content_blocks.text: Chief Myron Demkiw and Supt. Joe Matthews are set to speak to reporters at 11 a.m. ET, just over a week after the arrests of Bombardiers Sachintha Fernando and James Moreau were announced.
content_blocks.html: Chief Myron Demkiw and Supt. Joe Matthews are set to speak to reporters at 11 a.m. ET, just over a week after the arrests of Bombardiers Sachintha Fernando and James Moreau were announced.

content_blocks.text: Fernando, 22, and Moreau, 29, were arrested on Aug. 11 and face a total of 49 charges, including kidnapping for ransom, forcible confinement and use of a firearm during the commission of an indictable offence.

Fernando was also charged with multiple firearms-related offences, including unauthorized possession of a prohibited device, possession of property obtained by crime and careless storage of ammunition, a police spokesperson told Global News on Oct. 6.
Fernando and Moreau are members of the 7th Toronto Regiment, a spokesperson for the Department of National Defence told Global News last week.
Moreau enrolled in the Canadian Army as a reservist in March 2018 and Fernando enrolled in the Canadian Army as a reservist in January 2020, the spokesperson said.
Fernando has not been deployed on a CAF operation, whereas Moreau served on Operation Laser in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.
content_blocks.html: Fernando has not been deployed on a CAF operation, whereas Moreau served on Operation LASER in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

content_blocks.text: Both soldiers were removed from military duties after their arrests, and their access to military equipment, facilities and bases was restricted, the defence spokesperson said.

They remain members of the military pending the outcome of an administrative review, a formal process used to assess matters that May affect a member’s continued service while providing procedural fairness.

stories.title: Cross-border visits by Canadian and U.S. residents up from last year: StatCan
stories.summary: Statistics Canada says more Canadians and Americans have travelled across the border between the two countries over the last six months compared to last year.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Statistics Canada says more Canadians and Americans have travelled across the border between the two countries over the last six months compared to last year.

The agency says Canadian residents made 1.9 million return trips from the United States last month by automobile and by air, up 6.8 per cent compared to September 2025.

Statistics Canada says the spike marks the sixth consecutive month of year-over-year growth of visits to the U.S. by Canadian residents.

StatCan says trips by Canadian residents to the U.S. last month remain 31.1 per cent lower than in September 2024 despite the rise compared to the same month last year.

It says U.S. residents’ visits to Canada also increased by 17.2 per cent last month compared to the same month last year totaling 1.8 million trips.

The agency says the spike is the eighth consecutive month of year-over-year increase of travel of U.S. residents to Canada.

The rise in cross-border travel comes amidst an ongoing trade war between the two countries that saw U.S. President Donald Trump introduce outright bans on imports of certain Canadian goods last month including most Canadian-made booze, dairy byproducts and some motorcycles.

The bans marked the latest escalation of the trade war as the Trump administration seeks to pressure Canada into trade concessions after Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks in August.

Both countries accused each other of adding eleventh-hour changes to the agreement. U.S. tariffs hit $28 billion in Canadian goods the next day, followed by Canadian retaliatory tariffs on Sept. 8.

MIDDLESEX COUNTY(October 14,2026):Middlesex County was pleased to welcome three high school students from across the County as “Warden for a Day” on October 13, 2026. The initiative offered an engaging, hands-on opportunity for local students to experience municipal government in action and learn about the important role County Council plays in supporting Middlesex communities.

As part of the experience, students Katherine Legg, Kaevan Cormier, and Iver Clark joined Warden Sue Clarke for a full day of leadership and learning at the County Administration Building.

The day’s agenda will included a mock swearing-in ceremony, meetings with County staff, and a guided tour of the building, including the historic Middlesex County Gaol. Students also participated in job shadowing sessions with various departments including Forestry and Natural Heritage, Library Services, and the Middlesex-London Paramedic Service.

Later in the day, students sat down with Warden Clarke and County Councillors to discuss the challenges and rewards of municipal leadership and watched an official Middlesex County Council meeting. This provided students with a behind-the-scenes look at how decisions are made that shape services and support residents across the County.

The County of Middlesex extends its thanks to the participating students for their enthusiasm, thoughtful engagement, and interest in local government throughout the day.

“Spending time with young people always leaves me optimistic about the future of our communities,” said Warden Sue Clarke. “Programs like Warden for a Day help students connect with local government and recognize the important role they can play in shaping Middlesex County’s future.

Middlesex Countyis an innovative,well-run organization offering high-value programs and services to the best community in which to live, visit, and do business in Southwestern Ontario.The County serves a vibrant, growing community of 81,700 people and offers a great place to call home,offering exceptional lifestyle,a wide variety of local attractions,and wonderful sense of community.

MEDIA CONTACT: Middlesex County Media Relations Legislative Services Division mediarelations@middlesex.ca

Middlesex County is a great place to call home. Our modern telecommunications infrastructure, excellent health and social services, retail shopping, recreation facilities, beautiful landscapes and great people, make Middlesex the place to be!

stories.title: Statistics Canada reports building permits up $1.1B in August at $13.6B
stories.summary: Ottawa — Statistics Canada says the total value of building permits issued in Canada in August rose $1.1 billion month-over-month to $13.6 billion, boosted by strength in the residential sector.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Statistics Canada says the total value of building permits issued in Canada in August rose $1.1 billion month-over-month to $13.6 billion, boosted by strength in the residential sector.

The agency says construction intentions for the homebuilding sector rose $1.1 billion to $8.5 billion in August.

The increase came as permits for multi-unit buildings rose to $5.8 billion, while the total value of permits for single-family homes edged down to $2.6 billion.

The value of non-residential building permits edged lower by $29.8 million to $5.1 billion in August.

The move came as plans for commercial construction fell $380 million to $2.2 billion, offset in part by a $317.3-million gain in the industrial sector which totalled $1.1 billion.

The institutional building component rose $32.9 million to $1.8 billion.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.
