Indeed, much of the constitutional preferences that are discussed in the room during this event are distinctly American, emphasizing the first and second amendments, which protect free speech and the right to bear arms.

“In all of human history, only one factor has proven strong enough to resist this natural tendency towards endless government growth: The right to bear arms,” Jim Ostrowski, a lawyer and guns rights advocate based in New York state, said.

Another perspective uniting almost all people gathered here is the belief that the ideological left has grown into a cancer that undermines the foundations of Western society.

“The left-wing pathology recognizes no limits to its own goals,” Clayton Reeder, a senior associate at Kelowna, B.C.-based investment banking firm RWT Capital, said in his speech. “There are always more lines to cross.”

That left-wing pathology has materialized in countless ways, the idea goes, from the open-border immigration policies that have weakened Western identity to the institutionalized repression of free speech on university campuses.

In that way, Reeder said, culture warrior leftists are ultimately interested in destroying or undermining society rather than building it up. Because of this, it is a belief system that will not and cannot stop until only the rubble remains. And as it breaks down the pillars of society, it eventually begins to eat itself.

“In cosmological terms, this is chaos,” Reeder said. “In physics, it’s like entropy. In religious terms, it’s the waters of the flood. And that image — the waters of chaos unleashed — is rather applicable here.”

Reeder said that commentators on ancient biblical texts point out, for example, that the floods in the book of Genesis came after the society of the time had become so deeply corrupted that all societal boundaries had seemingly collapsed. The people had come unmoored from any moral law that bound them.

“But perhaps even more notable is what the serpent — the Nachash — said to Adam and Eve in the third chapter of the book of Genesis: ‘You shall be as gods. None shall be higher than you, and there should be no authority that binds you.’ So, perhaps this oneness and equality at the heart of leftism has this diabolical aspect that animates it,” Reeder said.

That sort of ideological rot — both ideologically and institutionally — is partly what prompted Fergus Hodgson, head of the Econ Americas, a financial consultancy based in Colorado, to host the event. It’s a problem that is as visible in Canada as any other Western nation, he said, and will only continue to divide society.

“I’m concerned that the intellectual class of Canada is captured,” he said in an interview. “They’re basically all government funded, or they get preferential treatment through tax subsidies or carve-outs or what have you. And so, I wanted a forum where we could get the best of the people who are much more independent in their perspectives.”

Hodgson, who was born in New Zealand but holds Canadian citizenship through his mother, describes the Canadian Prairies as a largely ideologically aligned region firmly rooted in a “mixture of laissez-faire capitalism and paleoconservatism.”

“Fundamentally, both of those strands are at direct odds with centralization in Ottawa,” he said.

Albertans, who were until recently a pioneering lot of oilfield wildcatters and farmers settling harsh terrain, inherently have far more in common with, say, the buffalo hunters of the U.S. plains than with Laurentian Canada. Hodgson sees Alberta, Saskatchewan and rural British Columbia as being ideologically similar to U.S. states such as Montana, Idaho and Wyoming.

“My strong view is that the prairie and mountain state people are the most freedom-oriented people on the planet, and therefore there is a very peculiar and unique opportunity to build a nation freer than any other, freer than the United States, freer than Switzerland, freer than New Zealand,” he said.

(Hodgson said he is entirely opposed to the idea of Alberta as a “51st state,” and said he hasn’t met many other separatists who want to join the U.S.)

While Albertan separatists are united in their desire to leave, they are in much less agreement over what a new nation might be composed of. Many don’t imagine an Albertan nation with radically less government intervention, but instead see the goal as giving Alberta more leverage to work in its own interests.

“I’m more of a pragmatist,” said Keith Wilson, the leader of pro-separatist advocacy group Let Alberta Decide.

Wilson said he sees the Oct. 19 referendum as an “historic opportunity” that could finally give Alberta voters a more meaningful seat at the political table in Canada’s political system.

“We need to gain leverage to have discussions with the federal government and try to address some of the long-standing grievances,” he said. “So, I hope more and more people realize that and choose to vote for Option 2, even if they don’t support independence.”

The 10th question on the Oct. 19 ballot will ask voters if they want to stay in Canada (Option 1) or “commence the legal process” to hold a binding referendum on separation at a later date (Option 2).

Wilson, who didn’t attend the Calgary event, said that the separatist movement is indeed made up of various factions or people with differing interests, but said that is no different from the range of opinions he witnessed when he was the president of his student society at Douglas College, or when he advocated on behalf of Alberta ranchers in the 2010s. People in the separatist camp often want Wilson to prioritize specific issues, but typically they tend to have a unified goal in mind, he said.

“The common theme across the board is that Canada is no longer working for Alberta, and that Alberta can do better by redefining its constitutional relationship.”

Also absent from the event are Jeff Rath and Mitch Sylvestre, perhaps the two most prominent advocates for separation and the organizers behind a petition that effectively prompted the referendum.

Sylvestre told National Post that he favours “more local government” and smaller government wherever possible. The owner of a gun store, he is opposed to greater firearm controls but said he was perfectly satisfied with Canada’s gun policies before the Trudeau era. He favours unlocking more oil and gas development for economic reasons, but considers himself environmentally minded when it comes to keeping bodies of water clean or limiting artificial spraying on agricultural lands — “I’m about as green a guy as there is,” he said.

A Christian, Sylvestre said he also believes that rights are God-given rather than afforded by human-designed governments.

“As far as I’m concerned, if there’s nothing above government, then they’ll just take all the rights and freedoms away,” he said. “I think that the biblical values are the path, I really do.”

Rath did not respond to National Post’s request for comment. In recent weeks, he has become the target of lawsuits from several First Nations that the Alberta lawyer had represented in their land claims against the federal government. He’s being sued for more than $100 million.

A few weeks before the Oct. 19 referendum, it doesn’t look as though the separatists have much of a shot at breaking away from the federation in favour of a small government oasis. Polling shows support for separatism has dwindled in recent months, although it’s remained roughly around 20 per cent in favour of leaving, while support for Smith’s United Conservative Party, which announced the referendum, has fallen in favour of the provincial NDP.

Wilson acknowledges that some of the separatist movement has lost momentum as the Liberal government under Prime Minister Mark Carney has sought, for now, to appease Alberta’s grievances by promising to fast-track a new oil pipeline and ratcheting back various climate-oriented energy policies.

Laughing, he points out that the pro-independence side’s position is much like the Liberals under Justin Trudeau, who is without question the separatists’ most disliked bogeyman of all.

“We’re in about the same place as the Liberals were two weeks before the vote in the last federal election, and they pulled it off. So, my view is you have to approach these things as though you’re not winning.”

Danielle Smith, premier of Alberta Smith has long said that she prefers “an independent Alberta within a united Canada,” and has urged voters to vote to stay in Canada. She has become more explicitly in favour of federalism as voting day nears, but has also sought to explain to non-Albertans why many in the province feel the need to separate.

As she put it in a recent forum hosted by former Reform Party leader Preston Manning: “When a proud, hardworking people feel their contribution is taken for granted and their livelihood is treated as something to be phased out, some begin to ask a painful question: “Does this country actually want us?”

Pierre Poilievre, Official Opposition leader of Canada Poilievre’s Conservative Party has long held the position that opposes Alberta’s separation. In a recent speech urging Albertans to vote to remain in Canada, he made the case for why Alberta separatists are actually opposed to Ottawa’s continued overreach rather than to the nation of Canada itself.

“Simply put, the last decade the federal government has done terribly at the things that are actually its job: immigration, crime, military spending, borders, while intruding into things that are not its job: regulating our resources, going after hunting rifles which are private property, just to name a few examples.”

Thomas Lukaszuk, founder of Forever Canadian Lukaszuk, the former deputy premier in Alberta’s Progressive Conservative government, has become a central voice of the federalist cause in the province. He has argued that separation is highly unpopular among the general population, and that the movement threatens to needlessly create uncertainty and drive away potential private investment. The former MLA launched his own advocacy group, Forever Canadian, to sway voters to reject the tenth referendum question on separation.

“A vast majority of Albertans, up to 80 per cent of Albertans, want nothing to do with separatism,” Lukaszuk said in an interview with Alberta Primetime last December. “They want both our federal government and provincial government to focus on what matters: affordability, health care, education. Not this silliness of separatism.”

Mark Carney, prime minister of Canada Carney was elected to office on a promise to fight back against U.S. trade aggression, and the prime minister has made Alberta central to his efforts to diversify trade away from America. He has opposed separation, but has also tried to convince non-Albertans to be sympathetic to the province’s complaints. Speaking with reporters in June, Carney rejected claims that the Alberta referendum could be used as a way to send a message to Ottawa, and warned voters against presuming that separation from Canada would be a simple process.

“This is a real referendum,” he said. “It’s not a question about a question, (or) a free option. I saw first-hand what happened, what gets sold in these referenda. The former Conservative prime minister took the unusual step of speaking at Prime Minister Mark Carney’s investment summit last month, and in a recent op-ed in the National Post, Harper said he didn’t see the upside of Alberta separating.

“I see no benefit and significant risk for Alberta to go down that path today. I believe Albertans’ energies are far better employed pushing for change in Ottawa and for the exercise of greater power by Alberta itself. Such efforts are far more likely to produce actual, positive results.”

paragraphs: It’s barely 8 a.m. and Darcy Gerow is talking about tearing Alberta’s political system down to its very foundations.

Gerow, a podcaster and former deputy leader of the Libertarian Party of Canada, is addressing a crowd of Alberta separatists in a low-ceilinged conference room a few minutes’ drive from the Calgary airport. In his speech, called “the anarcho-capitalist case for Alberta,” he advocates for a system of government by the same name, which would privatize all aspects of society.
“The long-term goal is the complete replacement of state monopoly,” Gerow said.

“The liberal experiment in Canada has run its course, and that’s why Alberta wants to separate. But an independent Alberta requires independent Albertans to follow the logic of private property and consent to its consistent end, which is a fully privatized civil society.”

While Gerow’s address proposed a decidedly more radical approach to forming a hypothetical new nation than others at this event, he is in good company. About 100 like-minded Alberta separatists — including a few of the most prominent voices in the pro-independence movement — are gathered in this small conference space to discuss the future of Alberta. That is: How the province should break free from Canada and establish itself as a free and independent nation.

The attendees are a collection of various anti-establishment or libertarian-leaning pundits, politicians and activists. Advocates for free speech on campuses network with American gun rights lobbyists. Anti-vaccine activists share tables with small-government libertarians and “anarcho capitalists.” While each has his or her own specific issues of interest, their fundamental values are mostly in agreement. They are united under one common belief: that the Canada of today has fallen into a state of serious disrepair.
“Our political system is extremely broken,” Drew Barnes, a former United Conservative Party MLA, tells the gathering during a speech later in the day.

The event, held on an uncommonly cold September weekend, comes just weeks before a referendum on whether Alberta should consider triggering negotiations to leave the Canadian federation. On Oct. 19, Albertans will vote in a referendum with 10 questions on the ballot, one of which will ask them whether they want to commence the legal process to hold a binding referendum on separating from Canada.

Alberta’s separatists, some of whom have been credited with getting Premier Danielle Smith elected by swaying the United Conservative Party vote in her favour, have been pushing their case for Alberta going it alone.

Media coverage of the resentments that have fuelled Alberta separatism tend to focus on matters such as Ottawa’s restrictive energy policies or the province’s systematic underrepresentation in Parliament. Flying more under the radar, and visible here at this gathering, is a separatism intellectually rooted in the basic beliefs of small government, God’s supremacy and individual rights.

Barnes, who was ousted from former Alberta premier Jason Kenney’s caucus in 2021 for speaking out against the government’s COVID vaccine and other policies, tells the crowd about how he was elected to the Alberta legislature on a promise to uphold a few fundamental principles: “smaller government, lower taxes, stronger property rights and more choice,” he says.
“And then I saw my party, my colleagues, drift away from that because of a strong administrative state and a desire for power.”

In many ways, the views expressed here are no different than the more classical conservative beliefs of minimal government intervention and a tendency to favour local centres of government over centralized ones. Last month, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, who has long said he opposes separation, made a case for Canada based on the idea that the federal government could, and must, be narrowed down in order to give provinces more control over their affairs.

“What Albertans are complaining about is not Canada,” he told a gathering of Conservative supporters in Edmonton. “It is the government policies that are actually inconsistent with how Canada was meant to work in the first place.”
Premier Smith, for her part, has also opposed separation, instead favouring a series of constitutional or other policy changes that would put more decision-making power in the hands of provinces.

For Barnes, who previously represented the Cypress–Medicine Hat riding in the legislature, such efforts are prone to get intercepted by a Parliament that inherently favours non-Albertan interests. He said he aims to combat what he views as that institutional rot with a new federal political party that will run strictly in Alberta’s 37 electoral ridings. Called Alberta Now, the party would, according to Barnes, give the province new sway in Ottawa by explicitly representing the interests of Alberta in the House of Commons. Much like the Bloc Québécois represents Quebec, the theory goes, such a party could tilt the balance of power in favour of Alberta’s voters.

“I think we have to accept that in our current first-past-the-post Westminster system, it’s going to lead to two parties,” he told attendees. “So let’s figure out a way for libertarian values to work strongly in a conservative party.”

The strategy has been tried before: The Alberta Now party is reminiscent of the now-defunct Maverick Party, which ran candidates solely in Alberta and Saskatchewan ridings in the 2021 election. (The party won less than two per cent of the vote in both provinces.)

Barnes’s Alberta Now gambit follows the thinking of the more pragmatic wing of the wider separatist movement, which tends to prefer to advocate for the province’s interests within Canada’s existing political system.

The pragmatists — who often want to “send a message to Ottawa” rather than actually separate from the country — see the upcoming referendum more or less as a negotiating tactic. By showing their discontent with Ottawa’s political class, they see an opportunity to gain the leverage needed to enact various policies that would reverse what they see as the country’s inherent political bias toward Ontario and Quebec. With that, they believe they could establish a provincial police force; push for constitutional changes that protect gun owners, secure greater provincial control over immigration rates; and eliminate Canada’s equalization program, among other things.

Such separatist sympathizers see Canada’s power structure as inherently anti-Albertan and fundamentally broken, but believe it can be reformed through effective political pressure. The hardcore separatists who are gathered here, by comparison, want to rip it all down to the studs. Where the pragmatists see a Canada that is damaged, the hardcore set see it as downright diseased.

For the former Libertarian Party of Canada candidate Gerow, the only remedy is to build a new nation of Alberta on a constitutional foundation that maximally prioritizes civil liberties over collective rule.
“Secession is the right step, but it is only a piece of the puzzle,” Gerow told the crowd.
Sadly, when we look closely at the history of the human race, we find that liberty is rare and tyranny is the norm
Modern societies are doomed to fail because the states that govern them inevitably work to enforce their own levers of control, Gerow argues, leading to ever increasing centralization of power.
“Alberta’s grievances — the extraction of wealth, regulatory constraints and the erosion of provincial jurisdiction — are not mistakes specific to Canada,” he said.

The state, Gerow said, possesses a “monopoly on ultimate decision-making and the power to impose compulsory payment” on its citizens through taxes. Over time, judges, legislators and the executive branch become “agents of the same apparatus whose power the constitution is supposed to limit,” he said.
“Alberta separatists have many valid reasons to leave Canada, but at its core, it’s because a limited state is a utopian fantasy, and that’s why Confederation failed.”

Only by privatizing every element of the public domain, from national defence to the courts, can citizens resist centralized control and win back their autonomy, Gerow argued. Under such a governing structure, public agencies ought to be broken up and divided among property owners and net tax contributors, who would ultimately make decisions about regulation and taxation.

Most other attendees here wouldn’t likely argue for such a radical vision for preserving civil rights. But the room is unanimous in its belief that Canada has become a victim of relentless government overreach, led by a bloated government that has extended its influence into too many areas of public life.

The Calgary event, called Capitalism and Morality and hosted by Econ Americas, an investment advisory firm, is an offshoot of similar conferences that have been held in Vancouver for over a decade. Held in Calgary’s Croatian-Canadian Cultural Centre, it was designed as a platform for guests to share politically incorrect and freedom-oriented ideas in the spirit of debate. Much of the talks at this particular event revolved around Alberta separatism, but its chief organizer said the event is not explicitly separatist.

Pardy is not actively involved in the separatist movement, but has often spoken publicly about how an independent Alberta could ensure freedom for its citizens.

The group aims to help get women more informed about, or involved in, the separation movement; a card on the table suggests that female supporters of the movement “transform your backyard into a space for open dialogue.”

Thomas Lukaszuk, founder of Forever Canadian Lukaszuk, the former deputy premier in Alberta’s Progressive Conservative government, has become a central voice of the federalist cause in the province. He has argued that separation is highly unpopular among the general population, and that the movement threatens to needlessly create uncertainty and drive away potential private investment. The former MLA launched his own advocacy group, Forever Canadian, to sway voters to reject the tenth referendum question on separation.

“A vast majority of Albertans, up to 80 per cent of Albertans, want nothing to do with separatism,” Lukaszuk said in an interview with Alberta Primetime last December. “They want both our federal government and provincial government to focus on what matters: affordability, health care, education. Not this silliness of separatism.”

Mark Carney, prime minister of Canada Carney was elected to office on a promise to fight back against U.S. trade aggression, and the prime minister has made Alberta central to his efforts to diversify trade away from America. He has opposed separation, but has also tried to convince non-Albertans to be sympathetic to the province’s complaints. Speaking with reporters in June, Carney rejected claims that the Alberta referendum could be used as a way to send a message to Ottawa, and warned voters against presuming that separation from Canada would be a simple process.

“This is a real referendum,” he said. “It’s not a question about a question, (or) a free option. I saw first-hand what happened, what gets sold in these referenda. It’s: ‘everything’s going to be easy, you can keep your passport, you can keep the currency, you can stay in the country and leave it at the same time,’” he said, referencing Britain’s vote to leave the European Union during his time as Bank of England governor.

Jason Kenney, former premier of Alberta Kenney has been one of the most vocal opponents of Alberta separation, and among the loudest critics of the movement’s leaders. In August, he teamed up with former Alberta premier Rachel Notley and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce on a campaign called Stronger Together, which sought to make a case for Canadian federalism.

“The national business community represented by the Canadian Chamber is an integrated network of hundreds of thousands of businesses of all sizes who know Alberta’s interests and theirs go hand in hand,” Kenney said in a statement announcing Stronger Together. “We’re ready to rally with facts and to make the case for a strong Alberta and a united Canada.”

Stephen Harper, former prime minister of Canada Harper had long refrained from making many public statements about Alberta separation, but started explicitly oppose the pro-independence movement in the weeks before the referendum. The former Conservative prime minister took the unusual step of speaking at Prime Minister Mark Carney’s investment summit last month, and in a recent op-ed in the National Post, Harper said he didn’t see the upside of Alberta separating.

“I see no benefit and significant risk for Alberta to go down that path today. I believe Albertans’ energies are far better employed pushing for change in Ottawa and for the exercise of greater power by Alberta itself. Such efforts are far more likely to produce actual, positive results.”

content_blocks.text: It’s barely 8 a.m. and Darcy Gerow is talking about tearing Alberta’s political system down to its very foundations.

Gerow, a podcaster and former deputy leader of the Libertarian Party of Canada, is addressing a crowd of Alberta separatists in a low-ceilinged conference room a few minutes’ drive from the Calgary airport. In his speech, called “the anarcho-capitalist case for Alberta,” he advocates for a system of government by the same name, which would privatize all aspects of society.
“The long-term goal is the complete replacement of state monopoly,” Gerow said.

“The liberal experiment in Canada has run its course, and that’s why Alberta wants to separate. But an independent Alberta requires independent Albertans to follow the logic of private property and consent to its consistent end, which is a fully privatized civil society.”

While Gerow’s address proposed a decidedly more radical approach to forming a hypothetical new nation than others at this event, he is in good company. About 100 like-minded Alberta separatists — including a few of the most prominent voices in the pro-independence movement — are gathered in this small conference space to discuss the future of Alberta. That is: How the province should break free from Canada and establish itself as a free and independent nation.

The attendees are a collection of various anti-establishment or libertarian-leaning pundits, politicians and activists. Advocates for free speech on campuses network with American gun rights lobbyists. Anti-vaccine activists share tables with small-government libertarians and “anarcho capitalists.” While each has his or her own specific issues of interest, their fundamental values are mostly in agreement. They are united under one common belief: that the Canada of today has fallen into a state of serious disrepair.
“Our political system is extremely broken,” Drew Barnes, a former United Conservative Party MLA, tells the gathering during a speech later in the day.

The event, held on an uncommonly cold September weekend, comes just weeks before a referendum on whether Alberta should consider triggering negotiations to leave the Canadian federation. On Oct. 19, Albertans will vote in a referendum with 10 questions on the ballot, one of which will ask them whether they want to commence the legal process to hold a binding referendum on separating from Canada.

Alberta’s separatists, some of whom have been credited with getting Premier Danielle Smith elected by swaying the United Conservative Party vote in her favour, have been pushing their case for Alberta going it alone.

Media coverage of the resentments that have fuelled Alberta separatism tend to focus on matters such as Ottawa’s restrictive energy policies or the province’s systematic underrepresentation in Parliament. Flying more under the radar, and visible here at this gathering, is a separatism intellectually rooted in the basic beliefs of small government, God’s supremacy and individual rights.

Barnes, who was ousted from former Alberta premier Jason Kenney’s caucus in 2021 for speaking out against the government’s COVID vaccine and other policies, tells the crowd about how he was elected to the Alberta legislature on a promise to uphold a few fundamental principles: “smaller government, lower taxes, stronger property rights and more choice,” he says.
“And then I saw my party, my colleagues, drift away from that because of a strong administrative state and a desire for power.”

In many ways, the views expressed here are no different than the more classical conservative beliefs of minimal government intervention and a tendency to favour local centres of government over centralized ones. Last month, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, who has long said he opposes separation, made a case for Canada based on the idea that the federal government could, and must, be narrowed down in order to give provinces more control over their affairs.

“What Albertans are complaining about is not Canada,” he told a gathering of Conservative supporters in Edmonton. “It is the government policies that are actually inconsistent with how Canada was meant to work in the first place.”
Premier Smith, for her part, has also opposed separation, instead favouring a series of constitutional or other policy changes that would put more decision-making power in the hands of provinces.

For Barnes, who previously represented the Cypress–Medicine Hat riding in the legislature, such efforts are prone to get intercepted by a Parliament that inherently favours non-Albertan interests. He said he aims to combat what he views as that institutional rot with a new federal political party that will run strictly in Alberta’s 37 electoral ridings. Called Alberta Now, the party would, according to Barnes, give the province new sway in Ottawa by explicitly representing the interests of Alberta in the House of Commons. Much like the Bloc Québécois represents Quebec, the theory goes, such a party could tilt the balance of power in favour of Alberta’s voters.

“I think we have to accept that in our current first-past-the-post Westminster system, it’s going to lead to two parties,” he told attendees. “So let’s figure out a way for libertarian values to work strongly in a conservative party.”
content_blocks.html: “I think we have to accept that in our current first-past-the-post Westminster system, it’s going to lead to two parties,” he told attendees. “So let’s figure out a way for libertarian values to work strongly in a conservative party.”

content_blocks.text: The strategy has been tried before: The Alberta Now party is reminiscent of the now-defunct Maverick Party, which ran candidates solely in Alberta and Saskatchewan ridings in the 2021 election. (The party won less than two per cent of the vote in both provinces.)

Barnes’s Alberta Now gambit follows the thinking of the more pragmatic wing of the wider separatist movement, which tends to prefer to advocate for the province’s interests within Canada’s existing political system.

The pragmatists — who often want to “send a message to Ottawa” rather than actually separate from the country — see the upcoming referendum more or less as a negotiating tactic. By showing their discontent with Ottawa’s political class, they see an opportunity to gain the leverage needed to enact various policies that would reverse what they see as the country’s inherent political bias toward Ontario and Quebec. With that, they believe they could establish a provincial police force; push for constitutional changes that protect gun owners, secure greater provincial control over immigration rates; and eliminate Canada’s equalization program, among other things.

Such separatist sympathizers see Canada’s power structure as inherently anti-Albertan and fundamentally broken, but believe it can be reformed through effective political pressure. The hardcore separatists who are gathered here, by comparison, want to rip it all down to the studs. Where the pragmatists see a Canada that is damaged, the hardcore set see it as downright diseased.

For the former Libertarian Party of Canada candidate Gerow, the only remedy is to build a new nation of Alberta on a constitutional foundation that maximally prioritizes civil liberties over collective rule.
“Secession is the right step, but it is only a piece of the puzzle,” Gerow told the crowd.
Sadly, when we look closely at the history of the human race, we find that liberty is rare and tyranny is the norm
Modern societies are doomed to fail because the states that govern them inevitably work to enforce their own levers of control, Gerow argues, leading to ever increasing centralization of power.
“Alberta’s grievances — the extraction of wealth, regulatory constraints and the erosion of provincial jurisdiction — are not mistakes specific to Canada,” he said.

The state, Gerow said, possesses a “monopoly on ultimate decision-making and the power to impose compulsory payment” on its citizens through taxes. Over time, judges, legislators and the executive branch become “agents of the same apparatus whose power the constitution is supposed to limit,” he said.
“Alberta separatists have many valid reasons to leave Canada, but at its core, it’s because a limited state is a utopian fantasy, and that’s why Confederation failed.”

Only by privatizing every element of the public domain, from national defence to the courts, can citizens resist centralized control and win back their autonomy, Gerow argued. Under such a governing structure, public agencies ought to be broken up and divided among property owners and net tax contributors, who would ultimately make decisions about regulation and taxation.

Most other attendees here wouldn’t likely argue for such a radical vision for preserving civil rights. But the room is unanimous in its belief that Canada has become a victim of relentless government overreach, led by a bloated government that has extended its influence into too many areas of public life.

The Calgary event, called Capitalism and Morality and hosted by Econ Americas, an investment advisory firm, is an offshoot of similar conferences that have been held in Vancouver for over a decade. Held in Calgary’s Croatian-Canadian Cultural Centre, it was designed as a platform for guests to share politically incorrect and freedom-oriented ideas in the spirit of debate. Much of the talks at this particular event revolved around Alberta separatism, but its chief organizer said the event is not explicitly separatist.

Tamara Lich, one of the key organizers behind the 2022 Freedom Convoy that protested the federal government’s lockdown measures, delivered a keynote speech at an exclusive dinner after she was handed a “Good Rebel Award.” According to a video posted online, Lich stuck mostly to speaking about her role in the Freedom Convoy and her legal battles and did not directly address separatism. She did not respond to an interview request.

Frances Widdowson, a former professor and campus free speech advocate, talked about the need for more intellectual freedom at universities. Bruce Pardy, a professor of law at Queen’s University, talked about the fundamental paradox of the state — that is, the inherent problem of how the state is both the thing that protects individual rights and the thing that restricts them. “You can’t be free with it, and you can’t be free without it,” he said.

Bruce Pardy, a professor of law at Queen’s University, talked about the fundamental paradox of the state — that is, the inherent problem of how the state is both the thing that protects individual rights and the thing that restricts them. “You can’t be free with it, and you can’t be free without it,” he said.

content_blocks.text: Widdowson told National Post she is not a separatist herself — “I don’t think it makes a lot of sense to break into smaller units,” she said. Pardy is not actively involved in the separatist movement, but has often spoken publicly about how an independent Alberta could ensure freedom for its citizens.

The event doubles as a networking and business event. At booths adjoining the main conference room, vendors sell handcrafted soap made from beef tallow or leather-bound copies of classic literary works.

At one table, two women with a grassroots organization called Alberta Women For Independence give away free T-shirts and other swag emblazoned with the Alberta flag. The group aims to help get women more informed about, or involved in, the separation movement; a card on the table suggests that female supporters of the movement “transform your backyard into a space for open dialogue.”

Calgary-based Bow Valley Credit Union, a sponsor of the event, hands out leaflets describing some of the financial services it offers, including a chequing account that lets customers seamlessly convert their Canadian dollars into bitcoin.

Some of the attendees here bristle at the “libertarian” label, given that the ideology, which essentially prioritizes personal freedoms above all else, has fallen into disrepute in recent years. A few of them say they adhere instead to the ideas of paleoconservatism, or a traditional brand of American conservatism that prioritizes regional values, nationalism and Christian values.

Phil Hart, a Republican member of the Idaho State Senate, spoke to the audience about the need for Alberta, once separated, to write its own Bill of Rights that restate and deepen civil liberties. Like others here, he prefers a constitution that mimics the American nation “under God,” as it’s written in the U.S. Pledge of Allegiance.
“If your rights come from God, the government can’t take them away,” he said to a burst of applause. “I can’t take them away. Only God can take them away.”

Hart talks about a theory held by some, which is that the American founding fathers based the spirit of the constitution (as it applies to the judiciary, legislative and executive branches) on the biblical book of Isaiah. Chapter 33:22 reads: “For the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king; it is He who will save us.”
If your rights come from God, the government can’t take them away

Indeed, much of the constitutional preferences that are discussed in the room during this event are distinctly American, emphasizing the first and second amendments, which protect free speech and the right to bear arms.

“In all of human history, only one factor has proven strong enough to resist this natural tendency towards endless government growth: The right to bear arms,” Jim Ostrowski, a lawyer and guns rights advocate based in New York state, said.
Another perspective uniting almost all people gathered here is the belief that the ideological left has grown into a cancer that undermines the foundations of Western society.

“The left-wing pathology recognizes no limits to its own goals,” Clayton Reeder, a senior associate at Kelowna, B.C.-based investment banking firm RWT Capital, said in his speech. “There are always more lines to cross.”

That left-wing pathology has materialized in countless ways, the idea goes, from the open-border immigration policies that have weakened Western identity to the institutionalized repression of free speech on university campuses.

In that way, Reeder said, culture warrior leftists are ultimately interested in destroying or undermining society rather than building it up. Because of this, it is a belief system that will not and cannot stop until only the rubble remains. And as it breaks down the pillars of society, it eventually begins to eat itself.

“In cosmological terms, this is chaos,” Reeder said. “In physics, it’s like entropy. In religious terms, it’s the waters of the flood. And that image — the waters of chaos unleashed — is rather applicable here.”

Reeder said that commentators on ancient biblical texts point out, for example, that the floods in the book of Genesis came after the society of the time had become so deeply corrupted that all societal boundaries had seemingly collapsed. The people had come unmoored from any moral law that bound them.

“But perhaps even more notable is what the serpent — the Nachash — said to Adam and Eve in the third chapter of the book of Genesis: ‘You shall be as gods. None shall be higher than you, and there should be no authority that binds you.’ So, perhaps this oneness and equality at the heart of leftism has this diabolical aspect that animates it,” Reeder said.

That sort of ideological rot — both ideologically and institutionally — is partly what prompted Fergus Hodgson, head of the Econ Americas, a financial consultancy based in Colorado, to host the event. It’s a problem that is as visible in Canada as any other Western nation, he said, and will only continue to divide society.

content_blocks.text: “I’m concerned that the intellectual class of Canada is captured,” he said in an interview. “They’re basically all government funded, or they get preferential treatment through tax subsidies or carve-outs or what have you. And so, I wanted a forum where we could get the best of the people who are much more independent in their perspectives.”

Hodgson, who was born in New Zealand but holds Canadian citizenship through his mother, describes the Canadian Prairies as a largely ideologically aligned region firmly rooted in a “mixture of laissez-faire capitalism and paleoconservatism.”
“Fundamentally, both of those strands are at direct odds with centralization in Ottawa,” he said.

Albertans, who were until recently a pioneering lot of oilfield wildcatters and farmers settling harsh terrain, inherently have far more in common with, say, the buffalo hunters of the U.S. plains than with Laurentian Canada. Hodgson sees Alberta, Saskatchewan and rural British Columbia as being ideologically similar to U.S. states such as Montana, Idaho and Wyoming.

“My strong view is that the prairie and mountain state people are the most freedom-oriented people on the planet, and therefore there is a very peculiar and unique opportunity to build a nation freer than any other, freer than the United States, freer than Switzerland, freer than New Zealand,” he said.
(Hodgson said he is entirely opposed to the idea of Alberta as a “51st state,” and said he hasn’t met many other separatists who want to join the U.S.)

While Albertan separatists are united in their desire to leave, they are in much less agreement over what a new nation might be composed of. Many don’t imagine an Albertan nation with radically less government intervention, but instead see the goal as giving Alberta more leverage to work in its own interests.
“I’m more of a pragmatist,” said Keith Wilson, the leader of pro-separatist advocacy group Let Alberta Decide.
Wilson said he sees the Oct. 19 referendum as an “historic opportunity” that could finally give Alberta voters a more meaningful seat at the political table in Canada’s political system.

“We need to gain leverage to have discussions with the federal government and try to address some of the long-standing grievances,” he said. “So, I hope more and more people realize that and choose to vote for Option 2, even if they don’t support independence.”

content_blocks.text: The 10th question on the Oct. 19 ballot will ask voters if they want to stay in Canada (Option 1) or “commence the legal process” to hold a binding referendum on separation at a later date (Option 2).

Wilson, who didn’t attend the Calgary event, said that the separatist movement is indeed made up of various factions or people with differing interests, but said that is no different from the range of opinions he witnessed when he was the president of his student society at Douglas College, or when he advocated on behalf of Alberta ranchers in the 2010s. People in the separatist camp often want Wilson to prioritize specific issues, but typically they tend to have a unified goal in mind, he said.
“The common theme across the board is that Canada is no longer working for Alberta, and that Alberta can do better by redefining its constitutional relationship.”
Also absent from the event are Jeff Rath and Mitch Sylvestre, perhaps the two most prominent advocates for separation and the organizers behind a petition that effectively prompted the referendum.

Sylvestre told National Post that he favours “more local government” and smaller government wherever possible. The owner of a gun store, he is opposed to greater firearm controls but said he was perfectly satisfied with Canada’s gun policies before the Trudeau era. He favours unlocking more oil and gas development for economic reasons, but considers himself environmentally minded when it comes to keeping bodies of water clean or limiting artificial spraying on agricultural lands — “I’m about as green a guy as there is,” he said.
A Christian, Sylvestre said he also believes that rights are God-given rather than afforded by human-designed governments.
“As far as I’m concerned, if there’s nothing above government, then they’ll just take all the rights and freedoms away,” he said. “I think that the biblical values are the path, I really do.”

content_blocks.text: Rath did not respond to National Post’s request for comment. In recent weeks, he has become the target of lawsuits from several First Nations that the Alberta lawyer had represented in their land claims against the federal government. He’s being sued for more than $100 million.

A few weeks before the Oct. 19 referendum, it doesn’t look as though the separatists have much of a shot at breaking away from the federation in favour of a small government oasis. Polling shows support for separatism has dwindled in recent months, although it’s remained roughly around 20 per cent in favour of leaving, while support for Smith’s United Conservative Party, which announced the referendum, has fallen in favour of the provincial NDP.

content_blocks.text: Wilson acknowledges that some of the separatist movement has lost momentum as the Liberal government under Prime Minister Mark Carney has sought, for now, to appease Alberta’s grievances by promising to fast-track a new oil pipeline and ratcheting back various climate-oriented energy policies.
Laughing, he points out that the pro-independence side’s position is much like the Liberals under Justin Trudeau, who is without question the separatists’ most disliked bogeyman of all.

“We’re in about the same place as the Liberals were two weeks before the vote in the last federal election, and they pulled it off. So, my view is you have to approach these things as though you’re not winning.”

stories.title: No injuries reported in South Huron house fire
stories.summary: A section of Crediton Road remains closed in South Huron following a residential structure fire early Wednesday morning.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A section of Crediton Road remains closed in South Huron following a residential structure fire early Wednesday morning.

According to South Huron fire all occupants of the home were safely evacuated and no injuries have been reported.

Crediton Road is fully closed between Babylon Line and Parr Line/King Street. Motorists were asked to avoid the area and seek alternate routes.

In an update issued around 6:20 a.m., OPP said officers had cleared the scene and that county officials would assume responsibility for managing access to the area while the closure remains in place.

No information has been released regarding the cause of the fire.

stories.title: As drones reshape modern warfare, the Canadian Army races to catch up
stories.summary: Minerva program launched a batch of tenders in recent months for a range of new drones
stories.author: Kyle Duggan
stories.content:
As drone-fuelled warfare rages on half a world away in Ukraine, the Canadian Army’s program for rapidly acquiring basic drones is just ramping up.

And the pressure is on for the Canadian Armed Forces to speed up its adoption of drones as the technology changes the nature of modern warfare.

Lt.-Col. Jonathan Penney is a reservist who previously worked in defence manufacturing and now co-ordinates the forces’ Minerva drone program. He said that while the army feels pressure to pick up the pace, it’s focused both on finding the right mix of tech for its current needs and on building up the domestic drone industry.

“The army is really good at adapting and evolving,” he said in an interview with The Canadian Press.

The Minerva program launched a batch of tenders in recent months for a range of new drones – everything from low-cost Arctic surveillance drones for the Canadian Rangers to ground and aerial drones that can conduct cargo supply runs.

“We are figuring out what ‘right’ looks like,” Penney said. “Instead of just jumping in, buying a whole bunch of things that we don’t need, we buy things that can use today and then let the system evolve so that it’s integrated in how we conduct operations.”

The Minerva program operates unlike a typical procurement, which sees the military draft a list of requirements.

Instead, Minerva launches what it calls “industry challenges” – ongoing projects which task companies with creating prototypes for specific uses. Army personnel will be testing those prototypes until roughly next summer or fall.

Another item the army is currently searching for is a low-cost targeting drone – an aerial spotter that allows artillery crews to hit targets they can’t see.

Penney said it’s safer to rely on an aerial drone for targeting instead of sending a soldier into the field with a set of binoculars and a laser rangefinder.

“If the drone gets shot down, we’ll just send up another one,” he said. “The reduction of risk to our personnel is significant.”

That kind of equipment is easy enough to buy off the shelf – but part of the goal of the Canadian Armed Forces drone program is to build up the domestic drone sector and ensure the tech can be easily absorbed by Canadian military units.

“Does it integrate with our systems and does it exist as-is produced in Canada?” Penney said. “That’s what we’re driving for.”

The army is expected to complete a new wish-list of drones for design and purchase over the next three to four months – including a breaching drone for dealing with ground-based obstacles such as mines.

The Minerva initiative launched roughly a year ago with the goal of quickly scaling up drone use in the army, rather than limiting it to ordering from the U.S. Defence Department’s approved list of drone manufacturers.

Army Commander Lt.-Gen. Michael Wright has said he wants to “flood” Canada’s land forces with drones.

Winning a drone prototype challenge is different from winning a large military production order, however.

The prototype challenge approach allows National Defence to cover research and development costs early in the process – which should encourage drone makers to take the risk of building prototypes with no guaranteed purchaser. The 15-month Arctic aerial drone challenge, for instance, has a $500,000 maximum funding award.

“Canadian companies, especially those small mid-sized companies that can offer some solutions, don’t really know how the military operates. So when they create a product, it’s not necessarily focused towards some of the things that we need,” Penney said.

“They actually understand things better. So if you’re working in the Arctic, you have big gloves on, it’s understood that you can’t operate with fine motor controls.”

Lt.-Gen. Darcy Molstad has been tasked with overseeing the integration of drones across the entire armed forces. He said in a previous interview the military is starting to approach uncrewed systems more like munitions, rather than traditional equipment or expensive vehicles.

“We have to treat it almost like an expendable commodity versus something that we have to keep in inventory and capitalize the cost over 20 years,” Molstad said. “These things just last a short amount of time.”

Penney said that’s particularly true for drones used by land forces.

“Especially from an army perspective, which will be different from the Air Force perspective, we are looking at … consumables, things that we’re going to use, and if it gets destroyed, fine, we’ll just send in another one,” he said. “Low-cost, high-use, high-value things.”

As Russia tests Nato allies in Europe with repeated drone incursions, Canada’s military is looking for ways to counter the emerging threat.

The Canadian Armed Forces recently put out a separate tender for a counter-aerial drone system that could be deployed at military installations across the country.

stories.title: Hundreds of doctors would leave if Alberta became an independent country, survey shows
stories.summary: Those who would elect to leave said they would move to another province or territory, while a small percentage would retire or leave the medical field earlier
stories.author: Fakiha Baig
stories.content:
Hundreds of physicians would not practise in Alberta if the province leaves Confederation, a survey by the organization that represents doctors in the province indicates.

Of the 1,649 physicians surveyed by the Alberta Medical Association, 15 per cent said they would continue living and practising in Alberta if it became an independent country, and less than a quarter were uncertain about what they would do.

Those who would elect to leave said they would move to another Canadian province or territory, while a small percentage would retire or leave the medical field earlier than planned.

The survey results were published Tuesday in a letter released by the association’s president Dr. Heidi Fell, which was the first of five days of advanced voting on separation ahead of the official referendum day on Oct. 19.

“As Albertans prepare to vote, the AMA is focused on an important question,” Fell said in the letter. “What could the referendum outcomes mean for patients, physicians and Alberta’s health-care system?”

Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative Party government has put 10 questions on the ballot. The 10th question asks whether the province should stay in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

The first nine questions are about Canada’s Constitution, as well as immigration, including whether the government should impose limitations and financial fees for newcomers and temporary workers accessing health care.

The AMA said if Albertans choose to separate, not only would the medical work force shrink, but health care in an independent Alberta would be left in limbo.

Fell said it’s unclear, for example, how an independent Alberta would fill the health-care funding gap that would be created after it loses federal money.

“In addition to assuming federal health-care funding responsibilities, significant health-care concerns remain, including maintaining access to medicines, equipment and medical services,” she said.

The association also has questions about the effects of the immigration questions on health care, Fell said, should the government receive a mandate on them.

Fell said she wrote to the province’s health ministers last week for more clarity.

She has asked them, for example, what doctors should do when someone needs necessary care but their eligibility can’t immediately be confirmed.

She has also asked how questions about eligibility should be resolved without delaying care.

“Physicians often need to make clinical decisions before a patient’s identity, residency status or coverage can be verified,” she said.

“Our position is straightforward: uncertainty about coverage should not unnecessarily delay care, and physicians and their staff should not be placed in the position of determining or enforcing a patient’s immigration or coverage status.”

Fell said the AMA hopes to hear from the government soon.

“Ultimately, we believe questions about coverage should be addressed through a reliable and timely administrative process so physicians can remain focused on clinical decisions and patients can receive the care they need.”

Hospitals Minister Adriana LaGrange’s office said it is reviewing the association’s letter.

“It would be inappropriate to speculate on the outcome of the referendum or any technical legislative, policy or program changes that May follow until Albertans have had their say,” her office said in an e-mail Tuesday.

stories.title: 3 Canadian Armed Forces members among 7 charged in Toronto crypto-motivated kidnapping investigation
stories.summary: The Canadian Armed Forces consist of personnel serving in the Royal Canadian Navy, Canadian Army and Royal Canadian Air Force.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Lucas Casaletto

Posted October 14, 2026 6:23 am.

Last Updated October 14, 2026 11:35 am.

Three members of the Canadian Armed Forces are among seven individuals charged following a Toronto police investigation into the kidnapping of a man who was allegedly targeted because of his access to cryptocurrency assets.

Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw announced Wednesday that investigators have laid a total of 82 criminal charges against seven accused after what began as a kidnapping probe evolved into a broader investigation involving firearms, stolen military ammunition and organized criminal activity.

Police allege the victim was abducted on July 25, 2026, as he approached his vehicle in the area of Finch Avenue East and Bayview Avenue in North York.

According to Detective Superintendent Joe Matthews, members of the Toronto police integrated kidnapping unit were called to investigate a reported abduction that day. Investigators allege the victim was forcibly taken and later released, but was threatened not to contact police.

“The victim was allegedly targeted because of his access to cryptocurrency assets,” Matthews told reporters. “… The victim was later released and was threatened not to contact police

Police said the investigation expanded after officers identified additional suspects and uncovered evidence beyond the original kidnapping allegation.

Within 24 hours of the abduction, investigators arrested two suspects identified as Saiefeddine Adem, 22, and Raheem Bishop-Jackson, 24.

Additional arrests followed on Aug. 11, when police took Talarambage Fernando, 22, James Moreau, 29, and Christian Darbandi, 39, into custody.

Police later arrested Jack Miley, 24, and Suhaib Alekozai, 39, ON Sept. 24.

Authorities say the accused face a range of charges, including kidnapping and numerous firearms-related offences.

Investigators identified Fernando, Moreau and Miley as members of the Canadian Armed Forces. Fernando and Moreau hold the rank of bombardier. The Department of National Defence announced last week that Fernando enrolled as a reservist in January 2020 but was never deployed, while Moreau enrolled as a reservist in March 2018 and was deployed in 2020 on Operation Laser, during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Police allege the three service members were involved in the offences linked to the kidnapping investigation and are facing criminal charges alongside the other accused.

Demkiw emphasized that no one is exempt from accountability under the law, regardless of their profession or position.

“Whether you are a member of the military or a member of a police service or a public official, no one is above the law,” he said.

The Toronto police chief also thanked the Canadian Armed Forces for assisting investigators throughout the probe.

Police say search warrants executed during the investigation led to the seizure of multiple weapons, including a shotgun, two firearm silencers and other firearms. Investigators also recovered more than 2,000 rounds of ammunition.

According to police, nearly all of the ammunition seized had been stolen from the Canadian Armed Forces.

Matthews described the case as one that grew significantly beyond the original kidnapping allegation as investigators uncovered additional evidence and suspects.

Police said there are currently no outstanding suspects and no further arrests are anticipated in the case.

“We’re still trying to determine how all of [the suspects] fit together in this puzzle,” Matthews noted.

The investigation remains ongoing.

stories.title: OPP yet to launch formal probe into alleged “egregious” Osap use at career colleges
stories.summary: In early October, the province sounded the alarm about six private career colleges and accused them of taking advantage the Osap program.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello, Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
As the Ford government faces increasing scrutiny over how a handful of private career colleges tapped into the Osap system, Ontario’s provincial police say they are reviewing the allegations but have yet to decide on whether to launch a formal criminal probe.

In early October, the Ministry of Colleges and Universities sounded the alarm about six private career colleges that were engaged in “egregious use of taxpayer dollars” and accused them of criminality by taking advantage of the student assistance program.

Nolan Quinn said an internal investigation found “unusually high concentrations of Osap applications submitted from the same geographic locations” and also pointed to the involvement of “immigration services firms” being directly tied to or co-owned by some career colleges in question.

After referring the findings to auditing firm Kpmg for a deeper dive, Quinn said the government had also “reported it to the OPP and the Auditor General.”

The OPP confirmed that it “received a referral from the Ontario government and that the allegations are “currently under review.”

“I am not able to provide an estimated timeline for the review,” an OPP spokesperson said in a statement. “As the matter remains under review, we are unable to provide any further detail or comment.”

Ontario’s Auditor General, however, said the office only received a “notification” from the government, but that the province stopped short of requesting a formal value-for-money audit.

“A statement was made by Minister Quinn on October 6 that states “As a result, the government notified the Auditor General last week and has also referred this matter to the Ontario Provincial Police,” the auditor’s office said in an email.

“We can confirm that the Office of the Auditor General received a notification from the government last week. This was separate from the request for an audit received from MPP Tyler Watt.”

While the minister has the power to request a “special assignment,” it’s unclear why the government chose to only notify the auditor as opposed to request a performance audit – similar to Liberal MPP Tyler Watt’s request.

The auditor’s office added that the office has been notified about similar issues in the past and stressed that it’s their “expectation that the government would inform us, as we are its independent auditor of the public accounts of Ontario.”

While the investigations remain in question, the Ford government continues to face calls to prevent the problem from spilling over into other institutions.

There are currently 242 career colleges that are eligible to receive Osap in Ontario, all of which have now been cut off from the provincial program as the province examines the scope of the problem.

Career Colleges Ontario, the association representing hundreds of institutions, is urging the Ford government to reinstate student financial aid for career college students who were already approved for funds and are actively attending in-person classes.

The association, which had been warning the government about possible misuse of Osap since 2023, says the government should be taking targeted action to address those concerns, not disrupting the education of students who have followed the rules.

The minister has only indicated that the pause in Osap grants will remain in effect until the government’s third-party auditors can complete a wider probe.

“The auditors, the third-party auditors, haven’t given us assurances yet, and I will respect the experts. And whenever they give me assurance to be able to release all of the institutions,” Quinn on Oct. 2.

“That’s when we’ll move forward with Osap for career colleges.”

stories.title: In Turkey, energetic Istanbul and spiritual Konya offer two different sides of the country
stories.summary: The nation features the iconic city with 2,500 years of history, as well as a lesser-known destination not yet on influencers’ radars
stories.author: Simona Choise
stories.content:
Turkish coffee has two uses. One is to help the traveller keep up with the energy of the country, and especially of Istanbul. The other is to predict the future.

We are in Sultanahmet Park, the landmark roof of the Hagia Sophia mosque, one of Istanbul’s most visited sites. One by one, my friends and I down our shots of coffee as our guide Şölen Mailoğlu says she will use her grandma’s technique to read the grounds. Proper fortune-telling form, she explains, is to first turn over the coffee cup against a saucer to let the remaining grinds distribute themselves in the cup in a pattern as unique as every person’s path through life.

Our fortune teller turns over the first cup.

“I see elephants,” she says to my friend. “Do you see a trunk, right there?” A coffee trail curls toward the wall of the cup, followed by a shorter lighter wisp behind. “And a baby elephant,” my friend says.

Two elephants foretell great movement in real estate, and the potential for good profit, the soothsayer predicts. My friend is thinking about a move, so this is welcome news.

I ask if the grinds can tell us what’s in the cards for Turkey.

“Of course not. Turkey makes its own future,” Mailoğlu says.

Over the centuries, the country has used its geography as a springboard for influence – whether through conquest, diplomacy and trade. Neighbouring conflicts between Iran and the United States, and Russia and Ukraine, has again put Turkey’s geography in focus, even as domestic political and economic tensions complicate its future.

For a tourist, these issues May feel urgent, perhaps even risky. But take the long view, one of our guides says. Istanbul is a city with a 2,500-year-old history.

Every human problem, from the rise and fall of an empire to personal heartbreak, has been felt by someone here in that time. To visit is to have the opportunity to glimpse how people live through and with the cracks of history all around.

For starters, they party.

On Saturday night in Istanbul, the streets and squares are spilling over with the city’s youth restlessly on the move, defying the bumper to bumper traffic. With a median age of 35, Turkey is young.

At the same time, generational mixing seems little changed from the family gatherings that fans of Orhan Pamuk’s Museum of Innocence would recognize. At Ruby, in the fashionable Ortaköy district, a mainstay restaurant in the city, everyone is out. A family is celebrating their patriarch’s birthday with hand-held sparklers and singing. Couples dressed for galas, not dates, whisper across intimate tables, waiting for the dance floor to open. The restaurant closes at 4 a.m.

And every patron makes their way to the outdoor patio to snap photos of the lights on the Bosphorus Bridge connecting Europe and Asia.

An even more polished image of Istanbul’s contemporary character is on display 20 minutes down the Bosphorus in the Galataport district.

Opened after a US$1.7-billion regeneration project, the district took approximately eight years to redevelop, transforming an industrial waterfront into a master-planned neighbourhood similar to New York’s Hudson Yards, Manchester’s Noma or Abu Dhabi’s Saadiyat Cultural District.

On the shoreline, “hans” – 19th-century industrial warehouses built to store merchandise bound for export – have been transformed into a luxury hotel, while a former post office and customs building is now home to more than 70 boutique Turkish brands. Shoppers disembarking from cruise ships are tempted by the oversized and elaborate jewellery of Sevan Bıçakçı, boxes of artisanal Turkish delight, photobooks by the country’s famed photographer Ara Güler, or a stop at the Istanbul Museum of Modern Art, designed by Renzo Piano.

Where Ruby serves perfect traditional meals of sea bass or lamb chops, the meze platter at Muutto, a second-storey restaurant overlooking the Bosphorus, nods to the cultural fusions created by trade.

Billing itself as an Anatolian tapas bar, Muutto – “migration” in Finnish – adds Mediterranean flavours to a foundation of Turkish cuisine. Its Michelin Guide entry compares it to a Spanish tapas bar. A roasted eggplant dip has the comforting smooth texture of baba ghanoush but is enlivened with mint and lemon, while a roasted mushroom dip is smoky with roasted red pepper.

Istanbul’s contemporary sheen can make it feel as if it represents the country’s future. But the country’s ambitions extend far beyond such photogenic areas. Increasingly, its influence will rise with the success of central areas, away from Istanbul. In central Anatolia, for example, secure land trade routes offer alternatives to increasingly contested sea routes.

An hour from Istanbul by plane, one region benefitting from proximity to economic investment in expanding trade is Konya. A destination not yet on influencers’ radars, Konya, the capital of the province, is a mix of intensive economic development and equally passionate spiritual devotion.

Konya is home to the resting place of Rumi, the 13th-century Persian poet and Sufi mystic, and his passing is marked by the religious order he founded, as well as by modern-day devotees drawn to his message of interfaith tolerance and love. Every December, millions of travellers arrive here to celebrate Rumi.

The rest of the year, Konya is a modern, 1.5 million person strong city. The sunrise behind the Taurus Mountains casts a magic light on the ring roads connecting newly built and spacious (by Turkish standards) apartments and townhouses, remarkable only in the precision of their planning.

And yet, again, history beats in each brick of the city’s modern façade.

In the city’s old centre, the Bedesten bazaar, dating from 1538, has been rebuilt as an open air mall. It would not seem out of place in a North American suburb. Go beyond the first few lanes to explore the 2,700 shops on the site and every lane reveals a new specialty: silver, nuts, high-quality clothing, shoes, knives, kitchen appliances, sweets, spices and peppers and on and on. Women shop arm-in-arm and happily offer their advice on the best goods to haul home.

Several streets are dedicated to jewellery, primarily gold. I go into a shop to explore.

As the vendor is weighing my purchase (gold is priced by weight not design), another customer walks in. He unwraps a large handkerchief to reveal a gold bar. A wafer is sliced from the bar along prescored markers in exchange for a stack of bills wrapped in paper. With inflation at over 30 per cent, the precious metal is a tangible store of value for households that can afford to maintain reserves.

This is not a man who would seek his fortune in a coffee cup, I think. In a country where the future is up for debate, people are forging their own.

Turkish Airlines offers direct flights from Toronto to Istanbul, with complimentary stopovers in the city for travellers wanting to connect further, either in Turkey or to further destinations. Turkish Airlines also offers packages to every region of the country, sometimes timed to local festivals.

The Galata Hotel Istanbul – Mgallery Collection has a terrific location on Bank Street in the Karaköy neighbourhood. Within walking distance are the Galata Tower, the Salt Galata cultural centre (once the headquarters for the Ottoman Bank, the empire’s central bank) and the Kamondo Stairs, which are favoured by short stay European travellers taking photos. Historical sites are a 10- to 20-minute walk across the Galata Bridge and the generous and artisanal breakfast offers fuel for adventures further afield. Rooms from $450 a night in low season.

We are in Sultanahmet Park, the landmark roof of the Hagia Sophia mosque, one of Istanbul’s most visited sites. One by one, my friends and I down our shots of coffee as our guide Şölen Mailoğlu says she will use her grandma’s technique to read the grounds. Proper fortune-telling form, she explains, is to first turn over the coffee cup against a saucer to let the remaining grinds distribute themselves in the cup in a pattern as unique as every person’s path through life.
Our fortune teller turns over the first cup.

“I see elephants,” she says to my friend. “Do you see a trunk, right there?” A coffee trail curls toward the wall of the cup, followed by a shorter lighter wisp behind. “And a baby elephant,” my friend says.
Two elephants foretell great movement in real estate, and the potential for good profit, the soothsayer predicts. My friend is thinking about a move, so this is welcome news.
I ask if the grinds can tell us what’s in the cards for Turkey.
“Of course not. Turkey makes its own future,” Mailoğlu says.

Over the centuries, the country has used its geography as a springboard for influence – whether through conquest, diplomacy and trade. Neighbouring conflicts between Iran and the United States, and Russia and Ukraine, has again put Turkey’s geography in focus, even as domestic political and economic tensions complicate its future.
For a tourist, these issues May feel urgent, perhaps even risky. But take the long view, one of our guides says. Istanbul is a city with a 2,500-year-old history.

Every human problem, from the rise and fall of an empire to personal heartbreak, has been felt by someone here in that time. To visit is to have the opportunity to glimpse how people live through and with the cracks of history all around.
For starters, they party.
On Saturday night in Istanbul, the streets and squares are spilling over with the city’s youth restlessly on the move, defying the bumper to bumper traffic. With a median age of 35, Turkey is young.

At the same time, generational mixing seems little changed from the family gatherings that fans of Orhan Pamuk’s Museum of Innocence would recognize. At Ruby, in the fashionable Ortaköy district, a mainstay restaurant in the city, everyone is out. A family is celebrating their patriarch’s birthday with hand-held sparklers and singing. Couples dressed for galas, not dates, whisper across intimate tables, waiting for the dance floor to open. The restaurant closes at 4 a.m.
And every patron makes their way to the outdoor patio to snap photos of the lights on the Bosphorus Bridge connecting Europe and Asia.
An even more polished image of Istanbul’s contemporary character is on display 20 minutes down the Bosphorus in the Galataport district.

Opened after a US$1.7-billion regeneration project, the district took approximately eight years to redevelop, transforming an industrial waterfront into a master-planned neighbourhood similar to New York’s Hudson Yards, Manchester’s Noma or Abu Dhabi’s Saadiyat Cultural District.

On the shoreline, “hans” – 19th-century industrial warehouses built to store merchandise bound for export – have been transformed into a luxury hotel, while a former post office and customs building is now home to more than 70 boutique Turkish brands. Where Ruby serves perfect traditional meals of sea bass or lamb chops, the meze platter at Muutto, a second-storey restaurant overlooking the Bosphorus, nods to the cultural fusions created by trade.
