stories.title: As drones reshape war around the world, the Canadian Armed Forces sprints to catch up
stories.summary: As drone-fuelled warfare rages on half a world away in Ukraine, the Canadian Army’s program for rapidly acquiring basic drones is just ramping up.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — As drone-fuelled warfare rages on half a world away in Ukraine, the Canadian Army’s program for rapidly acquiring basic drones is just ramping up.

And the pressure is on for the Canadian Armed Forces to speed up its adoption of drones as the technology changes the nature of modern warfare.

Lt.-Col. Jonathan Penney is a reservist who previously worked in defence manufacturing and now co-ordinates the forces’ Minerva drone program. He said that while the army feels pressure to pick up the pace, it’s focused both on finding the right mix of tech for its current needs and on building up the domestic drone industry.

“The army is really good at adapting and evolving,” he said in an interview with The Canadian Press.

The Minerva program launched a batch of tenders in recent months for a range of new drones — everything from low-cost Arctic surveillance drones for the Canadian Rangers to ground and aerial drones that can conduct cargo supply runs.

“We are figuring out what ‘right’ looks like,” Penney said. “Instead of just jumping in, buying a whole bunch of things that we don’t need, we buy things that can use today and then let the system evolve so that it’s integrated in how we conduct operations.”

The Minerva program operates unlike a typical procurement, which sees the military draft a list of requirements.

Instead, Minerva launches what it calls “industry challenges” — ongoing projects which task companies with creating prototypes for specific uses. Army personnel will be testing those prototypes until roughly next summer or fall.

Another item the army is currently searching for is a low-cost targeting drone — an aerial spotter that allows artillery crews to hit targets they can’t see.

Penney said it’s safer to rely on an aerial drone for targeting instead of sending a soldier into the field with a set of binoculars and a laser rangefinder.

“If the drone gets shot down, we’ll just send up another one,” he said. “The reduction of risk to our personnel is significant.”

That kind of equipment is easy enough to buy off the shelf — but part of the goal of the Canadian Armed Forces drone program is to build up the domestic drone sector and ensure the tech can be easily absorbed by Canadian military units.

“Does it integrate with our systems and does it exist as-is produced in Canada?” Penney said. “That’s what we’re driving for.”

The army is expected to complete a new wish-list of drones for design and purchase over the next three to four months — including a breaching drone for dealing with ground-based obstacles such as mines.

The Minerva initiative launched roughly a year ago with the goal of quickly scaling up drone use in the army, rather than limiting it to ordering from the U.S. Defence Department’s approved list of drone manufacturers.

Army Commander Lt.-Gen. Michael Wright has said he wants to “flood” Canada’s land forces with drones.

Winning a drone prototype challenge is different from winning a large military production order, however.

The prototype challenge approach allows National Defence to cover research and development costs early in the process — which should encourage drone makers to take the risk of building prototypes with no guaranteed purchaser. The 15-month Arctic aerial drone challenge, for instance, has a $500,000 maximum funding award.

“Canadian companies, especially those small mid-sized companies that can offer some solutions, don’t really know how the military operates. So when they create a product, it’s not necessarily focused towards some of the things that we need,” Penney said.

“They actually understand things better. So if you’re working in the Arctic, you have big gloves on, it’s understood that you can’t operate with fine motor controls.”

Lt.-Gen. Darcy Molstad has been tasked with overseeing the integration of drones across the entire armed forces. He said in a previous interview the military is starting to approach uncrewed systems more like munitions, rather than traditional equipment or expensive vehicles.

“We have to treat it almost like an expendable commodity versus something that we have to keep in inventory and capitalize the cost over 20 years,” Molstad said. “These things just last a short amount of time.”

Penney said that’s particularly true for drones used by land forces.

“Especially from an army perspective, which will be different from the Air Force perspective, we are looking at … consumables, things that we’re going to use, and if it gets destroyed, fine, we’ll just send in another one,” he said. “Low-cost, high-use, high-value things.”

As Russia tests Nato allies in Europe with repeated drone incursions, Canada’s military is looking for ways to counter the emerging threat.

The Canadian Armed Forces recently put out a separate tender for a counter-aerial drone system that could be deployed at military installations across the country.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

“The army is really good at adapting and evolving,” he said in an interview with The Canadian Press.

The Minerva program launched a batch of tenders in recent months for a range of new drones — everything from low-cost Arctic surveillance drones for the Canadian Rangers to ground and aerial drones that can conduct cargo supply runs.

“We are figuring out what ‘right’ looks like,” Penney said. “Instead of just jumping in, buying a whole bunch of things that we don’t need, we buy things that can use today and then let the system evolve so that it’s integrated in how we conduct operations.”
The Minerva program operates unlike a typical procurement, which sees the military draft a list of requirements.

Instead, Minerva launches what it calls “industry challenges” — ongoing projects which task companies with creating prototypes for specific uses. Army personnel will be testing those prototypes until roughly next summer or fall.
Another item the army is currently searching for is a low-cost targeting drone — an aerial spotter that allows artillery crews to hit targets they can’t see.
Penney said it’s safer to rely on an aerial drone for targeting instead of sending a soldier into the field with a set of binoculars and a laser rangefinder.
“If the drone gets shot down, we’ll just send up another one,” he said. “The reduction of risk to our personnel is significant.”

That kind of equipment is easy enough to buy off the shelf — but part of the goal of the Canadian Armed Forces drone program is to build up the domestic drone sector and ensure the tech can be easily absorbed by Canadian military units.
“Does it integrate with our systems and does it exist as-is produced in Canada?” Penney said. “That’s what we’re driving for.”

The army is expected to complete a new wish-list of drones for design and purchase over the next three to four months — including a breaching drone for dealing with ground-based obstacles such as mines.

The Minerva initiative launched roughly a year ago with the goal of quickly scaling up drone use in the army, rather than limiting it to ordering from the U.S. Defence Department’s approved list of drone manufacturers.
Army Commander Lt.-Gen. Michael Wright has said he wants to “flood” Canada’s land forces with drones.
Winning a drone prototype challenge is different from winning a large military production order, however.

The prototype challenge approach allows National Defence to cover research and development costs early in the process — which should encourage drone makers to take the risk of building prototypes with no guaranteed purchaser. The 15-month Arctic aerial drone challenge, for instance, has a $500,000 maximum funding award.

“Canadian companies, especially those small mid-sized companies that can offer some solutions, don’t really know how the military operates. So when they create a product, it’s not necessarily focused towards some of the things that we need,” Penney said.
“They actually understand things better. So if you’re working in the Arctic, you have big gloves on, it’s understood that you can’t operate with fine motor controls.”

Lt.-Gen. Darcy Molstad has been tasked with overseeing the integration of drones across the entire armed forces. He said in a previous interview the military is starting to approach uncrewed systems more like munitions, rather than traditional equipment or expensive vehicles.

“We have to treat it almost like an expendable commodity versus something that we have to keep in inventory and capitalize the cost over 20 years,” Molstad said. “These things just last a short amount of time.”
Penney said that’s particularly true for drones used by land forces.

“Especially from an army perspective, which will be different from the Air Force perspective, we are looking at … consumables, things that we’re going to use, and if it gets destroyed, fine, we’ll just send in another one,” he said. “Low-cost, high-use, high-value things.”
As Russia tests Nato allies in Europe with repeated drone incursions, Canada’s military is looking for ways to counter the emerging threat.
The Canadian Armed Forces recently put out a separate tender for a counter-aerial drone system that could be deployed at military installations across the country.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.
Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: What about Alberta’s nine other referendum questions?
stories.summary: Premier Danielle Smith is asking voters to consider policies that would upend immigration and require reopening the Constitution
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Albertans will head to the polls and make themselves heard in a provincial referendum next Monday.

Voters will face 10 questions. The last one – on whether Alberta should remain in Canada or trigger a secession vote – has dominated headlines and consumed the debate around the vote.

But the other nine, on topics including migrants’ access to social programs, judicial appointments and the future of the Senate, could also lead to consequential changes in the province or even a push to reopen the Constitution. Voters are declaring whether they support the proposals by checking one of two boxes: yes or no.

Ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has spent $4-million on government advertising focused mostly on the first nine questions. She says to implement her political agenda, she needs direct input from the electorate. Her detractors, meanwhile, have argued the referendum is harmful. They say its questions stoke anti-immigration rhetoric and feed oxygen to the province’s separatist fire.

Here’s what you need to know about the nine questions Canadians have heard less about.

To help understand her immigration proposals, the Premier has asked voters to consider the province that’s recently become Alberta’s unlikely ally: Quebec. The francophone province reached an agreement with the federal government in 1991 that gave it exclusive control over the selection of incoming economic migrants, a unique carve-out Ms. Smith is hoping to mirror in Alberta.

“We have to make sure that we’re involved at the very beginning stages of determining what the market need is,” she said.

She has provided only loose details around how it would be managed. Her government has not said what “sustainable” immigration levels would be, nor who would qualify as an “Albertan.”

While the question proposes decreasing immigration levels, the Premier has recently suggested that she wants to admit more people under the provincial nominee program. Between 2022 and 2025, provincial nominees comprised roughly 58 per cent of economic migrants to Alberta, according to figures from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada.

The proposals are being floated at a time when migration into Alberta is nosediving after surging from 2022 to 2024, and Ottawa has curbed the number of non-permanent residents entering Canada.

This proposal would narrow which newcomers are eligible for social services and, in the government’s words, allow Alberta to “distinguish between the temporary residents it has approved and those it has not.” Unapproved temporary residents would therefore be ineligible for certain provincial benefits, according to a website created by Ms. Smith’s government.

All temporary residents are currently eligible for those services. However, Ms. Smith hasn’t set criteria for how people with “Alberta-approved immigration status” would be selected, nor has she committed to whether the change would affect non-permanent residents already living in Alberta.

In February, when Ms. Smith unveiled a projected $9.4-billion deficit for the current fiscal year, she blamed two things: low oil prices and immigration. The Premier has since justified her proposals by arguing non-permanent residents are a drag on the province’s finances.

This referendum question doesn’t specify which social support programs would be off-limits to new non-permanent residents.

But according to the government’s website, this proposal would exclude all non-permanent residents from accessing benefits such as child care subsidies, student aid, income supports and other benefits – but not health care and education. The province estimates non-permanent residents’ use of these services cost roughly $100-million annually.

The Premier frequently points to a statistic that says non-permanent residents cost the public system roughly $1-billion for health care and education, while delivering $150-million in taxes in return.

Experts dispute this number. Mikal Skuterud, an economist at the University of Waterloo, said many Canadian citizens cost the public system more than they pay in taxes. Children, for example, don’t pay taxes but are expected to contribute later in life, he said.

“That’s just not the right way to do the fiscal impact analysis,” said Mr. Skuterud, who has advised Prime Minister Mark Carney and his predecessor, Justin Trudeau , on immigration policy. Experts have also pointed out that immigrants often arrive in better health than Canadian-born populations and use fewer health services than non-immigrants.

As with the other questions, Ms. Smith hasn’t said how this proposal would work – whether it would affect current non-permanent residents, for example, or only those who move to Alberta after the province changes the law.

The Alberta government has not said what it would charge non-permanent residents, but last month Ms. Smith mused about a $1,900 premium for health care, suggesting businesses could shoulder the cost. She didn’t say whether the fee would recur annually but pointed to Britain, which requires temporary residents to pay an annual surcharge for health care.

The Calgary Chamber of Commerce has pushed back on the immigration questions, finding in a poll that only one-third of its membership supports increasing provincial control over immigration, though 41 per cent support limiting eligibility for provincially funded programs.

Alberta Finance Minister Jason Nixon has suggested the government’s immigration proposals wouldn’t be implemented until after the next provincial election, scheduled for October, 2027, when Ms. Smith would seek a second mandate from voters.

The province says this measure would help ensure only Canadian citizens living in Alberta would be able to vote in provincial elections by requiring voters to produce proof of citizenship at the polls.

Earlier this year, Ms. Smith’s government made that easier by adding citizenship markers to provincial identification and drivers’ licences.

It is unclear what problem this proposal would solve. Elections Alberta currently requires voters to prove their address and accepts 50 forms of identification, including more than 30 types of government-issued ID.

The electoral agency has reported only four instances of ineligible voters casting ballots since 2015, and it verifies voters’ citizenship when they are added to the provincial list of electors. Provincial law requires voters be 18 or older, Canadian citizens and Alberta residents.

“You’re not going to be on that list if you’re not a Canadian citizen,” Shaun Fluker, law professor at the University of Calgary, said of the provincial electors list. He said forcing voters to bring citizenship documents to the polls would add an unnecessary barrier to voting.

This proposal follows on the coattails of Ms. Smith’s roughly year-long push for judicial appointments to be made by the provincial government.

In January, Ms. Smith wrote to Mr. Carney proposing more provincial involvement in judicial appointments, citing what she described as Alberta’s “distinct legal traditions.”

The Premier hasn’t said how Alberta’s justice system operates differently than other provinces. (The justice system in Alberta, like elsewhere in Canada outside Quebec, is rooted in the same common law that stretches back centuries to England.)

This question goes one step further, proposing full provincial control over judicial appointments to the King’s Bench and Appeal courts.

The federal government currently names judges to those courts with the help of 17 judicial advisory committees, including one for Alberta, that assess applicants and make recommendations to Ottawa.

Each committee has seven members: Ottawa names three; the provincial government names one; the province’s chief justice names one; and two lawyers’ groups – one national and one provincial – each get one pick.

Like for all constitutional changes, Ms. Smith would need to convince seven provincial legislatures covering 50 per cent of Canada’s population to endorse reopening the Constitution.

The federal Senate – the upper house whose members are appointed by the governor-general on the advice of the prime minister – has been a source of discontent among Western premiers for decades over frustrations around underrepresentation.

The “chamber of sober second thought” scrutinizes bills passed by the House of Commons and must approve legislation for it to become law.

Like British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, Alberta is currently allocated six of the 105 Senate seats – a contrast to the 30 collectively held by the four Atlantic Provinces.

Alberta has attempted to pressure Ottawa into picking its preferred candidates by holding Senate nominee elections, in which residents vote for candidates they want nominated to the chamber.

The vote is more of a poll than an election. The results aren’t binding for Ottawa, and in the five Senate nominee elections held in Alberta since 1989, only a handful of winners have subsequently been tapped by the prime minister.

While Ms. Smith would again need seven legislatures covering half of the national population to be on board with opening the Constitution for amendments, the Senate would only be abolished if all 10 provinces agreed. (The Territories aren’t required to sign off.)

Ottawa transfers billions of dollars to provinces every year to help run programs – funding that comes with strings attached, such as complying with the Canada Health Act, the legislation that requires provinces to provide universal health care in exchange for health care transfer payments.

The province is technically free to run its health care system how it likes, said Lorian Hardcastle, assistant professor at the University of Calgary’s Faculty of Law. But Alberta risks losing federal funding if it runs afoul of the conditions set by Ottawa.

This question proposes cutting those strings while allowing Alberta to continue receiving that federal money, Prof. Hardcastle said.

Such a constitutional amendment could come with major consequences, she said, because it could functionally neuter legislation like the Canada Health Act.

The Alberta government says this proposal would shift “default authority” to the provinces when they clash with federal laws – a change that would dramatically reshape the country’s constitutional order.

Federal environmental laws have frustrated Ms. Smith during her premiership, as well as previous Alberta governments.

In 2023, the Supreme Court of Canada found the federal Impact Assessment Act was unconstitutional because aspects of it went beyond Ottawa’s legal authority. The matter had originally been referred to Alberta’s Court of Appeal by the provincial government in 2019.

This referendum proposal is built on Ms. Smith’s trademark Alberta Sovereignty Within a United Canada Act, the first bill she introduced as Premier in 2022, which targeted federal legislation the province believes is harmful.

Ms. Smith has since wielded the sovereignty act in bids to subvert federal electricity and gun laws, but the bill hasn’t been tested in court and legal scholars have panned it as unconstitutional.

Prof. Fluker with the University of Calgary characterized the question as a “rephrased version” of the sovereignty act, adding there are few occasions in which federal and provincial laws directly clash.

“The Constitution is wired around the idea that … federal legislation applies across the country,” he said.

content_blocks.text: Question 2: Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status will be eligible for provincially-funded programs, such as health care, education and other social services?

content_blocks.text: This proposal would narrow which newcomers are eligible for social services and, in the government’s words, allow Alberta to “distinguish between the temporary residents it has approved and those it has not.” Unapproved temporary residents would therefore be ineligible for certain provincial benefits, according to a website created by Ms. Smith’s government.

content_blocks.text: All temporary residents are currently eligible for those services. However, Ms. Smith hasn’t set criteria for how people with “Alberta-approved immigration status” would be selected, nor has she committed to whether the change would affect non-permanent residents already living in Alberta.

content_blocks.text: Question 3: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially funded social support programs?

content_blocks.text: In February, when Ms. Smith unveiled a projected $9.4-billion deficit for the current fiscal year, she blamed two things: low oil prices and immigration. The Premier has since justified her proposals by arguing non-permanent residents are a drag on the province’s finances.

stories.title: The shrinking neighbourhoods in Canada’s biggest cities
stories.summary: A Globe analysis found that the populations of several neighbourhoods in Toronto and Vancouver are declining
stories.author: The Decibel Staff, Sherrill Sutherland, Alex Bozikovic
stories.content:
The populations of Vancouver and Toronto have doubled in the past 50 years, but in certain neighbourhoods of those cities, populations have declined by as much as 40 per cent .

The Globe’s architecture critic Alex Bozikovic explains why neighbourhoods have lost so many residents, what that means for the areas, and how it might present a solution to the housing crises.

stories.title: Three B.C. party leaders to face off in only televised debate of election
stories.summary: The leaders of British Columbia's three main parties are to face off today in their only debate of the snap provincial election.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
flag wire: true flag sponsored: false article_type: pubinfo.section: cms.site.custom.site_domain : thestar.com sWebsitePrimaryPublication : publications/toronto_star bHasMigratedAvatar : false firstAuthor.avatar :

By Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press

British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby repeatedly acknowledged his government’s imperfections in a debate where his B.C. Conservative and Green Party rivals railed against his record on the economy, health care and Indigenous rights.

“Look, I’m not perfect, but I will always act in the best interests of British Columbians, and that’s my commitment to you and your family,” he said Wednesday.

He repeated his statement during a later question period with reporters, saying he held himself “accountable to British Columbians.”

His acknowledgment was in response to questions from Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson and Green Leader Emily Lowan about his party’s record after nearly a decade in government.

“We are here because David Eby called a snap election,” Doerkson said. “He called a snap election, because he saw opportunity for himself, and I see opportunity for British Columbians.”

Asked why he called a snap election less than two years into his mandate, Eby said he needed a stronger mandate, noting the Conservatives tried to bring down his government 13 times.

“This was not a government that was able to deliver the big swings that you and your family need government to be taking for you,” he said.

The debate, held 10 days before the Oct. 24 provincial election, was carried on all major television and radio stations Wednesday and is the only one between the three leaders.

There was a surprise at the end of the event when the leaders of CentreBC and OneBC each delivered brief statements.

Moderator Shachi Kurl said neither party qualified for the debate because they did not have enough candidates.

While the debate covered a range of issues, including housing, public safety, and health care, the three leaders frequently returned to economic issues.

Doerkson said his party would “supercharge” the provincial economy, without raising existing taxes or introducing new ones. He also promised to cut taxes and bureaucratic bloat, while fully funding public health care.

He told reporters after the debate that he was committed to releasing a fully costed-out platform before residents have the opportunity to vote.

Advance voting begins Friday.

Eby questioned Doerkson’s campaign promises, saying they could only mean “dramatic cuts.”

Eby said he’d never seek to balance the province’s budget “on the backs of British Columbians,” as the province faces a record deficit of $14 billion.

In an apparent reference to previous B.C. Liberal administrations, he said their “so-called balanced budgets” came at the expense of school land being sold off.

Instead, he is focused on growing the economy and addressing wasteful spending, Eby said.

“We know what Conservatives do when they need money,” he said. “They cut … and they will do it again.”

Doerkson responded by saying Eby was guilty of fearmongering.

“The reality is you refuse to talk about your own record in this province, which is one of devastation,” he said.

The debate came hours after the NDP released the costings for its platform, showing a $2 billion reduction of the province’s deficit by 2028-29.

When Eby tried to defend his economic record, Doerkson said nobody believed him anymore, while Lowan said it was “staggering” that 1.2 million British Columbians do not have access to a family doctor.

“Your record has been marred with broken promises,” she said. “This year’s election bribes are next year’s broken promises.”

The Green leader also accused the Conservatives of being unclear about their financial plans. She promised to push for electoral reform if her party held the balance of power.

“A voting system where we’re not caught between lesser evils, where we are choosing between broken promises or service cuts, and I think we can find that system in proportional representation,” she said.

There have been three previous attempts in recent decades to change B.C.‘s first-past-the-post system. They failed to gain public support.

The debate got off to a fractious start. Eby interrupted Doerkson with a question about why he had not removed his campaign director Katy Merrifield over online posts about Islam that he likened to “the worst corners of the dark web.”

Doerkson said Merrifield was a survivor of sexual violence and that she “acted out in a moment of trauma.”

He said he was shocked Eby would go after Merrifield.

“The fact is that I’ve given her grace, I would have hoped that you might have too,” he told Eby, adding that he would “always stand against hate.”

He pointed to allegations of antisemitism in the NDP caucus from former legislature member Selina Robinson.

The debate swiftly shifted to the state of the province’s economy and the deficit under Eby.

Doerkson, whose Conservatives are the only party yet to release a costed platform, said Eby had “promised a $7-billion deficit just a few years ago.”

“It’s at 14. The reality is that doesn’t account for the things that you promised,” he said. “You challenge my thoughts on growing an economy.

“The problem Mr. Eby is you cannot continue to attack the residents of British Columbia through taxation.”

He added that British Columbians would see a fulsome plan from his party before they go to the polls.

Lowan said her party had a “fully costed, credible plan” to deal with the deficit.

“We’ve launched a tax on B.C.‘s ultra wealthy and mega corporations,” she said, adding it would generate $22.2 billion in its first year and around $5.4 billion in subsequent years.

Major differences were revealed in all three leaders’ approaches toward the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act. Kurl pointed to concerns about its impact and fears over private property rights.

Eby said while there had been “challenging” court rulings in relation to Indigenous rights and that the government was appealing them, the only path forward was in partnership with Indigenous Peoples.

“We cannot afford to have major projects tied up in the court,” he said, pointing to the need to work with Indigenous stakeholders.

Doerkson said he was committed to repealing the act known as Dripa, saying it had created division.

Lowan said the Greens took advice from First Nations leaders and they have been “unequivocal” about the need to implement Dripa. When Doerkson said the province was “at odds” as a result of Dripa, Lowan called his conclusion “ridiculous.”

Toward the end of proceedings, Kurl introduced CentreBC leader Elenore Sturko and OneBC leader Dallas Brodie, who were not in the debate auditorium but gave remarks by video. Both are former B.C. Conservatives from different ends of the party’s ideological spectrum.

Sturko said she was not asking British Columbians “to pretend that CentreBC will form government.”

“I’m asking them a different question: Who will hold the next government accountable?” she said.

“CentreBC is a socially progressive, environmentally pragmatic, and fiscally responsible party. Divisiveness and extremes on the left and on the right aren’t helping British Columbians.”

Brodie said OneBC would push for a 25 per cent income tax cut for both individuals and corporations, and a two per cent cut in the PST.

“As well, we will fight against these land back giveaways that are being done by the current government. We will read the treaties and let you know what is going on,” she said.

“We will stop the greed and corruption of the reconciliation industry in British Columbia and put B.C. back in the hands of British Columbians.”

By Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press

British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby repeatedly acknowledged his government’s imperfections in a debate where his B.C. Conservative and Green Party rivals railed against his record on the economy, health care and Indigenous rights.
“Look, I’m not perfect, but I will always act in the best interests of British Columbians, and that’s my commitment to you and your family,” he said Wednesday.
He repeated his statement during a later question period with reporters, saying he held himself “accountable to British Columbians.”
His acknowledgment was in response to questions from Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson and Green Leader Emily Lowan about his party’s record after nearly a decade in government.
“We are here because David Eby called a snap election,” Doerkson said. “He called a snap election, because he saw opportunity for himself, and I see opportunity for British Columbians.”
Asked why he called a snap election less than two years into his mandate, Eby said he needed a stronger mandate, noting the Conservatives tried to bring down his government 13 times.
“This was not a government that was able to deliver the big swings that you and your family need government to be taking for you,” he said.
The debate, held 10 days before the Oct. 24 provincial election, was carried on all major television and radio stations Wednesday and is the only one between the three leaders.
There was a surprise at the end of the event when the leaders of CentreBC and OneBC each delivered brief statements.
Moderator Shachi Kurl said neither party qualified for the debate because they did not have enough candidates.
While the debate covered a range of issues, including housing, public safety, and health care, the three leaders frequently returned to economic issues.

Doerkson said his party would “supercharge” the provincial economy, without raising existing taxes or introducing new ones. He also promised to cut taxes and bureaucratic bloat, while fully funding public health care.
He told reporters after the debate that he was committed to releasing a fully costed-out platform before residents have the opportunity to vote.
Advance voting begins Friday.
Eby questioned Doerkson’s campaign promises, saying they could only mean “dramatic cuts.”
Eby said he’d never seek to balance the province’s budget “on the backs of British Columbians,” as the province faces a record deficit of $14 billion.
In an apparent reference to previous B.C. Liberal administrations, he said their “so-called balanced budgets” came at the expense of school land being sold off.
Instead, he is focused on growing the economy and addressing wasteful spending, Eby said.
“We know what Conservatives do when they need money,” he said. “They cut … and they will do it again.”
Doerkson responded by saying Eby was guilty of fearmongering.
“The reality is you refuse to talk about your own record in this province, which is one of devastation,” he said.
The debate came hours after the NDP released the costings for its platform, showing a $2 billion reduction of the province’s deficit by 2028-29.

When Eby tried to defend his economic record, Doerkson said nobody believed him anymore, while Lowan said it was “staggering” that 1.2 million British Columbians do not have access to a family doctor.
“Your record has been marred with broken promises,” she said. “This year’s election bribes are next year’s broken promises.”
The Green leader also accused the Conservatives of being unclear about their financial plans. She promised to push for electoral reform if her party held the balance of power.

“A voting system where we’re not caught between lesser evils, where we are choosing between broken promises or service cuts, and I think we can find that system in proportional representation,” she said.
There have been three previous attempts in recent decades to change B.C.‘s first-past-the-post system. They failed to gain public support.

The debate got off to a fractious start. Eby interrupted Doerkson with a question about why he had not removed his campaign director Katy Merrifield over online posts about Islam that he likened to “the worst corners of the dark web.”
Doerkson said Merrifield was a survivor of sexual violence and that she “acted out in a moment of trauma.”
He said he was shocked Eby would go after Merrifield.
“The fact is that I’ve given her grace, I would have hoped that you might have too,” he told Eby, adding that he would “always stand against hate.”
He pointed to allegations of antisemitism in the NDP caucus from former legislature member Selina Robinson.
The debate swiftly shifted to the state of the province’s economy and the deficit under Eby.
Doerkson, whose Conservatives are the only party yet to release a costed platform, said Eby had “promised a $7-billion deficit just a few years ago.”
“It’s at 14. The reality is that doesn’t account for the things that you promised,” he said. “You challenge my thoughts on growing an economy.
“The problem Mr. Eby is you cannot continue to attack the residents of British Columbia through taxation.”
He added that British Columbians would see a fulsome plan from his party before they go to the polls.
Lowan said her party had a “fully costed, credible plan” to deal with the deficit.
“We’ve launched a tax on B.C.‘s ultra wealthy and mega corporations,” she said, adding it would generate $22.2 billion in its first year and around $5.4 billion in subsequent years.

Major differences were revealed in all three leaders’ approaches toward the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act. Kurl pointed to concerns about its impact and fears over private property rights.

Eby said while there had been “challenging” court rulings in relation to Indigenous rights and that the government was appealing them, the only path forward was in partnership with Indigenous Peoples.
“We cannot afford to have major projects tied up in the court,” he said, pointing to the need to work with Indigenous stakeholders.
Doerkson said he was committed to repealing the act known as Dripa, saying it had created division.

Lowan said the Greens took advice from First Nations leaders and they have been “unequivocal” about the need to implement Dripa. When Doerkson said the province was “at odds” as a result of Dripa, Lowan called his conclusion “ridiculous.”

Toward the end of proceedings, Kurl introduced CentreBC leader Elenore Sturko and OneBC leader Dallas Brodie, who were not in the debate auditorium but gave remarks by video. Both are former B.C. Conservatives from different ends of the party’s ideological spectrum.
Sturko said she was not asking British Columbians “to pretend that CentreBC will form government.”
“I’m asking them a different question: Who will hold the next government accountable?” she said.
“CentreBC is a socially progressive, environmentally pragmatic, and fiscally responsible party. Divisiveness and extremes on the left and on the right aren’t helping British Columbians.”
Brodie said OneBC would push for a 25 per cent income tax cut for both individuals and corporations, and a two per cent cut in the PST.
“As well, we will fight against these land back giveaways that are being done by the current government. We will read the treaties and let you know what is going on,” she said.
“We will stop the greed and corruption of the reconciliation industry in British Columbia and put B.C. back in the hands of British Columbians.”

stories.title: Emily Lowan's journey from coffee-grounds advocacy to BC Greens' leadership
stories.summary: When Emily Lowan was in her late teens, not so long ago, she would pedal around Victoria collecting coffee grounds for local farms to use as fertilizer.
stories.author: Brenna Owen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
When Emily Lowan was in her late teens, not so long ago, she would pedal around Victoria collecting coffee grounds for local farms to use as fertilizer.

Now, the 26-year-old from the Saanich Peninsula is leading British Columbia’s Green Party in a snap election campaign and running to represent the same region where she camped, snorkelled and crabbed in her childhood.

Lowan credits those experiences with inspiring a “deep reverence” for the natural world, and activating her political convictions.

“As a young person, I saw how deeply these ecosystems are under threat,” she said in an interview.

Ever since, Lowan said she has been on a mission to challenge what she described as “the politicians and the corporate forces that are threatening our democracy and a livable future on this planet” and put power in the hands of communities.

Lowan played a key role in a student-led campaign that pressured the University of Victoria into directing its investments away from fossil fuels, before climate advocacy with the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives and Climate Action Network Canada.

She won the Greens’ leadership contest last year, succeeding Sonia Furstenau.

Lowan said she recognizes why climate action isn’t top of mind for many voters.

“People have a really hard time thinking about climate when they don’t have their basic needs met, and so I want to do both,” she said.

“I want to take climate action and deliver that affordable life for regular people with, you know, a guarantee on good, green jobs, with universal child care and social housing.”

Lauren Latour was Lowan’s manager while she worked at Climate Action Network Canada between 2023 and 2025, co-ordinating efforts among non-profit and Indigenous groups while pushing for phasing out the extraction of fossil fuels.

Latour said Lowan has a “positive magnetism” that served her well in her bridge-building role with the network, along with her knowledge of climate policy in Canada and experience with organizing at the community level.

“She’s incredibly audacious. She’s not afraid to be bold in her campaign ideas and in her dreams and aspirations for her (work),” Latour said.

Outgoing Green legislator Rob Botterell, too, said Lowan has a clear vision for bringing young people into politics and pushing for “bold, courageous change” to tackle climate change, affordability and health-care challenges.

“Here is the leader of the future,” Botterell said of his first impression of Lowan.

Botterell had always intended to serve one term after winning in Saanich North and the Islands in 2024, becoming one half of a two-member Green caucus along with Jeremy Valeriote, who is seeking re-election in West Vancouver-Sea to Sky.

The retired lawyer said he “would have loved to carry on for the next couple of years” in the legislature and directed his ire at NDP Leader David Eby for “calling a completely unnecessary election” with two years left in the government’s term.

But Botterell said he was “thrilled” Lowan is running in Saanich North, where he fondly recalled knocking on doors alongside her and “watching constituents’ eyes light up when they recognize her and just seeing how well they connect.”

Botterell said Lowan is a leader beyond her years, and “somebody that you can trust.”

Lowan’s campaign in Saanich North is a family affair, with her grandmother — who previously ran a children’s book shore in Sidney, B.C. — dropping off signage materials at her office shortly before she spoke to The Canadian Press.

Lowan said her grandparents worked blue-collar jobs and opened a small business, enough to buy a home and provide generational wealth for the family.

“That is just not the reality for my generation,” she said.

“I’ve spent my whole adult life watching establishment parties manage decline as the lives of young and working people get harder.”

Lowan said people have “lost trust in a political class” across B.C.‘s major parties, whose politicians have “bought in and sold out” to corporate interests.

But the Greens offer a different vision, she said, one that centres on young people, workers, renters and “everyone else who is being crushed by the status quo in B.C.”

Lowan said the province has a revenue problem, allowing major corporations to walk away with billions of dollars in what she described as “corporate welfare.”

She said the Greens’ platform will outline how to find the money required to fund affordable housing, child care and health care, including taxing the ultra-wealthy, while building up the economy to be more independent and resilient to shocks.

“We need leadership that isn’t corrupted by the system,” Lowan said. “We need young leaders with bold ideas and real hope to bring back half the population who has stopped voting, who has given up and tuned out.”

Lowan has said the two Greens had made a difference in the legislature and the snap election offered a path to growing and holding the balance of power.

paragraphs: When Emily Lowan was in her late teens, not so long ago, she would pedal around Victoria collecting coffee grounds for local farms to use as fertilizer.

Now, the 26-year-old from the Saanich Peninsula is leading British Columbia’s Green Party in a snap election campaign and running to represent the same region where she camped, snorkelled and crabbed in her childhood.
Lowan credits those experiences with inspiring a “deep reverence” for the natural world, and activating her political convictions.
“As a young person, I saw how deeply these ecosystems are under threat,” she said in an interview.

Ever since, Lowan said she has been on a mission to challenge what she described as “the politicians and the corporate forces that are threatening our democracy and a livable future on this planet” and put power in the hands of communities.

Lowan played a key role in a student-led campaign that pressured the University of Victoria into directing its investments away from fossil fuels, before climate advocacy with the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives and Climate Action Network Canada.
She won the Greens’ leadership contest last year, succeeding Sonia Furstenau.
Lowan said she recognizes why climate action isn’t top of mind for many voters.
“People have a really hard time thinking about climate when they don’t have their basic needs met, and so I want to do both,” she said.
“I want to take climate action and deliver that affordable life for regular people with, you know, a guarantee on good, green jobs, with universal child care and social housing.”

Lauren Latour was Lowan’s manager while she worked at Climate Action Network Canada between 2023 and 2025, co-ordinating efforts among non-profit and Indigenous groups while pushing for phasing out the extraction of fossil fuels.

Latour said Lowan has a “positive magnetism” that served her well in her bridge-building role with the network, along with her knowledge of climate policy in Canada and experience with organizing at the community level.
“She’s incredibly audacious. She’s not afraid to be bold in her campaign ideas and in her dreams and aspirations for her (work),” Latour said.

Outgoing Green legislator Rob Botterell, too, said Lowan has a clear vision for bringing young people into politics and pushing for “bold, courageous change” to tackle climate change, affordability and health-care challenges.
“Here is the leader of the future,” Botterell said of his first impression of Lowan.

Botterell had always intended to serve one term after winning in Saanich North and the Islands in 2024, becoming one half of a two-member Green caucus along with Jeremy Valeriote, who is seeking re-election in West Vancouver-Sea to Sky.

The retired lawyer said he “would have loved to carry on for the next couple of years” in the legislature and directed his ire at NDP Leader David Eby for “calling a completely unnecessary election” with two years left in the government’s term.

But Botterell said he was “thrilled” Lowan is running in Saanich North, where he fondly recalled knocking on doors alongside her and “watching constituents’ eyes light up when they recognize her and just seeing how well they connect.”
Botterell said Lowan is a leader beyond her years, and “somebody that you can trust.”

Lowan’s campaign in Saanich North is a family affair, with her grandmother — who previously ran a children’s book shore in Sidney, B.C. — dropping off signage materials at her office shortly before she spoke to The Canadian Press.
Lowan said her grandparents worked blue-collar jobs and opened a small business, enough to buy a home and provide generational wealth for the family.
“That is just not the reality for my generation,” she said.
“I’ve spent my whole adult life watching establishment parties manage decline as the lives of young and working people get harder.”
Lowan said people have “lost trust in a political class” across B.C.‘s major parties, whose politicians have “bought in and sold out” to corporate interests.
But the Greens offer a different vision, she said, one that centres on young people, workers, renters and “everyone else who is being crushed by the status quo in B.C.”
Lowan said the province has a revenue problem, allowing major corporations to walk away with billions of dollars in what she described as “corporate welfare.”

She said the Greens’ platform will outline how to find the money required to fund affordable housing, child care and health care, including taxing the ultra-wealthy, while building up the economy to be more independent and resilient to shocks.

“We need leadership that isn’t corrupted by the system,” Lowan said. “We need young leaders with bold ideas and real hope to bring back half the population who has stopped voting, who has given up and tuned out.”
Lowan has said the two Greens had made a difference in the legislature and the snap election offered a path to growing and holding the balance of power.
“We can hold the government to account and get real results to make our province safer, healthier and more democratic,” she told a campaign event last month.

stories.title: Trial for man accused in Pearson gold heist set to hear more from key figure in case
stories.summary: The man who received a prison sentence for his role in the Toronto Pearson airport gold heist is expected to continue his testimony today at the trial of another man accused in the case.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The testimony of a key player in the Toronto Pearson airport gold heist has been adjourned until next week after he told a Brampton, Ont., court Wednesday that recalling details of his alleged abduction in Pakistan on the stand has left him traumatized.

Arsalan Chaudhary is serving a four-year prison sentence after pleading guilty to theft over $5,000 in what police have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.

He took the stand Tuesday in the trial of Parmpal Sidhu, who has pleaded not guilty to charges of theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the 2023 heist.

Chaudhary testified that he’d planned the heist with Simran Preet Panesar, who is still wanted by authorities, and ended up taking 30 per cent of boxes full of one-ounce gold bars. He said he melted some of the gold and sold it for cash before travelling to Pakistan, where he claimed people in police uniforms kidnapped and abused him.

He said he believed the kidnappers learned he had money from a man who helped him procure his gold-melting machine. He said he was released after giving up the remaining gold he kept in a Greater Toronto Area condo and the cash he had at his cousin’s house in Pakistan.

When Chaudhary returned to the witness stand on Wednesday, he said he couldn’t sleep the previous night after telling the story of his abduction.

“My memory is very vague when I have locked out a lot of stuff from my memory, so that’s why I cannot remember,” he said in response to questions from the Crown.

“If you’ve been through the trauma that I’ve been through, and been shocked and had bruises, you would probably understand where I’m coming from.”

Chaudhary said he has been kept at Maplehurst Correctional Complex for about three weeks, where he didn’t receive his prescribed medications including melatonin and vitamins.

“Last night, I couldn’t sleep. I had terrors, night terrors. I couldn’t eat when I got back, so it does affect me,” he said. “So, that’s why I’m not able to help you, but I would like to.”

He asked the court to send him back to the Collins Bay Institution, a federal prison in Kingston, Ont., where he is serving his sentence.

“I’ve been in Maplehurst, living with three people in a cell by a toilet, and I’ve been not getting no medical attention. I’ve asked for it,” he said.

“I’m not in the right state of mind to remember stuff you’re asking me,” he told the Crown.

After some discussions between prosecutors and defence lawyers, Superior Court Justice Gordon Cudjoe issued an order to return Chaudhary to the Collins Bay Institution and bring him back to the Brampton courthouse on Monday morning to resume his testimony.

Cudjoe also told Chaudhary he will make a recommendation to the prison to have him assessed by a medical professional.

During his testimony on Tuesday, Chaudhary said he didn’t really know Sidhu and that he only called or texted him when he couldn’t get ahold of Panesar.

The Crown asked Chaudhary about text and group chat messages related to the heist, but he repeatedly said he did not remember or recall the content of these conversations, nor who was involved in them.

Prosecutors allege that Sidhu, an Air Canada employee at the time, provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22 million in gold and currency from a Pearson airport cargo bay.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from the airport on April 17, 2023, after the shipment arrived from Switzerland.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Ontario blocks a few career colleges from Osap for three additional years
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario's colleges and universities minister has barred three career colleges from being able to offer publicly funded student financial assistance until at least 2030, after previously blocking them from the program just for this year.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Ontario’s colleges and universities minister has barred three career colleges from being able to offer publicly funded student financial assistance until at least 2030, after previously blocking them from the program just for this year.

An order in May from Nolan Quinn meant that six schools, including four Academy of Learning locations, could not access the Ontario Student Assistance Program for the 2026-27 academic year, which most of them are fighting in court.

Quinn’s decision followed government inspections that found evidence suggesting third parties were completing the coursework — sometimes entire courses in one day — and a few students who couldn’t name their school or program, officials allege in documents filed in court.

Three Academy of Learning locations, who share a parent company, updated their court complaint earlier this month to say that Quinn has now blocked them from Osap for three more years following a “final” decision by his ministry.

Quinn’s office would not comment, but rules governing the sector say that if an institution is found to be in non-compliance with those rules, they will not be eligible for Osap for three years.

The schools argue in their court application that Quinn’s decision was unreasonable and procedurally unfair.

The ministry “imposed and relied upon new approval criteria and evidentiary standards without adequate prior notice, and relied upon adverse information and analyses that was not adequately disclosed,” the schools wrote.

Concerns about the use of Osap at some career colleges are not limited to the six locations initially targeted by Quinn’s order. Career Colleges Ontario began raising concerns in 2023, and in February highlighted 14 campuses whose application patterns “include indicators consistent with possible suspicious activity,” they wrote to the government in a letter filed as part of the court case.

Quinn announced last week that the government called in auditors Kpmg in August and based on “serious concerns” in their preliminary findings, the province has referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police.

The concerns include the involvement of immigration services firms and co-location between private career colleges and immigration recruitment or services firms, inadequate student validation and verification of course enrolment and outcomes, and unusually high concentrations of Osap applications submitted from the same geographic locations, Quinn said.

He did not say if those issues apply to the three Academy of Learning locations he has now blocked from Osap until 2029-30, though ministry inspectors expressed concerns about student validation and course enrolment verification at those schools, court records show.

None of the findings and allegations have been proven in court.

The Academy of Learning said in a statement that it takes the integrity of its programs seriously.

“Over the past year, we have made significant investments to strengthen admissions, identity verification, academic monitoring and compliance, and we remain committed to fully implementing our corrective action plan,” they wrote.

“Our priority remains our students. A further three-year bar from Osap would have serious consequences for adult learners who rely on financial assistance to access career training, which is why we are asking the court to review the decision.”

The Academy of Learning has previously also said students May not have responded to government verification attempts because they believed them to be scam calls, and other students May have had language difficulties.

As well, the schools had submitted corrective action plans in response to their failed inspections, showing dozens of actions taken to remedy problems identified by the province including two-factor authentication and investigation of unusual login activity, they noted.

The instances of unusually rapid completion of courses warrants review, the Academy acknowledged, but said some students download materials to study off-line. The schools have implemented additional monitoring of files before exam codes are issued, they said.

Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request shows that the Academy of Learning’s Bay Street location went from 996 students on Osap in 2021-22 to 7,435 in 2024-25. In that year, students qualified for more than $108 million in provincial Osap grants.

The Brampton East location went from about 74 students accessing Osap in 2020-21 to 4,260 in 2024-25, for a total of more than $64 million in provincial Osap grants in the latter year.

Those two schools, plus the North York location, which is a campus of the Brampton East location, accounted for one-fifth of the nearly $1 billion in provincial Osap grants that went to all career colleges that year.

The Academy of Learning says high growth in applications was due to offering programs relevant to workforce needs.

In response to rising Osap costs, Quinn earlier this year announced that career college students would no longer be able to access grants, and students at publicly funded colleges and universities would qualify for much lower grant amounts, with a higher proportion of loans.

When Quinn announced last week that he had referred concerns to the OPP, he also said that Osap loan payments for students at all career colleges and private post-secondary institutions across the province are paused while the Kpmg audit is ongoing.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Father set to be sentenced in New York for the murder of nine-year-old Montreal girl
stories.summary: Elizabethtown - A Montreal man found guilty of drowning his daughter in a creek in Upstate New York is set to be sentenced today in Essex County Court.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Elizabethtown - Luciano Frattolin’s face remained expressionless on Wednesday as a judge sentenced him to life in prison for killing his daughter and leaving her in a marsh in rural New York.

Wearing a rumpled black suit and large black glasses, he shook his head slightly as Judge Tatiana Coffinger described the second crime he was convicted of — concealing the nine-year-old girl’s body.

“I hope, at some point in your life, you realize what you have done, what you have done to a family, and moreover, how you let down your daughter. Nothing brings her back, and we will all live with this,” said Coffinger, moments before Frattolin was led out of the courtroom, chained and in handcuffs.

In the back of the room, the girl’s mother, grandparents, and other relatives and loved ones had been watching intently. Some wiped their eyes after the judge announced her ruling in the Essex County Court.

“We continue to suffer deeply since the day Melina was brutally murdered,” the family said in a statement read outside the courthouse by District Attorney Michael Langey after the hearing.

“Nothing can bring Melina back, but we are relieved that this chapter is over. We are sincerely grateful to everyone who worked on the case. Your dedication and persistence, your efforts helped bring a measure of justice for our family.”

The sentence comes two months after a jury convicted Luciano Frattolin of second degree murder and concealment of a human corpse in the death of Melina Frattolin.

Judge Tatiana Coffinger delivered the sentence after rejecting a defence motion to set aside the guilty verdict. Frattolin would not be eligible for parole before 25 years and is expected to serve his sentence in New York.

He was also sentenced to one to three years for the charge of concealing a human corpse and was fined $5000.

“We will never know exactly what happened on the evening of July 19, 2025. We do know that at a moment (when) Melina needed her father the most, he was not her protector,” said Coffinger.

The defence issued a notice of appeal following the sentence.

“Mr. Frattolin maintains his innocence,” Brian Pilatzke, Frattolin’s lawyer, told the judge in court before she announced the sentence.

Melina Frattolin had been living in Montreal with her mother and had gone on a road trip to the United States with her father in July 2025.

On the night they were scheduled to return home, Luciano Frattolin called 911, reporting she had been kidnapped after he had stopped the car he was driving on the side of the road.

The prosecution called several police officers and experts over the trial who used car location data, cellphone data and surveillance camera footage to recreate Frattolin’s movements on the day his daughter died.

The data showed Frattolin’s car and phone were stopped for close to an hour in the area where Melina’s body was later found. Police also found a bag of muddy clothing Frattolin had been wearing on the side of the road.

During the hearing, Coffinger accused Frattolin of having lied in his statements to police and likened his kidnapping story to “a Hollywood script.”

“Mr. Frattolin, you live in a world of self-made delusion of wealth and image,” she said. “When the greatest accomplishment of your life would have been to be a great father, that is not what you are going to be remembered for.”

Coffinger also granted a protective order for Melina’s mother, Kali Galanis, meaning Frattolin will be forbidden from contacting her in any way.

Outside the courthouse, Langey said he was satisfied with the sentence.

“Hopefully the parole board doesn’t parole him, and he does serve most of his life in prison,” he added.

Asked about Frattolin’s possible motive, Langey said he believed the Montreal man had wanted a life of wealth and success.

“He had an obsession and hatred of Melina’s mom, Kali, and he wanted a different life,” he said.

During the three-week-long trial, the defence had tried to argue that local police had not adequately investigated Frattolin’s claims that his daughter was kidnapped.

The jury spent an hour deliberating on Aug. 10 at the end of the trial, before concluding that Frattolin was guilty.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: 'Fjord' drew early criticism for its supposed anti-wokeness. The director says decide for yourself
stories.summary: Toronto - Director Cristian Mungiu knows there are people with strong opinions about his latest film — even though they haven't seen it yet.
stories.author: Nicole Thompson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Director Cristian Mungiu knows there are people with strong opinions about his latest film — even though they haven’t seen it yet.

In some ways, he says, that proves the point he’s making in “Fjord.”

“I think that it confirms a lot what the film is about: people do express firm opinions, even without knowing the content, even before they watch the film,” he said in an interview ahead of the movie’s screening at the Toronto International Film Festival last month.

At that point, the number of people who’d seen the film was relatively small. It premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in May, where it won the top prize, the Palme d’Or. It then screened at Telluride in September. Toronto was to be its third stop on the festival circuit before its theatrical release in Canada this Friday.

But the film, which stars Sebastian Stan as a devoutly Christian father of five who comes under suspicion when his oldest daughter shows up to school bruised, already had an outsized reaction.

Some on social media called “Fjord” a Maga movie; others said it was “anti-woke.”

The Norway-set film asks questions about what religious tolerance looks like in secular communities, while examining the consequences of the country’s child protection system.

Mungiu said he wants people to come to their own opinions about the movie.

“I think the worst thing you can do is to have firm opinions about things that you haven’t seen yet,” the Romanian filmmaker said.

He added that he wants people to go into the film with an open mind, shedding their preconceived notions.

For instance, he said, he’s been accused of casting Stan to make his character — a conservative, somewhat standoffish man with traditional ideas about childrearing — more sympathetic to audiences.

Mungiu said that’s not the case — people only think that because they have existing positive feelings about Stan.

“This is your problem as spectators that you like Sebastian. I mean, from my point of view, you need to listen to the arguments in the film,” he said.

Mungiu said even those who have seen the film May not be opening their minds to its message.

“In every screening, let’s say that 80, 90 per cent of the spectators come in and get out with the same ideas that they had before,” he said. “And the film will just only confirm their own ideas. But you know there are 10, 15, 20 per cent of people who think about the point of view of the other. And this is where the conversation can start.”

He said he wants that conversation to be about more than just the movie.

“It can start about something more important, which is what happens in the society today, this conflict between these groups that don’t talk and don’t communicate.”

To do that, Stan said, people “might have to put their phones down.”

“I think online unfortunately is just a made-up place in a lot of ways, you know, and I think it’s quite dangerous in that regard because you can just live in your own little bubble, which a lot of people do, and never once think for yourself or never once go out and see anything,” he said.

“Instead of going to your social media for some sort of opinion, go and actually form one for yourself.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: A policing dynasty meets Project South
stories.summary: In today’s First Up: Kawhi Leonard returns to the Raptors and a tale of two Chows.
stories.author: Paige Oldfield
stories.content:
Because Braeden Chow shares a surname with incumbent Toronto mayor Olivia Chow, confusion at polling stations has followed — even from the mayor herself.

Courtesy Braeden Chow

Franco Bisceglia has been racing pigeons since he was 7 years old, now at 50 he’s still loving the sport and the companionship it comes with.

Nick Lachance/Toronto Star

Morning News Digest

Morning News Digest

In today’s First Up: Kawhi Leonard returns to the Raptors and a tale of two Chows.

Toronto star illustration using photos from X and Dreamstime[](http://www.thestar.com/news/morning-digest/a-policing-dynasty-meets-project-south/article_1de09df2-6027-4d6b-9419-1b378aca3c2f.html)

ByPaige Oldfield Digital producer

Good morning. This is the Wednesday, Oct. 14 edition of First Up, the Star’s daily morning digest. Sign up to get it earlier each day, in your inbox.

With less than two weeks to election day, a new poll shows an already tight mayoral race could hinge on voter turnout in all corners of the city. Edward Keenan is off till Thursday but joins us briefly today to write about the matter of the two very different Chows listed on the ballot in the race for mayor of Toronto. More on that below.

Three generations of the Madeley family have worked for the Toronto Police Service: grandfather, father and son, each named John Madeley. But a shadow was cast on that policing legacy after two of them were charged in Project South, a sprawling investigation into allegations of police corruption. The middle John, a retired officer, was arrested for allegedly improperly using a police database and was accused of working with an alleged loan shark. Weeks later, his constable son Madeley Jr. was arrested and charged with unlawful computer searches and breach of trust. Lawyers for the pair declined to comment.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

How a former actress turned private eye ended up in the crosshairs of the Project South police corruption probe.

She hasn’t been charged. But the Project South allegations have branded her with a “scarlet letter.”

Watch: We untangle the web of alleged connections between accused crime figures and Toronto police officers.

“All options are on the table”: Ottawa could sue Stelco at any time over the up to 500 layoffs it has planned in Hamilton.

Shareholders for Roots, the decades-old Canadian brand best known for its comfy sweatpants, have approved a deal to take it private under U.S. ownership, with a Canadian operating partner.

This nail salon chain owes more than $50,000 in unpaid wages to nine workers. Immigration and work reporter Ghada Alsharif spoke with the employees and the salon owners.

Cycling advocates want to take the fight to save key downtown bike lanesto the Supreme Court of Canada. The Ford government began removing them on Bloor Street Tuesday and were temporarily thwarted by protests.

A record 222,550 Torontonians cast early ballots, marking the highest advance voting turnout in more than 10 years.

David Miller: Brad Bradford is promising to fix a water problem that doesn’t exist. His “solution” is bad news for all Torontonians.

Six years after Regis Korchinski-Paquet fell to her death during a police call, a coroner’s inquest examines whether her history of epilepsy and seizures played a role.

Toronto police have arrested and charged a 29-year-old man with arson after Israeli flags were burned near a North York church on Oct. 7.

With just days left before Albertans decide on whether to set the path for provincial secession, separatist campaign groups are not preparing to quit.

ICYMI: In his Thanksgiving video Monday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is “worth fighting for.”

When Mayor Olivia Chow came out of the voting booth last week, she made a startling admission: she almost voted for someone else. “I just noticed there is two ‘Chow’ on the ballot, and there is one before me,” she said.

That’s when many people would have learned for the first time that a man named Braeden Chow is also running for mayor. Alongside dozens of other people, which is part of what might make this a problem: the ballot is very long and formed into a grid crowded with names. Scanning the names, it is very easy to see how the boldface Chow listed eighth, the Chow listed ninth and the Choy listed tenth could lead to some confusion. You have to squint a bit at the fainter first names listed way over on the opposite side of the column to be sure who is who.

Olivia Chow’s campaign is now engaged in a public message push to alert people to the possible confusion. With polls tightening, there’s some fear miscast ballots could wind up being decisive. It would certainly seem like a travesty if that wound up being the case.

The Star’s Elissa Mendes spoke with Braeden Chow about his previously under-the-radar campaign. He denied that he was encouraged to run by the current mayor’s opponents. “I did this for a love of the game,” he said. “I have real plans, and I think it’s time for a change in the city.”

As a reader named Chris said in the comments, “The guy’s allowed to use his own name. It’s up to voters to show due diligence and double-check before voting.” Certainly, most of us would agree. But Chris points at another problem some would think is evident on that ballot: “I’m more concerned about these dozens of candidates for the same job in some elections. The elections people need to put a reasonable upper limit and have criteria to weed out nuisance candidates.”

This is a sentiment you hear — that perhaps the required monetary deposit or minimum number of signatures needed to register should be higher, to discourage fringe candidates (including any whose motive for running might be mischievous). But that strategy limits access to running for office to those with more resources. I’ve heard plenty of objections to that over the years.

I wonder if there isn’t a way the ballot could be designed to be less confusing. Something as simple as putting the first and last names closer together. Or changing the spacing between the names.

What do you think? Do you have a suggestion to make the long ballot less confusing? Do you think it’s a problem that so many people are able to run no-hope campaigns? Or do you think all’s fair in love and elections, and it’s up to voters to avoid confusion themselves? Let us know in the comments section here.

— Edward Keenan, host of First Up

SUSAN DELACOURT:Chrystia Freeland’s book is a plea to all those dealing with Donald Trump to be the bad cop.

ADAM RADWANSKI:Mark Carney says he might ramp up immigration again. We need to see his plan first.

MARTIN REGG COHN:Doug Ford is at the middle of an actual scandal, but this isn’t it.

Pigeon racing involves champion birds fetching high prices. As Mark Colley reports, the sport is “dying.” Can these Ontarians save it from extinction?

John Green talks with us about his first adult novel, “Hollywood, Ending,” centered on two young actors navigating sudden fame after starring in an Andy Warhol biopic.

Basketball: Kawhi Leonard took to an NBA court in a Toronto uniform again Tuesday night and it was nothing but good.

Hockey: The Maple Leafs couldn’t outscore their many flaws on display in a 5-4 loss to the Utah Mammoth on Tuesday.

In the Star’s recent profile on Toronto-Centre, city hall bureau chief Ben Spurr spoke with residents about how homelessness and public safety concerns are shaping up the race to become councillor there. There was a lot of discussion on what harm reduction actually does:

“The very term ‘harm reduction’ says it all, if the only way we can help these people is to stop them from killing themselves, I would argue we’re not doing a good enough job.” — Peter

Others pointed out the need to do more to solve the housing issue:

“We need to look at why they lost their housing in the first place to find out the best way to help them be successfully housed now.” — Susan

Before you go, do you play pickleball at (checks notes) Ashbridge’s Bay Sports Hub? As Libaan Osman reports, tempers are running high at the park over a lack of signs outlining which of the 11 courts to use and how long players can play.

Thanks for starting your day with us. If you enjoy First Up, please share it with a friend. And let us know what you think of the changes we’ve made, and what you’d like to see. Email firstup@thestar.ca. Ed will see you back here tomorrow morning.

Editor: Maryam Shah

Senior editor: Christine Loureiro

How a family with a policing legacy was swept up in a corruption scandal

Three generations of the Madeley family have worked for the Toronto Police Service: grandfather, father and son, each named John Madeley.
