stories.title: Alberta government recommended Sam Mraiche-linked company to build recovery centre, lawyer alleges
stories.summary: Former lawyer for Tsuut’ina Nation says province played role in First Nation’s selection of Melewka Homes Ltd.
stories.author: Tom Cardoso, Carrie Tait
stories.content:
The Alberta government recommended a company linked to businessman Sam Mraiche to build a $35-million addiction recovery centre on a First Nation near Calgary, according to the community’s former lawyer.

Tsuut’ina Nation, which broke ground on its recovery centre in 2024, is one of several Indigenous communities building addiction treatment facilities funded by the provincial government.

Terry Braun, the nation’s former lawyer, alleges in a court document that the government of Alberta played a role in Tsuut’ina’s selection of Melewka Homes Ltd. The builder has been linked in court filings to Mr. Mraiche, who is a central figure in a health care procurement controversy in the province and has connections to powerful figures in Alberta Premier Danielle Smith ’s government.

While Mr. Braun’s filing does not detail who made the recommendation, his assertion is the first indication that Ms. Smith’s government suggested a candidate to build Tsuut’ina’s health care facility.

“The Government of Alberta recommended Melewka Homes Ltd. for the construction of the Project as Melewka Homes was constructing comparable recovery facilities elsewhere in Alberta as part of a broader recovery model within the province,” Mr. Braun said. A lawyer representing Mr. Braun declined to comment on the filing, and a lawyer for Melewka Homes did not respond to a request for comment.

Three Indigenous communities collectively received more than $100-million in grants from the province to build their respective recovery centres. Each awarded its contract to Melewka Homes Ltd., a company with a history of residential construction that is mired in litigation and allegations that subcontractors on its recovery centre projects have gone unpaid .

Ms. Smith has repeatedly told the public that the three communities – Tsuut’ina Nation, Enoch Cree Nation and the Métis Nation of Alberta – were responsible for selecting Melewka Homes.

“We know nothing about them,” she said of the company during a session in the legislature in late March, “which is why we rely on the First Nations and the Métis, when we give them a grant, to manage their own contracts.”

In November, 2025, while responding to an NDP statement alleging that companies owned or affiliated with Mr. Mraiche had received contracts to build recovery centres, Ms. Smith told the legislature that purchasing decisions were left up to Indigenous communities.

“The way we operate with our partnership with Indigenous communities,” she said, “is that we give them a grant, and they do the procurement.”

Spokespersons for Ms. Smith and the Alberta government did not respond to messages from The Globe and Mail seeking comment. A lawyer for Mr. Mraiche also did not respond to a request for comment.

Tsuut’ina sued Mr. Braun in July, alleging negligence, breach of contract and other wrongdoing in connection with the procurement process for its unfinished recovery centre, which it says was sole-sourced and has been marred by “red flags.” The Dene community of roughly 2,500 citizens also alleged that Mr. Mraiche – a medical-supply executive and entrepreneur whose business and government contracts are part of an RCMP investigation – played an undisclosed role in the construction project.

Mr. Braun has denied any wrongdoing, and denied any knowledge that Mr. Mraiche would benefit from the project. He also said he had no dealings of substance with the businessman and “only interacted with Mraiche on a single occasion.” Mr. Mraiche is not a party to Tsuut’ina’s lawsuit.

The United Conservative Party government has been entangled in a purchasing controversy since early 2025 after the province fired Athana Mentzelopoulos as the chief executive of Alberta Health Services, a health care agency that employed more than 100,000 people.

After her termination, Ms. Mentzelopoulos sued the government for wrongful dismissal and alleged that government officials had pressed her to shut down an internal investigation she had been conducting into potential conflicts of interest in the purchasing decisions made by senior procurement officials at her agency. Ms. Mentzelopoulos’s investigation did not focus on recovery centres, which are under the purview of the Ministry of Mental Health and Addiction.

Her investigation focused, in part, ON contracts awarded to Mr. Mraiche’s company, MHCare Medical Corp., which had received roughly $614-million in business from Alberta Health Services since 2020; Mr. Mraiche is also connected to companies that were vying for an estimated $430-million in contracts for private surgical facilities.

The government says it fired Ms. Mentzelopoulos because she failed to execute its vision for the health care system. Neither party’s allegations have been tested in court.

The Globe has reported that Mr. Mraiche hosted the Premier, cabinet ministers and senior staff at NHL hockey games; that he joined Ms. Smith’s inner circle in a hotel suite in May, 2023, to watch the province’s election results; that he was under an election-finance investigation by Elections Alberta around the time his long-time friend and relative , Justice Minister Mickey Amery, tightened the regulator’s timelines for issuing sanctions for violations ; and, earlier this year, that the RCMP searched the offices of MHCare and an accounting business owned by an MHCare executive and Alberta government appointee .

Mr. Mraiche has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing in connection with the controversies.

The recovery centres being built by Tsuut’ina, Enoch and the Métis Nation of Alberta are part of a broader provincial response to the opioid epidemic. That strategy was championed by Marshall Smith, the Premier’s former chief of staff, who The Globe reported lived in a $1.6-million home owned by Mr. Mraiche’s sister while he was one of Ms. Smith’s top aides. Lawyers for Mr. Smith did not respond to a request for comment.

In March, 2025, the Alberta government inquired into how the three Indigenous communities awarded the construction contracts for their recovery centres, documents tabled in the legislature show.

“If you could also please confirm how Melewka was selected to perform the work, we will update our files accordingly,” Yvonne Carignan, an executive director at the Ministry of Mental Health and Addiction – which paid out the grants for the three recovery centre projects – said in an e-mail to the Enoch Cree Nation.

“The Nation followed its own internal procurement process, soliciting bids from potential vendors in the Edmonton-area,” the Indigenous community replied. In an e-mailed statement to The Globe, Enoch spokesperson Erin Stroud said that Melewka Homes’ “existing design and relationship with other First Nations added strength to their proposal,” and that the nation expects to open its recovery centre in early December.

When Tsuut’ina’s then-chief Roy Whitney responded to Ms. Carignan, he said the nation had chosen Melewka Homes based on “a review of construction companies that were familiar with the construction of recovery facilities in Alberta.”

The nation entered into a contract with Melewka Homes in February, 2024, court filings show. At the time, Melewka had one other recovery centre contract, with the Métis Nation, which it had signed a month prior.

Ellery Starlight, who was elected as Tsuut’ina Nation’s chief in late 2025, said in an interview that his community is still investigating how its recovery centre contract was managed.

“The whole project – as positive as it is sounding, everybody was in the dark of the process,” he said.

Mr. Starlight estimated Tsuut’ina’s recovery centre is about 80 per cent complete, and he wants to see its doors open.

“A recovery centre is a godsend,” he said. “I actually have a good team now that’s overseeing the project in a responsible way. And we’re moving forward. We’re not mothballing anything.”

The projects at Tsuut’ina, Enoch and the Métis Nation fell into a legal morass after a dispute emerged between Melewka Homes and a business development partner , the similarly named Melewka Construction Management Services Ltd., owned by Mohamed Eldassouki, an MHCare executive and Mr. Mraiche’s brother-in-law.

Mr. Eldassouki alleges that Melewka Homes president Lewis Semashkewich took control of his business and bank account by using a forged share sale agreement. Mr. Semashkewich, meanwhile, alleges that Mr. Mraiche was the undisclosed “directing mind” of Melewka Construction and that he had worked with others to withhold payments on various projects, including the recovery centres, until Melewka Homes agreed to pay him.

While the two Melewkas continue their court battle, The Globe has reported that subcontractors allege they have gone unpaid, and some have taken to placing liens or suing to recoup their costs. None of the allegations in those proceedings have been proven in court.

Mr. Mraiche has denied any wrongdoing in his court filings and said his involvement in Melewka Construction was limited to providing “casual, unofficial and informal business advice.” Lawyers for Mr. Eldassouki and Mr. Semashkewich did not respond to a request for comment, and the litigation continues.

stories.title: B.C.’s Eby declines to reveal size of donation after $10-a-day daycare revelation
stories.summary: British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby says he and his wife donated the difference in costs after their children's daycare fell under the $10-a day program a couple years ago, but he declined to specify the amount.

stories.content:
The leaders of the two major parties running in British Columbia’s election pitched business leaders with infrastructure commitments, including a new shipyard and promises of tax cuts.

NDP Leader David Eby and Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson appeared at a Greater Vancouver Board of Trade event on Tuesday along with Green Leader Emily Lowan to speak for 10 minutes each and then take pre-selected questions in advance of the Oct. 24 election.

Eby said his party would build a new shipyard in partnership with the federal government, so new B.C. ferries and other vessels, such as icebreakers, can be built in British Columbia.

His appearance came just hours after he faced more questions about his family’s use of $10-a-day childcare.

He said earlier Tuesday that he and wife Cailey Lynch, a doctor, didn’t need the daycare discount that has only reached a minority of parents in the province.

Eby said they wanted other families to benefit after the centre switched to the subsidized rate, so they made a donation to the facility.

While Eby initially declined to reveal the size of the donation, his campaign later said that the family will have contributed $8,000 between 2024 and the end of 2026 for both of their children who are at the facility.

Eby promised business leaders that in addition to building a new shipyard his government would make permanent a manufacturing jobs fund worth $60 million that was announced days before he called an election.

His government would also expand food processing opportunities across the provincial Agricultural Land Reserve.

Doerkson told the crowd that his party would supercharge the provincial economy by cutting taxes and trimming permitting times for large investments.

He said a Conservative government would establish a 120-day approval process for capital projects worth more than $250 million, permanently cancel the proposed expansion of the provincial sales taxes, and exempt machinery, equipment and software from PST for three years.

Green Leader Emily Lowan pledged to implement a new industrial strategy that would lessen B.C.’s dependence on exploiting natural resources, while the party’s proposed tax on the ultra-wealthy would help pay down the deficit and provide public services.

Bridgitte Anderson, president of the Greater Vancouver Board of Trade, moderated the event and opened it by revealing the results of a survey that asked its members about their top concerns.

Anderson said 78 per cent of those who responded to the survey said the provincial economy is heading in the wrong direction, while 74 per cent expressed concerns about the deficit, which was forecast to hit $13.8 billion.

Eby said that the challenges facing the business community are not unique to the province, and the question facing the province right now is how to get through this existential moment, referring to the trade war with the United States.

“We’re going to stand up, we’re going to protect, and we’re going to build,” he said.

Standing up, he said, means in part that U.S. liquor won’t be back on local shelves until there is a fair deal for the provincial forest sector. It also means standing up against U.S.-style politics coming to British Columbia, he added.

Eby said his party would also protect British Columbians against high prices by regulating profits on basic grocery items and the cost of fuel.

“But let’s also be frank: the path forward for us as a province is to build,” he said.

A change in government, he said, would cast doubt on projects worth $130 billion.

“We cannot afford chaos,” he said.

Doerkson said British Columbians are ready for a change, pointing to business concerns about the economic direction of the province and the deficit.

“We’re spending a lot, but we are not seeing the results that British Columbians expect,” Doerkson said.

“ Four out of five of you are not confident in the provincial government’s economic strategy, and what troubles me the most of all, is more than 30 per cent (of board members) say that their businesses have considered moving outside of British Columbia.”

Doerkson said Conservatives are ready to govern and will create the conditions for economic growth.

“With a Conservative government, you will have an ally in Victoria,” he said.

Both Eby and Doerkson faced pointed questions about their financial plans.

When asked about the deficit, Eby said his party would release a fully-costed platform and reduce the deficit over time, without giving an exact time frame.

But the Conservatives have made billions of dollars of unfunded commitments, and that the party is on track to almost double the deficit, without citing concrete figures, Eby said.

“The only way to achieve that and drive down the deficit is massive cuts to public services,” he said.

When Anderson asked Doerkson about his plans for the deficit without raising new taxes, he said his party would cut red tape, while fully funding health care.

“The part that we are forgetting in this province is what happens when we create GDP and that is overlooked all the time,” he said. Doerkson said two per cent growth would probably generate $11 to $12 billion worth of GDP.

Lowan questioned both Eby’s and Doerkson’s focus on resource projects.

“This is the politics of imagination and hope that is desperately needed when times feel bleak. This is not the time to hunker down in old ideas.”

A televised leaders’ debate is set for Wednesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

Wolfgang Depner, The Canadian Press

stories.title: France won't grant crab licence off Newfoundland without discussion, ambassador says
stories.summary: ST. John's - France's ambassador to Canada says her country has not issued a fishing licence off the coast of Newfoundland, despite a reported pledge from the French president.
stories.author: Sarah Smellie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - France’s ambassador to Canada says her country has not issued a fishing licence off the coast of Newfoundland, despite a reported pledge from the French president.

Hélène Farnaud-Defromont said France would not take such a step without consulting Canada, as per the agreements between the two countries. And France has no intention of challenging those fishing agreements with Canada, she said.

stories.title: The Campaign Pitch: How a new program could give us clean parks, clear winter sidewalks and youth jobs
stories.summary: Hiring young people to fill in gaps for seasonal maintenance could help both youth and the city
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
stories.content:
The Star is partnering with the School of Cities at the University of Toronto to pitch big ideas during the run-up to this month’s municipal election . Affiliated faculty at the school have taken on some of the city’s thorniest problems and the Star has presented their solutions to the two main contenders running to be mayor. In the fourth edition, the case for hiring more young people to fill the gaps in city maintenance.

Last winter while pushing a stroller through uncleared, hazardous snowy sidewalks on the school run, Kofi Hope had an idea: What if the city deployed hundreds or thousands of young people to clear the streets within a day of a snowfall?

stories.title: Missing Person – Richard Pitre
stories.summary: London, ON (October 13, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 40-year-old Richard Pitre, of London.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 13, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 40-year-old Richard Pitre, of London.

The missing person is described as male, White, approximately 5’8”, short brown hair, and unshaven. He was last seen wearing light blue jeans, a camouflage rain jacket, and white shoes.

The missing person was last seen on October 11, 2026, in the area of High Street and Base Line Road East. He was reported missing on October 13, 2026.

Family and police are concerned for her welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Police charge suspect after Israeli flags burned near North York church on Oct. 7 anniversary
stories.summary: Toronto police have arrest and charged a 29-year-old male suspect with arson after Israeli flags burned near North York church on Oct. 7 anniversary.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
stories.content:
A Toronto man is facing charges including arson after several Israeli flags were found burned at a North York church, police say.

Around 1:02 a.m. on Oct. 7, officers say a man went to the area of Sunrise Avenue and O’Connor Drive, removed Israeli flags placed in front of a church, lit them on fire and fled the scene, police said in a release Tuesday.

stories.title: Traffic stop leads to arrest
stories.summary: General Releases
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 13, 2026) – A London man is facing a number of charges after a traffic stop by a member of the London Police Service (LPS) Road Safety Section in the south end of the city last week.

At approximately 11:30 a.m., ON Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, a London police officer operating an unmarked police vehicle on Wharncliffe Road South near Belmont Drive observed a driver using a cellphone while stopped at a red light. The officer conducted a traffic stop and learned that the G1 driver was alone in the vehicle without an accompanying driver present.

The officer observed that the vehicle did not have a muffler attached and directed the driver to pull off the road for an inspection. Multiple deficiencies were identified, and the vehicle was deemed unfit to drive.

Further investigation revealed the driver was breaching court-imposed conditions.

The driver was arrested and transported to the LPS Headquarters Detention Centre.

A search incident to arrest yielded a quantity of suspected controlled substances.

As a result of the investigation, Koch Bill Agok, 25, of London, has been charged with:

Two counts of failing to comply with a release order;

Possession of a Schedule III substance;

Breach of probation;

Drive-hand-held communication device;

Class G1 licence holder – unaccompanied by a qualified driver

No muffler-motor vehicle; and

Drive commercial motor vehicle not in accordance with emissions regulations.

The accused remains in custody and is scheduled to appear in London court today, in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information about this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be submitted anonymously online to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Ontario to change how people with addictions get safer-supply opioids, in a bid to stop drugs being diverted to the street
stories.summary: It will mark a big shift in how people with opioid use disorder access potent pharmaceutical opioids from a safe source.
stories.author: Omar Mosleh
stories.content:
The regulatory body for Ontario physicians has introduced stricter rules for prescribing safer supply opioids , aiming to reduce the rate of those drugs being diverted to the street.

The change will mark a major shift in how people addicted to opioids access potent pharmaceutical opioids such as hydromorphone from a safe source. Some experts say the changes seem reasonable and will lead to greater oversight of prescribing practices, while others argue it could drive patients to obtain street fentanyl, which is much more toxic and dangerous.

The first formal safer supply program was introduced in 2016 in London, Ont., as fentanyl was sweeping through the opioid street supply and overdose deaths were soaring. Safer supply typically involves the prescribing of hydromorphone, a potent short-acting pharmaceutical opioid that is about five to 10 times stronger than morphine, to help people get off street opioids. It’s sometimes used as an alternative to opioid agonist treatment, which uses medications such methadone and Suboxone to reduce withdrawal symptoms, but are not as effective for people with high tolerances to opioids.

Ontario's medical regulator has approved significant changes to the way doctors prescribe safer supply drugs, in an effort to reduce the amount of opioids making their way to the streets. (Oct. 13, 2026)

But there have also been longstanding concerns that the programs result in more pharmaceutical pills being sold on the street.

On Tuesday, the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario voted to move forward with three main measures: Requiring that physicians only prescribe safer supply medications in concert with opioid agonist treatment; mandating a comprehensive in-person clinical assessment at least monthly for patients receiving the medication; and perhaps most controversially, requiring the medication to be consumed under supervision, effectively eliminating what are known as “carries” (prescriptions that can be taken home).

“Taken together, these changes were intended to reduce the risk of diversion, strengthen clinical oversight, and support a transition to” opioid agonist treatment, said Dr. Anil Chopra, associate registrar at Cpso.

In January, British Columbia introduced restrictions to its safer supply program, requiring the drugs to be taken under medical supervision due to concerns about the drugs being diverted to the street. At Tuesday’s board meeting, the Cpso’s CEO and registrar Dr. Nancy Whitmore characterized Ontario as “the only jurisdiction now that has open prescribing of safer supply without any checks and balances in the system.”

Another provision that was heavily criticized was limiting safer supply prescribing to a maximum of eight weeks, which the board removed from the proposal due to feedback from experts.

“They noted that it could lead to rapid tapering, make it more difficult to retain patients in treatment, and destabilize patients who had been stable on long-term safer supply,” Chopra said. “Based on this feedback, Cpso determined that the proposed eight-week limit was unnecessarily prescriptive and could lead to unintended harm to some patients.”

Michael Parkinson, executive director of the Drug Strategy Network of Ontario, said the eight-week limit was most problematic but also took issue with the requirement for doses to be supervised, which he says will disproportionately affect people who are employed or who live in rural and remote areas, which would make it hard for them to get to a pharmacy several times a day for the medication.

“It’s not a question of if a number of patients in Ontario are going to be harmed,” Parkinson said. “They are. The changes are guaranteed to impact those most in need of health care and least likely to receive it.”

Dr. Meldon Kahan, an addictions specialist and former medical director of the Substance Use Service at Women’s College Hospital, said safer supply programs were previously overseen and funded by the federal government. When the feds stopped funding programs in 2025, private fee-for-service doctors “filled the gap.” The medications are covered by Ohip.

“There are some doctors who are prescribing conscientiously and carefully, but there are also clinics that are just handing out massive amounts of this drug without anything else, with no counselling, with no careful patient selection,” Kahan said. “It’s unethical, in my view.”

Kahan is not opposed to safer supply — he said a number of observation studies clearly show that people enrolled in safer supply programs do better than patients not undergoing any treatment. He added that they tended to have good treatment retention rates. Patients receiving safer supply are less likely to end up in hospital and less likely to die of overdose, Kahan said.

He said he supports safer supply being prescribed in conjunction with opioid agonist treatment, highlighting a B.C. study that patients were more likely to stay in treatment if they received both simultaneously.

He said one of the primary issues is that patients are being given far more doses of hydromorphone than he believes is reasonable or medically necessary — ranging from 14 to 24 or 30 eight-milligram tablets per day.

“What we need to do is take steps to stop diversion while also attempting to retain patients in treatment,” Kahan said.

It’s unclear how much of hydromorphone sold on the street is being diverted from safer supply prescriptions. On Tuesday, Chopra said police informed the college the amount of illicit hydromorphone they’ve seized increased by 12 times from 2022 to 2025. But experts say there are other ways hydromorphone pills are diverted for street sales, including prescriptions for other medical conditions and black market production.

stories.title: Fanshawe College opens the Wsib Centre of Excellence in Immersive Technologies Simulation for Workplace Safety
stories.summary: State-of-the-art facility will leverage XR and AI to advance workplace safety, training a
stories.content:
State-of-the-art facility will leverage XR and AI to advance workplace safety, training and mental health supports for public safety personnel

Today, Fanshawe College, the Workplace Safety and Insurance Board (Wsib) and community partners celebrated the grand opening of the Wsib Centre of Excellence in Immersive Technologies Simulation for Workplace Safety. This research and production facility will use extended reality (XR) and artificial intelligence (AI) to develop immersive training and therapeutic simulations to help public safety personnel prepare for high-pressure scenarios, strengthen decision-making skills, and support recovery and return-to-work outcomes after a mental stress injury.

"The Wsib Centre of Excellence in Immersive Technologies Simulation for Workplace Safety demonstrates what is possible when organizations come together around a shared commitment to innovation, well-being and solving real-world challenges," said Peter Devlin, President of Fanshawe College. "By bringing together expertise in immersive technology, applied research and education, we are creating opportunities to improve safety outcomes, support public safety personnel and prepare the next generation of leaders and innovators. We thank the Wsib for its generous support, and our public safety partners for their leadership in developing this state-of-the-art centre of excellence."

, in partnership with the WorkSafe Ontario Fund, the centre brings together researchers, educators, students, industry partners and public safety leaders to develop innovative training and therapeutic simulations designed to address some of the most pressing challenges facing the public safety sector today.

“Today marks the beginning of a new way to understand, prevent and treat mental stress injuries and we’re excited about the important work Fanshawe College will be doing at this centre,” said Jeff Lang, Wsib President and CEO. “Two years ago, this was a dream. Now it’s a real space that will change lives - and save lives too - especially for our first responders.”

Students from a variety of disciplines, including health sciences, public safety, information technology, artificial intelligence, digital media, gaming, business and design, will have opportunities to contribute to projects undertaken through the centre. The facility will serve as a living lab where students, faculty and industry partners collaborate on complex real-world challenges while developing the critical-thinking, problem-solving and teamwork skills increasingly sought by employers.

“This centre is about the people it will protect,” said Joshua Workman, President and CEO, WorkSafe Ontario Fund. “By bringing students, researchers and first responders together in one space, we will help public safety personnel prepare for the toughest moments of the job, recover from mental stress injuries and safely return home to their families. The WorkSafe Ontario Fund is honoured to partner with the Wsib and Fanshawe College to bring the Wsib Centre of Excellence in Immersive Technologies Simulation for Workplace Safety to life.”

The centre builds on Fanshawe's growing leadership in immersive technology and applied AI. The College has established a comprehensive XR ecosystem across sectors including health care, public safety, construction, advanced manufacturing and digital media, helping organizations explore new approaches to training, workforce development and innovation.

stories.title: Missing person –
stories.summary: Original - London, ON (October 13, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 40-year-old Richard Pitre, of London.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
Update – London, ON (October 16, 2026) – Police continue to search for missing person, Richard Pitre.

Investigators have received information that he was last seen at approximately 11:40 a.m., ON October 11, 2026, in the area of Commissioners Road East and Adelaide Street North.

Original - London, ON (October 13, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 40-year-old Richard Pitre, of London.

The missing person is described as male, White, approximately 5’8”, short brown hair, and unshaven. He was last seen wearing light blue jeans, a camouflage rain jacket, and white shoes.

The missing person was last seen on October 11, 2026, in the area of High Street and Base Line Road East. He was reported missing on October 13, 2026.

Family and police are concerned for her welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Toronto robotics startup hopes to expand options for surgical procedures
stories.summary: Revolve Surgical says its device is cheaper than other robotic aids used for laparoscopy
stories.author: Chris Hannay
stories.content:
Trauma surgeon Joao De Rezende-Neto stands by an operating table in the simulation area of St. Michael’s Hospital in downtown Toronto.

On the table in front of him is a silicone replica of part of a human abdomen. His eyes remain fixed on the screen above the table, showing the view of a camera inside the abdominal cavity.

In Dr. De Rezende-Neto’s hands are the controls for slim robotic arms that are, currently, inside the abdomen and grabbing at a fake gall bladder. With the twist of a wrist, the roll of a thumb or the pull of a trigger, the surgeon can use the tiny grabbers at the ends of the robotic arms to perform delicate tasks, such as stitching up an incision.

The makers of the device – Toronto startup Revolve Surgical Inc. – hope to bring it to hospitals across Canada and the United States in the coming years.

They say the tool makes it easier for surgeons to conduct laparoscopic procedures, in which a surgeon makes small incisions in a patient’s abdomen and inserts tools and a camera. The company says its device expands options for these procedures, which improve patient outcomes, at a price that is far more affordable for cash-strapped hospitals than other robotic aids.

The team recently celebrated a major milestone: bringing the device from simulations to a real operating table. Dr. De Rezende-Neto performed the first human surgery – an appendix removal – with the Revolve arm on Oct. 1.

The road to that first real human operation has been a long one for the co-founders. Matthew Kang and Peter Francis first met during placements working on surgical tools at the Hospital for Sick Children in the summer of 2015, while they were graduate students in engineering at the University of Toronto. (Another co-founder, Alex Gordon, left Revolve this summer to join another company.)

Mr. Kang said their goal was to create and commercialize a new surgical device that helped patients. “We wanted to make something that would have a real, truly positive impact on people,” he said.

They founded Revolve in 2019, and went through two startup programs shortly after: the Creative Destruction Lab at U of T in 2020 and the famed Y Combinator in Silicon Valley in 2021.

Since then, Revolve has held some early fundraising rounds and continued to iterate and improve the technology. Its surgical arm received investigational testing approval from Health Canada and premarket clearance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration last year.

The human testing at Unity Health Toronto is the team’s first pilot project. It began this year with a goal of using the device in three patients who needed their appendix removed and met certain eligibility criteria.

Dr. De Rezende-Neto, who has given advice to the Revolve team for years, says their device fills a gap in the market that few other technologies can fill in North America right now.

At the low end of the market are regular laparoscopic procedures that allow the surgeon to operate without needing to open larger holes in the patient, greatly improving recovery.

But Dr. De Rezende-Neto says that traditional laparoscopic tools have limited range of motion. The robot-assisted Revolve system can do much more, which opens up options for procedures that can be performed laparoscopically. “This, to me, is the main advantage of this robot,” he said.

At the high end of the market are remote-controlled robotic systems that can be operated from a console at a further distance. Revolve’s system is not as advanced as those options, but also not nearly as expensive. Mr. Kang said Revolve is hoping to price its system to be a fraction of the seven-figure cost of the more advanced robotics – such that a hospital could stock all their operating rooms with Revolve systems at the price of one advanced system.

The team is also building capacity into the Revolve system to eventually integrate AI, Mr. Kang said, with the hopes it will assist surgeons with precise movements.

Developing the technology has been slow in some ways because of the need to be careful and keep patients safe, he said.

But “truthfully, some of the harder challenges are working within systems that move maybe at a different pace than we’re used to,” he said.

Medical technology companies founded in Canada have long said it is hard to build a sustainable business selling to Canadian hospitals and health authorities because of limited budgets and risk aversion.

Mr. Kang said Revolve’s main market for selling devices will be U.S. health care providers.

“While we are so proud to be Canadian and love our health care system here, the truth is just that the American market is more primed for innovation and adopting newer technologies earlier,” he said.

Even so, the Revolve team has been making the devices in-house so far, and is in talks with local manufacturers to continue making them in Canada when they are ready to build at scale, Mr. Kang said. The team hopes to make its official commercial launch next year.

stories.title: Watch: Mayoral hopefuls square off in CTV News London debate
stories.summary: The gloves came off during a spirited mayoral debate hosted by CTV News London on the key issues facing the city ahead of the municipal election.
stories.content:
The gloves came off during a spirited mayoral debate hosted by CTV News London on the key issues facing the city ahead of the municipal election.

Incumbent Mayor Josh Morgan and challengers Susan Stevenson and Kirsten Krose squared off on a range of topics, including homelessness, property taxes, traffic congestion, public transit, downtown revitalization, climate change and public safety for women and girls.

Several exchanges grew tense as the candidates challenged each other’s positions during rebuttal periods.

The one-hour special aired commercial-free and unedited on CTV London on Monday, Oct. 12, in place of the 6 p.m. newscast.

stories.title: Canada 'stronger together' than apart, Carney says in Thanksgiving message ahead of Alberta visit
stories.summary: Mark Carney appealed for Canadian unity Monday as both the Prime Minister and the Conservative leader prepare to travel to Alberta this week
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre are set to travel this week to address some of the weightiest and most consequential issues facing the country.

Carney, who appealed directly in his Thanksgiving message Monday to Albertans, will visit the Western province this week ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum question on separation.

Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre, meanwhile, is also expected in Alberta this week, after first visiting Detroit on Tuesday to meet with business leaders and media outlets to push for the removal of cross-border tariffs and champion the Conservatives’ proposed tariff-free auto pact.

“Canada is facing real threats to our economy, to our security, to our way of life. We have to be strong, and we are stronger together,” Carney said in a short video message released on YouTube on Monday.

“A week from today Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future, whether to remain part of Canada or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada,” the prime minister said as he sat in a classroom at his old Edmonton high school, St. Francis Xavier High School.

Carney, who was born in Fort Smith, N.W.T., but raised in Alberta, said he’s “back home a lot these days” because his government is building “big things” in Alberta, including a new pipeline to the West Coast.

But Canada can’t build big things “on fault lines” while the country is already facing serious threats to its economy, security and way of life, he said.

“Generations of Albertans helped build this country. It’s yours, it’s ours and it’s worth fighting for.”

On Oct. 19, Albertans will be asked whether they wish to remain in Canada or begin a legal process to hold a binding referendum on leaving. More than 300 advance polls opened across the province on Tuesday.

The prime minister is scheduled to attend a rally hosted by the pro-Canada group, Forever Canadian, at the Edmonton Expo Centre on Friday.

That same day, Poilievre, who is also appealing to Albertans to vote to stay, is scheduled to speak in Calgary.

Poilievre, who seemed poised to lead the government before U.S. President Donald Trump’s belligerent threats to make Canada the 51st state, will visit Detroit Tuesday to pitch a proposed plan unveiled earlier this year that the party says would restore the nation’s auto production to two million cars per year over the next decade. Canada built 2.3 million vehicles in 2016. That fell by nearly half, to 1.2 million, last year.

Under the Conservatives’ proposed auto trade deal, “for every car produced in Canada, the same manufacturer would get to sell a car in Canada, duty-free, from a Cusma partner, ON a dollar-for-dollar basis,” similar to the old 1965 trade agreement.

It also calls for ending Liberal electric vehicle subsidies.

“My message to Americans is simple: these tariffs drive up costs and put jobs at risk in both our countries,” Poilievre said in a statement Monday.

“For decades, free trade has helped our workers build things together, sell to each other and bring home bigger paycheques,” the Conservative leader said.

“Let’s get tariffs out of the way so workers and businesses on both sides of the border can get ahead.”

According to the latest poll by Leger, backing for a united Canada is holding, and growing: 70 per cent of Alberta residents said the province should remain in Canada, up five points from 65 per cent in August.

In her Saturday call-in radio show, Premier Danielle Smith said outsiders like billionaire Elon Musk suggesting that the province should separate from Canada are out of touch.

Musk last week responded to a post from prediction market platform Polymarket on his social media platform X regarding the possibility of Quebec separating from Canada after it elected the sovereigntist Parti Quebecois to a minority government.

“They would be better off,” Musk wrote of Quebec leaving Canada, adding, “Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too.”

On her radio show, Smith responded to a text message suggesting she should heed Musk’s advice. “I don’t know that outsiders commenting on this have really been all that helpful with the debate,” she said.

“I hear more backlash when Americans weigh in on our debate here. I think this is for Albertans to decide. They’ll get a chance on Oct. 19.”

National Post, with a file from Matthew Black, Postmedia News

stories.title: ‘Breaking Bad’ actor, RJ Mitte, dead at 34: report
stories.summary: RJ Mitte, most known for his role as Walter White Jr. on the hit series "Breaking Bad" is dead according to multiple reports.
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
LOS Angeles (AP) — Actor and disability rights advocate RJ Mitte , who brought a lifetime of experience with cerebral palsy to fictional family struggles in an essential role on “Breaking Bad,” died Monday at age 34, authorities and his representatives said.

Cameron County Justice of the Peace Cyndi Hinojosa told The Associated Press she declared Mitte dead at about 1:30 p.m. at what she believed was his home in Brownsville, Texas. She said she was unable to provide a cause, but an autopsy will be performed.

Mitte played Walter White Jr., the son of Bryan Cranston’s chemistry teacher-turned-meth dealer Walter White on nearly every episode of the five seasons of the AMC show, which recently ranked as the best of the 21st century in a New York Times poll.

Diagnosed at age 3, Mitte told the AP in 2014 that his disability and the surrounding struggles with physical therapy, family problems and exorbitant medical bills – all key subjects on the show – made him better at his job.

“You develop a different mentality and you develop a different look at how the world sees you and how you see the world,” he said. “You’re able to use that. And I think it’s an asset instead of something that would hinder.”

Mitte was born and raised in Jackson, Mississippi.

He landed small guest roles on sitcoms after moving to Los Angeles to act in 2006. Like his character, he was in his mid-teens when he began his work on “Breaking Bad,” starting in 2007. The show ran from 2008 to 2013.

“Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion,” the actor’s representatives said in a statement announcing his death. The statement said he used “his platform to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation.”

His later credits included the ABC Family series “Switched at Birth” and the superhero satire series “Guardians of Justice.”

He was also a producer of several independent films.

As an advocate, he served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s. He was also president of his own Mitte Foundation supporting philanthropic and community initiatives around disabilities.

stories.title: Eby slams U.S.-style health care privatization, Conservatives claim 'fearmongering'
stories.summary: Eby signed what his party calls its "public health-care guarantee" which promises to protect the system from changes that would charge patients for necessary care, let people pay to jump the queue or pull staff from public health care.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby took aim at the premier next door while campaigning in this month’s election, promising not to implement what he called the “U.S.-style privatization” of health care.

Eby told a group of supporters asking him questions in Delta on Monday that Alberta’s United Conservative Party government made vague promises about protecting public health care, but are now creating a system where doctors can charge families money for medically necessary surgeries.

Eby says B.C. Conservatives are advocating for the same thing, but the Conservatives say they are committed “keeping B.C.‘s system universal and publicly funded” and accuse Eby of “tired health-care fearmongering.”

On a stage surrounded by supporters and backed by a large Canadian flag, Eby signed what his party calls its “public health-care guarantee” which promises to protect the system from changes that would charge patients for necessary care, let people pay to jump the queue or pull staff from public health care.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s UCP government passed a law late last year to allow doctors to work simultaneously in both the private and public tracks.

Critics have said the law has muddied the waters for the national health-care plan and moves Alberta closer to a U.S.-styled, two-tier health-care model.

“We’ve seen the Conservative playbook in action. They pretend health care is safe to get your vote. Then the moment they get into power, it’s carved up for profit,” Eby said in a statement. “The same thing would happen here under (interim leader Lorne) Doerkson and the B.C. Conservatives.

The Conservatives responded that Doerkson has already promised to protect health-care funding and noted that “British Columbians will never need anything more than their health card.”

They said Eby is trying to keep people from looking at his record which includes emergency rooms that are closing and more than one-million British Columbians who don’t have a family doctor.

“David Eby is increasingly desperate, so we fully expect him to resort to the Ndp’s usual fear campaign. He is running on fear because he cannot run on his record,” their statement said.

“A Conservative Party of BC government will keep emergency rooms open, recruit the doctors and nurses this province needs, and protect the public health care British Columbians rely on.”

Eby told the crowd that the Alberta model means doctors are pulled from the public system to work in the private system, calling in “anti-Canadian” to make people pay for things that used to be covered by the public health-care system.

Maddison McKee, press secretary for Alberta’s Ministry of Hospital and Surgical Health Services, issued a statement also accusing the B.C. NDP of “fearmongering.”

“The reality is that dual practice brings Alberta more in line with other top-performing health systems, including many European nations, who combine strong public funding with modern, flexible delivery models,” she said.

Smith’s government has repeatedly defended the move, saying the current status quo isn’t serving Albertans well and the government wants to create more options. The province has also said it thinks the model will attract more doctors to Alberta.

Smith has also said the move doesn’t violate the Canada Health Act and that she expects Ottawa to respect the province’s jurisdiction over health care.

Health care has become a central issue ahead of the Oct. 24th election, and the the BC NDP have suggested that promises by the Conservatives under Doerkson to cut taxes, while not providing details on how they will pay for those cuts, means health-care funding is at risk.

Eby’s New Democrats, meanwhile, are running on a promise to create a new tax bracket for people who make more than $1 million and increasing the top two existing brackets to pay for health-care costs.

The Conservatives say the NDP plan to raise taxes will drive doctors away.

The Conservative health-care platform includes a promise for a $50-million emergency fund to help prevent rural practices from closing and help recruitment.

Doerkson has also promised to establish an expert panel to look at publicly funded health-care systems around the world with an eye to reducing wait times and keeping emergency rooms and maternity wards open.

— With files from Fakiha Baig in Edmonton

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 12, 2026

stories.title: Canada signs joint statement denouncing Iran’s apparent plot to attack U.K. air base
stories.summary: More than two dozen countries say they ‘condemn in the strongest terms Iran’s use of violent attacks’
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Canada has joined more than two dozen other countries in denouncing Iran’s apparent involvement in a planned attack on an air base in England.

The countries said in a joint statement Monday they “condemn in the strongest terms Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners.”

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that a suspected terror plot at a U.S.-run military air base last month was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard.

“We recognize the United Kingdom’s attribution of Iran’s involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford on 27 September,” the statement says.

“The U.K. has also confirmed this event demonstrates the Irgc’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors.”

The statement also notes a “recent campaign of attacks across Europe targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists and U.S. interests, claimed by Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya,” a pro-Iran group.

The signatories include the United States, France, Germany and Australia, among others. They say any attempt by Iran to threaten individuals on their territory through proxies is unacceptable.

“Anyone who conducts hostile activities on behalf of Iran, or any other state, should know that we will take action to identify, investigate, disrupt and prosecute these acts,” the statement says.

Police have arrested seven men in the investigation into the alleged plot at RAF Fairford, but all suspects have been released on bail and no one has been charged so far.

The RAF Fairford air base has been used by American bombers to strike Iran in the ongoing war.

Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

stories.title: Alberta Chief Justice Ritu Khullar used her ‘superpowers’ to help others
stories.summary: Known for her intellectual rigour and compassionate leadership, she was unafraid of making decisions that went against public opinion
stories.author: Lisa Fitterman
stories.content:
One day, after watching The Incredibles , an animated Pixar film about a family of superheroes, Ritu Khullar told her son Samir Reynolds that everyone has a superpower and the trick is deciding what to do with it.

“You can choose to help others, or you can choose to help yourself,” she said.

For her, it was a simple choice. The daughter of immigrants to this country who always identified herself as a proud Canadian first and foremost, she spent her life advocating for others, as a wife and mother, as a lawyer who specialized in areas such as labour and human rights, and as Chief Justice of Alberta and the courts of Appeal of Alberta, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut.

Chief Justice Khullar, who was appointed to the Alberta Court of Queen’s Bench in March, 2017, promoted to the province’s Court of Appeal the following year and named Chief Justice in November, 2022, died on Sept. 3 after being diagnosed with cancer this year. She was 62 years old.

“She was the rare person who was able to make a massive impact on the lives of many,” her son said at the provincial memorial held for her at the Northern Alberta Jubilee Auditorium in Edmonton. “She always used her superpowers to help others.”

With a moral imperative, Chief Justice Khullar saw the Constitution as a living tree that was constantly growing and changing, and justice itself as the application of law to life.

As a lawyer, this led her to represent clients such as Linda McKay-Panos in a case against Air Canada that revolved around the rights of those who are disabled. Ms. McKay-Panos was morbidly obese and made to pay for a second seat on a flight because her weight was not considered a disability.

In 2008, the Supreme Court rejected an application for permission to appeal a Canadian Transportation Agency ruling that airlines must offer a “one person, one fare” policy to disabled people who require room for an attendant or a wheelchair, or take up more than one seat because of their disability, including some individuals whose obesity was determined to be disabling.

“Ritu was skeptical that disability could be understood in the abstract because it was about individuals,” said Paula Simons, a senator who knew Chief Justice Khullar through their children and interviewed her while a columnist at the Edmonton Journal. “She had a razor-sharp intellect grounded in common sense that helped guide her way.”

She was unafraid of making decisions that went against public opinion, such as one in which she and two colleagues ruled that two accused men’s Charter rights were violated when Canadian border officials searched their cellphones and laptop computers for no specific reason other than a suspicion that something was off; this, even though the officials found pornographic images of children.

In September of last year, she took the entire Alberta Appeal Court bench and northern judges to Nunavut, so they could participate in cultural activities, visit correctional institutions and speak with representatives from local community organizations about their experiences with the justice system. The idea was to sensitize judges to the ways of life and challenges faced by the people affected by the decisions made in courtrooms 2,400 kilometres due south.

In a statement, Alberta Justice Minister Mickey Amery lauded the intellectual rigour and compassionate leadership she brought to her role as Chief Justice. “She worked tirelessly to strengthen the justice system and to advance meaningful access to justice while preserving the independence and integrity of the courts.”

Peter Sankoff, a criminal defence lawyer in Edmonton and law professor at the University of Alberta, called Chief Justice Khullar one of the best listeners he has ever encountered.

“You could feel the sea change with her appointment. She brought a freshness to the court,” he said. “I always had a feeling of real confidence when she was appointed to a hearing. She was genuinely interested the issues, always having done her research beforehand. Whether … I won or lost, I always felt I had a fair hearing before her.”

Ritu Khullar was born on May 7, 1964, in Fort Vermilion, Alta., about 660 km north of Edmonton. She was the youngest of Jitendra and Pritam Khullar’s three daughters. Her father was Hindu and her mother, Sikh, both immigrants from India who arrived in the early 1960s to build a new life in a frigid climate.

Her parents were teachers, working first in a Mennonite community southeast of Fort Vermilion called La Crête, then in Jamaica and finally in Morinville, a suburb just north of Edmonton, and they instilled in young Ritu and her sisters the importance of curiosity, reading and recognizing that there was always more to learn. They also made sure their children understood the importance of community and contributing to the country that had given them a home.

Much of Ritu’s childhood was spent in Morinville, at the time a rural community with a large francophone population. While living there, she made friends who would last her lifetime and developed a love of places such as Jasper National Park, to which she would return again and again throughout her life.

In 1981, she graduated from Old Scona Academic, a public college-preparatory school in Edmonton’s Old Strathcona neighbourhood, then went on to do a bachelor’s in political science at the University of Alberta. Upon graduation, she worked in the province’s department of federal and intergovernmental relations, where she met Robert Reynolds, whom she refused to go out with until one of them quit to study or work somewhere else.

The couple had their first date when Mr. Reynolds decided in 1987 to go to law school. A little over a year later, when she was back in Edmonton for Thanksgiving after having moved east to study law at the University of Toronto, he proposed marriage.

“Ritu said she would consider it. Finally, in February, she got back to me and said ‘yes,’” Mr. Reynolds recalled. “I was admitted to the [Alberta] bar on a Thursday, and we got married two days later, ON the Saturday.”

After getting her law degree from U of T in 1991, she was admitted to the Alberta Bar in 1992 and practised in the fields of constitutional, labour and human-rights law while raising two sons, teaching as a sessional instructor at the University of Alberta’s law school and serving on the boards of the Alberta Law Reform Institute and the Centre for Constitutional Studies.

In 2014, she was named a Queen’s Counsel in recognition of her exemplary service to Canada’s justice system.

She was focused, with a ferocious work ethic and an ability to organize and compartmentalize. When she was with her family, they had her attention. Ditto with Bentley, the family’s labradoodle, whom she would walk every morning, no matter the weather.

Each Saturday, she had her walking club, and as the boys became more involved in sports such as hockey, she became an avid Edmonton Oilers fan.

In November, 2022, she ignored a call from then-federal-justice-minister David Lametti, who wanted to tell her she had been selected to become Alberta’s chief judge, because she was invested in watching Jeopardy on TV.

“Ritu was my soulmate,” Mr. Reynolds said. “When you have spent a lifetime together – we were married for 35 years – every day there is something that strikes home what a good person she was.

“She worked hard as a judge to do what she thought was right and I think she had a real gift for making people feel comfortable. She showed. She listened. She cared.”

Chief Justice Khullar leaves her husband and her sons, Samir and Nikhil Reynolds.

Chief Justice Khullar, who was appointed to the Alberta Court of Queen’s Bench in March, 2017, promoted to the province’s Court of Appeal the following year and named Chief Justice in November, 2022, died on Sept. 3 after being diagnosed with cancer this year. She was 62 years old.

“She was the rare person who was able to make a massive impact on the lives of many,” her son said at the provincial memorial held for her at the Northern Alberta Jubilee Auditorium in Edmonton. “She always used her superpowers to help others.”
With a moral imperative, Chief Justice Khullar saw the Constitution as a living tree that was constantly growing and changing, and justice itself as the application of law to life.

As a lawyer, this led her to represent clients such as Linda McKay-Panos in a case against Air Canada that revolved around the rights of those who are disabled. Ms. McKay-Panos was morbidly obese and made to pay for a second seat on a flight because her weight was not considered a disability.

In 2008, the Supreme Court rejected an application for permission to appeal a Canadian Transportation Agency ruling that airlines must offer a “one person, one fare” policy to disabled people who require room for an attendant or a wheelchair, or take up more than one seat because of their disability, including some individuals whose obesity was determined to be disabling.

“Ritu was skeptical that disability could be understood in the abstract because it was about individuals,” said Paula Simons, a senator who knew Chief Justice Khullar through their children and interviewed her while a columnist at the Edmonton Journal. “She had a razor-sharp intellect grounded in common sense that helped guide her way.”

She was unafraid of making decisions that went against public opinion, such as one in which she and two colleagues ruled that two accused men’s Charter rights were violated when Canadian border officials searched their cellphones and laptop computers for no specific reason other than a suspicion that something was off; this, even though the officials found pornographic images of children.

In September of last year, she took the entire Alberta Appeal Court bench and northern judges to Nunavut, so they could participate in cultural activities, visit correctional institutions and speak with representatives from local community organizations about their experiences with the justice system. The idea was to sensitize judges to the ways of life and challenges faced by the people affected by the decisions made in courtrooms 2,400 kilometres due south.

In a statement, Alberta Justice Minister Mickey Amery lauded the intellectual rigour and compassionate leadership she brought to her role as Chief Justice. “She worked tirelessly to strengthen the justice system and to advance meaningful access to justice while preserving the independence and integrity of the courts.”
Peter Sankoff, a criminal defence lawyer in Edmonton and law professor at the University of Alberta, called Chief Justice Khullar one of the best listeners he has ever encountered.

“You could feel the sea change with her appointment. She brought a freshness to the court,” he said. “I always had a feeling of real confidence when she was appointed to a hearing. She was genuinely interested the issues, always having done her research beforehand. Whether … I won or lost, I always felt I had a fair hearing before her.”

Ritu Khullar was born on May 7, 1964, in Fort Vermilion, Alta., about 660 km north of Edmonton. She was the youngest of Jitendra and Pritam Khullar’s three daughters. Her father was Hindu and her mother, Sikh, both immigrants from India who arrived in the early 1960s to build a new life in a frigid climate.

Her parents were teachers, working first in a Mennonite community southeast of Fort Vermilion called La Crête, then in Jamaica and finally in Morinville, a suburb just north of Edmonton, and they instilled in young Ritu and her sisters the importance of curiosity, reading and recognizing that there was always more to learn. They also made sure their children understood the importance of community and contributing to the country that had given them a home.

Much of Ritu’s childhood was spent in Morinville, at the time a rural community with a large francophone population. While living there, she made friends who would last her lifetime and developed a love of places such as Jasper National Park, to which she would return again and again throughout her life.

In 1981, she graduated from Old Scona Academic, a public college-preparatory school in Edmonton’s Old Strathcona neighbourhood, then went on to do a bachelor’s in political science at the University of Alberta. Upon graduation, she worked in the province’s department of federal and intergovernmental relations, where she met Robert Reynolds, whom she refused to go out with until one of them quit to study or work somewhere else.

The couple had their first date when Mr. Reynolds decided in 1987 to go to law school. A little over a year later, when she was back in Edmonton for Thanksgiving after having moved east to study law at the University of Toronto, he proposed marriage.

“Ritu said she would consider it. Finally, in February, she got back to me and said ‘yes,’” Mr. Reynolds recalled. “I was admitted to the [Alberta] bar on a Thursday, and we got married two days later, ON the Saturday.”

After getting her law degree from U of T in 1991, she was admitted to the Alberta Bar in 1992 and practised in the fields of constitutional, labour and human-rights law while raising two sons, teaching as a sessional instructor at the University of Alberta’s law school and serving on the boards of the Alberta Law Reform Institute and the Centre for Constitutional Studies.
In 2014, she was named a Queen’s Counsel in recognition of her exemplary service to Canada’s justice system.

She was focused, with a ferocious work ethic and an ability to organize and compartmentalize. When she was with her family, they had her attention. Ditto with Bentley, the family’s labradoodle, whom she would walk every morning, no matter the weather.
Each Saturday, she had her walking club, and as the boys became more involved in sports such as hockey, she became an avid Edmonton Oilers fan.

In November, 2022, she ignored a call from then-federal-justice-minister David Lametti, who wanted to tell her she had been selected to become Alberta’s chief judge, because she was invested in watching Jeopardy on TV.
“Ritu was my soulmate,” Mr. Reynolds said. “When you have spent a lifetime together – we were married for 35 years – every day there is something that strikes home what a good person she was.
“She worked hard as a judge to do what she thought was right and I think she had a real gift for making people feel comfortable. She showed. She listened. She cared.”
Chief Justice Khullar leaves her husband and her sons, Samir and Nikhil Reynolds.

stories.title: SIU invokes mandate after man died in OPP custody in Orillia
stories.summary: Orillia — Ontario’s police watchdog says it has launched an investigation after a 44-year-old man died in police custody in Orillia.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Orillia — Ontario’s police watchdog says it has launched an investigation after a 44-year-old man died in police custody in Orillia.

The Special Investigation Unit says Ontario Provincial Police officers responded to a disturbance Sunday shortly after 6:45 p.m.

The SIU says three man were arrested and taken to the OPP’s Orillia detachment and lodged into cells after being searched.

It says one of the men was found without vital signs during a routine check Monday at around 6:30 a.m.

The Special Investigation Unit says the man was pronounced dead after unsuccessful resuscitation efforts.

Three investigators and one forensic expert are assigned to examine the circumstances surrounding the death.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 12, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: As protests continue in their home country, Indians in Montreal gather in solidarity
stories.summary: Montreal - A dozen people rallied in downtown Montreal on Monday to express solidarity with protesters in India.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - A dozen people rallied in downtown Montreal on Monday to express solidarity with protests in India, where thousands of demonstrators who oppose contentious revisions to the country’s voter lists have been detained.

“It’s been very, very painful,” said Bhaskar, who was born in India and moved to Montreal in 2018. Bhaskar asked for his last name not to be published for fear of retaliation from the Indian government.

“There have been some very blatant violations of democratic principles. The government has been disenfranchising people, voters en masse,” he added.

The rally was organized by the South Asian Diaspora Action Collective and the Center for Study and Research in South Asia.

India’s Election Commission has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists in the last few months. With India’s population at close to 1.5 billion, according to UN data, this represents close to 10 per cent of the total population.

Opposition parties and protest groups have said the changes disproportionately erased voters who oppose the party in power. The Indian government has denied these claims.

Among the protesters in Montreal on Monday was Najmi, who used a pseudonym to protect her from reprisals. Born in India, she has lived in Montreal for over 20 years and now watches anxiously as her family faces the political upheaval of her home country.

Government workers have been going door to door, asking people for a list of documents to prove their citizenship, she said, adding that some of her family are waiting to see if they will keep their right to vote.

“People have been holding their breath and waiting for the list (of voters) to come out,” she said.

Najmi believes it’s part of an effort to push out Muslim and Christian people in favour of the Hindu majority.

A youth movement in India known as the Cockroach Janata Party has been leading protests against these changes.

NEW Delhi (AP) — Leaders of a popular Indian youth movement vowed to continue protests Sunday after being released from detention, a day after…

On Saturday, Indian police detained three movement leaders and thousands of protesters in New Delhi. Police released the three leaders on Sunday, and they vowed to continue protesting.

“It’s enraging what happened, and at the same time it’s beautiful how people are rising,” said Najmi.

The protests occur as Canada’s International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu visits India this week. The two countries are looking to reach a free-trade agreement by the end of the year.

Mark Carney made resetting relations with India a priority after he became prime minister in 2025. He visited Mumbai and New Delhi in March, the first visit by a Canadian prime minister in eight years.

Some protesters in Montreal on Sunday called on the Carney government to cut ties with India in response to the Indian government’s actions.

“There are many reasons for Canada to actually boycott India and have clear demands for human rights for people,” said Najmi.

Veena Gokhale, who left India 32 years ago, said she was worried by how little her Canadian friends knew about the tensions in her home country.

“It really makes me very concerned and very put off. Look at this,” she said, pointing at the handful of protesters at the rally. “This is a huge thing. … People don’t want to engage.”

— With files from Catherine Morrison and The Associated Press

stories.title: Stelco pushes back on Ottawa amid threats of legal action over layoffs
stories.summary: Stelco has reportedly pushed back on accusations it breached its agreement with the federal government, saying they are "false," and it "stands ready to protect its interests."
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Stelco has reportedly pushed back on accusations it breached its agreement with the federal government, saying they are “false,” and it “stands ready to protect its interests.”

This comes as Stelco begins laying off hundreds of workers , and faces threats of legal action from the federal government if those jobs are not preserved.

The Ontario-based steel manufacturer sent a letter responding to Industry Minister Melanie Joly after she sent a letter to Cleveland-Cliffs , the U.S.-based company which acquired Stelco in 2024. She also gave the company five days to respond.

Cleveland-Cliffs told Global News it sent a letter in response to Joly’s office on Oct. 9, although the response was not initially shared publicly.

Stelco’s letter to Joly, which was written by the company’s president and general counsel, Paul Simon, was shared with Global News Monday via a source who asked not to be named.

“Through our regular contact, the government has had significant advance notice of the impact these unprecedented market conditions have had on our business, and in more recent communications dating back to July 2026,” the letter said.

“Our early September meetings with several senior government officials, including representatives from your office, led Stelco to believe that the government understood the market realities confronting Stelco’s Hamilton Works finishing lines.”

Stelco, like Algoma and other Canadian steel manufacturers have been hit hard by U.S. tariffs of 50 per cent on Canadian steel imports , which led to a steep decline in sales to U.S. customers. The company said these market conditions have forced it to layoff up to 500 workers.

Joly responded on social media on Oct. 10 after reportedly receiving the letter from Stelco.

“The Government of Canada continues to expect Stelco to meet its legally binding commitments to employees. These commitments were agreed upon as undertakings under the Investment Canada Act and do not cease to apply because of changing business strategy or market conditions,” said Joly in the statement.

“As our legal team reviews the Stelco letter, all options are on the table.”

Canada gave U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs the go-ahead to purchase Stelco back in 2024 under the Investment Canada Act (ICA), which regulates foreign takeovers.

Speaking in the letter to Stelco last week, Joly said Canada’s approval of the deal was contingent on the new owner maintaining the number of union jobs and the majority of non-union positions.

Those conditions don’t expire just because “business strategy or market conditions have changed,” she added.

“This is particularly relevant here, where Cleveland-Cliffs has cited trade disruptions as affecting its operations at Hamilton Works, notwithstanding its chief executive officer’s public support for Section 232 tariff measures,” Joly said.

Stelco pushed back on Joly’s accusations in its letter, and said it “remains in compliance” with the undertakings in the agreement from 2024.

“Stelco submitted its annual report confirming its compliance with the employment undertakings in November 2025. That report highlighted that Stelco was facing significant challenges due to the unforeseen consequences stemming from unprecedented U.S. tariffs and Canada’s failure to advance an effective ‘Fortress North America’ trade regime,” the letter said.

“Your representation that Stelco’s planned layoffs cause it to breach its undertakings is false as the undertakings do not stipulate a commitment to avoid layoffs.”

When the layoffs were first announced last month, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the company “betrayed” Canadian workers and insisted “there’s money on the table” to keep employees on the job.

In an exclusive interview with Global News from Sept. 30, Lourenco Goncalves, the chairman and CEO of Cleveland-Cliffs, said the company’s decision was purely market-driven and that financial incentives could not fix the fundamental issues.

“I’m not shutting down, I’m not dismantling,” Goncalves said during a 10-minute phone call. “There’s no market in Canada for the amount of galvanized steel we produce in Canada. We need to export… to the United States.”

“Until we reestablish that, there’s nothing we can do, nothing.”

The union representing the roughly 500 steel workers facing potential layoffs, USW Local 1005, said it was not consulted nor did it have an opportunity to review those undertakings in the ICA.

“We were assured by both Cleveland Cliff’s and the Federal Government that bargaining unit employment levels would remain the same for 5 years. In other words no layoffs,” said the union’s president Ron Wells in a statement.

“Although we weren’t privileged to the signed agreement between Cliff’s and the Government, the response reeks of desperation as the original explanation of Stelco being victims of Trump’s steel tariffs wasn’t flying.”

Stelco, in the letter to Joly, denied wrongdoing, and based on the information presented to the federal government throughout the trade war, and the government’s own guidelines, the company said:

“In a situation such as this, Stelco should not be responsible for any non-compliance with its undertakings. Stelco stands ready to protect its interests consistent with the Investment Canada Act and its guidelines.”

Global News sent requests for comment to Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs, but neither responded by publication.

– With files from Global News’ Colin D’Mello and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada signs joint statement denouncing Iran after UK air base plot
stories.summary: Canada is joining more than two dozen other countries in denouncing Iran’s apparent involvement in a planned attack on an air base in England.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Canada is joining more than two dozen other countries in denouncing Iran’s apparent involvement in a planned attack on an air base in England.

The countries say in a joint statement they “condemn in the strongest terms Iran’s use of violent attacks.”

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that a suspected terror plot at a U.S.-run military air base last month was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard.

The RAF Fairford air base has been used by American bombers to strike Iran in the ongoing war.

The countries that signed the joint statement say any attempt by Iran to threaten individuals on their territory through proxies is unacceptable.

The signatories include the United States, France, Germany and Australia, among others.
