stories.title: “We’re laughing every single night’: Senior theatre company prepares for the Matchmaker at the Grand Theatre
stories.summary: Silver Spotlight Theatre Inc. (Ssti) is rehearsing for its first production as its own charitable non-profit.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Silver Spotlight Theatre Inc. (Ssti) is rehearsing for its first production as its own charitable non-profit. The group of senior actors is rehearing three times per week in preparation for a five-day run of The Matchmaker production later this month.

“If you know the story for Hello Dolly!, the Matchmaker is what it’s based on,” said Rick Smith, director of the Matchmaker for Ssti. “Dolly Levi is hired by Horace van der Gelder to find himself a new wife. Little does he know, her plan is to marry him herself.

Along the way, she’s brought in other members of his of his crew and people he knows to mess things up a little bit so that she has a better chance of winning the prize at the end.” In 2025 Ssti separated from the umbrella of Musical Theatre Productions which got them started in 2023.

After doing musicals including Babes in Arms, Grease, Into the Woods and Showtune this will be the first non-musical production. “I’ve wanted to work with this group for quite some time,” said Sam Sabathy, who plays Dolly and is doing her first Ssti production.

“I’ve seen all their shows and when I found out that they were doing a play, that’s their inaugural production for Ssti, I thought, I’ve got to audition and Rick picked me, so here we are.” Sabathy has a degree in drama from Western University and studied in New York.

She moved back to Canada and got into local theatre around Southwestern Ontario. Over the past four years, the senior actors have not only made great shows but great friends. “We have people that we’ve known through every production, but then also we meet new people,” said Mitchell Zimmer, who plays Rudolph in the play.

“We meet behind the scenes at restaurants, breakfasts, get togethers. It’s become bigger than just theatre, it’s family.” Sabathy describes the cast and crew as having an “absolute blast”. “We’re laughing every single night, and it’s just so much fun and encourage everyone to try and do it,” she said.

For this production, half of the cast is new to Ssti and others have experience with the company. “You can see the development over the past five productions,” said Smith. “They continue getting that support from our other experienced cast members.

So, it really is that community and they’re all supportive of each other as we’ve gone through the process.” The five-day run on the Auburn Stage at the Grand Theatre takes place Oct. 28-Nov. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home raided by U.S. Homeland Security agents
stories.summary: Ilhan Omar accused the administration of targeting political opponents following a raid of her home just three weeks before the midterms.
stories.author: AFP
stories.content:
U.S. federal agents searched the Washington home of Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar on Monday as part of a criminal investigation, officials said, marking a dramatic escalation in President Donald Trump’s confrontation with the outspoken lawmaker.

Omar said she was “ok” following the operation but accused the administration of targeting political opponents just three weeks before she seeks re-election in the November 3 midterms.

The early morning search was conducted by agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of U.S. immigration enforcement.

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar wrote on X.

“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”

The operation also sparked a furious backlash from Democrats who accused Trump of abusing government powers to pursue his political opponents.

Fox News reported that the search was linked to a criminal fraud investigation concerning immigration paperwork submitted on behalf of the Somali-born congresswoman by her late father when she was a child.

Trump’s border enforcement chief Tom Homan told Fox News he was unwilling to give details ahead of any official announcement but confirmed that an “investigation was ongoing for a while” and that “there was a warrant executed this morning.”

U.S. media quoted the Justice Department confirming that agents had carried out a court-authorized search in the Washington area, but officials did not identify Omar or disclose the nature of the investigation.

Omar, 44, is a leftist Democrat and fierce critic of Trump, particularly his administration’s sweeping crackdown on immigration.

The Republican president has repeatedly clashed with Omar, who came to the United States from Somalia as a child and has frequently been the target of his political attacks.

Political backlash

Top House Democrat Hakeem Jeffries and his leadership team called the raid “deeply disturbing” and raised questions about “the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries.”

Minnesota’s Democratic Governor Tim Walz accused Trump of “abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election.”

Republican congresswoman Nancy Mace, meanwhile, said Omar should be stripped of her U.S. citizenship and deported if fraud was proven.

“NO ONE is above the law,” she wrote on X.

The timing also drew criticism from Xochitl Hinojosa, a former director of public affairs at the Justice Department.

“There’s a longstanding rule at DOJ that you don’t take overt actions like this before an election, especially when there’s a candidate on the ballot,” she wrote on X.

Omar said in September that Homeland Security officials had not contacted her about any investigation, dismissing the allegations against her as politically motivated attacks.

Omar was first elected to Congress in 2018 and represents a district including Minneapolis, home to one of the largest Somali communities in the United States.

She is a member of the group of left-wing Democratic lawmakers known as “The Squad,” who have been among Trump’s most vocal opponents in Congress.

No charges against Omar were announced in connection with Monday’s search.

stories.title: I sell an unusual crop at the local farmers’ market: a historical thriller
stories.summary: While some people sell fruit and veggies, I’m renting a stall to hawk my book – and building community along the way
stories.author: Doug Ronson
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

As I sat at my market stall, I pondered how in the exact same spot in the early 1800s, you could purchase venison from a local hunter, fresh fish from Lake Ontario and hay to feed your livestock.

I didn’t have any of those items on sale at Kingston Public Market – or anything remotely similar. I was there to promote my new novel.

“Selling books at a farmers’ market? What a ridiculous idea,” scoffed one friend.

Turns out he was wrong. Very wrong.

Kingston’s market has a rich history. Established in 1801, it is the oldest in Ontario, serving the community continuously for more than two centuries. When it started, butchers and farmers operated from poorly constructed wooden stalls, so ramshackle that the area was called “the market shambles.” On July 1, 1867, Canadian Confederation was proclaimed in the market square. It has always been a gathering point for people to socialize and catch up on the latest news and gossip.

Of course, the vendors have changed. There are still farmers who get out of bed at 4 a.m. to load their trucks and get to the market in the early morning hours. Current sellers include a Canadian newcomer barbecuing Syrian-style corn and other delights. There are organic farmers and artists selling photographs.

Early on Saturday mornings, I arrive at my spot overlooking the British Whig building, where I had once happily toiled as a reporter and editor. Just like the market, it’s changed. The Whig-Standard’s handful of remaining employees all work from home and the paper that once proudly proclaimed to be Canada’s oldest daily now appears just four times a week. The British Whig building currently serves as an office for city employees.

At the market, I was given a hearty welcome by people at the adjacent stalls. One was an expert on growing succulent plants and was happy to share her knowledge with curious marketgoers. Another had beautiful handcrafted glass on display. She promised to buy The Admiral’s Daughter – as soon as she made enough sales to pay for my book. Sure enough, within an hour she was back at my stall to obtain a copy.

Market vendors embrace the spirit of co-operation, not competition. If a customer is looking for zucchini, everyone knows how to guide them. The spouses of some vendors hang around for the entire day, ready to watch the stand during the inevitable washroom breaks. At lunch, my neighbour complimented my use of chopsticks as I struggled to eat my Thai noodle lunch – I had forgotten to ask the takeout joint for a fork.

On this particular day, tourists and locals were flocking through the aisles. When they stopped to talk with me, people were fascinated by the fact that the book was based on the true story of my father moving from Canada to Washington to take a position with the British embassy in 1941. He handled top secret cables as Winston Churchill desperately begged the United States to join the war against Hitler.

At the market, I had the chance to chat with visitors from across Canada, the U.S. and Europe. They told me their own stories of family members’ experiences in the war – one woman’s father served in Europe in an artillery unit from Newfoundland. People liked the fact that the book is partly set in Kingston, with the hockey-playing protagonist skating on Lake Ontario.

As it turns out, bookselling is not new at this market. In the 19th century, books were mostly published by local newspapers who wanted to keep their presses running after the papers were on the streets. The Kingston Gazette set up stalls adjacent to the market to hawk their books.

I’m simply following in the lead of another local author who has been offering his Viking-era novels for several years here. When I recently published my historical thriller, he kindly suggested that I rent a stall. It proved to be a fabulous idea.

Holding court at my stall during the summer and fall, I’m proud to be part of this tradition.

Doug Ronson lives in Kingston.

stories.title: Violent incidents caught on camera during anti-Israel protests in Toronto and Montreal
stories.summary: Police in Toronto are looking for a male suspect who allegedly attacked another man from behind unprovoked during an anti-Israel protest.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
Two people suffered apparent injuries after altercations with anti-Israel demonstrators in Toronto and Montreal on Saturday.

Police said the victim “was engaged in conversation with another demonstrator” and was headed north on Yonge Street near the intersection of Grosvenor Street when “the suspect approached the victim from behind and punched the victim several times in the head without provocation, causing the victim to fall to the ground.”

They suffered facial and leg injuries, according to police.

The suspect is described as five-foot-five with a thin build and black hair. At the time of the alleged attack, police said he wore prescription lenses, a grey jacket, dark grey sweatpants and a black Under Armour backpack.

It starts with Hancock panning over the marching protest and then panning forward to see a white, middle-aged man in sunglasses and a black leather jacket saying to a demonstrator, “Do something about it, c— sucker.”

The man behind him, matching the police’s description, immediately sucker-punches him from behind and then drags him to the ground and punches him five more times in quick succession. Demonstrators on both sides quickly gather around and attempt to pry the victim free from the suspect, who keeps trying to land more blows before they’re pulled apart.

As the man claims his knee is broken, the suspect briefly disappears before returning and appearing to throw something at the man, opening a wound above his eyebrow.

“Mitch, get me out of here,” he says from the ground. “Where are the guys?”

Some people can be seen and heard mocking him as he waits for help, including one wearing a sweater with an inverted red triangle, a symbol popularized by Hamas terrorists.

The edited clip begins with two older women already on the ground, one of whom kicks towards a younger brown-haired woman standing over her, who responds with a kick of her own. A Montreal police vehicle pulls up to block the scene, an officer quickly hops out to intervene and the camera follows to show one of the women leaning over the other.

As it continues, police are seen detaining and speaking to the younger woman, before cutting to one of the older women appearing to cry while her friend checks on her. By the video’s end, the apparent victim is on her feet and demonstrating again.

National Post has contacted Montreal police for more information.

stories.title: Carney makes case for united Canada ahead of Alberta separation vote
stories.summary: In video tied to the Thanksgiving holiday, Prime Minister says Canada can’t build big things if it is divided
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is making the case for a united Canada as Albertans prepare to vote in a referendum on the province’s place in Confederation.

In a video posted online on Monday, Mr. Carney said Albertans helped build Canada, and he raised concerns about uncertainty linked to the sovereignty vote.

“A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future – whether to remain part of Canada or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada,” Mr. Carney said in a Thanksgiving message.

Mr. Carney filmed the video in a classroom at St. Francis Xavier High School in Edmonton, which he attended as a student.

Mr. Carney talked about his government’s record in the province, citing federal support for building new homes, high-speed rail and a new pipeline to the West Coast .

But he said Canada can’t build big things if it is divided, and that the country is facing threats to its economy, security and way of life.

“We are stronger together. Generations of Albertans helped build this country. It’s yours. It’s ours. And it’s worth fighting for.”

Advance voting opens Tuesday in the referendum, with a vote to follow on Oct. 19 on 10 questions that include whether the province should stay in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

Mr. Carney will be in Alberta this week to make the case for remaining in Canada. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and other leaders are also scheduled to speak in the province.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith launched the referendum process, saying it was necessary to allow Albertans to resolve the question of the province’s place in Canada.

Ms. Smith has said she supports Alberta remaining a part of Canada.

On Sunday, Ms. Smith’s press secretary, Sam Blackett, said Alberta’s government will continue its advertising campaign urging Albertans to vote in support of a strong and sovereign Alberta in a united Canada.

“The Premier has been clear that our government, caucus, and party support Alberta remaining in Canada, and we will continue to work to get a strong mandate from Albertans for more sustainable immigration policies and to pursue constitutional reforms that increase our province’s sovereignty within Canada,” Mr. Blackett said.

stories.title: Prime minister’s Thanksgiving message addresses Alberta separation referendum
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is "worth fighting for," a week ahead of Alberta’s separation referendum.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney focused his Thanksgiving Day message on Alberta’s upcoming separation referendum, saying Canada is “worth fighting for.”

“This year, Thanksgiving is a bit different,” he said in the video message. “A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future: whether to remain part of Canada or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada.”

Albertans will vote on Oct. 19 on whether the province should stay in Canada or hold a second, binding separation referendum.

In the video posted Monday and filmed in his old high school in Edmonton, Carney noted he grew up in Alberta.

Carney said the federal government is building “big things” in Alberta, including a new pipeline to the West Coast, but that Canada can’t achieve those goals if the country is divided.

“ You can’t build big things on fault lines,” he said.

Carney also said the country must be strong as it faces threats to its economy, security and culture, and that we are “stronger together.”

“Generations of Albertans helped build this country. It’s yours, it’s ours, and it’s worth fighting for,” he said.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is scheduled to speak in Calgary on Friday, urging the province to stay within Canada.

In his own Thanksgiving message, BC NDP Leader David Eby, who is in the middle of a provincial election campaign, encouraged Albertans to vote for unity with Canada. He said the two provinces have bonds of family, friendship and business and are “stronger together.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 12, 2026.

— With files from Lisa Johnson

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Plane bound for Amsterdam lands safely in St. John's, N.L. after engine issues
stories.summary: ST. John's - An international flight bound for the Netherlands was diverted to Newfoundland early Monday morning.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
United Airlines says flight UA 946 from Washington, D.C. to Amsterdam was diverted to St. John’s International airport to address an engine issue.

It says the plane landed safely and passengers exited the aircraft normally.

There were 122 passengers and nine crew members aboard the Boeing 767.

The airline says it arranged overnight hotel accommodation for the passengers, and it is sending a different aircraft to take them to Amsterdam.

stories.title: 1 dead in collision between motorcycle and SUV in Ottawa
stories.summary: Ottawa police say a 21-year-old man who was riding the motorcycle died in the crash. The female driver of the SUV sustained minor injuries and was transported to hospital.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
One person is dead after a weekend collision between a motorcycle and an SUV in Ottawa’s east end.

Ottawa police say a 21-year-old man who was riding the motorcycle died in the crash.

Officers responded to the collision on Trim Road, south of Watters Road, around 9:30 p.m. Saturday.

The female driver of the SUV sustained minor injuries and was transported to hospital.

Police are asking anyone who witnessed the collision or who May have dashcam or video footage to come forward.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the Ottawa Police Service Fatal Collision Investigation Unit.

stories.title: Toronto voters want action on affordability, housing ahead of municipal election
stories.summary: Toronto - As Toronto's leading mayoral candidates criss-cross the city, pitching their vision ahead of this month's municipal elections, voters say affordability, housing, public safety and transit are the top issues they want to see addressed.
stories.author: Sharif Hassan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - As Toronto’s leading mayoral candidates criss-cross the city, pitching their vision ahead of this month’s municipal elections, voters say affordability, housing, public safety and transit are the top issues they want to see addressed.

More than 50 people are vying to lead Canada’s largest city for the next four years, but polls suggest it will be a tight race between incumbent Olivia Chow and councillor Brad Bradford in the Oct. 26 vote.

Chow’s key promises include measures to help lower grocery prices in the city, free lunches in schools and building more affordable housing units, while Bradford has pledged to freeze property tax rates in his first year as mayor and scrap the land transfer tax for homes under $1.1 million.

Ilham Saydna, who has lived in Toronto for 30 years, said many in the city are struggling financially and she will vote for anyone whose top priority is to make life more affordable.

“I am looking to see who is going to be having a good platform for food security because a lot of people are hungry right now, and people are going to food banks and they cannot afford to pay rent,” the North York resident said.

Saydna, who is a tenant, also said the city needs to do more to support renters, including redefining what affordable housing means.

While some voters have expressed public safety concerns, Saydna said she feels safe in the city because the crime rate is trending downward. Toronto police data show homicides, shootings and robberies have decreased this year.

Saydna believes homelessness is a far greater issue.

“If we tackle poverty and people’s needs, crime will go down,” she said. “If people are not properly housed and they live on the streets, you can’t blame them for trying to survive.”

Terry Chamberlain, who lives in the Don Mills area, said the city should do more to encourage building new housing.

“As long as the development is done in a reasonable manner and it fits into the area, I’m all for it,” he said.

Chamberlain said his neighbourhood is in need of a community centre and more facilities for children.

He said while public transit in the area is “quite good” and reliable, the city should lobby the province to extend the 15.6-kilometre Ontario Line subway currently under construction beyond Eglinton Avenue.

Ross Rowlands, who lives in the Beaches, said he will vote for a candidate who stands up to Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whom he criticized for his controversial decisions to ban municipal speed cameras and remove some bike lanes on stretches of major city roads.

“It’s terrible,” Rowlands, who cycles regularly, said of the planned bike lane removals. “It’s unsafe, and despite all the empirical studies that have been done showing that it makes roads safer.”

While Chow has strongly opposed the Ford government’s speed camera and bike lane removals, she and the premier have worked closely on many issues and Ford has described their relationship as “phenomenal.”

Rowlands also said he wants the next mayor to invest in preventive measures when it comes to crime and mental health, rather than spend money on what he called reactionary policing.

The homelessness crisis is another key issue in municipal elections across the province, but Toronto’s 10-year plan to open more shelters, including some outside the downtown core, has received mixed reactions, with some living in communities hosting them raising safety concerns.

One was built two years ago near Patty Wegrzyn’s home in Scarborough, and she isn’t happy about it.

“Everybody has a right to have a home,” she said. “But do not put homeless shelters where there are small children and families.”

Chow has said that her approach to reducing homelessness has been working, while Bradford said that his strategy would include more supportive and transitional housing.

Wegrzyn, who said she sold her home because she could no longer afford property tax increases, added that she will vote for any candidate who is more sympathetic to Toronto’s ratepayers.

“We’re all still coming out of the pandemic, half (of) these families … are struggling themselves trying to keep everything afloat, why raise taxes?” she asked.

Peter Formica, a Scarborough resident who lives in senior co-operative housing, said the city could sell the underused high-value properties it owns to address the issue of affordable housing for seniors. The city could also increase the supply of affordable housing by freeing up larger, underused units, he suggested.

Chow and Bradford have faced off in several debates so far, including one focused on issues in Scarborough, a district of more than 600,000 people often described as a “transit desert.”

The Toronto Transit Commission recently opened a four-kilometre Scarborough Busway connecting Kennedy Station and Scarborough Town Centre, replacing Line 3 train service that was shut down after a derailment more than three years ago.

The city hailed the bus-only roadway as a major achievement because it opened six months ahead of schedule. But for many Scarborough residents, that’s too little, too late.

Leonel Juan said he can’t wrap his head around why a subway line has been extended as far as Vaughan in the north, but Scarborough has not yet been fully integrated in Toronto’s transit system, nearly three decades after amalgamation.

The long-awaited Scarborough subway extension line is still years away from opening.

The Scarborough East Rapid Transit, an 18.6-kilometre light-rail transit, which connects Kennedy to Malvern Town Centre via the University of Toronto’s Scarborough campus, is still in the design phase nearly two decades after it was first proposed.

Formerly known as the Eglinton East LRT, the project has been marred by significant delays due to lack of funding and political disagreements, and Juan said the next mayor should expedite the work on it.

The city needs to address Scarborough’s housing shortage by allowing more development in the district’s waterfront areas, Juan said.

“Downtown Toronto or other areas of Toronto are being prioritized more so,” he said. “I think a lot of focus should also be placed on Scarborough.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 12, 2026.

stories.title: London’s Thanksgiving Monday forecast: warm start with drizzle, turning wet mid-week
stories.summary: Londoners can expect a mild, but cloudy Thanksgiving Monday.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
Londoners can expect a mild, but cloudy Thanksgiving Monday.

Environment Canada says the week ahead is looking unsettled, bringing a mix of showers, a risk of thunderstorms on Tuesday, and gradually cooler temperatures as the week progresses.

Thanksgiving Monday begins mainly cloudy with morning fog patches and a 40 per cent chance of drizzle. Winds will become southwest 20 km/h, gusting to 40 km/h near noon. The high will be 24C (Humidex 29, UV 5 Moderate). Monday night, conditions clear to partly cloudy with southwest winds at 20 km/h and a low of 18C.

Here’s the forecast for the rest of the week:

Tuesday: Expect mainly cloudy skies with a 40 per cent chance of showers and a risk of thunderstorms. Winds will be strong from the southwest at 30 km/h, gusting to 50 km/h. The high will be 25C (Humidex 30, UV 6 High). Tuesday night brings cloudy periods with a 30 percent chance of showers and a low of 14C.

stories.content:

Officers say a BMW sedan that traveled eastbound on Lawrence Avenue East collided with a westbound Ford Escape turning left into a driveway

stories.title: Raise the Roar; Lions fans gather for watch party in London, Ont. as Detroit blows out Arizona
stories.summary: In what has been a roller coaster season so far for Detroit Lions fans, they couldn’t have picked a better game to have a watch party with a few hundred supporters.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
In what has been a roller coaster season so far for Detroit Lions fans, they couldn’t have picked a better game to have a watch party with a few hundred supporters.

Members of the ‘One Pride’ community packed the Canadian Brewhouse in north London, Ont. for the third annual stop on the Detroit Lions’ Raise the Roar Canadian Bar tour.

“As a Lions fan I love this,” said Aaron Bayer from London.

“Pulling up and seeing all the blue and white all that Honolulu Blue, it’s as close to being at a tailgate in Detroit as we get here right now.”

The past two years, the party was held on Dundas Place and the watch party inside Canada Life Place. This time, the Lions switched to a bar tour.

“I’m from Windsor, and me and my dad were season ticket holders back home, so it is awesome to see stuff like this,” said Lions fan Ryan Walker.

“It still seems like a decent enough crowd here. Obviously when it was downtown they had a bigger venue, different experience and they were able to put more stuff on. But I mean, I think they’ve done a good job here with what they’ve had.”

Outside in the parking lot, they had games and photo opportunities with a giant helmet and signs. Inside they had a DJ, the Lions cheerleaders, more games and a photo booth.

After an up and down 2-2 start to the year, this date couldn’t have been better to watch a game. Detroit blew out Arizona 45-17.

The Lions were granted marketing rights in Canada in April 2024 and hosted its first Canadian watch party later that year. There are two more area stops to come in Kitchener on Nov. 15 for the US Thanksgiving game, and in Windsor on Nov. 26.

“It’s nice seeing that Canada is getting stuff like this now,” added Walker.

“It’s nice that they finally saw that there’s a lot of fans in Ontario and to put something like this together is awesome, especially for the city.”

stories.title: Trump’s diesel deal with Putin in ‘direct opposition’ to Ukraine’s efforts, Carney’s office says
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy Sunday about U.S. President Donald Trump’s new diesel fuel supply agreement with Russia.
stories.author: Devika Desai, Daniel Otis
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy Sunday about U.S. President Donald Trump’s new diesel fuel supply agreement with Russia.

The Prime Minister’s Office says the two leaders discussed the new agreement for Russia to supply millions of tonnes of diesel fuel to the United States, which Trump announced on Friday.

“The Prime Minister was clear: this agreement is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe,” a readout from the PMO explained. “It will provide additional revenue for Russia and help finance its illegal, unjustifiable war against Ukraine.”

The two leaders also talked about increasing coordination with allies to help Ukraine with its air defence needs.

Trump posted on his Truth Social platform on Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an “energy ceasefire,” which appeared to be news to Zelenskyy.

Zelenskyy said on social media that he would support a ceasefire but is awaiting details from the White House.

He also said Russia must back it up by ending its strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, which reportedly continued after Trump’s Truth Social Post.

“We support it, but I have not heard approval of this proposal from the Russian side,” Zelenskyy said from the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland on Monday. “This energy ceasefire can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war.”

Russia has repeatedly targeted energy infrastructure in order to deny Ukrainians power and heat, especially in colder months. Ukraine has retaliated with strikes against Russian energy sites like oil refineries. Ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November, Trump has publicly blamed Ukraine for rising diesel prices, although experts say they are largely being pushed upwards by the effects of the Iran War.

Our offer is honest and clear – we are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same – we agree if they agree. And we have already shown that we mean it. Last night, Russian oil refineries were not burning. But at midnight, a Russian jet-powered “shahed”… pic.twitter.com/Oxta11C1wy — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 12, 2026

“For Russia, of course, gasoline shortages and burning oil refineries – because of our strikes in response – are painful,” Zelenskyy said. “But if Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure. This is only fair.”

The prime minister also spoke with Trump on the energy ceasefire between Ukraine Russia on Sunday.

A readout from his office states that Carney thanked Trump for his efforts securing the ceasefire and reiterated Canada’s support for the agreement.

He also reiterated Zelenskyy’s call for Russia to uphold it.

With files from The Canadian Press and The Associated Press

stories.title: Alberta referendum campaigns enter homestretch with speeches and rallies
stories.summary: Advance voting stations open Tuesday and Oct. 19 is the official polling day
stories.author: Lisa Johnson
stories.content:
The referendum campaigns on Alberta’s place in Confederation have entered the homestretch, with politicians set to speak and groups ready to rally.

Advance voting stations open Tuesday.

Less than a week later, ON Monday, Oct. 19, it’s the official polling day. Albertans are answering 10 questions, including whether the province should stay in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

It promises to be a busy week.

Former Alberta United Conservative premier Jason Kenney and one-time NDP rival and fellow premier Rachel Notley will speak for a united Canada at an event in Edmonton on Tuesday.

On Friday, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith will speak in Calgary. Both are urging Alberta stay in the Canadian fold.

The federalist Forever Canadian group will gather supporters in Calgary Thursday and Edmonton Friday.

On the weekend, duelling rallies are scheduled in Edmonton at the legislature grounds. The pro-separation group Let Alberta Decide has announced an event on Saturday and the Alberta Federation of Labour is sponsoring a unity rally on Sunday.

On the ground, MP Dane Lloyd has been leading the federal Conservative party’s pro-Canada drive with door knocking and public events. Lloyd said turnout will be key. “There is no substitute for direct engagement,” he said in a statement.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Liberal cabinet ministers have not announced plans but have been in Alberta numerous times in recent months to, among other things, announce a fast-track plan for a new Alberta oil pipeline and remind Albertans of billions of dollars in ongoing military spending.

Carney made a pitch for Canada in a Thanksgiving video on Monday, noting the holiday was a day to slow down and reflect, and a chance for Albertans to give thanks to Canada for the rights, freedoms and opportunities it offers.

The Alberta Opposition NDP says it has been going all out, with more than 15,000 volunteers, door knocking and phoning to keep Albertans in Confederation.

NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said they are stepping into a void left by Smith and her UCP colleagues.

Nenshi has lambasted Smith for not following through on her promise to actively campaign for a united Canada. Last week, Nenshi noted that not only are Smith’s cabinet members not getting out the vote, many have left on foreign trips during the critical lead-up to the vote.

“They should bloody be knocking on doors. They should be getting out the vote,” Nenshi said. “They’re behaving like separatists.”

Smith rejects the criticism, saying she has made her pro-Canada sentiments clear in speeches and at coffee parties. Her government has put $4-million into an advertising campaign encouraging people to vote for “a strong and sovereign Alberta within a united Canada.”

“I go into some pretty tough rooms, and I talk to a lot of people who are voting for [the separatist option],” Smith said last week on the Ryan Jespersen podcast. “I make my case about why it is that I think Canada can work – is [in fact] working better than ever.”

The separation question is the last of the 10 issues Albertans are being asked to mark an X on. The first nine focus on immigration and the Constitution. Smith has said she hopes Albertans vote yes to first nine to give her some leverage to negotiate with the federal government.

The immigration questions ask Albertans whether the province should have more say on who comes here to work and whether it’s time to put more limitations – and perhaps introduce fees – on some who arrive and seek access to health care and education.

The constitutional questions ask Albertans for a blessing to pursue talks with other provinces on wresting power from the federal government and abolishing the Senate.

Smith’s UCP never campaigned on holding a separation vote in the last election in 2023. However, Smith says some Albertans’ anger and disillusionment with the country spread during the term of former Liberal prime minister Justin Trudeau to the point that hundreds of thousands have signed petitions for and against Confederation. A referendum, she has said, is now necessary to resolve the matter once and for all.

She has taken heat from both sides. Some separatists have derided her pro-separation question as a weak-kneed plan to make a plan. Some critics on the pro-Canada side say Smith is both arsonist and firefighter – rolling the dice on the future of the country while framing herself as its champion.

Polls before Smith announced the referendum and after have suggested Albertans are consistently in favour of staying in the Confederation fold. To that end, critics, including Nenshi, say the referendum was never about Canada but merely about Smith placating separatist hardliners in her party to keep them from fracturing the movement or rising up against her.

Recent events suggest Smith and her party are taking a hit for calling the referendum in the first place. Polls show Smith’s UCP bleeding support to the benefit of the NDP with the next election scheduled for a year from now. Last month, Smith’s party lost a Calgary by-election to the NDP in what had been a longtime UCP stronghold.

Smith has also been forced into pretzel-style arguments when pushed on why her caucus and party are formally pro-Canada yet allow at least one pro-separatist legislature member to remain in their ranks. Smith has said the party can still be officially pro-Canada while allowing for a diversity of opinion.

On referendum night, Elections Alberta officials say the separation question will be counted first. The result should be known sometime early the following morning. Smith has said a simple majority one way or the other will carry the day.

The other nine questions, however, have spawned more questions, such as what exactly the new immigration rules would look like and whom they would apply to.

Smith’s government has said that will be decided later this fall by her government should it get a mandate on those questions. And what does a mandate on those questions look like? Smith was asked by reporters last week.

“We’ll look at the voter turnout, and we’ll look at the result, and we will be able to give you some clear direction on Oct. 20th,” she replied.

Nenshi has lambasted Smith for not following through on her promise to actively campaign for a united Canada. Last week, Nenshi noted that not only are Smith’s cabinet members not getting out the vote, many have left on foreign trips during the critical lead-up to the vote.
“They should bloody be knocking on doors. They should be getting out the vote,” Nenshi said. “They’re behaving like separatists.”

Smith rejects the criticism, saying she has made her pro-Canada sentiments clear in speeches and at coffee parties. Her government has put $4-million into an advertising campaign encouraging people to vote for “a strong and sovereign Alberta within a united Canada.”

“I go into some pretty tough rooms, and I talk to a lot of people who are voting for [the separatist option],” Smith said last week on the Ryan Jespersen podcast. “I make my case about why it is that I think Canada can work – is [in fact] working better than ever.”

The separation question is the last of the 10 issues Albertans are being asked to mark an X on. The first nine focus on immigration and the Constitution. Smith has said she hopes Albertans vote yes to first nine to give her some leverage to negotiate with the federal government.

The immigration questions ask Albertans whether the province should have more say on who comes here to work and whether it’s time to put more limitations – and perhaps introduce fees – on some who arrive and seek access to health care and education.
The constitutional questions ask Albertans for a blessing to pursue talks with other provinces on wresting power from the federal government and abolishing the Senate.

Smith’s UCP never campaigned on holding a separation vote in the last election in 2023. However, Smith says some Albertans’ anger and disillusionment with the country spread during the term of former Liberal prime minister Justin Trudeau to the point that hundreds of thousands have signed petitions for and against Confederation. A referendum, she has said, is now necessary to resolve the matter once and for all.

She has taken heat from both sides. Some separatists have derided her pro-separation question as a weak-kneed plan to make a plan. Some critics on the pro-Canada side say Smith is both arsonist and firefighter – rolling the dice on the future of the country while framing herself as its champion.

Polls before Smith announced the referendum and after have suggested Albertans are consistently in favour of staying in the Confederation fold. To that end, critics, including Nenshi, say the referendum was never about Canada but merely about Smith placating separatist hardliners in her party to keep them from fracturing the movement or rising up against her.

Recent events suggest Smith and her party are taking a hit for calling the referendum in the first place. Polls show Smith’s UCP bleeding support to the benefit of the NDP with the next election scheduled for a year from now. Last month, Smith’s party lost a Calgary by-election to the NDP in what had been a longtime UCP stronghold.

Smith has also been forced into pretzel-style arguments when pushed on why her caucus and party are formally pro-Canada yet allow at least one pro-separatist legislature member to remain in their ranks. Smith has said the party can still be officially pro-Canada while allowing for a diversity of opinion.

On referendum night, Elections Alberta officials say the separation question will be counted first. The result should be known sometime early the following morning. Smith has said a simple majority one way or the other will carry the day.
The other nine questions, however, have spawned more questions, such as what exactly the new immigration rules would look like and whom they would apply to.

Smith’s government has said that will be decided later this fall by her government should it get a mandate on those questions. And what does a mandate on those questions look like? Smith was asked by reporters last week.
“We’ll look at the voter turnout, and we’ll look at the result, and we will be able to give you some clear direction on Oct. 20th,” she replied.

stories.title: France open to defence deals with Canada despite its push for arms autonomy, envoy says
stories.summary: In February, Canada became the first non-European partner in an EU loan program for joint defence projects called Security Action for Europe, or Safe
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
France’s new ambassador in Ottawa says her country is open to working closer with Canada on defence procurement, despite its push for Europe to develop a fully autonomous arms industry.

“In the defence sector and in other equally strategic sectors, France advocates for a European preference in procurement,” French Ambassador Hélène Farnaud-Defromont said in a French-language interview.

“The ideal for us would be to achieve 100 per cent European content but, once again, we’re being realistic. We know we’re all going to need a bit of time to reach that goal.”

Farnaud-Defromont said France can help Canada build up its defence base by sharing best practices.

“France is the only member state of the European Union today to have retained a comprehensive defence industrial and technological base,” she said. “We have some really interesting ideas to put forward and develop together.”

In February, Canada became the first non-European partner in an EU loan program for joint defence projects called Security Action for Europe, or Safe. Only one contract for Canada has emerged from the program so far.

The program allows EU countries to access low-interest loans to buy military gear and weapons. It’s part of an initiative called ReArm Europe aimed at weaning the continent off its reliance on American weapons.

“The fact that Canada has joined Safe, I think that’s a very good thing,” she said. “We now need to see things come to fruition. We need this partnership to actually take shape.”

Much of Canada’s defence industrial base is made up of branches of American corporations. Farnaud-Defromont would not speculate on how that continental integration might affect Canada’s participation in Safe.

The ambassador said 65 per cent of the components in each piece of defence equipment France procures are of European origin – a threshold the EU is trying to apply to Safe projects.

Farnaud-Defromont said the people of France are “extremely concerned and worried” about the war in Ukraine and its implications for freedom across Europe.

Canada’s strong support for Ukraine is deeply appreciated across the continent, she said.

“We are in fact facing an all-out war on European soil following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine,” Farnaud-Defromont said.

“The front line is just a few hundred kilometres from Paris. It is not that far away.”

She said France is still trying to work toward peace through multilateralism, despite dozens of armed conflicts that – like those in the Middle East – have implications far beyond one region.

“The international order has been profoundly disrupted,” said Farnaud-Defromont, a career diplomat for 32 years.

“The environment in which I work today as a French diplomat bears no resemblance to the one I knew.”

While France is a founding member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, it has always maintained some autonomy.

France pulled out of Nato’s command structure for most of the Cold War and advocated for nuclear energy autonomy to avoid relying on others for electricity.

The country has for years advocated a vision of European collective security that runs at odds with American leadership. France ramped up its push for continental autonomy after U.S. President Donald Trump’s demands for control of Greenland.

“We have long been committed to developing, within the European Union and within Nato, a European pillar, and within the European Union a community that is also strategic,” Farnaud-Defromont said.

“We are by no means pleased with the situation within Nato, which is, to say the least, very confused.”

Kerry Buck, a former Canadian ambassador to Nato, has warned that Ottawa would be less safe if the alliance turned its focus more to the defence of Europe.

“Canada had long resisted the creation of a European pillar within Nato for fear of being sidelined, and because we didn’t want the EU exercising ‘strategic autonomy’ in decision-making, or otherwise competing with Nato,” she wrote in a June, 2025 commentary in Policy Magazine.

This two-bedroom plus den unit in a 15-year-old building on Avenue Road was open to visits from potential buyers over two months this summer. After the asking price was reduced from $2.275-million to $2.15-million and around the time it recorded its 60 th guest, two offers came in.

“Sixty showings was astounding,” said agent Paul Maranger, and was an indication that buyers felt they could bide their time. “Buyers don’t see a need to rush; they can sit and wait. Once they see there’s an offer, they jump forward.”

This 1,658-square-foot unit has two parking spots and a 770-square-foot terrace, two prime assets, Mr. Maranger said. “Once you get into larger apartments, it’s almost imperative to have two-car parking.”

“Most balconies are simply too tiny, but on this one, the seller had potted plants and herbs, and a barbecue area. It’s also L-shaped with a lounge area protected from the sun, and a dining area.”

This corner unit has a terrace with a built-in irrigation system and entrances into four rooms, including the den, kitchen, and primary bedroom. The living room also has windows facing east and south, and a gas fireplace.

There is a laundry room and three bathrooms, including one with heated flooring.

The unit comes with two storage lockers. Monthly fees of $2,059 cover internet, heating and water, as well as concierge, valet parking and amenities.

“Most kitchens in condos don’t have a window, and this had patio doors,” Mr. Maranger said.

“There’s a nice, boutique grocery store on the main floor of the building, and it’s on a lovely section of Avenue Road with bakeries, cafes, and restaurants.”

stories.title: Ottawa bankrolls push to protect existing affordable housing
stories.summary: Canada Rental Protection Fund was announced in the 2024 budget and is a Build Canada Homes initiative
stories.author: Howard Chai
stories.content:
On Sept. 22, the Government of Canada announced the launch of the Canada Rental Protection Fund, the latest – and now largest – program in the push to preserve existing affordable housing.

Various other governments have launched similar programs in recent years, including Toronto’s Multi-Unit Residential Acquisition Program in 2021, British Columbia’s Rental Protection Fund in 2023, Nova Scotia’s Community Housing Capital Fund in 2024 and the Edmonton Rental Protection Program this summer.

The Canada Rental Protection Fund was announced in Budget 2024 and is an initiative under Build Canada Homes, the new Crown corporation. Seeded with $1.5-billion, it will disburse grants or loans to non-profits, housing societies and co-ops, among other mission-driven groups, to allow them to buy existing affordable rental buildings, shielding them from redevelopment.

“This is one of the gaps in the National Housing Strategy,” said Ray Sullivan, Board Chair of the Canadian Housing Acquisition Fund (Chaf), which will administer the program. “The underlying principles seem to be supply, supply, supply, and we will build our way out of this problem, but we know from research we’re actually losing more affordable housing in the private market than what we’re building through programs in the National Housing Strategy.”

According to Mr. Sullivan, the national ratio is 1 to 11, meaning that for every home being built with government assistance, 11 existing affordable homes in the private market are being lost. The ratio varies by market. Ottawa, for example, is 1 to 30, according to Mr. Sullivan, who calls the growing momentum of such programs a “welcome shift.”

The federal program is modelled on B.C.’s program. Non-profits become prequalified, scour the market for potential buildings to acquire, and bring proposals to the Crpf, which then vets the proposal to ensure it meets the directives of the program.

The general guideline is that buildings have at least 40 per cent of their units at 30 per cent of the median renter household income. From that starting point, the building will then be assessed in a more local context, with factors including how existing rents compare to the market, the depth of affordability within the building, and local housing needs.

“We know that when non-profits – instead of a Reit, speculator, or private owner – buy these buildings, they will stabilize those rents and those tenancies are more protected,” said Mr. Sullivan. “Far too often we see that when that ‘for sale’ sign goes up on the front lawn, too many tenants end up on the street.”

Similar to the B.C. Rental Protection Fund, which has disbursed more than half of the $500-million it launched with so far, the federal program will hope to achieve equitable geographical results, meaning the goal is to spread the money around.

The federal government says the $1.5-billion program has the potential to protect 7,000 affordable rental units, which implies an average price of $214,000 per unit. According to commercial real estate firm Colliers, the average price per unit for buildings that transacted in the second quarter of 2026 was $308,000 per unit in the Greater Toronto Area and $325,355 in Metro Vancouver, meaning the funding will have to be spread out across different markets if they want to get to 7,000 units.

The Canada Housing Acquisition Fund (Chaf) is led by a nine-person board of directors, while the Canada Rental Protection Fund (Crpf) will be led by a seven-person investment committee that will review the acquisition proposals. Similar to the B.C. Rental Protection Fund, the federal government is not directly involved in the operations of the Crpf, which operates like an arm’s-length organization.

To help get the Crpf up and running, Chaf has brought in several members of the B.C. RPF, including T’Brenn Kelly-McKinnon, who is serving as interim-CEO of the B.C. RPF and also chief investment officer of Chaf. The entities remain separate, although they are well co-ordinated due to their shared mission, and could also potentially co-invest together.

Where the federal program differs from other existing programs is that funding can be provided as a grant, but also a repayable loan, the latter of which would have a 10-year term and allow the Crpf’s purse to be replenished over time.

Mr. Sullivan says that around $1-billion of the $1.5-billion for the program will be distributed as low-interest loans while around $480-million will be distributed as grants. Mr. Kelly-McKinnon says the Crpf is envisioned as a 30-year program, but the intent is to deploy the vast majority of the $1.5-billion within the first five years, so capital can be redeployed in later years.

Groups that receive funding for acquisitions will have to remain in compliance – with affordability, financials and more – through regular reporting.

One recurring criticism of B.C.’s program is that taxpayer money is going toward “protecting” old buildings that May need to be redeveloped down the line regardless and that the funding would be better used to subsidize new affordable housing.

Asked to address that critique, Mr. Sullivan said both of those things are needed, the latter continues to happen, and that programs like this are doing more of the former.

“What we’re doing is taking an asset and moving it into the non-market column. That not only stabilizes those tenancies and those rents, but then becomes an asset that is removed from the speculative private market,” he said. “If that means 30 or even 25 years from now that non-profit redevelops that property, that’s an opportunity. But the people who live there right now would otherwise be displaced, and that’s a lot of what’s driving homelessness and other issues across the country.”

Mr. Sullivan says they’re actively trying to fill the seven-person investment committee, they’ve already received dozens of applications since the program was announced, and they’re aiming to help groups close on acquisitions in early 2027. The hope is that if the program is successful, other governments will create similar programs and the federal government will make another contribution in the future.

stories.title: A new airport facility will speed up vital deliveries to Canada’s northern communities
stories.summary: Cargo planes are vital lifelines for remote communities in Canada’s north, delivering food, medicine and other essentials.
stories.author: Katie Griffin
stories.content:
Ottawa - Cargo planes are vital lifelines for remote communities in Canada’s north, delivering food, medicine and other essentials.

To get those critical items to people faster, Canadian North, has opened a new cargo facility at the Ottawa International Airport. The airline serves more than 20 destinations across Nunavut, Nunavik and the Northwest Territories.

“It represents the beginning of a new, exciting chapter for Canadian North as we continue to strengthen our operations and enhance the services we provide,” said Shelly De Caria, Canadian North’s president and CEO.

De Caria, who was born and raised in Kuujjuaq, Que., said she understands the vital importance of this infrastructure.

“I remember when the cargo came in and my brother ran to the fridge and said ‘we’re rich’ because we had food in our fridge.”

The airline transports thousands of boxes of groceries, essential medical supplies and materials for businesses every week, often to communities only accessible by air.

The expansion project received $11 million from the federal government’s National Trade Corridors Fund.

“A sovereign Arctic depends on moving goods safely and reliably across the north. That is why this building matters so much,” said Defence Minister David McGuinty.

The warehouse’s general cargo capacity has increased by 40 per cent. Its cold storage capacity has nearly doubled.

“Alongside faster cargo processing and cargo loading, truck wait times will come down from as much of an hour to just five to 10 minutes,” said Rebecca Alty, minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations.

The facility aims to move cargo more quickly to ensure supplies arrive faster and fresher.

“Reliable northern supply chains depend on everyday links like this from the southern facilities where goods are handled to the airports and communities where they arrive,” said Rebecca Chartrand, minister of northern and arctic affairs.

stories.title: Ontario’s taxing delay on property assessments
stories.summary: A decade gap in provincewide property valuations has created huge gaps in tax bills, and fairness
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
Imagine an out-of-date tax structure that leaves a lot of people paying less than they should. At this time of affordability concerns that sounds pretty good – for them, at least. But what if that missing tax revenue is being covered by other people, who are paying more than they should? Suddenly this seems grossly unfair.

Unfortunately, this is not just a thought exercise. This is exactly the situation facing people in Ontario, where municipal property reassessments have not been done in a decade.

Having left the system on hold for so long, the government says somewhat unconvincingly that it is consulting on how best to resume normal assessments. Here’s some free advice: just do it. There’s no excuse for continuing to force some people to carry an undue share of the tax burden.

The Globe and Mail has been running a series of articles and columns recently on how to overhaul the tax system to boost productivity, improve fairness across generations and encourage construction of rental homes. But the existing system also has to be run better. And the situation in Ontario is a good place to start.

Property taxes in Ontario are determined based on two factors: the local tax rate, as set by local politicians, and the estimated value of the property. That value is determined by the Municipal Property Tax Assessment Corporation, which answers to the province.

Until 2016, Mpac did reassessments every four years and phased in any changes in value over the ensuing four-year period. However, the 2020 assessment was derailed by the COVID-19 pandemic. There has not been another one since, even though property values have changed a lot over those 10 years.

The value of a property is used to determine how much tax it is levied because that value has been seen as a proxy for owner wealth. It’s an imperfect rationale – other approaches could involve taxing property size, which affects the cost of providing municipal services, or taxing improvements to the land or property – but this is longstanding policy in Ontario.

It’s important to note that a changed value assigned to a property by Mpac does not, in and of itself, lead to property tax increases or decreases. In Ontario, what matters is how its value changes compared to the average in that community. Properties that go up more than the average face higher taxes. Those that lag the average get tax cuts. The pie remains the same size but its composition gets rebalanced.

And therein lies the problem. The properties with above-average value increases since 2016 are not being charged the higher taxes they should be. These fortunate people are being subsidized by people whose properties had below-average appreciation. Let the unfairness of that sink in.

At this point it’s impossible to know for sure just who is in which group. But since not all properties in the province have appreciated at exactly the average over the last 10 years, not doing reassessments has created winners and losers. And that situation is being exacerbated the longer the system is left out of balance.

According to Paul Sullivan, a B.C. property-tax consultant quoted in a recent Globe story , property owners likely to be paying more than they should be include residents of a Toronto inner suburb called Scarborough and fully half of Toronto condo owners.

This issue affects commercial properties as well. Mr. Sullivan believes that many small main-street retailers are paying more than their share. At the same time, reassessments could hurt other small retailers, because zoning changes to what is allowed near transit, for example, could lead to higher tax bills.

The situation is undoubtedly thorny. Ontarians who are reassessed and face spikes in their tax bill will not be happy. But these same people have been getting a break for years. And the money has to come from somewhere, so contriving some way to cushion them from any coming increase just perpetuates the unfairness of the current situation. There are no easy solutions and the government is simply making the problem worse by letting it drag on year after year.

It’s wrong to argue, as Ontario Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy did when glossing over government’s lack of urgency, that “what people want is certainty” in this time of economic peril. In fact, the looming threat of a tax increase is the opposite of certainty. Even if that were not the case, stability cannot come at the price of unfairness.

stories.title: How a Mexico-U.S. trade deal could set the terms for Canada
stories.summary: 2027’s Cusma review looms as U.S.-Mexico talks advance while negotiations with Canada stall.
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — Washington is gearing up for next year’s review of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement, but signs of negotiating progress have come mainly from the U.S.-Mexico trade teams in recent weeks, while formal talks between the U.S. and Canada remain stalled.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says he speaks frequently with Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, but there have been no formal meetings between the U.S. and Canadian sides since talks collapsed in August.

The Mexican and U.S. teams met for a round of formal talks in July and were supposed to meet again in September, but that has been postponed, likely until sometime this month.

Mexico’s Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard recently expressed optimism that new agreements are coming soon. “We are getting closer on many issues, resolving problems, and we are making progress,” he said at last week’s G-20 meeting in Milwaukee, Wisc., after meeting with Greer. “Every day we are closer to reaching new agreements.”

Washington has opened public consultations for next year’s Cusma review while maintaining bilateral engagement with Mexico — and not with Canada, which raises concerns about Ottawa’s ability to influence the process. Experts say there is no reason for Canada to panic, but they also warn that a Mexican agreement could set terms that Washington later expects Ottawa to accept.

Mexico was seemingly on the back burner while Canada made progress in late summer, said Diego Marroquín Bitar, a fellow with the Americas Program at Washington’s Csis.

“The Canadians made a lot of progress before negotiations collapsed,” he said. “So they could jump back … to the negotiation table at any moment and be very close to where the Mexicans are actually.”

The arrangement the U.S. and Mexico are working toward centres on tariff relief and policy concessions, rather than a comprehensive rewrite of Cusma.

Marroquín Bitar referred to it as a “skinny deal,” or a preliminary bilateral deal, that would give Mexico tariff relief in exchange for domestic-policy concessions and closer alignment with U.S. trade policy toward non-market economies.

This could help prepare the ground for the 2027 Cusma review, he said, but it’s not a final settlement or replacement for the trilateral agreement.

Carlo Dade, director of international policy and the New North America Initiative at the School of Public Policy at the University of Calgary, agrees.

“Mexico can sign an agreement on reciprocal trade with the U.S. to set a new tariff regime and to set a new economic security regime,” he said, noting that Ustr calls them agreements on reciprocal trade.

Dade also rejects the notion that Canada is being left out, noting that not every communication is shared with the public.

“I wouldn’t read this as necessarily being sidelined,” he said.

As for what Mexico and the U.S. could hash out bilaterally, there are a number of issues, but trade experts believe it will largely focus on immediate issues while laying a path for continued talks on tougher debates.

“I think there’s a lot that bilaterally can be addressed without Canada,” said Inu Manak, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, pointing to energy investments and reform in Mexico, labour reform and enforcement, including collective bargaining rights, Mexico’s external trade policies, and some agricultural disputes over seasonal produce.

Still, the bilateral bargains are closely tied to Cusma’s future, as Washington is using the prospect of renewal to press for settlements on other trade disputes, according to Christopher Sands, director of the Center for Canadian Studies at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies in Washington.

“The way that the Trump administration has taken this, the review, as you know from last year, is to hold the renewal of the agreement hostage until other trade issues are resolved,” he said.

One possible development that could really impact Canada, trade watchers say, is an agreement on sectoral tariffs. Any settlement by Mexico on the Section 232 tariffs, Marroquín Bitar warned, could become Canada’s benchmark.

“Whatever Mexico accepts in this interim deal will very likely become the floor rather than the ceiling for whatever Canada negotiates when it eventually returns to the table,” he said. “Every Mexican concession becomes the opening term of Canada’s negotiations.”

Manak largely agreed and pointed to the automotive industry.

“So let’s say Mexico can negotiate down … from the 25 per cent … auto or auto parts tariff, a tariff at 15 per cent or lower, for example … that would be something that would create … a baseline even for Canada,” she said.

Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute in Washington, also expressed concern over this, noting that the U.S. is unlikely to agree to a better deal for Canada later.

“If Mexico agrees to it, I find it difficult to believe that the Trump administration would … be open to being flexible when it comes to Canada specifically,” he said.

Even if Canada’s formal talks remain on hold, Sands says closer Canada–Mexico ties could help Ottawa stay informed about Washington’s demands.

“What we will have now that we didn’t have reliably before is … a Mexico-Canada dialogue where I’m sure they’ll pick up the phone and say, ‘Hey, this is what the Americans are asking us to … sign, and here’s where we’re trying to modify it,’” Sands said.

And while this approach May not stop Washington from using a “divide and conquer” approach, Sands said he thinks the “Mexicans are … trying anyway to be much better partners.”

“They May be forced to do a bilateral on security, or just a U.S.-Mexico agreement on some aspect, but I think they want to keep the band together.”

Changes to Cusma itself, however, require agreement among all three countries.

“Any changes to the agreement would need the concurrence of all three parties,” said Dade.

Marroquín Bitar said any deal the U.S. and Mexico might strike this autumn would leave broader trilateral issues — including rules of origin — for the next phase.

He referred to this as merely the beginning of a “15-round fight.”

“It’s going to be a very long and painful process, but I think Usmca will survive it,” he added.

“It’s not going to be the same agreement that we have now, but it’s still going to be a framework that’s going to give Mexico and Canada, I think, better market access compared to any other country or any other trading block in the world.”

“Mexico can sign an agreement on reciprocal trade with the U.S. to set a new tariff regime and to set a new economic security regime,” he said, noting that Ustr calls them agreements on reciprocal trade.
Dade also rejects the notion that Canada is being left out, noting that not every communication is shared with the public.
“I wouldn’t read this as necessarily being sidelined,” he said.

As for what Mexico and the U.S. could hash out bilaterally, there are a number of issues, but trade experts believe it will largely focus on immediate issues while laying a path for continued talks on tougher debates.

“I think there’s a lot that bilaterally can be addressed without Canada,” said Inu Manak, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, pointing to energy investments and reform in Mexico, labour reform and enforcement, including collective bargaining rights, Mexico’s external trade policies, and some agricultural disputes over seasonal produce.

Still, the bilateral bargains are closely tied to Cusma’s future, as Washington is using the prospect of renewal to press for settlements on other trade disputes, according to Christopher Sands, director of the Center for Canadian Studies at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies in Washington.
“The way that the Trump administration has taken this, the review, as you know from last year, is to hold the renewal of the agreement hostage until other trade issues are resolved,” he said.

One possible development that could really impact Canada, trade watchers say, is an agreement on sectoral tariffs. Any settlement by Mexico on the Section 232 tariffs, Marroquín Bitar warned, could become Canada’s benchmark.

“Whatever Mexico accepts in this interim deal will very likely become the floor rather than the ceiling for whatever Canada negotiates when it eventually returns to the table,” he said. “Every Mexican concession becomes the opening term of Canada’s negotiations.”
Manak largely agreed and pointed to the automotive industry.

“So let’s say Mexico can negotiate down … from the 25 per cent … auto or auto parts tariff, a tariff at 15 per cent or lower, for example … that would be something that would create … a baseline even for Canada,” she said.
Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute in Washington, also expressed concern over this, noting that the U.S. is unlikely to agree to a better deal for Canada later.
“If Mexico agrees to it, I find it difficult to believe that the Trump administration would … be open to being flexible when it comes to Canada specifically,” he said.
Even if Canada’s formal talks remain on hold, Sands says closer Canada–Mexico ties could help Ottawa stay informed about Washington’s demands.

“What we will have now that we didn’t have reliably before is … a Mexico-Canada dialogue where I’m sure they’ll pick up the phone and say, ‘Hey, this is what the Americans are asking us to … sign, and here’s where we’re trying to modify it,’” Sands said.
And while this approach May not stop Washington from using a “divide and conquer” approach, Sands said he thinks the “Mexicans are … trying anyway to be much better partners.”
“They May be forced to do a bilateral on security, or just a U.S.-Mexico agreement on some aspect, but I think they want to keep the band together.”
Changes to Cusma itself, however, require agreement among all three countries.
“Any changes to the agreement would need the concurrence of all three parties,” said Dade.
Marroquín Bitar said any deal the U.S. and Mexico might strike this autumn would leave broader trilateral issues — including rules of origin — for the next phase.
He referred to this as merely the beginning of a “15-round fight.”
“It’s going to be a very long and painful process, but I think Usmca will survive it,” he added.

“It’s not going to be the same agreement that we have now, but it’s still going to be a framework that’s going to give Mexico and Canada, I think, better market access compared to any other country or any other trading block in the world.”

stories.title: France open to defence deals with Canada despite its push for arms autonomy: envoy
stories.summary: France's new ambassador in Ottawa says her country is open to working closer with Canada on defence procurement, despite its push for Europe to develop a fully autonomous arms industry.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

Posted October 12, 2026 6:00 am.

Last Updated October 12, 2026 8:07 am.

Ottawa — France’s new ambassador in Ottawa says her country is open to working closer with Canada on defence procurement, despite its push for Europe to develop a fully autonomous arms industry.

“In the defence sector and in other equally strategic sectors, France advocates for a European preference in procurement,” French Ambassador Hélène Farnaud-Defromont said in a French-language interview.

“The ideal for us would be to achieve 100 per cent European content but, once again, we’re being realistic. We know we’re all going to need a bit of time to reach that goal.”

Farnaud-Defromont said France can help Canada build up its defence base by sharing best practices.

“France is the only member state of the European Union today to have retained a comprehensive defence industrial and technological base,” she said. “We have some really interesting ideas to put forward and develop together.”

In February, Canada became the first non-European partner in an EU loan program for joint defence projects called Security Action for Europe, or Safe. Only one contract for Canada has emerged from the program so far.

The program allows EU countries to access low-interest loans to buy military gear and weapons. It’s part of an initiative called ReArm Europe aimed at weaning the continent off its reliance on American weapons.

“The fact that Canada has joined Safe, I think that’s a very good thing,” she said. “We now need to see things come to fruition. We need this partnership to actually take shape.”

Much of Canada’s defence industrial base is made up of branches of American corporations. Farnaud-Defromont would not speculate on how that continental integration might affect Canada’s participation in Safe.

The ambassador said 65 per cent of the components in each piece of defence equipment France procures are of European origin — a threshold the EU is trying to apply to Safe projects.

Farnaud-Defromont said the people of France are “extremely concerned and worried” about the war in Ukraine and its implications for freedom across Europe.

Canada’s strong support for Ukraine is deeply appreciated across the continent, she said.

“We are in fact facing an all-out war on European soil following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine,” Farnaud-Defromont said.

“The front line is just a few hundred kilometres from Paris. It is not that far away.”

She said France is still trying to work toward peace through multilateralism, despite dozens of armed conflicts that — like those in the Middle East — have implications far beyond one region.

“The international order has been profoundly disrupted,” said Farnaud-Defromont, a career diplomat for 32 years.

“The environment in which I work today as a French diplomat bears no resemblance to the one I knew.”

While France is a founding member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, it has always maintained some autonomy.

France pulled out of Nato’s command structure for most of the Cold War and advocated for nuclear energy autonomy to avoid relying on others for electricity.

The country has for years advocated a vision of European collective security that runs at odds with American leadership. France ramped up its push for continental autonomy after U.S. President Donald Trump’s demands for control of Greenland.

“We have long been committed to developing, within the European Union and within Nato, a European pillar, and within the European Union a community that is also strategic,” Farnaud-Defromont said.

“We are by no means pleased with the situation within Nato, which is, to say the least, very confused.”

Kerry Buck, a former Canadian ambassador to Nato, has warned that Ottawa would be less safe if the alliance turned its focus more to the defence of Europe.

“Canada had long resisted the creation of a European pillar within Nato for fear of being sidelined, and because we didn’t want the EU exercising ‘strategic autonomy’ in decision-making, or otherwise competing with Nato,” she wrote in a June 2025 commentary in Policy Magazine.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 12, 2026.

— With files from Émilie Bergeron
