stories.title: 'Hardly surprising' many Alberta business leaders staying mum on separation: expert
stories.summary: Calgary - The silence from many Alberta business leaders on the upcoming provincial referendum comes as no surprise to one corporate leadership expert.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel The Canadian Press
stories.content:
CALGARY - Some prominent business leaders have taken a public stand on Alberta remaining a part of Canada, but many more remain on the sidelines as a provincial referendum on that question, and others, fast approaches.

Monday’s vote includes 10 questions: one on whether should Alberta stay in Confederation or move toward a binding separation referendum; five on immigration and four on constitutional matters.

“It’s a mixed bag right now so far,” said Bob Pickard, principal at Leadership Communication Inc., a Calgary-based firm that advises executives and newsmakers on public relations.

“Some leaders have spoken out with conviction. Others have remained quiet.”

Pickard’s firm was one of more than 80 that have signed an open letter from the Calgary Chamber of Commerce warning of the economic fallout if Alberta were to break from Canada.

The chamber and other business advocacy groups have been vocal in warning of the consequences of a split, as well as measures that could make it harder to attract newcomers into the provincial workforce. But relatively few individual corporate CEOs have taken a public stand.

“It’s hardly surprising that a majority of CEOs are not speaking up,” said Richard Leblanc, a professor of governance, law and ethics at York University. “You can alienate customers. You can alienate investors, so there’s more to be lost than gained, generally, by speaking up about a political matter.”

CEOs of public companies answer to their boards of directors and shareholders, who are often loath to take on undue risks to a firm’s reputation, he added. Top executives are often limited to speaking on matters that directly affect the company itself.

“There’s a tradition in Canada of really staying in your lane,” Leblanc said.

But he said there may be times a company’s board of directors agrees that a CEO should speak out on a matter that affects the well-being of the business. Various economic analyses have flagged higher trade costs, decreased investment and reduced employment should Alberta choose to go it alone.

“Sometimes the risk of not doing something can be far greater than doing something and dealing with the blowback,” Leblanc said.

Oilpatch CEOs — many are geologists or engineers by trade — might not have it in their natures to be outspoken on politics, Pickard said. Some might not want to be seen as “showboating” or “grandstanding.”

“They don’t get the top job because of acts of risky courage,” Pickard said. “Many of them get that top job because they’re cautious careerists.”

But Pickard said the separatism issue goes beyond being a political controversy, and is a legitimate concern for every business in Alberta.

“I think we’ve seen way too much passivity here,” he said. “And what we need is candid, transparent, courageous leadership communication on this most existential of issues.”

Getting board sign-off on a CEO’s public message is no easy feat and there are likely to be divisions among directors, said Leblanc, the York governance expert.

Some corporations have former prime ministers, premiers and cabinet ministers as directors on their boards, who can advise on when and how to weigh in on politics, Leblanc noted.

Atco Ltd.‘s board includes former Alberta premier Jason Kenney, who has been a fervent voice in the “stay” camp, as well as former federal cabinet minister Rona Ambrose.

Atco CEO Nancy Southern is among a handful of leaders at big, publicly traded companies to sign the Calgary Chamber’s open letter. Others include the CEOs of AltaGas Ltd., Keyera Corp. and Capital Power Corp., as well as the heads of Berkshire Hathaway Energy businesses BHE Transmission and AltaLink.

“What we kept hearing was people wanted safety in numbers to sign,” said chamber president and CEO Deborah Yedlin. “I’m not sure that safety in numbers actually materialized the way we thought it would.”

The chamber and other umbrella groups can speak on behalf of members, but Yedlin said C-suite voices can have a greater impact because there’s more skin in the game.

“At the end of the day, the chamber is not risking that capital, the companies are.”

Financial disclosures filed with Elections Alberta show Calgary-based energy infrastructure company AltaGas has donated $5,000 to the third-party advertiser group Vote to Stay.

No prominent corporations or executives can be found on the disclosures of pro-separation-referendum groups.

A few top executives have made their views known.

“We believe a strong Alberta and a strong Canada go hand in hand,” Imperial Oil chief executive John Whelan wrote on LinkedIn last month after delivering that message to a Calgary Chamber of Commerce luncheon featuring Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

Atco’s Southern, who describes herself as a proud Albertan and Canadian, told reporters after the company’s annual meeting in May that she can’t imagine how businesses could operate efficiently if Alberta were to separate.

Cenovus Energy Inc. CEO Jon McKenzie told a conference in mid-2025 — as separatist sentiment bubbled up following the federal Liberals’ election victory — that the movement is rooted in legitimate grievances with federal policy, but is not a constructive way to address those issues. He said he expected separatism to dissipate once those concerns were addressed.

Since that time, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has made a number of policy moves embraced by the oilpatch. Several Trudeau-era environmental policies have been rolled back, legislation has been brought in to speed up infrastructure approvals and Ottawa has deemed a new million-barrel-per-day Alberta-to-B.C. pipeline to be in the national interest.

All this, as global geopolitical upheaval casts Canada as a reliable energy supplier.

“We could have a boom in this province that we’ve never seen before,” said Yedlin. “And we could also ruin it if we’re not careful.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Supreme Court hears challenge of law clearing path for Ontario Place redevelopment
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Supreme Court of Canada plans to hear arguments today from a coalition challenging the constitutionality of legislation that smooths the way for major changes at Ontario Place.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The Supreme Court of Canada heard arguments Thursday from a coalition challenging the constitutionality of legislation that clears the way for major changes at Ontario Place.

Judges on the top court peppered counsel for the coalition and the Crown with questions and comments about their respective legal positions before reserving the court’s decision until a later date.

The case unfolding in the Supreme Court could reverberate far beyond the Toronto waterfront park that opened in 1971.

Over the years, Ontario Place has featured a spherical theatre that showed movies on a huge screen, children’s play areas, a revolving concert stage and several pavilions suspended above the water.

The provincial government wants to redevelop the theme park to include an elaborate spa operated by a private company, a relocated Ontario Science Centre, revamped play and shoreline areas, a parking facility and a provincial police detachment.

The coalition Ontario Place Protectors challenged the province’s Rebuilding Ontario Place Act, arguing that it insulates state action from scrutiny by the courts and therefore violates the Constitution.

The coalition also argued that exemptions from environmental and heritage laws and municipal noise regulations amount to a breach of public trust.

An Ontario judge dismissed the application in 2024 and a challenge of the ruling in the provincial Court of Appeal was also unsuccessful.

Writing on behalf of a unanimous Court of Appeal, Justice Grant Huscroft said there’s no doubt the provincial government’s decision to redevelop Ontario Place is strongly opposed by a number of concerned citizens and organizations.

Political opposition to the plan has not swayed the government and the coalition has turned to the court in an effort to stop it, Huscroft said.

“But there is no basis for the court to do so. The court is not an alternative forum for resolving political grievances. The only legitimate question for the court is whether the impugned provisions of ROPA violate the law or the Constitution,” he said.

“They do not, and the appeal must be dismissed.”

In January, the Supreme Court agreed to hear the Ontario Place Protectors’ case.

The coalition says provincial superior courts have historical and inherent jurisdiction to review laws and government actions protected under section 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867, and to provide effective remedies when governments do not respect the limits on their powers.

The coalition says the Rebuilding Ontario Place Act’s scope is unprecedented and it appears to violate section 96 by removing the essential core powers of the courts.

It argues the legislation severely limits or eliminates the ability of courts to hold Crown officials accountable through declaratory actions, damage awards and injunctions when they have acted beyond their powers.

The coalition is also seeking to have the doctrine of public trust acknowledged as an unwritten constitutional principle rooted in English common law and inherited by Canada.

It argues the doctrine of public trust maintains that natural and cultural assets are essential to public welfare and must be safeguarded by the state in its role as trustee.

Margie Zeidler, the daughter of Ontario Place architect Eberhard Zeidler, remembers visiting the park as a child.

“It was extraordinary. It was a public place,” she said in an interview. “You could have a picnic in the forest. You could watch films at Cinesphere. You could watch any musical performance at the forum.”

Zeidler, a member of the Ontario Place Protectors coalition, said the provincial government’s actions have made the fight about more than just the historic theme park.

“It became more, not about Ontario Place, but about, wait a minute, what democracy are we living in here?” she said. “I didn’t know governments could do that.”

In their written submission to the Supreme Court, the Crown and the Ontario attorney general say the case should be dismissed.

The immunity provided by the provincial legislation does not go as far as the coalition alleges, the submission says: ”(The act) does not make Ontario Place a lawless zone.”

Rather, it immunizes the Crown, its servants and agents from civil causes of action arising from specific circumstances, the submission says.

The Crown and attorney general are also urging the court to reject the claim that the legislation is invalid because of the doctrine of public trust.

“The novel doctrine articulated by the Appellant is not an unwritten constitutional principle, and even if such a doctrine existed in law, which is denied, there is no evidence in the record that could warrant applying this far-reaching new doctrine to Ontario Place,” the submission says.

The case has attracted submissions from interveners, including the federal attorney general, several provinces, First Nations, civil liberties groups and environmental organizations.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Zeidler, a member of the Ontario Place Protectors coalition, said the provincial government’s actions have made the fight about more than just the historic theme park.
“It became more, not about Ontario Place, but about, wait a minute, what democracy are we living in here?” she said. “I didn’t know governments could do that.”
In their written submission to the Supreme Court, the Crown and the Ontario attorney general say the case should be dismissed.
The immunity provided by the provincial legislation does not go as far as the coalition alleges, the submission says: ”(The act) does not make Ontario Place a lawless zone.”
Rather, it immunizes the Crown, its servants and agents from civil causes of action arising from specific circumstances, the submission says.
The Crown and attorney general are also urging the court to reject the claim that the legislation is invalid because of the doctrine of public trust.

“The novel doctrine articulated by the Appellant is not an unwritten constitutional principle, and even if such a doctrine existed in law, which is denied, there is no evidence in the record that could warrant applying this far-reaching new doctrine to Ontario Place,” the submission says.
The case has attracted submissions from interveners, including the federal attorney general, several provinces, First Nations, civil liberties groups and environmental organizations.

stories.title: Fatal crash on Highway 401 near London
stories.summary: Highway 401 eastbound lanes are closed following a fatal multi-vehicle collision south of London.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Highway 401 eastbound and westbound lanes are closed following two collisions on the eastbound side, one being a fatal multi-vehicle collision south of London.

The first collision was at about 2:15 p.m. near Colonel Talbot Road and involved approximately three vehicles.

Just after 4 p.m. OPP responded to a second collision involving a transport truck and passenger vehicle, further down the highway near Union Road.

The transport truck collided with the rear of a passenger vehicle, that according to OPP was stopped in traffic. The vehicle burst into flames.

OPP says Highway 401 is closed between Colonel Talbot Road and Iona Road.

The number of deceased individuals is unknown at this time.

Motorists are being urged to plan alternate routes.

stories.title: Quebec publishing house stands by author amid AI allegations
stories.summary: Montreal - A Quebec publisher says it will keep Thélyson Orélien’s novel on bookstore shelves despite allegations that it was written using artificial intelligence.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - A Quebec publisher is standing by a novel by author Thélyson Orélien, saying it will remain on bookstore shelves despite allegations that it was written using artificial intelligence.

In a statement released Wednesday, Éditions du Boréal said it received the manuscript on Sept. 12, 2025 and could not verify allegations about the evolution of the book, ‘’C’était ça ou mourir,’’ which translates to “It was either that or dying,” before that date.

The decision to keep the book on sale comes despite lingering questions about the author’s writing process and earlier statements indicating Orélien and his publisher were gathering evidence to support his denial of using AI to write the novel.

The new statement came one day after the publisher released a statement from Orélien, admitting plagiarism in some of his earlier writings in Quebec and French media, while reiterating that he had not used AI for the book.

Orélien said in the statement that he began writing his novel in the fall of 2017, while living in Laval, north of Montreal, completing a first draft of more than 300 pages in 2019, around the time he learned of his mother’s death. He said he spent the following years revising scenes, characters and passages.

The publisher did not confirm this timeline in its new statement. It said it would have liked to provide definitive answers to the allegations, but that it had no evidence beyond Orélien’s word to establish how the novel was written before it was submitted.

Boréal said on Wednesday that the author’s decision not to disclose further details about his writing process was his to make, arguing that publishers should not be expected to monitor authors.

“The publisher’s role is not to demand proof from authors, but to stand by them, and that is what we are doing,” the publishing house said.

The new statement contrasts with what Orélien and his publisher said in September, when Boréal announced it was collaborating with him to compile a detailed record of his work related to his manuscript, before the publisher got involved.

While Orélien told French media outlet Libération the compilation would prove what he was saying about his work, the publisher did not confirm this.

“We would have liked to provide a definitive answer,” the publisher said at the time, adding that it was unable to either confirm or refute the allegations related to AI use.

In his latest statement released on Tuesday through Boréal, Orélien said he had nothing to prove to those making accusations against him.

The publisher’s Wednesday statement did not address the earlier efforts to compile records.

Éditions du Boréal did not immediately respond to questions from The Canadian Press about whether it had revised its efforts or approach.

Orélien also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The author previously said the novel draws on his experiences of migration and exile, as well as stories he heard from others.

He acknowledged occasionally using tools for research, including to look up foreign expressions, but insisted that no sentence in the novel had been generated by a machine.

“I wrote this novel myself,” he said, describing the allegations as an attack not only on his identity as a writer but also on his humanity.

In its Wednesday statement, Boréal unequivocally condemned the plagiarism in Orélien’s earlier writings, saying the findings violated some of its most deeply held values.

But it also defended the author against personal attacks, arguing that the controversy over artificial intelligence did not justify making him a scapegoat for broader fears about the technology’s growing role in creative work.

Orélien said Tuesday that he had faced threats, racist harassment and what he described as a media lynching over the allegations.

He said that after leaving Haiti following the devastating 2010 earthquake, he became fascinated by the work of numerous authors and sometimes sought to imitate their styles, and admitted making some mistakes.

“Admiration does not give you the right to take, to claim as your own texts that are not yours,” he wrote, apologizing for what he described as unacceptable mistakes.

The allegations have triggered some consequences. Orélien’s novel was removed from the running for France’s prestigious Prix Goncourt earlier this month amid the AI allegations and separate questions about plagiarism in his previous work.

Boréal also suspended promotional activities surrounding the novel in September, citing concerns for Orélien’s well-being.

In its latest statement, the publisher said the novel would continue to be sold in bookstores in the absence of definitive findings about the AI allegations, leaving readers to decide whether to purchase it.

According to the websites of major bookstore chains Renaud-Bray and Indigo, the novel remains available for purchase at most of their locations across Quebec.

’‘It is our job as booksellers to make books accessible to our customers,’’ said Renaud-Bray spokesperson Floriane Claveau.

Claveau said no major variation in the book sales had been observed over the past few weeks.

Boréal acknowledged Wednesday in its statement that the controversy raises questions extending well beyond one novel, particularly about the trust between authors, publishers and readers.

It said it was undertaking a broader reflection on the lessons to be learned from the case and how to continue protecting and promoting human creativity.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Key figure in Pearson gold heist says he’s having trouble testifying due to trauma
stories.summary: A man who admitted his role in the Toronto Pearson airport gold heist is telling the trial for another man accused in the case that recalling his alleged abduction in Pakistan on the stand is leaving him traumatized.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The testimony of a key player in the Toronto Pearson airport gold heist has been adjourned until next week after he told a Brampton court Wednesday that recalling details of his alleged abduction in Pakistan on the stand has left him traumatized.

Arsalan Chaudhary is serving a four-year prison sentence after pleading guilty to theft over $5,000 in what police have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.

He took the stand Tuesday in the trial of Parmpal Sidhu, who has pleaded not guilty to charges of theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the 2023 heist.

Chaudhary testified that he’d planned the heist with Simran Preet Panesar, who is still wanted by authorities, and ended up taking 30 per cent of boxes full of one-ounce gold bars. He said he melted some of the gold and sold it for cash before travelling to Pakistan, where he claimed people in police uniforms kidnapped and abused him.

He said he believed the kidnappers learned he had money from a man who helped him procure his gold-melting machine. He said he was released after giving up the remaining gold he kept in a Greater Toronto Area condo and the cash he had at his cousin’s house in Pakistan.

When Chaudhary returned to the witness stand on Wednesday, he said he couldn’t sleep the previous night after telling the story of his abduction.

“My memory is very vague when I have locked out a lot of stuff from my memory, so that’s why I cannot remember,” he said in response to questions from the Crown.

“If you’ve been through the trauma that I’ve been through, and been shocked and had bruises, you would probably understand where I’m coming from.”

Chaudhary said he has been kept at Maplehurst Correctional Complex for about three weeks, where he didn’t receive his prescribed medications including melatonin and vitamins.

“Last night, I couldn’t sleep. I had terrors, night terrors. I couldn’t eat when I got back, so it does affect me,” he said. “So, that’s why I’m not able to help you, but I would like to.”

He asked the court to send him back to the Collins Bay Institution, a federal prison in Kingston, Ont., where he is serving his sentence.

“I’ve been in Maplehurst, living with three people in a cell by a toilet, and I’ve been not getting no medical attention. I’ve asked for it,” he said.

“I’m not in the right state of mind to remember stuff you’re asking me,” he told the Crown.

After some discussions between prosecutors and defence lawyers, Superior Court Justice Gordon Cudjoe issued an order to return Chaudhary to the Collins Bay Institution and bring him back to the Brampton courthouse on Monday morning to resume his testimony.

Cudjoe also told Chaudhary he will make a recommendation to the prison to have him assessed by a medical professional.

During his testimony on Tuesday, Chaudhary said he didn’t really know Sidhu and that he only called or texted him when he couldn’t get ahold of Panesar.

The Crown asked Chaudhary about text and group chat messages related to the heist, but he repeatedly said he did not remember or recall the content of these conversations, nor who was involved in them.

Prosecutors allege that Sidhu, an Air Canada employee at the time, provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22 million in gold and currency from a Pearson airport cargo bay.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from the airport on April 17, 2023, after the shipment arrived from Switzerland.

stories.title: Longtime London MP Irene Mathyssen dies at age 75
stories.summary: Former NDP MP Lindsay Mathyssen announced her mother's passing on Tuesday, saying she always strived to make the world a better place.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Longtime member of Parliament Irene Mathyssen, who served the London, Ont., region both provincially and federally under the NDP banner, has died at the age of 75. She had been battling cancer.

Former NDP MP Lindsay Mathyssen announced her mother’s passing on social media on Tuesday.

“To Londoners and Canadians, she was known for her public service, her dedication to her community, and her commitment to the people and causes she believed in,” she said in a statement on Facebook.

“She believed that our responsibility is to leave this world a better place than we found it. That belief is part of her legacy and I will do my best to honour it throughout my life.”

Mathyssen was first elected provincially in 1990 and served as Ontario’s tourism minister.

She was elected to represent London federally in 2006 and held her seat of London—Fanshawe until her retirement from politics in 2019.

During her time as MP, Mathyssen notably led a successful effort to remove the federal portion of the sales tax from menstrual products.

NDP Leader Avi Lewis said she will be remembered as someone “who fought relentlessly for our movement, and for a Canada that upholds the dignity of every person.”

“In calling for a housing bill of rights, the expansion of EI for workers, and fighting for women’s liberation, Irene pushed to make life better for people on every front,” Lewis said in a statement.

Conservative London-area MP Andrew Lawton said in a media statement that Mathyssen was “a tireless advocate for her values and her constituents and was always generous with her time when I was working in radio.

“My thoughts are with Keith (Irene’s husband) and Lindsay.”

Peter Fragiskatos, Liberal MP for London Centre, called her a “profoundly important” community voice.

“She spoke up for those who had been forgotten and ignored and always approached her work with kindness, humility and dedication. This was a true public servant,” he said in a media statement.

Mathyssen was succeeded in the House of Commons by her daughter Lindsay, who held the seat of London—Fanshawe until 2025.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Father receives life sentence in New York for murder of Montreal girl
stories.summary: Elizabethtown — A Montreal man has been sentenced to life in prison for killing his nine-year-old daughter and leaving her in a marsh in rural New York.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
ELIZABETHTOWN — Luciano Frattolin’s face remained expressionless on Wednesday as a judge sentenced him to life in prison for killing his daughter and leaving her in a marsh in rural New York.

Wearing a rumpled black suit and large black glasses, he shook his head slightly as Judge Tatiana Coffinger described the second crime he was convicted of — concealing the nine-year-old girl’s body.

“I hope, at some point in your life, you realize what you have done, what you have done to a family, and moreover, how you let down your daughter. Nothing brings her back, and we will all live with this,” said Coffinger, moments before Frattolin was led out of the courtroom, chained and in handcuffs.

In the back of the room, the girl’s mother, grandparents, and other relatives and loved ones had been watching intently. Some wiped their eyes after the judge announced her ruling in the Essex County Court.

“We continue to suffer deeply since the day Melina was brutally murdered,” the family said in a statement read outside the courthouse by District Attorney Michael Langey after the hearing.

“Nothing can bring Melina back, but we are relieved that this chapter is over. We are sincerely grateful to everyone who worked on the case. Your dedication and persistence, your efforts helped bring a measure of justice for our family.”

The sentence comes two months after a jury convicted Luciano Frattolin of second degree murder and concealment of a human corpse in the death of Melina Frattolin.

Judge Tatiana Coffinger delivered the sentence after rejecting a defence motion to set aside the guilty verdict. Frattolin would not be eligible for parole before 25 years and is expected to serve his sentence in New York.

He was also sentenced to one to three years for the charge of concealing a human corpse and was fined $5000.

“We will never know exactly what happened on the evening of July 19, 2025. We do know that at a moment (when) Melina needed her father the most, he was not her protector,” said Coffinger.

The defence issued a notice of appeal following the sentence.

“Mr. Frattolin maintains his innocence,” Brian Pilatzke, Frattolin’s lawyer, told the judge in court before she announced the sentence.

Melina Frattolin had been living in Montreal with her mother and had gone on a road trip to the United States with her father in July 2025.

On the night they were scheduled to return home, Luciano Frattolin called 911, reporting she had been kidnapped after he had stopped the car he was driving on the side of the road.

The prosecution called several police officers and experts over the trial who used car location data, cellphone data and surveillance camera footage to recreate Frattolin’s movements on the day his daughter died.

The data showed Frattolin’s car and phone were stopped for close to an hour in the area where Melina’s body was later found. Police also found a bag of muddy clothing Frattolin had been wearing on the side of the road.

During the hearing, Coffinger accused Frattolin of having lied in his statements to police and likened his kidnapping story to “a Hollywood script.”

“Mr. Frattolin, you live in a world of self-made delusion of wealth and image,” she said. “When the greatest accomplishment of your life would have been to be a great father, that is not what you are going to be remembered for.”

Coffinger also granted a protective order for Melina’s mother, Kali Galanis, meaning Frattolin will be forbidden from contacting her in any way.

Outside the courthouse, Langey said he was satisfied with the sentence.

“Hopefully the parole board doesn’t parole him, and he does serve most of his life in prison,” he added.

Asked about Frattolin’s possible motive, Langey said he believed the Montreal man had wanted a life of wealth and success.

“He had an obsession and hatred of Melina’s mom, Kali, and he wanted a different life,” he said.

During the three-week-long trial, the defence had tried to argue that local police had not adequately investigated Frattolin’s claims that his daughter was kidnapped.

The jury spent an hour deliberating on Aug. 10 at the end of the trial, before concluding that Frattolin was guilty.

paragraphs: ELIZABETHTOWN — Luciano Frattolin’s face remained expressionless on Wednesday as a judge sentenced him to life in prison for killing his daughter and leaving her in a marsh in rural New York.
Wearing a rumpled black suit and large black glasses, he shook his head slightly as Judge Tatiana Coffinger described the second crime he was convicted of — concealing the nine-year-old girl’s body.

“I hope, at some point in your life, you realize what you have done, what you have done to a family, and moreover, how you let down your daughter. Nothing brings her back, and we will all live with this,” said Coffinger, moments before Frattolin was led out of the courtroom, chained and in handcuffs.

In the back of the room, the girl’s mother, grandparents, and other relatives and loved ones had been watching intently. Some wiped their eyes after the judge announced her ruling in the Essex County Court.
“We continue to suffer deeply since the day Melina was brutally murdered,” the family said in a statement read outside the courthouse by District Attorney Michael Langey after the hearing.

“Nothing can bring Melina back, but we are relieved that this chapter is over. We are sincerely grateful to everyone who worked on the case. Your dedication and persistence, your efforts helped bring a measure of justice for our family.”
The sentence comes two months after a jury convicted Luciano Frattolin of second degree murder and concealment of a human corpse in the death of Melina Frattolin.

Judge Tatiana Coffinger delivered the sentence after rejecting a defence motion to set aside the guilty verdict. Frattolin would not be eligible for parole before 25 years and is expected to serve his sentence in New York.
He was also sentenced to one to three years for the charge of concealing a human corpse and was fined $5000.
“We will never know exactly what happened on the evening of July 19, 2025. We do know that at a moment (when) Melina needed her father the most, he was not her protector,” said Coffinger.
The defence issued a notice of appeal following the sentence.
“Mr. Frattolin maintains his innocence,” Brian Pilatzke, Frattolin’s lawyer, told the judge in court before she announced the sentence.
Melina Frattolin had been living in Montreal with her mother and had gone on a road trip to the United States with her father in July 2025.
On the night they were scheduled to return home, Luciano Frattolin called 911, reporting she had been kidnapped after he had stopped the car he was driving on the side of the road.

The prosecution called several police officers and experts over the trial who used car location data, cellphone data and surveillance camera footage to recreate Frattolin’s movements on the day his daughter died.

The data showed Frattolin’s car and phone were stopped for close to an hour in the area where Melina’s body was later found. Police also found a bag of muddy clothing Frattolin had been wearing on the side of the road.
During the hearing, Coffinger accused Frattolin of having lied in his statements to police and likened his kidnapping story to “a Hollywood script.”

“Mr. Frattolin, you live in a world of self-made delusion of wealth and image,” she said. “When the greatest accomplishment of your life would have been to be a great father, that is not what you are going to be remembered for.”
Coffinger also granted a protective order for Melina’s mother, Kali Galanis, meaning Frattolin will be forbidden from contacting her in any way.
Outside the courthouse, Langey said he was satisfied with the sentence.
“Hopefully the parole board doesn’t parole him, and he does serve most of his life in prison,” he added.
Asked about Frattolin’s possible motive, Langey said he believed the Montreal man had wanted a life of wealth and success.
“He had an obsession and hatred of Melina’s mom, Kali, and he wanted a different life,” he said.
During the three-week-long trial, the defence had tried to argue that local police had not adequately investigated Frattolin’s claims that his daughter was kidnapped.
The jury spent an hour deliberating on Aug. 10 at the end of the trial, before concluding that Frattolin was guilty.

Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman, The Canadian Press

stories.title: 3 people suffer life-threatening injuries in Kincardine crash
stories.summary: Police, along with Kincardine Fire and Emergency Services, were called to the scene shortly after 3 p.m. on Tuesday.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Three people suffered life-threatening injuries, following a crash near Kincardine.

The collision happened shortly after 3 p.m. on Tuesday, ON Highway 21, in front of Kincardine Township-Tiverton Public School, just north of Kincardine.

Police say four vehicles were involved.

A section of Highway 21 was closed for several hours, as police investigated the cause of the crash.

Anyone with information regarding this incident is asked to contact the Ontario Provincial Police at 1-888-310-1122. Should you wish to remain anonymous, you May call Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 where you May be eligible to receive a cash reward of up to $2000.

stories.title: Neurologist to continue testifying at inquest into Toronto woman's fatal balcony fall
stories.summary: A neurologist who examined Regis Korchinski-Paquet's records after her death is set to continue testifying today at a coroner's inquest.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - A neighbour broke up a fight between Regis Korchinski-Paquet and her brother hours before the 29-year-old fell to her death from a highrise balcony while police were inside the home, a coroner’s inquest heard Wednesday.

Doreen Gayle, who lived next door to Korchinski-Paquet and her family, told a police watchdog agency what she remembered of May 27, 2020 in an interview less than a week after the fatal fall. The roughly 50-minute recording was played on the second day of the inquest.

Gayle said both Korchinski-Paquet and her mother, Claudette Beals, had come by her apartment to chat and smoke in the morning.

Hours later, she told the Special Investigations Unit, Beals came back, asking her to break up a fight between Korchinski-Paquet and her 26-year-old brother, Reece Korchinski — something Gayle said she’d had to do multiple times in the past. She didn’t know what triggered the fight, but said Korchinski-Paquet often got “angry” after experiencing seizures and she’d had two that morning.

The two women rushed next door and found Korchinski had his sister in a chokehold on the bed, trying to restrain her as she struggled, Gayle said. He told them the fight started because his sister broke his TV, she said, adding it took a few minutes to pull them apart.

“He let go of his sister and he says, ‘Mom, look what’s going to happen. She’s gonna go get knives’ — exactly what happened,” she said.

Korchinski-Paquet “went straight to the kitchen” and grabbed two knives, she said. Gayle, who had told the family to go to her unit, stopped Korchinski-Paquet in the hallway before deciding she’d had enough, she told the SIU.

She went back to her apartment and stayed with Korchinski’s girlfriend and their children, she said. Soon after, Korchinski came in and flung a chair, breaking a lamp, she said.

“I got mad and I said, all of you, leave,” she said, adding she locked the door behind them.

When they came to her door again later that day, it was to share the devastating news, she said.

“I saw Reece and he said: ‘Regis went over the balcony,’” she said. “I couldn’t understand and then I saw them crying.”

Gayle told the SIU she didn’t know what happened after the family left her apartment, and choked up as she recalled chatting and laughing with Korchinski-Paquet earlier that day. “She didn’t have to die so tragically,” she said.

The two households were close like family, with Gayle offering her apartment as refuge whenever arguments broke out next door, she said. Between Korchinski-Paquet’s state after her seizures and the presence of her brother, his girlfriend and their children, “it was a volatile situation,” she said.

The inquest has heard Korchinski-Paquet had a long history of seizures from epilepsy, often followed by confusion, aggressive behaviour and temporary amnesia.

She had two seizures the morning of the day she died. Police were called in the late afternoon over a “rapidly developing and violent family disturbance that involved knives,” the inquest heard.

Five calls were made to 911, three of them by Korchinski-Paquet, the inquest heard. Those calls are expected to be played for the jury, along with CCTV footage from the hallway outside the apartment.

Six police officers and two paramedics responded to the calls.

Gayle wasn’t clear on the timeline of what she described to the SIU, but said Beals took her phone when she came to ask for help and used it to call 911. The phone’s logs showed a call to 911 at 2:27 p.m. and another at 5:13 p.m., she said in the interview.

Investigators asked her if Korchinski-Paquet had ever walked between their balconies in the past, and Gayle said she hadn’t. Beals and Korchinski, however, had previously gone over the part connecting the two balconies to get into their unit when they were locked out, but they never went over the outside railing, she said. Gayle said that was no longer possible since her balcony now had netting to repel pigeons.

The inquest also heard the agency’s interview with a bystander who saw Korchinski-Paquet holding on to the outside of the balcony, then after briefly turning away, witnessed the woman fall.

Earlier Wednesday, lawyers representing Korchinski-Paquet’s family, the Black Legal Action Centre, and others who have standing at the inquest questioned a neurologist who examined her records after her death.

Dr. Julien Hébert told the inquest that it would be “nearly impossible” to determine that someone was acting aggressively due to delirium or psychosis after an epilepsy seizure without knowing their medical history.

“If a patient has signs of seizures that could obviously alert one to the possibility of postictal psychosis or delirium, but absent that history and absent signs of seizures or psychosis I agree that for a lay person or a police officer it would be ... extremely difficult or nearly impossible to distinguish from other causes,” he said in response to a lawyer for the Toronto Police Association.

Hébert said Tuesday that in the years preceding her death, Korchinski-Paquet on several occasions showed symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium or postictal psychosis, both mental states that can occur after seizures.

Her death, which came soon after the police killing of George Floyd in Minneapolis, fuelled protests and revived calls to defund the police. It was also one of several deaths to bring attention to how police respond to calls involving mental health.

The inquest was announced earlier this year and is slated to last 14 days.

Korchinski-Paquet’s mother, father and brother have been named as potential witnesses, as have five of the police officers who attended the scene.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. An earlier version mistakenly said Hébert had finished testifying.

stories.title: As drones reshape war around the world, the Canadian Armed Forces sprints to catch up
stories.summary: Ottawa — As drone-fuelled warfare rages on half a world away in Ukraine, the Canadian Army's program for rapidly acquiring basic drones is just ramping up.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — As drone-fuelled warfare rages on half a world away in Ukraine, the Canadian Army’s program for rapidly acquiring basic drones is just ramping up.

And the pressure is on for the Canadian Armed Forces to speed up its adoption of drones as the technology changes the nature of modern warfare.

Lt.-Col. Jonathan Penney is a reservist who previously worked in defence manufacturing and now co-ordinates the forces’ Minerva drone program. He said that while the army feels pressure to pick up the pace, it’s focused both on finding the right mix of tech for its current needs and on building up the domestic drone industry.

“The army is really good at adapting and evolving,” he said in an interview with The Canadian Press.

The Minerva program launched a batch of tenders in recent months for a range of new drones — everything from low-cost Arctic surveillance drones for the Canadian Rangers to ground and aerial drones that can conduct cargo supply runs.

“We are figuring out what ‘right’ looks like,” Penney said. “Instead of just jumping in, buying a whole bunch of things that we don’t need, we buy things that can use today and then let the system evolve so that it’s integrated in how we conduct operations.”

The Minerva program operates unlike a typical procurement, which sees the military draft a list of requirements.

Instead, Minerva launches what it calls “industry challenges” — ongoing projects which task companies with creating prototypes for specific uses. Army personnel will be testing those prototypes until roughly next summer or fall.

Another item the army is currently searching for is a low-cost targeting drone — an aerial spotter that allows artillery crews to hit targets they can’t see.

Penney said it’s safer to rely on an aerial drone for targeting instead of sending a soldier into the field with a set of binoculars and a laser rangefinder.

“If the drone gets shot down, we’ll just send up another one,” he said. “The reduction of risk to our personnel is significant.”

That kind of equipment is easy enough to buy off the shelf — but part of the goal of the Canadian Armed Forces drone program is to build up the domestic drone sector and ensure the tech can be easily absorbed by Canadian military units.

“Does it integrate with our systems and does it exist as-is produced in Canada?” Penney said. “That’s what we’re driving for.”

The army is expected to complete a new wish-list of drones for design and purchase over the next three to four months — including a breaching drone for dealing with ground-based obstacles such as mines.

The Minerva initiative launched roughly a year ago with the goal of quickly scaling up drone use in the army, rather than limiting it to ordering from the U.S. Defence Department’s approved list of drone manufacturers.

Army Commander Lt.-Gen. Michael Wright has said he wants to “flood” Canada’s land forces with drones.

Winning a drone prototype challenge is different from winning a large military production order, however.

The prototype challenge approach allows National Defence to cover research and development costs early in the process — which should encourage drone makers to take the risk of building prototypes with no guaranteed purchaser. The 15-month Arctic aerial drone challenge, for instance, has a $500,000 maximum funding award.

“Canadian companies, especially those small mid-sized companies that can offer some solutions, don’t really know how the military operates. So when they create a product, it’s not necessarily focused towards some of the things that we need,” Penney said.

“They actually understand things better. So if you’re working in the Arctic, you have big gloves on, it’s understood that you can’t operate with fine motor controls.”

Lt.-Gen. Darcy Molstad has been tasked with overseeing the integration of drones across the entire armed forces. He said in a previous interview the military is starting to approach uncrewed systems more like munitions, rather than traditional equipment or expensive vehicles.

“We have to treat it almost like an expendable commodity versus something that we have to keep in inventory and capitalize the cost over 20 years,” Molstad said. “These things just last a short amount of time.”

Penney said that’s particularly true for drones used by land forces.

“Especially from an army perspective, which will be different from the Air Force perspective, we are looking at … consumables, things that we’re going to use, and if it gets destroyed, fine, we’ll just send in another one,” he said. “Low-cost, high-use, high-value things.”

As Russia tests NATO allies in Europe with repeated drone incursions, Canada’s military is looking for ways to counter the emerging threat.

The Canadian Armed Forces recently put out a separate tender for a counter-aerial drone system that could be deployed at military installations across the country.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Rides closed at Canadian theme parks after deadly fall from Six Flags coaster in U.S.
stories.summary: Rides at two Canadian theme parks were closed after a man in the United States fell to this death from a Six Flags roller-coaster in Georgia.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Rides at two Canadian theme parks were closed after a man in the United States fell to this death from a Six Flags roller-coaster in Georgia.

Two rides at Canada’s Wonderland in Toronto and another at La Ronde in Montreal were temporarily shuttered “out of an abundance of caution,” the parks said. Six Flags owns Wonderland and recently sold La Ronde.

A 42-year-old man was killed while riding a roller-coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday, prompting the theme park operator to close nine similar rides across Canada and the United States. The man was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride, police said Tuesday.

The Leviathan and Behemoth roller-coasters at Canada’s Wonderland were closed, said a spokesperson for the park. There was no timeline for their reopening.

“The safety of our guests and team members remains on our highest priorities,” the spokesperson said in a written statement.

The Goliath roller-coaster at La Ronde was also closed and the park’s owner said it would carry out a safety review with the ride’s manufacturer.

“We are taking this additional time to carefully review the attraction. It will not reopen until this review is complete and we are fully satisfied that it can be operated safely,” read the statement.

The temporarily shuttered Canadian rides were manufactured by the same company as the coaster involved in the incident in Georgia.

Six Flags Entertainment did not immediately respond Tuesday to emailed questions about why specific rides were shut down and what would be done before they reopen.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct 13, 2026.

– With files from The Associated Press.

The Canadian Press
paragraphs: Rides at two Canadian theme parks were closed after a man in the United States fell to this death from a Six Flags roller-coaster in Georgia.

Two rides at Canada’s Wonderland in Toronto and another at La Ronde in Montreal were temporarily shuttered “out of an abundance of caution,” the parks said. Six Flags owns Wonderland and recently sold La Ronde.

A 42-year-old man was killed while riding a roller-coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday, prompting the theme park operator to close nine similar rides across Canada and the United States. The man was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride, police said Tuesday.
The Leviathan and Behemoth roller-coasters at Canada’s Wonderland were closed, said a spokesperson for the park. There was no timeline for their reopening.
“The safety of our guests and team members remains on our highest priorities,” the spokesperson said in a written statement.
The Goliath roller-coaster at La Ronde was also closed and the park’s owner said it would carry out a safety review with the ride’s manufacturer.

“We are taking this additional time to carefully review the attraction. It will not reopen until this review is complete and we are fully satisfied that it can be operated safely,” read the statement.
The temporarily shuttered Canadian rides were manufactured by the same company as the coaster involved in the incident in Georgia.
Six Flags Entertainment did not immediately respond Tuesday to emailed questions about why specific rides were shut down and what would be done before they reopen.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct 13, 2026.
– With files from The Associated Press.
The Canadian Press

stories.title: More than 300 advance polls open across Alberta in historic referendum on separation
stories.summary: Roughly 310 advance polling stations open across Alberta Tuesday in a historic vote on the province's place in Canada.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Roughly 310 advance polling stations open across Alberta Tuesday in a historic vote on the province’s place in Canada.

Albertans are to begin marking an X on ballots listing 10 questions.

The first nine focus on Canada’s Constitution and immigration.

The 10th and most contested one will ask voters whether they want to remain in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on quitting Confederation.

Elections Alberta has said it’s preparing for a record voter turnout in the referendum.

The official vote day is on Monday and results on the separation question are set to be announced the next day — Oct. 20.

stories.title: Swath of Ontario boreal forest larger than Toronto to be protected from development
stories.summary: A chunk of Ontario's northern boreal forest bigger than Toronto is set to be protected from industrial development.
stories.author: Jordan Omstead The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Nature Conservancy of Canada says it has acquired 814 square kilometres of boreal forest and peatlands south of Kapuskasing, previously owned by a company selling carbon offset credits.

The non-profit says where the landscape is healthy and free of vulnerable species, some day-use recreational activities such as hiking and paddling May continue, in line with provincial laws.

Article continues below

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

The federal government says it’s contributing $13 million to the project as part of a total $64-million investment from both public and private donors.

The announcement comes ahead of next week’s annual United Nations biodiversity summit, where the talks are expected to focus on global progress toward conservation goals.

Ottawa unveiled a new $3.8-billion nature protection strategy earlier this year intended to put Canada’s goals within reach, months after the federal environmental watchdog found it to be more than one-million square kilometres short of its 2025 goal to protect 25 per cent of its lands and inland water.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

stories.title: New Brunswick gets $219 million loan from Ottawa for hydroelectric dam repair work
stories.summary: Mactaquac - The federal government says it will spend more than $260 million to help New Brunswick modernize a pair of energy projects.
stories.author: Eli Ridder The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MACTAQUAC - The federal government is investing nearly $270 million in loans and grants to help New Brunswick modernize energy facilities that officials say are key to Ottawa’s plan to double the capacity of Canada’s electrical grid by 2050.

The bulk of the money is a $219-million loan from the Canada Infrastructure Bank to extend the life of the province’s largest hydroelectric dam, located west of Fredericton on the Saint John River.

The province will also receive a $50-million grant to upgrade its Salisbury Terminal near Moncton, which officials say is key to managing the flow of electricity across the provincial grid.

The federal government is investing $269 million in loans and grants to help New Brunswick modernize a pair of energy facilities that officials say are key to the country's electricity goals. (Oct. 13, 2026)

Federal Energy Minister Tim Hodgson made the announcements Tuesday during a news conference in front of the massive Mactaquac Dam.

“New Brunswick is critical to this plan and so are today’s investments,” he said. “Together, these two projects will strengthen New Brunswick’s electricity system while creating jobs, attracting investment, supporting affordability, and lowering emissions.”

New Brunswick’s Crown-owned electric utility is preparing the 672-megawatt Mactaquac Generation Station for a multibillion-dollar overhaul aimed at extending its operational life to 2068.

The new funding will pay for technical studies, regulatory reviews, First Nations engagement and planning for the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project, according to Natural Resources Canada.

In 2016, NB Power agreed to a plan in 2016 to spend up to $3.6 billion to prolong the life of the dam, which would have otherwise been decommissioned by 2030 due to concrete swelling.

The new funding will support technical studies, regulatory reviews, First Nations engagement and planning for the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project, according to Natural Resources Canada.

On Tuesday, NB Power CEO Lori Clark said the total cost for the project is now expected to be close to $9 billion.

Hodgson would not commit the federal Liberal government to spending more on the dam, noting that electricity generation is within provincial jurisdiction.

However, he said the federal government will need to help provinces and territories keep costs low as they work to meet federal clean energy regulations that call for a net-zero electricity grid by 2050.

“In the budget coming up, you will see a number of initiatives we are working on to work ... with provinces and territories to help them realize the growth that they need in an affordable way,” the minister told reporters.

“This is clearly an indication that we understand how important it is for our prosperity to grow our electricity generating capabilities and we understand that the federal government needs to do its part in helping to make that affordable.”

New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt said the Mactaquac Generating Station is important to the entire Maritime region.

In the event of a system-wide blackout, the dam can start generating electricity without relying on an external power supply, making the largest so-called “black-start” facility in the region.

“We often call it the battery of the Maritimes,” said Holt. “Having this kind of renewable energy that we can turn on and off is critical, not only to our province, but to our neighbours in Prince Edward Island and in Nova Scotia and beyond.” The dam supplies 30 per cent of the province’s renewable energy requirements and 20 per cent of its overall electricity demand, officials said.

The investments come as NB Power is looking for ways to fix ageing infrastructure without imposing massive rate hikes on its customers.

Since the 1980s, concrete portions of the the dam have been affected by a chemical process called alkali-aggregate reaction. The reaction causes concrete to swell and crack, requiring substantial repairs and maintenance.

Just last week, NB Power applied to the provincial regulator to raise rates by 17.4 per cent over the next three years as it plans to spend $4 billion on maintaining the provincial grid.

Some of that money will be used to transition the province’s only remaining coal-fired generating plant to a facility that burns wood pellets to generate electricity.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

Note to readers: This is a corrected story. A previous version said Ottawa was spending nearly $270 million to help New Brunswick modernize its electrical grid. In fact, Ottawa’s investment is through a loan and a grant.

stories.title: Key figure in Pearson airport gold heist testifying at trial of another accused man
stories.summary: Arsalan Chaudhary was sentenced this spring to four years in prison after pleading guilty to theft over $5,000, and he was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A man who admitted his role in the massive gold heist at Toronto’s Pearson airport told a Brampton, Ont., court that he melted and sold some of the gold before travelling to Pakistan, where he claims he was kidnapped and abused to give up the loot.

Arsalan Chaudhary started testifying Tuesday in the trial of Parmpal Sidhu, a former Air Canada employee who has pleaded not guilty to charges of theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the April 2023 heist.

Prosecutors allege that Sidhu provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22 million in gold and currency from a Pearson airport cargo bay in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.

Chaudhary, who was sentenced this spring to four years in prison after pleading guilty to theft over $5,000, told Sidhu’s trial that he planned the heist with Simran Preet Panesar, who is wanted by authorities.

He said they divided boxes full of one-ounce gold bars and he took 30 per cent of the boxes while Panesar took 70 per cent.

“That’s the deal we made,” he said. “I didn’t know at first it was going to happen. So, I was like ‘OK, and if it does happen, 30 per cent of that, I’m pretty happy with it.’”

Chaudhary said he didn’t really know Sidhu and that he only called or texted him when he couldn’t get a hold of Panesar.

He said the gold bars had TD Bank markings and he took his share to a condo in the Greater Toronto Area, adding that he doesn’t remember its address. Chaudhary said he started melting the gold for sale, acquiring $200,000 to $300,000 in cash.

“Whatever gold I had, I started melting it ... I had a machine, a gold melting machine,” he said. “It’s not brain surgery. It’s pretty simple: Turn it on, heat it up, put it in there, it melts.”

He said he doesn’t recall how much gold he melted each time nor how much of his share he melted, but said he was doing it so the gold could not be traced.

Chaudhary said he travelled to Mexico and Portugal before he ended up in Pakistan to “invest the money and buy a business or something.”

He testified that a group of people in police uniforms abducted him in Pakistan and abused him, so he was forced to let people they worked with take the remaining gold and cash from his condo in Canada, as well as the cash he left at his cousin’s house in Pakistan.

“They took me to (an) area. I was blindfolded so I couldn’t tell. When I got there they abused me,” he testified. “Before they could do anything further, I ... told them, ‘I will give you everything. You don’t need to do anything. You have me. My life is worth more than any money.’”

Chaudhary said he believed the kidnappers learned he had money from a man he met in Pakistan, who had helped him procure his gold-melting machine and transfer cash from Canada to Pakistan.

He said the kidnappers let him go and he went to Dubai, where he stayed at his cousin’s house looking for work until he came back to Canada on Jan. 12, 2026.

As part of his sentencing, Chaudhary was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.

“All of this was not even worth it. I destroyed people’s lives. I did everything for nothing,” he said on the witness stand. “Now, I’m here.”

The Crown asked Chaudhary about text and group chat messages related to the heist, but he repeatedly said he did not remember or recall the content of these conversations, nor who was involved in them.

The stolen gold and foreign currency were ordered from Zurich, Switzerland, and transported in the hull of an Air Canada flight to Toronto, police said when they released details of the investigation dubbed Project 24K. The shipment was then brought to an Air Canada cargo facility at the airport, police said.

Later that day, a suspect presented a fraudulent airway bill to warehouse employees, who loaded the shipment onto his five-tonne truck, police alleged.

Chaudhary is expected to continue his testimony on Wednesday.

stories.title: B.C. party leaders make campaign stop at Vancouver trade board ahead of election
stories.summary: Vancouver - The leaders of British Columbia's three major political parties will pitch their plans to business leaders in Vancouver with less than two weeks to go before the provincial election.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The leaders of the two major parties running in British Columbia’s election pitched business leaders with infrastructure commitments, including a new shipyard and promises of tax cuts.

NDP Leader David Eby and Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson appeared at a Greater Vancouver Board of Trade event on Tuesday along with Green Leader Emily Lowan to speak for 10 minutes each and then take pre-selected questions in advance of the Oct. 24 election.

Eby said his party would build a new shipyard in partnership with the federal government, so new B.C. ferries and other vessels, such as icebreakers, can be built in British Columbia.

All three major party leaders in the B.C. election campaign made promises to business leaders at a board of trade event. The NDP’s David Eby, Conservatives’ Lorne Doerkson and Greens’ Emily Lowan spoke at an event hosted by the Greater Vancouver Board of Trade. (Oct. 13, 2026)

His appearance came just hours after he faced more questions about his family’s use of $10-a-day childcare.

He said earlier Tuesday that he and wife Cailey Lynch, a doctor, didn’t need the daycare discount that has only reached a minority of parents in the province.

Eby said they wanted other families to benefit after the centre switched to the subsidized rate, so they made a donation to the facility.

While Eby initially declined to reveal the size of the donation, his campaign later said that the family will have contributed $8,000 between 2024 and the end of 2026 for both of their children who are at the facility.

Eby promised business leaders that in addition to building a new shipyard his government would make permanent a manufacturing jobs fund worth $60 million that was announced days before he called an election.

His government would also expand food processing opportunities across the provincial Agricultural Land Reserve.

Doerkson told the crowd that his party would supercharge the provincial economy by cutting taxes and trimming permitting times for large investments.

He said a Conservative government would establish a 120-day approval process for capital projects worth more than $250 million, permanently cancel the proposed expansion of the provincial sales taxes, and exempt machinery, equipment and software from PST for three years.

Green Leader Emily Lowan pledged to implement a new industrial strategy that would lessen B.C.‘s dependence on exploiting natural resources, while the party’s proposed tax on the ultra-wealthy would help pay down the deficit and provide public services.

Bridgitte Anderson, president of the Greater Vancouver Board of Trade, moderated the event and opened it by revealing the results of a survey that asked its members about their top concerns.

Anderson said 78 per cent of those who responded to the survey said the provincial economy is heading in the wrong direction, while 74 per cent expressed concerns about the deficit, which was forecast to hit $13.8 billion.

Eby said that the challenges facing the business community are not unique to the province, and the question facing the province right now is how to get through this existential moment, referring to the trade war with the United States.

“We’re going to stand up, we’re going to protect, and we’re going to build,” he said.

Standing up, he said, means in part that U.S. liquor won’t be back on local shelves until there is a fair deal for the provincial forest sector. It also means standing up against U.S.-style politics coming to British Columbia, he added.

Eby said his party would also protect British Columbians against high prices by regulating profits on basic grocery items and the cost of fuel.

“But let’s also be frank: the path forward for us as a province is to build,” he said.

A change in government, he said, would cast doubt on projects worth $130 billion.

“We cannot afford chaos,” he said.

Doerkson said British Columbians are ready for a change, pointing to business concerns about the economic direction of the province and the deficit.

“We’re spending a lot, but we are not seeing the results that British Columbians expect,” Doerkson said.

“Four out of five of you are not confident in the provincial government’s economic strategy, and what troubles me the most of all, is more than 30 per cent (of board members) say that their businesses have considered moving outside of British Columbia.”

Doerkson said Conservatives are ready to govern and will create the conditions for economic growth.

“With a Conservative government, you will have an ally in Victoria,” he said.

Both Eby and Doerkson faced pointed questions about their financial plans.

When asked about the deficit, Eby said his party would release a fully-costed platform and reduce the deficit over time, without giving an exact time frame.

But the Conservatives have made billions of dollars of unfunded commitments, and that the party is on track to almost double the deficit, without citing concrete figures, Eby said.

“The only way to achieve that and drive down the deficit is massive cuts to public services,” he said.

When Anderson asked Doerkson about his plans for the deficit without raising new taxes, he said his party would cut red tape, while fully funding health care.

“The part that we are forgetting in this province is what happens when we create GDP and that is overlooked all the time,” he said. Doerkson said two per cent growth would probably generate $11 to $12 billion worth of GDP.

Lowan questioned both Eby’s and Doerkson’s focus on resource projects.

“This is the politics of imagination and hope that is desperately needed when times feel bleak. This is not the time to hunker down in old ideas.”

A televised leaders’ debate is set for Wednesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

stories.title: A timeline of key events in the Regis Korchinski-Paquet case
stories.summary: A coroner’s inquest is scheduled to start Tuesday in the case of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman who fell from a Toronto highrise balcony while police were in her home in 2020.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — A coroner’s inquest is scheduled to start Tuesday in the case of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman who fell from a Toronto highrise balcony while police were in her home in 2020.

Here is a timeline of key events in the case:

May 27, 2020: The Special Investigations Unit says it is investigating the death of a woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in the apartment. Korchinski-Paquet’s death sparks questions from her family, local politicians, and on social media about the role of police officers in the incident.

In the days that follow, Korchinski-Paquet’s mother says she called police that day hoping they would take her daughter to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health but instead the woman ended up dead.

May 30, 2020: Thousands of people take to the streets in Toronto to protest against racism and demand answers in Korchinski-Paquet’s case. Several smaller marches follow over the next few weeks.

June 3, 2020: The SIU urges police to stop speaking on the case after Korchinski-Paquet’s family postpones meeting the watchdog, citing concerns about possible police leaks.

June 8, 2020: Two Toronto city councillors put forward a motion to defund the city’s police force by 10 per cent and use the money for community resources.

June 10, 2020: Korchinski-Paquet’s family says it will talk to the SIU.

June 11, 2020: The family holds a small funeral for her.

June 29, 2020: Toronto city council votes against defunding the police budget but approves numerous reforms to the service, including anti-racism measures and the implementation of body-worn cameras.

July 25, 2020: Family, friends and community members gather for a memorial and walk to honour Korchinski-Paquet.

Aug. 26, 2020: The SIU clears police of wrongdoing in her death, finding the officers tried to de-escalate the situation and “though their efforts were unsuccessful,” none of them broke the law. Korchinski-Paquet’s family rejects the findings.

Feb. 3, 2021: Toronto announces a pilot project to send crisis-support workers instead of police to certain 911 calls in the city. The pilot, set to begin the following year, comes after widespread calls for police reform, including improvements to how police deal with those experiencing mental-health crises.

May 26, 2021: A lawyer for Korchinski-Paquet’s family says they recently filed a complaint with the Office of the Independent Police Review Director because they believe the report by the SIU doesn’t make sense. The Oiprd confirms it is investigating but declines to comment further, citing confidentiality.

June 19, 2021: Korchinski-Paquet’s relatives speak at Juneteenth event in Ottawa aimed at demanding accountability and changes to the justice system. Several Black and Indigenous families whose loved ones were harmed or killed by police also attend the event organized by Black Lives Matter Toronto.

June 2022: Korchinski-Paquet’s family files a $10-million lawsuit against several police officers and the head of Ontario’s police watchdog, as well as Ontario’s attorney general, the City of Toronto and the Toronto Community Housing Corporation.

The lawsuit alleges her relatives suffered severe emotional distress after they were provided with “misleading information” at the time of her death.

April 2, 2026: Coroner Dr. Richard Wells announces that an inquest into Korchinski-Paquet’s death will be held.

May 27, 2026: Korchinski-Paquet’s parents join advocates at the provincial legislature to call for reforms, including that the recommendations issued by coroner’s inquests be binding and implemented in a reasonable time frame.

Sept. 15, 2026: The date of the coroner’s inquest is announced.

Oct. 13, 2026: The coroner’s inquest begins.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Coroner's inquest set to begin examining death of Toronto woman who fell from balcony
stories.summary: A coroner’s inquest is set to begin today to examine the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — A coroner’s inquest is set to begin today to examine the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago.

Korchinski-Paquet, a woman of Ukrainian, Black and Indigenous ancestry, died on May 27, 2020 after police responded to calls about a family dispute at the apartment. She was 29.

Her death came on the heels of the police killing of George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, spurring further protests amid growing calls to defund the police.

It also cast a spotlight on how police interact with people experiencing mental health crises.

Ontario’s police watchdog investigated the case and eventually cleared Toronto police of wrongdoing in Korchinski-Paquet’s death.

The Special Investigations Unit found it happened as she was trying to move from her apartment balcony to an adjacent one.

The inquest was announced earlier this year and is slated to last 14 days, with 15 witnesses expected to take the stand.

The inquest jury does not assign criminal responsibility but May make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future. The chief coroner’s office does not have the authority to impose the recommendations, however.

On the anniversary of her death this year, Korchinski-Paquet’s parents joined advocates in calling for the recommendations issued in coroner’s inquests to be binding and implemented within a reasonable timeframe.

Her mother, Claudette Beals, also said there should be a different system in place to investigate allegations of wrongdoing against police officers, adding she has no faith in “police investigating police.”

“My daughter’s been gone for six years and no one’s held responsible for that,” she said in a news conference at the provincial legislature.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

Paola Loriggio, The Canadian Press

News Home

Tuesday, 13 October 2026 07:29

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Share on Facebook

The Braves sit on top of the Doherty Division standings and the Trojans are at the bottom of the Yeck Division standings.

PJHL - It was a mixed weekend for Oxford County's Junior C hockey teams.

The Norwich Merchants suffered a 6-1 loss to the New Hamburg Firebirds on Friday, but they were able to bounce back with a 5-2 victory over the Dorchester Dolphins on Saturday. Liam Nunn scored the lone goal for Norwich on Friday, while Jack Birkbeck, Gavin Balazs, Logan Van Den Akker, Boden Brimmell, and Tyler McDole scored during Saturday's game.

The Tavistock Braves doubled the Dolphins 4-2 on Friday with Jacob Skuta, Tucket Otto, Nolan Miller, and Carter Otto scoring for the home team. The Braves went on to suffer a 7-6 loss to the Firebirds on Saturday with Kaiden Cormier scoring the game winning goal for New Hamburg in overtime.

The Thamesford Trojans only had one game over the long weekend, where they lost to the Aylmer Spitfires 3-2 in overtime on Friday. Yusuf Jomaa scored the first goal of the game from Thamesford, and Rowan Reid scored in the second period for the Trojans.

The Braves sit on top of the Doherty Division standings with 17 points. The Firebirds are tied with the Wellesley Applejacks for second place with 14 points, and the Merchants are in third place with eight points. The Paris Mounties are in fourth place with seven points, while the Dolphins are in fifth place with four points, only one ahead of the last place Hespeler Shamrocks with three points.

The Trojans sit at the bottom of the Yeck Division standings with five points. They're only one point behind the Lucan Irish with six points, while the Port Stanley Sailors sit in fifth place with seven points, and the Petrolia Flyers sit in fourth place with nine points. The Spitfires and tied with the Exeter Hawks for third place with 10 points each, while the North Middlesex Stars sit in second place with 12 points, and the Mount Brydges Bulldogs top the standings with 14 points.

The Woodstock Navy Vets suffered two losses over the Thanksgiving long weekend.

WOODSTOCK/CAMBRIDGE - It was a rough weekend for the Woodstock Navy Vets.

They suffered a 5-4 loss to the Strathroy Rockets at Southwood Arena on Friday. Woodstock had the lead close to the end of the game, by Strathroy scored twice in the final 3.5 minutes to secure the victory. Evan Giannone scored twice for Woodstock, while the other goals were scored by Sebastien Fortin and captain Will McGregor.

The Vets also lost to the Cambridge Redhawks 5-2 on Saturday. Maddyx Chaput and Cole Bonneville scored for the Vets, and Landyn Quirk made 39 saves in the Woodstock net.

The Vets only have one game on the schedule for this coming weekend, with a home game against the London Nationals on Friday.

Woodstock is currently in a three-way tie for sixth place in thre GOHL Western Conference standings. The Vets have eight points, matching the Komoka Kings and the LaSalle Vipers. The Nationals are tied with the Elmira Sugar Kings for fifth place with nine points each, while the Stratford Warriors sit in fourth place with 10 points. The Listowel Cyclones are in third place with 11 points, the Chatham Maroons and the St. Thomas Stars are tied for second place with 16 points each, and the St. Mary's Lincolns sit on top of the standings with 18 points.

The Rockets are one point behind the Vetd with seven points, and the Sarnia Legionnaires sit at the bottom of thes standings with zero points.
